We have restricted the charge-mass ($\varepsilon-m$) parameter space for millicharged particles by simulating the rotational evolution of neutron stars, incorporating an additional deceleration effect caused by the accretion of millicharged dark matter. For a standard neutron star with a mass of $M=1.4~M_{\odot}$, a radius of $R=10~{\rm km}$, and a typical magnetic field strength of $B_{0}=10^{12}$ G, we derived an upper limit on millicharged particles that aligns with recent experimental and observational constraints. Furthermore, we investigated how variations in the magnetic field $B_{0}$ and the local dark matter density $\rho_{\rm{DM}}$ near the neutron star affect the $\varepsilon-m$ phase space of these particles.

Classifying cough audio signals offers a promising method for screening respiratory conditions, including COVID-19. Due to the risks associated with collecting data from contagious patients, researchers have increasingly relied on crowdsourcing to amass cough recordings, a strategy exemplified by the creation of the COUGHVID dataset. In that project, expert physicians diagnosed a limited set of uploaded recordings; however, this method is prone to labeling errors and significant inter-expert disagreement. To address these issues, this study employs a semi-supervised learning (SSL) approach to enhance labeling consistency and improve the robustness of distinguishing between COVID-19 and healthy coughs. First, we apply existing SSL techniques for aggregating expert knowledge to mitigate labeling inconsistencies and data sparsity. Subsequently, our SSL method identifies a subset of COUGHVID audio samples for re-labeling, which can then train or augment future classification models. The re-labeled data demonstrates superior class separability—three times greater than the original user-labeled data—despite the inherent inconsistencies in the initial expert labels. Additionally, the spectral distinctions between healthy and COVID-19 coughs are accentuated in the re-labeled set, yielding markedly different power spectral densities and confirming both the dataset's improved consistency and its acoustic interpretability. Finally, we show how this refined dataset can effectively train a cough classifier. This SSL framework can integrate the knowledge of multiple experts to boost database consistency for various diagnostic classification tasks.

This study reports on a single-dish survey targeting 95 Very Low Luminosity Objects (VeLLOs) using optically thick HCN (1-0) and optically thin $\rm N_2H^+$ (1-0) emission lines to elucidate the physical mechanisms driving inward motions within VeLLO envelopes and to define their intrinsic nature. Normalized velocity differences ($\delta V_{HCN}$) between the peak velocities of these two lines were calculated for 41 VeLLOs detected in both tracers. The resulting $\delta V$ distribution exhibits a significant blueward skew, suggesting that infalling motions dominate the envelopes of these objects. Infall velocities were estimated for 15 candidates utilizing the HILL5 radiative transfer model, yielding speeds between 0.03 and 0.3 $\rm km~s^{-1}$ with a median of 0.16 $\rm km~s^{-1}$. These values align with gravitational free-fall speeds expected from pressure-free envelopes. Calculated mass infall rates are predominantly around $10^{-6} M_{\odot}~yr^{-1}$, with a median of $\rm 3.4 \pm 1.5 \times 10^{-6} M_{\odot}~yr^{-1}$. These rates are consistent with predictions from the inside-out collapse model and display a strong correlation with the internal luminosities of the VeLLOs, further supporting the conclusion that the observed motions are gravitational infalls. Finally, the findings suggest that the majority of VeLLOs represent faint protostars, whereas two specific objects may be proto-brown dwarf candidates.

While the clustering of inertial particles is crucial in various astrophysical and geophysical turbulent systems, previous research has focused mainly on incompressible flows. This study examines compressible flows, contrasting clustering in turbulence driven by solenoidal (vortical) versus irrotational (compressive) forces. These flows are stochastically driven by circular expansion waves for compressive cases and solenoidal waves for vortical cases. For compressively forced flows, the power spectrum of inertial particle density serves as an effective metric for comparing particle clustering against fluid density enhancements. Results indicate that power spectra are especially sensitive to large-scale clustering, whereas traditional methods like radial distribution functions better capture small-scale clustering. Our main conclusion is that shock-induced particle clustering is most pronounced in turbulence generated by spherical expansion waves, characterized by a double-peaked spectral power distribution dependent on the Stokes number. These two peaks correspond to distinct mechanisms: shock interaction for lower Stokes numbers and the centrifugal sling effect for higher ones. Since inertial particle clustering is linked to caustic formation—a phenomenon observable only in Lagrangian descriptions—we used this framework to evaluate the relative significance of caustics in both vortical and compressive turbulence. Furthermore, we demonstrate that statistical noise arising from the finite number of particles in Lagrangian simulations can be eliminated from power spectra, enabling a more precise comparison of residual spectra. Although our analysis centers on the Epstein drag law applicable to rarefied gases, we confirm that these findings extend to the standard Stokes drag regime.

Over the past few decades, the twisted Alexander polynomial has become a significant tool in low-dimensional topology. For Montesinos links, we have established an efficient approach to calculate the twisted Alexander polynomial corresponding to any linear representation. Consequently, formulas for the multi-variable Alexander polynomials of these links can be readily derived.

The initial case of the novel coronavirus (COVID-19) was identified in Hubei, China, in December 2019. Since then, the pandemic has expanded across 214 countries and regions, profoundly impacting daily life worldwide. As of July 13, 2020, the situation remained uncontrolled, with global case numbers reaching approximately 13.1 million and deaths totaling 571,527. Driven by recent breakthroughs in artificial intelligence (AI) and big data, this paper underscores the critical role of these technologies in managing the outbreak and mitigating its severe consequences. The article begins with an overview of AI and big data, followed by an analysis of their applications in combating COVID-19. It subsequently examines the challenges and limitations of current solutions and offers recommendations for effective communication strategies to control the crisis. Ultimately, this work aims to provide researchers and communities with fresh perspectives on how AI and big data can alleviate the pandemic, thereby inspiring further research to halt its spread.

Browsers enforce security policies to mitigate malicious activities. Cross-Origin Read Blocking (CORB) serves as a specific browser policy designed to prevent side-channel attacks like Spectre. This paper introduces CorbFuzz, a fuzzer for web browser security policies aimed at validating CORB and comparable mechanisms. During the implementation of such policies, browsers rely exclusively on HTTP requests and responses to determine actions. Conversely, CorbFuzz employs a policy oracle that monitors web application behavior and deduces the intended policy actions based on the application's state. By contrasting the oracle's expectations with actual browser behavior, CorbFuzz identifies vulnerabilities within these security policies. The tool achieves this by fuzzing a collection of web applications, utilizing symbolic evaluation for state-related queries to enhance coverage and automation. Furthermore, CorbFuzz gathers type information from database queries and branch conditions to ensure data consistency during the fuzzing process. Evaluations were conducted on CORB implementations in Chromium and Webkit, as well as the Opaque Response Blocking (ORB) policy in Firefox, using web applications sourced from GitHub. The study uncovered three distinct classes of weaknesses in Chromium's CORB implementation.

A continuous-time quantum walk on a graph is governed by the unitary operator $e^{-iAt}$, where $A$ denotes the graph's adjacency matrix. Perfect state transfer (PST) refers to the movement of a quantum state between two nodes with 100% fidelity. Since the adjacency matrix of a cubelike graph can be expressed as a finite sum of tensor products of Pauli $X$ operators, we leverage this property to design an efficient quantum circuit for such walks. Building on characterizations of integer weighted cubelike graphs that exhibit periodicity or PST at $t=\pi/2$ (as detailed in \cite{Cao2021, rishi2021(2)}), we utilize these circuits to verify PST and periodicity on IBM's quantum computing platform~\cite{Qiskit, IBM2021}.

This study investigates the use of directed energy in spacecraft mission design, specifically targeting rapid transit to Mars. It assumes the availability of an unprecedented Earth-based laser array, measuring 10 meters in diameter and delivering 100 MW of power, made possible by advancements in photonic laser technology. A phased-array laser of this magnitude, equipped with atmospheric compensation, can transmit power to spacecraft in cislunar space, where an inflatable reflector focuses the beam into a hydrogen heating chamber. Exhausting the hydrogen propellant through a nozzle achieves specific impulses of 3000 seconds. The system is designed for immediate reusability, utilizing a burn-back maneuver to return the propulsion unit while it remains within the Earth-based laser's range. The capacity to withstand significantly higher laser fluxes allows for the simultaneous achievement of high thrust and high specific impulse, positioning this approach as superior to laser-electric propulsion and comparable to gas-core nuclear thermal rockets without the need for a reactor. This research places special emphasis on the heating chamber, along with its regenerative cooling and propellant handling systems. Furthermore, the study analyzes the associated astrodynamics and the extreme aerocapture maneuver necessary upon Mars arrival following a 45-day transit. Finally, the potential of laser-thermal propulsion as an enabling technology for rapid transit missions throughout the solar system and beyond is discussed.

We introduce an algorithm designed to denoise single-microphone audio streams affected by dynamic, non-stationary noise. Drawing inspiration from recent neural network successes in separating speakers from other voices or isolating vocals from instrumental tracks, our method utilizes embedding spaces generated through source-contrastive estimation—a technique adapted from negative sampling in natural language processing—to produce continuous inference masks. Unlike previous approaches, this embedding space directly optimizes for distinguishing speech from noise by jointly modeling their features; it is generalizable, meaning it can denoise speech from speakers never encountered during training. Training employs dual objectives: one to create a selective bandpass filter that removes noise where signal power is insufficient, and another to proportionally allocate time-frequency content between signal and noise. When compared to state-of-the-art methods and traditional sparse non-negative matrix factorization, our algorithm achieves competitive accuracy while significantly reducing computational burden through a more intuitive and easily optimized framework.

We introduce an algorithm that compiles arbitrary unitaries into sequences of gates native to quantum processors. Given that precise CNOT gates remain challenging to implement on Near-term Noisy-Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) devices, our A*-inspired method prioritizes minimizing their usage while respecting hardware connectivity constraints. We detail the search strategy and metrics used to expand the solution frontier. For circuit workloads suitable for the NISQ era, our approach generates solutions that fall well within the best published upper bounds, matching or surpassing hand-tuned implementations and other existing synthesis methods. Specifically, compared to state-of-the-art synthesis packages, we achieve an average 2.4x reduction in CNOT count, with improvements reaching up to 5.3x. Furthermore, we demonstrate the algorithm's adaptability to different chip topologies and native gate sets while maintaining comparable result quality. We contend that empirical tools like ours can support algorithmic exploration, aid gate set discovery for processor designers, and offer valuable optimization modules within the quantum compilation workflow.

One method for defining intention involves applying counterfactual tools originally created to establish causality. In common law, direct intention represents the highest tier of intent and is a requisite element for the gravest crimes. Broadly, it entails performing actions to achieve a specific, desired result. However, direct intention is not always required for the most serious offenses; consequently, legal theory has evolved to address side-effects through the concept of oblique (or indirect) intent. This framework ensures that moral harms, which were unintended by the actor but were natural consequences of their actions, do not escape punishment. This paper utilizes the canonical case of a plane owner who plants a bomb to collect insurance to demonstrate how two existing counterfactual intent frameworks fail to conclude that the deaths of the passengers and crew were directly intended. We expand upon both of these frameworks by incorporating a definition of oblique intent drawn from Ashton (2021).

Understanding vocal entrainment, a social adaptation mechanism in human interaction, provides valuable insights into an individual's cognitive and behavioral traits. We introduce a context-aware framework designed to measure vocal entrainment within dyadic conversations. This approach utilizes conformers—a hybrid of convolutional networks and transformers—to capture both short-term and long-term conversational contexts, thereby modeling entrainment patterns across various domains. Specifically, we employ cross-subject attention layers to extract intra- and inter-personal signals from these interactions. We first validate the proposed method through classification experiments that distinguish between authentic (consistent) and artificial (inconsistent or shuffled) conversations. Furthermore, experimental results involving individuals with Autism Spectrum Disorder demonstrate a statistically significant correlation between our proposed entrainment metric and clinical scores related to symptoms, a finding that holds true across different genders and age groups.

In recent decades, technological advancements have spurred significant growth in numerous methodologies. Among these, Evolutionary Algorithms have emerged as a popular heuristic approach. Nevertheless, computational costs rise exponentially as problem dimensions expand. This paper proposes integrating Principal Component Analysis (PCA), a dimensionality reduction technique, into the iterative process of Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy (CMA-ES). CMA-ES is a robust numerical Evolutionary Algorithm applicable to a wide range of problems. We evaluate the proposed method's performance by analyzing its convergence rate on multi-modal benchmarks from the Black-Box Optimization Benchmarking (BBOB) suite. Additionally, we utilize the COmparing Continuous Optimizers (COCO) framework to track the new method's progress and benchmark it against existing algorithms.

This study examines an Unruh-DeWitt detector, modeled as a harmonic oscillator interacting with a massless quantum scalar field within (2+1)-dimensional Minkowski spacetime. Treating the detector as an open quantum system, we utilize a quantum Langevin equation to govern its temporal evolution, where the field—defined by a frequency-independent spectral density—functions as a stochastic force. We analyze the dynamics of a point-like detector undergoing constant acceleration through the Minkowski vacuum alongside an inertial detector submerged in a thermal reservoir at the Unruh temperature, aiming to explore the consequences of the established non-equivalence between these scenarios. Our findings reveal that both the dissipation rate and the frequency shift induced by the field coupling for the accelerated detector rely on the acceleration temperature. This result contrasts not only with inertial motion in a heat bath but also with standard quantum Brownian motion models in open systems, where such temperature dependencies are typically absent. Nevertheless, we demonstrate that the fluctuation-dissipation theorem remains valid for this detector-field system, and under weak-coupling conditions, an accelerated detector approaches a thermal equilibrium state at the Unruh temperature over time.

We demonstrate that within a globally deterministic universe, all spatiotemporally symmetric processes must adhere to counterfactual parameter independence. We show that the Tsirelson bound follows from this counterfactual parameter independence, and that the quantum monogamy bound can likewise be derived from global determinism. Leveraging these findings, we propose a new solution to the horizon problem. Additionally, we clarify the relationship between global determinism and contextuality in quantum mechanics.

Solitons are ubiquitous, shape-preserving waveforms found in nonlinear dynamical systems, categorized into bright solitons (occurring in anomalous group velocity dispersion) and dark solitons (in the normal dispersion regime). While both have been observed in contexts ranging from hydrodynamics and BECs to mode-locked lasers, they are especially significant for generating microresonator-based frequency combs (microcombs) used in timing, spectroscopy, and communications. Although bright solitons and dark pulses (derived from interlocking switching waves) have been extensively studied for microcombs, theoretically predicted localized dissipative structures lying between these two categories have remained experimentally elusive. This work reports the discovery of such hybrid structures, termed "zero-dispersion solitons," which exist where group velocity dispersion is nearly vanishing and third-order dispersion dominates. These structures form clusters of quantized sub-structures through the collapse of switching wave fronts, which are generated directly via synchronous pulse-driving in a Si3N4 photonic chip microresonator. The resulting frequency combs exhibit extreme spectral broadness, spanning 136 THz or nearly an octave (97%) in both the switching wave and zero-dispersion soliton regimes. Furthermore, engineering fourth-order dispersion leads to dual-dispersive wave formation and a novel quasi-phase matched wave associated with Faraday instability. This unexpected dissipative structure extends the boundaries of Kerr cavity physics into the near-zero-dispersion regime and may offer a superior method for broadband comb generation compared to conventional solitons.

A defining characteristic of the Landau-Zener transition is that the survival probability remains largely unaffected by the decay rate of the excited state. Specifically, the likelihood of a particle initially in the ground state staying there is robust against decay mechanisms, such as coupling to a continuum, a phenomenon documented by Akulin and Schleich (1992). While this insensitivity has been established for scenarios where the continuum's density of states is constant with respect to energy, this study examines the contrasting limit where the density of states behaves as a step-like function of energy. Consequently, the decay rate of a driven excited level undergoes a temporal jump at a specific moment, $t_0$. By leveraging known analytical solutions for time periods before and after $t_0$, we demonstrate that decay effects become significant in the survival probability when $t_0$ is comparable to the transition time.

The RuNNE Shared Task addresses the challenge of nested named entity recognition (NER) using an annotation schema that permits entities to partially overlap or nest within one another. For instance, the organization "The Yermolova Theatre" contains the person entity "Yermolova." The task utilizes the Russian NEREL dataset, which consists of news articles from the Wikinews portal and features 29 distinct entity types with a nesting depth of up to six levels. The shared task investigates two configurations: a general setup where entities appear with roughly equal frequency, and a few-shot setup where most entity types are common in training data, though some remain rare and difficult to identify, despite having balanced frequencies in the test set. This paper presents the task results, noting that 156 submissions from nine teams participated, with half surpassing a standard BERT-based baseline in both scenarios. Additionally, the paper reviews the task design, analyzes the submitted systems, and offers meaningful insights into nested NER challenges. All evaluation platform links and data are accessible via the project's GitHub repository: https://github.com/dialogue-evaluation/RuNNE.

This paper introduces a brain-inspired cognitive architecture integrating sensory processing, classification, contextual prediction, and emotional tagging. Implemented as three modular web servers, the system supports both centralized and distributed network deployment. Experimental results identify two distinct behavioral modes—high- and low-salience operations—that closely emulate brain-based attention. Beyond modeling the cortex, this bio-inspired approach also demonstrates improved processing efficiency. Published as open-source software, the platform is readily extensible for future research. Ultimately, this work establishes foundational principles for bio-realistic attention direction and sensory selection, representing a significant step toward creating bio-realistic artificial intelligence.

Given the current and anticipated transformations in energy generation, gas trading and transportation are becoming increasingly dynamic, volatile, and unpredictable. Consequently, the role of computer-aided support for rapid simulation and control optimization is growing significantly in gas network dispatching. This paper introduces and openly releases two novel mathematical models for regulators, or control valves, which, alongside compressors, constitute the most intricate active components of gas network infrastructure. These elements exert direct control over the network but operate based on target values, or set-points. Our models accommodate up to six dynamic target values to specify desired transient states for the local network environment. Specifically, every pair of these targets establishes a bounding box for inlet pressure, outlet pressure, and gas mass flow. In these models, the target values hold varying priorities and compete with one another, a conflict that is resolved dynamically during the execution of simulation or optimization processes. Following rigorous derivation, we validate our models by comparing simulation and optimization outcomes against predictions from the commercial software SIMONE.

The Aslamazov-Larkin conductivity (ALC) within Weyl semi-metals has been computed for both Type-I and Type-II phases across various dimensionalities and magnetic field strengths. This conductivity exhibits a significant dependence on the tilt parameter of the dispersion cone. In three-dimensional and two-dimensional systems, ALC shows only a slight variation with tilt in the Type-I phase but increases in the Type-II phase; conversely, in one-dimensional systems, ALC decreases in the Type-I phase, approaching zero near the boundary with the Type-II phase. These findings are contextualized against recent experiments on the layered Weyl semi-metal HfTe5, leading to the conclusion that one-dimensional AL conductivity effectively accounts for the observed experimental data.

Strained graphene subjected to external magnetic fields offers an ideal experimental platform that combines Abelian ($B$) and axial ($b$) magnetic fields. In this configuration, we numerically evaluate the two-terminal conductance ($G$) and the four- and six-terminal Hall conductivity ($\sigma_{xy}$) for spinless fermions. In unstrained graphene ($b=0$), the $B$-field generates quantized plateaus where $G=\pm |\sigma_{xy}|=(2n+1) e^2/h$ for $n=0,1,2, \cdots$. The strain-induced $b$-field removes the two-fold valley degeneracy of higher Landau levels, creating additional even-integer plateaus at $G=\pm |\sigma_{xy}|= (2,4,\cdots)e^2/h$ when $B>b$. Although the same sequence of plateaus occurs for $G$ when $b>B$, clear quantization of $\sigma_{xy}$ in Hall bar geometries disappears due to numerical instability. Furthermore, the emergence of a charge-density-wave order always results in a plateau where $G=\sigma_{xy}=0$, which induces a staggered fermionic density pattern between the two sublattices of the honeycomb lattice.

Developing high-efficiency actuators serves as a critical enabler for constructing the next generation of large-format deformable mirrors. The Netherlands Organization for Applied Scientific Research (TNO) has engineered a novel variable-reluctance actuator that consumes roughly eighty times less power than conventional voice-coil actuators. This report details laboratory performance data from a 57-actuator large-format deformable mirror developed by TNO, evaluating metrics such as influence functions, linearity, hysteresis, natural shape flattening, actuator cross-coupling, creep, repeatability, and actuator lifetime. Over a 10-micron stroke, the system achieved a linearity of 99.4 ± 0.33% and a hysteresis of 2.10 ± 0.23%, suggesting significant potential for deployment in on-sky adaptive secondary mirrors (ASMs). Finally, we outline plans for future laboratory prototypes and ASMs intended to further validate this technology.

The increasing prevalence of misinformation and fake news via online platforms necessitates an automated detection mechanism. While existing research rarely distinguishes between reliable news and other categories like satire, propaganda, or hoaxes, none of these studies model interactions between sentences within a document. We have identified a distinct pattern in how sentences relate to one another across various news types. To capture these dynamics in lengthy articles, we introduce a graph neural network-based approach that eliminates the need for manual feature engineering in fine-grained fake news classification. Experimental results demonstrate that our method outperforms strong neural baselines and achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on current datasets. Furthermore, we validate the model's generalizability by testing it on out-of-domain scenarios. The code is accessible at https://github.com/MysteryVaibhav/fake_news_semantics.

We introduce a novel approach to collision-free planning that leverages Conditional Generative Adversarial Networks (cGANs) to map a robot's joint space to a latent space representing exclusively obstacle-free regions, conditioned on an obstacle map. This capability facilitates the generation of multiple viable trajectories, which is particularly advantageous for robot arm manipulation, allowing for the selection of paths that avoid collisions with the robot or its surroundings. In our method, various obstacle-avoiding trajectories are produced by linking start and goal states via arbitrary line segments within this synthesized latent space. By providing such a collision-free latent space, our approach enables any planner, utilizing any specific optimization criteria, to generate optimal paths dynamically. We validated this method through both simulations and experiments with a physical UR5e 6-DoF robotic arm, confirming that distinct trajectories can be generated based on varying optimization conditions.

Athletes frequently undergo fitness assessments to monitor their training advancements, a process that typically involves a trained specialist using specialized tools such as force plates. During these tests, athletes execute drop and squat jumps while critical metrics like velocity, flight duration, and stabilization time are recorded. However, amateur athletes often lack access to the necessary professionals or equipment for such evaluations. This study explores the viability of deriving these key metrics from video footage. We prioritize jump velocity as our initial focus due to its strong correlation with other variables and its significance in assessing posture and lower-limb strength. Our findings indicate that velocity can be estimated with high precision across various athlete groups, yielding an average R-value of 0.71 (SD = 0.06).

We employ magnetotransport measurements in dual-gated magnetic topological insulator heterostructures to chart the phase diagram of the topological Hall and quantum anomalous Hall effects, varying the chemical potential (mainly controlled by the back gate) and the asymmetric potential (mainly controlled by the top gate). A theoretical framework incorporating both surface states and valence band quantum well states enables the assessment of how the Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction and carrier density change with gate voltages. The qualitative match between experimental results and theoretical predictions offers robust evidence for the presence of a topological Hall effect in the investigated system, thereby establishing a novel pathway for comprehending and manipulating chiral magnetic spin textures in real space.

The illicit transport of special nuclear materials (SNM) and nuclear devices across borders and ports poses a significant threat to global security, necessitating reliable technologies to detect high-$Z$ substances like uranium and plutonium within commercial flows. This paper presents an experimental proof-of-concept for a technique utilizing inelastic ($p,p'$) nuclear reactions to produce monoenergetic photons, enabling the precise measurement of an object's areal density and effective atomic number ($Z_{\text{eff}}$) with accuracy exceeding current methods. By employing an ION-12$^{ \text{SC}}$ superconducting 12~MeV proton cyclotron, we generated photons at energies of 4.4, 6.1, 6.9, and 7.1~MeV through various nuclear reactions. In a transmission configuration, these photons allowed for the accurate reconstruction of both areal density and $Z_{\text{eff}}$ for a test object. This approach has the potential to facilitate mobile screening of commercial cargo with high material specificity, effectively distinguishing standard materials from high-$Z$ threats such as uranium and plutonium.

Traditionally, generating text from semantic graphs relies on deterministic methods that produce a single, fixed description for a given input. However, the generation task inherently allows for a variety of valid textual outputs, characterized by variations in lexicon, syntax, and semantics. To bridge this gap, we introduce two primary contributions. First, we develop a stochastic graph-to-text model featuring a latent variable within an encoder-decoder architecture, applied within an ensemble framework. Second, we propose a novel automatic evaluation metric designed to jointly assess both output diversity and quality in a multi-reference context. Our evaluation on WebNLG datasets in English and Russian demonstrates that an ensemble of stochastic models yields diverse sentence sets while maintaining quality comparable to state-of-the-art deterministic approaches.

The Volume of Fluid (VOF) method is a sharp interface technique used for simulating two-phase flows, typically representing the interface with piecewise linear segments within each grid cell based on the volume fraction field. Although VOF achieves exact mass conservation in Cartesian coordinates, current algorithms fail to maintain machine-precision mass conservation in axisymmetric systems. This study introduces analytic formulae for interface reconstruction in axisymmetric coordinates, analogous to those developed by Scardovelli and Zaleski (J. Comput. Phys. 2000) for Cartesian grids. Furthermore, we propose modifications to existing VOF advection schemes for axisymmetric coordinates to enhance mass conservation accuracy.

Although Thomas Ehrhard and Laurent Regnier introduced differential lambda-calculus in 2003, there has been limited research into a version incorporating integration over its fifteen-year history. This paper presents a programming-centric approach to developing a differential calculus that includes integration. We demonstrate a strong alignment with mathematical principles, evidenced by the construction of our reduction rules and the preservation of key mathematical theorems within the system. Furthermore, we emphasize the calculus's utility in incremental computation, automatic differentiation, and approximation algorithms.

Upcoming datasets will facilitate cross-correlations between redshift space distortions (RSD) and weak lensing (WL). Although photometric lensing and clustering cross-correlations have currently offered some of the most stringent cosmological constraints, the optimal methods for conducting lossless RSD/WL joint analyses remain unclear. Since RSD is generally measured in three-dimensional redshift space while WL is inherently a projected signal, angular statistics represent a logical approach for combined analysis. Consequently, this study investigates the quantity of RSD information recoverable via projected statistics. Specifically, we employ a Fisher analysis to forecast constraints and evaluate model bias by comparing two distinct Fingers-of-God (FoG) models using both the 3D power spectrum, $P(k, \mu)$, and tomographic $C(\ell)$. Our results indicate that naive tomographic projection, which conflates large scales with poorly modeled nonlinear radial modes, fails to yield competitive constraints relative to the 3D RSD power spectrum unless model bias becomes unacceptably high; this holds true even with narrow tomographic bins. Addressing this limitation, we propose a novel radial weighting scheme that disentangles radial RSD scales during projection, thereby achieving constraints competitive with the 3D RSD power spectrum while maintaining low model bias. This research establishes a foundation for optimal joint analyses of RSD and cosmic shear.

We investigate actions of the mapping class group on an orientable surface $\Sigma_{g,n}$ of genus $g$ with $n$ punctures using arithmetic and Hodge-theoretic methods. Our main result demonstrates that if $\rho: \pi_1(\Sigma_{g,n}) \to GL_r(\mathbb{C})$ is a representation with a finite orbit under the mapping class group, and if $r < \sqrt{g+1}$, then $\rho$ must have a finite image. This finding resolves inquiries posed by Junho Peter Whang and Mark Kisin. Furthermore, we apply these techniques to the Putman-Wieland conjecture, the Fontaine-Mazur conjecture, and a question raised by Esnault and Kerz. The proofs are grounded in non-abelian Hodge theory, our previous research on the semistability of isomonodromic deformations, and recent contributions by Esnault-Groechenig and Klevdal-Patrikis regarding Simpson's integrality conjecture for cohomologically rigid local systems.

Resistive Plate Chambers (RPCs) are established gaseous detectors in High Energy Physics (HEP), valued for their excellent tracking performance, high efficiency, superior time resolution, and affordable manufacturing costs. However, their primary drawback is a limited capacity to handle high particle rates. To address this, various experimental teams have created advanced techniques to enhance rate handling and minimize noise. This article examines a novel method involving linseed oil coating applied to bakelite-based RPCs, demonstrating the resulting efficiency when utilizing a standard gas mixture.

Third-party automotive dongles, such as those provided by insurance firms, can access sensitive information and transmit commands to vehicles through the standardized OBD-II interface. The absence of message authentication mechanisms creates significant security risks, particularly when connecting to malicious devices. To address this, we propose a modular, protocol-independent firewall strategy that positions a man-in-the-middle between the dongle and the car's OBD-II port. Leveraging this privileged network location, we demonstrate the ability to alter or restrict data flows accessible via the OBD-II interface. By employing fine-grained, configurable rewriting rules designed to be protocol-agnostic, we can modify message contents or delay their transmission. We have successfully implemented and tested this modular firewall approach against commercially available third-party dongles. Consequently, our solution provides a security layer that enhances the privacy and safety of dongle users, addressing the critical lack of message authentication at the electronic control unit level.

Leveraging the MeerKAT radio telescope, a cutting-edge SKA precursor, we investigate the constraints on millisecond pulsar timing precision imposed by pulse stochasticity, or jitter. Our study presents new jitter measurements for 15 out of 29 pulsars in our sample, revealing significant variability in jitter levels across different sources. While some pulsars, such as the 2.2-ms PSR J2241--5236, exhibit extremely low jitter of approximately 4 ns/hr, others, like the 3.9-ms PSR J0636--3044, are constrained to about 100 ns/hr. Although jitter is recognized as a primary factor limiting arrival time precision in high signal-to-noise observations, its impact on dispersion measure (DM) determination—especially in broad-band contexts—remains unreported. Utilizing MeerKAT's superior sensitivity, we analyzed the DM of every individual pulse for the bright millisecond pulsar PSR J0437--4715. Our results show that single-pulse DMs typically deviate by 0.0085 cm$^{-3}$ pc from the mean, with the most accurate DM estimates being capped by differential jitter across the frequency band. We propose that each millisecond pulsar possesses a unique limit on DM precision, surmountable only through extended integration times. Furthermore, employing high-time resolution filterbank data with 9 $\mu$s sampling, we conducted a statistical analysis of single-pulse phenomenology and outlined optimization strategies for the MeerKAT pulsar timing program within the framework of the International Pulsar Timing Array (IPTA).

We present the inaugural application of lean methodology to machine learning initiatives. Drawing parallels with lean startups and manufacturing, we contend that Lean Machine Learning (LeanML) can significantly eliminate avoidable waste in commercial ML projects, lower business risks associated with investing in ML capabilities, and thereby broaden access to machine learning. This proposed design pattern rests on two key insights. First, one can estimate the optimal achievable performance for predicting an outcome $y \in \mathcal{Y}$ given a set of explanatory variables $x \in \mathcal{X}$ across various metrics, all without training a predictive model. Second, this estimation process is markedly simpler, quicker, and less expensive than learning the optimal predictive model. We derive formulas that express the maximum $R^2$, MSE, classification accuracy, and log-likelihood per observation attainable when using $x$ to predict $y$ as a function of mutual information $I\left(y; x\right)$, along with a measure of $y$'s variability (such as Shannon entropy for classification accuracy or variance for regression MSE). We demonstrate the effectiveness of the LeanML design pattern across a diverse array of synthetic and real-world regression and classification tasks.

Recent research indicates that quantum field stress tensor components, including pressure and energy density, undergo significant vacuum fluctuations. To obtain finite values, these quantities must be averaged over time, and the likelihood of substantial fluctuations can exceed Gaussian predictions depending on the specific averaging method. This study investigates fluctuations in vacuum radiation pressure acting on Rydberg atoms and their potential observable consequences. The process of Rydberg atom excitation and de-excitation serves as a concrete model for time-averaging radiation pressure, as the atom's polarizability varies dynamically, changing by several orders of magnitude. This switching behavior in polarizability can generate large vacuum pressure fluctuations, which may momentarily impart linear momentum to the atom, resulting in a detectable recoil.

This paper investigates the diffusion approximation of multi-scale McKean-Vlasov stochastic differential equations. Specifically, we establish the weak convergence of the slow component $X^\varepsilon$ within the space $C([0,T];\mathbb{R}^n)$ to a limiting process $X$, which satisfies a distribution-dependent stochastic differential equation featuring novel drift and diffusion terms absent in the original formulation. Our primary contribution involves employing two distinct methodologies to explicitly derive the limiting equations. Although the resulting diffusion coefficients differ in form across these approaches, we demonstrate their equivalence through a comparative analysis.

This research examines an abstract framework describing the co-evolution of mutating viruses and the adaptive immune system. Within sequence space, both populations cluster around transiently dominant strains. We observe a new interdependence between delocalization and error thresholds, as the immune response relies on viral attack. Stochastic fluctuations trigger an evolutionary chase that may proceed through periodic or intermittent cycles. Through simulations and stochastic analysis, we demonstrate how the shift between these dynamic regimes is governed by mutation rates, immune response intensity, and population size.

Large Pre-trained Language Models (PLMs) have become central to language understanding and many AI breakthroughs. Although English PLMs have achieved unprecedented progress, similar advancements in Hebrew are scarce. This gap stems from two main issues: the scarcity of training data for Hebrew NLP models compared to English, and the lack of established tasks and benchmarks to evaluate Hebrew PLM performance. This work addresses both challenges. First, we introduce AlephBERT, a large Hebrew PLM trained on a significantly larger dataset and vocabulary than any previous Hebrew model. Second, leveraging AlephBERT, we achieve state-of-the-art results across multiple Hebrew benchmarks, including segmentation, part-of-speech tagging, full morphological tagging, named-entity recognition, and sentiment analysis. By making AlephBERT publicly available, we provide a unified resource to accelerate the development of Hebrew NLP applications.

Image-to-Image (I2I) translation is a demanding computer vision task applied across various domains, with ophthalmology emerging as a key area for its rapid adoption. A specific use case involves generating synthetic retinal optical coherence tomography (OCT) scans. However, current I2I approaches necessitate training separate models for each target pathology, which restricts their utility due to inherent complexity. To overcome this limitation, we introduce an unsupervised multi-domain I2I network featuring a pre-trained style encoder capable of converting retinal OCT images from a single source domain into multiple target domains. Our method operates on the premise that images can be decomposed into domain-invariant content and domain-specific style codes, with the latter being pre-trained. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed model surpasses state-of-the-art techniques, such as MUNIT and CycleGAN, in synthesizing diverse pathological scans.

This study addresses the intricate pathological characteristics inherent in retinal edema lesion segmentation from OCT images, specifically challenges such as indistinct boundaries, significant scale variations among symptoms, and background noise interference, with the goal of enhancing result reliability. We introduce a novel Reliable Multi-Scale Wavelet-Enhanced Transformer Network capable of delivering precise segmentation accompanied by reliability assessments. To better capture complex pathological features, we designed a new segmentation backbone that combines a wavelet-enhanced feature extractor with a custom multi-scale transformer module. Furthermore, to ensure robustness, we incorporated a novel uncertainty segmentation head grounded in subjective logical evidential theory, which produces final segmentation outputs alongside a corresponding overall uncertainty evaluation map. Comprehensive experiments conducted on the AI-Challenge 2018 public dataset demonstrate that our method outperforms other state-of-the-art approaches in both segmentation accuracy and reliability. The source code is available at: https://github.com/LooKing9218/ReliableRESeg.

The scripting language outlined in this document is primarily designed for robots created by Anja M{\o}lle Lindelof and Henning Christiansen within a research initiative focused on stage performances. These target robots are envisioned to resemble familiar household items that appear to possess a life of their own, potentially interacting with human performers to create the illusion of mutual communication. In its current iteration, the robots' collective behavior is exclusively governed by scripts written in this language; the only autonomy they possess is the ability to dynamically self-correct for inaccuracies that occur during a performance. This work is currently in a preliminary stage, lacking rigorous comparison with other research in the field, and testing remains limited. An initial implementation on small Lego Mindstorms robots is currently being developed by Mads Saustrup Fox as part of his master's thesis.

We created models and algorithms to characterize two primary artifacts of Atomic Force Microscopy (AFM): profile broadening and reduced heights for individual objects adsorbed on hard substrates. We also demonstrated a method for measuring the elastic properties of single adsorbed microobjects. From the perspective of contact deformation theory, we examined the mechanisms underlying AFM's visualization of the atomic or molecular structure of flat surfaces. Additionally, we evaluated a technique for immobilizing free single-stranded RNA molecules in an extended conformation on a substrate. Using AFM, we visualized the stages of RNA release from the protein coat of tobacco mosaic virus particles and confirmed the asymmetry of this process at the two ends of the macromolecule. We tracked the compaction dynamics of T4 DNA molecules in real-time AFM mode, clearly resolving partially compacted structures. Our analysis revealed that these partially compacted forms consist of toroidal sections made from different macromolecular strands. Based on systematic AFM measurements, we reconstructed the real geometry of these compacted structures, which enabled us to calculate the number of molecules comprising each condensed DNA particle. We also highlighted the advantages of the horizontal deposition method for creating Langmuir-Blodgett (LB) films. Through AFM, we achieved molecular resolution for certain thin film coatings and determined lattice parameters with a precision limited by errors of only a few percent. Finally, we demonstrated that film structure is governed by the interplay of several factors: the closest packing principle for hydrocarbon tails, the surface areas of polar heads at the water subphase, and the influence of the substrate.

Hafnia (HfO2) holds significant promise for next-generation chip technology owing to its high-k dielectric characteristics, compatibility with negative capacitance heterostructures, scalable ferroelectricity, and ability to integrate with silicon. However, its lattice dynamics and phononic attributes—including thermal conductivity, contraction, and heat capacity—remain largely unexplored, largely because high-quality single crystals have been unavailable. This study investigates the vibrational properties of yttrium-stabilized HfO2 crystals (with Y concentrations of 20, 12, 11, 8, and 0%) and contrasts these findings with symmetry analyses and lattice dynamics simulations. By validating our calculations against experimental Raman and infrared spectra across cubic, antipolar orthorhombic, and monoclinic phases, we disentangle the specific effects of yttrium and identify the characteristic modes of the polar orthorhombic phase. Ultimately, this work establishes a spectroscopic fingerprint for various HfO2 phases, facilitating future investigations into how specific vibrational modes contribute to the high-k dielectric and ferroelectric behaviors essential for advanced chip applications.

The detection of gravitational waves from merging black-hole binaries has revived the hypothesis that dark matter comprises, at least in part, primordial black holes (PBHs). Yet, this theory faces significant challenges from various observational constraints that limit PBH abundance across a wide spectrum of masses. Notably, microlensing surveys provide the most stringent limits for masses between $\sim 10^{-10}$ and a few solar masses ($M_{\odot}$). This specific mass window aligns with the region where PBH formation is enhanced by the QCD phase transition in the early universe, underscoring the critical role of microlensing. Although it has been suggested that PBH clustering on small scales could substantially weaken or eliminate these bounds, the effect of such clustering on the microlensing event rate remains largely unexplored. In this Letter, we examine this gap and demonstrate that clusters generated by isocurvature perturbations—derived from Gaussian initial curvature perturbations linked to PBH formation—do not modify existing microlensing constraints, as these clusters lack sufficient compactness.

We establish sharp generalization and excess risk guarantees for full-batch Gradient Descent (GD) applied to smooth losses, even when they are non-Lipschitz or nonconvex. Central to our analysis is an upper bound on generalization error, demonstrating that average output stability combined with a bounded expected optimization error at termination ensures generalization. This finding indicates that generalization error remains small throughout the optimization trajectory, enabling us to circumvent the Lipschitz or sub-Gaussian assumptions typically required in prior research. For nonconvex, convex, and strongly convex settings, we explicitly detail how generalization error depends on the accumulated path-dependent optimization error, terminal optimization error, sample size, and iteration count. In the case of nonconvex smooth losses, we prove that full-batch GD efficiently generalizes to any stationary point reached at termination, recovering the guarantees of stochastic algorithms under fewer assumptions. For smooth convex losses, our derived generalization error bounds are tighter than existing SGD bounds by approximately one order of magnitude, resulting in excess risk that matches SGD performance with quadratically fewer iterations. Finally, for strongly convex smooth losses, we demonstrate that full-batch GD achieves an excess risk rate comparable to state-of-the-art SGD methods but requires an exponentially smaller number of iterations, which scales logarithmically with dataset size.

Academic norms typically assess model performance using in-domain evaluation data reserved from the training set; however, real-world applications often involve data that significantly diverges from training characteristics. This paper addresses Finnish out-of-domain parsing by introducing a new Universal Dependencies (UD) Finnish-OOD treebank. This resource aggregates five distinct data sources—web documents, clinical texts, online discussions, tweets, and poetry—comprising 19,382 syntactic words across 2,122 sentences, all released under the UD framework. Alongside this new treebank, we conduct extensive out-of-domain parsing evaluations using section-level data from three existing Finnish UD treebanks (TDT, PUD, and OOD). Unlike previous resources, the Finnish-OOD treebank includes sections that pose greater challenges for general parsers, thereby establishing a compelling evaluation scenario and providing valuable insights for deploying parsers beyond their training domains.

Utilizing integral field spectroscopy from the PHANGS-MUSE survey, which achieves ~50 pc resolution for the ionized interstellar medium in 19 nearby spiral galaxies, we investigate the origins of diffuse ionized gas (DIG). To analyze the physical properties of this gas, we first exclude morphologically defined HII regions and then bin low-surface-brightness areas to ensure robust detections of key nebular lines. A straightforward model describing the leakage and propagation of ionizing radiation from HII regions successfully reproduces the observed H$\alpha$ distribution within the DIG. Furthermore, this leaking radiation accounts for the decline in low-ionization line ratios ([SII]/H$\alpha$, [NII]/H$\alpha$, and [OI]/H$\alpha$) as H$\alpha$ surface brightness increases. However, emission from hot low-mass evolved stars is necessary to explain three specific phenomena: (1) elevated low-ionization line ratios in the central regions of certain galaxies; (2) trends showing flat or decreasing [OIII]/H$\beta$ with increasing $\Sigma_{H\alpha}$; and (3) DIG regions offset from the standard HII region locus in the Baldwin-Phillips-Terlevich (BPT) diagram, extending toward low-ionization nuclear emission-line regions (LINERs). Although hot low-mass evolved stars contribute only a small fraction (2%) to the galaxy-integrated H$\alpha$ energy budget, their harder spectra are crucial for [OIII] production. Consequently, the DIG likely arises from a superposition of two components: an energetically dominant source from young stars and a more diffuse background of harder ionizing photons from older stars. This unified framework connects Milky Way DIG observations with LINER-like emission found in the bulges of nearby galaxies.

The rapid global spread of COVID-19 has created an urgent demand for affordable, rapid, and dependable diagnostic tools for physicians. While medical imaging like CT scans plays a vital role alongside molecular diagnostics, deep learning has shown promise in analyzing CT and X-ray data. This study advocates for the expanded use of point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) to guide COVID-19 detection, leveraging its non-invasive nature and widespread availability in healthcare settings worldwide. Our work has three main components. First, we compiled a lung ultrasound dataset comprising 1,103 images (654 from COVID-19 patients, 277 from bacterial pneumonia cases, and 172 from healthy controls) derived from 64 videos sourced online and processed for deep learning; this resource is intended as a foundation for an open-access initiative. Second, we trained a deep convolutional neural network, POCOVID-Net, on this three-class dataset, achieving an overall accuracy of 89% and a video-level accuracy of 92% via majority voting. Specifically for COVID-19 detection, the model demonstrated a sensitivity of 0.96, specificity of 0.79, and an F1-score of 0.92 during 5-fold cross-validation. Third, we launched an open-access web service, POCOVIDScreen (https://pocovidscreen.org), which deploys the predictive model for analyzing lung ultrasound images and allows medical personnel to upload their own screenings to expand the public pathological image database. The dataset and code are accessible at: https://github.com/jannisborn/covid19_pocus_ultrasound. NOTE: This preprint has been superseded by our paper in Applied Sciences: https://doi.org/10.3390/app11020672

This study examines a Kerr-like black hole situated within a Randall-Sundrum warped spacetime under the conformal dilaton-Higgs $(\omega,\Phi)$ gravity framework. By imposing antipodal boundary conditions on the Klein surface via $\mathds{Z}_2$-symmetry along the "large" (bulk) extra dimension, the pseudo-Riemannian 5D manifold is effectively represented as a 4D Riemannian brane spacetime, $\mathds{R}^2_+\times\mathds{R}^1\times S^1$, where $\mathds{R}^2_+$ exhibits conformal flatness. The derived solution remains valid across both manifolds and can be equivalently characterized as an instanton solution. A significant benefit of this approach is that antipodicity is preserved without resorting to the "cut-and-paste" technique or quantum cloning when analyzing the scattering aspects of Hawking radiation evaporation; only the winding number is required as the quantum number. Furthermore, the equations demonstrate invariance under time reversal. The challenge of matching the near-horizon approximation with the distant Regge-Wheeler approximation may be addressed by decomposing the spacetime into a dilaton field multiplied by an "un-physical," conformally flat spacetime. Specifically, for a constant gauge field, the conformally invariant mass term $\sim \Phi^2\omega^2$ in the Lagrangian emerges directly from the dilaton equation, provided the scale of the extra dimension is appropriately selected.

We have enhanced our prior constituent quark model by incorporating a full set of three-dimensional harmonic oscillator bases into the spatial component of the total wave function. To validate this approach, we benchmarked the calculated binding energies against exact values from the hydrogen model. Following a fit to the masses of ground-state hadrons, we applied the refined method to investigate doubly-heavy tetraquark states ($qq'\bar{Q}\bar{Q'}$), comparing our binding energy results with existing literature. Additionally, we computed the ground-state masses for $T_{sc} (ud\bar{s}\bar{c})$ and $T_{sb} (ud\bar{s}\bar{b})$ with isospin and spin quantum numbers $(I,S) = (0,1)$ and $(0,2)$. Our findings indicate that $T_{bb} (ud\bar{b}\bar{b})$ and $us\bar{b}\bar{b}$, both with $(I,S) = (0,1)$, are stable against the two lowest meson thresholds, exhibiting binding energies of $-145$ MeV and $-42$ MeV, respectively. We also determined that $T_{cb} (ud\bar{c}\bar{b})$ lies near its lowest threshold. Finally, the spatial dimensions of these tetraquarks were analyzed.

Remote sensing datasets frequently contain quality flags indicating whether observations are reliable, acceptable, or poor; however, this fidelity information is often overlooked in subsequent analyses. Drawing on data from NASA's Atmospheric Infrared Sounder (AIRS) aboard the Aqua satellite, we introduce a latent variable co-kriging model utilizing separable Gaussian processes to analyze extensive remote sensing datasets alongside their quality metadata. By augmenting the posterior distribution with an imputation strategy, we decompose large covariance matrices into computationally efficient components that leverage the input data's structure. Within this augmented framework, we implement a Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm primarily based on direct simulations from conditional distributions and propose a recursive prediction method for improved computational efficiency. Applied to AIRS air temperature data, our approach demonstrates that integrating quality flag information significantly enhances prediction accuracy compared to models that ignore such flags.

This study examines a logistic differential equation with impulsive delayed harvesting, where the harvest deduction depends on the population size at a previous impulse moment. By leveraging a strong link to high-order difference equation dynamics, we demonstrate that although delay in the impulsive condition does not affect yield optimality, it significantly influences sustainability, which is generally dependent on the delay. The analysis explores various yield types and establishes sharp stability tests along with explicit sufficient conditions. Furthermore, we show that persistence is not assured for all positive initial conditions, and finite-time extinction can occur, a finding supported by simulation results.

Extracting low-dimensional representations from long-timescale biomolecular trajectories, such as protein folding or ligand-receptor binding, is crucial, with kinetic models like Markov modeling being particularly effective. Recently, VAMPNet was introduced as an unsupervised machine learning method that end-to-end learns both low-dimensional representations and linear dynamical models based on the Variational Approach to Markov Processes (VAMP) using neural networks to capture coarse-grained dynamics. This work integrates VAMPNet with graph neural networks to create an end-to-end framework that efficiently derives high-level dynamics and metastable states from extensive molecular dynamics simulations. By leveraging graph representation learning and message-passing operations to generate embeddings for each data point, this approach feeds into VAMPNet to produce a coarse-grained representation. The resulting molecular representation yields a higher-resolution and more interpretable Markov model than standard VAMPNet, facilitating a more detailed kinetic analysis of biomolecular processes. Furthermore, our GraphVAMPNet method incorporates an attention mechanism to identify key residues essential for classifying different metastable states.

Neural models, capable of generating novel representations, have demonstrated promising outcomes in healthcare prediction tasks. Nevertheless, patient demographics, medical technologies, and care quality evolve over time, often causing a decline in neural model performance for future patients, particularly regarding calibration. The deep kernel learning (DKL) framework offers robustness against such temporal shifts by integrating neural networks with Gaussian processes, which account for prediction uncertainty. We hypothesize that out-of-distribution inputs will yield probabilities nearer to the global mean, thereby mitigating overconfidence and enhancing calibration on prospective data. This study examines DKL's behavior during a temporal shift naturally introduced by an update to the information system feeding a cohort database. We compare DKL against a recurrent neural network baseline, demonstrating that DKL delivers superior calibrated predictions with less sharp probability estimates. Furthermore, DKL exhibited improved discrimination ability, achieving an AUC of 0.746 (+- 0.014 std) compared to the baseline's 0.739 (+- 0.028 std). These findings underscore the critical importance of incorporating uncertainty into neural computing, especially for prospective applications.

We report initial findings from an intensive, multi-wavelength monitoring campaign of the luminous Seyfert 1 galaxy Mrk 817. Although this active galactic nucleus was originally chosen for its lack of historical obscuration, our data reveal a highly absorbed X-ray spectrum and newly identified blueshifted, broad, and narrow UV absorption lines. These features indicate that a dust-free, ionized obscurer situated within the inner broad line region partially covers the central engine. Despite this absorption, we detect UV and optical continuum reverberation lags consistent with a centrally illuminated Shakura-Sunyaev thin accretion disk, alongside expected lags from the optical broad line region. However, during the first 55 days of the observation when obscuration peaked, we observed a decoupling between UV continuum variability and UV broad emission line fluctuations. This correlation re-established itself over the subsequent 42 days as Mrk 817 transitioned to a less obscured state. Furthermore, the short time lags in CIV and Ly alpha suggest that the accretion disk extends beyond the region of UV broad emission lines.

This paper proves noncommutative Burkholder inequalities featuring asymmetric diagonals within symmetric operator spaces. The demonstration primarily depends on a novel complex interpolation theorem for asymmetric vector-valued spaces alongside a duality method. Additionally, we present the asymmetric counterparts of the noncommutative Johnson-Schechtman inequalities.

We establish the theoretical framework for magnetic-field-induced Wigner crystallization in recently discovered charged interlayer excitons (CIE) within transition-metal-dichalcogenide (TMD) heterobilayers. For many-particle CIE systems under perpendicular magnetic fields of varying strengths, we calculate the ratio of mean potential to kinetic energy, examine both weak and strong field limits, and investigate the 'cold' crystallization phase transition occurring in strong fields. Additionally, we extend the concept of the effective g-factor for interlayer excitons to encompass CIE formation in electrostatically doped TMD heterobilayers. We demonstrate that both the magnetic-field-induced Wigner crystallization and melting of CIEs are observable through strong-field magneto-photoluminescence experiments on TMD heterobilayers with systematically adjusted electron-hole doping levels. These findings enhance the potential of this emerging class of transdimensional quantum materials.

We present M2DGR, a new large-scale dataset gathered by a ground robot equipped with a comprehensive sensor suite. This suite features six fish-eye and one sky-pointing RGB cameras, an infrared camera, an event camera, a Visual-Inertial Sensor (VI-sensor), an IMU, a LiDAR, a consumer-grade GNSS receiver, and a GNSS-IMU navigation system utilizing real-time kinematic (RTK) signals. All sensors were meticulously calibrated and synchronized, ensuring simultaneous data recording. Ground truth trajectories were derived from a motion capture system, a laser 3D tracker, and an RTK receiver. The dataset consists of 36 sequences totaling approximately 1TB, captured across varied indoor and outdoor environments. We assessed state-of-the-art SLAM algorithms on M2DGR, revealing that current solutions struggle in certain scenarios. To support the research community, we have made the dataset and associated tools publicly available at https://github.com/SJTU-ViSYS/M2DGR.

MAELAS is a computational tool designed to automatically determine magnetocrystalline anisotropy energy, anisotropic magnetostrictive coefficients, and magnetoelastic constants. The initial methodology used in MAELAS version 1.0 relied on the unit cell length optimization technique proposed by Wu and Freeman to calculate anisotropic magnetostrictive coefficients. This document introduces an updated version (v2.0) that incorporates a new approach for deriving anisotropic magnetoelastic constants through a linear fit of energy against applied strain. By comparing the accuracy of both techniques, we demonstrate that the new method is more robust and reliable, particularly for non-cubic crystal symmetries. Furthermore, this analysis suggests that the version 1.0 method could achieve higher accuracy by utilizing deformation gradients from the equilibrium magnetoelastic strain tensor, with potential future improvements via strain optimization methods. Additionally, we clarify the influence of the demagnetized state on fractional length changes and derive expressions for saturation magnetostriction in polycrystals exhibiting trigonal, tetragonal, and orthorhombic symmetries. Finally, this updated version rectifies specific issues regarding trigonal crystal symmetry that were present in version 1.0.

While some deep learning studies \citep[e.g.,][]{zhang2016understanding} have noted that over-parametrized networks can achieve minimal testing error despite near-zero training error, this paper explores an alternative approach to enforcing zero training error without over-parametrization by utilizing a data interpolation mechanism. We specifically examine a range of interpolated weighting schemes within nearest neighbors (NN) algorithms. By precisely characterizing the multiplicative constant in statistical risk, we demonstrate a U-shaped performance curve associated with varying levels of data interpolation for both classification and regression tasks. These findings refine existing conclusions \citep{belkin2018does} suggesting that zero training error does not inherently compromise predictive performance, and they present a counter-intuitive result: a moderate degree of data interpolation {\em strictly} enhances both prediction performance and statistical stability compared to standard (un-interpolated) $k$-NN methods. Finally, we discuss the universality of these results, including variations in distance measures and the presence of corrupted testing data.

Parallel-in-time algorithms like Parareal and multigrid reduction-in-time (MGRIT) offer a promising avenue for enhancing concurrency in high-performance computing simulations of time-dependent partial differential equations (PDEs). Although these methods excel with parabolic equations, they frequently exhibit severe performance degradation when applied to advection-dominated or purely hyperbolic PDEs using conventional rediscretization strategies on coarse grids. This paper investigates MGRIT and Parareal applied to the constant-coefficient linear advection equation, leveraging existing convergence theory to explain the often non-scalable or divergent behavior observed in such scenarios. To address these limitations, we substitute standard rediscretization with optimized coarse-grid operators designed to minimize error estimates derived from convergence theory. A primary conclusion is that achieving rapid convergence comparable to parabolic problems requires coarse-grid operators to account for hyperbolic characteristics by tracking characteristic curves. We validate this approach across various scheme orders, combining explicit and implicit Runge-Kutta time integrators with upwind finite-difference spatial discretizations. In every test case, we achieve scalable convergence within a few iterations, with parallel experiments demonstrating substantial speed-ups over sequential time-stepping. The strategy of tracking characteristics on coarse grids offers a crucial insight for resolving the longstanding challenge of efficient parallel-in-time integration for hyperbolic PDEs.

This study examines the failure dynamics of fiber bundles on complex networks, specifically investigating how the disorder in fiber strength influences the shift from localized to mean-field behavior. Beginning with a regular square lattice, we utilize the Watts-Strogatz rewiring method to incorporate long-range random connections, analyzing how the bundle's ultimate strength and the statistical distribution of failure cascade sizes evolve as the rewiring probability increases. Our results indicate that the level of strength disorder among network nodes significantly impacts the transition from localized to mean-field regimes. Specifically, we demonstrate that this transition occurs at a finite rewiring probability that increases as strength disorder decreases. The transition is confined to a specific disorder range, implying a threshold level of strength disorder below which randomizing the network structure fails to enhance either the system's overall load-bearing capacity or its tolerance to cascades. Consequently, networks with low strength disorder achieve maximum stability when fully random, whereas those with high disorder exhibit optimal cascade tolerance at intermediate levels of structural randomness. Finally, we develop an analytical framework based on the interaction between network topology and strength disorder that effectively explains the observed numerical results.

During an ALMA survey of the 1-3 Myr old Lupus association, we identified circumstellar dust and CO gas around the K7 class III star NO Lup. Our analysis reveals that the $J=3-2$ CO emission is both spectrally and spatially resolved, exhibiting a broad velocity width of approximately 19 km/s across a resolved size of roughly 1 arcsecond (equivalent to ~130 au). Modeling this gas emission as a Keplerian disk yields consistency only with a central mass of ~11 $M_{\odot}$, a value that is implausible given the star's spectral type and X-Shooter data. Conversely, the data can be well-fitted by modeling the CO as outflowing gas with a radial velocity of ~22 km/s. We interpret NO Lup's CO emission as the first imaged class III circumstellar disk containing outflowing gas. We conclude that the CO is continuously replenished, though we cannot yet determine if this source is the fragmentation of icy planetesimals or the final remnants of the protoplanetary disk. We recommend further investigation into the origin of this CO and its unexpectedly high velocity relative to photoevaporative models.

Influence Maximization (IM), a field focused on identifying a subset of social network users to maximize the spread of influence, has recently gained prominence in mass communication and commercial marketing. Current IM research relies heavily on the assumption that selected seed users are eager to disseminate information after receiving incentives from an organization. However, in practice, some seeds may be unwilling to share information or require higher compensation. Moreover, existing IM studies often overlook the potential for influence propagation in future time periods. This paper introduces a novel problem called the Reconnecting Top-l Relationships (RTlR) query, which seeks to identify $l$ previously existing but now estranged relationships such that re-establishing them maximizes the expected benefit to influenced users in the future. We demonstrate that the RTlR problem is NP-hard. To address this, we propose an efficient greedy algorithm that combines influence estimation with a tailored link prediction method to forecast near-future network structures. Additionally, we develop a pruning technique to minimize unnecessary edge probing and introduce a carefully designed order-based algorithm to accelerate query processing. Finally, extensive experiments on real-world datasets validate the effectiveness and efficiency of our proposed approaches.

Beginning in October 2018, the Large Sky Area Multi-Object Fiber Spectroscopic Telescope (LAMOST) initiated a median-resolution spectroscopic survey (MRS, R$\sim$7500) aimed at studying binary stars, pulsators, and other variable stars through time-domain observations. Accurate radial velocity measurements for this survey require careful attention to systematic errors, such as those arising from wavelength calibration biases and variations between different spectrographs. This study presents a correction technique for wavelength calibration systematics derived from relative radial velocity measurements within LAMOST MRS spectra. We demonstrate that for stars observed across multiple epochs, systematic biases caused by exposures taken on different nights can be effectively corrected for each spectrograph, achieving a radial velocity zero-point precision of better than 0.5 km/s. Additionally, we identify candidate constant stars that could serve as secondary radial-velocity standards for LAMOST MRS time-domain surveys.

In the context of search and recommendation systems, diversifying multi-aspect search results can reduce redundancy and surface items that would otherwise be overlooked. While numerous prior methods have addressed this, they often fail to explicitly account for class uniformity or evenness, potentially compromising search and recommendation quality. To overcome this limitation, we propose a novel approach that adapts Simpson's Diversity Index from biology, enabling a more effective and efficient quadratic algorithm for diversifying search results. Furthermore, we extend this method to balance diversity across multiple aspects using weighted factors and enhance computational efficiency through a fast approximation algorithm. We validate the feasibility of our approach using the publicly available Kaggle shoes competition dataset. Experimental results indicate that our method surpasses previous state-of-the-art diversification techniques while simultaneously lowering computational complexity.

This paper presents a deep multiple description coding (MDC) framework optimized by minimizing multiple description (MD) compressive loss. Initially, an MD multi-scale-dilated encoder network produces multiple description tensors that are discretized via scalar quantizers; subsequently, these quantized tensors are reconstructed using MD cascaded-ResBlock decoder networks. To significantly minimize the total number of artificial neural network parameters, an auto-encoder architecture integrating these components is designed with a symmetrical parameter-sharing structure. Second, this auto-encoder network, along with a pair of scalar quantizers, undergoes simultaneous learning through an end-to-end self-supervised approach. Third, to address variations in image spatial distribution, each scalar quantizer utilizes an importance-indicator map to generate MD tensors instead of applying direct quantization. Fourth, we propose a multiple description structural similarity distance loss that implicitly regularizes diverse MD generation and explicitly supervises diversified MD decoding alongside the standard MD reconstruction loss. Finally, experimental results on several widely used datasets demonstrate that our MDC framework achieves superior image coding efficiency compared to various state-of-the-art MDC methods.

I provide an overview of models that expand the Standard Model's scalar sector through the inclusion of extra gauge singlets or multiplets. I examine existing constraints on these frameworks, along with potential signatures and discovery opportunities at both present and upcoming colliders.

The widespread presence of computer software has made software vulnerabilities (SVs) a prevalent and critical issue. Numerous machine learning techniques have been developed to address software vulnerability detection (SVD), yet two major challenges remain: i) developing automatic representations to enhance predictive accuracy, and ii) overcoming the scarcity of labeled vulnerability datasets, which typically require extensive manual labeling by experts. This paper introduces a novel end-to-end solution to address these key problems. First, we utilize automatic representation learning combined with deep domain adaptation for SVD. Second, we propose a new cross-domain kernel classifier based on the max-margin principle, designed to significantly improve the transfer of knowledge from labeled projects to unlabeled ones. Experiments on real-world software datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. Specifically, our approach achieves a notable improvement in F1-measure—the most critical metric in SVD—rising from 1.83% to 6.25% compared to the second-best method on the tested datasets. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/vannguyennd/dam2p.
