Deep learning has emerged as a promising technology for precision radiotherapy in prostate cancer, where accurate segmentation facilitates both detection and treatment. Yet, the clinical applicability of trained models is often restricted by varying acquisition protocols and the scarcity of small, publicly available datasets. To address these issues and identify a generalizable solution, this study reviews state-of-the-art deep learning algorithms for MR prostate segmentation, analyzes their strengths and limitations, and proposes an optimized 2D U-Net. We assess performance across four public datasets using the Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC), conducting both within-dataset and cross-dataset evaluations. Our results show the highest DSC of 0.9427 on the Decathlon test set via composite evaluation, while the lowest DSC of 0.5892 occurred during cross-dataset testing on the Prostate X training set and Promise 12 testing set. We discuss existing challenges and offer recommendations for future research. This work provides a fresh perspective on MR prostate segmentation and establishes standardized experimental settings for algorithm evaluation. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/AIEMMU/MRI_Prostate.

For a finite cocommutative Hopf algebra $A$ defined over a commutative regular ring $R$, the lattice of localising tensor ideals within the stable category of Gorenstein projective $A$-modules can be characterized by the lattices associated with the fibres of $A$ over $\text{Spec}(R)$. When specific natural conditions regarding the cohomology of $A$ over $R$ are satisfied, this characterization induces a stratification of the stable category. These findings are applicable to cases where $A$ is the group algebra of a finite group over $R$, as well as when $A$ is the exterior algebra on a finite free $R$-module.
The complete characterization of real or complex polynomial maps between affine spaces that possess a Lipschitz-trivial value is established.

Molecular dynamics simulations were conducted on Poiseuille flow of liquid methane within planar graphite channels spanning diameters from 3 to 135 nm. At this scale, a transition occurs between a regime where wall-induced local ordering governs the entire system and one characterized by larger channel diameters where boundary slip remains present but is more confined. This transition does not impact the validity of Darcy's law for pressure-driven flow through porous media.

Albert Einstein's profound physical insight and genius gave rise to the general theory of relativity, which unifies gravity with the geometry of spacetime. Yet, this theory has generated perspectives that extend far beyond Einstein's original vision, many of which were not revealed until after his death in 1955. These breakthroughs emerged from a new generation of relativists, including Penrose, Hawking, and Geroch, who applied a greater level of mathematical rigor than their predecessors. Significant among these advances was the contribution of Amal Kumar Raychaudhuri (AKR), whose derived equation became a fundamental component of the singularity theorems in general relativity. This article elucidates AKR's contributions using accessible language.

Fractals have recently been central to geophysical and geospatial research. This study investigates the emergent fractal nature of water vapor distributions above Earth's surface, analyzing variations in image resolution (pixel count) and moisture content percentiles. Using computational algorithms, we compute physically significant metrics, including fractal dimension, cluster count, and the size of the largest cluster across different vapor percentiles. We evaluate the applicability of Korcak's law to this system and assess the goodness of fit using the Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic. Our findings indicate that the fractal character of the distribution is exact with respect to image resolution but approximate under certain regimes regarding vapor percentiles.

Multi-label datasets frequently exhibit a mix of highly common and extremely rare labels, creating a class imbalance that poses significant hurdles for developing efficient multi-label classification models. To address this, we introduce UCLSO, a minority class oversampling framework that combines Unsupervised Clustering with Label-Specific data Oversampling. First, clustering identifies key, locally connected regions within the dataset independent of label information. Subsequently, for each specific label, we analyze the distribution of minority instances within these clusters. Synthetic minority points are generated exclusively from minority instances found inside clusters, ensuring that while the underlying cluster sets remain consistent across all labels, the resulting synthetic distributions vary by label. The training data is then augmented with these label-specific synthetic points, and classifiers are trained to independently predict label relevance. Empirical evaluations on twelve multi-label datasets using various algorithms demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms competing approaches.

This study investigates the regularity of entropy solutions for scalar conservation laws featuring discontinuous fluxes. As established by Adimurthi et al. (Comm. Pure Appl. Math., 2011), such equations generally do not yield entropy solutions with BV regularity, even if the initial data is in BV. Consequently, fractional BV spaces with exponents $0 < s \leq 1$ (where $BV = BV^1$) are necessary to accommodate this behavior. A longstanding open problem remains identifying the optimal regularizing effect for these equations with $L^\infty$ initial data. Using control theory, the optimal regularizing effect within fractional BV spaces has been proven for a significant specific case, revealing that the fractional exponent $s$ is bounded above by $1/2$, even when the fluxes are uniformly convex.

Digital platforms have facilitated access to an unprecedented volume of literary data, empowering authors, readers, and researchers to share extensive information regarding books and their creators. However, digital archives remain imbalanced, as writers from non-Western regions are underrepresented, a disparity that perpetuates historical discrimination. To address this issue, we introduce the Under-Represented Writers Knowledge Graph (URW-KG), a resource that aggregates and maps data on authors and works from Wikidata alongside three additional sources: Open Library, Goodreads, and Google Books. Experimental results utilizing KG embeddings demonstrate that the integrated graph enhances the exposure of scholars and users to non-Western literary figures and works compared to using Wikidata alone. Consequently, this advancement paves the way for developing more equitable and effective tools for discovering and exploring authors.

The quantum description of a test field within a quantum cosmological spacetime can be interpreted as a theory of that field propagating on an emergent classical background. In this scenario, the effective metric governing field propagation depends on the quantum fluctuations of the underlying geometry. When backreaction effects are insignificant, massive modes evolve against an anisotropic Bianchi type I background. Consequently, field modes traversing this quantum-gravity-induced spacetime may reveal intriguing phenomenological implications of super-Planckian scales, such as gravitational particle creation. This paper focuses on investigating gravitational particle production for massive modes within such an anisotropic dressed spacetime. By applying an appropriate adiabatic condition to the vacuum state and calculating the energy density of the generated particles, we examine the relevance of this particle production for the universe's dynamics during the Planck era.

The study examines transverse momentum ($j_{\rm T}$)-dependent jet fragmentation functions within proton-proton (p+p) and proton-lead (p+Pb) collisions at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}} = 5.02~{\rm TeV}$, utilizing a multiphase transport model that integrates a basic quark coalescence mechanism with a novel hybrid hadronization approach combining coalescence and fragmentation. When employing this new hadronization scheme, the AMPT model successfully provides a quantitative match to the $j_{\rm T}$-dependent jet fragmentation functions observed by ALICE. Furthermore, the analysis reveals no significant evidence of jet-medium interactions or cold nuclear matter effects influencing these functions in p+Pb collisions. For the proposed hybrid mechanism, the $j_{\rm T}$-dependent jet fragmentation functions are primarily driven by the quark coalescence contribution, which can be separated into narrow and wide components. The root mean square value of the wide component varies with the jet radius $R$ and jet transverse momentum $p_{\rm{T,jet}}$, making it sensitive to the specific hadronization mechanisms and their constituent parts. Consequently, $j_{\rm T}$-dependent jet fragmentation functions are suggested as an effective probe for investigating the non-perturbative hadronization effects of jets in small collision systems.

We explore attractor quantum neural networks (aQNNs) using coherence theory. Our findings demonstrate that: i) aQNNs correspond to quantum channels that do not generate coherence; ii) the network's depth reflects the decohering strength of the associated quantum map; and iii) the attractor linked to any input state is the one that minimizes relative entropy. Additionally, we investigate faulty aQNNs modeled by noisy quantum channels, outline their physical realization, and determine the conditions under which entanglement or coherence can serve as external resources to improve their performance.

Many unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) approaches leverage domain adversarial training to align features and minimize the domain gap, involving a feature extractor trained to deceive a domain discriminator. However, as training progresses and feature distributions become increasingly aligned, the discriminator's ability to distinguish domains diminishes, ultimately hindering its capacity to effectively guide the feature extractor. To address this, we introduce Re-enforceable Adversarial Domain Adaptation (RADA), an efficient optimization strategy that revitalizes the domain discriminator through dynamic domain labeling. Specifically, well-aligned target samples are dynamically relabeled as source samples during training. This relabeling enhances the separability of previously indistinct distributions, resulting in a more potent domain classifier adapted to the new data, which subsequently reinforces feature alignment. Comprehensive experiments across various UDA benchmarks validate the effectiveness and superiority of our proposed RADA method.

In electron magnetohydrodynamics, Hall instability is understood as a shear-Hall instability caused by the combined influence of shear and helicoidal oscillations within the electron current velocity. This framework posits that the essential requirement for such instability is an antiparallel alignment between the background magnetic field and the vorticity of the current velocity. Numerical simulations in plane slab geometry have validated this condition, demonstrating that unstable eigenmodes are confined to regions where the field and vorticity are antiparallel. These findings, which cover tearing-type modes, align closely with asymptotic analytical estimates applicable at large Hall numbers. Furthermore, the study identifies and explains how perfect conductor boundary conditions exert a stabilizing influence. Regarding large Hall numbers, growth rates exhibit a power-law relationship with magnetic field ($B$) and diffusivity ($\eta$) expressed as $\sigma \propto B^\alpha\eta^{1-\alpha}$. While nearly all calculations yield a power index of $\alpha = 3/4$, the tearing-type mode under vacuum boundary conditions is an exception, resulting in $\alpha = 2/3$.

We investigate superconductor diodes, characterized by a critical current magnitude that varies with reversal direction, using a generalized Ginzburg-Landau framework that incorporates higher-order momentum terms in the order parameter. Applying this theory to systems with Rashba spin-orbit coupling yields analytical relationships between nonreciprocal critical currents and system parameters. Additionally, mean-field theory numerical calculations explore wider parameter ranges. These findings provide a comprehensive description and design guidelines for superconductor diodes.

Although the initial 5G New Radio Release-15 has been finalized, its specifications currently address only unicast technologies, leaving point-to-multipoint (PTM) scenarios unexplored. Consequently, this paper begins by reviewing the latest LTE PTM technology, known as eMBMS, and evaluates its physical layer performance using link-level simulations. Building on these results, we examine potential enhancements for the two existing eMBMS approaches: MBSFN and SC-PTM. The study specifically concentrates on integrating 5G candidate technologies, such as multi-antenna systems and millimeter-wave communications, into current eMBMS frameworks to assess their viability for meeting next-generation PTM transmission demands.

Symbol-level precoding (SLP) has demonstrated its efficacy in mitigating interference within multiuser downlink systems and boosting received signal strength. This study introduces an unsupervised learning approach for SLP tailored to quantized deep neural networks (DNNs). Instead of relying on supervised training, the proposed method unfolds a power minimization SLP formulation designed for imperfect channel conditions, utilizing the interior point method (IPM) with a proximal 'log' barrier function. To compress DNN weights, both binary and ternary quantization schemes are employed. Simulation results indicate substantial memory reductions compared to existing full-precision SLP-DNNs, achieving approximately 21x and 13x model compression for binary DNN-based SLP (RSLP-BDNet) and ternary DNN-based SLP (RSLP-TDNets), respectively.

The emergence of spatiotemporal patterning in multicellular tissues, ranging from somitogenesis to cartilage condensation, is believed to be driven by the interplay between cellular contractility and active phase separation within cell-matrix composites. To analyze these mechanisms, we present a generalized theory that extends the classical Cahn--Hilliard-Larch{\'e} model for phase separation in passive viscoelastic solids by incorporating active cellular contractility. Our investigation into the dynamics of this modified model demonstrates that activity can destabilize a homogeneous mixture through either a pitchfork or Hopf bifurcation, leading to stable phase separation and/or traveling waves. Numerical simulations of the complete equations enable us to trace the evolution of self-organized patterns in periodic and mechanically constrained domains across various geometries. Collectively, this study highlights the necessity of combining cellular activity with mechanical phase separation to comprehend patterning in soft, active biosolids, offering potential explanations for prior experimental observations of cartilage condensation in both in-vivo and in-vitro contexts.

This study examines multiple teleportation processes using nonmaximally entangled channels, calculating and comparing the efficiencies of the separate multiple teleportation protocol (SMTP) and the global multiple teleportation protocol (GMTP). Our results demonstrate that GMTP achieves higher efficiency than SMTP.

The discrepancy between early- and late-Universe measurements of the Hubble constant presents a major challenge to contemporary cosmology. Researchers have explored modifications to the standard flat, homogeneous, and isotropic $\Lambda$CDM framework, which includes dark energy, cold baryonic matter, and dark matter. These alternatives rely on general relativity and meet two criteria: first, the Hubble constant derived from the recombination-era Hubble parameter using flat $\Lambda$CDM formulas must match 92% of the value inferred from low-redshift observations; second, deviations from the $\Lambda$CDM model must not produce effects that conflict with astronomical data or derived estimates. The analysis indicates limited viable options: either dark matter must possess negative pressure ($-\rho_{dm}c^2 \ll p_{dm} < 0$), exerting only a weak influence on cosmic evolution and observed dark matter phenomena, or a mechanism for generating new matter—such as dark energy decay—must be accepted.

This study examines a coupled system of partial differential equations (PDEs) involving multilayered (thick layer) waves, thin-layer waves, and heat transfer within a fluid. These models are frequently employed in literature to simulate blood transport in mammalian vascular networks, specifically modeling boundary interface deformations using a two-dimensional elastic equation. The research investigates how fluid dissipation beneath the interface stabilizes both the thick and thin structural components, with all three PDE components evolving on their distinct geometries. Our primary contribution is establishing uniform decay rates for classical solutions of this multilayered PDE framework. To achieve these estimates, we first derive necessary a priori inequalities for specific static multilayered PDE models, which then facilitate the application of a standard resolvent criterion to determine rational decay.

Although radiative models currently interpret experimental phenomena like the mass hierarchy effect, their validity hinges on the often-overlooked contribution of collisional energy loss. To date, no direct link between collisional energy loss and heavy quark mass has been established, nor is there a specific observable to quantify this phenomenon. However, forthcoming high-precision heavy flavor data from RHIC and LHC's high-luminosity runs offer a unique chance to investigate quark-gluon plasma interaction mechanisms using high-pT heavy flavor data. Leveraging a newly developed DREENA framework grounded in our dynamical energy loss formalism, this study examines the mass hierarchy in heavy flavor suppression by achieving three goals: i) deriving an analytical relationship connecting collisional suppression/energy loss to heavy quark mass; ii) introducing a novel observable exclusively sensitive to collisional energy loss for future experimental verification; and iii) analytically and numerically extracting the mass hierarchy within collisional energy losses using this new observable.

The Poisson-Nernst-Planck-Bikermann (PNPB) framework accounts for steric and correlation effects in ionic solutions—phenomena overlooked by point-charge-based Poisson-Nernst-Planck and Poisson-Boltzmann theories—by modeling ions and water molecules as distinct species with varying sizes, valences, and interstitial voids. Within this model, the electric potential satisfies the fourth-order Poisson-Bikermann (4PBik) equation rather than the standard Poisson equation to capture correlation effects. Additionally, steric effects are quantified through Fermi-like equilibrium distributions and incorporated into the fluxes for both ions and water via a steric potential. This study performs a nondimensionalization to examine the self-adjointness and kernel of the 4PBik operator's fourth-order term, while also demonstrating the positivity of the void volume function and the convexity of the free energy. These properties establish the well-posedness of the PNPB model at equilibrium. Leveraging the model's energy-dissipating structure, a finite volume scheme is developed that maintains this property at the semi-discrete level. Finally, numerical simulations illustrate how the steric effect influences the steady state in relation to various parameters.

Electrophoretic (EP) mobility reversal is a well-documented phenomenon for highly charged macromolecules in multivalent salt environments. This intriguing effect occurs, for instance, when a charged polymer like DNA adsorbs an excess of counterions, causing the counterion-dressed surface charge to flip signs and thereby reversing the polymer's drift under an external electric field. To analyze this counterintuitive process, which electrostatic mean-field theories fail to describe, we apply a previously established strong-coupling-dressed Poisson-Boltzmann formalism to the cylindrical geometry of polyelectrolyte-salt systems. Using this framework, we derive an analytical expression for polymer mobility that accounts for charge correlations. Qualitatively consistent with experimental polymer transport data, this mobility formula indicates that increasing monovalent salt concentration, reducing the valency of multivalent counterions, and raising the background solvent's dielectric permittivity all diminish charge correlations and elevate the multivalent bulk counterion concentration needed for EP mobility reversal. These findings are supported by coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations, which demonstrate how multivalent counterions trigger mobility inversion at low concentrations but suppress this inversion at high concentrations. This re-entrant behavior, previously noted in the aggregation of like-charged polymer solutions, warrants verification through polymer transport experiments.

This paper introduces a novel framework for designing and analyzing strategyproof mechanisms, inspired by the growing field of "learning-augmented algorithms." While traditional computer science focuses on worst-case performance, this emerging approach designs algorithms enhanced by machine-learned predictions of the optimal outcome. These algorithms use such predictions to guide decisions, aiming for strong consistency guarantees when predictions are accurate while retaining robust, near-optimal performance even when they are inaccurate. Although previous research has been confined to algorithms, we argue that mechanism design offers a promising new avenue for this framework.

We begin by developing strategyproof mechanisms augmented with predictions about agents' private information. To demonstrate the value of this method, we re-examine the classic facility location problem involving strategic agents in a two-dimensional Euclidean space, considering both egalitarian and utilitarian social cost functions. We propose new mechanisms that utilize predictions to achieve an optimal balance between consistency and robustness, offering designers a range of options based on their confidence in prediction accuracy. Additionally, we establish parameterized approximation results relative to prediction error, proving that our mechanisms maintain high performance even when predictions are imperfect.

Jointed assemblies with frictional nonlinearities display stiffness and dissipation that vary with amplitude. To enable predictive and design-oriented numerical simulations, macro-scale High Fidelity Models (HFMs) of contact interfaces are necessary, yet their substantial computational expense hinders practical application. Consequently, we introduce a model-driven approach to build hyper-reduced order models for these systems. Centering on steady-state analysis, we employ the Multi-Harmonic Balance Method (MHBM) to express equations of motion in the frequency domain, constructing the reduction basis by solving vibration problems under hypothetical interface conditions. A Galerkin projection is then applied to reduce the model's order. However, the need for fine interface discretization limits the potential for significant speedups. To overcome this bottleneck, we implement an adapted Energy Conserving Weighting and Sampling (ECSW) technique for Hyper Reduction (HR), enabling substantial performance gains even on arbitrarily fine meshes. This capability is crucial because analysts often face a difficult trade-off between accuracy and computational cost when selecting mesh sizes, a challenge especially acute for such problems. To evaluate accuracy without relying on the high-fidelity solution, we propose an error indicator featuring thresholds validated through our analyses. Ultimately, the method's accuracy and efficiency are validated through two case studies.

We examine the octonionic eigenvalue problem through a geometric lens, specifically investigating the tautological sheaf on the Ogievetski\^i-Dray-Manogue sextic associated with this problem. We subsequently introduce and analyze a twisted variant of the octonionic eigenvalue problem, which gives rise to a new sextic and its corresponding tautological sheaf. This twisted formulation exhibits significantly greater symmetry than the original, as demonstrated by our final result: the automorphism group of the twisted problem, although not isomorphic to $\mathrm{E}_6$, acts prehomogeneously on the exceptional Jordan algebra $\mathrm{J}_{3}(\mathbb{O})$. This stands in stark contrast to the classical octonionic eigenvalue problem, where the generic orbit under the action of its automorphism group has a codimension of at least $6$ within $\mathrm{J}_{3}(\mathbb{O})$.

First suggested in 1937, the Collatz conjecture has captured the attention of mathematicians and computer scientists because of its deceptively simple premise but notoriously difficult proof. This paper introduces new theorems, corollaries, and algorithms that investigate the connections among natural numbers, their maximum values, and the conjecture. These contributions mainly examine how many Collatz steps are required for a specific integer to reach 1 or a smaller number, as well as the relationship between an initial number and its peak value.

We demonstrate that viable electroweak baryogenesis can occur without a first-order phase transition, provided that the plasma is heated unevenly by non-gravitational structure formation within certain particle species. Yukawa interactions facilitate relatively long-range attractive forces in the early Universe, triggering an instability that fosters structural growth in some species even during the radiation-dominated era. At temperatures beneath the electroweak scale, the collapse and annihilation of halos generate fireballs that heat the plasma; these fireballs expand to establish the out-of-equilibrium, high-temperature conditions necessary for baryon asymmetry generation. The plasma temperature during baryogenesis may be as low as 10 MeV, aligning with both standard and low-reheat cosmological models.

We examine two extensions of the Standard Model that introduce new particles, yielding extra scalar states and viable dark matter candidates. We also provide a brief overview of existing constraints and discuss production cross-sections at current and upcoming collider experiments.

Complex systems conceal information within their patterns, necessitating exploration. This study introduces a simplified model of cytokine and T-cell interactions, analyzed through a stochastic framework by formulating and solving the system's Master equation. The resulting probability distribution function reveals a classical Poisson pattern in the large population limit ($M,Z \rightarrow \text{large}$), suggesting the system attracts numerous small-scale random cytokine processes toward its basin of attraction by filtering out nonrandom ones. Additionally, as the mean $\langle Z\rangle$ increases, the pattern transitions to a classical Normal distribution, where uncorrelated small-scale fluctuations are suppressed, yielding a regular yet memoryless spatiotemporal aggregation. Finally, Fano factor-based noise estimation confirms that cytokine dynamics are driven by noise, pushing the system far from equilibrium.

Small covers derived from 3-dimensional simple polytopes constitute a fascinating category of 3-manifolds. For broad classes of 3-manifolds, especially orientable Haken manifolds—which encompass orientable small covers—the fundamental group serves as a robust invariant. Leveraging a Morse-theoretic method, we outline a procedure to construct an explicit, balanced presentation of the fundamental group for closed, orientable 3-dimensional simple covers with the fewest possible generators. Additionally, this presentation identifies the minimal Heegaard splitting.

This study examines the Cauchy problem associated with the inhomogeneous Helmholtz equation featuring a non-uniform refractive index. To address the ill-posed nature of this problem, the variational form of mollification is employed. The approach is demonstrated to be consistent, and the resulting numerical simulations yield encouraging results.

This study reports measurements of the branching fraction ratios for the decays $B_{s}^{0} \to D_{s}^{\mp} K^{\pm}$ and $B^{0} \to D_{s}^{-} K^{+}$, normalized to the decays $B_{s}^{0} \to D_{s}^{-} \pi^{+}$ and $B^{0} \to D^{-} \pi^{+}$, respectively. The analysis utilizes data from proton-proton collisions with an integrated luminosity of 3.0 fb$^{-1}$. The determined ratios are $\dfrac{\mathcal{B}(B_{s}^{0} \to D_{s}^{\mp} K^{\pm})}{\mathcal{B}(B_{s}^{0} \to D_{s}^{-} \pi^{+})} = 0.0752 \pm 0.0015 \pm 0.0019$ and $\dfrac{\mathcal{B}(B^{0} \to D_{s}^{-} K^{+})}{\mathcal{B}(B^{0} \to D^{-} \pi^{+})} = 0.0129 \pm 0.0005 \pm 0.0008$, where the errors represent statistical and systematic uncertainties, respectively.

Quantum technologies are poised to surpass current classical devices, making it essential to identify inherently non-classical features to achieve superior performance. This thesis investigates two such behaviors: quantum contextuality and Wigner negativity. Contextuality, which generalizes nonlocality, has primarily been examined in discrete-variable settings where it is both necessary and sufficient for certain quantum advantages. Conversely, Wigner negativity is a distinct non-classical property of continuous-variable quantum states arising from phase-space formulations, which are promising for quantum computation. While negativity is a known necessary resource for speedups in continuous variables, the role of contextuality in these scenarios remains poorly understood.

This work establishes a robust framework for analyzing contextuality in continuous variables, utilizing infinite-dimensional optimization theory to quantify it. We demonstrate that Wigner negativity is equivalent to contextuality under Pauli measurements in continuous-variable systems, providing an analogue to a celebrated result by Howard et al. Furthermore, we develop experimentally feasible witnesses for the Wigner negativity of single-mode and multimode states based on their fidelity with Fock states, again leveraging infinite-dimensional optimization techniques. Finally, we extend existing discrete-variable findings connecting contextuality and advantage into the new domain of information retrieval.

Validating quantum devices from unidentified sources is a fundamental prerequisite before employing them for information processing. This work introduces a certification protocol for a specific class of $d$-outcome quantum measurements (where $d$ is arbitrary) within a framework involving sequential preparation and two measurements. We define a set of temporal inequalities, varying with different $d$, based on correlation functions of consecutive outcomes that quantum devices fail to satisfy. By leveraging violations of these inequalities, we certify particular $d$-outcome measurements under minimal, experimentally feasible assumptions. This certification method requires neither entanglement nor prior knowledge of the system's dimension. Additionally, we demonstrate the protocol's resilience against practical imperfections. Finally, as an extension, we propose a scheme for securely certifying genuine quantum randomness.

Black holes are traditionally viewed as unique regarding their temporal evolution and information processing, but recent proposals suggest these traits are actually characteristic of a broader class of objects known as saturons—entities that reach the maximum entropy allowed by unitarity. This paper confirms that link using a renormalizable $SU(N)$ invariant framework. We demonstrate that the theory's spectrum includes a series of bubbles, which are bound states composed of $SU(N)$ Goldstones. Remarkably, even without gravity, a saturated bound state mirrors a black hole: its entropy adheres to the Bekenstein-Hawking formula; semi-classically, the bubble evaporates thermally at a rate inversely proportional to its radius; and the time required for information retrieval matches Page's time. This alignment is mediated by a trans-theoretic entity called the Poincaré Goldstone. The established correspondence between black holes and saturons holds significant implications for black hole physics, spanning both fundamental theory and observational studies.

It is established that the boundary charge accumulating at the edge of a one-dimensional single-channel insulator exhibits a universal property: shifting the lattice by one site toward the edge changes this charge by the sum of the average bulk electronic density and a topologically invariant term limited to values of 0 or -1 [Phys. Rev. B 101, 165304 (2020)]. This quantized contribution, linked to particle-hole duality, guarantees charge conservation and resolves the mod(1) ambiguity inherent in the Modern Theory of Polarization. In this study, we extend these single-channel findings to multichannel systems using boundary Green's functions. We demonstrate that the topological invariant governing the change in boundary charge upon a lattice shift in multichannel models can be represented as a winding number of specific combinations of bulk Green's function components with respect to complex frequency, as they encircle the energy axis segment corresponding to the occupied spectrum. We find that this winding number is constrained to values between $-N_c$ and $0$, where $N_c$ denotes the number of channels (orbitals) per site. Additionally, we examine translationally invariant one-dimensional multichannel models containing an impurity, introducing topological indices that correspond to the quantized charge accumulating around this defect. These invariants are also expressed via winding numbers of bulk Green's function combinations. Through this framework, we offer a rigorous mathematical proof of the nearsightedness principle, originally formulated by W. Kohn [Phys. Rev. Lett. 76, 3168 (1996)], for noninteracting multichannel lattice models.

We have determined the dynamic critical exponent $z$ for both two-dimensional and three-dimensional Ising universality classes using a minimally subtracted five-loop $\varepsilon$-expansion derived for the one-component model A. This achievement becomes feasible through the effective application of the Sector Decomposition technique to critical dynamics problems. By combining the resulting fifth-order perturbative calculation with sophisticated resummation methods for asymptotic series, we derived precise numerical estimates for $z$: $\boldsymbol{2.14(2)}$ for the 2D case and $\boldsymbol{2.0235(8)}$ for the 3D case. These findings align well with recent outcomes from alternative methodologies.

This study addresses the question posed by Vidaux and Videla regarding the distribution of Northcott numbers within the context of the Weil height, and it resolves the same issue for weighted Weil heights. These heights encompass both the absolute and relative Weil heights as special cases. Furthermore, our findings improve upon the results established by Pazuki, Technau, and Widmer.

This work extends the resistivity calculations for Kondo lattice systems presented in \cite{konav}, shifting the focus from $3d$ to $2d$ frameworks. By computing the memory function for a $2d$ system, I observe distinct results compared to the $3d$ case. Specifically, in the low-temperature regime ($k_{B}T\ll \mu_d$), the $2d$ resistivity follows a power law proportional to $1/T$, whereas the $3d$ system exhibits the same $1/T$ dependence. Conversely, in the high-temperature regime ($k_{B}T\gg\mu_d$), the $2d$ resistivity increases linearly with temperature, differing from the $3d$ behavior which scales as $T^{3/2}$.

This paper demonstrates that the wavelength shift in a non-pumped light-emitting diode (LED) varies practically linearly with temperature, a new implication derived from Varshni's widely recognized empirical formula. This equation describes bandgap changes in most semiconductors across a range from 0 K to their high-temperature limits, relying on specific fitting parameters. Consequently, we propose an external thermal mechanism capable of tuning and stabilizing the wavelength of LEDs operating under constant current bias. We validate this approach using published AlN data, showing that the fitting parameters are straightforward. Additionally, we introduce a novel technique for characterizing semiconductors and present experimental results from measurements on various commercial LEDs.

We investigate and define windings along Brownian trajectories within the octonionic Euclidean, projective, and hyperbolic spaces, which correspond to 8-dimensional Riemannian model spaces. Specifically, we demonstrate that the asymptotic distributions of these windings follow a Gaussian pattern in flat and spherical geometries, whereas hyperbolic winding displays distinct long-term behavior.

While the decidability and complexity of reachability and model-checking for flat counter machines are well-understood, knowledge regarding flat (lossy) FIFO machines remains limited to specific scenarios, such as single loops or bounded expressions. This paper demonstrates that numerous verification challenges—including reachability, non-termination, and unboundedness—are NP-complete for flat FIFO machines by establishing reductions between properties and mapping SAT to a subset of these problems, thereby extending similar findings for flat counter machines. Furthermore, we establish that reachability is NP-complete for both flat lossy and flat front-lossy FIFO machines. We also present a trace-flattable system of counter machines communicating via rendez-vous that is bisimilar to any given flat FIFO machine, enabling model-checking of the original system. These findings provide the theoretical groundwork and pave the way for developing verification tools for general FIFO machines by analyzing their flat sub-machines.

Assessing normal brain development is a critical aspect of pediatric neuroradiology and neurology. While infant brain MRI reveals specific developmental patterns extending beyond myelination, relying on myelination, morphology, and size to gauge age-appropriate maturity demands years of specialized experience. In the absence of standardized criteria, visually estimating structural maturity in children under three remains plagued by significant inter- and intra-observer variability. An objective method for estimating developmental age could enable physicians to detect neurodevelopmental disorders earlier and with greater reliability; however, acquiring such data is challenging, and the "gold standard" is limited by the inherent subjectivity of human assessment. Consequently, this study investigates the feasibility of addressing this task and evaluates various approaches, including two- and three-dimensional convolutional neural networks (CNNs) trained on fused T1-weighted, T2-weighted, and proton density (PD) sequences from 84 subjects across four age groups ranging from birth to three years. The top-performing method achieved an accuracy of 0.90 [95% CI: 0.86–0.94] using a 2D CNN on a central axial thick slab. We compare this result with 3D networks and assess performance when using only T1-weighted sequences. Ultimately, despite the theoretical advantages of 3D CNNs, they prove inferior to simpler architectures in data-limited scenarios. The source code is available at https://github.com/shabanian2018/Age_MRI-Classification.

This paper investigates monomial operators on $L^2[0,1]$, defined as bounded linear operators that transform every monomial $x^n$ into a scalar multiple of $x^{p_n}$ for some sequence $p_n$. We demonstrate that all such operators are unitarily equivalent to weighted composition operators acting on a Hardy space. Furthermore, we identify the admissible sequences $p_n$ and, specifically when $p_n$ corresponds to a fixed translation of $n$, establish a criterion for the boundedness of the operator.

Let $(M,g)$ be a closed Riemannian manifold and $\eta$ a closed real 1-form. We define $d_z$, $\delta_z$, and $\Delta_z$ as Witten-type perturbations of the de~Rham derivative, coderivative, and Laplacian, respectively, parameterized by $z \in \mathbb C$. The associated zeta function $\zeta(s,z)$ is given by $\operatorname{Tr}^s({\eta\wedge}\,\delta_z\Delta_z^{-s})$ for sufficiently large $\Re s$. For specific classes of Morse forms $\eta$, we demonstrate that $\zeta(s,z)$ is smooth at $s=1$ when $|\Re z|$ is large. Furthermore, the zeta invariant $\zeta(1,z)$ converges uniformly in $\Im z$ to a real value $\mathbf z$ as $\Re z \to +\infty$. We characterize $\mathbf z$ using instantons of an auxiliary Smale gradient-like vector field $X$ and the Mathai-Quillen current on $TM$ determined by $g$. Every real cohomology class admits a representative $\eta$ meeting these criteria. When $n$ is even, we can prescribe any real value for $\mathbf z$ by adjusting $g$, $\eta$, and $X$, and the same limit holds as $\Re z \to -\infty$. This framework allows for the definition and description of certain tempered distributions generated by $g$ and $\eta$. These distributions correspond to contributions from compact leaves preserved by the flow within a trace formula for simple foliated flows on closed foliated manifolds, providing a solution to a problem posed by C.~Deninger.

A central challenge in Geometric Tomography involves deducing the properties of a specific convex body based on known attributes of its sections or projections. Numerous significant results exist that characterize spheres and ellipsoids through these sectional or projected properties. Additionally, ellipsoids can be characterized via support cones; however, existing characterizations typically focus on a single convex body, analyzing its own sections, projections, or cones. This article presents new findings that characterize Euclidean balls and ellipsoids when sections or projections are derived from a pair of nested convex bodies, specifically two bodies $K$ and $L$ where $L$ lies strictly within the interior of $K$. By establishing specific relationships between the corresponding sections or projections, we derive apparently novel characterizations of the ball or ellipsoid. Furthermore, we examine support cone properties and point source shadow boundaries, assuming the apexes are located on the boundary of $K$.

This study provides perturbative results regarding the renormalization of the supercurrent operator, $S_\mu$, within ${\cal N} =1$ Supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory. At the quantum level, $S_\mu$ mixes with both gauge invariant and noninvariant operators sharing identical global transformation properties; specifically, there are 13 linearly independent operators of the same or lower dimension involved in this mixing. Using lattice perturbation theory, we calculate the first two rows of the mixing matrix, which correspond to the renormalization of $S_\mu$ and the gauge invariant operator $T_\mu$. To derive these mixing coefficients in the ${\overline{\rm MS}}$ scheme at one-loop order, we evaluate the necessary two-point and three-point Green's functions for $S_\mu$ and $T_\mu$ using two regularization methods: dimensional and lattice. In our lattice calculations, we utilize the plaquette gluonic action and the fermionic Wilson action with clover improvement for the gluinos.

Creative Problem Solving (CPS) represents a specialized domain within Artificial Intelligence (AI) dedicated to addressing off-nominal or anomalous challenges in autonomous systems. Although significant progress has been made in planning and learning, the ability to resolve novel issues or adapt prior knowledge to new contexts—particularly when environments shift unpredictably after deployment—continues to hinder the safe and effective integration of intelligent systems. As systems become increasingly autonomous, there is a growing imperative for AI agents to navigate environmental uncertainty through creative capabilities. To advance research in CPS, we introduce a formal definition and framework to classify existing AI methodologies in this area. This framework outlines four core components of a CPS problem: 1) problem formulation, 2) knowledge representation, 3) knowledge manipulation techniques, and 4) evaluation methods. The survey concludes by highlighting open research questions and proposing directions for future inquiry.

We develop invariants for both bosonic and spinning tensionless (null) strings within backgrounds characterized by mixed-type Killing tensors or Killing-Yano tensors. This approach is enabled by the strong connection between these strings and point particles. The method is applied to both Minkowski and Kerr-Newman spacetimes.

A primary objective in observing active galactic nuclei via radio and gamma-ray instruments is to analyze their temporal variability to uncover the physical mechanisms driving their radiation. This presentation outlines algorithms for essential time-series analysis techniques—including correlation functions, Fourier and wavelet amplitude and phase spectra, structure functions, and time-frequency distributions—designed to handle arbitrary data modes and sampling schemes. These methods facilitate the cross-analysis of radio measurements with time-tagged gamma-ray photon streams. Central to this approach is the Bayesian block scheme, which serves both to identify local structures within light curves and to preprocess raw data for subsequent analysis algorithms. The aim of this talk is to encourage discussion regarding these methodologies during the workshop.

The integration of the LoRa communication protocol into next-generation transceivers offers significant advantages for search and rescue (SaR) operations, particularly due to their ability to function in rugged environments over extensive areas with minimal power usage. Equipping helmets with LoRa radios and installing transceivers in unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) can expedite the localization of potentially unconscious targets. This paper theoretically and experimentally assesses the achievable communication ranges for these links within a basic SaR scenario on flat terrain, accounting for different positions of the helmet wearer (standing or lying). Simulations and experimental tests revealed that for a standing subject, ground-bounce multi-path effects cause significant fluctuations in received power relative to the transmitter-receiver distance; however, reducing the UAV altitude can confine these fluctuations within 100 meters of the target. Conversely, in the more critical lying position, the received power profile is monotonic and largely unaffected by posture. Across all scenarios, the signal from the body-worn transceiver can be utilized for localization based on signal strength, and it is theoretically detectable by the UAV radio up to a distance of 5 kilometers on flat ground.

We introduce a novel cyclic proof system designed for automated equational reasoning concerning the behavior of pure functional programs. Central to this system is the integration of contextual substitution as a cut rule, which mediates between cyclic proofs and equational reasoning. We demonstrate that, despite its simplicity, this framework subsumes multiple existing methods for implicit induction, including "inductionless induction," "rewriting induction," and "proof by consistency." By constraining the structure of traces, we establish that global correctness can be verified incrementally by leveraging the well-known size-change principle, thereby enabling an efficient proof search implementation. Our CycleQ tool, available as a GHC plugin, yields promising results when applied to various standard benchmarks.

Video super-resolution (VSR) methods typically involve more intricate architectures than their image-based counterparts due to the necessity of leveraging the temporal dimension. This study aims to simplify these complex designs by re-evaluating four fundamental functionalities: Propagation, Alignment, Aggregation, and Upsampling. By integrating existing components with minimal modifications, we introduce BasicVSR, a streamlined framework that delivers significant enhancements in both restoration quality and processing speed compared to many state-of-the-art algorithms. We provide a systematic analysis to elucidate the source of these gains and identify potential pitfalls. Furthermore, we demonstrate the extensibility of BasicVSR through an information-refill mechanism and a coupled propagation scheme designed to improve information aggregation. Both BasicVSR and its extension, IconVSR, establish robust baselines for future VSR research.

Connecting electronics to optical fiber networks is essential for transmitting both classical and quantum information over long distances. While piezo-optomechanical transducers offer a pathway for this by using gigahertz acoustic vibrations to convert microwave photons into optical photons through combined optomechanical and piezoelectric effects, their efficiency remains elusive due to difficulties in hybrid material integration and losses from piezoelectric components in the quantum regime. In this work, we present an alternative method that generates 5-GHz phonons within a standard silicon-on-insulator platform. Our setup uses electrostatic forces in a charge-biased narrow-gap capacitor to resonantly drive a phononic crystal oscillator with microwave photons. These mechanical vibrations are then routed via a phonon waveguide to an optomechanical cavity, where they are converted into optical photons at the sideband of a pump laser. Operating under room temperature and atmospheric conditions, we achieved a microwave-to-optical photon conversion efficiency of $1.8 \times 10^{-7}$ within a 3.3 MHz bandwidth and demonstrated effective phase modulation with a half-wave voltage of $V_\pi = 750$ mV. These findings represent a significant step toward quantum transduction using integrated crystalline silicon devices, which offer prospects for efficient high-bandwidth operation and compatibility with superconducting qubits. Furthermore, because this approach does not rely on piezoelectricity or other intrinsic nonlinearities, it is adaptable to various materials, enabling potential applications extending beyond quantum technologies.

This paper investigates the application of the Euler characteristic within multiparameter topological data analysis. As a classical and well-established topological invariant, the Euler characteristic has been utilized in various fields, including the study of random fields. The primary objective is to demonstrate how this invariant can be extended to higher-dimensional parameter spaces. Although the analysis of such spaces using more complex invariants like homology remains a vigorous area of research, the Euler characteristic offers significant advantages in terms of theoretical tractability and computational efficiency, serving as a vital intermediate stage in multi-parameter topological data analysis. The utility of these techniques is validated through both synthetic examples and a real-world case study involving the detection of diabetic retinopathy in retinal imagery.

Rhodium-based compounds provide an ideal environment for investigating novel materials exhibiting superconductivity and other remarkable electronic correlation phenomena. We successfully synthesized a new ternary rhodium-antimonide, La$_2$Rh$_{3+\delta}$Sb$_4$ ($\delta\approx 1/8$), using a Bi-flux technique. This material adopts an orthorhombic structure analogous to Pr$_2$Ir$_3$Sb$_4$, belonging to the space group $Pnma$ (No. 62). Its crystal lattice consists of stacked two-dimensional networks of RhSb$_4$ and RhSb$_5$ polyhedra along the $\mathbf{b}$ axis, with lanthanum atoms occupying the voids within these frameworks. Band structure computations identify it as a multi-band metal featuring a van-Hove singularity near the Fermi level, where the density of states is predominantly derived from Rh-4$d$ and Sb-5$p$ orbitals. The calculations further indicate that excess rhodium atoms function as charge dopants. Superconductivity was detected in this sample with an onset transition temperature of approximately 0.8 K. Measurements of magnetic susceptibility and specific heat at ultra-low temperatures characterize it as an s-wave type-II superconductor. These findings suggest that the broader $Ln_2$$Tm_{3+\delta}$Sb$_4$ family ($Ln$=Rare earth, $Tm$=Rh, Ir, etc.) could serve as a promising source for discovering new materials capable of hosting superconductors, quantum magnetism, and other correlated electronic effects.

A regular continuant $K$ represents the denominator of a terminating regular continued fraction, viewed as a function of its partial quotients. We define $K$ on the set of all finite words over the alphabet $1<2<3<\dots$, mapping to positive integers. For a word $w=w_1\cdots w_n$ where $w_i\in\mathbb{N}$, the multiplicity $\mu(w)$ is the count of distinct permutations within the Abelian class $\mathcal{X}(w)$ that yield the value $K(w)$. We establish the existence of infinitely many distinct lacunary alphabets of the form $\{b_1<\dots <b_t<l+1<l+2<\dots <s\}$, with natural number parameters $b_j, t, l, s$ and $s$ sufficiently large, for which $\mu$ attains arbitrarily large values on words formed from these alphabets. The proof methodology partially utilizes a combinatorial characterization of the specific word $w_{max}$ in the class $\mathcal{X}(w)$ at which $K$ reaches its maximum.

This study introduces MDD-CF, a cell-free massive MIMO architecture utilizing multicarrier-division duplexing. This scheme allows for the simultaneous transmission of downlink data and uplink data or pilots on orthogonal subcarriers within distributed CF systems. To evaluate MDD-CF's benefits, we first analyze spectral efficiency (SE) over a single coherence interval (CT), focusing on access point selection, power control, and subcarrier allocation. Addressing the NP-hard nature of the resulting mixed-integer non-convex optimization, we exploit variable interdependencies to convert the problem into a continuous-integer convex-concave form. A quadratic transform-assisted iterative algorithm is then developed to maximize SE. The analysis is subsequently expanded to a radio frame comprising multiple CT intervals, where a novel two-phase CT (TPCT) scheme is introduced to enhance SE and ensure consistent data transmission across rapidly varying channels. To support this, a two-step iterative algorithm is proposed that links the two TPCT phases via an iteration factor. Simulation outcomes indicate that MDD-CF significantly surpasses in-band full duplex (IBFD)-CF in interference management and demonstrates greater robustness and superior SE performance compared to time-division duplex (TDD)-CF in high-mobility environments.

This study aims to measure the non-normality of the most amplified resolvent modes and forecast their properties using the features of the base or mean velocity profile. A 2-by-2 linear Navier-Stokes (LNS) operator model demonstrates how mean shear-induced non-normality redistributes perturbation energy across various velocity components in both forcing and response modes. We propose using the reciprocal of their inner product—as unity in purely normal mechanisms—as a metric for quantifying non-normality. In flows with downstream spatial variation, mean flow advection decouples the spatial support of forcing and response modes, thereby affecting the inner product. The efficacy of mean stability analysis relies on the normality of amplification; if amplification is normal, the dyadic representation of the resolvent operator shows that adjoint and forward stability modes are proportional to the corresponding forcing and response modes. Conversely, when amplification is non-normal, resolvent analysis becomes essential to explain the emergence of observed flow structures, which are characterized using eigenspectra and pseudospectra. Two test cases are examined: low Reynolds number cylinder flow and turbulent channel flow. The cylinder flow case primarily involves normal mechanisms, where the quantified non-normality via the inverse inner product of the leading modes aligns well with the product of the resolvent norm and the distance from the imaginary axis to the least stable eigenvalue. In the turbulent channel flow, structures arise from both normal and non-normal mechanisms; while mean shear is utilized most effectively by stationary disturbances, pseudospectral bounds demonstrate how non-normality drives the amplification of disturbances at specific spatial wavenumbers and temporal frequencies associated with recognized turbulent structures.

Identifying large or heavy matchings in graphs constitutes a pervasive combinatorial optimization challenge. This paper presents the first non-trivial implementations for approximating the dynamic weighted matching problem. Our primary algorithm integrates random walks or paths with dynamic programming. A second algorithm, previously proposed by Stubbs and Williams but lacking an implementation, leverages dynamic unweighted matching algorithms as subroutines within a multilevel framework; this approach enables us to treat prior work on dynamic unweighted matching as a black box to construct a fully-dynamic weighted matching solution. We empirically evaluated both algorithms across a broad range of dynamic instances against optimal weighted matchings. Our results indicate that the random walk algorithm generally outperforms the Stubbs/Williams method in terms of the time-quality tradeoff, with its outcomes frequently remaining close to the optimum.

This work addresses Far-Field 3D Detection (Far3Det), which targets objects located beyond a specific range, such as greater than 50 meters. This capability is critical for autonomous vehicles (AVs) traveling at highway speeds, as detecting distant obstacles is essential for maintaining adequate braking distances. However, existing AV benchmarks like nuScenes largely overlook this challenge by restricting performance evaluation to distances within 50 meters. This limitation stems partly from the difficulty of generating far-field 3D annotations, especially for LiDAR sensors, which often yield sparse point returns for distant objects; our analysis reveals that nearly 50% of objects beyond 50 meters have zero LiDAR points. Additionally, current 3D detection metrics apply uniform tolerance thresholds to both near and far objects, a "one-size-fits-all" approach that contradicts the varying tolerances inherent in human vision and stereo disparity. These factors result in an incomplete assessment of Far3Det. For instance, despite the conventional belief that high-resolution RGB sensors are crucial for detecting distant objects, LiDAR-based methods currently outperform RGB counterparts on standard benchmark leaderboards. As an initial step toward a dedicated Far3Det benchmark, we identified well-annotated scenes within the nuScenes dataset to create a robust far-field validation set. We also introduced a new evaluation protocol and tested various 3D detection methods specifically for this task. Our findings strongly validate the established wisdom that high-resolution RGB significantly enhances far-field 3D detection. Furthermore, we propose a simple yet effective fusion method combining RGB and LiDAR detections via non-maximum suppression, which substantially surpasses state-of-the-art 3D detectors in the far-field.

Gradient-based approaches for two-player games generate complex dynamics capable of addressing difficult challenges, though they often prove hard to stabilize and comprehend. A significant source of this intricacy lies in the discrete update steps of simultaneous or alternating gradient descent, which cause players to diverge from the continuous gradient flow—a phenomenon termed "discretization drift." By applying backward error analysis, we construct modified continuous dynamical systems that accurately track these discrete behaviors. These adjusted dynamics offer valuable insights into the well-known difficulties of zero-sum games, such as those found in Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). Specifically, we isolate distinct components of discretization drift that can degrade performance or induce instability. Furthermore, quantifying this drift enables the development of regularizers designed to counteract detrimental drift patterns or amplify advantageous ones, thereby enhancing GAN training outcomes.

Dispersion error frequently dominates numerical solutions to wave propagation problems containing high-frequency components. This paper introduces and provides explicit examples of $\alpha$-dispersion-relation-preserving schemes, which are dual-pair finite-difference methods for systems of hyperbolic partial differential equations. These schemes maintain the continuous problem's dispersion relation within a uniform $\alpha \%$-error tolerance. We present a general framework for designing provably stable finite-difference operators that preserve the dispersion relation for hyperbolic systems, such as the elastic wave equation. The derived operators can resolve the highest frequency ($\pi$-mode) on any equidistant grid with a $5\%$ error tolerance, a marked improvement over the current standard, which allows for up to $100 \%$ error.

This study introduces HD-TESS, a catalog comprising 1,709 bright ($V\sim3-10$) red giants listed in the Henry Draper Catalog, for which we derived asteroseismic measurements using photometric data from NASA's TESS mission. By analyzing light curves covering at least six months within a single observing cycle, we determined global asteroseismic parameters ($\nu_{\mathrm{max}}$ and $\Delta\nu$) and evolutionary states for all stars. Leveraging literature-based atmospheric parameters and asteroseismic scaling relations, we estimated the masses and radii of these giants, noting that HD-TESS red giants generally possess larger masses than their Kepler counterparts. Furthermore, we report the detection of oscillations in 99 red giants belonging to astrometric binary systems, some of which feature subdwarf or white dwarf companions. Finally, we compared asteroseismic radius estimates against those obtained via long-baseline interferometry for 18 stars, demonstrating that applying correction factors to the scaling relations reduces the discrepancy between the two methods to approximately 3%.

New experiments designed to detect neutrinos in the far-forward region of the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) are currently being prepared or designed. Among these, FASER$
u$ and SND@LHC are slated to operate during Run 3, aiming to capture neutrinos generated by high-energy proton-proton collisions and traveling along the beam line's tangent. The primary source of tau neutrinos and antineutrinos is the production of $D_s^\pm$ mesons, which subsequently decay leptonically. These future experiments focus on neutrino pseudorapidities exceeding 6.9 and 8.9. At such extreme forward angles and high energies, theoretical models for the tau neutrino flux depend on parton distribution functions (PDFs) spanning both very small and large parton-$x$ values. This study evaluates PDF uncertainties within a next-to-leading order (NLO) QCD framework for calculating the $
u_	au$ and $ ar{
u}_	au$ flux from $D_s^\pm$ decays in the far-forward LHC region. Uncertainties derived from the 40 PROSA19 PDF sets contribute a $\pm (20-30)$\% variation to the predicted number of charged-current events. However, scale uncertainties are significantly larger, causing predictions for CC events to fluctuate between roughly 70\% below and 90\% above the central value. Comparisons with central PDFs from the CT14, ABMP16, and NNPDF3.1 collaborations reveal that far-forward neutrino energy distributions can differ by a factor of 2 to 4 from PROSA19 predictions at TeV-scale energies. Ultimately, data from the Forward Physics Facility during the high-luminosity LHC era will be instrumental in constraining these NLO QCD evaluations across various PDF sets.

Gravitational wave observations of binary black hole mergers have started to probe the cosmic black hole mass distribution. Stellar evolution models for single cores suggest a gap in this distribution caused by pair-instability supernovae (PISN). Identifying the boundaries of this upper mass gap is crucial for interpreting gravitational wave data from merging black holes. Using \MESA, we simulated the evolution of non-rotating, massive helium cores at a metallicity of $Z = 10^{-5}$ until they either collapsed into black holes or exploded as PISNs without leaving remnants. We determined the lower edge of the mass gap for S-factors ranging from S(300 keV) = (77,203) keV b, reflecting the $\pm 3\sigma$ uncertainty in the high-resolution tabulated probability distribution for the $^{12}$C($\alpha$,$\gamma$)$^{16}$O reaction rate. We rigorously tested temporal and mass resolution to accurately capture the theoretical peak of the black hole mass spectrum across the gap. Our analysis of convergence regarding convective mixing and nuclear burning revealed that high time resolution is essential. We also investigated the impact of adopting a minimum diffusion coefficient to assist lower-resolution models in reaching convergence. Based on the $\pm 3\sigma$ uncertainty in the $^{12}\text{C}(\alpha, \gamma) ^{16}\text{O}$ rate, we established a new lower edge for the upper mass gap at M\textsubscript{lower} $\simeq$\,60$^{+32}_{-14}$\,\Msun. Furthermore, we examined how an increased 3-$\alpha$ rate affects this lower edge, yielding M\textsubscript{lower} $\simeq$\,69$^{+34}_{-18}$\,\Msun. Finally, we compared these findings with black hole candidates listed in the Gravitational-Wave Transient Catalog.

Although air travel is expanding rapidly, its growth is being constrained by the adverse effects of aircraft noise on nearby communities. To investigate and reduce this impact, numerous airports continuously monitor ambient noise levels. However, analyzing these recordings is challenging because non-aircraft noise sources also contribute to the data. This study demonstrates that Convolutional Neural Networks are highly effective at distinguishing non-aircraft noise events. When trained on 900 manually labeled events, our system achieved an accuracy of 0.970. The training dataset and a TensorFlow implementation of the model can be accessed at https://github.com/neheller/aircraftnoise.

Kenneth G. Wilson offered profound and perceptive advancements in statistical physics, particle physics, and associated disciplines. Beyond his scientific achievements, he was also a considerate and kind individual.

Recent years have seen significant interest in self-supervised representation learning via Contrastive Learning (CL), driven by its ability to achieve strong performance on various downstream tasks, especially classification, without relying heavily on labeled data. However, most standard CL algorithms (including SimCLR, MoCo, BYOL, and Barlow Twins) are ill-suited for pixel-level applications. An existing method, PixPro, addresses this by filtering positive and negative image crops based on their distance within the full image. We propose enhancing this approach by integrating semantic cues from external data as an additional filter to refine the selection of pixel-level samples during training. Specifically, we focus on depth information, derivable from depth estimation networks or sources like stereovision, parallax, and LiDAR, which offers valuable signals to differentiate pixels across distinct objects. Incorporating this exogenous information into the contrastive loss yields better results and ensures learned representations more accurately capture object shapes. Furthermore, we introduce a multi-scale loss to address challenges in adapting training parameters to varying object sizes. Our method demonstrates effectiveness on Breakout Segmentation for Borehole Images, achieving a 1.9% improvement over PixPro and nearly 5% over supervised baselines. We also validate our approach on indoor (ScanNet) and outdoor (CityScapes) scene segmentation, securing gains of 1.6% and 1.1% over PixPro, respectively.

This paper introduces a novel adaptive strategy for resource optimization in multi-device terahertz (THz) Internet of Things (Tera-IoT) networks, which simultaneously allocates subwindows and transmit power. Diverging from previous research that primarily maximized total distance, our formulation integrates both data rate and transmission distance into the objective function, explicitly accounting for THz-specific characteristics such as spreading and molecular absorption losses. Specifically, we utilize transport capacity (TC)—the aggregate of rate-distance products across all users—as the performance metric, a measure widely used in large-scale ad hoc networks and well-suited for assessing diverse Tera-IoT applications. We formulate an optimization problem to maximize TC. Furthermore, recognizing that transmission distance is severely constrained by high path loss in THz bands, we extend the optimization to jointly allocate subwindow, transmit power, and transmission distance. We propose an efficient two-stage resource allocation strategy to solve these problems and demonstrate, through extensive numerical simulations across various large-scale Tera-IoT environmental scenarios, that our adaptive approach outperforms existing benchmark methods.

The Standard Model of particle physics forecasts quantum tunnelling events between topologically distinct vacua, referred to as Instantons. Within the electroweak framework, these instantons act as a generator for baryon asymmetry, while in Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD), they are associated with chiral symmetry breaking and confinement. Consequently, directly observing Instanton-induced phenomena would represent a significant advancement in modern particle physics. Recent publications detailing QCD Instanton processes in proton-proton collisions indicate potentially large cross-sections and viable detection signatures at the LHC. This study investigates analytical methods for identifying QCD Instanton effects at the LHC and establishes an initial constraint using available Minimum Bias data.

Data-driven decision-making significantly shapes finance, yet our capacity to fully grasp the informational depth of datasets is often constrained by current analytical tools, particularly when dealing with high-dimensional data. This paper introduces the Ball Mapper algorithm from Topological Data Analysis as a novel approach to revealing data details through its underlying shape. By comparing this method to existing techniques and providing illustrative examples, the study demonstrates its value. Furthermore, it outlines practical applications for Ball Mapper and reviews its associated benefits.

To enhance generalization in deep learning and automate learning rate scheduling, we introduce SALR, a sharpness-aware technique for updating learning rates aimed at recovering flat minimizers. Our approach dynamically adjusts the learning rates of gradient-based optimizers by evaluating the local sharpness of the loss landscape. This mechanism enables optimizers to automatically raise learning rates within sharp valleys, thereby increasing the likelihood of escaping them. We validate the efficacy of SALR across a wide range of networks and various algorithms. Our experimental results demonstrate that SALR accelerates convergence, improves generalization, and steers solutions toward significantly flatter regions.

This study investigates an exact solution to a novel generalized nonlinear KdV partial differential equation using the homotopy analysis technique. Specifically, the equation was solved via the homotopy perturbation method (HPM). The research is structured into two distinct scenarios: the first involves selecting the linear component as the time-derivative term, with the initial guess derived from initial conditions or boundary values. The second scenario employs multiple linear terms from the original equation to construct a simplified partial differential equation with an easily obtainable solution. Finally, graphical representations of the derived solutions illustrate their convergent behavior.

Nonlinearities in optical fibers, which cause nonlinear signal interference (NLI), are conventionally treated as an instantaneous reaction to the optical field. Yet, the fiber's nonlinear response includes a delayed component known as the Raman response. The imaginary component of its Fourier transform, termed the Raman gain spectrum, drives inter-channel stimulated Raman scattering (ISRS), a phenomenon that shifts optical power from higher to lower frequencies as the signal propagates. Because the nonlinear fiber response must be causal, the Raman spectrum adheres to the Kramers-Kronig relations, generating a real component in the complex-valued spectrum. While the effects of the imaginary part (ISRS) are well-documented, the direct influence of its corresponding real part on NLI remains uninvestigated. This work introduces a theory to analytically measure the impact of the real Raman spectrum on nonlinear interference power. By extending the ISRS Gaussian Noise (GN) model based on a generalized Manakov equation, the study incorporates the real Raman spectrum to fully account for the nonlinear Raman response. The authors derive precise integral expressions and propose closed-form approximations, developing specific formulations for both single- and dual-polarized signals alongside new analytical approximations for the real Raman spectrum. Furthermore, it is demonstrated analytically that the real Raman spectrum modulates the magnitude of instantaneous nonlinear distortions based on the frequency spacing between interacting signals, leading to a simple functional form for assessing NLI scaling. The validity of this theory is confirmed through numerical simulations across C- and C+L bands using experimentally obtained fiber data.

Active learning seeks to maximize benefits in resource-constrained settings. This study employs COMET-QE, a reference-free metric, to identify sentences for low-resource neural machine translation. Experiments conducted on Swahili, Kinyarwanda, and Spanish demonstrate that COMET-QE significantly surpasses two Round Trip Translation Likelihood (RTTL) variants and random selection methods, achieving up to 5 BLEU points higher when selecting 20k sentences via Active Learning compared to a 30k baseline. These findings indicate that COMET-QE is a highly effective instrument for sentence selection in extremely low-resource scenarios.

Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) are powerful astrophysical objects driven by the accretion of material onto supermassive black holes, exhibiting distinctive observational signatures across the entire electromagnetic spectrum and beyond, spanning roughly twenty orders of magnitude in frequency. We begin by reviewing the primary characteristics and variety of AGN, demonstrating that these phenomena can be accounted for by a limited set of parameters. Next, we examine Unification Models for non-jetted AGN, which propose that these sources share an identical nuclear engine and circumnuclear environment with a consistent geometry for obscuring structures. However, this streamlined framework fails to address all observed complexities, such as multiple absorbers at various physical scales, including recent X-ray data regarding circumnuclear matter. Finally, we briefly explore AGN evolution within the X-ray and $\gamma$-ray domains.

I examine compact metric spaces that possess intrinsic isometries to d-dimensional Euclidean space. My primary finding is that the collection of such spaces is essentially identical to the class of inverse limits formed by d-dimensional Euclidean polyhedra.

We examine the higher-order Schrödinger operator $H=(-\Delta)^m+V(x)$ in $n$ dimensions, where $n>4m-1$ and $m$ is a natural number, featuring a real-valued potential $V$. We demonstrate that for any $\frac{2n}{n-4m+1}<p\leq \infty$ and $0\leq \alpha<\frac{n+1}{2}-2m-\frac{n}p$, there exists a real-valued, compactly supported potential $V\in C^{\alpha}(\mathbb R^n)$ such that the wave operators $W^{\pm}$ fail to be bounded on $L^p(\mathbb R^n)$. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that for the standard second-order Schrödinger operator $-\Delta+V$, the wave operators are unbounded on $L^p(\mathbb R^n)$ when $n>3$ and $\frac{2n}{n-3}<p\leq \infty$, provided the potential $V$ lacks sufficient differentiability. Additionally, we identify a breakdown in $L^{p'}\to L^p$ dispersive estimates, a result that may hold independent significance.

We investigate the verification of distributed systems composed of finite automata processes utilizing a shared lock pool. Our analysis focuses on objectives defined as boolean combinations of local regular constraints. While the general problem is PSPACE-complete, we demonstrate that under specific assumptions regarding the system, it resides in NP. These assumptions involve limiting the number of locks a process can access and constraining the order of lock releases. Furthermore, we establish tight complexity bounds and identify a particularly relevant subcase solvable in polynomial time (PTIME).

This study utilizes the Tuffs et al. attenuation and inclination models across UV, optical, and near-infrared wavelengths to examine global dust properties in galaxies relative to stellar mass ($M_{*}$), stellar mass surface density ($\mu_{*}$), star-formation rate (SFR), specific star-formation rate (sSFR), star-formation main-sequence offset ($dMS$), and SFR surface density ($\Sigma_{SFR}$) at redshifts $z \sim 0$ and $z \sim 0.7$. Our low-redshift sample ($0.04 < z < 0.1$) comprises $\sim$20,000 star-forming galaxies from SDSS and $\sim$2,000 from GAMA, while the $z \sim 0.7$ sample consists of $\sim$2,000 star-forming galaxies from COSMOS ($0.6 < z < 0.8$). We observe that galaxies at $z \sim 0.7$ exhibit greater optical depth ($\tau_{B}^{f}$) and clumpiness ($F$) compared to those at $z \sim 0$. The elevated $F$ suggests that stars in $z \sim 0.7$ galaxies are less likely to escape their birth clouds, potentially indicating larger cloud sizes. Additionally, $\tau_{B}^{f}$ increases with both $M_{*}$ and $\mu_{*}$ regardless of the sample or redshift, whereas no clear trends emerge between $\tau_{B}^{f}$ or $F$ and SFR, implying that dust mass distribution—and consequently the balance of dust formation and destruction—may be independent of SFR. Finally, analyzing the inclination dependence of the Balmer decrement reveals that reproducing Balmer line emission requires not only the standard optically thick dust component linked to star-forming regions but also an additional optically thin dust component within birth clouds.
