Through interactions, agents learn about their neighbors' trustworthiness, causing their behaviors to evolve accordingly. Empirical tests on realistic social networks reveal that when given the choice, many agents become highly trustworthy; notably, when trustworthiness is inferred from past interactions rather than known beforehand, most or all agents tend to become highly trustworthy. This behavior stems not from altruism but from intrinsic competitive motivation. Two key insights emerge: first, trustworthy actions boost the utility of all agents, where maintaining a moderate level of trustworthiness can increase net utility by up to 14.5%, and if just one self-centered agent acts modestly trustworthy, it can raise its average utility by as much as 25% in specific scenarios. Second, counter-intuitively, an abundance of partnership opportunities leads agents to become less trustworthy.

This report presents measurements of the inclusive J/$\psi$ elliptic ($v_2$) and triangular ($v_3$) flow coefficients at forward rapidity (2.5 $<y<$ 4), alongside the midrapidity $v_2$ ($|y|<$ 0.9), obtained from Pb-Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}$ = 5.02 TeV using the ALICE detector at the LHC. The analysis utilizes the complete Run 2 Pb-Pb dataset, corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 750 $\mu$b$^{-1}$ at forward rapidity and 93 $\mu$b$^{-1}$ at midrapidity. Derived via the scalar product method, these results are presented as functions of transverse momentum $p_{\rm T}$ and collision centrality. At midrapidity, the J/$\psi$ $v_2$ aligns with the forward rapidity findings. Centrality-averaged data reveal a positive J/$\psi$ $v_3$ with a significance exceeding 5$\sigma$ at forward rapidity for $2<p_{\rm T}<5$ GeV/$c$. In the low to intermediate $p_{\rm T}$ range ($p_{\rm T} \lesssim 8$ GeV/$c$), the forward rapidity $v_2$, $v_3$, and $v_3$/$v_2$ values display a mass hierarchy relative to pions and D mesons, converging to a species-independent trend at higher $p_{\rm T}$. These low and intermediate $p_{\rm T}$ results suggest a later thermalization of charm quarks compared to light quarks, whereas high $p_{\rm T}$ behavior indicates dominance by path-length dependent effects. The J/$\psi$ $v_2$ data are compared with microscopic transport model calculations. Furthermore, applying a simplified extension of the quark scaling approach that incorporates both light and charm quark flow components, it is demonstrated that D-meson $v_{\rm n}$ measurements can be reproduced using the flow characteristics of charged pions and J/$\psi$.

This study addresses the exponential stabilization of underactuated linear homogeneous systems consisting of $m$ parabolic partial differential equations (PDEs) arranged in cascade (reaction-diffusion systems), where only the first state is actuated, either internally or at the right boundary, and the diffusion coefficients are distinct. For distributed control, an explicit proportional-type stabilizing controller is presented. Following modal decomposition, this control law relies on transforming the ordinary differential equation (ODE) system associated with the relatively unstable modes into a target system; crucially, calculating this law does not depend on the arbitrarily large number of such modes. This is accomplished by recursively solving generalized Sylvester equations. In the boundary control scenario, provided the coupling matrix (reaction term) satisfies specific sufficient conditions, the proposed controller is dynamic. This involves first applying a dynamic extension technique through a trigonometric change of variables to internalize the control, followed by modal decomposition and a state transformation of the ODE system to facilitate the selection of a dynamic law. For both distributed and boundary control configurations, a constructive and scalable stabilization algorithm is developed, as the selection of controller gains is independent of the count of unstable modes and relies solely on stabilizing the reaction term. This approach resolves the stabilization challenge for underactuated systems with distinct diffusion coefficients, a problem that remains unsolvable via direct methods typically used for scalar PDEs.

We provide a novel proof for the block structure within the representation category of a reductive algebraic group $\mathbf{G}$ over a field of positive characteristic $\ell$ (an original result by Donkin). This approach utilizes the Satake category of the Langlands dual group alongside Smith-Treumann theory, as formulated by Riche and Williamson. From a representation-theoretic perspective, our methodology establishes an upper bound on the length of the shortest chain connecting two weights within the same block and offers an alternative proof for the block decomposition of quantum groups evaluated at an $\ell$-th root of unity.

Drawing inspiration from the similar characteristics of the $Z_c(3900/3885)$ and $Z_{cs}(3985/4000)$ systems, we preliminarily identify the $Z_c(4020/4025)$ as an $A\bar{A}$-type hidden-charm tetraquark with quantum numbers $J^{PC}=1^{+-}$, where $A$ represents axialvector diquarks. Using QCD sum rules, we systematically investigate these $A\bar{A}$-type tetraquarks in scenarios without strange quarks, with strange quarks, and with hidden-strange components. Furthermore, relying on rigorous quark-hadron duality within the QCD sum rule framework, we determine the hadronic coupling constants for the strong two-body decays of both non-strange and strange tetraquarks to calculate their respective partial and total decay widths. Our calculations reinforce the assignment of the $Z_c(4020/4025)$ as an $A\bar{A}$-type tetraquark with $J^{PC}=1^{+-}$, and the predicted properties of its strange counterpart, $Z_{cs}$, are positioned for future experimental verification.

This study examines chaotic dynamics in multidimensional Hamiltonian systems subject to nonlinearity and disorder. While Anderson localization (AL) causes initial excitations in sufficiently large linear disordered systems to spread briefly before halting permanently, the impact of introducing nonlinearity remains a subject of intense debate due to computational challenges, particularly in multi-dimensional settings. Because the spreading of localized wave packets constitutes a non-equilibrium thermalization process linked to ergodicity and chaos, our research investigates these chaotic properties by analyzing observables derived from the system's tangent dynamics. Specifically, we analyze the disordered discrete nonlinear Schrödinger (DDNLS) equation across one and two spatial dimensions. We provide detailed calculations of the time evolution of the maximum Lyapunov exponent (MLE, $\Lambda$) and the associated deviation vector distribution (DVD). Our findings indicate that, despite the MLE decreasing over time according to a power law $t^{\alpha_\Lambda}$ (where $\alpha_\Lambda < 0$) in both weak and strong chaos regimes, no transition to the behavior $\Lambda \propto t^{-1}$—characteristic of regular motion—is observed. Furthermore, DVD analysis reveals random fluctuations of chaotic hotspots with growing amplitudes within the excited wave packet region, which facilitate the homogenization of chaos and promote the thermalization of additional lattice sites.

This work investigates solutions within non-linear electrodynamics (NED) to derive several broad conclusions. We demonstrate that the $SO(2)$ electric-magnetic duality symmetry is sufficiently constraining to enable the reconstruction of the NED Lagrangian from a spherically symmetric, electrostatic (Coulomb-like) solution. Although infinitely many distinct NED theories can accommodate a specific solution, exactly one remains invariant under $SO(2)$. We present a general algorithm for building new $SO(2)$ invariant NED theories using the conventional method, addressing a gap where such examples are scarce. Additionally, we outline the procedure for deriving the Lagrangian of the unique $SO(2)$ invariant theory corresponding to a given electrostatic solution. Through a simple example, we show that certain NED theories necessitate sources with finite, non-zero dimensions. Such extended sources not only prevent the infinite energy associated with point charges but also ensure regularity by maintaining a zero electric field at the origin. This condition was previously established as necessary and sufficient for NED solutions to produce regular black holes via the double copy construction, a property also shared by solitons. We propose an extensive class of solitonic NED solutions that yield regular black holes through the double copy mechanism and encompass both Maxwell and Born-Infeld theories as limiting cases. As the asymptotics of the corresponding regular black hole approaches Minkowski space, this class of NED solutions exhibits two novel characteristics: it generates regular higher-spin black holes via a generalized "higher-copy" construction, and at very short distances, it inverts the force sign, rendering it repulsive or attractive depending on whether the charges are opposite or similar.

It remains an open question whether Yao-Yao graphs $\mathsf{YY}_k$ (also called sparse-Yao graphs) function as spanners for sufficiently large integer values of $k$. This paper demonstrates that for any integer $k \geq 42$, the graph $\mathsf{YY}_{2k}$ is indeed a $t_k$-spanner, achieving a stretch factor of $t_k = 6.03 + O(k^{-1})$ as $k$ approaches infinity. This finding extends the strongest existing result, which established that all $\mathsf{YY}_{6k}$ are spanners for large enough $k$ [Bauer and Damian, SODA'13], and our proof approach is notably simpler.

Machine Learning-based Programming Language Processing (PLP) has seen significant advancements recently, sparking growing interest in the field. However, new researchers and developers face difficulties in assembling their own ML pipelines due to the wide variety of PLP tasks, the abundance of available datasets and models, and the complexity of the compilers and tools required. To enhance the findability, accessibility, interoperability, and reusability (FAIRness) of these components, we gathered and analyzed a selection of representative papers on machine learning-driven PLP. We subsequently identified and characterized essential concepts, such as PLP tasks, model architectures, and supporting tools. Finally, we demonstrate practical use cases that leverage these reusable components to build ML pipelines for addressing various PLP tasks.

Anomaly detection can be approached either by generating regular training data or by discriminating against negative training data, each with distinct failure modes. This makes hybrid algorithms a promising research direction. However, dense anomaly detection demands translational equivariance and high-resolution inputs, which, to our knowledge, disqualify all existing hybrid methods. To address this, we propose a novel hybrid algorithm that reinterprets discriminative logits as the logarithm of the unnormalized joint distribution $\hat{p}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y})$. Our model utilizes a shared convolutional representation to derive three dense outputs: i) the closed-set class posterior $P(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x})$, ii) the dataset posterior $P(d_{in}|\mathbf{x})$, and iii) the unnormalized data likelihood $\hat{p}(\mathbf{x})$. The latter two are trained on both standard and generic negative datasets. We combine these predictions into a hybrid anomaly score that enables dense open-set recognition on large natural images. Furthermore, we introduce a specialized loss function for the data likelihood to circumvent backpropagation through the intractable normalizing constant $Z(\theta)$. Evaluations on standard dense anomaly detection benchmarks and a new metric, open-mIoU, demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art results with negligible computational overhead compared to standard semantic segmentation baselines.

We examine entropy solutions to the two-dimensional eikonal equation $|\nabla u|=1$. Inspired by a specific class of variational problems, these solutions generally lack bounded variation; however, they retain several fine properties characteristic of BV functions. Specifically, we demonstrate that the set of non-Lebesgue points possesses a co-dimension of at least one.

The Fisher-Stefan model integrates the Fisher-KPP equation with a boundary that evolves under a Stefan-like condition. This approach overcomes two key practical constraints of the standard Fisher-KPP model in biological invasion contexts. First, unlike the Fisher-KPP equation, the Fisher-Stefan model yields solutions with compact support, allowing for a clear definition of the interface between inhabited and uninhabited areas. Second, it permits solutions where the population goes extinct, a scenario the Fisher-KPP equation cannot represent. While prior studies established that survival or extinction in the Fisher-Stefan model hinges on a critical length within one-dimensional Cartesian or radially symmetric settings, the behavior in general two-dimensional regions has not been examined. This work combines analytical methods with level-set numerical simulations to explore survival-extinction thresholds for rectangular initial domains. The findings indicate that extending critical length conditions to a critical area in two dimensions is inadequate; instead, the specific geometry of the region must be understood to predict whether a population will persist or perish.

This study investigates how population-based engagement prediction can tackle cold-start challenges at scale within extensive learning resource collections. It presents three key contributions: i) VLE, a new dataset featuring content and video attributes extracted from open-access scientific lectures, combined with implicit and explicit learner engagement signals; ii) two standard tasks involving the prediction and ranking of context-agnostic engagement in video lectures, accompanied by preliminary baselines; and iii) experiments validating the utility of the proposed dataset. Our results demonstrate that the VLE dataset enables the development of significantly more effective context-agnostic engagement models compared to those using prior datasets, primarily due to the increased volume of training examples. The dataset's applicability to building models for Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence education within e-learning and MOOC contexts is also confirmed. Additionally, experiments integrating the model with personalization algorithms yield promising results in mitigating cold-start issues in educational recommendation systems. To our knowledge, VLE represents the largest and most diverse public dataset addressing learner engagement prediction. The dataset, along with auxiliary tools, descriptive statistics, and code examples, is publicly accessible.

Supersymmetry (SUSY) offers a solution to the hierarchy problem in high-energy physics and serves as a natural basis for unifying gravity with other fundamental forces. Although it is one of the most compelling frameworks for physics beyond the Standard Model, direct experimental confirmation of SUSY in nature has yet to be found. In this study, we present the experimental realization of a supersymmetric quantum mechanics (SUSY QM) model—a simplified version of SUSY quantum field theory used to investigate its core properties—by employing a trapped ion quantum simulator. We confirm the energy degeneracy resulting from SUSY within this model and observe spontaneous SUSY breaking. Through partial quantum state tomography of the spin-phonon coupled system, we explicitly measure the supercharge of the degenerate ground states, which manifest as superpositions of bosonic and fermionic states. Our findings establish the trapped-ion quantum simulator as a cost-effective yet potent platform for exploring diverse physical phenomena within a single, well-controlled system.

This study demonstrates that an abelian category can be embedded exactly and fully faithfully into a module category as the right perpendicular subcategory to a set of modules or morphisms if and only if it is a locally presentable abelian category possessing a projective generator. Equivalently, such categories correspond to the models of additive algebraic theories with possibly infinite bounded arity, encompassing instances like contramodules over topological rings and similar examples. The analysis examines various formulations of the right perpendicular subcategory, all of which identify the same class of abelian categories. Furthermore, sufficient conditions are provided for the natural forgetful functors mapping from contramodule categories to their associated module categories to be fully faithful.

Discovering causality in data influenced by unobserved factors is a challenging yet critical task. The impact of these hidden variables on observed relationships is particularly intricate in nonlinear scenarios compared to linear ones. This study examines causal additive models under the influence of unobserved variables, which are characterized by structural equations where variables and error terms are additive. We consider the presence of both unobserved common causes and intermediate variables. Our theoretical findings indicate that when causal links are nonlinear and unobserved variables exist, regression and independence tests cannot fully identify all causal relationships among observed variables. However, these results also demonstrate that avoiding incorrect inferences remains feasible. We introduce a method to identify all theoretically recoverable causal relationships without bias from unobserved factors. Empirical evaluations using synthetic data and simulated fMRI data confirm that our approach effectively infers causal structures despite the presence of unobserved variables.

Hydrogen cyanide (HCN) is widely regarded as a reliable tracer of dense molecular gas, the primary fuel for star formation. Nevertheless, recent extensive surveys of giant molecular clouds (GMCs) have revealed extended HCN line emission, often resolving the J=1-0 hyperfine structure (HFS). Accurately determining the physical conditions of this gas necessitates accounting for HFS line overlap effects. This study investigates HCN HFS excitation and emission using nonlocal radiative transfer models that incorporate line overlaps and newly calculated HFS-resolved collisional rate coefficients for inelastic collisions between HCN and both para-H2 and ortho-H2 (derived via the scaled-IOS approximation up to 500 K). Furthermore, we consider the impact of electron collisions on HFS level excitation. Our findings indicate that line overlap and opacity effects frequently generate anomalous HCN J=1-0 HFS intensity and width ratios, contradicting the standard assumption of uniform excitation temperatures across all HFS lines. Additionally, these factors, along with electron collisions, enhance the excitation of higher rotational J lines. Electron excitation plays a significant role in molecular gas with H2 densities below a few $10^5$ cm$^{-3}$ and electron abundances exceeding $\sim 10^{-5}$. Notably, electron excitation can produce low-surface-brightness HCN emission from highly extended, low-density regions within GMCs. The presence of such a pervasive emission component could alter the interpretation of the extragalactic correlation between HCN luminosity and star-formation rate. Alternatively, extended HCN emission might originate from dense star-forming cores and be resonantly scattered by lower-density envelopes. Two distinct scenarios—electron-assisted collisional excitation versus scattering—yield different HCN J=1-0 HFS intensity ratios, providing testable predictions for observational verification.

Serving as the cornerstone of particle physics, Quantum Field Theory has provided profound insights into the fundamental nature of the universe. Despite its remarkable achievements, its reliance on local interactions leads to divergent quantities in intermediate calculation steps, necessitating regularization and renormalization techniques. As an alternative to conventional methods that utilize analytic continuation of space-time dimensions, approaches operating strictly within physical dimensions have developed, with Implicit Regularization being a prominent example. This work offers a brief overview of the method, demonstrating how Implicit Regularization aligns with the BPHZ theorem, thereby ensuring compliance with unitarity and locality to arbitrary loop orders.

Flavor-changing neutral current decays in leptonic and semileptonic mesons serve as powerful tools for investigating both the Standard Model and physics beyond it. This work provides explicit calculations of the Wilson coefficients for the weak effective Lagrangian governing these decays, applicable to any perturbative framework where such processes occur at the one-loop level. We demonstrate that our findings are both finite and gauge-independent, and we supply Mathematica code to facilitate the practical application of these results.

The shuffle model of differential privacy represents a new distributed framework that integrates local privacy mechanisms with a secure shuffler. Research indicates that the extra randomization introduced by the shuffler yields superior privacy bounds compared to local mechanisms alone. However, calculating precise bounds remains challenging due to the complexity added by the shuffler. Recent numerical techniques for assessing $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-differential privacy have demonstrated the ability to provide tighter bounds than traditional methods for composing complex mechanisms. This paper demonstrates how to derive accurate bounds for adaptive compositions of general $\varepsilon$-LDP shufflers using the analysis by Feldman et al. (2021) and tight bounds for adaptive compositions of shufflers applied to $k$-randomised response mechanisms via the analysis by Balle et al. (2019). Furthermore, we present a method to accelerate the evaluation of the resulting privacy loss distribution from $\mathcal{O}(n^2)$ to $\mathcal{O}(n)$, where $n$ denotes the number of users, without significantly altering the resulting $\delta(\varepsilon)$-upper bounds. Finally, we highlight the looseness of existing bounds and methodologies in the literature, thereby substantially improving prior composition results.

Beginning with the creation of the first webpage three decades ago, the Web has transformed significantly, shifting from static HTML to dynamic content, and from text-dominated pages of the 1990s to today's multimedia-rich environments. While these shifts are widely acknowledged anecdotally, there remains a lack of quantitative documentation regarding their timing and scope. This study addresses that gap by analyzing the top 100 Alexa-ranked websites over a 25-year period using data from the Internet Archive (Wayback Machine). The research examines popularity trends, tracing the shift from mid-to-late 1990s giants like Geocities and Yahoo! to contemporary leaders such as Google, Facebook, and TikTok. Additionally, the paper categorizes websites by type to reveal a decline in news and education sites, which have been supplanted by social networking and streaming media platforms. Finally, it investigates the evolution of various MIME types—including text, images, video, JavaScript, and JSON—to determine whether text usage on the Internet is decreasing.

This study addresses distributed convex optimization within a time-varying network that lacks consistent strong connectivity. Each node's local cost function is influenced by a stochastic process, and the collective goal is to minimize the average of these functions. The primary challenge lies in the unavailability of cost function gradients, necessitating their estimation solely through numerical observations of the cost values; this framework is termed zeroth-order stochastic convex optimization (ZOSCO). This paper presents an initial approach to distributed optimization under ZOSCO conditions. The proposed algorithm operates in two stages per iteration: first, each node updates its local variable using a single-point gradient estimator based on random perturbations of its own cost function; second, nodes exchange local variables with direct neighbors and compute a weighted average. For smooth and strongly convex cost functions, the algorithm achieves an optimization error of $O(T^{-1/2})$ after $T$ iterations, matching the optimal convergence rate for ZOSCO problems. Additionally, we examine the optimization error for general Lipschitz convex functions, yielding a rate of $O(T^{-1/4})$.

Path-independent (PI) quantum control was recently introduced to unify quantum error correction with control mechanisms, enabling fault-tolerant gates resilient to ancilla errors [Phys. Rev. Lett. 125, 110503 (2020)]. This work uncovers the algebraic foundation of PI quantum control, demonstrating that its Hamiltonians and propagators reside within an algebra isomorphic to standard matrix algebra, termed the PI matrix algebra. Defined over the Hilbert space of a composite system comprising both ancilla and central components, this algebra is isomorphic to the matrix algebra acting solely on the ancilla's Hilbert space. By generalizing the PI matrix algebra to the Hilbert-Schmidt space of the composite system, we establish an exact and comprehensive criterion for achieving PI quantum control in the presence of ancilla noise.

We develop a local-to-global principle applicable to higher moments within the holomorphy rings of global function fields, subsequently utilizing this framework to calculate the higher moments of rectangular unimodular matrices and Eisenstein polynomials possessing coefficients in these rings.

We categorize pairs $(S, \gamma)$, comprising a rational elliptic surface $S$ and a Galois cover $\gamma$ of the base, that meet our defined criterion of $\mathcal{L}$-stability. We demonstrate how Mordell-Weil lattice theory can be applied to determine the kernel of restriction maps between Weil-Chatelet groups for these $\mathcal{L}$-stable pairs. Furthermore, we establish findings regarding the injectivity of such restriction maps for certain pairs that do not satisfy $\mathcal{L}$-stability.

We introduce the inaugural investigation into baryon-baryon interactions within the continuum limit of lattice QCD, revealing surprisingly significant lattice artifacts. Specifically, we calculate the binding energy of the $H$ dibaryon at one specific quark-mass value. This calculation utilizes six different lattice spacings $a$, employing O($a$)-improved Wilson fermions at the SU(3)-symmetric point where $m_\pi=m_K\approx 420$ MeV. Energy levels are derived by applying a variational method to correlation matrices of bilocal two-baryon operators, computed via the distillation technique. Our approach uses L\"uscher's finite-volume quantization condition to interconvert the spectrum and scattering phase shifts, both above and below the two-baryon threshold. We conduct global fits to the lattice spectra using phase-shift parametrizations augmented with terms for discretization effects, followed by an extrapolation to zero lattice spacing. The resulting phase shift and binding energy are shown to be heavily influenced by lattice artifacts. Our estimate for the binding energy in the continuum limit of three-flavor QCD is $B_H^{\text{SU(3)}_{\rm f}}=4.56\pm1.13_{\rm stat}\pm0.63_{\rm syst}$ MeV.

This paper presents findings from incorporating a semi-boosted transition region into the reconstruction of top quark pairs within the $\ell$ + jets channel, bridging the gap between resolved and boosted analyses. Although this region is frequently excluded because its complex reconstruction typically reduces efficiency, it has been fully reconstructed here across all three topologies to facilitate comparison and combination. A hypothetical $Z'$ particle served as the probe to investigate the resulting increase in event counts within the analyzed energy range.

In a three-level quantum system at resonance, electrons transition between energy levels—either absorbing photons to move from low to high states or emitting photons to drop from high to low states—based on the two lattice points with the strongest Hamiltonian coupling. This process facilitates quantum walking along a straight line under equal probability conditions. The resulting optical radiation from this quantum walk is modeled as a Gaussian electric field pulse, and Maxwell's equations are solved using the three-dimensional finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) method to determine the spatial electric field distribution. Furthermore, the study explores quantum walking across two parallel lines, examining physical attributes such as electromagnetic coupling, coherence, and quantum state exchange. Calculating the electric field coupling between these lines via FDTD offers a valuable tool for the design and analysis of quantum devices.

This paper investigates bifurcations in generalized periodic Hamiltonian systems by employing the Clarke-Ekeland dual variational principle and abstract bifurcation theory concepts from the author's prior work or its proofs. Numerous new results are established without imposing any restrictions on the growth of Hamiltonian functions.

Consider a $C^2$ Axiom A diffeomorphism $f : M \longrightarrow M$ defined on a compact Riemannian manifold. We establish that for a basic set $X$ of $f$, if $\mu$ is a Gibbs measure associated with a H\"older continuous potential and the Oseledets subspaces $E_i(x)$ vary upper semi-continuously with $x \in X$, then a Pesin set with exponentially decaying tails exists for $\mu$. This theorem is subsequently applied to open billiard flows in $\R^d$. As a result, we demonstrate that the non-wandering set of such flows possesses a Pesin set with exponentially small tails relative to any Gibbs measure. This finding is anticipated to yield results concerning exponential mixing for open billiard flows, analogous to those previously obtained for contact Anosov flows in \cite{St4}.

As robots increasingly adopt massive models to enhance functionality and precision, they face escalating computational demands, leading to critical bottlenecks in processing power and battery life. Consequently, fog and cloud robotics have emerged as promising solutions. While cloud robotics approaches have evolved from system-level to node-level architectures, current node-level systems lack the flexibility to dynamically adapt to shifting conditions. To overcome this limitation, we introduce ElasticROS, which transforms existing node-level frameworks into algorithm-level collaborative computing systems. Built upon ROS and ROS2, ElasticROS represents the first robot operating system for fog and cloud environments to operate at the algorithm level. Its core innovation lies in developing elastic collaborative computing to ensure adaptability in dynamic scenarios.

The collaborative computing algorithm serves as the central challenge of ElasticROS. We formulated the problem and developed an algorithm called ElasAction to solve it. ElasAction is a dynamic action decision mechanism based on online learning that orchestrates cooperation between robots and servers. By dynamically updating parameters to respond to real-time environmental changes, it achieves the elastic distribution of computational tasks across robots and servers based on specific configurations. Furthermore, we demonstrated that the regret upper bound of ElasAction is sublinear, ensuring convergence and guaranteeing the stability of ElasticROS's elasticity. Finally, experiments conducted on common robotic tasks—including SLAM, grasping, and human-robot dialogue—measured performance metrics such as latency, CPU usage, and power consumption. The results indicate that the algorithm-level ElasticROS significantly outperforms traditional node-level systems.

This paper investigates a specific class of coagulation equations featuring a source term that introduces clusters of unit order into the system. The coagulation kernel is homogeneous with a degree $\gamma < 1$, behaving approximately as $x^{\gamma + \lambda} y^{-\lambda}$ when $x > y$. The analysis focuses on the regime where $\gamma + 2 \lambda \geq 1$. In this range, the movement of mass toward infinity results from collisions between particles of disparate sizes, contrasting with the scenario where $\gamma + 2 \lambda < 1$, in which mass transport is driven by collisions among particles of similar sizes. For $\gamma+2\lambda\geq 1$, interactions between differently sized particles generate an additional transport term in the coagulation equation that approximates the solution of the original equation with injection at large times. We demonstrate the existence of self-similar solutions for appropriate choices of $\gamma$ and $\lambda$ within this transport-inclusive class of equations, whereas we prove that such solutions do not exist in the complementary case.

This paper employs the $f$-deformed oscillator framework to derive the dynamical algebra of a particle within an infinite spherical well. Specifically, we examine an exciton possessing definite angular momentum inside a large quantum dot that interacts with two laser beams. Under conditions of weak confinement and quantized center-of-mass motion, we demonstrate that the exciton's stationary state can be modeled as a distinct type of nonlinear coherent state characterized by quadrature squeezing.

Energy storage offers a robust mechanism for balancing temporal supply and demand, thereby substantially lowering costs under time-of-use pricing structures. However, the high expense of current storage technologies hinders widespread practical adoption. A more feasible strategy to enhance cost-efficiency involves sharing resources through models like community pooling, cloud storage, and peer-to-peer exchange. Yet, disclosing private consumption data to external operators risks user privacy and exposes data to potential misuse or breaches. This paper introduces a novel privacy-preserving framework for energy storage sharing, leveraging privacy-preserving blockchain and secure multi-party computation. The proposed integrated solution facilitates storage service scheduling and cost allocation without revealing individual user demand profiles. Additionally, it allows grid operators to perform auditing and verification through the blockchain. Crucially, the system protects against a dishonest majority of colluding users without relying on a trusted third party. We deployed this solution as a smart contract on the real-world Ethereum blockchain and present an empirical evaluation in this study.

Building upon recent findings regarding the exact hydrodynamics of diffusive active particles undergoing motility-induced phase separation, we incorporate typical fluctuations of the dynamical fields. Through the exact calculation of correlation functions within the homogeneous phase, we identify the emergence of two macroscopic length scales: one associated with particle diffusion and the other with collective behavior. The latter scale diverges as the system approaches the critical point. Our analysis demonstrates that, under a specific thermodynamic limit, the one-dimensional critical behavior of this model aligns with the mean-field Ising universality class for both static and dynamic properties. When compared to the ABC model, our results reveal a key distinction: unlike the ABC model, the Gaussian approximation of the density large deviation function lacks algebraically decaying interactions. Instead, it exhibits a finite, macroscopic extent governed by the diverging correlation length.

Air pollution stands as a critical global public health crisis, responsible for approximately seven million deaths each year. In Africa, the issue is exacerbated by swift urbanization and inadequate transportation systems. This study examines the spatio-temporal fluctuations of PM2.5 across various African regions. West Africa emerges as the most impacted area, with certain cities such as Lagos, Abuja, and Bamako recording daily averages of 40.856 $\mu g/m^3$. In East Africa, Uganda exhibits the highest pollution levels at 56.14 $\mu g/m^3$, followed by Kigali at 38.65 $\mu g/m^3$. Meanwhile, N'Djamena in Central Africa recorded the peak daily average concentration of 90.075 $\mu g/m^3$. The research further evaluates three data-driven models for forecasting pollution trends, revealing that neural networks outperform both Gaussian processes and ARIMA models.

This paper introduces general one-loop form factors for the process $H\rightarrow \gamma^* \gamma^*$ within the $R_{\xi}$ gauge, covering scenarios where the final photons are two on-shell, one on-shell, or two off-shell. The computations are carried out in both the Standard Model and various Beyond the Standard Model frameworks involving charged scalar particles in one-loop diagrams. Analytic expressions for the form factors are derived in general forms using Passarino-Veltman functions. We further validate our findings against previous calculations applicable to the two on-shell photon case and discuss the $\xi$-independence of the results. Additionally, we demonstrate that numerical outcomes exhibit robust stability across varying values of $\xi$, specifically for $\xi=0$, $\xi=1$, and the limit $\xi\rightarrow \infty$.

Current artificial assistants generally execute tasks based on explicit, imperative instructions like "Set a timer" or "Pick up the box." To advance toward more natural human-agent interactions, it is crucial to comprehend how non-imperative statements can subtly prompt an addressee to act. This study examines command types within a grounded, collaborative game environment, specifically focusing on the less explored category of locative utterances, such as "The chair is in the other room," which serve as indirect commands depending on the specific game context. Our findings demonstrate that models equipped with domain-specific grounding can successfully perform the pragmatic reasoning required for more resilient natural language interaction.

Submatrices of the Fourier matrix are recognized for their ill-conditioned nature. In a recent SIAM Review publication, A. Barnett introduced new bounds regarding the rate of this ill-conditioning for discrete Fourier submatrices. The current paper concentrates on the associated singular value decomposition, where the singular vectors are identified as periodic discrete prolate spheroidal sequences (P-DPSS). These singular values display an initial plateau determined by the submatrix dimensions, followed by a rapid decay known as the plunge region, a behavior consistent with their ill-conditioning. While the discrete prolate sequences have been less explored than their continuous counterparts—the prolate spheroidal wave functions linked to continuous Fourier transforms and extensively studied since Slepian's 1970s work—this paper compiles and extends existing findings on the stable numerical calculation of the singular values and vectors of Fourier submatrices. Furthermore, we demonstrate these computations and highlight several applications involving Fourier submatrices.

Social recommendation systems have demonstrated significant advantages over traditional methods by utilizing social correlation data as an extra input. However, most current research assumes that all necessary data is accessible to a single platform. In reality, user-item interactions (such as ratings) and user-user social connections are typically generated by separate platforms, each holding sensitive information. Consequently, developing a secure and efficient method for cross-platform social recommendation that addresses the inherent sparsity of the data remains a critical challenge. This study integrates secure computation techniques into social recommendation by introducing S3Rec, a sparsity-aware framework designed for secure cross-platform operations. This model enhances recommendation accuracy on the rating platform by incorporating sparse social data from the social platform while simultaneously safeguarding the privacy of both entities. Furthermore, to boost training efficiency, we develop two secure sparse matrix multiplication protocols utilizing homomorphic encryption and private information retrieval. Experimental results on two benchmark datasets validate the effectiveness of the proposed S3Rec framework.

Communication overhead represents the primary bottleneck in distributed training, a challenge frequently addressed through gradient compression to minimize traffic. When integrated with parallel communication strategies such as pipelining, these compression techniques significantly mitigate the impact of communication costs. Nevertheless, two critical issues remain: first, the additional computational burden introduced by compression can delay subsequent training iterations, and second, these methods often result in a reduction of convergence accuracy.

This paper introduces Orthogonal Time Sequency Multiplexing (OTSM), an innovative single-carrier modulation technique that maps information symbols into the delay-sequency domain before applying a series of Time-Division Multiplexing (TDM) and Walsh-Hadamard sequence multiplexing steps. Leveraging the Walsh-Hadamard Transform (WHT), both modulation and demodulation processes avoid complex domain multiplications. For OTSM, the study first establishes the input-output relationship within the delay-sequency domain and introduces a low-complexity detection approach that utilizes zero-padding. Simulation results indicate that OTSM achieves superior performance compared to Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiplexing (OFDM) and performance comparable to Orthogonal Time Frequency Space (OTFS), all with reduced complexity due to the use of WHT. Additionally, a computationally efficient time-domain channel estimation method is proposed. Finally, the paper demonstrates the integration of an outer error control code and a turbo decoder to enhance the error performance of the coded system.

Recent studies on discourse relations indicate that they are signaled not only by discourse markers but also through various other textual cues, with these signaling patterns reflecting specific genres. Although resources like the Penn Discourse Treebank (PDTB) and the Rhetorical Structure Theory Signalling Corpus (RST-SC) contain annotated signaling data, both are restricted to the news domain of the Wall Street Journal within the Penn Treebank. Consequently, this study extends the signal identification and anchoring framework (Liu and Zeldes, 2019) to three additional genres, investigates how signaling devices are distributed across different relations and genres, and establishes a taxonomy for the indicative signals identified in this new dataset.

Let $\omega$ denote a weight defined on a right cancellative semigroup $S$, and let $\|\cdot\|_{\omega}$ represent the corresponding weighted norm on the discrete semigroup algebra $\ell^1(S, \omega)$. This paper establishes that $\omega$ possesses the F-property if and only if the operator norm $\| \cdot \|_{\omega op}$ of $\| \cdot \|_{\omega}$ coincides precisely with a different weighted norm $\| \cdot \|_{\widetilde{\omega}_1}$, as stated in Theorem 2.5 ($iii$). Although the proof is straightforward, the finding is notably counterintuitive; specifically, on $\ell^1(S)$, the operator norm $\| \cdot \|_{1 op}$ is identical to $\| \cdot \|_1$. Furthermore, the study examines various examples to clarify the relationships among $\| \cdot \|_{\omega op}$, $\| \cdot \|_{\omega}$, and the space $\ell^1(S, \omega)$.

This study examines the phase structure of baryonic matter, emphasizing fluctuations that exceed the mean-field approximation. The analysis utilizes the chiral nucleon-meson model as a primary test case, supplemented by observations regarding the chiral quark-meson model. The work explores applications to the liquid-gas phase transition within nuclear matter and extends these findings to dense matter environments. A systematic investigation into the influence of both vacuum fluctuations and thermal excitations reveals that these factors tend to stabilize the hadronic phase, which is defined by spontaneously broken chiral symmetry. Consequently, this stabilization shifts the chiral restoration transition to significantly higher densities. Furthermore, the application of functional renormalisation group methods to account for additional dynamical fluctuations demonstrates that this stabilizing effect is further amplified.

Scale invariance of intrinsic patterns is a fundamental concept in geology, observable across a wide range of geological objects and phenomena. These entities are characterized by statistically self-similar patterns, frequently modeled using fractal geometry. This mathematical framework has been widely applied to describe pore space and fracture distributions in both carbonate and clastic rocks, as well as to analyze transport properties and fluid flow within porous media and reservoirs. Typically, fractal properties are derived from thin-section photomicrographs or scanning electron microscope images. However, for complex rocks like carbonates, automatic feature detection often yields inaccurate results. Furthermore, facies-selective diagenesis can preferentially alter specific rock fabrics, further complicating the automated identification of certain features. To address these challenges, we introduce GeoBoxCount, an interactive program designed for analyzing thin-section images and computing fractal dimensions. By leveraging a geologist's expertise to interpret features of interest, this tool significantly enhances the accuracy of feature selection. The program offers two methods for calculating fractal dimension: the Hausdorff and the Minkowski-Bouligand box-counting techniques.

Continual shifts in traffic patterns, notably those caused by the COVID-19 pandemic, underscore the need to align public transport systems with evolving user requirements. This study demonstrates that single and multi-objective approaches can be synergistically integrated to enhance transit network design problem (TNDP) solutions. In single-objective formulations, network ratings from an approximated multi-objective Pareto front are dynamically analyzed using regression to determine optimal weights for transfer needs, travel times, distances, coverage, and costs. Applied as a case study to Lisbon, Portugal's multimodal network, the system utilizes smartcard data from CARRIS buses and the METRO subway to estimate origin-destination demand. Genetic Algorithms, incorporating both single and multi-objective strategies, are then employed to redesign the bus network to better match observed traffic patterns. The proposed optimization significantly improved outcomes, achieving reductions in objective functions of up to 28.3%. The redesigned network substantially decreased the number of routes while significantly enhancing all passenger-centric metrics, such as travel time and transfers per trip. Based on automated fare collection data, the system enables the incremental redesign of bus networks to dynamically adapt to ongoing urban traffic changes.

Self-interacting dark matter (SIDM) naturally produces a cored isothermal density profile, a feature favored by observations of numerous dwarf galaxies. When a central black hole exists within such an isothermal halo, the dark matter distribution forms a density spike following a power law of $r^{-7/4}$. This profile is notably shallower than the $r^{-7/3}$ power law anticipated for collisionless dark matter (CDM). Consequently, indirect detection limits on dark matter annihilation derived from these spikes can be less stringent in SIDM scenarios. Using Draco, the Milky Way's densest satellite galaxy, as a case study, we establish upper bounds on the annihilation cross-section and black hole mass for both SIDM and CDM halos. In the SIDM context, Draco could potentially host an intermediate-mass black hole even if dark matter consists of thermal relics. We further examine constraints from the Milky Way and M87, which contain supermassive black holes, demonstrating that upper limits on the annihilation cross-section are significantly relaxed under SIDM assumptions. Additionally, our findings suggest that the Event Horizon Telescope offers a distinctive opportunity to test the existence of SIDM spikes.

We demonstrate a factorization theorem applicable to invertible, cross-symmetric, totally nonnegative matrices and apply this theoretical framework to confirm the total nonnegativity of specific instances of Holte's Amazing Matrix.

This study addresses the challenge of maximizing downlink sum-rates with cost awareness by jointly optimizing radio access technology (RAT) assignment and power allocation within next-generation heterogeneous wireless networks (HetNets). The scenario involves a future HetNet featuring multiple RATs and edge devices (EDs) utilizing multi-connectivity. The problem is formulated as a mixed-integer non-linear programming (MINP) task. Given the problem's high complexity, combinatorial nature, and the limitations of conventional solution methods, we introduce DeepRAT, a hierarchical multi-agent deep reinforcement learning (DRL) framework designed for efficient resolution and system dynamics learning. Specifically, DeepRAT splits the task into two phases: an RAT-to-ED assignment phase employing a single-agent Deep Q-Network (DQN), and a power allocation phase utilizing a multi-agent Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG). Simulation results illustrate how these DRL agents interact effectively to learn system dynamics and determine a global optimal policy. Moreover, the simulations indicate that the DeepRAT algorithm surpasses current state-of-the-art heuristic methods regarding network utility. Finally, quantitative analysis confirms the model's capacity to rapidly and dynamically adjust to sudden shifts in network conditions, such as ED mobility.

While the Bloch Sphere effectively illustrates single-qubit states by mapping them one-to-one to a three-dimensional space, it falls short when addressing multi-qubit phenomena like entanglement, which exist in unvisualizable six-dimensional or higher spaces. This paper addresses that limitation by constructing geometric maps for 1- and 2-qubit subspaces that encode state properties both qualitatively and quantitatively. Specifically, a toroidal representation of 2-qubit states reveals the complex topology of the state space while enabling the simultaneous assessment of entanglement levels and the mixed-state characteristics of individual qubits through distances and angles. By minimizing reliance on mathematical formalism, these visualizations aim to clarify fundamental concepts in quantum mechanics and information for introductory learners. Interactive versions of these tools can be accessed at https://quantum.bard.edu/.

Predicting the nature and quantity of plutonium emissions during industrial accidents, such as solvent fires at PUREX reprocessing plants, is a primary focus for nuclear safety authorities. Under accident conditions involving oxygen and water vapor, plutonium is anticipated to form three primary volatile species: $\rm{PuO_2}$, $\rm{PuO_3}$, and $\rm{PuO_2(OH)_2}$. However, the thermodynamic data required for these predictions—specifically enthalpies of formation and heat capacities—currently suffer from significant uncertainties or are entirely absent. This study seeks to address these gaps by deriving the necessary data through relativistic correlated electronic structure calculations using a two-step multi-reference method (MS-CASPT2 with SO-RASSI), a technique capable of accurately modeling the multireference nature of the ground-state wave functions for $\rm{PuO_3}$ and $\rm{PuO_2(OH)_2}$. The validity of this approach is verified by benchmarking it against relativistic coupled cluster calculations for the ground, ionized, and excited states of $\rm{PuO_2}$. Our findings predict enthalpies of formation at $\rm{298.15~K}$ of $\rm{-449.5\pm8.8}$, $\rm{-553.2\pm27.5}$, and $\rm{-1012.6\pm38.1~kJ\;mol^{-1}}$ for $\rm{PuO_2}$, $\rm{PuO_3}$, and $\rm{PuO_2(OH)_2}$, respectively. These results confirm the dominance of plutonium dioxide while also indicating that plutonium trioxide exists in the gas phase under oxidative conditions, although its partial pressures remain low in wet atmospheres. Furthermore, our calculations allow for a re-evaluation of previous $\rm{PuO_2}$ data, confirming that the molecule's ground state is predominantly of $\rm{^{5}\Sigma_{g}^+}$ character and validating the experimental adiabatic ionization energy of $\rm{PuO_2}$.

This work provides analytical findings regarding the structural evolution of networks that develop through a mix of growth mechanisms (node addition and random attachment) and contraction mechanisms (random node deletion). We examine a model where, at each time step, a node is added with probability $P_{add}$ and deleted with probability $P_{del}=1-P_{add}$. The interplay between these opposing forces is defined by the parameter $\eta=P_{add}-P_{del}$. Pure growth corresponds to $\eta=1$. When $0<\eta<1$, node addition outpaces deletion, resulting in overall network expansion. Conversely, if $-1<\eta<0$, the network contracts overall, whereas $\eta=0$ implies a stable expected network size subject only to fluctuations. By applying the master equation, we derive a closed-form solution for the time-dependent degree distribution $P_t(k)$. This distribution comprises a term dependent on the initial distribution $P_0(k)$, which diminishes over time, and an asymptotic distribution $P_{st}(k)$. For pure growth ($\eta=1$), $P_{st}(k)$ is exponential; however, for $-1<\eta<1$, it consists of a sum of Poisson-like terms with a Poisson-like tail. In scenarios of overall growth ($0 < \eta < 1$), $P_t(k)$ converges to $P_{st}(k)$. During overall contraction ($-1 < \eta < 0$), two distinct regimes emerge: for $-1/3 < \eta < 0$, $P_t(k)$ rapidly approaches $P_{st}(k)$, but for $-1 < \eta < -1/3$, convergence is initially sluggish, occurring only just before the network disappears.

Although deep learning has proven effective for tree monitoring and object detection, research regarding tree crowns and fallen trees in flooded zones remains underexplored. Detecting damaged tree trunks in natural settings like water, mudflats, and vegetated areas is difficult due to complex, mixed-color backgrounds. This study utilized Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) equipped with RGB cameras to capture images of fallen *Acacia Xanthophloea* trees across six specific plots surrounding Lake Nakuru, Kenya. To address the need for detecting these fallen trees, two established deep neural networks—Faster R-CNN and RetinaNet—were employed. The research utilized a dataset comprising 7,590 annotations across three classes derived from 256 x 256 pixel image patches. Experimental outcomes demonstrate the applicability of deep learning in this domain, with the RetinaNet model yielding a precision of 38.9% and a recall of 57.9%.

This study addresses the communication of a general bivariate function derived from two classical sources observed at the encoders of a classical-quantum multiple access channel. Leveraging techniques established for classical channels, we introduce and evaluate a coding strategy utilizing coset codes. This approach allows the decoder to reconstruct the target function without needing to recover the original sources. Furthermore, we establish a novel set of sufficient conditions that are less restrictive than existing known conditions for specific identified cases. Our work relies on a new ensemble of coset codes, which are demonstrated to achieve the capacity of a classical-quantum point-to-point channel.

This study examines Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM), a gradient-based technique for deep networks that has demonstrated enhanced performance in image and language tasks. When applied to convex quadratic objectives, we demonstrate that for the majority of random initializations, SAM converges to an oscillating cycle near the minimum along the direction of maximum curvature, and we establish bounds on its convergence rate. In non-quadratic scenarios, these oscillations function similarly to gradient descent but with a reduced step size regarding the spectral norm of the Hessian. Consequently, SAM's update mechanism can be interpreted as a third-order derivative—specifically, the derivative of the Hessian along the leading eigenvector direction—that promotes convergence toward wider minima.

Following the groundbreaking discoveries by LIGO/Virgo, determining the astrophysical origins of gravitational wave (GW) transients remains a critical unresolved issue. In active galactic nuclei (AGNs), the dense stellar populations and gaseous disks facilitate the efficient formation and evolution of binaries. Previous research indicates that stellar-mass black hole (BH) mergers within these environments can account for observed merger rates and suspected hierarchical events. The distribution of binary eccentricity offers a valuable metric for discriminating between competing astrophysical models. This study derives the eccentricity distribution of BH mergers occurring in AGN disks. We determine that binary-single (BS) interactions are the primary driver of eccentricity, resulting in most AGN disk mergers possessing significant eccentricity at $0.01\,\mathrm{Hz}$, a signal detectable by LISA. If BS interactions occur isotropically in three dimensions, between $8$ and $30\%$ of mergers will exhibit eccentricities at $10\,\mathrm{Hz}$ exceeding $e_{10\,\rm Hz}\gtrsim 0.03$ (observable by LIGO/Virgo/KAGRA), with $5$--$17\%$ reaching $e_{10\,\rm Hz}\geq 0.3$. Conversely, if disk torques restrict BS interactions to the AGN-disk plane—allowing for 1–20 intermediate binary states—or if BHs migrate to distances less than $\lesssim10^{-3}\,\mathrm{pc}$ from the central supermassive black hole, then $10$--$70\%$ of mergers will be highly eccentric ($e_{10\,\rm Hz} \geq 0.3$), a scenario consistent with the high eccentricity potentially observed in GW190521.

The debate over whether artificial entities or machines can achieve self-awareness or consciousness has persisted in philosophy for centuries. The core challenge lies in the fact that self-awareness cannot be observed externally, and determining if a system is truly conscious or merely simulating it requires intimate knowledge of its internal mechanisms. This review examines the current state of these advancements and analyzes common machine learning approaches regarding their potential for self-awareness. We find that many critical algorithmic steps toward machines with core consciousness have already been developed. However, achieving human-level intelligence will require the discovery of numerous additional techniques.

Electrons traversing noncoplanar magnetic textures accumulate a Berry phase, interpretable as an effective magnetic field, a phenomenon identified as the topological Hall effect observed in topological spin structures. Driven by recent experimental advances, we investigate the Hall effect within a non-topological magnetic configuration called a target skyrmion. Beginning with a simplified semiclassical framework, we demonstrate that the Hall signal varies nonmonotonically with both electronic energy and the target skyrmion's radius. This finding persists in a fully quantum mechanical approach utilizing the Landauer-Büttiker formalism within a mesoscopic context. Consequently, our results challenge the prevailing community belief that a nonzero skyrmion number is a prerequisite for the Hall effect in such systems.

This study examines an extension of the influential Granovetter model of social behavior, where individual actions are driven by personal preferences and the observed behavior of neighbors. Individuals are positioned within a network—typically a square lattice—and possess a specific state along with a fixed threshold for behavioral change. The system is simulated asynchronously through two mechanisms: randomly selecting an individual to update its state or to exchange places with another randomly chosen individual (mixing). Analytically, the dynamics are described in the fast-mixing limit using mean-field approximation, while numerical investigation focuses on scenarios with finite mixing rates. We demonstrate that the system's dynamics converge to a manifold within the state space that defines possible equilibria, and we outline a method to estimate this manifold's projection by analyzing simulated trajectories originating from various initial conditions. Furthermore, we show that the impact of network structure can be decomposed into finite-neighborhood effects and finite-mixing-rate effects, which exhibit qualitatively similar outcomes. Both factors enhance the system's propensity to transition from less-desired equilibria toward the "ground state." These findings offer a framework for investigating shifts in behavioral norms and provide insights into how information flow influences the persistence or disappearance of unpopular social norms, such as foot binding or female genital cutting.

While algorithmic recourse has been studied for supervised machine learning to enhance the interpretability, transparency, and robustness of decision support systems, its application to anomaly detection—particularly for tabular data with discrete features—remains largely unexplored. In this domain, the objective is to generate a set of counterfactuals classified as normal by the anomaly detection model, enabling explanations and the recommendation of countermeasures. We introduce CARAT (Context-preserving Algorithmic Recourse for Anomalies in Tabular data), an approach that is effective, scalable, and model-agnostic regarding the underlying anomaly detection method. CARAT employs a transformer-based encoder-decoder architecture to identify features with low likelihood, thereby explaining the anomaly. It then produces semantically coherent counterfactuals by modifying these highlighted features while maintaining the overall context of the anomalous instance. Comprehensive experiments validate the efficacy of CARAT.

Cosmic Ray (CR) impacts represent the primary source of contamination in astronomical imaging and spectroscopic data acquired with solid-state detectors. Accurately identifying and masking these events is essential within image processing workflows to prevent false detections. To address this, we developed and evaluated a novel Deep Learning framework for the automated detection of CR hits in data from two distinct imagers: the Dark Energy Camera (DECam) and the Las Cumbres Observatory Global Telescope (LCOGT). Our approach builds upon two state-of-the-art baseline models, deepCR (trained on Hubble Space Telescope ACS/WFC data) and Cosmic-CoNN (trained on LCOGT Network images), by experimenting with the integration of Attention Gates (AGs) to enhance detection performance. Models were trained on DECam data, yielding consistent marginal gains in True Positive Rate (TPR) at a 0.01% False Positive Rate (FPR) and Precision at 95% TPR compared to the baselines. Furthermore, testing on previously unseen LCO data comprising images from three different telescope classes revealed that the AG-augmented models significantly improved TPR at 0.01% FPR. We also demonstrated that both our baseline models and their AG-augmented variants outperformed existing state-of-the-art solutions, including Astro-SCRAPPY, Maximask (natively trained on DECam), and the pre-trained ground-based Cosmic-CoNN. Ultimately, this study confirms that augmenting deepCR and Cosmic-CoNN with AG modules enhances their generalization capabilities on unseen datasets.

Planar Josephson junctions offer a flexible alternative to nanowire geometries for generating Majorana bound states, primarily due to the enhanced phase tunability they provide for topological superconductivity. Previous work demonstrated significant potential in manipulating this phenomenon through the proximity induction of chiral magnetism and superconductivity within a two-dimensional electron gas. In this study, we examine a Josephson junction incorporating a skyrmion crystal, revealing that the skyrmions' chiral magnetism can generate and regulate Majorana bound states without necessitating intrinsic Rashba spin-orbit coupling. Notably, these states emerge robustly at zero phase difference across the junction. Furthermore, the externally tunable skyrmion radius, adjustable via magnetic fields or magnetic anisotropy, introduces a distinctive mechanism for controlling the Majorana bound states.

We present an extension of Kaczynski's theorem concerning boundary functions within $n$-dimensional space. Let $H$ represent the upper half-plane and $X$ denote its boundary, the $x$-axis. Consider a function $f$ that maps $H$ into a metric space $Y$. For any subset $E \subseteq X$, a function $\varphi: E \rightarrow Y$ is defined as a boundary function for $f$ if and only if, for every $x \in E$, there exists an arc $\gamma$ terminating at $x$ such that $\lim_{z\rightarrow x \atop z\in\gamma} f(z) = \varphi(x)$.

The century-old Abraham-Minkowski dilemma in macroscopic electrodynamics centers on observing the Abraham force term, defined as ${\bf f}^{\rm Aterm} = [(\varepsilon\mu-1)/c^2] \partial/\partial t ({\bf E}\times {\bf H})$. Although recent radiation optics experiments have yielded elegant results, they typically fail to detect this term because it fluctuates away, leaving researchers reliant on indirect confirmations such as Jones {et al.}'s 1950s measurements of radiation pressure on a mirror within a dielectric liquid. A distinct approach involves utilizing low (quasi-stationary) frequencies to directly observe the force's sinusoidal variation. Walker {\it et al.} pioneered such experiments in the 1970s using BaTiO$_3$ as a high-permittivity dielectric ($\varepsilon \sim 3600$). Given the emergence of modern dielectric materials with permittivities reaching $10^5$ or higher, it is logical to revisit Walker's methodology to determine if the experiment can be made more accessible and accurate, which is the primary focus of this paper. Successful outcomes from these trials robustly support the Abraham energy-momentum tensor in low-frequency regimes, whereas the Minkowski tensor predicts no torque whatsoever. Consequently, low- and high-frequency behaviors stand in stark contrast; while the Minkowski tensor remains the most practical choice for optical experiments, the Abraham tensor is favored at lower frequencies. The note concludes by addressing the Einstein-Laub tensor's (1908) applicability to this scenario and examining the effects of air friction.

The Gaussian mechanism (GM) stands as a foundational instrument for ensuring differential privacy (DP), inspiring extensive research. We propose that the three dominant frameworks for interpreting GM—$(\varepsilon, \delta)$-DP, $f$-DP, and Rényi DP—can be unified through a single parameter, $\psi$, which we designate the sensitivity index. This index uniquely defines the GM and its characteristics by integrating its two core components: query sensitivity and noise magnitude. Leveraging connections to ROC curves and the hypothesis-testing perspective of DP, $\psi$ equips practitioners with a robust framework for analyzing, comparing, and conveying the privacy assurances of Gaussian mechanisms.

This paper employs an optimal partition approach to investigate the parametric analysis of a second-order conic optimization problem with an objective function perturbed in a fixed direction. We define and characterize the invariancy set and nonlinearity interval, which act as stability regions for the optimal partition. Additionally, assuming the strict complementarity condition, we introduce an iterative algorithm to calculate a nonlinearity interval. Under conditions of primal and dual nondegeneracy, we demonstrate that boundary points of a nonlinearity interval can be numerically determined via a nonlinear reformulation of the parametric problem. These theoretical findings are validated through numerical experiments.

Incorporating physics models into machine learning offers significant potential for creating robust systems with enhanced interpretability and extrapolation capabilities. This study specifically addresses the integration of incomplete physics models into deep generative frameworks. We propose a variational autoencoder (VAE) architecture where a segment of the latent space is anchored by physical laws. A primary technical hurdle involves balancing these incomplete physics constraints with trainable neural network components to ensure the physics module functions meaningfully. To address this, we introduce a regularized learning approach that modulates the influence of trainable elements while safeguarding the intended semantics of the physics-driven latent variables. Our results demonstrate superior generative performance across various synthetic and real-world datasets, alongside the ability to learn robust models that reliably extrapolate beyond the training distribution. Furthermore, we illustrate that the generative process can be steered in an interpretable fashion.

Non-rigid registration serves as a fundamental element in soft-tissue navigation, specifically within laparoscopic liver surgery. This process involves aligning a preoperative CT-derived organ model with an intraoperative surface reconstructed from laparoscopic video. The task is complex due to factors such as sparse and noisy real-time data, numerous unknowns regarding tissue properties and boundary conditions, and the difficulty of establishing correspondences between pre- and intraoperative datasets. These challenges are exacerbated by the liver's lack of distinct surface features and the disparate noise characteristics of the imaging modalities used. To address this, we developed a convolutional neural network that simultaneously performs surface correspondence search and non-rigid registration. The network was trained on physically accurate biomechanical simulations of randomly generated, deforming organ-like structures, enabling immediate generalization to new patients without retraining. By incorporating varying levels of noise into the intraoperative surfaces during training, the model achieves robustness against noisy data. During inference, the network generates a displacement field that aligns the preoperative volume with the partial intraoperative surface. Experimental results demonstrate that the approach effectively translates to real-world data while maintaining high inference speed, and the source code is publicly available.

Linearizability, the conventional correctness criterion for concurrent data structures, is deemed inadequate for non-volatile shared memory environments where processes recover after crashing. In this crash-recovery context, strict-linearizability is the preferred standard because, unlike standard linearizability, it guarantees that operations either complete before a crash or do not occur at all. This study formally addresses whether an implementation designed for the crash-stop model remains strict-linearizable within the crash-recovery framework. Through a rigorous analysis, we demonstrate that helping mechanisms, common in non-blocking designs, serve as the algorithmic distinction between linearizability and strict-linearizability. Our primary contribution involves formalizing the crash-recovery model and illustrating how explicit crashes and recoveries add complexity beyond the standard crash-stop model. Our specific technical contributions include: (i) proving that strict-linearizability is independent of existing help definitions; (ii) introducing a natural definition of "help-freedom" to show that any obstruction-free, linearizable, and help-free implementation of a total object type is also strict-linearizable; and (iii) establishing that for a broad class of object types, a non-blocking strict-linearizable implementation cannot utilize helping. Collectively, this work offers the first precise characterization of the complexities involved in adapting concurrent implementations between the crash-stop and crash-recovery models.

This study provides an analytical solution to the quantum absorption refrigerator within the space of holomorphic functions equipped with a Gaussian measure. Our methodology streamlines computations because the coordinate representation of any quantum state is inherently more intricate than its expression in terms of phase-space coordinates, $z_{i}$. We conclude by examining the computational complexity of the holomorphic representation, contrasting it with the standard operator method, and demonstrating the efficiency of the former for specific tasks. Furthermore, our framework is universally applicable to all quantum heat engines and refrigerators.

We begin by re-examining the search for BPS solutions within $\mathcal{N}=4$ SU(2)$\times$SU(2) gauged supergravity. We present a novel supersymmetric solution located in the Abelian sector, representing a globally regular soliton that preserves 1/4 of the supersymmetry. This solution arises via a double analytic continuation of a planar solution originally identified by Klemm in hep-th/9810090. Within the same Abelian sector, but utilizing a spherically symmetric ansatz, we discover another new solution whose supersymmetric character was previously missed. Shifting to the non-Abelian sector, we employ the meron ansatz for SU(2) to construct electric-meronic and double-meron solutions; the latter yield singular 1/4 BPS configurations that possess an additional conformal Killing vector. Extending beyond the standard supergravity framework, we modify the scalar self-interaction while retaining the meron ansatz for a single, dilatonically coupled gauge field. In this context, we derive exact black holes for two families of self-interactions that include topologically Lifshitz black holes, alongside other solutions featuring distinctive causal structures and asymptotic behaviors, and we investigate their thermal properties.

Histopathological tissue classification is a cornerstone of pathomics cancer research, where accurately distinguishing tissue types significantly benefits downstream applications such as diagnosis and prognosis. While existing methods typically rely on standard computer vision classification backbones, this paper introduces a super lightweight, plug-and-play module called Pyramidal Deep-Broad Learning (PDBL). Designed to enhance classification performance without requiring retraining, PDBL mimics the multi-magnification observation process of pathologists by constructing an image pyramid to capture pyramidal contextual information. For each pyramid level, a proposed Deep-Broad block (DB-block) extracts multi-scale deep-broad features. The module was integrated into three popular backbones—ShuffleNetV2, EfficientNet-B0, and ResNet50—to evaluate its effectiveness and efficiency on the Kather Multiclass and LC25000 datasets. Experimental results confirm that PDBL consistently improves tissue-level classification across various CNN architectures, particularly benefiting lightweight models when training data is scarce (under 10%), thereby substantially reducing computational costs and annotation efforts.

When a climate system approaches a tipping point, its linear response to disturbances becomes degenerate, often corresponding to extreme values of equilibrium climate sensitivity (ECS). This study compares linearized (instantaneous) and fully nonlinear geometric (two-point) definitions of ECS, examining both scenarios where tipping points exist and where they do not. Using a stochastic energy balance model of global mean surface temperature featuring two stable states, we demonstrate that tipping events induce extreme values in both ECS concepts. Additionally, the two-point ECS reveals multiple regimes with distinct mean sensitivities. We further validate these results using a physics-based multi-box model of the climate system.

This paper introduces the Brand-Topic Model (BTM), designed to identify topics linked to brands that carry sentiment polarity within product reviews. Unlike current sentiment-topic extraction models that restrict topics to discrete sentiment categories like `positive`, `negative`, or `neutral`, the BTM automatically derives continuous, real-valued sentiment scores for brand-associated topics. This capability allows for the generation of fine-grained sentiment-topics where one can observe gradual sentiment shifts within a specific topic (e.g., regarding `shaver` or `cream`) as associated words transition from negative to positive. Built upon a Poisson factorization framework enhanced with adversarial learning, the BTM was assessed using a dataset derived from Amazon reviews. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that the BTM surpasses several competitive baselines in brand ranking, successfully achieving a superior balance between topic coherence and uniqueness while extracting more distinctly separated polarity-bearing topics.

Accreting protoplanets offer critical understanding of planetary assembly within their natal disks. While Zhou et al. (2021) previously detected the young accreting planet PDS 70 b in the F656N ($\mathrm{H}\alpha$) band with a signal-to-noise ratio (S/N) of 7.9 using angular differential imaging (ADI) on HST/WFC3, this study presents an efficient alternative by applying reference star differential imaging (RDI) to the identical dataset. We constructed a reference library from the Space Telescope Science Institute's database of WFC3 point-spread functions (PSFs) and established morphology-significance criteria to optimize the pre-selection of reference frames for improved subtraction. Although RDI utilizing this PSF library yielded a lower S/N of 5.3 for PDS 70 b, we calibrated its astrometry and photometry via forward-modeling and injection-recovery tests, determining a separation of $186 \pm 13$ mas, a position angle of $142 \pm 5^\circ$, and an $\mathrm{H}\alpha$ flux of $(1.7 \pm 0.3)\times10^{-15}$ erg s$^{-1}$ cm$^{-2}$. The reduced detection significance in the RDI results stems from the reference PSFs having peak-to-background ratios approximately 100 times lower than those of the ADI PSFs. Constructing high-quality WFC3 reference libraries offers distinct advantages for investigating short-timescale accretion variability without roll-angle scheduling limitations and for efficiently identifying actively accreting protoplanets in $\mathrm{H}\alpha$ around targets unsuitable for ground-based adaptive optics, such as faint transition disk hosts.

We examine $\mathbb{Z}_2$-synchronization on the Euclidean lattice, where each vertex in $\mathbb{Z}^d$ is assigned an independent symmetric random sign $\theta_u$. For every edge $(u,v)$, the product $\theta_u\theta_v$ is observed after being independently flipped with probability $p$. The objective is to reconstruct these products for vertex pairs separated by arbitrary distances. Abbé, Massoulié, Montanari, Sly, and Srivastava (2018) established that synchronization is achievable if and only if $p$ remains below a critical threshold $\tilde{p}_c(d)$, with efficient recovery possible for sufficiently small $p$.
