We extend this framework by incorporating a side-information model that maintains the sign symmetry of $\theta$, introducing an \emph{efficient} algorithm capable of synchronizing a randomly selected distant pair of vertices on average, up to a distinct critical threshold $p_c(d)$. We conjecture that $p_c(d) = \tilde{p}_c(d)$ for all dimensions $d \ge 2$. Our approach involves \emph{renormalizing} the synchronization model to lower the effective noise parameter, followed by the application of a modified multiscale algorithm based on AMMSS. The viability of this renormalization relies on a credible yet unproven assumption regarding the regularity of the free energy in an Ising spin glass model on $\mathbb{Z}^d$.

This study examines the incompressible limit of the compressible magnetohydrodynamic equations, featuring vanishing viscosity coefficients and general initial data defined over the entire space $\mathbb{R}^d$ (where $d=2$ or $3$). It is rigorously demonstrated that as the Mach number, shear viscosity coefficient, and magnetic diffusion coefficient simultaneously approach zero, the weak solution of the compressible magnetohydrodynamic equations converges to the strong solution of the ideal incompressible magnetohydrodynamic equations, provided the latter exists.

Enhancing code sharing in programs is beneficial for reducing size and preventing redundant runtime computations, which accelerates execution. We demonstrate how to achieve maximum sharing for programs represented as lambda calculus terms with `letrec`. We define a concept of "maximal compactness" for these terms based on their infinite unfolding, utilizing graph semantics rather than purely syntactic definitions. Specifically, `lambda-letrec` terms are interpreted as first-order term graphs, ensuring that unfolding equivalence is maintained and reflected through graph bisimilarity. Consequently, the compactness of these graphs can be evaluated using functional bisimulation.

We outline practical and efficient solutions for two key challenges: converting a `lambda-letrec` term into its most compact form and determining if two such terms are unfolding-equivalent. The transformation of a term $L$ into a maximally compact version $L_0$ involves three stages: (i) translating $L$ into its term graph $G = [[ L ]]$; (ii) calculating the bisimulation collapse $G_0$ to obtain the maximally shared form of $G$; and (iii) reconstructing a `lambda-letrec` term $L_0$ from $G_0$ such that $[[ L_0 ]] = G_0$. This ensures $L_0$ and $L$ share the same unfolding while $L_0$ maximizes sharing.

To decide unfolding-equivalence between two terms $L_1$ and $L_2$, the procedure computes their respective term graph interpretations, $[[ L_1 ]]$ and $[[ L_2 ]]$, and verifies if these graphs are bisimilar. Additionally, we provide a functional implementation to demonstrate these concepts.

Although advancements in scientific instruments have expanded the capabilities of Mars rover missions, the resulting surge in data complexity has strained the operations teams of the Mars Science Laboratory (MSL) and future rovers. These staff members face increasing pressure to rapidly analyze intricate datasets within progressively tighter tactical and strategic planning windows. MSLWEB serves as an internal tracking utility for operations personnel, facilitating initial assessments of MSL image sequences captured by the Mastcam. Because Mastcam's multiband multispectral imagery demands more sophisticated analysis than standard 3-band RGB photos, traditional methods are often used to pinpoint unique features. However, the urgency of tactical planning—requiring the analysis of downlinked images within 5 to 10 hours prior to the next uplink—necessitates a triage strategy to prioritize critical sequences and segments. To address this, we developed MSLWEB products leveraging novelty detection to assist staff in flagging anomalous data that may indicate novel or atypical mineralogies and compositions within imaging scenes. This was accomplished through two mechanisms: 1) generating per-sequence products to highlight novel image regions, and 2) assigning multispectral sequences a sortable novelty score. These innovations produce colorized heat maps of inferred novelty, enabling staff to swiftly review downlinked data and concentrate on potentially new diagnostic multispectral signatures. Ultimately, this methodology holds the promise of guiding scientists toward new discoveries by rapidly highlighting subtle variations that are often invisible in simple color composites.

We investigate the relationship between embedded young massive star clusters (YMCs) and (sub-)millimeter line observations that map the excitation and dissociation of molecular gas within the starburst ring of NGC 1365. This galaxy is notable for hosting one of the most intense nuclear starbursts and the densest populations of YMCs within 20 Mpc. By combining new ALMA multi-J CO (1-0, 2-1, and 4-3) and [CI](1-0) data with near-/mid-IR PHANGS-JWST imaging, we trace gas properties at 330 pc resolution. Specifically, we use the ratios R42 = I_CO(4-3)/I_CO(2-1) and R21 = I_CO(2-1)/I_CO(1-0) to assess CO excitation, and RCICO = I_[CI](1-0)/I_CO(2-1) to measure dissociation. Our analysis reveals that gas flowing from the northeast to the southwest into the starburst ring is significantly impacted by stellar feedback, exhibiting reduced excitation (lower R42) and enhanced dissociation signatures (higher RCICO) in downstream areas. Radiative transfer modeling indicates that in these regions, molecular gas density drops while temperature and the [CI/CO] abundance ratio rise. Comparing R42 and RCICO with local conditions shows that both correlate with near-IR 2 $\mu$m emission from YMCs, as well as PAH (11.3 $\mu$m) and dust continuum (21 $\mu$m) emission. Notably, RCICO demonstrates approximately 0.1 dex tighter correlations than R42, suggesting that [CI] is a more sensitive tracer of varying physical conditions in the NGC 1365 starburst than CO (4-3). These findings support a scenario where gas enters the two arm regions along the bar, undergoes condensation and shock, forms YMCs, and subsequently, these clusters heat and dissociate the surrounding gas.

Mining Software Repositories (MSR) has emerged as a critical component of software development, with a growing focus on extracting architectural data to facilitate tasks like architecture recovery and comprehension. Despite this interest, a holistic view of the current research landscape in this area remains lacking. This study aims to systematically identify, analyze, and synthesize existing literature regarding the mining of architectural information from software repositories, specifically examining the types of information and sources extracted, the architecting activities supported, the methodologies and tools employed, and the associated challenges. A Systematic Mapping Study (SMS) was conducted on publications released between January 2006 and November 2021. The analysis of 79 primary studies revealed eight categories of mined architectural information, with architectural descriptions being the most frequently extracted; 12 architecting activities can be supported by these insights, led by architecture understanding; 81 distinct approaches and 52 tools have been proposed and utilized; and four primary challenges were identified. Ultimately, this SMS offers researchers valuable future research directions and assists practitioners in understanding which approaches and tools are available to extract specific architectural information from various sources to support diverse architecting activities.

This study applies the Orthonormal Polynomial Expansion Method (OPEM) to approximate the previously estimated excess specific heat ratio, $C^{excess}/T^{5}$, for two fluoropolymers: PTFE and PCTFE. A novel aspect of this OPEM implementation is the incorporation of experimental errors at each data point as weighting functions. The temperature-dependent behavior of $C^{excess}/T^{5}$ is analyzed across the full ranges of 0.4–8 K for PTFE and 2.5–7 K for PCTFE, with additional subdivision into (0.4–2) K and (2.5–8) K intervals for PTFE. The paper presents numerical results quantifying the deviations between the experimental data and the approximated values. Furthermore, it proposes standard polynomial coefficients derived via orthonormal methods within the OPEM framework, alongside calculated absolute, relative, and specific sensitivities at every point for the thermal characteristic. The approximation parameters for this thermal property are illustrated in the accompanying figures and tables.

Uncertainty quantification for intricate technical systems frequently relies on computer simulations. However, since every model, including these computational ones, inherently fails to perfectly capture reality, this article reviews methods that incorporate observed system data to address such modeling deficiencies in uncertainty analysis. These techniques are demonstrated and evaluated through their application to problems in mechanical engineering.

The Quantum Fisher Information matrix (QFIM) serves as a pivotal metric for advanced algorithms like Quantum Natural Gradient Descent and Variational Quantum Imaginary Time Evolution. However, calculating the complete QFIM for a model with $d$ parameters is computationally intensive, typically demanding $\mathcal{O}(d^2)$ function evaluations. To address these escalating costs within high-dimensional parameter spaces, we introduce an approach utilizing simultaneous perturbation stochastic approximation to estimate the QFIM with constant computational expense. We detail this new algorithm and demonstrate its efficacy in preparing Hamiltonian ground states and training Variational Quantum Boltzmann Machines.

This paper presents a reformulation of a three-dimensional polynomial affine gravity model, which is constructed without explicitly relying on a metric tensor field. By decomposing the affine connection, we examine consistently truncated sectors. Applying a cosmological ansatz to the connection, we investigate cosmological solutions within these truncated sectors and discuss how various types of metrics emerge.

Symmetry invariants of a group define the quantum numbers of quasiparticles in systems possessing that symmetry. Discrete point groups possess more known symmetry invariants than the full rotation group $\mathrm{O(3)}$, leading to the emergence of "new fermions" as lattice-restricted excitations with no vacuum counterparts. This study examines fermion excitation classes under spin-space group symmetries, relevant to materials featuring coexisting long-range magnetic order and itinerant electrons. We provide a list of symmetry invariants exclusive to spin-space groups, which facilitate novel quasiparticles, including a 12-fold Dirac fermion and a 13-nodal-line-nexus fermion, previously unproposed in the literature.

We demonstrate that a pair of singularities linked by a transformation derived from the McKay correspondence are orbifold equivalent, which subsequently implies a McKay-type categorical equivalence for their respective matrix factorization categories.

This paper applies Faa di Bruno's formula to link Bell polynomial values with differential equations of the form $y^{\prime}=f(y)$. Specifically, we employ partial Bell polynomials to express the solution to these equations and subsequently utilize that solution to determine special values of the partial Bell polynomials.

This study examines the average order of a connected induced subgraph within a graph, extending the concept of the average order of a subtree in a tree. While Jamison established in 1984 that the path $P_n$ minimizes the average order across all trees of order $n$, Kroeker, Mol, and Oellermann conjectured in 2018 that $P_n$ achieves this minimum for all connected graphs. The primary finding of this paper validates that conjecture.

Standard methods for pinpointing information sources in complex networks typically rely on the assumption of full and precise knowledge of the network's topology. This study evaluates three such algorithms—LPTVA, GMLA, and the Pearson correlation method—under conditions where this assumption is violated by altering the network structure before localization. Modifications include inserting unnecessary links, concealing existing ones, or reattaching links based on the network's structural Hamiltonian. Our findings indicate that GMLA demonstrates high resilience against the addition of extra edges, with precision dropping beyond statistical uncertainty only when the link count roughly doubles. Conversely, GMLA's performance declines significantly if the edge set is underestimated or if links are reattached. In these instances, the Pearson algorithm is superior, maintaining most of its efficacy when simulation parameters favor localization, such as high observer density and deterministic propagation. Furthermore, the Pearson method is generally more accurate than LPTVA and operates orders of magnitude faster. While these algorithmic differences can be intuitively understood, further theoretical research is required.

We rely more and more on diverse algorithmic systems driven by data to support us in numerous areas of daily life. Beyond search engines, recommender systems serve as vital sources of information, aiding decisions ranging from choosing restaurants and books to selecting friends and career paths. This growing reliance has sparked significant concerns about the fairness of these technologies. In this paper, we introduce a comprehensive toolkit comprising definitions, models, and methods designed to ensure fairness in rankings and recommendations. Our goals are threefold: (a) to establish a robust framework within a rapidly evolving and impactful field, (b) to review existing methods and contextualize them, and (c) to identify open challenges and potential research directions for future work.

Robot planning often involves a trade-off between model fidelity and performance. Analytical models offer rapid evaluation but are restricted to specific conditions, whereas physics simulators capture complex object interactions at a higher computational cost. Learning when to switch between these models can significantly enhance both planning speed and task success reliability. This study introduces Model Deviation Estimators (MDEs) to forecast discrepancies between real-world states and those predicted by transition models. These estimators define preconditions that identify when specific transitions are accurately modeled. Consequently, we propose a planner that leverages these learned preconditions to dynamically switch between models, prioritizing faster options when they remain accurate. The method's effectiveness is validated on two real-world tasks: inserting a rod into a box and placing a rod into a closed drawer.

Current continual learning strategies typically address either task incremental learning (TIL) or class incremental learning (CIL) in isolation, as these two scenarios differ fundamentally: TIL provides task identifiers for test samples, whereas CIL does not. Methods designed for one scenario often fail to perform adequately in the other. To overcome this limitation, this paper introduces CLOM, a unified framework leveraging out-of-distribution (OOD) detection and task masking. The core innovation involves training each task as an OOD detector instead of a standard supervised model, while simultaneously training a task mask to mitigate forgetting. Experimental results demonstrate that CLOM significantly surpasses existing state-of-the-art baselines, achieving an average accuracy of 87.6% for TIL and 67.9% for CIL across six experiments, compared to the best baselines' 82.4% and 55.0%, respectively.

This study introduces a new approach to classifying Type Ia supernovae by leveraging convolutional neural networks, a technique traditionally associated with image recognition. Our model relies exclusively on photometric data, thereby removing the dependency on precise redshift measurements. Photometric inputs are pre-processed using 2D Gaussian process regression to generate two-dimensional images representing flux values across wavelength-time coordinates. These "flux heatmaps," paired with corresponding "uncertainty heatmaps" derived from Gaussian process uncertainty, form the training dataset. This preprocessing strategy not only mitigates irregular sampling intervals between filters but also ensures that SCONE remains independent of the specific filter sets used during training. The model demonstrates exceptional performance in in-distribution SNIa classification without redshift data, achieving a test accuracy of $99.73 \pm 0.26$% with no signs of overfitting or underfitting on a subset of supernovae from PLAsTiCC's unblinded test set. Additionally, we attained a $98.18 \pm 0.3$% test accuracy in a 6-way classification task to distinguish supernovae by type. However, out-of-distribution performance lags behind in-distribution results, indicating that discrepancies between training and test sample characteristics significantly influence model efficacy. We examine the implications of these findings and outline directions for future research. All data processing scripts and model code utilized in this work are available in the SCONE software package at github.com/helenqu/scone.

We introduce cKAM, or cyclical Kernel Adaptive Metropolis, which utilizes a cyclical stepsize mechanism to regulate exploration and sampling. Our findings demonstrate that on a specifically designed bimodal distribution, traditional Adaptive Metropolis algorithms fail to converge to the true posterior. This failure occurs because adaptive samplers estimate covariance structures based on the chain's historical data, causing them to become trapped in local modes. In contrast, cKAM promotes thorough exploration of the posterior, enabling the sampler to escape local modes while retaining the high performance characteristic of adaptive methods.
It has been demonstrated that the Landauer erasure principle prevents the exploitation of Maxwell's demon to circumvent tests of quantum non-locality.

This study introduces and validates a straightforward adaptive surface remeshing method designed to migrate history-dependent variables from a degrading mesh to a new one during finite element analyses of elastic surface deformation. By employing this approach, we minimize errors caused by severe mesh distortion while retaining data regarding the mesh's original configuration and its associated history-dependent variables. The proposed method generates the new mesh's initial state by accounting for the distortion of the previous mesh elements and projecting backward in time. With this reconstructed initial configuration, stress and strain calculations on the new mesh become straightforward. Following an outline of the reconstruction steps, we demonstrate that this relatively simple transfer strategy enhances simulation stability and decreases both spatial and strain errors across the domain. Ultimately, the novel technique described here offers an easy-to-implement solution for stabilizing simulations subjected to large deformations.

Precise predictions for non-linear power spectra across various redshifts ($z$) are essential for interpreting data from future mass-probe cosmological surveys to constrain the nature of Dark Energy. This objective necessitates high-precision simulations that span the entire functional space of the Dark Energy equation of state, $w(z)$, while accounting for permissible variations in other cosmological parameters—a formidable challenge. A previous method was proposed to achieve accuracy up to $k \sim 3 \, h\text{Mpc}^{-1}$ at $z=0$ for nearly arbitrary $w(z)$ models by leveraging results from $N$-body simulations with constant $w$. In this study, we extend this methodology to high redshifts and validate it using a suite of $N$-body gravitational simulations of diverse models, including one consistent with WMAP5 and complementary observations. Our approach successfully identifies constant-$w$ models that satisfy the $z=0$ criteria within 1% and achieve even superior precision at higher redshifts, reaching close to the permil level. Conversely, existing Halofit expressions, even when extended to constant $w \neq -1$, prove unsuitable for fitting the spectra of the physical models examined here. Nevertheless, extending these expressions to cover the required range appears feasible, which would allow for the matching of spectra from any Dark Energy equation of state.

We investigate integral curvature conditions imposed on a Riemannian metric $g$ defined on $S^4$ to determine the optimal bilipschitz constant relative to the standard metric on $S^4$. Our findings demonstrate that this optimal constant is bounded by the $L^2$-norm of the Weyl tensor and the $L^1$-norm of the $Q$-curvature, provided these values are sufficiently small, the metric possesses a positive Yamabe constant, and the $Q$-curvature exhibits a mean-positive property. The proof proceeds in two stages: first, we construct a quasiconformal map connecting two metrics within the same positive Yamabe class, and second, we utilize the Ricci flow to establish bilipschitz equivalence between this conformal class and the standard conformal class on $S^4$.

Although widespread acceptance of climate change and its escalating consequences exists, meaningful dialogue remains scarce, thereby hindering the pace of societal transformation required to mitigate it. To facilitate more effective climate communication, our objective is to develop a system that delivers climate predictions tailored to an individual's specific personal values, thereby maximizing their motivation and inspiration to act. To overcome the cold-start challenge, this system utilizes a knowledge base known as ClimateKB, which maps the causes and effects of climate change to personal values. As no comprehensive ClimateKB currently exists, we are revisiting knowledge base construction methodologies to generate one from free-text sources. Furthermore, we intend to release the ClimateKB and its accompanying code as open-source resources to foster future research and practical applications.

In their 2012 *AMS Notices* piece, "Debunking Myths about Gender and Mathematics Performance," Kane and Mertz assert that the greater male variability hypothesis regarding math abilities has been disproven. However, the logical and statistical arguments they present, which are frequently cited in scientific literature, suffer from fundamental errors. Their methodology is critically defective, their primary logical premise is incorrect, and they fail to cite numerous published studies that contradict their results. Most significantly, their ultimate conclusion—that their data refute the greater male variability hypothesis—is erroneous. The purpose of this note is to rectify the scientific record concerning these assertions. Furthermore, by exposing these mistakes, the *Notices* can help prevent similar errors from being repeated in the future.

We employ manifestly covariant quantization for a scale-invariant gravity model coupled with a scalar field, which, through a scalar field redefinition, corresponds to the established Brans-Dicke gravity under the de Donder (harmonic) gauge condition for general coordinate invariance. Initially, without committing to a specific gravitational action, we formulate various equal-time (anti-)commutation relations (ETCRs), specifically those concerning the Nakanishi-Lautrup field, FP ghosts, and FP antighosts, relying solely on the de Donder gauge. We demonstrate that chiral symmetry—a Poincaré-like $IOSp(8|8)$ supersymmetry—emerges from such a general action when the de Donder gauge is applied. Subsequently, treating the scale-invariant gravity with a scalar field as a classical framework, we derive the ETCRs for the gravitational sector involving the metric tensor and scalar fields. Furthermore, we elucidate the spontaneous breaking of scale symmetry in quantum gravity, establishing that the dilaton functions as a massless Nambu-Goldstone boson.

For the first time, the doubly Cabibbo-suppressed decay $\Xi_{c}^{+}\to p\phi$ (where $\phi\to K^{+}K^{-}$) has been observed with a statistical significance exceeding fifteen standard deviations. This result is based on an integrated luminosity of 2 fb$^{-1}$ collected by the LHCb detector from proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 8 TeV. The measured ratio of branching fractions for the decay $\Xi_{c}^{+}\to p\phi$ relative to the singly Cabibbo-suppressed mode $\Xi_{c}^{+}\to pK^{-}\pi^{+}$ is given by
\begin{equation*} \frac{\mathcal{B}(\Xi_{c}^{+}\to
p\phi)}{\mathcal{B}(\Xi_{c}^{+}\to pK^{-}\pi^{+})} = (19.8 \pm 0.7 \pm 0.9 \pm
0.2) \times 10^{-3}, \end{equation*}
where the uncertainties correspond to statistical, systematic, and the precision of the $\phi\to K^{+}K^{-}$ branching fraction, respectively.

Digital quantum simulation necessitates algorithms feasible within finite quantum resources. Recent efforts have successfully applied digital quantum simulation to open quantum systems on Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) hardware. This study introduces quantum circuits designed for the optimal simulation of both Markovian and Non-Markovian open quantum systems. These circuits employ ancilla qubits to model the environment, generating memory effects by retaining system information on additional qubits. We validate the framework by simulating amplitude damping and dephasing channels, using the monotonic or non-monotonic evolution of dynamics to infer (Non-)Markovianity. Furthermore, we propose an optimization strategy that decomposes intricate open quantum dynamics into manageable segments, enabling simulation with fewer qubits. This approach demonstrates a reduction in quantum space complexity for environment simulation from $O(l)$ to $O(1)$.

This paper focuses on automatic structures defined over finite words and trees (both ranked and unranked), which are infinite systems finitely described by synchronized finite-state automata. We examine the "directed" variant of Ramsey quantifiers, which assert the existence of an infinite directed clique, noting that this generalizes the standard "undirected" Ramsey quantifiers. The study establishes significant links between these quantifiers and two verification challenges: (1) reachability under Büchi and generalized Büchi conditions in regular model checking corresponds to Ramsey quantification over transitive automatic graphs, and (2) verifying the monadic decomposability (or recognizability) of automatic relations equates to Ramsey quantification over co-transitive automatic graphs. We map out the complexity landscape for Ramsey quantifiers across these three scenarios—general, transitive, and co-transitive—all situated between NL and EXP. Consequently, we derive numerous new results with exact complexity bounds, including verification of subtree/flat prefix rewriting and monadic decomposability for tree-automatic relations. Additionally, we present notably streamlined proofs, such as demonstrating NL complexity for monadic decomposability over word-automatic relations represented by DFAs.

While Computer Vision techniques often utilize fixed-size 2D spectrograms as image-like inputs for Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) in audio tasks, the musical domain typically requires variable-duration outputs. This paper introduces VQCPC-GAN, an adversarial framework designed to synthesize variable-length audio by leveraging Vector-Quantized Contrastive Predictive Coding (VQCPC). By using a sequence of VQCPC tokens derived from real audio as conditional inputs, the model provides time-dependent features for generation step-by-step, while a fixed noise vector (z) ensures global temporal consistency. The proposed model was evaluated against various strong baselines using diverse metrics. Although the baselines achieved superior scores, VQCPC-GAN demonstrated comparable performance specifically in generating variable-length audio. Sound examples are available on the project website, and the code has been released to ensure reproducibility.

Language models (LMs) are increasingly ubiquitous across various global language-based applications. While these models enhance our daily interactions with digital tools, concerns persist regarding whether their open-ended outputs or generated text exhibit biases toward specific groups, potentially compromising product usability. Identifying such biases is essential to enhancing model fairness. This need drives our ongoing research, which evaluates two dimensions of bias within GPT-3-generated text using a disability perspective.

Estimating electric fields in straightforward scenarios offers a valuable chance to cultivate intuition regarding physics models. We present an activity for university-level General Physics students that involves comparing the electric field of a finite line of charge—analytically or numerically—with those of an infinite line and a point charge. Contrary to common intuition, a finite line does not need to be approached extremely closely to be approximated as infinite, nor does one need to move very far away for its field to resemble that of a point charge. After implementing this activity with a student group, we observed that many participants had not yet developed a sufficient intuition for the approximations inherent in electromagnetism.

Accurately measuring and analyzing customer traffic in retail environments is vital for understanding consumer behavior and informing strategic decisions. However, the creation of advanced technologies for automatic person counting has received limited attention. This paper introduces LRCN-RetailNet, a recurrent neural network designed to learn a non-linear regression model that precisely estimates the number of people from video feeds captured by affordable surveillance cameras. The system utilizes the recently proposed RGBP image format, which integrates color data with foreground (person) information. The architecture effectively processes two key dimensions: spatial features derived from RGBP images via convolutional layers, and temporal consistency managed by recurrent layers. Through supervised learning, the trained models demonstrate high accuracy in predicting crowd sizes. Furthermore, we show that a simple modification to the method successfully excludes sales staff from the count. Extensive experiments were conducted to validate, assess, and compare the proposed architecture. Results indicate that LRCN-RetailNet significantly surpasses the previous RetailNet architecture, which processed only a single image per iteration, as well as current state-of-the-art object detection neural networks. Finally, computational tests confirm that the entire methodology is efficient enough for real-time person counting.

It is established that classical randomization, whether implemented via behavioral or mixed strategies, fails to enhance the optimal cost in team decision problems. This work introduces a novel class of stochastic strategies for static team decision problems that leverage quantum entanglement to produce randomness. Through a numerical example of a static team decision problem, we present a physically realizable quantum strategy that achieves a cost strictly lower than the best possible outcome using classical methods, thus proving the existence of a quantum advantage in decentralized control. We demonstrate that the optimal quantum cost corresponds to optimizing a linear objective over an abstractly defined convex set. Furthermore, we offer a computable linear programming relaxation to determine lower bounds on this optimal quantum cost. Our research establishes a new paradigm in decision and control, expanding the space of achievable control policies through quantum physical architectures.

Unsupervised reinforcement learning seeks to develop a generalist policy capable of rapid adaptation to downstream tasks without relying on external rewards. Current approaches predominantly utilize surprise-based intrinsic rewards, where maximizing surprise encourages exploration while minimizing it aids in gaining environmental control. However, both strategies depend on the strong assumption that the environment's dynamics possess either consistently high or low entropy, an assumption that often fails in real-world settings where entropy levels are unknown. This creates a dilemma in selecting an appropriate objective. To resolve this, we introduce a novel and straightforward mixture of policies that simultaneously optimizes for both maximizing and minimizing surprise. Specifically, we train one policy component to maximize surprise and another to minimize it, thereby eliminating the need to assume a specific entropy level for the environment. We name this approach $\textbf{M}\text{ixture }\textbf{O}\text{f}\textbf{S}\text{urprise}\textbf{S}$ (MOSS) for unsupervised reinforcement learning. Experimental evaluations on the URLB benchmark demonstrate that our simple method achieves state-of-the-art performance, surpassing previous methods based solely on surprise maximization. Our code is available at: https://github.com/LeapLabTHU/MOSS.

This study investigates various facets of fluctuations and correlations within the box-ball system (BBS), a one-dimensional integrable cellular automaton. We analyze an ensemble of microscopic configurations characterized by independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) box occupancies with a fixed mean ball density. In this homogeneous stationary state, we calculate exact values for several quantities: the mean and variance of the ball count $N_t$ crossing the origin over time $t$, the scaled cumulants generating function for $N_t$, and two spatially integrated current-current correlations. The first correlation, representing the long-time limit known as the Drude weight, is derived via the thermodynamic Bethe Ansatz (TBA), while the equal-time current-current correlation is determined using a transfer matrix method. Furthermore, we construct a family of generalized currents linked to conserved charges and distinct time evolutions. Their long-time correlation limits, which extend the concepts of the Drude weight and the second cumulant of $N_t$, satisfy nontrivial symmetry relations. These are computed using TBA and show strong agreement with microscopic simulations. Additionally, TBA is employed to explicitly calculate the entire family of flux Jacobian matrices. Finally, select findings are extended to a non-i.i.d. two-temperature generalized Gibbs state, where parameters couple to the total number of balls and solitons.

We introduce CALIPSO (Conic Augmented Lagrangian Interior-Point SOlver), a novel solver tailored for non-convex trajectory optimization in robotics. By integrating multiple constrained numerical optimization strategies, it natively manages second-order cones and complementarity constraints. This approach reliably addresses difficult motion-planning scenarios—such as those involving contact-implicit impact and Coulomb friction formulations, conic thrust limits, and state-triggered constraints—where general-purpose solvers like SNOPT and Ipopt often fail to converge. Furthermore, CALIPSO facilitates efficient differentiation of solutions regarding problem data, supporting bi-level optimization tasks such as the auto-tuning of feedback policies. The solver's robust convergence is validated across diverse applications in manipulation, locomotion, and aerospace fields, and an open-source version is publicly available.

We conducted a census of young stellar populations near the Corona Australis molecular cloud by utilizing photometric and kinematic data from multiple sources, with a focus on Gaia EDR3, alongside spectroscopy of hundreds of candidate members. This effort resulted in a catalog of 393 Corona Australis members, including 39 with spectral types later than M6, of which 293 (36 with >M6) were spectroscopically classified for the first time in this study. Our findings indicate that Corona Australis comprises two distinct stellar populations: a younger group (a few Myr) partially embedded in the cloud, known as the Coronet Cluster, and an older group (~15 Myr) that envelops and extends beyond the cloud, termed Upper Corona Australis. Despite their age difference, these populations share similar space velocities, revealing no evidence for separate kinematic groups within Corona Australis, a result that contrasts with a recent study utilizing Gaia DR2. The spectral type distribution peaks at M5 (~0.15 M_sol), suggesting the initial mass function possesses a characteristic mass comparable to other nearby star-forming regions. Furthermore, we compiled mid-infrared photometry from the Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer and the Spitzer Space Telescope for the catalog members to identify and classify their circumstellar disks; excess emission was detected in 122 stars, with one-third of these discoveries reported here for the first time.

A new algorithm has been created to locate the global minimum of a multidimensional error function by aligning model spectral maps with observed data. Principal component analysis (PCA) is employed to lower the model's dimensionality, decouple parameter interactions, and identify the minimum's region, while the k-nearest neighbors method determines the optimal parameters. This approach was applied to estimate the physical characteristics of the contracting dense star-forming core in L1287. The method fitted observed maps of HCO+(1-0), H13CO+(1-0), HCN(1-0), and H13CN(1-0) lines against those calculated using a 1D microturbulent model. The analysis yielded estimates for the core's physical parameters, including radial profiles for density ($\propto r^{-1.7}$), turbulent velocity ($\propto r^{-0.4}$), and contraction velocity ($\propto r^{-0.1}$), along with calculated confidence intervals. Considering determination errors, the absolute value of the power-law index for the contraction-velocity radial profile is lower than the theoretical expectation for free-fall gas collapse onto a protostar. This finding supports a global contraction model for the L1287 core.

This study utilizes FIRE-2 zoom cosmological simulations of Milky Way-mass galaxy halos to determine astrophysical J-factors for dark matter annihilation and indirect detection. Beyond calculating J-factors for velocity-independent (s-wave) cross sections, we also derive effective J-factors for velocity-dependent scenarios, specifically p-wave ($\propto v^2/c^2$) and d-wave ($\propto v^4/c^4$) models. Our analysis employs 12 simulation pairs, each executed with both dark-matter-only (DMO) and FIRE-2 physics. We find that FIRE simulations yield central dark matter velocity dispersions that are systematically $2.5-4$ times larger than those in DMO runs. Furthermore, due to the interplay between baryonic contraction and feedback, FIRE runs exhibit a wider range of central ($\sim 400$ pc) dark matter densities compared to DMO runs ($\rho_{\rm FIRE}/\rho_{\rm DMO} \simeq 0.5 - 3$). At 3 degrees from the Galactic Center, J-factors in FIRE runs are $5-50$ times higher for p-wave and $15-500$ times higher for d-wave relative to DMO runs. While the change in s-wave signals at this distance is more variable ($\sim 0.3-6$), the resulting emission profiles in FIRE runs are flatter and more circular than in DMO runs. Our s-wave results align broadly with assumptions in existing indirect detection studies, whereas our p-wave J-factors are significantly enhanced compared to previous estimates. Consequently, thermal models involving p-wave annihilation may become detectable in the near future.

We examine the Maximum-Profit Routing Problem (MPRP), a pick-up routing variant introduced in \cite{Armaselu-arXiv-2016, Armaselu-PETRA} aimed at maximizing total profit. While the original MPRP restricts vehicles to visiting each site only once, this paper explores extensions allowing multiple visits per site. Specifically, we analyze two scenarios: MPRP-M, where pickup quantities remain constant over time, and MPRP-VS, where supplied quantities grow linearly with time. For both versions, we develop constant-factor polynomial-time approximation schemes.

Upcoming redshift drift observations in both optical and radio frequencies are expected to yield precise $H(z)$ measurements across the redshift intervals of $0<z<0.3$ and $2<z<5$. Furthermore, gravitational wave (GW) standard siren observations may enable the measurement of luminosity distance dipole anisotropy, offering $H(z)$ data for the range $0<z<3$. This study proposes a multi-messenger, multi-wavelength strategy utilizing the next-generation E-ELT, SKA, and DECIGO projects to measure $H(z)$, aiming to determine if future data can tightly constrain dark-energy parameters. The analysis examines $\Lambda$CDM, $w$CDM, CPL, HDE, and I$\Lambda$CDM models. Results indicate that E-ELT, SKA1, and DECIGO are highly complementary; while each dataset individually provides only weak constraints on the considered models, their combination effectively breaks parameter degeneracies and significantly tightens constraints on nearly all cosmological parameters. Additionally, incorporating CMB data alongside E-ELT, SKA1, and DECIGO further refines dark-energy constraints, achieving $\sigma(w_0)=0.024$ and $\sigma(w_a)=0.17$ within the CPL model. These findings suggest that these three promising probes will be essential in uncovering the true nature of dark energy.

This work investigates left-invariant conformal Killing-Yano (CKY) 2-forms on Lie groups equipped with left-invariant metrics. We provide a classification of all 5-dimensional metric Lie algebras that support CKY tensors derived from 4-dimensional metric Lie algebras via a one-dimensional central extension and possessing an invertible parallel skew-symmetric tensor. Additionally, we classify 5-dimensional metric Lie algebras with a center of dimension exceeding one that admit strict CKY tensors, and we identify all possible CKY tensors on these algebras. Notably, we present the first examples of CKY 2-forms on metric Lie algebras that do not possess any Sasakian structure.

Most existing adversarial attack methods are effective in white-box scenarios against deep face recognition systems where the attacker has full system knowledge, but they fail in gray-box settings where face templates remain hidden. This paper introduces SGADV, a similarity-based gray-box adversarial attack that employs a novel objective function. By leveraging dissimilarity scores to generate optimized adversarial examples, SGADV targets authentication systems that distinguish genuine users from imposters based on these scores, functioning effectively in both white-box and gray-box contexts. Extensive experiments were conducted on the LFW, CelebA, and CelebA-HQ datasets against FaceNet and InsightFace models in both attack settings. The findings demonstrate that SGADV significantly surpasses current adversarial techniques within gray-box environments. Consequently, we conclude that similarity-based approaches for crafting adversarial examples are highly suitable for achieving de-authentication in gray-box scenarios.

This work examines the theoretical foundations for investigating the lifetimes of heavy hadrons. Following an introduction to key concepts such as the effective weak Hamiltonian and heavy quark effective theory (HQET), we detail the construction of the heavy quark expansion (HQE). This framework enables the systematic calculation of total decay widths for heavy hadrons through an expansion in inverse powers of the heavy quark mass. We provide a thorough discussion of the HQE's structure and explicitly outline the computation of its lowest-dimensional contributions. Special attention is given to expanding the quark propagator in an external gluon field within the Fock-Schwinger (FS) gauge, a critical component of the calculation. A primary outcome of this study is the determination of the dimension-six contribution arising from the Darwin operator, a recently identified term with significant impact. Furthermore, we apply the HQE to two phenomenological scenarios in the charm sector: analyzing the lifetimes of charmed mesons and examining GIM cancellations in neutral $D$-meson mixing. By comparing our findings with recent data from the LHCb, Belle-II, and BESIII collaborations, we demonstrate that the HQE successfully reproduces the experimental lifetime patterns for charmed mesons, despite substantial theoretical uncertainties. Additionally, we propose a potential resolution to the discrepancies between previous theoretical predictions for $D$-mixing and experimental observations.

This study offers three key contributions. First, it extends the Lindeberg-Feller and Lyapunov Central Limit Theorems to Hilbert spaces via $L^2$ formulations. Second, it broadens these findings to accommodate scenarios involving sample failures and missing data. Third, it demonstrates that satisfying the Lindeberg-Feller Condition within such spaces ensures the consistency of all inferences drawn from partially observed functional data relative to fully observed data. These latter two advancements are particularly significant due to the growing focus on statistical inference with incomplete functional datasets. Unlike prior research, this paper establishes straightforward boundedness conditions that guarantee the consistent estimation of *all* inferences, rather than merely a subset, primarily by aggregating conditional expectations across the space of missingness patterns. To the authors' knowledge, this is the first application of this specific technique.

Self-sovereign identity constitutes a decentralized approach to credential management. In the verification process, data exchange occurs exclusively between the data owner and the verifier, bypassing any intermediaries. Although this method prioritizes privacy, it introduces a significant challenge: how can verifiers trust that a credential is endorsed by a legitimate source? Specifically, how can they ascertain the issuer's reputation or authorization? This paper presents a trust registry design to address the dimension of human trust within self-sovereign identity. Furthermore, we introduce an incentive mechanism for the registry to encourage active and honest participation from all stakeholders.

Second-order accurate Cartesian grid methods are well-established in the literature for interface problems; however, creating methods with third-order or higher accuracy for curved interfaces and internal boundaries remains difficult. This paper introduces alternative approaches utilizing two distinct grids for specific interface and internal layer problems, differing from adaptive mesh refinement (AMR) techniques. For one-dimensional or two-dimensional cases involving straight interfaces or boundary layers parallel to an axis, the analysis is straightforward. A key challenge lies in constructing a fourth-order compact finite difference scheme at border grid points where two meshes connect. A proposed two-grid method applies second-order discretization near the interface within the fine mesh, while employing fourth-order discretization away from the interface in the coarse mesh and border points. For two-dimensional problems featuring curved interfaces or internal layers, a level set representation is adopted to construct a fine mesh within a tube defined by $|\varphi({\bf x}) | \le \delta h$ around the interface. A novel super-third seven-point discretization capable of ensuring the discrete maximum principle has been developed for hanging nodes. The coefficient matrices of the finite difference equations presented herein are M-matrices, ensuring the convergence of the schemes. Non-trivial numerical examples included in this study confirm the desired accuracy and convergence.

Attention mechanisms are gaining prominence in Natural Language Processing (NLP) due to their superior performance compared to convolutional and recurrent models. Nevertheless, standard platforms like CPUs and GPUs struggle with attention inference because of complex data movement and low arithmetic intensity. Furthermore, current neural network accelerators primarily optimize for convolutional or recurrent tasks, failing to efficiently handle attention operations. This paper introduces SpAtten, an efficient algorithm-architecture co-design that exploits token sparsity, head sparsity, and quantization to minimize both computation and memory access. Drawing inspiration from the inherent redundancy in human language, we propose a novel cascade token pruning method to eliminate irrelevant tokens, alongside cascade head pruning to discard unnecessary heads. Unlike weight pruning, which modifies trainable parameters, cascade pruning selects tokens and heads dynamically at runtime without altering weights. To support this on hardware, we developed a new top-k engine capable of ranking importance scores for tokens and heads with high throughput. Additionally, we introduced progressive quantization, which initially retrieves only Most Significant Bits (MSBs) for computation; if confidence is low, it fetches Least Significant Bits (LSBs) to recompute results, effectively trading computation for reduced memory usage. Comprehensive experiments across 30 benchmarks demonstrate that SpAtten reduces DRAM access by an average of 10.0x without any accuracy degradation. Compared to the A3 accelerator, MNNFast accelerator, TITAN Xp GPU, and Xeon CPU, SpAtten achieves speedups of 1.6x, 3.0x, 162x, and 347x, respectively, while delivering energy savings of 1.4x, 3.2x, 1193x, and 4059x.

We utilize graph neural networks trained on halo catalogues derived from Gadget N-body simulations to conduct field-level, likelihood-free inference of cosmological parameters. These catalogues encompass fewer than 5,000 halos with masses exceeding $10^{10}~h^{-1}M_\odot$ within a periodic box of $(25~h^{-1}{\rm Mpc})^3$, where each halo is defined by attributes including position, mass, velocity, concentration, and maximum circular velocity. Our models are constructed to maintain invariance under permutation, translation, and rotation, allowing them to extract information without a minimum scale constraint. When utilizing position-velocity or position-mass data, these models infer $\Omega_{\rm m}$ and $\sigma_8$ with a mean relative error of approximately 6%. Crucially, the models demonstrate high robustness, successfully inferring these parameters across thousands of N-body simulations generated by five distinct codes: Abacus, CUBEP$^3$M, Enzo, PKDGrav3, and Ramses. Remarkably, a model trained specifically for $\Omega_{\rm m}$ also performs effectively on thousands of advanced CAMELS hydrodynamic simulations produced by four different codes with various subgrid physics. However, incorporating halo properties like concentration and maximum circular velocity enhances information extraction at the cost of model robustness, likely because the N-body codes have not yet converged on the scales relevant to these specific parameters.

This research investigates the asymptotic properties of sub-solutions to non-uniformly elliptic equations featuring nonstandard growth conditions. Specifically, we establish Harnack-type inequalities. Our methodology yields novel findings for scenarios involving (p,q) nonlinearity as well as generalized Orlicz growth.

For every type of Coulomb (Newton) charge, there exists a corresponding Coulomb (Newton) mass. This mass-charge duality accounts for the existence within a neutrino of a unified rest mass and charge, encompassing all its constituent electric, weak, strong, and other innate components. Similarly to other quantum matter possessing Coulomb (Newton) mass and charge, the neutrino supports the concept of a mononeutrino, characterized by a magnetocoulomb (magnetonewton) rest mass and charge that includes all its magnetoelectric, magnetoweak, magnetostrong, and other innate parts. We propose a theory where the symmetry between electricity and magnetism emerges at the level of grand unification mathematical logic as a defined symmetry between gravity and magnetogravity, both operating within a single allgravity responsible for all phenomena in curved space-time. This allgravity relates the graviton and monograviton as outcomes of force unification, forming one unified allgraviton. Consequently, this framework establishes a set of forces and defines their role in generating mass and charge, thereby directly revealing previously unknown, diverse properties of curved space.

We progress toward structurally characterizing signed graphs $H$ for which the list switch $H$-colouring problem, denoted as $\operatorname{LSwHom}(H)$, admits a polynomial-time solution. We propose a conjecture characterizing signed graphs that can be switched into graphs where all negative edges are effectively positive, and we establish this characterization specifically for the case where the signed graph is reflexive.

Inadequate coordination of laryngeal muscles leading to abnormal glottal configuration is considered a primary cause of common voice disorders, particularly non-phonotraumatic vocal hyperfunction. It is hypothesized that the irregular activity of opposing laryngeal muscles significantly alters normal vocal fold biomechanics, resulting in the associated dysphonia. However, existing low-order vocal fold models are insufficient for testing this hypothesis because they fail to account for the simultaneous contraction of antagonist muscle pairs. To overcome this shortcoming, a new self-sustained triangular body-cover model with complete intrinsic muscle control has been developed. This proposed framework demonstrates strong alignment with previous research involving finite element models, excised larynges, and clinical observations of both steady and dynamic vocal gestures. Simulations utilizing distinct activation patterns for antagonistic muscles reveal significant variations in kinematic, aerodynamic, and acoustic metrics. Consequently, this tool is regarded as both accurate and adaptable for future in-depth studies of non-phonotraumatic vocal hyperfunction and other laryngeal motor control disorders.

This study introduces a new large-scale quantum circuit simulator utilizing the tensor network contraction method for circuit representation. We develop a novel parallelization algorithm grounded in the \stepslice approach. Furthermore, we refine the estimates regarding the quantum computer size required to demonstrate the benefits of the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA). Specifically, we simulated QAOA circuits comprising 210 qubits and 1,785 gates across 1,024 nodes of the Cray XC 40 supercomputer, Theta. To our knowledge, these results represent the largest QAOA quantum circuit simulations reported to date.

Decentralization serves as a fundamental element in the design of Cameroon's government institutions. This chapter presents a straightforward hierarchical model to analyze the consequences of power devolution. The model forecasts that decentralization yields overall positive outcomes, particularly when local authorities possess valuable information regarding optimal resource allocation. Empirical estimates concerning the 2010 power devolution to Cameroonian municipalities indicate a beneficial impact on the early accumulation of human capital. Furthermore, the added value of decentralization remains consistent across both Anglophone and Francophone municipalities, though its effects are more pronounced at advanced levels of primary education.

The electric fields generated by relativistic electrons within the ultraviolet and extreme ultraviolet undulators of a synchrotron light source were characterized using spectral phase interferometry for direct electric-field reconstruction (SPIDER). This process involved a tandem undulator equipped with a phase shifter, which generated a pair of wavelength-shifted wave packets separated by a specific delay. By applying the widely used SPIDER algorithm to analyze the interferogram created between these wave packets, researchers reconstructed a 10-cycle square-shaped electric field. This waveform accurately reflects the radiation emitted by an electron accelerated through an undulator composed of 10 periods of permanent magnets.

Tailoring the electronic characteristics of quantum materials and devices through orbital engineering in multilayered oxide heterostructures offers a promising approach. This study demonstrates that the interaction between interlayer charge imbalance and ligand distortions serves as a mechanism to adjust the sequence of electronic levels, even within inherently stacked oxides. Using electron spin resonance, we have clarified the $d$-level structure of layered Sr$_2$IrO$_4$. Although standard ligand-field theory predicts $g_{\parallel}$-factors less than 2 for the positive tetragonal distortions found in Sr$_2$IrO$_4$, experimental results show $g_{\parallel} > 2$. This discrepancy indicates an inversion of the iridium $d$ levels relative to their conventional ordering. Advanced electronic-structure calculations validate this level switching in Sr$_2$IrO$_4$, whereas in Ba$_2$IrO$_4$, the levels remain in their normal order. Considering the nonpolar nature of the metal-oxygen layers, these findings position tetravalent transition-metal 214 oxides as excellent systems for investigating $d$-orbital reconstruction within oxide electronics.

A spacetime is classified as a pure radiation field when its energy-momentum tensor indicates that all energy propagates in a single direction at the speed of light. In 1989, Wils, followed by Ludwig and Edgar in 1997, examined the physical characteristics of pure radiation metrics, noting their conformal relationship to vacuum spacetimes. This paper investigates the curvature properties of a specific class of these metrics introduced by Ludwig and Edgar. The study demonstrates that such spacetimes are semisymmetric, Ricci simple, and qualify as $R$-spaces according to Venzi, with Ricci tensors that are Riemann compatible. Furthermore, it is proven that both the conformal curvature 2-forms and Ricci 1-forms exhibit recurrence. The authors also introduce a pure radiation type metric, analyze its curvature properties alongside its energy-momentum tensor structure, and observe that this metric satisfies the conditions for being $Ein(3)$ and 3-quasi-Einstein. Additionally, sufficient conditions are derived for this metric to represent a generalized pp-wave, pure radiation, or perfect fluid. Finally, a comparison is drawn between the curvature properties of the Ludwig and Edgar pure radiation metric and those of pp-wave metrics.

Label Distribution Learning (LDL) serves as a technique to stabilize classification and regression tasks involving ambiguous or imbalanced labels, with a primary application being human age estimation from profile images. To address this regression challenge, a method known as Deep Label Distribution Learning (DLDL) was introduced, which jointly regresses the label distribution and its expected value. However, the original DLDL approach employs loss components grounded in different mathematical principles and scales, necessitating the use of hyperparameters. This work presents a new loss function for DLDL where all components are defined by Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergences, allowing them to be directly comparable without requiring additional hyperparameters. Furthermore, this approach extends the DLDL concept to broader applications, specifically targeting multi-dimensional or multi-scale distribution learning tasks.

This paper presents a novel dataset comprising 4,836 annotated images of room interiors featuring overlaying and scene text across 25 product categories. We detail the dataset's collection and annotation procedures alongside an analysis of its statistics. Additionally, we introduce a baseline method for detecting overlaid text that utilizes a character region-aware text detection framework to guide a classification model. Our validation demonstrates the approach's efficiency, achieving a binary classification F1 score of 0.95, with corresponding false positive and false negative rates of 0.02 and 0.06.

This study reports measurements of azimuthal correlations between charged hadron pairs in Au+Au collisions at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s_{_{NN}}}=200$ GeV, with trigger particles in the range $1<p_T^t<10$~GeV/$c$ and associated particles in $0.5<p_T^a<10$~GeV/$c$. Following the subtraction of the underlying event using a model incorporating higher-order azimuthal anisotropies ($v_2$, $v_3$, and $v_4$), the away-side yield for high-$p_T$ trigger particles ($p_T^t>4$~GeV/$c$) is found to be suppressed relative to $p$$+$$p$ collisions. Additionally, at the lowest associated particle transverse momentum ($0.5<p_T^a<1$ GeV/$c$), both the away-side shape and yield differ from those observed in $p$$+$$p$ collisions. These findings align with the radiative-jet energy loss scenario. For low-$p_T$ trigger correlations ($2<p_T^t<4$ GeV/$c$), a finite away-side yield is present, and the shape dependence is investigated within the framework of an underlying-event model. The analysis also examines correlations differentially with respect to the event-plane angles $\Psi_2$ and $\Psi_3$. Angular correlations exhibit an asymmetry when selecting the sign of the difference between the trigger-particle azimuthal angle and the $\Psi_2$ event plane. This asymmetry, along with the measured suppression of pair yield out of the plane, supports a path-length-dependent energy loss mechanism. No significant dependence on $\Psi_3$ could be resolved given the experimental uncertainties.

Variable selection for linear models continues to be a significant field of study. This article examines numerous recent advancements in Bayesian model selection and shrinkage prior research. We introduce a posterior variable selection summary that condenses a complete posterior distribution of regression coefficients into a series of sparse linear predictors.

This work introduces an enhanced rotational invariance technique, termed I-HAD-ESPRIT, designed for hybrid analog-digital (HAD) transceivers to accurately estimate the Direction of Arrival (DOA) of target users while effectively resolving phase ambiguities inherent in HAD architectures. To further enhance measurement precision, a machine-learning (ML) framework is developed. During the training phase, the HAD transceiver functions as a receiver, repeatedly calculating DOA values using I-HAD-ESPRIT to construct a slightly large training dataset (TDS). Histogram analysis of this TDS reveals that the probability density function (PDF) of the DOA measurement error (DOAME) approximates a Gaussian distribution. This dataset enables the learning of the mean DOA and the variance of DOAME, which are subsequently leveraged to refine these estimates in real-time operations. In the real-time phase, the transceiver rapidly acquires several DOA measurements to form a smaller real-time set (RTS), allowing for the determination of real-time mean and variance values. Three weight combiners are then proposed to integrate the maximum-likelihood outputs from both the TDS and RTS, with weighting factors determined by the dataset sizes and signal-to-noise ratios of each stage. By utilizing the learned mean and variance, the PDFs of DOA and DOAME are directly established, facilitating the design of a robust beamformer for a directional modulation (DM) transmitter equipped with HAD technology. This robust analog beamformer on the RF chain fully exploits the known PDFs. Simulation results demonstrate that: 1) the proposed I-HAD-ESPRIT achieves the Cramér-Rao Lower Bound (CRLB) for HAD systems; 2) the ML-based framework significantly outperforms real-time approaches lacking a training stage; and 3) the proposed robust DM transmitter yields superior bit error rates and secrecy rates compared to non-robust counterparts.

By integrating advanced optical technologies with antiferromagnetic spintronics, we introduce a technique to achieve ultrafast spin transport. Through the optical Barnett effect, we generate quasiequilibrium Bose-Einstein condensates (BECs) of magnons linked to a fully spin-polarized state within insulating antiferromagnets (AFs). This optomagnonic Barnett effect allows us to utilize high-frequency coherent magnons, surpassing the conventional sub-terahertz magnons tied to N\'eel magnetic order. We demonstrate that the macroscopic coherence of these optical magnon BECs drives a spin current across the interface of weakly coupled insulating AFs, manifesting as an optomagnonic Josephson effect that facilitates ultrafast spin transport. Notably, the period of the resulting optomagnonic Josephson oscillation is significantly shorter than the conventional picosecond-scale period. Consequently, we propose a strategy to realize ultrafast spin transport in AFs by leveraging the macroscopic coherence of optical magnon BECs.

Neural oscillations refer to brain electrical activities that can be measured across various frequencies. This study investigates the interplay between rapid and sluggish neural processes. We obtained intracranial recordings from simple Wistar rats, processed the signals, and calculated the correlation between the envelopes of the high-frequency gamma rhythm and a low-frequency ECoG signal. The analysis reveals that the low-frequency delta rhythm modulates the gamma rhythm with a minimal time lag. Additionally, we employed basic excitable neuron models, specifically the FitzHugh-Nagumo and Hindmarsh-Rose models, to simulate the gamma rhythm. In these simulations, the low-frequency delta rhythm served as an input to influence the threshold, thereby generating the gamma rhythm.

Data augmentation plays a pivotal role in unsupervised contrastive learning (CL), as it defines positive samples and directly influences representation quality. Although effective augmentation strategies exist for standard vision benchmarks like ImageNet, developing them for other domains—such as medical imaging or datasets with trivial but irrelevant features—remains an open challenge. This study introduces a novel approach to defining positive samples using kernel theory, coupled with a new loss function termed decoupled uniformity. We further propose integrating prior knowledge, sourced from generative models or auxiliary attributes, into contrastive learning to reduce its reliance on data augmentation. By linking contrastive learning to conditional mean embedding theory, we establish tight bounds on downstream classification performance. In an unsupervised context, our empirical results show that incorporating generative models like VAEs and GANs allows CL to function with diminished dependence on data augmentation. We validate this framework across vision datasets (CIFAR10, CIFAR100, STL10, and ImageNet100) and a brain MRI dataset, demonstrating state-of-the-art performance in weakly supervised settings.

Software caches enhance the efficiency of various storage systems, databases, and applications. While current research predominantly relies on fully associative cache architectures, our study highlights limited associativity as a viable and promising approach for concurrent software caching. We demonstrate that this design facilitates straightforward yet efficient implementations of multiple cache management strategies that can be easily parallelized. Our results indicate that hit ratios remain comparable to those of fully associative caches under the same management policies, while throughput improves by up to 5x over existing production-grade caching libraries, particularly in multi-threaded scenarios.

We introduce a self-supervised learning (SSL) framework tailored for semi-global applications like object detection and semantic segmentation. This approach enforces local consistency among self-learned features by minimizing a pixel-level local contrastive (LC) loss, ensuring that corresponding image locations in transformed versions of the same image align. The LC loss can be integrated into existing SSL methods with negligible computational overhead. We assess our SSL strategy on object detection and semantic segmentation using the COCO, PASCAL VOC, and CityScapes datasets. Our method surpasses current state-of-the-art SSL techniques, achieving improvements of 1.9% on COCO object detection, 1.4% on PASCAL VOC detection, and 0.6% on CityScapes segmentation.

We demonstrate that recent refinements to the $O(\alpha)$ long-distance quantum electrodynamics (QED) corrections for the radiative inclusive $K_{e3}$ decay rate, utilizing the Sirlin representation, are devoid of infrared divergences and collinear electron mass singularities as $m_e\rightarrow0$, in accordance with the Kinoshita-Lee-Nauenberg theorem. Furthermore, we confirm that massless QED, when employing simultaneous dimensional regularization for both QED photon infrared divergences and electron mass singularities, yields an identical inclusive rate result in the limit of four space-time dimensions. This equivalence arises partly from a notable interplay between a minor chirality-breaking effect in the massless electron limit and the extension of space-time algebra and phase space integrals to $d>4$ dimensions. Our findings bolster the assertion of minimal theoretical uncertainty for $K_{e3}$ radiative inclusive rates and reinforce their value in precision unitarity tests of the quark mixing matrix.

This work examines the efficacy of cross-attention within Transformer architectures specifically for transfer learning in machine translation, building upon previous research regarding cross-attention in models trained from scratch. We performed experiments by fine-tuning translation models on datasets where either the source or target language shifted. The results indicate that fine-tuning exclusively the cross-attention parameters achieves performance nearly equivalent to fine-tuning the entire model. We offer explanations for this phenomenon and note that such constrained fine-tuning produces cross-lingually aligned embeddings. The practical implications of this discovery include mitigating catastrophic forgetting, enabling potential zero-shot translation, and allowing machine translation models to be extended to new language pairs with reduced parameter storage requirements.

The distorted diamond spin chain with $S=1/2$ and anisotropic ferromagnetic interactions was examined through numerical diagonalization and level spectroscopy analysis. While it is established that the system displays a magnetization plateau at one-third of saturation, this study reveals that varying the anisotropy induces a quantum phase transition between two distinct mechanisms underlying this 1/3 plateau. Additionally, the phase diagram, plotted against anisotropy and ferromagnetic coupling, is provided.

This study investigates the ground state of the Hubbard model on a square lattice featuring two degenerate orbitals per site at integer fillings, examining its dependence on the onsite Hubbard repulsion $U$ and Hund's intra-atomic exchange coupling $J$. We employ a variational slave-spin mean field (VSSMF) approach, which facilitates the analysis of symmetry-broken states within a computationally efficient slave-spin mean field framework, thereby enhancing its capability to explore strongly correlated electron systems. Our findings indicate that at half-filling, the ground state for lower $U$ values is a Slater antiferromagnet (AF) exhibiting significant local charge fluctuations. As $U$ increases, this AF state transitions toward Heisenberg behavior before undergoing a first-order phase transition into a Mott insulating AF state at a critical interaction $U_c$ comparable to the bandwidth. The introduction of Hund's coupling $J$ further correlates the system and significantly lowers $U_c$. At quarter-filling (one electron per site), the ground state for small $U$ is a paramagnetic metal. With finite $J$, increasing the interaction beyond a lower critical threshold $U_{c1}$ drives the system into a fully spin-polarized ferromagnetic state coexisting with antiferro-orbital order, which eventually becomes Mott insulating at a higher critical value $U_{c2}$. We provide a comprehensive discussion of these results across the $U$ and $J$ parameter space.

We introduce an automatic cough classification system powered by deep learning, capable of distinguishing between tuberculosis (TB), COVID-19, and healthy coughs. Both TB and COVID-19 are highly contagious respiratory illnesses that cause significant mortality annually, with coughing being a primary symptom. The dataset comprises audio recordings gathered in diverse indoor and outdoor environments and via smartphones from participants worldwide, resulting in varied noise levels. Specifically, the data includes 1.68 hours of TB coughs, 18.54 minutes of COVID-19 coughs, and 1.69 hours of healthy coughs, sourced from 47 TB patients, 229 COVID-19 patients, and 1,498 healthy individuals. This data was utilized to train and assess Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN), Long Short-Term Memory networks (LSTM), and ResNet50 architectures. To enhance performance, these models were pre-trained on 2.14 hours of sneezing, 2.91 hours of speech, and 2.79 hours of noise. To mitigate class imbalance, we employed the SMOTE technique and evaluated the models using F1-scores and AUC. Our findings indicate that a pre-trained ResNet50 achieved the highest F1-scores of 0.9259 for the two-class task (TB vs. COVID-19) and 0.8631 for the three-class task (TB vs. COVID-19 vs. healthy). The application of deep transfer learning improved classifier robustness and generalization across cross-validation folds, with performance levels surpassing the World Health Organization's (WHO) requirements for TB triage. Analysis reveals that the most effective features involve higher-order Mel-frequency cepstral coefficients (MFCCs), implying that the distinctions between TB and COVID-19 coughs are imperceptible to the human ear. As this non-contact, cost-effective method can be easily deployed on smartphones, it serves as a promising tool for screening both TB and COVID-19.

The structural, electronic, and magnetic characteristics of the half-Heusler compounds XVSb (where X represents Fe, Co, or Ni) were examined using density functional theory combined with the generalized gradient approximation (GGA) and the Tran-Blaha modified Becke-Johnson (TB-mBJ) exchange potential. Results indicate that the mBJ method generally yields wider half-metallic gaps compared to GGA. Within the mBJ framework, the magnetic properties of these compounds are clearly defined, yielding precise integer values for the magnetic moment. The band gap values obtained via TB-mBJ align well with existing theoretical data. Specifically, FeVSb displays semiconducting behavior, whereas CoVSb and NiVSb exhibit half-metallic properties with total magnetic moments of $1\mu_\text{B}$ and $2\mu_\text{B}$, respectively, consistent with the Slater-Pauling rule. Consequently, these alloys appear promising for application in spintronic devices.

We establish a Riemann-Hilbert correspondence on the product of a complex manifold $X$ and a complex curve $S$, which serves as a parameter space. This correspondence links regular holonomic relative $\mathcal D$-modules (and their complexes) to relative perverse complexes (and $S$-$\mathbb{C}$-constructible complexes).

While the existing separation between the network control plane and applications offers significant advantages, a notable drawback is that the network lacks insight into application goals, preventing it from optimizing accordingly. This paper explores an alternative where applications explicitly declare their abstract intents and assumptions to the network—such as identifying traffic as a "Tweet" or noting that an app operates within a local domain. By enriching this semantic context, the network can better align with application requirements and improve resource efficiency across the system. We term this paradigm "intent-driven networking" (IDN) and outline an incrementally deployable architecture designed to facilitate a practical implementation of IDN within today's Internet.

This study introduces a data segmentation algorithm that integrates t-SNE, DBSCAN, and a Random Forest classifier into an end-to-end pipeline. This system divides data into natural clusters and generates a characteristic profile for each based on key features. It enables the inference of cluster labels for out-of-sample data and demonstrates strong generalization on real-world datasets. The paper details the algorithm and presents case studies using the Iris and MNIST datasets, along with real Instagram social media data. Serving as a proof of concept, this work lays the groundwork for future in-depth theoretical analysis.

Diffusion, a core internal mechanism prevalent across numerous physical processes, characterizes interactions between various entities. In learning scenarios constrained by limited training data, diffusion bridges labeled and unlabeled samples, serving as a vital element for attaining superior classification performance. While many current deep learning methods directly apply fusion loss during neural network training, this study introduces a novel Diffusion Residual Network (Diff-ResNet), inspired by convection-diffusion ordinary differential equations (ODEs), which embeds diffusion directly into neural network architectures. Based on the structured data assumption, we demonstrate that the proposed diffusion block enhances the distance-diameter ratio, thereby improving the separation between inter-class points while minimizing distances among intra-class points. Furthermore, this characteristic facilitates the construction of separable hyperplanes within residual networks. Extensive experiments across synthetic binary classification, semi-supervised graph node classification, and few-shot image classification on diverse datasets confirm the efficacy of the proposed approach.

Evolutionary Neural Architecture Search (ENAS) has recently gained significant attention for its ability to identify high-quality neural networks, though it typically incurs substantial computational expenses by training every individual architecture for full epochs during evaluation. While various ENAS methods have emerged to lower these costs, many struggle to maintain high evaluation accuracy. To resolve this, we introduce MFENAS, an accelerated ENAS framework utilizing multi-fidelity evaluation. This approach drastically reduces individual evaluation costs by training each architecture for only a limited number of epochs. By integrating evaluations across varying epoch counts, MFENAS effectively balances cost and accuracy, identifying promising candidates that might otherwise be eliminated prematurely. Furthermore, to ensure high architectural diversity, a novel population initialization strategy generates varied structures ranging from ResNet-like to Inception-like designs. Experiments on CIFAR-10 demonstrate that the architecture discovered by MFENAS achieves a 2.39% test error rate while consuming merely 0.6 GPU days on a single NVIDIA 2080Ti, outperforming state-of-the-art NAS methods in both efficiency and quality.
