Additionally, when transferred to CIFAR-100 and ImageNet, the proposed architecture exhibits competitive performance against existing approaches. The source code for MFENAS is accessible at https://github.com/DevilYangS/MFENAS/.

The inverse eigenvalue problem for graphs investigates real symmetric matrices where the off-diagonal structure corresponds to the graph's adjacencies. The strong spectral property (SSP) serves as a key instrument in this field. This note introduces the bifurcation lemma, asserting that if a spectrum is realizable by an SSP-compliant matrix for a given graph, then all sufficiently close spectra are also realizable by such matrices. This concept extends to other strong properties and applies even when matrices are not necessarily symmetric. These insights facilitate new methods for verifying spectrally arbitrary or inertially arbitrary patterns. Furthermore, the bifurcation lemma offers a unified theoretical basis for several established results, including the stable northeast lemma and the nilpotent-centralizer method.

When cracks encounter material heterogeneities, their fronts become distorted and adopt intricate, winding shapes that reflect the energy barriers involved in propagation. Consequently, investigating these front deformations is essential for understanding the effective failure characteristics of micro-structured solids and interfaces. However, the influence of localized dissipation within a finite region trailing the crack front, known as the process zone, has frequently been ignored. This study derives the governing equation for 3D coplanar crack growth in heterogeneous cohesive materials where crack opening is resisted by traction in its wake. We demonstrate that the process zone exerts two opposing effects on front deformation: (i) it increases the front's compliance to small-wavelength perturbations, and (ii) it averages out local variations in strength and process zone dimensions, thereby generating heterogeneities in fracture energy. The distinct impacts of these factors on front stability and their stationary configurations when interacting with arrays of tough obstacles are significant. Overall, this theoretical framework offers a unified approach to predicting the diverse front profiles seen in experiments, even when the small-scale yielding assumption of linear elastic fracture mechanics is no longer valid.

This study addresses network topology inference, aiming to reconstruct an unknown graph from node-level observations. A key innovation is the integration of prior knowledge regarding motif density within the target graph to improve upon classical Gaussian graphical models. Directly handling motif density presents a difficult combinatorial challenge; however, we observe that graphs with comparable motif densities yield similar expected values when a polynomial is applied to their empirical spectral distributions. Leveraging this insight, we assume the availability of a reference graph with similar motif densities and incorporate a similarity constraint alongside a regularization term into the optimization framework for inferring network topology. The paper analyzes the non-convexity of this problem and proposes a computationally efficient alternating majorization-minimization algorithm. Finally, the method's efficacy is evaluated through extensive numerical experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets, comparing various constraints against established baseline algorithms.

Developing efficient techniques to fingerprint microstructural data is essential for leveraging data-centric machine learning, with a specific focus on materials science. A systematic statistical framework has been established for the compressed characterization of image populations, encompassing traditional computer vision methods as special cases. The primary goal is to rapidly fingerprint sample images within high-throughput design, manufacturing, and testing workflows. These applications extend to quantifying microstructural disparities for quality control, classifying microstructures, predicting material properties from images, and identifying processing routes for engineering new materials with desired characteristics. This study examines microstructure classification and applies the derived features across supervised, semi-supervised, and unsupervised learning tasks.

The methodology was tested on two distinct datasets to demonstrate various capabilities, yielding several key recommendations. Notably, methods utilizing transfer learning with ImageNet-pretrained convolutional neural networks (CNNs) consistently outperformed alternative approaches. Furthermore, dimensionality reduction of these CNN-based fingerprints had a negligible effect on classification accuracy in supervised scenarios. In cases involving large datasets with very few labeled images, graph-based label propagation to unlabeled data proved superior to discarding unlabeled data for supervised learning alone. Specifically, label propagation via Poisson learning demonstrated high effectiveness even at low labeling rates.

The most recent findings regarding collective phenomena in proton-proton interactions at the U-70 accelerator at IHEP (Protvino) are reported. This long-term study was conducted using the SVD-2 configuration. We have obtained evidence supporting the formation of a pion (Bose-Einstein) condensate. Two distinct peaks observed in the angular distribution of charged pions are interpreted as Cherenkov radiation emitted by quarks from gluons. Furthermore, the leading effect vanishes, and the secondary system becomes isotropic across all directions within the high multiplicity region.

This study highlights the efficacy of statistical disclosure control in safeguarding data for training recommender systems. By employing a synthetic data generation technique, we conceal specific details within the user-item matrix through a transformation that modifies certain values while retaining others. This process yields a partially synthetic dataset suitable for recommendation tasks that obscures granular information regarding individual user preferences. Such synthetic data offers significant value to corporations seeking to share datasets with external developers for algorithm innovation—such as in recommender system competitions—while simultaneously mitigating risks of data misuse. Experimental evaluations applied various recommender algorithms to both the partially synthetic and original datasets, revealing that the relative performance rankings remain consistent between the two. Additional analysis confirms that key data properties are preserved during synthesis, yet specific attributes accessible in the original data are effectively hidden in the synthesized version.

This chapter presents findings from a test bed comprising a microgrid and a wireless network built on realistic premises. The setup is designed to assess application protocols operating at the transport layer of the standard IEC-61850. Specifically, it examines a data collection system where IEC-61850 messages travel between various utility grid components, including IEDs, publishers, and subscribers. While IEC-61850 defines multiple protocols like SV, GOOSE, and MMS—each with unique requirements but sharing common transport mechanisms such as TCP and UDP—a dedicated testing framework was employed to evaluate their performance for real-world microgrid deployments. IEC-61850 messages carried over TCP or UDP were directed to a centralized database, which stored data under various test scenarios and transmission sample intervals. The results are promising, suggesting that TCP-based protocols combined with a 5G cellular architecture are well-suited for most applications within the studied microgrid. Conversely, UDP performance revealed specific limitations tied to the multiple access nature of simultaneous transmissions and Signal-to-Interference-plus-Noise Ratio (SINR).

A Data Ecosystem functions as a keystone-player or alliance-based infrastructure that facilitates stakeholder interaction and resolves interoperability challenges within shared data. Nevertheless, despite extensive research in data governance and management, trust remains compromised due to a lack of transparent and traceable data pipelines. This study addresses the requirements and challenges data ecosystems encounter when guaranteeing data transparency, deriving these needs from data and organizational management, alongside broader legal and ethical factors. We introduce a novel, knowledge-driven architecture for data ecosystems designed to satisfy these identified requirements. We demonstrate the proposal's potential through a real-world case study and conclude by evaluating and rating its capacity to meet the stated requirements.

Quantum simulation has emerged as a vital research direction, enabling the study of High Energy Physics models that are currently too complex or beyond reach for experimental realization. This work demonstrates the simulation of such a model—a quantum mechanical system featuring spatial noncommutativity—drawing inspiration from Noncommutative Geometry and Noncommutative Field Theory for implementation on a universal quantum computer. By employing a novel group theoretical formalism, we transform the Hamiltonian of this noncommutative system into an ordinary quantum mechanical Hamiltonian, facilitating simulation via the Trotter-Suzuki product formula. Additionally, we analyze the influence of the noncommutativity parameter on the simulation, particularly regarding Trotter error, and determine how a large value of this parameter degrades the simulation's accuracy.

We introduce TNCR, a novel dataset featuring table images with diverse quality levels sourced from free online platforms. This resource supports table detection in scanned documents and classification into five distinct categories, comprising 9,428 high-quality labeled images. To establish robust baselines, we applied state-of-the-art deep learning techniques for table detection. Among the evaluated methods, Cascade Mask R-CNN utilizing the ResNeXt-101-64x4d backbone delivered superior results on the TNCR dataset, achieving a precision of 79.7%, a recall of 89.8%, and an F1 score of 84.4%. To foster further research in table detection, classification, and structure recognition, we have open-sourced the dataset and trained model checkpoints, which can be accessed at https://github.com/abdoelsayed2016/TNCR_Dataset.

This study numerically examines the scattering and absorption cross-sections of a massless scalar field interacting with several well-established regular black holes using the partial wave method. The computational findings reveal that as the parameters increase, the peaks of the total absorption cross-section decrease. Compared to the Schwarzschild black hole, certain regular black hole spacetimes exhibit an enhanced scattering cross-section, though the scattering width remains narrow in the forward direction. Additionally, it is observed that the null geodesics corresponding to the critical impact parameter and the geometrical optical value display similar trends in the high-frequency regime.

Recent approaches leverage the invariance of prediction models across varying environments to identify subsets of causal parents for a response variable. However, if environments affect only a limited number of underlying mechanisms, methods like Invariant Causal Prediction (ICP) may yield a small or even empty set. We introduce the concept of minimal invariance and propose Invariant Ancestry Search (IAS). In its population formulation, IAS produces a set containing only the response's ancestors, which serves as a superset of the ICP output. When applied to empirical data, corresponding theoretical guarantees hold asymptotically provided the underlying invariance test possesses asymptotic level and power. We have developed scalable algorithms and validated our approach through experiments on both simulated and real-world datasets.

Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have ruled the computer vision landscape for the past decade thanks to their proficiency in capturing local features. However, their restricted receptive fields prevent them from effectively modeling global context. Conversely, transformer architectures, which rely on attention mechanisms, excel at capturing global context. Nevertheless, few studies have explored the potential of transformers for crowd counting. Furthermore, most current crowd counting approaches rely on regressing density maps, necessitating laborious and error-prone point-level annotations for every individual in a scene. This has driven a shift toward weakly-supervised methods that only require count-level annotations. In this paper, we introduce a weakly-supervised crowd counting framework utilizing a pyramid vision transformer. We performed comprehensive evaluations to demonstrate the method's efficacy, achieving performance comparable to state-of-the-art models on benchmark datasets. Most significantly, the proposed approach exhibits remarkable generalizability.

This work theoretically proposes a method to achieve a $p$-wave superfluid Fermi gas. To circumvent the experimental challenge where $p$-wave pairing interactions that form Cooper pairs destroy the system before condensation can occur, we first generate a $p$-wave pair amplitude ($\Phi_{p}$) within a spin-orbit coupled $s$-wave superfluid Fermi gas in the absence of any $p$-wave interaction. Subsequently, by abruptly switching the $s$-wave interaction to a $p$-wave interaction ($U_{p}$) via a Feshbach resonance, the system transitions into the $p$-wave superfluid phase, characterized by an order parameter symbolically expressed as $\Delta_{p}\sim U_{p}\Phi_{p}$. In this letter, we evaluate this proposal using time-dependent Bogoliubov-de Gennes theory. Our findings aim to advance the investigation of unconventional pairing states in ultracold Fermi gases.

We show that Monte Carlo Search (MCS) algorithms, specifically Nested Monte Carlo Search (NMCS) and Nested Rollout Policy Adaptation (NRPA), can construct graphs and identify counter-examples to spectral graph theory conjectures within minutes.

Heteroatom doping is recognized as an effective strategy for modulating the electronic states and transition channels within carbon nano-dots (CNDs), thereby altering their photoluminescence (PL) characteristics. To advance CNDs as materials for optoelectronic applications, developing practical heteroatom doping techniques is crucial. This study presents the synthesis of multi-color fluorescent, nitrogen-doped CNDs (N-CNDs) using a rapid and efficient microwave approach. We investigated how varying the ratios of raw materials influence the structural and optical properties of the resulting N-CNDs. The findings indicate that adjusting the mass ratio of precursors to 1:1, 1:2, and 1:3 yields blue (445 nm), green (546 nm), and orange (617 nm) fluorescence, respectively. Furthermore, variations in nitrogen content modify the surface/edge states within the $n-\pi^*$ domain, allowing for the tuning of PL emission wavelengths through controlled nitrogen doping. Additionally, the PL intensity of N-CNDs is primarily positively correlated with the concentration of surface/edge C-O groups. Ultimately, this research offers an effective experimental method and technical pathway to enhance fluorescent emission and precisely modulate the color of PL from CNDs.

Extracting phenotypes from clinical narratives proves beneficial for diverse applications, including the identification of patients with rare conditions. Nevertheless, reasoning with numerical data remains a significant hurdle in clinical phenotyping; for instance, interpreting "102°F" as "Fever" is difficult. While current state-of-the-art models can identify general phenotypes, they struggle significantly when numerical reasoning is required. This study introduces a novel unsupervised approach that utilizes external knowledge and contextualized word embeddings from ClinicalBERT to enhance numerical reasoning across various phenotypic contexts. Against unsupervised benchmarks, this method demonstrates substantial performance gains, achieving absolute improvements in generalized Recall and F1 scores of up to 79% and 71%, respectively. Furthermore, in a supervised setting, it outperforms alternative methods with absolute gains in generalized Recall and F1 scores reaching up to 70% and 44%, respectively.

As reinforcement learning becomes more prevalent in real-world decision-making, focus has shifted to how these algorithms handle potentially sensitive information. We address the challenge of training a policy that maximizes rewards while minimizing the leakage of specific sensitive state variables through actions. We illustrate how this framework applies to privacy concerns in sequential decision-making scenarios. Our solution, implemented within the policy gradients framework, introduces a mutual information (MI) regularizer that limits the information revealed between sensitive states and actions at each timestep. Furthermore, we propose a model-based stochastic gradient estimator to optimize these privacy-constrained policies. Additionally, we present an alternative MI regularizer that acts as an upper bound to our primary method and can be optimized in a model-free context. We compare our mutual-information approach to existing differentially-private reinforcement learning techniques. Experimental results demonstrate that our training method successfully produces policies that effectively conceal sensitive state information.

This research investigates neural networks (NNs) through the framework of classical nonparametric regression, specifically targeting their capacity to adaptively estimate functions exhibiting heterogeneous smoothness, as characterized by Besov or Bounded Variation (BV) classes. While prior studies necessitate adjusting NN architectures according to specific function spaces and sample sizes, we introduce a "Parallel NN" variant of deep ReLU networks. We demonstrate that standard weight decay in this architecture effectively promotes $\ell_p$-sparsity ($0<p<1$) within the coefficient vector of an end-to-end learned function basis, or dictionary. Leveraging this equivalence, we prove that merely tuning the weight decay allows such Parallel NNs to achieve estimation errors arbitrarily close to minimax rates for both Besov and BV classes. Significantly, the approach converges exponentially closer to minimax optimality as network depth increases. These findings offer new insights into the significance of depth and illustrate the superior power of neural networks compared to kernel methods.

Quantum computing offers substantial enhancements to computational power across diverse domains, including machine learning and intricate optimization challenges. Emerging technological progress indicates that the adiabatic quantum computing framework could soon yield practical utility. This study utilizes this paradigm to create a quantum solver for the weapon-target assignment problem, a classic NP-hard nonlinear integer programming task. The viability of the proposed model is validated through numerical simulations of adiabatic evolution, tracking a quantum bit system as it converges toward the optimal solution embedded in the model Hamiltonian. Ultimately, the methodology extends beyond weapon management; with minor adjustments to the Hamiltonian, it is applicable to general worker-task allocation optimization.

Near the deconfinement transition, the behavior of the interquark potential can be accurately forecasted using Effective String Theory (EST). Should the transition be continuous, combining EST findings with conformal perturbation analysis allows for the precision required to identify corrections exceeding the Nambu-Goto approximation. We examine this scenario in detail for the SU(2) gauge theory in $(2+1)$ dimensions—specifically within the universality class of the 2d Ising model—through extensive high-precision simulations. Our results demonstrate that the SU(2) Polyakov loop correlator is precisely matched by the 2d Ising spin-spin correlator, a correspondence that holds not only at the critical point but extends down to approximately $0.8 T_c$. Leveraging the exact integrability of the Ising model, we extend this comparison across the full spectrum of Polyakov loop separations, surpassing the conformal perturbation regime. Utilizing these findings, we quantify the leading EST correction beyond the Nambu-Goto approximation, confirming its compatibility with bootstrap analysis constraints. This correction carries significant physical insight and may clarify the nature of the flux tube and its representation within EST.

We examine graviton scattering within maximal supergravity on $(d+1)$-dimensional Anti-de Sitter (AdS) space, specifically for $d=3, 4,$ and $6$, assuming no additional compact spacetime dimensions. Holographic principles indicate that this setup corresponds to an unconventional, maximally supersymmetric conformal field theory (CFT) in $d$ dimensions characterized by having only the stress tensor as a light single-trace operator. This stands in contrast to conventional examples, such as Type IIB string theory on $AdS_5 \times S^5$ dual to $\mathcal{N}=4$ Super-Yang-Mills, where the CFT features light single-trace operators associated with every Kaluza-Klein mode on the $S^5$. We calculate the one-loop correction to the pure AdS$_{d+1}$ theory using a small Planck length expansion, which maps to the large central charge expansion in the dual CFT. Our results demonstrate that this correction reaches the most general non-perturbative conformal bootstrap bounds for the relevant correlator in the large central charge limit for $d=3, 4, 6$, whereas one-loop corrections in CFTs possessing string or M-theory duals remain strictly within the permitted region.

Grant-free random access (RA) methods are well-suited for machine-type communication (MTC) networks but must adapt to MTC traffic patterns, which differ significantly from human-type communication. Traditional RA protocols, such as exponential backoff (EB) within slotted-ALOHA, often result in excessive collisions and are not directly compatible with MTC traffic models. This study introduces a multi-agent deep Q-network (DQN) featuring parameter sharing to establish a unified collision resolution policy for all machine-type devices (MTDs) in the network. Additionally, we employ binary broadcast feedback shared among all devices to minimize signaling overhead. Performance evaluations comparing our proposed DQN-RA approach against EB schemes for up to 500 MTDs demonstrate that the DQN-based method outperforms EB policies, achieving a superior balance of throughput, delay, and collision rates.

The kinetic Sunyaev-Zel'dovich (kSZ) effect generates secondary anisotropies in the cosmic microwave background (CMB) via the scattering of CMB photons by intervening electrons. By cross-correlating these effects with large-scale structure tracers, researchers can reconstruct the three-dimensional radial-velocity field, a method termed kSZ tomography. This study investigates the cross-correlation between the CMB and line-intensity fluctuations to recover the late-time kSZ signal over a broad redshift span. Specifically, we examine CII emission lines and forecast the signal-to-noise ratio for kSZ tomography between redshifts $z=1$ and $z=5$ for future experiments. Our findings indicate that while instruments currently being built may achieve only low-significance detections, next-generation observatories will attain significantly higher sensitivity, with detection significance levels of $\mathcal{O}(10^2-10^3)$. Leveraging sample-variance cancellation, the cross-correlation between the velocity field derived from kSZ tomography and intensity fluctuations can enhance measurements of scale-dependent bias contributions from new physics at large scales. To demonstrate this gain, we analyze early Universe models featuring primordial local-type non-gaussianity and correlated compensated isocurvature perturbations. We demonstrate that utilizing CMB-S4 alongside an AtLAST-like survey could reduce uncertainties in $f_{\rm NL}$ and $A_{\rm CIP}$ by approximately a factor of three, yielding $\sigma(f_{\rm NL}) \lesssim 1$. Furthermore, we establish that observing both low and high redshifts is essential for breaking the degeneracy between these two parameters.

Function-as-a-Service (FaaS) has recently gained prominence as a means to lower the deployment costs of cloud applications compared to Infrastructure-as-a-Service (IaaS). Operating on a serverless "pay-as-you-go" model, FaaS incurs a higher cost per unit of execution time but generally offers faster function provisioning with minimal startup latency. In contrast, IaaS relies on Virtual Machines, which often endure prolonged cold-start delays, resulting in increased queuing times and higher rates of dropped requests. We introduce LIBRA, a balanced hybrid strategy that utilizes both VM-based and serverless resources to optimize cloud resource management for applications. LIBRA continuously monitors application demand to provision the necessary mix of VMs and serverless functions, thereby minimizing running costs while adhering to Service-Level Agreements (SLAs). Unlike existing state-of-the-art solutions, LIBRA not only mitigates VM cold-start delays to reduce response times by leveraging serverless capabilities but also routes low-rate, bursty demand to serverless environments where it is more cost-effective than instantiating new VMs. We evaluated LIBRA using real-world traces in a simulated setting as well as on the AWS commercial cloud. Our findings demonstrate that LIBRA surpasses other resource-provisioning policies, including a recent hybrid approach, achieving over an 85% reduction in SLA violations and up to 53% in cost savings.

Celestial bodies like stars and planets can potentially capture significant quantities of dark matter particles via dark matter-nucleon scattering. Previous research has treated various celestial objects, including the Earth and the Sun, as natural dark matter detectors to derive strict constraints on the dark matter-nucleon scattering cross-section. In this work, we utilize the approximately 10 MeV electron neutrino flux limits from the Super-Kamiokande experiment, employing the Earth as a massive natural detector to place tighter constraints on the dark matter-nucleon scattering cross-section. Our findings indicate that this approach generally yields more restrictive limits. Specifically, for certain dark matter mass ranges involving annihilation through the $b\bar{b}$ channel, the derived limits for both isospin-independent scattering and proton-only scattering surpass the constraints established by the PICO direct-detection experiment.

Terahertz frequencies represent an untapped resource for enabling high-speed, short-range communications, making the study of their propagation characteristics and the development of corresponding channel models a priority. While prior research utilized a measurement-based approach to create an accurate channel model for line-of-sight (LoS) links, this paper extends that work by developing models for non-line-of-sight (NLoS) links involving a single reflection. Specifically, we investigate reflections off both metal plates and wooden surfaces. Our model for received signal magnitude accounts for standing waves that form between the transmitter and receiver, with measurements demonstrating excellent agreement between empirical data and the proposed model. Furthermore, we analyzed the phase of the reflected signal across the 320–480 GHz frequency range. Although a linear error was observed between predicted and actual phase values, we developed a model to address this discrepancy. The resulting phase prediction model proves highly accurate across the entire 320–480 GHz spectrum and for both tested materials.

This study investigates conformal matter collineations of the energy-momentum tensor within a general spherically symmetric static spacetime. When the energy-momentum tensor is non-degenerate, the general form of these collineations is determined, with a maximum of fifteen independent conformal matter collineations possible. Conversely, in cases where the energy-momentum tensor is degenerate, these collineations exhibit infinite degrees of freedom. Furthermore, for certain subcases involving degenerate energy-momentum tensors where the Ricci tensor remains non-degenerate, non-degenerate Ricci inheritance collineations are found to exist.

We present and theoretically examine an experiment in which the displacement sensing of an optically levitated nanoparticle positioned near a surface enables the measurement of the induced dipole-dipole interaction between the particle and its thermal image. This measurement utilizes a surface that is transparent to trapping light yet reflective to infrared radiation, with a reflectivity that can be time-modulated. The underlying dipole-dipole interaction depends on the thermal radiation emitted by a silica nanoparticle possessing sufficient temporal coherence to correlate reflected radiation with the dipole's thermal fluctuations. The resulting force is orders of magnitude stronger than the thermal gradient force and exhibits a strong dependence on the nanoparticle's internal temperature for distances exceeding two micrometers. We contend that using displacement sensing of a levitated nanoparticle near a surface as an internal thermometer is experimentally viable. Gaining experimental access to the internal physics of a levitated nanoparticle in a vacuum is essential for understanding how decoherence limits current attempts to prepare a nanoparticle in a macroscopic quantum superposition state.

This study introduces a unified framework designed to address key challenges in dense cloud radio access networks (C-RAN), such as excessive power usage, restricted fronthaul bandwidth, high computational demands, and the lack of complete channel state information (CSI). Specifically, the work seeks to jointly optimize remote radio head (RRH) selection, user equipment (UE)-RRH associations, and beam-vectors to minimize total network power consumption (NPC) in dense multi-channel downlink C-RAN scenarios with imperfect CSI. This optimization must adhere to per-RRH power limits, individual UE rate requirements, and fronthaul capacity constraints, forming an NP-hard problem. Given the incomplete CSI, the exact rate expression for UEs is intractable; therefore, we conservatively substitute it with a lower-bound. Leveraging the successive convex approximation (SCA) technique and the link between data rate and mean square error (MSE), we develop a single-layer iterative algorithm with guaranteed convergence to solve the NPC minimization. Within each iteration, the Lagrange dual decomposition method determines the optimal beam-vector structure, enabling parallel computations at the Baseband unit (BBU) pool. Additionally, a bisection-based UE selection algorithm is introduced to ensure problem feasibility. Simulation outcomes demonstrate the advantages of the proposed algorithms and indicate that limited CSI is sufficient to achieve performance nearly equivalent to that obtained with perfect CSI.

The inverse and linear seesaw mechanisms serve as prominent extensions of the standard seesaw framework, featuring a larger number of sterile degrees of freedom that naturally account for the minimal masses of three active neutrinos at relatively low energy scales, such as the TeV range. To comprehensively characterize the mixing involving three active neutrinos, three sterile neutrinos, and three additional gauge-singlet neutral fermions within these paradigms, we provide the {\it first} complete parametrization of the $9\times 9$ flavor mixing matrix, defined by 36 rotation angles and 36 CP-violating phases. Furthermore, we derive the precise formulas for both the inverse and linear seesaw scenarios and examine potential deviations of the $3\times 3$ active neutrino mixing matrix from its unitary limit by computing effective Jarlskog invariants and unitarity nonagons.

We report multi-colour CCD photometric data for GSC4589-2999 collected in 2008 and 2009, which identify the object as an active Algel binary system. Analysis of this new data reveals a declining mean brightness of the system between 2007 and 2009. Light curves from 2008 to 2009 were analyzed using the Wilson-Devinney code, alongside an examination of the system's light and color variations across different orbital phases. The observed fluctuations in brightness and color are attributed to the rotation of irregularly distributed starspots on both stellar components.

Future wireless communication systems are constrained by the scarcity of conventional spectrum resources alongside an explosive increase in service demand, making millimeter-wave communication a viable solution for next-generation broadband cellular networks. Nevertheless, significant transmission path loss and severe absorption by oxygen and water molecules present substantial challenges, necessitating technical approaches distinct from those used in low-frequency wireless communication. Following an analysis of millimeter-wave transmission characteristics, this work comprehensively reviews the progress of millimeter-wave technology and RF front-ends. It thoroughly examines the technical challenges associated with millimeter-wave communication and proposes corresponding research directions.

Unsupervised relation discovery seeks to identify novel relationships within a text corpus without relying on labeled data, yet it frequently overlooks existing human-annotated knowledge bases even when they are pertinent. This paper investigates leveraging knowledge bases containing out-of-relation information—where the target relations differ entirely from those in the base—to supervise the discovery of unseen relations. We generate constraints between entity pairs using knowledge base embeddings and integrate these constraints into the discovery process via a variational auto-encoder. Experimental results demonstrate that this proposed approach significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in relation discovery.

Recent studies in robust optimization have identified an overfitting-like behavior where models trained to withstand adversarial attacks demonstrate superior robustness on training data than on test data. While prior research offered theoretical insights into this issue using a robust PAC-Bayesian bound over adversarial test error, existing algorithmic approaches remain only loosely tied to this bound, creating a disconnect between empirical performance and theoretical understanding of adversarial robustness. To bridge this gap, we propose a distinct formulation of the robust PAC-Bayesian bound and directly optimize it with respect to the model posterior. Our derivation links PAC-Bayesian learning to the geometry of the robust loss surface via a Trace of Hessian (TrH) regularizer, which quantifies surface flatness. Practically, we apply the TrH regularizer exclusively to the final layer, yielding an analytical solution with computational costs independent of network depth. We evaluate our TrH regularization method on CIFAR-10/100 and ImageNet using Vision Transformers (ViT), comparing it against baseline adversarial robustness techniques. Results indicate that TrH regularization enhances ViT robustness to match or exceed current state-of-the-art methods while simultaneously reducing memory usage and computational expenses.

Oscillatory magnetoresistance measurements in graphene have uncovered extensive new physics, typically investigated under low-current conditions. However, at high currents, electrons are driven far from equilibrium with the atomic lattice, causing their kinetic energy to surpass phonon thermal energy. This study reports three non-equilibrium phenomena in high-current monolayer graphene: (i) a "Doppler-like" frequency shift and splitting of transverse acoustic (TA) phonons emitted during inter-Landau level transitions; (ii) an intra-LL Mach effect involving TA phonon emission as electrons approach supersonic speeds; and (iii) the emergence of elastic inter-Landau level transitions at a critical carrier drift velocity, similar to the superfluid Landau velocity. All three quantum effects are unified by a single resonance equation and provide new pathways for exploring out-of-equilibrium phenomena in other two-dimensional fermion systems.

Recently, there has been significant interest in certifying model performance robustness against bounded data distribution shifts, a concept often categorized under distributional robustness. However, current methods are constrained by either stringent assumptions regarding model classes and loss functions—such as Lipschitz continuous gradients—or the need to solve intricate optimization problems. Consequently, their practical utility is hampered by limitations in scalability and flexibility; they frequently fail to scale to large-scale datasets with modern deep neural networks or accommodate non-smooth loss functions like the 0-1 loss. This paper addresses the certification of distributional robustness for blackbox models with bounded loss functions by introducing a novel framework grounded in Hellinger distance. Our approach successfully scales to ImageNet-sized datasets, complex architectures, and a wide variety of loss functions. We further demonstrate a specific application of this scalability: certifying out-of-domain generalization for large neural networks using metrics such as accuracy and AUC. Experimental validation across multiple datasets, including ImageNet where we achieve the first non-vacuous certified out-of-domain generalization, as well as smaller classification tasks where we outperform state-of-the-art methods, confirms the efficacy of our technique.

Machine Learning (ML) has been utilized within the high energy physics (HEP) community since the early 1980s to address a wide range of challenges. This study investigates the potential of Deep Learning techniques for estimating elliptic flow ($v_2$) in heavy-ion collisions at RHIC and LHC energies. A new approach is introduced to process input observables derived from particle kinematics. The proposed Deep Neural Network (DNN) is trained using Minimum Bias Pb-Pb collision simulations at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}} = 5.02$ TeV generated by the AMPT model. ML predictions are benchmarked against both experimental data and simulations. Results indicate that the Deep Learning model effectively maintains the centrality and energy dependence of $v_2$ across both RHIC and LHC energy scales. Furthermore, the DNN demonstrates significant success in predicting the $p_{\rm T}$ dependence of $v_2$. Even when event simulations include additional noise, the proposed DNN retains robustness and prediction accuracy to a considerable degree.

This study investigates self-excited dust acoustic waves (DAWs) and their propagation within a magnetized radio-frequency discharge plasma. These waves arise spontaneously in dusty plasma once additional particles are introduced into the confining potential well, subsequently traveling in the direction of streaming ions. Such spontaneous excitation of low-frequency modes occurs due to instabilities generated by streaming ions moving through the dust grain medium. The stability of these excited DAWs is governed by the background electric field and neutral gas pressure. Furthermore, the characteristics of DAWs are heavily influenced by the intensity of the external magnetic field. Specifically, a magnetic field strength of B < 0.05 T merely alters the properties of propagating waves under moderate conditions (P = 3.5 W, p = 27 Pa). However, when the magnetic field exceeds B > 0.05 T, DAWs begin to dampen, eventually being completely suppressed at B ~ 0.13 T. Conversely, when power and pressure are reduced to 3 W and 23 Pa, respectively, DAWs in the absence of a magnetic field exhibit slight instability; in this scenario, increasing the magnetic field up to 0.1 T or higher stabilizes the waves and modifies their propagation. The primary mechanism driving both the modification and damping of DAWs in a magnetized rf discharge plasma is the alteration of the sheath electric field where particles are confined in the presence of an external magnetic field.

The second African Conference on Fundamental and Applied Physics (ACP2021) occurred from March 7 to 11, 2022. Throughout the event, special sessions were dedicated to the African Strategy for Fundamental and Applied Physics (ASFAP) working groups to examine their scope, past and current activities, and shared areas of interest. This report aims to encapsulate the discussions held by ASFAP working groups regarding societal engagements, specifically focusing on Physics Education, Community Engagement, Young Physicists, and Women in Physics. Additionally, the report outlines recommended future activities within these societal engagement domains.

As facial biometrics become more prevalent, the challenge of differentiating between identical twins and non-twin look-alikes has grown in significance for automated facial recognition (FR) systems. Both groups present the most difficult scenarios for these tools due to their striking facial resemblance. This study leverages one of the most extensive twin datasets available to tackle two key FR issues: establishing a baseline for facial similarity among identical twins and evaluating how "doppelgangers" or look-alikes affect FR performance on large-scale datasets. A deep convolutional neural network was employed to calculate this similarity, trained on a specific verification task designed to cluster highly similar face pairs within the embedding space, achieving a test AUC of 0.9799. The resulting network generates quantitative similarity scores for any pair of faces and has been utilized to identify similar pairs across large face datasets. Furthermore, an analysis was conducted to correlate the scores produced by the proposed network with those from standard facial recognition tools.

Solar flares originate from magnetic eruptions within active regions on the sun's surface, events that significantly affect human activities but can often be mitigated through timely forecasting. While previous machine learning approaches for flare prediction relied on physics-based attributes derived from active region images, recent studies have begun utilizing features automatically extracted via deep learning techniques like convolutional neural networks. This work introduces a novel suite of shape-based features extracted from solar magnetogram images using computational topology and geometry. We assess the efficacy of these features within a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) framework, comparing them against conventional physics-based attributes. Our results demonstrate that these abstract shape-based features surpass those selected by human experts, and that integrating both feature sets further enhances forecasting performance.

The 1T$^\prime$-MoS$_2$ material displays valley-spin-polarized tilted Dirac bands when subjected to an external vertical electric field and experiences a topological phase transition between a topological insulator and a band insulator near a critical field strength. Utilizing linear response theory, we theoretically examine the anisotropic longitudinal optical conductivities of these tilted Dirac bands in both undoped and doped 1T$^\prime$-MoS$_2$, accounting for the impact of the vertical electric field. Our analysis elucidates how the spin-orbit coupling gap, band tilting, and vertical electric field influence the optical conductivities of the tilted Dirac bands. Furthermore, we propose a theoretical framework for detecting the topological phase transition in 1T$^\prime$-MoS$_2$ through the distinctive behaviors of longitudinal optical conductivities. Given the similarities in their band structures, these findings for 1T$^\prime$-MoS$_2$ are anticipated to be qualitatively applicable to other monolayer tilted gapped Dirac materials, including $\alpha$-SnS$_2$, TaCoTe$_2$, and TaIrTe$_4$.

This paper presents $(p, q)$-deformed versions of generalized Touchard polynomials and Stirling numbers, serving as post-quantum extensions of their $q$-deformed counterparts. We establish the relationship between these deformations and derive a recurrence relation for the $(p, q)$-deformed generalized Touchard polynomials, which provides a $(p, q)$-deformation of Spivey's relation.

Investigating the impact of stellar mass on planetary properties requires detecting and characterizing exoplanets and brown dwarfs (BDs) orbiting massive AF-type stars. However, radial velocity (RV) surveys have largely overlooked these targets due to their sparse, rotation-broadened, and jitter-blended spectral lines, resulting in limited knowledge about planet and BD formation around hot stars. This study aims to expand the sample by precisely determining the masses and eccentricities of giant planets and BDs transiting AF-type stars identified by the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS). We utilized ground-based photometry and high-precision RV data from CORALIE, CHIRON, TRES, FEROS, and MINERVA-Australis spectrographs to analyze bright (V < 12 mag) stars with $T_{\mathrm{eff}}$ > 6200 K hosting giant companions (R > 7 $\mathrm{R_{\rm \oplus}}$). Through this effort, we report the discovery of three brown dwarf companions—TOI-629b, TOI-1982b, and TOI-2543b—and one massive planet, TOI-1107b. Joint analysis reveals the BDs possess masses of 66–68 $\mathrm{M_{\rm Jup}}$, orbital periods ranging from 7.54 to 17.17 days, and radii between 0.95 and 1.11 $\mathrm{R_{\rm Jup}}$. The hot Jupiter TOI-1107b orbits every 4.08 days with a radius of 1.30 $\mathrm{R_{\rm Jup}}$ and a mass of 3.35 $\mathrm{M_{\rm Jup}}$. Additionally, the survey identified four low-mass eclipsing components: TOI-288b, TOI-446b, TOI-478b, and TOI-764b. Notably, both TOI-1107b and TOI-1982b exhibit anomalously inflated radii relative to their system ages, and TOI-629 represents one of the hottest stars hosting a known transiting brown dwarf. Furthermore, TOI-629b and TOI-1982b rank among the most eccentric brown dwarfs discovered.

Well-known in high-energy physics, Higgs and Goldstone modes have been observed across various condensed matter systems, such as magnetism and superconductivity, and the Goldstone-Higgs framework offers new perspectives on structural phase transitions. This study demonstrates that the Leggett mode, a collective excitation in multi-band superconductors, possesses a counterpart in crystallographic phase transitions. These structural Leggett modes manifest as antiphase Goldstone modes (anti-phasons) within the phase channel, analogous to Leggett's original findings in *Prog. Theor. Phys.* 36, 901 (1966). Furthermore, a novel collective mode emerges in the amplitude channel: an out-of-phase (antiphase) Higgs mode, which is expected to be detectable in multi-band superconductors. We substantiate the existence and characteristics of these structural Leggett modes through the case study of the pyrochlore relaxor ferroelectric, Cd$_2$Nb$_2$O$_7$.

Building upon the Regularized Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (RLTH), which posits the existence of smooth, non-binary subnetworks within dense networks capable of matching the performance of the full network, we introduce a few-shot class incremental learning (FSCIL) approach named \emph{Soft-SubNetworks (SoftNet)}. This method aims to enable incremental learning across multiple sessions, where each session contains only a limited number of training examples per class, while retaining knowledge from prior sessions. SoftNet simultaneously optimizes model weights and adaptive non-binary soft masks during a base training session; each mask comprises a major and a minor subnetwork. The major subnetwork is designed to mitigate catastrophic forgetting, whereas the minor subnetwork prevents overfitting to the scarce samples in new sessions. Extensive empirical evaluations demonstrate that SoftNet effectively addresses the few-shot incremental learning challenge, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines across various benchmark datasets.

This study investigates a parabolic partial differential equation featuring a non-linear, non-local term in time. This term represents the product of an interaction potential and the solution itself. The interaction potential relies on a weighted integral of the solution across the entire time domain and adheres to fairly broad conditions. Specifically, it is assumed to be a continuous function bounded from below, capable of behaving arbitrarily at infinity. Consequently, the interaction term does not constitute a lower-order term within the equation. The paper establishes the weak solvability of the corresponding initial boundary value problem. Notably, the proof relies solely on energy estimates and avoids any assumptions regarding the solution's continuity with respect to time.

Melt pools formed from molten metal exhibit highly non-linear behaviors that are extremely sensitive to boundary conditions. Numerical simulations of these melt pools frequently overlook temporal and spatial fluctuations in energy flux distribution. Furthermore, researchers often artificially adjust thermo-physical properties to align predicted melt-pool shapes with experimental macrographs. This study examines laser spot melting in conduction mode, specifically investigating how dynamically modified energy flux distributions and variable thermo-physical properties influence melt pool oscillatory behavior under both deformable and non-deformable gas-metal interface assumptions. The findings indicate that modifying the absorbed energy flux alters oscillatory fluid dynamics, thereby impacting the predicted melt pool's shape and dimensions. Additionally, the study demonstrates that artificially altering thermophysical properties or employing a non-deformable surface assumption results in significant deviations in oscillatory behavior compared to simulations without these adjustments.

We examine several models common in quantum optics by representing their Hamiltonians within Fock-state lattices. The limited degrees of freedom inherent to these systems, combined with their symmetries, result in relatively simple lattice structures that can be mapped onto established condensed matter models, thereby offering fresh insights into quantum optical phenomena. Although we compile an extensive catalog of such models and their associated lattices, we highlight specific cases to illustrate the method's efficacy. For instance, the three-mode boson model exhibits a fractal spectrum and chiral evolution within the Fock-state lattice, characterized by localized distributions moving along symmetric paths. In another example, the central spin model produces a Fock-state lattice analogous to the SSH-model, supporting topological edge states. Furthermore, we demonstrate how flat bands observed in lattice models can appear in corresponding Fock-state lattices, a phenomenon connected to so-called dark states.

We examine the principal steps of the recently introduced relativistic fluid dynamics framework incorporating spin degrees of freedom. By deriving from the foundational definitions of quantum kinetic theory regarding equilibrium phase space distributions, we establish the equations of motion for the system's expansion. Furthermore, we analyze the evolution of spin polarization within a Bjorken hydrodynamical background.

Prior research established a scaling law linking Language Model (LM) size to zero-shot performance across various NLP tasks. However, our findings reveal that this relationship breaks down when large LMs are evaluated on tasks using negated prompts, exhibiting an inverse scaling law instead. We assessed nine such tasks across four categories: (1) pretrained LMs (OPT and GPT-3) ranging from 125M to 175B parameters, (2) models fine-tuned for prompt generalization (InstructGPT), (3) models given few-shot examples, and (4) models specifically fine-tuned on negated prompts. In all cases, performance degraded as model size increased, creating a substantial gap between human performance and model scores on both original and negated prompts. By exposing a fundamental limitation in current LM architectures and training methods, we call for the development of new strategies to ensure models adhere strictly to instructions. To facilitate further research, we have released our code and datasets at https://github.com/joeljang/negated-prompts-for-llms.

For an associative ring $R$ with identity, we investigate the non-existence of $k$-torsion within $NK_1GQ(R)$, which represents the Bass nil-groups associated with general quadratic or Bak's unitary groups. Furthermore, by employing a graded extension of Quillen–Suslin theory, we establish a corresponding result for graded rings.

This study presents a unique chance to investigate the inner dust coma environments of comets 45P/Honda-Mrkos-Pajdušáková (45P/HMP) and 46P/Wirtanen, where dust and gas remain partially coupled, using visible light observations from December 26, 2016 to March 15, 2017 for 45P/HMP, and November 10, 2018 to February 13, 2019 for 46P/Wirtanen. Radial profile slopes were determined in the R and HB-BC filters, which best represent dust, revealing significant deviations from a purely radially expanding coma. For 45P/HMP, the azimuthally averaged radial profile slope shifted gradually from -1.81 ± 0.20 five days before perihelion to -0.35 ± 0.16 seventy-four days after. In contrast, 46P/Wirtanen maintained a relatively steady radial profile slope of -1.05 ± 0.05 throughout the observation window. Furthermore, 46P/Wirtanen's radial profile exhibited dependence on the skyplane-projected solar position angle, whereas 45P/HMP's did not. These findings indicate that the two comets possess markedly different coma dust environments and distinct dust characteristics, underscoring the importance of well-resolved inner comae for accurately characterizing dust conditions.

We characterize the Weyl-Hörmander symbol classes $S(M,g)$ by examining how the associated $\Psi$DOs act on time-frequency shifts of a single test function. To facilitate this, we introduce a geometric short-time Fourier transform tailored for the analysis of $S(M,g)$. Furthermore, we define new modulation spaces and establish the characterization of these Weyl-Hörmander classes by demonstrating that they correspond to intersections of such modulation spaces, which are appropriate for time-frequency analysis.

London-van der Waals dispersion forces play a pivotal role in condensed matter, biological phenomena, and self-assembly. This letter introduces a computational approach for determining the C6 coefficients that define non-retarded dispersion interactions within molecules existing in coherent superpositions of excited states. We examine various ultrafast femtosecond pump-probe methodologies. Applying this technique to LiH molecules reveals that their London-van der Waals interactions can undergo significant alterations following exposure to a pump pulse. Specifically, the pulse modulates the C6 coefficients, and the complex interplay among molecular polarization, orientation, and dipole fields generates a diverse array of interaction combinations.

We introduce a technique to estimate spectral gaps for reversible Markov jump processes featuring chaotic invariant measures, subsequently utilizing it to validate the Kac conjecture regarding hard sphere collisions in three dimensions.

This paper investigates the exact controllability of two one-dimensional coupled wave equations featuring first-order coupling terms, where the coefficients vary with both space and time. We establish a necessary and sufficient condition for exact controllability in high frequencies within the general case and for unique continuation in the cascade scenario.

While most rainfall extreme models concentrate on point data, there is greater interest in precipitation aggregated over areas ranging up to river catchment scales. To effectively and parsimoniously model the extremes of these aggregates across varying spatial resolutions, one must understand the underlying spatial processes. Precipitation results from a mix of processes operating at different intensities and scales, such as convective and frontal systems. Typically, extremes in aggregates for standard catchment sizes stem from the extremes of a single process type rather than a combination of both. The process dominating aggregate extremal behavior shifts depending on the aggregation area: high-intensity convective events drive extremes at small scales, whereas the contribution of lower-intensity, large-scale fronts grows as the aggregation area expands. Consequently, a unified approach to modeling spatial aggregates from small to large scales requires a framework capable of accurately capturing the extremal properties of both convective and frontal events. Previous extreme value methods overlooked this mixture structure; therefore, we propose a spatial extreme value model composed of two components with distinct marginal and dependence models. This approach captures the extremal behavior of both rainfall types and more faithfully reproduces spatial aggregates across a broad range of scales. Modeling the frontal component presents new challenges due to its strong long-range extremal spatial dependence. Applied to fine-scale, high-dimensional gridded precipitation data, our method demonstrates that accounting for this mixture structure significantly improves joint inference regarding extremes of spatial aggregates across regions of differing sizes.

We identify a flaw in the proof asserting that Island Finder conditions guarantee the existence of islands. By examining cases that meet these criteria yet lack actual islands—termed "island mirages"—we demonstrate this discrepancy. Additionally, we present and resolve two novel puzzles related to islands, one of which directly conflicts with the quantum Bousso bound.

This paper investigates the formation and structure of multidimensional shock waves for the first-order conservation law $\partial_t u+\partial_x F(u)+\partial_y G(u)=0$, given smooth initial data $u_0(x,y)$. It is established that when $\min{H(\xi,\eta)}<0$, the smooth solution $u$ undergoes blow-up at the critical time $T^*=-\frac{1}{\min{H(\xi,\eta)}}$, where $H(\xi,\eta)=\partial_{\xi}(F'(u_0(\xi,\eta)))+\partial_{\eta}(G'(u_0(\xi,\eta)))$. Specifically, while the first-order derivatives $\nabla_{t,x,y}u$ become unbounded at $t=T^*$, the solution $u$ itself remains continuous up to this point. Assuming a generic nondegenerate condition on $H(\xi,\eta)$, we construct a local weak entropy solution $u$ valid for $t\ge T^*$. This solution exhibits non-uniform Lipschitz continuity on both sides of the resulting shock surface $\Sigma$. The shock strength begins at zero along the initial blow-up curve $\Gamma$ and subsequently increases for $t>T^*$. Furthermore, precise and detailed characterizations of the singularities of $u$ within the vicinity of $\Gamma$ are provided.

This research examines the cycle counts within permutations of $\{1, \dots, n\}$ generated by the Mallows distribution, where the probability of selecting a permutation $\pi \in S_n$ is proportional to $q^{\text{inv}(\pi)}$ for a parameter $q>0$, with $\text{inv}(\pi)$ representing the inversion count. For a fixed integer $\ell$, we analyze the vector of cycle counts $(C_1(\Pi_n),\dots,C_\ell(\Pi_n))$, where $C_i(\pi)$ represents the number of cycles of length $i$ in $\pi$, and $\Pi_n$ is drawn from the Mallows distribution. We demonstrate that when $0<q<1$ is fixed and $n$ approaches infinity, there exist positive constants $m_i$ such that the expected value of each $C_i(\Pi_n)$ is asymptotically $(1+o(1)) \cdot m_i\cdot n$. Furthermore, an appropriately rescaled version of this cycle count vector converges to a joint Gaussian distribution. In contrast, for $q>1$, a notable divergence emerges between the behaviors of even and odd cycles. While even cycle counts maintain linear means and converge to a multivariate Gaussian distribution after rescaling, the limiting behavior of odd cycles depends on the parity of $n$. Specifically, for both even ($2n$) and odd ($2n+1$) cases, the vectors of odd cycle counts converge to distinct discrete limiting distributions without requiring renormalization. These distributions are characterized using Gnedin and Olshanski's bi-infinite extension of the Mallows model. Additionally, we investigate these limiting distributions and the constants governing the Gaussian limits. For instance, as $q$ decreases toward 1, the expected number of 1-cycles converges to $1/2$, a value distinct from the case where $q=1$. Finally, we highlight an intriguing "oscillating" phenomenon in the limiting probability measures for $q>1$, which varies depending on whether $n$ is even or odd.

Weakly-supervised text classification seeks to build classifiers using only a limited set of user-provided seed words. Most prior research presupposes the availability of high-quality seed words, yet obtaining expert-annotated terms can be challenging. Moreover, without labeled documents in this setting, it is impossible to evaluate the quality of selected seed words, rendering the selection process akin to "walking in the dark." This study eliminates the reliance on expert-curated seeds by first extracting (potentially noisy) candidate words linked to category names. Individual interim models are then trained using these candidates, and their error rates are estimated unsupervised. Candidates producing the lowest estimated errors are selected for the final seed set. Comprehensive testing across six binary classification tasks on four widely used datasets shows that the proposed approach surpasses baselines relying solely on category names and achieves performance comparable to methods using expert-annotated seeds.

This study reviews the impact of stellar flybys and encounters on protoplanetary discs surrounding young stars, drawing on three decades of published literature. Given that the majority of stars younger than 2 Myr possess these discs, tidal disturbances significantly influence planet formation. First, we assess the likelihood of such encounters: in a typical star-forming region, over 50% of stars with planet-forming discs are expected to undergo a close stellar flyby or encounter within 1,000 astronomical units. Second, we outline the specific dynamical consequences of these interactions. Prograde, parabolic, and disc-penetrating flybys are the most destructive; notably, grazing and penetrating encounters can cause the secondary star to capture disc material, forming a highly misaligned circumsecondary disc relative to the primary's disc. These events may trigger extreme accretion and outbursts akin to those seen in FU Orionis-type stars, while retrograde flybys distinctly produce warped or fragmented discs. Third, we examine recently observed stellar systems suspected of having experienced flybys or encounters, such as UX Tau, RW Aur, AS 209, Z CMa, and FU Ori. Finally, we discuss the broader implications for planet formation and exoplanet demographics, including potential signatures of a flyby within our own Solar System, such as anomalies in the orbits of trans-Neptunian objects and the Sun's axial tilt.

We introduce a novel, compact, all-glass vapor cell that incorporates hollow-core photonic crystal fibers. By eliminating metals typically found in traditional vacuum chambers and adopting a significantly smaller geometry, this design enables rapid and uniform heating. Consequently, the fibers can be filled within much shorter timeframes, spanning from minutes to hours. Furthermore, the entirely glass construction provides optical access along the fiber, facilitating real-time monitoring of rubidium atom diffusion through frequency-dependent fluorescence measurements. Finally, the atomic density is determined numerically by applying a 5-level system of Bloch equations.

We compute the form factors for $B 	o\pi\ell
u$ and $B_s 	o K \ell
u$ decays using dynamical lattice QCD. Our calculations rely on (2+1)-flavor gauge-field ensembles from RBC-UKQCD, which were generated employing domain-wall fermions and Iwasaki gauge actions. The $b$ quarks are treated via an anisotropic clover action interpreted within the relativistic heavy-quark framework. We examine two lattice spacings, approximately $0.11$ and $0.086$ fm, utilizing unitary pion masses down to roughly $290$ MeV. By applying SU(2) "hard-pion" chiral perturbation theory, we simultaneously extrapolate our data to physical light-quark masses and the continuum limit while interpolating in pion and kaon energy. We present comprehensive error budgets for the form factors $f_+(q^2)$ and $f_0(q^2)$ at three momentum values covering the accessible $q^2$ range. Furthermore, we extrapolate to $q^2 = 0$ using a model-independent $z$-parametrization, reporting the final results as $z$-coefficients alongside their correlation matrix. Our findings align with other lattice determinations utilizing staggered light quarks, offering crucial independent verification. Since both decay modes allow for the extraction of the CKM matrix element $|V_{ub}|$, we demonstrate this by performing a combined $z$-fit of our $B	o\pi\ell
u$ form-factor data with experimental branching fractions, treating the relative normalization as a free parameter. This yields $|V_{ub}| = 3.61(32) 	imes 10^{-3}$, with errors encompassing both statistical and systematic components. A similar procedure can be applied to $B_s	o K \ell
u$ once experimental data becomes available. In preparation for future measurements, we also provide predictions for the Standard Model differential branching fractions and forward-backward asymmetries for these decays.

The interactivism model offers a dynamic perspective on language, communication, and cognition. This study examines that foundational theory within the realm of dialogue modelling for spoken dialogue systems (SDS). To broaden this theoretical framework, we introduce a collection of design principles grounded in core psycholinguistic and communication theories to realize interactivism in SDS. These principles are derived from essential concepts that form the foundation of our proposed design guidelines.

Convolutional Neural Network (CNN)-based generative deep learning methods serve as powerful instruments for forecasting non-linear structures within cosmology. This study utilizes these techniques to derive high-resolution dark matter halos from large-scale, low-resolution dark matter-only simulations. The approach involves mapping density fields from lower to higher resolutions while maintaining identical cosmological parameters, initial conditions, and box sizes. By employing a U-Net variant integrated with a conditional GAN, we successfully resolve structures with an eightfold increase in mass resolution. The generated outputs align exceptionally well with high-resolution targets both visually and statistically. Consequently, this methodology enables the production of high-resolution density data across Gpc/h box sizes from low-resolution simulations with minimal computational cost.

We propose a chiral anomalous fermion Hamiltonian to investigate higher-order topological (HOT) phases exhibiting chiral symmetry $\mathcal{C}$ fractionalized as $\mathcal{C}_{x}\mathcal{C}_{y}\mathcal{C}_{z}$. Initially, we address the $\mathcal{C}$-chiral symmetry constraints within eight-band models and characterize those arising from partial $\mathcal{C}_{i}$ components. Subsequently, we derive explicit expressions for the fractional states defining HOT matter, discuss their interrelations and connections to standard Altland-Zirnbauer gapless modes, and outline the distinctive properties of these gapless fractional states alongside their contribution to the topological index of the chiral model. These results are demonstrated to be essential for exploring and managing higher-order topological phases.

We analyze connectivity fluctuations in networks constructed via the horizontal visibility (HV) algorithm applied to trajectories from nonlinear circle maps near the quasiperiodic transition to chaos. The resulting HV graphs exhibit significant anomalies, characterized by degree fluctuations across all scales with amplitudes that grow as network size increases. We identify families of Pesin-like identities linking entropy growth rates to generalized graph-theoretical Lyapunov exponents, where each family is defined by an irrational winding number possessing a purely periodic continued fraction. Our findings are demonstrated using the golden, silver, and bronze numbers.

Symptom data is largely recorded in free-text clinical notes, making it difficult to access for downstream tasks. To overcome this, we require information extraction techniques capable of managing linguistic variations in clinical language across different institutions and specialties. This paper introduces a domain generalization approach for symptom extraction using pretraining and fine-tuning datasets that differ from the target domain regarding institution, specialty, or patient demographics. We utilize a transformer-based joint entity and relation extraction method to identify symptom events. To minimize dependence on domain-specific features, we propose a domain generalization strategy that dynamically masks frequent symptom terms in the source domain. Furthermore, we pretrain the transformer language model on unlabeled, task-relevant texts to enhance representation learning. Experimental results demonstrate that both masking and adaptive pretraining substantially improve performance when the source domain is significantly distant from the target domain.

The CEV model is defined by the stochastic differential equation $X_t=X_0+\int_0^t\mu X_sds+\int_0^t\sigma (X^+_s)^pdW_s$, where $\frac{1}{2}\le p<1$. This model exhibits a non-Lipschitz diffusion coefficient and possesses a positive probability of absorption at zero. We demonstrate the weak convergence of Euler-Maruyama approximations $X_t^n$ to the process $X_t$ over the interval $0\le t\le T$ within the Skorokhod metric. Furthermore, we introduce a novel approximation using continuous processes that relaxes certain technical requirements found in \cite{HZa}, where weak convergence was previously proven via the discrete time martingale problem. As an illustrative application, we compute ruin probabilities. We find that ruin probabilities derived from simulations are not assured to converge to their theoretical counterparts because zero acts as a discontinuity point for the limiting distribution. To prove convergence, we employ the Levy metric and validate the results numerically. Although our findings are presented for this specific model, the methodology extends to a broader class of non-Lipschitz diffusions involving absorption.

We introduce a data-driven pipeline designed to generate exogenous observation data for the New Fashion Product Performance Forecasting (NFPPF) challenge, which involves predicting the success of brand-new apparel without historical data. This pipeline constructs the missing historical context by starting with a single image of the new clothing item. It begins by expanding textual tags linked to the image and searching for relevant fashionable or unfashionable images from specific past periods available online. Using confident learning, a binary classifier is robustly trained on these web-sourced images to understand past fashion trends and assess how well the new item aligns with them. This alignment generates the POtential Performance (POP) time series, which estimates how the item would have performed had it been available earlier. The POP metric demonstrates high predictive power for future performance, significantly improving sales forecasts across all state-of-the-art models on the recent VISUELLE fast-fashion dataset. Furthermore, we show that POP accurately reflects the ground-truth popularity of new style ensembles on the Fashion Forward benchmark, proving that our web-derived signal truthfully captures popularity, is universally accessible, and generalizes to any analysis period. The forecasting code, data, and POP time series can be accessed at: https://github.com/HumaticsLAB/POP-Mining-POtential-Performance

SARS-CoV-2 is the virus responsible for causing COVID-19 in humans. Similar to other coronaviruses, it possesses the ability to adapt to various hosts and evolve into distinct lineages, which are primarily defined by mutations in the spike protein. Grasping the structure of the spike protein and how it can be altered is essential for assessing the risk of specific lineages, a critical step in managing current outbreaks and averting future pandemics. While machine learning (ML) offers a promising solution due to the vast amount of available sequencing data—much of which remains unaligned or unassembled—traditional ML methods struggle because they rely on fixed-length numerical vectors within Euclidean space, a format ill-suited for biological sequence classification and clustering. To address this, we developed a method that transforms spike protein sequences into a Sequence Similarity Network (SSN). This SSN serves as input for classical graph mining algorithms to perform tasks like classification and clustering. Our results demonstrate that this alignment-free approach outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in clustering accuracy. Furthermore, using Node2Vec-based embeddings on our network yields higher classification accuracy compared to other baseline embedding techniques.

This study examines a symmetric deformed random matrix generated by perturbing the diagonal entries of a Wigner matrix. We observe that the eigenvector $\vec{x}_{\rm min}$ associated with the minimal eigenvalue $\lambda_{\rm min}$ of this deformed matrix exhibits a tendency to condense at a single site. Under specific perturbation types and in the limit of large components, this condensation manifests as a sharp phase transition, mathematically analogous to Bose-Einstein condensation. Using the replica method, we investigate this Bose-Einstein-like phenomenon by first deriving a formula to compute both the minimal eigenvalue and the overlap of $\vec{x}_{\rm min}$. We then apply this formula to two solvable scenarios: one where the perturbation distribution features a double peak, and another where it follows a continuous distribution. In the double peak case, we find that at the transition point, the participation ratio shifts discontinuously from a finite value to zero. Conversely, for the continuous distribution case, the participation ratio approaches zero either continuously or discontinuously, contingent upon the specific nature of the distribution.

For a subset $E \subset {\Bbb F}_q^d$ with $d \ge 2$, where ${\Bbb F}_q$ denotes the finite field of order $q$, we examine the distance graph ${\mathcal G}^{dist}_t(E)$ for $t \not=0$. In this graph, vertices correspond to elements of $E$, and an edge exists between $x$ and $y$ if their squared Euclidean distance satisfies $||x-y|| = \sum_{i=1}^d (x_i-y_i)^2 = t$. We demonstrate that when $|E| \ge C_k q^{\frac{d+2}{2}}$, the graph ${\mathcal G}^{dist}_t(E)$ contains a statistically expected number of cycles of length $k$. Furthermore, we analyze the dot-product graph ${\mathcal G}^{prod}_t(E)$ for $t \not=0$, where edges connect $x$ and $y$ if $x \cdot y = \sum_{i=1}^d x_i y_i = t$. By employing more advanced techniques to address the lack of translation invariance in the dot-product function, we derive analogous results for this case. Additionally, for sufficiently long cycles, the exponent $\frac{d+2}{2}$ is improved.

Drawing inspiration from detailed models of biological neurons, Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) have been explored for their potential to offer more biologically realistic and powerful neural computation, as well as to harness the energy efficiency of biological systems. However, their performance has historically lagged behind that of classical Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs). In this study, we present a novel approach combining a surrogate gradient with recurrent networks of tunable, adaptive spiking neurons, achieving state-of-the-art results for SNNs on difficult time-domain tasks such as speech and gesture recognition. These results surpass the performance of standard classical Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) and rival the best modern ANNs. Furthermore, due to the sparse spiking activity exhibited by these SNNs, they are theoretically one to three orders of magnitude more computationally efficient than RNNs with similar performance. Collectively, these findings position SNNs as a promising solution for AI hardware implementation.

Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) ranks as the fourth leading global cause of mortality. However, diagnosis depends heavily on spirometry and functional airway assessment, leading to significant underdiagnosis, particularly in early stages. Although recent advancements in deep learning (DL) demonstrate promising potential for identifying COPD from CT scans, these models often fail to generalize across different medical centers due to heterogeneous syndromes and distinct phenotypes. Furthermore, privacy regulations prevent the aggregation of distributed CT images into a single centralized repository. While federated learning (FL) offers a solution by training on distributed private data, standard FL methods degrade in performance when data is non-independent and identically distributed (Non-IID). To address this, we propose a novel personalized federated learning (PFL) method utilizing vision transformers (ViT) for distributed and heterogeneous COPD CT datasets. Specifically, our approach partially personalizes certain heads within multi-headed self-attention layers to capture local data nuances while retaining shared heads to extract common features. To our knowledge, this represents the first PFL framework specifically designed for ViT-based COPD identification. Evaluations on a curated dataset from six medical centers demonstrate that our method outperforms existing PFL approaches based on convolutional neural networks.

Using 9 fb$^{-1}$ of proton-proton collision data recorded by the LHCb detector from 2011 to 2018, researchers have analyzed $B^+\rightarrow J/\psi \pi^+ \pi^- K^+$ decays. This study reports precise branching fraction ratios for intermediate states including $\psi_2(3823)$, $\chi_{c1}(3872)$, and $\psi(2S)$. For the first time, the decay $B^+\rightarrow \psi_2(3823)K^+$ (where $\psi_2(3823)\rightarrow J\psi\pi^+\pi^-$) is observed with a statistical significance of 5.1 standard deviations. The mass differences among these three states are determined as follows:
$$
\begin{array}{rcl} m_{\chi_{c1(3872)}} - m_{\psi_2(3823)} &= & 47.50 \pm 0.53 \pm 0.13\,\mathrm{MeV/}c^2\,, \\ m_{\psi_2(3823)} - m_{\psi(2S)} &= & 137.98 \pm 0.53 \pm 0.14\,\mathrm{MeV/}c^2\,, \\ m_{\chi_{c1}(3872)} - m_{\psi(2S)} &= & 185.49 \pm 0.06 \pm 0.03\,\mathrm{MeV/}c^2\,, \end{array} $$
