Additionally, we discuss effective flavor-changing interactions among Standard Model fermions induced by the bulk scalar and comment on the potential influence of the bulk scalar's Higgs portal interaction on Higgs boson couplings.

This study introduces a new method for authorship verification using handwritten word images. The proposed approach is text-independent and imposes no constraints on the size of the input images. First, the SIFT algorithm extracts key points across different levels of abstraction (individual letters, characters, or character combinations). These points are fed into a trained Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) to generate feature maps. However, because SIFT key points vary in scale, the resulting feature maps may differ in size. To resolve this, a Histogram of Gradients (HOG) is applied to create a fixed representation. Since CNNs typically increase the number of filters per block with network depth, calculating HOG features for every convolutional map would significantly increase dimensionality and computational cost. To mitigate this, an entropy-based method is employed to learn weights for the feature maps of a specific CNN layer during training. The system's effectiveness was validated on two public datasets, CVL and IAM, demonstrating promising results compared to prior research.

Using Ohi's criterion for the faithful flatness of commutative ring extensions, we demonstrate that any \'etale extension $k[Y_1, \ldots, Y_n]\subseteq k[X_1, \ldots, X_n]$ of polynomial rings over a commutative ring $k$ is faithfully flat. Consequently, when $k$ is an algebraically closed field, every \'etale polynomial map $k^{n} \to k^{n}$ is surjective.

Driven by the rapid advancement of deep learning, recent studies have increasingly applied graph neural networks (GNNs) to tackle NP-hard challenges like Boolean Satisfiability (SAT), highlighting their potential to merge machine learning with symbolic reasoning. Yet, existing literature has largely overlooked the quality of the solutions GNNs generate. This paper examines the ability of GNNs to solve the Maximum Satisfiability (MaxSAT) problem from both theoretical and practical standpoints. We develop two distinct GNN architectures trained on benchmark MaxSAT instances and demonstrate through experimental analysis that GNNs hold significant promise for addressing MaxSAT. Furthermore, we provide the first theoretical explanation, grounded in algorithmic alignment theory, for how GNNs can effectively learn to solve the MaxSAT problem to a certain degree.

Although molecular simulations frequently assist in analyzing neutron reflectometry data, the technique's focus on large-scale structures often renders all-atom simulations unnecessary. This study offers the inaugural direct comparison between reflectometry profiles derived from various all-atom and coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations, benchmarking them against traditional model layer structure analysis to identify the minimum simulation resolution needed for accurate experimental reproduction. Our findings indicate that systematic limitations hinder the efficacy of the MARTINI potential model, whereas both the Berger united-atom and Slipids all-atom models align closely with experimental data. While the model layer structure yields the strongest agreement, higher-resolution simulation-dependent methods achieve comparable results. Ultimately, we employ atomistic simulations to guide refinements to model layer structures, resulting in a more realistic monolayer representation.

Acquiring semantically meaningful sentence embeddings remains an unresolved challenge in natural language processing. This study introduces a novel method for learning sentence embeddings that leverages both visual and textual data through a multimodal contrastive objective. Experiments across multiple semantic textual similarity tasks reveal that our approach consistently enhances performance across diverse datasets and pre-trained encoders. Specifically, by integrating a modest amount of multimodal data with a substantial text-only corpus, we achieve a 1.7% increase in the state-of-the-art average Spearman's correlation. Furthermore, an analysis of the textual embedding space demonstrates that our model effectively aligns semantically similar sentences, offering insight into its superior performance.

Contrastive learning (CL) has recently become a highly effective approach for unsupervised graph representation learning. Typically, graph CL techniques generate two views of a graph through stochastic augmentation and then optimize for representation consistency between these views. Although graph CL has advanced significantly, the design of augmentation strategies—a critical element of CL—has been largely overlooked. We contend that augmentation schemes must safeguard the intrinsic structures and attributes of graphs, compelling models to learn representations that remain robust against perturbations in less significant nodes and edges. Conversely, most current methods rely on uniform augmentation, such as randomly dropping edges or shuffling features indiscriminately, which results in suboptimal performance. This paper introduces a novel graph contrastive representation learning framework featuring adaptive augmentation that integrates diverse priors regarding both the topological and semantic characteristics of graphs. At the topological level, we develop augmentation strategies grounded in node centrality metrics to emphasize key connectivity patterns. At the node attribute level, we degrade node features by injecting additional noise into less important ones, thereby forcing the model to discern underlying semantic information. Through extensive node classification experiments across multiple real-world datasets, we demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art baselines and even exceeds the performance of certain supervised approaches, confirming the efficacy of our adaptive augmentation-enhanced contrastive framework.

This study introduces polarization profiles for 23 millisecond pulsars observed at 820 MHz and 1500 MHz using the Green Bank Telescope within the NANOGrav pulsar timing array project. Data calibration relies on Mueller matrix solutions derived from observations of PSRs B1929+10 and J1022+1001. We examine these polarization profiles, which offer constraints on pulsar emission geometry, presenting the first published radio polarization profiles for nine pulsars and identifying very low-intensity average profile components, or "microcomponents," in four others. By analyzing Faraday rotation measures, we determine the Galactic magnetic field parallel to the line of sight through various paths in the interstellar medium. After fitting linear and sinusoidal time trends to dispersion measures and Galactic magnetic fields, we detect one-year magnetic field variations in certain pulsars, though overall, the variations in these parameters appear to stem from a stochastic origin.

This paper aims to demonstrate that the evolution of the Riemann-Christoffel (curvature) tensor can be fully described by an arbitrary timelike vector field, and that the curvature tensor reverts to its initial state upon changing a specific index. This finding suggests that Poincaré's recurrence theorem holds true within this cosmological framework. Furthermore, it has been established that geodesics are capable of both diverging and converging. As this outcome implies, there exists a point of exclusivity—the antithesis of a singularity.

Open Relation Extraction (OpenRE) involves identifying relation schemes within open-domain corpora. However, most current OpenRE approaches either fail to fully leverage high-quality labeled datasets or cannot directly learn semantic representations, which hinders downstream clustering performance. To overcome these limitations, this study introduces MORE (Metric learning-based Open Relation Extraction), a new framework. By employing deep metric learning, MORE extracts abundant supervisory signals from labeled data and enables the neural model to directly acquire semantic relational representations. Experimental results on two real-world datasets demonstrate that our approach surpasses other state-of-the-art baselines, and the source code is publicly available on Github.

The standard assumption regarding code smells relies on a causal relationship: identifying a smell, removing it, and consequently improving code quality. We empirically tested this assumption's validity. We established a set of criteria that code smells must meet to genuinely cause reduced quality. Our evaluation analyzed 151 code smells detected by CheckStyle across 31,687 Java files from 677 GitHub repositories (each with over 200 commits in 2019), measuring their impact on quality, productivity, and bug detection metrics. Results indicate that less than 20% of these smells are potentially causal, with only a few showing robustness. The most impactful smells relate to simplicity, defensive programming, and abstraction. Files lacking these potentially causal smells are 50% more likely to be of high quality. Unfortunately, most smells persist because developers tend to remove the easily identifiable ones rather than the effective ones.

At filling factors $
u=0,\pm1$, graphene's ground state manifests as a specific SU(4) ferromagnet characterized by a complex phase diagram and various magnon modes related to spin, pseudospin, or entanglement. Inspired by recent experimental findings, we investigate a Fabry-P'erot magnonic junction operating at $
u=-1|0|-1$. When the $
u=0$ ground state exhibits spin polarization, two spin modes interfere to generate a beating pattern, whereas pseudospin modes undergo reflection. Conversely, if the $
u=0$ ground state is pseudospin polarized, the situation reverses: pseudospin magnons display interference while spin modes are reflected. Detecting such interference patterns would reveal details about low-energy anisotropies and, consequently, the nature of the ground state.

We observe that finding the extremal values of the Sombor index for trees with a specified degree sequence falls under the scope of Hua Wang's results in [Cent. Eur. J. Math. 12 (2014) 1656-1663], which indicates that the greedy tree achieves the minimum Sombor index, whereas an alternating greedy tree achieves the maximum.

Pre-trained language models (PLMs) such as BERT have achieved substantial advancements across numerous downstream NLP tasks. Nevertheless, recent studies utilizing cloze-style evaluations reveal that PLMs struggle to acquire knowledge from unstructured text. To investigate the internal mechanisms of PLMs regarding knowledge retrieval, we introduce the concepts of knowledge-bearing (K-B) and knowledge-free (K-F) tokens within unstructured text, labeling specific samples through manual annotation by experts. Our findings indicate that PLMs tend to produce incorrect predictions on K-B tokens and allocate reduced attention to them within the self-attention mechanism. Leveraging these insights, we propose two strategies designed to enhance the model's ability to learn from unstructured text via fully self-supervised learning. Experimental results on knowledge-intensive tasks demonstrate the efficacy of our methods. To the best of our knowledge, this work represents the first exploration of fully self-supervised knowledge learning during continual pre-training.

This paper explores a generalization of the Böttcher-Wenzel inequality, which originally established a sharp upper bound for the Frobenius norm of a standard commutator. We extend this investigation to the $q$-deformed commutator, defined for $n \times n$ complex matrices $A$ and $B$ as $[ A, B ]_q := A B - q BA$, where $q$ is a real parameter. The study focuses on determining sharp upper bounds for this deformed commutator across two contexts: general matrices and traceless matrices. We provide partial results and conjectures for both positive and negative values of $q$. Specifically, for positive $q$, we prove that if either $A$ or $B$ is normal, the inequality $|| [ A , B ]_q||_F^2 \le \left(1+q^2 \right) ||A||_F^2 ||B||_F^2$ holds and is sharp. We further conjecture that this same bound applies when either matrix is traceless and $q$ is positive. For negative $q$, we propose alternative sharp upper bounds for both general and traceless scenarios. These conjectures are validated numerically and rigorously proven for the case where $n=2$.

This research introduces a computational consciousness framework designed for non-interacting agents, positing that this phenomenon sequentially relies on cognitive functions including sensation, perception, emotion, affection, attention, awareness, and consciousness. Building upon the Smart Sensing prodromal study, the model formally defines and evaluates the cognitive levels linked to attention, awareness, and consciousness alongside the other sensory and emotional processes. The model generates an index that integrates energetic and entropic contributions of consciousness from a computational moral standpoint. Attention was simulated using a bottom-up method, whereas awareness and consciousness were distinguished by separating environmental inputs from subjective cognitive operations. When tested against visual stimuli triggering happiness, anger, fear, surprise, contempt, sadness, disgust, and neutrality, the model aligned with scientific data on covert attention. Similar findings emerged in relation to awareness resulting from visual repetition and moral judgments regarding stimuli evoking disgust and sadness. Ultimately, this solution offers a new methodology for defining computational consciousness via artificial emotional activity and morality.

Driven by the challenges of constructing de Sitter vacua within string theory, a novel framework was introduced in arXiv:1807.01570 and arXiv:1907.04268, depicting four-dimensional de Sitter space as an effective cosmology containing matter and radiation on an expanding spherical bubble. This bubble mediates the decay from a non-supersymmetric $AdS_5$ to a more stable $AdS_5$ configuration. In this third installment, we extend the scenario by analyzing the backreaction of bulk and brane matter through the lens of brane bending. We calculate the backreacted metric for both the bent brane and the five-dimensional bulk. To clarify the implications of brane bending, we contrast our findings with an explicit computation of the five-dimensional graviton propagator via a holographic method. Lastly, we discuss potential four-dimensional gravity localization within this model involving two colliding branes.

Although the enumerative investigation of pinnacle sets in permutations was initially launched by Davis, Nelson, Petersen, and Tenner (2018) and has since garnered significant interest, this article introduces a recurrence relation for efficiently calculating $|\mathfrak{S}_n(P)|$, the count of size-$n$ permutations with a specific pinnacle set $P$. This method achieves an arithmetic complexity of $O(k^4 + k\log n)$ for a set $P$ of size $k$ and also yields a symbolic expression for pinnacle sets of fixed size. Regarding the weighted sum $q_n(P)$ of $|\mathfrak{S}_n(P)|$ introduced by Davis et al. (2018), which appears to possess a simple structure and for which a conjectural form was recently proposed by Flaque, Novelli, and Thibon (2021+), we resolve the issue by presenting and proving an alternative formulation with distinct combinatorial properties. Furthermore, we examine admissible orderings of a given pinnacle set, a concept first explored by Rusu (2020) and later characterized by Rusu and Tenner (2021), and we develop an efficient algorithm for counting them.

The Generalized Uncertainty Principle (GUP) extends the Heisenberg uncertainty principle, originating from phenomenological quantum gravity models that posit a minimum measurable length. A recent development, the Linear GUP (LGUP), incorporates both a minimum length and a maximum momentum, yielding a phase space volume proportional to $(1 - \alpha p)^{-4} d^3x d^3p$, where $\alpha$ remains an undetermined GUP parameter. This study investigates the mass-radius relationships of white dwarfs modified by LGUP, introducing radial perturbations to examine dynamical instability through oscillations. Our findings indicate that LGUP leads to a reduced maximum mass for white dwarfs, an effect that becomes more pronounced as $\alpha$ increases. Furthermore, we observe that the maximum mass corresponds to the point where the square of the fundamental frequency, $\omega_0$, vanishes. The dynamical instability analysis confirms that instability occurs across all values of $\alpha$, emerging at lower central densities (and thus lower maximum masses) as $\alpha$ rises, thereby corroborating the mass-radius relation results. Finally, the preservation of the mass limit in LGUP-modified white dwarfs suggests that this framework supports gravitational collapse in compact objects.

Compositional generalization refers to the ability to identify and conceptualize vast arrays of new combinations derived from familiar elements. While this capability is fundamental to human intelligence, existing neural networks typically fail to possess it. This report synthesizes a series of our research efforts on compositional generalization and outlines a specific methodology. The initial section defines relevant concepts and properties, while the second explores a machine learning strategy that employs architectural design and regularization to manage representation information. Focusing on core principles with intuitive and illustrative explanations, we aim to clarify the fundamentals of compositional generalization and advance artificial intelligence.

This work addresses chance-constrained optimization, aiming to optimize a function while satisfying constraints under uncertainty, a scenario often characterized by high computational costs in real-world applications. To address these challenges, we introduce a novel Bayesian optimization approach suitable for cases where uncertainty stems from specific inputs, allowing for the definition of an acquisition criterion within the joint space of controlled and uncontrolled variables. The primary contribution is an acquisition criterion that balances expected objective function improvement with constraint reliability. Derived using Stepwise Uncertainty Reduction principles, maximizing this criterion yields optimal values for both controlled and uncontrolled parameters. We provide analytical formulas for efficient criterion calculation and present numerical experiments on test functions. Comparative studies with alternative sampling methods demonstrate that the alignment between the sampling criterion and the problem structure significantly enhances overall optimization efficiency. Additionally, as a secondary outcome, we derive an expression for the variance of the improvement.

Higher-order multiway data is prevalent in statistics and machine learning, frequently displaying community-like structures where nodes within each mode belong to specific communities. This paper introduces the tensor mixed-membership blockmodel, an extension of the tensor blockmodel that allows memberships to be continuous convex combinations of latent communities rather than strictly discrete. We prove the model's identifiability and present a computationally efficient estimation method combining the higher-order orthogonal iteration algorithm (HOOI) for tensor singular value decomposition with a simplex corner-finding algorithm. Furthermore, we establish the consistency of this procedure by deriving a per-node error bound that illustrates the impact of higher-order structures on accuracy. To support this consistency result, we develop an $\ell_{2,\infty}$ tensor perturbation bound for HOOI under independent, potentially heteroskedastic, subgaussian noise, a contribution of independent interest. Our analysis employs a novel leave-one-out construction for iterates, yielding bounds dependent solely on the spectral properties of the underlying low-rank tensor under nearly optimal signal-to-noise ratios that ensure computational feasibility for tensor SVD. Unlike standard leave-one-out analyses that typically remove only a small portion of noise from algorithmic outputs, our approach utilizes both prior iterates and additional tensor structure to mitigate an extra source of error. Finally, we validate our methodology using real and simulated data, including two flight datasets and a trade network dataset, revealing effects that remain unidentifiable when assuming discrete community memberships.

This paper introduces a simplified second-order Gaussian Poincaré inequality designed for the normal approximation of functionals involving infinitely many Rademacher random variables. This result relies on a novel bound for the Kolmogorov distance between a general Rademacher functional and a Gaussian random variable, which was derived using the discrete Malliavin-Stein method and holds independent significance. Applications include an analysis of the count of vertices with a specified degree and subgraph counting statistics within Erdős-Rényi random graphs. Additionally, the study examines the number of vertices with a fixed degree in the context of percolation on the Hamming hypercube, as well as the number of isolated faces in Linial-Meshulam-Wallach random $\kappa$-complexes and infinite weighted 2-runs.

The widespread adoption of the Internet of Things (IoT) introduces significant privacy threats, as billions of connected devices are authorized to monitor user data and transmit it across the internet. Adversaries particularly target user identity, which is crucial for initiating attacks. While the risks associated with exposing specific physical biometrics or device identifiers have been widely investigated, the combined impact of leakage from both sources remains unexplored in multi-modal sensing contexts. This study investigates the feasibility of compound identity leakage across cyber-physical domains, revealing that co-located smart device identifiers (such as smartphone MAC addresses) and physical biometrics (such as facial or vocal samples) serve as side channels for one another. The findings demonstrate that the proposed method remains robust against various real-world observation noises, enabling attackers to comprehensively profile victims across multiple dimensions with minimal analytical effort. Two real-world experiments involving different biometric types and device IDs indicate that this approach can successfully compromise over 70% of device IDs while simultaneously harvesting multiple biometric clusters with approximately 94% purity.

This work introduces a significant application of Lebesgue integral quadrature, detailed in arXiv:1807.06007. By addressing two random processes, $f(x)$ and $g(x)$, the study formulates and resolves two generalized eigenvalue problems. This approach yields Lebesgue quadratures for both $f$ and $g$ derived from the respective eigenproblems. Furthermore, projecting the $f$- and $g$-eigenvectors onto one another enables the construction of a joint distribution estimator, with the most comprehensive version being a density-matrix correlation. This correlation encompasses both a value-correlation, $V_{f^{[i]};g^{[j]}}$, akin to standard correlation metrics, and a novel probability-correlation, $P_{f^{[i]};g^{[j]}}$. Utilizing the average of the Christoffel function rather than a standard average extends the methodology to estimate the joint probability of three or more random processes. The theoretical framework has been numerically implemented, and the associated software is released under the GPLv3 license.

Efficient approximation is fundamental to solving large-scale machine learning challenges. This paper introduces a new, robust maximum entropy algorithm designed to handle hundreds of moments while enabling computationally efficient approximations. We illustrate the method's utility, demonstrate its equivalence to constrained Bayesian variational inference, and highlight its advantages over current techniques in two specific applications: rapid log determinant estimation and information-theoretic Bayesian optimization.

Let $X$ be a measure space equipped with a measure-preserving action of an abelian group $G$. We investigate the structure of measurable tilings $F \odot A = X$ of $X$ using a measurable tile $A \subset X$ shifted by a finite subset $F \subset G$, where the translates $f \cdot A$ for $f \in F$ partition $X$ modulo null sets. By adapting techniques from prior work, we prove a "dilation lemma" which essentially states that if $F \odot A = X$, then $F^r \odot A = X$ for a broad class of integer dilations $r$. Leveraging this result, we derive a structure theorem for such tilings, mirroring one recently established by the second and fourth authors. As applications, we fully characterize random tilings of finitely generated abelian groups that are "factors of iid" and demonstrate that measurable tilings of a torus $\mathbb{T}^d$ can always be continuously (specifically linearly) deformed into a tiling with rational shifts. Notably, we obtain particularly strong outcomes for low-dimensional cases $d=1,2$, including a resolution of a conjecture by Conley (the first author) and Pikhurko in the $d=1$ scenario.

To accommodate diverse display devices, frequently accessed video streams are often pre-transcoded into multiple formats. However, the traditional method of storing these varied formats incurs significant costs for providers. In contrast, cloud services offer greater flexibility at a relatively lower price, leading many video companies to migrate their storage to the cloud. While consolidating all streams into a single cloud storage type initially appears efficient, costs tend to rise gradually over time. Crucially, fluctuating access patterns to popular content can drastically increase storage expenses. To address this and optimize costs, we propose a method that leverages cloud hierarchy storage. Specifically, our algorithm identifies frequently accessed video segments and stores them in the most appropriate cloud storage tier. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach reduces cloud storage costs by 18.75%.

Recently, Alexandersson and colleagues established combinatorial formulas for the Schur function expansion of the horizontal-strip LLT polynomial $G_\lambda(x;q)$ in specific scenarios. By associating a weighted graph $\Pi$ with $\lambda$, we derive a linear relationship among LLT polynomials. Applying this relation, we demonstrate an explicit combinatorial Schur-positive expansion for $G_\lambda(x;q)$ whenever $\Pi$ contains no triangles. Furthermore, we show that the highest power of $q$ appearing in the LLT polynomial corresponds to the total edge weight of the graph $\Pi$.

We investigate quantum phase transitions emerging from the fracton-ordered phase of the $\mathbb{Z}_N$ X-cube model. These transitions are triggered by the condensation of various sub-dimensional excitations and their composites. The resulting condensed phases are either trivial paramagnets or consist of stacked deconfined gauge theories in $d=2$ or $d=3$ spatial dimensions. The specific character of these transitions varies depending on the type of excitation condensed. When dipolar bound states of fractons or lineons are condensed for $N \geq 4$, stable critical points emerge, characterized by decoupled stacks of $d=2$ conformal field theories. Similarly, condensing lineon excitations with $N > 4$ yields a gapless intermediate phase between the X-cube and condensed states, described as an array of $d=1$ conformal field theories. Across all these scenarios, effective subsystem symmetries derived from the mobility constraints inherent to the X-cube phase's excitations are crucial for analyzing the phase transitions.

This study calculates the thermodynamic properties of spin-polarized strange quark matter at finite temperatures within a strong magnetic field, employing the MIT bag model. Furthermore, we derive the equation of state for this matter under these conditions and subsequently utilize it to examine the structural characteristics of spin-polarized strange quark stars across varying temperatures and magnetic field strengths.

This paper introduces a mechanism for the emergence of strange attractors within a one-parameter family of differential equations defined on a 3-dimensional sphere. At the zero parameter value, the system's flow displays an attracting heteroclinic network, known as a Bykov network, composed of two 1-dimensional connections and one 2-dimensional separatrix linking hyperbolic saddles-foci with distinct Morse indices. Upon slightly increasing the parameter while maintaining the 1-dimensional connections, we focus on the scenario where the 2-dimensional invariant manifolds of the equilibria do not intersect. We demonstrate that for a set of parameters sufficiently close to zero with positive Lebesgue measure, the dynamics generate strange attractors that wind around an annulus in phase space and support Sinai-Ruelle-Bowen (SRB) measures. Furthermore, we prove the existence of a sequence of parameter values yielding a superstable sink and characterize the transition from a Bykov network to a strange attractor.

Generalized from topological crystalline insulators (TCIs), high-order topological insulators (HOTIs) are defined by lower-dimensional metallic boundary states safeguarded by spatial symmetries. The standard theoretical basis for HOTIs, relying on band inversion at specific $k$-points, fails to apply to quasicrystals due to incompatible rotational symmetries and the absence of a well-defined momentum quantum number. In this study, we establish a low-energy effective model describing HOTI phenomena in 2D quasicrystals across all rotational symmetries. By utilizing a recent Fourier transform technique for quasicrystals and approximating long-wavelength dynamics through large-scale averaging, we formulate an effective $k \cdot p$ Hamiltonian that captures band inversion at the center of a pseudo-Brillouin zone (PBZ). We demonstrate that an in-plane Zeeman field can create mass-kinks at the intersections of adjacent edges in a 2D quasicrystal topological insulator, thereby generating corner modes (CMs) with fractional charge protected by rotational symmetries. These predictions are validated by numerical tight-binding simulations. Additionally, when the quasicrystal is coupled to an \textit{s}-wave superconductor, Majorana corner modes can be realized by adjusting the field strength and chemical potential. Our findings provide a general framework for investigating the low-energy physics of quasicrystals, particularly regarding topological excitations and fractional statistics.

This paper introduces the inaugural outer approximation algorithm designed for multi-objective mixed-integer linear programming (MOMILP) problems, regardless of the number of objectives, and it also addresses specific classes of non-linear programming issues. The method generates both non-dominated extreme points and the facets of their convex hull. By utilizing an oracle to solve single-objective weighted-sum problems, the authors demonstrate that the number of required oracle calls scales polynomially with the number of facets in the convex hull of non-dominated extreme points for MOMILP cases. Consequently, when the weighted-sum problem is solvable in polynomial time, these facets can be computed with incremental-polynomial delay. Practically, the algorithm begins with a valid lower bound set for non-dominated extreme points and iteratively refines it, making it suitable for multi-objective branch-and-bound frameworks where a valid bound set remains available at any stage, even if the process is interrupted before convergence. Additionally, because the oracle yields Pareto optimal solutions, the approach offers significant advantages from a primal perspective within multi-objective branch-and-bound contexts. The oracle can also operate on any relaxation of the primal problem, ensuring that the resulting points and facets continue to form a valid lower bound set. Finally, a computational study evaluates the method using benchmark instances from existing literature alongside newly generated non-linear multi-objective problems.

It is universally acknowledged that an equation corresponds to a multivariate function. Typically, such functions contain multiple unknown variables, making it difficult to reduce them to a single unknown. This paper addresses that challenge by introducing function promotion, which transforms a function with fewer variables into one with more, and by developing multivariate function composition based on the concept of unary composition. We also define inverse multivariate functions, extending the idea of inverse unary functions, allowing the solution to be expressed via an inverse multivariate function whenever the equivalent function is invertible. For cases where the function is irreversible, we introduce the concept of a relation, treating the multivariate function as a special type of multivariate relation; thus, the solution can always be expressed as an inverse multivariate relation. After reading this paper and understanding the significance of multivariate function composition in solving general equations, one might realize that this concept is not as widely appreciated as it should be. Furthermore, we explore the possibility of representing the solution—whether as a multivariate function or relation—for a general equation through the superposition of unary functions, a topic that connects to Hilbert's 13th problem. Given the fundamental nature of the subject, this research could open new avenues for mathematicians.

We demonstrate that any connected Cayley graph $\Gamma$ defined on an Abelian group of order $2n$ with degree $\tilde{\Omega}(\log n)$ contains no more than $2^{n+1}(1 + o(1))$ independent sets. This upper bound is asymptotically tight, up to the $o(1)$ term, specifically when $\Gamma$ is bipartite. Our proof relies on Sapozhenko's graph container method and incorporates the Pl\"{u}nnecke-Rusza-Petridis inequality from additive combinatorics.

We introduce a comprehensive framework for quantum interference (QI) involving multiple, fundamentally distinct processes. This framework highlights the critical role of shaped input wavefunctions in facilitating QI and forecasts novel interactions among free electrons, bound electrons, and photons. Specifically, it predicts: (i) the suppression of the zero-loss peak through destructive QI when a shaped electron wavepacket interacts with light, even in scenarios where the zero-loss peak typically dominates; and (ii) QI between spontaneous emission from free electrons and atoms, which remains significant despite large separations, thereby challenging the conventional belief that electrons and atoms must be in close proximity to significantly influence one another. Our findings demonstrate that advanced quantum waveshaping techniques expand the versatility of light-matter interactions and broader quantum processes.

Graph neural networks (GNNs) have been widely developed for graph representation learning across various application domains. However, like other neural network models, GNNs face the black-box problem, making their underlying mechanisms difficult to understand. To address this, several GNN explainability methods have been introduced to clarify the decisions made by GNNs. In this survey, we provide an overview of state-of-the-art GNN explainability techniques and their evaluation methods. Additionally, we propose a novel evaluation metric and conduct comprehensive experiments to compare these methods on real-world datasets. Finally, we suggest future directions for GNN explainability.

This paper examines the one-dimensional compressible Navier-Stokes-Vlasov-Fokker-Planck system featuring density-dependent viscosity and drag coefficients. Within a spatially periodic domain, the study establishes the existence, uniqueness, and regularity of global weak solutions for general initial data, while also analyzing their long-term behavior. The results demonstrate that as time progresses, the particle distribution function approaches the global Maxwellian, with both the fluid velocity and the macroscopic particle velocity converging to a common speed.

Accurately segmenting cells in volumetric fluorescence microscopy is essential for investigating diverse cellular mechanisms, spanning from cancer research to embryonic behavioral analysis. While recent computer vision techniques typically rely on large convolutional neural networks (CNNs) or vision transformers (ViTs), the scarcity of 3D microscopy data necessitates a distinct strategy. We propose a lightweight CNN designed for volumetric cell segmentation. Unlike prior segmentation models, our architecture features an asymmetric encoder-decoder structure with a highly parameter-efficient decoder, and training is further accelerated through transfer learning. Additionally, we implement Context Aware Pseudocoloring to leverage spatial context along the z-axis during slice-wise processing. Evaluated on various 3D datasets from the Cell Tracking Challenge's Cell Segmentation Benchmark, our method achieves top-tier performance while utilizing up to 25 times fewer parameters than leading alternatives. The code and pretrained models are accessible at: https://github.com/roydenwa/efficient-cell-seg

Future low-carbon grid scenario studies require power sector capacity expansion models (CEMs) to include detailed grid operation representations. Typically, CEMs model operations over representative periods selected via clustering algorithms from original input data. However, these representative period selection (RPS) approaches are constrained by the clustering algorithm's decreasing effectiveness as input dimensionality grows and fail to account for the relative significance of input variations on CEM results. This paper introduces an RPS method that overcomes these issues by applying dimensionality reduction through neural network-based autoencoders before clustering. This reduction enhances clustering performance and enables the inclusion of additional features, such as estimated outputs from simplified parallel CEM solutions for each disjoint period (e.g., weekly). The impact of integrating dimensionality reduction into RPS is measured by comparing the error between reduced-space and full-space CEM outcomes. Extensive numerical experiments across diverse networks and technology and policy scenarios demonstrate the superiority of dimensionality-reduction-based RPS methods.

One of the most enigmatic predictions of Einstein's relativity concerns the peculiar visual appearance of objects, a phenomenon arising from the distinction between measuring and seeing. While measurement adheres to the Lorentz Transformation, visual perception accounts for the travel time of light rays from every point on an object to the observer. By calculating the apparent position based on velocity, initial location, and observation time, we determine that an object's apparent speed can exceed the speed of light as it approaches the observer, mimicking superluminal motion. For parameterizable surfaces, we examine apparent shape properties such as curvature and torsion, mathematically proving that a sphere maintains a circular silhouette regardless of initial conditions. We generate plots illustrating apparent speed and length, compute the metric tensor for a distorted sphere, and derive a generalized equation for the Doppler effect and relativistic aberration to analyze redshift and blueshift regions. Applying Born-rigidity conditions, we calculate the hyperbolic trajectories of points on an extended object given specific initial velocities, positions, and proper accelerations, thereby justifying the claim that an accelerating rigid body in Special Relativity cannot surpass a certain length under specific circumstances. We present numerous non-trivial results, verified algebraically and via light cones, which are validated by taking the zero-acceleration limit to recover constant velocity scenarios. Ultimately, these visualizations offer an intuitive tool for educators teaching Special Relativity, and we conclude with an overview of extending this framework to curved spacetime and its potential applications.

Image super-resolution is vital for domains like surveillance and remote sensing. Nevertheless, infrared (IR) images typically suffer from low resolution due to the high cost of optical hardware. Although deep learning has revolutionized super-resolution for visible images, IR applications have garnered less focus. The scarcity of patterns in IR data makes it challenging for deep neural networks (DNNs) to extract diverse features. To address this, we propose HetSRWGAN, a framework utilizing heterogeneous convolution and adversarial training for IR super-resolution. HetSRWGAN is a lightweight GAN architecture featuring a plug-and-play heterogeneous kernel-based residual block. Additionally, we introduce a novel gradient-based loss function applicable to any model. Experimental results demonstrate that HetSRWGAN consistently outperforms existing methods in both qualitative and quantitative metrics, while ensuring a more stable training process.

The objective is to design a frame capable of stably reconstructing signals from transmitted coefficients in a channel affected by additive noise and adversarial erasures. To address this, we propose numerically erasure-robust frames. Our analysis examines various constructions, such as random frames, equiangular tight frames, and group frames. We subsequently demonstrate that arbitrarily high erasure rates inevitably lead to numerical instability during signal reconstruction. Finally, we offer several insights, including implications for maximal equiangular tight frames and sparse frames.

The Polyhedral Active Set Algorithm (PASA) is engineered to optimize general nonlinear functions within a polyhedral domain. Its first phase utilizes a nonmonotone gradient projection method, whereas the second phase employs an active set strategy to traverse the faces of the constraint polyhedron. A gradient-based implementation is detailed, featuring a projected conjugate gradient approach for the second phase. Asymptotically, the process relies exclusively on phase two. The method's performance is evaluated against IPOPT using polyhedral constrained problems from the CUTEst suite and the Maros/Meszaros quadratic programming test collection.

This article demonstrates the application of Zamolodchikov's higher equations of motion within Liouville field theory to derive explicit $N$-point correlation numbers in minimal Liouville gravity for cases where $N>4$. We provide a closed-form expression for the 5-point correlation numbers and compare these results with those obtained from one-matrix model calculations.

The azimuthal instability of a self-excited spinning mode within an annular combustor featuring non-swirling flow is examined via Large Eddy Simulation (LES). This study solves compressible Navier-Stokes equations incorporating a flamelet combustion model to represent subgrid-scale chemistry-turbulence interactions. Two distinct flamelet models—one including and one excluding heat loss—are contrasted to clarify the impact of non-adiabatic wall conditions on thermoacoustic instability. Both models effectively capture azimuthal modes, yielding only minor discrepancies in calculated frequencies and amplitudes. When compared against experimental data, the LES frequencies are roughly 10% higher, while the predicted amplitudes align well. Additional analysis of both experimental and LES datasets reveals a dominant anti-clockwise spinning mode, characterized by strong agreement in phase-averaged heat release rate fluctuations. Dynamic Mode Decomposition (DMD) is utilized to further investigate this spinning mode; the reconstructed DMD modes for azimuthal frequencies from both LES and experiments show excellent correspondence regarding heat release fluctuations. However, the DMD mode structure for acoustic pressure derived from the LES exhibits a significant non-zero profile at the combustor outlet, a feature potentially critical for establishing azimuthal modes in this annular system. Furthermore, a low-order modeling study was performed using an acoustic network coupled with a flame transfer function extracted from the LES. Results indicate that the dominant mode is linked to the plenum, displaying a mixed first longitudinal and azimuthal structure. By adjusting the plenum length to match the effective volume, the predicted frequency closely approximates the measured value.

This study examines the Vlasov-Poisson-Boltzmann system without angular cutoff and the Vlasov-Poisson-Landau system with Coulomb interaction within a bounded domain defined as a union of cubes. We demonstrate global stability and exponential decay over large time intervals under specular-reflection boundary conditions, assuming the initial data is close to a Maxwellian equilibrium. Furthermore, we derive a compatible specular boundary condition for high-order derivatives and establish a velocity-weighted energy estimate.

This study analyzes the production and signatures of charged Higgs bosons $H_2^{\pm}$ within a 3-3-1 model incorporating heavy leptons at the CLIC (Cern Linear Collider). We find that the production rate is substantial for the direct process $e^{-} e^{+} \rightarrow H_{2}^{+} H_{2}^{-}$, and we investigate the feasibility of identifying these bosons through their respective branching ratios.

Current high-frequency very-long-baseline interferometry (VLBI) enables the resolution of horizon-scale emissions from supermassive black holes in our immediate vicinity. Future space-based VLBI missions will observe highly lensed features, specifically photon rings, offering precise probes of strong-field gravity. Focusing on M87*, this study investigates diverse accretion flows onto Kerr black holes to understand their resulting images and visibilities. A primary interest lies in space-baseline visibilities, which encode photon ring geometry and could provide a rigorous test of the Kerr hypothesis. We construct a fully analytical model of stationary, axisymmetric accretion flows featuring variable disk thickness and a four-velocity that smoothly transitions between purely azimuthal rotation and radial infall. By incorporating thermal synchrotron emission and absorption effects, we determine the observational signatures of these flows. The resulting images typically exhibit a "wedding cake" structure, consisting of discrete, narrow photon rings (n=1, 2, ...) stacked atop broader primary emission surrounding a central brightness depression of varying size. We conclude that the "black hole shadow" is model-dependent—even for diffuse, optically thin sources—and should not be considered a universal prediction of general relativity. At 230 GHz, the n=1 ring is consistently visible, whereas the n=2 ring is occasionally suppressed by absorption. At 345 GHz, the medium is more optically thin, allowing the n=2 ring to appear clearly in both image and visibility data, making this frequency more suitable for future space-VLBI measurements of photon ring morphology.

This note addresses the problem of homogeneous $ L^2 L^{\infty} $ Strichartz estimates for the Wave equation in dimensions $ n \geq 4 $, a question posed by Fang and Wang. While Guo, Li, Nakanishi, and Yan recently demonstrated that this estimate fails using probabilistic methods, we provide a deterministic counterexample to disprove it.

Long-duration gamma-ray bursts are theorized to originate from rapidly rotating Wolf-Rayet stars, yet verifying this hypothesis observationally presents significant challenges. Since spectral lines in these stars arise from their expanding winds, accurately measuring their rotational speeds spectroscopically is difficult. However, intrinsic polarization caused by the rotational modulation of the stellar wind could offer an indirect method to estimate these velocities, provided detailed wind models are available. We utilized 2.5D hydrodynamical simulations to model the structure of rotating Wolf-Rayet winds, incorporating factors such as stellar surface deformation from rotation, gravity darkening, and nonradial forces. These simulations, which scaled the mass loss rate to reflect realistic wind densities, yielded a prolate wind structure that results in relatively low polarization levels. Consequently, even substantial rotational velocities remain consistent with observational constraints. The derived wind structure aligns with previous findings for rotating optically thin winds, and the upper limits on rotational velocities obtained do not contradict the long-duration gamma-ray burst progenitor model.

This paper presents an overview of the ALICE detector's performance and experimental results obtained from proton-proton collisions at center-of-mass energies of 0.9, 2.76, and 7 TeV, as well as lead-lead collisions at 2.76 TeV at the LHC. The study focuses on hadron spectroscopy at low to moderate transverse momentum ($p_T$) within proton-proton interactions. Additionally, lead-lead measurement results are compared with those from proton-proton collisions to investigate the properties of hot quark matter.

Given an infinite-dimensional Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ and $G$ as its formal series representation derived from the algebraic completion, we apply Schottky's method—constructing a genus $g$ Riemann surface by attaching multiple handles to a complex sphere—to build a family of coboundary operator extensions. These extensions operate on double complexes of specific meromorphic functions of predetermined nature, which are associated with elements of $G$.

We examine a nonlinear stochastic partial differential equation (SPDE) in divergence form, driven by Gaussian noise that is white in time and colored in space, resulting in a solution gradient that is Hölder-continuous but non-differentiable. Subsequently, we establish a generalized Taylor expansion for the discrepancy between the SPDE's solution and the solution to its linearization around a fixed reference point. This finding aligns with the framework of (controlled) rough paths and supports the broader insight that, in contexts involving a rough driver, the difference between the actual solution and the linearized solution exhibits enhanced regularity.

The chromatic vertex (resp. edge) stability number, denoted ${\rm vs}_{\chi}(G)$ (resp. ${\rm es}_{\chi}(G)$) for a graph $G$, is defined as the smallest count of vertices (resp. edges) that must be removed to produce a subgraph $H$ where $\chi(H) = \chi(G)-1$. The primary theorem establishes that for any graph $G$ where $\chi(G)$ is either $\Delta(G)$ or $\Delta(G)+1$, the equality ${\rm vs}_{\chi}(G) = {\rm ivs}_{\chi}(G)$ holds, with ${\rm ivs}_{\chi}(G)$ representing the independent chromatic vertex stability number; however, this relationship does not necessarily apply to graphs satisfying $\chi(G) \le \frac{\Delta(G)+1}{2}$. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that when $\chi(G) > \frac{\Delta(G)}{2}+1$, then ${\rm vs}_{\chi}(G) = {\rm es}_{\chi}(G)$. Additionally, the paper presents a Nordhaus-Gaddum-type theorem concerning the chromatic vertex stability number.

This paper introduces an efficient frontier detection method utilizing an adaptive Rapidly-exploring Random Tree (RRT) for autonomous robot exploration, enabling real-time incremental detection in unknown environments. First, the detector dynamically adjusts the RRT sampling space based on perceived environmental structures, significantly boosting the sampling success rate and regulating expansion bias. Second, by employing non-uniform sample distribution, the approach addresses the over-sampling issue inherent in RRT's sliding windows, where uniform random sampling leads to redundancy in overlapping regions. This strategy prioritizes sampling in recently explored areas, enhancing detection efficiency and facilitating incremental updates. Validation across three simulated benchmarks demonstrates that our method reduces frontier detection runtime by approximately 40% compared to the state-of-the-art DSV Planner.

Text-to-image generative models offer a potent method for creating visual art. However, the unstructured nature of text-based interaction presents a dual challenge: although it enables an unlimited variety of outputs, users often resort to iterative trial and error when prompt quality is unsatisfactory. This study investigates which prompt elements and model settings facilitate coherent results, specifically analyzing prompts organized by subject and style to understand both successful and failed outcomes. Our assessment, based on 5,493 generations across five experiments, covers 49 concrete and abstract subjects alongside 51 abstract and figurative styles. Consequently, we offer design guidelines aimed at assisting users in achieving superior results from text-to-image systems.

This paper investigates a new privacy-preserving anonymization approach for pedestrian images, designed to retain personal identity information (PII) for authorized models while preventing third-party recognition. Traditional anonymization methods inevitably result in semantic information loss, thereby limiting data utility. Furthermore, existing learned anonymization techniques, despite maintaining various identity-irrelevant utilities, alter pedestrian identities, rendering them unsuitable for training robust re-identification models. To address the privacy-utility trade-off in pedestrian images, we introduce a joint learning reversible anonymization framework capable of generating full-body anonymous images with minimal performance degradation on person re-identification tasks. Our core strategy involves using desensitized images from conventional methods as initial privacy-preserving supervision to jointly train an anonymization encoder, a recovery decoder, and an identity-invariant model. Additionally, we propose a progressive training strategy that iteratively enhances the initial anonymization supervision to improve overall performance. Experimental results confirm the effectiveness of our anonymized pedestrian images in balancing privacy protection and re-identification performance. The code is available at \url{https://github.com/whuzjw/privacy-reid}.
A strategic document outlining the United States' computing initiative.

This study demonstrates that the discrete approximate volume preserving mean curvature flow within the flat torus $\mathbb{T}^N$, when initiated near a strictly stable critical set $E$ of the perimeter, converges exponentially quickly to a translation of $E$ over the long term. As an intermediate finding, we derive a novel quantitative estimate of Alexandrov type applicable to periodic strictly stable constant mean curvature hypersurfaces. Furthermore, in two dimensions, we offer a comprehensive characterization of the long-term behavior of the discrete flow for initial sets with arbitrary finite perimeter.

On the occasion of my eighty-fifth birthday, I wish to acknowledge the pivotal role my advisor, Professor Ayalam Balachandran, played in guiding my transition from engineering to physics. Decades later, this student presents his most recent work on the significance of asymmetry within Yukawa matrices. Beginning with a purely phenomenological approach that utilizes Tri-Bi-Maximal mixing as input, the model predicts the CP-violating angle and the three mixing angles within one sigma of their probability density function values. To maximize naturalness, we also examine a model extending from $SU_5$ to $E_6$ in the context of finite family groups, specifically subgroups of $G_2$.

We analyze a system generating acceleration radiation at two distinct temperatures, where equilibrium states emerge asymptotically as Planck distributions and transitions occur non-thermally. The model's simplicity allows for an analytical global solution of the radiation spectrum. We propose this framework as a valuable tool for studying non-thermal vacuum acceleration radiation alongside final or initial asymptotic thermodynamic horizon states that remain in equilibrium.

A core challenge in array signal processing involves designing sensor arrays that offer high degrees of freedom (DOFs) or low redundancy alongside minimized mutual coupling, as these attributes are critical for enhancing direction-of-arrival (DOA) estimation performance. An array is defined as low-redundancy when the ratio $R=N(N-1)/(2L)$ approaches the Leech's bound ($1.217\leq R_{opt}\leq 1.332$), where $N$ represents the number of physical sensors and $L$ denotes the maximum inter-sensor spacing. Currently, the most advanced infinite classes of low-redundancy arrays (LRAs) achieve a ratio of $R\leq1.5$. This paper introduces a novel LRA configuration with $R<1.5$ applicable for any $N\geq18$. The proposed array retains the advantageous traits of existing sparse arrays, including a hole-free difference co-array and sensor locations defined by a closed-form expression dependent on the sensor count. Significantly, it mitigates mutual coupling effects more effectively than prior sparse arrays by minimizing the number of sensor pairs with the smallest inter-spacing to just one. Numerical simulations are presented to demonstrate the proposed array's superiority over other established sparse array designs.

The widespread adoption and ongoing expansion of personal electronic devices constitute a vast, underutilized reservoir of computational resources. To harness this potential, we introduce Pando, a volunteer computing framework built on a declarative concurrent programming paradigm and realized through JavaScript, WebRTC, and WebSockets. This system allows a fluctuating cohort of unreliable personal devices, donated by volunteers, to parallelize the execution of functions across value streams by utilizing their browsers. We demonstrate that Pando achieves superior throughput compared to a solitary device across various compute-intensive tasks, such as animation rendering and image processing. Furthermore, we illustrate the adaptability of our method by deploying Pando across diverse environments: personal devices on a local network, Grid5000 (a French national grid accessible via VPN), and seven PlanetLab nodes distributed across a European wide-area network.

This work revisits Stone duality for lattices equipped with various quasioperators, an area initially explored in [14], offering a novel duality result that advances the previous findings in two key ways. Firstly, the axiomatization of frames from [14], which was previously cumbersome, has been streamlined by integrating Gehrke's [8] concept of section stability for relations. Secondly, morphisms have been redefined to preserve Galois stable (and co-stable) sets; this relies partly on Goldblatt's [11] recent definition of bounded morphisms for polarities, although our definition requires strengthening to achieve a Stone duality result. Furthermore, by examining dual algebraic structures linked to polarities with relations, we show that stable/co-stable set operators emerge as the Galois closure of restricted classical image operators (generated by frame relations) applied to Galois stable/co-stable sets. This offers a representation-level proof that non-distributive logics can be regarded as fragments of sorted, residuated (poly)modal logics, a line of inquiry begun in [16,17].

This paper investigates the regularity of Gaussian Bessel potentials and Gaussian Bessel fractional derivatives within variable Gaussian Besov-Lipschitz spaces $B_{p(\cdot),q(\cdot)}^{\alpha}(\gamma_{d})$, which were introduced in a prior work \cite{Pinrodurb}, subject to specific constraints on the functions $p(\cdot)$ and $q(\cdot)$.

The Software-Defined Networking (SDN) paradigm, which enables the programmability of both control and data planes, offers a promising foundation for developing new operational and management strategies, with this work specifically targeting DDoS attack detection using machine learning. To achieve this, the paper introduces ORACLE (cOllaboRation of dAta and Control pLanEs), an architecture designed to coordinate these planes for effective network attack detection. Its primary contribution involves delegating the extraction and processing of per-flow traffic data to the data plane. This approach streamlines the calculation and classification of features required for detection by ensuring that necessary flow information is already prepared when it reaches the control plane. Furthermore, the architecture's second contribution is its ability to overcome limitations in traditional OpenFlow-based environments, allowing for the calculation of certain features that were previously unfeasible. In the evaluation phase, the ORACLE system achieved an accuracy rate of up to 96% during testing when utilizing a K-Nearest Neighbor model.

LHAASO has identified 12 gamma-ray sources exceeding 100 TeV, which are potential origins for Galactic cosmic rays. We review neutrino data from IceCube and ANTARES near these LHAASO sources to limit the fraction of gamma-rays produced via hadronic processes. Our results indicate that current observations restrict hadronic contributions to no more than approximately 60% of the gamma-ray emission from the Crab Nebula. Under the assumptions used in the IceCube analysis, the gamma-rays from LHAASO J1825-1326 and LHAASO J1907+0626 are dominated by leptonic mechanisms up to roughly 200 TeV. We also discuss the uncertainties associated with these constraints on hadronic gamma-ray emission and further limit the total 100 TeV gamma-ray output from TeV pulsar wind nebulae (PWNe), leveraging LHAASO's exceptional sensitivity at these energies.

This study reports the inaugural detection of instability within pressure-dominated, weakly magnetized plasma Couette flow, occurring squarely within the Hall regime. Intense Hall currents interact with a low-frequency electromagnetic mode fueled by high-$\beta$ ($>1$) pressure distributions. Spectroscopic data reveal a threefold increase in temperature for cold, unmagnetized ions, resulting from a resonant Landau damping mechanism. Furthermore, a developed linear theory forecasts positive growth rates at finite $\beta$ and identifies the stabilizing influence of extremely high $\beta$ values, consistent with the observed phenomena.

TOI-1266c, a newly identified super-Venus orbiting an early M dwarf within the radius valley, exhibits a bulk density of approximately 2.2 g cm$^{-3}$. This value aligns with a substantial volatile content, implying the survival of volatile reservoirs despite receiving more than double Earth's insolation over billions of years. Conversely, the upper mass constraint suggests a composition resembling a cool super-Mercury, dominated by an iron core exceeding 50% of the mass ($\sim$9.2 g cm$^{-3}$), indicating it has reached the collisional stripping threshold and entered the radius gap. This study investigates various hypothetical scenarios for TOI-1266c by integrating updated and novel open-source models for atmospheric escape, radiative-convective processes, and photochemistry. Results indicate that water-rich atmospheres containing trace H$_{2}$ and CO$_{2}$ could be detected with a signal-to-noise ratio greater than 5 in under 20 hours of JWST observation time. Furthermore, water vapor spectral signatures appear largely unaffected by high-altitude water or ice clouds, as significant water vapor exists above the cloud deck, though self-consistent cloud modeling remains necessary for confirmation. Regardless of its specific mass, TOI-1266c serves as a critical testbed for hypotheses concerning the evolution of sub-Neptunes and Venus-analogues, especially those situated near the radius valley.

This paper introduces a novel class of bi-univalent functions and investigates the upper bound of the second Hankel determinant, $|H_2(2)|$, for a subclass of $\Sigma$ defined by subordination. Additionally, the study derives several results as special cases of the main findings and corrects errors in previous research that were based on miscalculations.

In 2020, the XENON1T experiment detected an excess of events corresponding to electron recoil energies ($E_R$) between 2 and 3 keV. This anomaly could stem from various origins, including solar axions, neutrino magnetic moments, or inelastic dark matter scattering off xenon nuclei, where the resulting electron recoil energy is determined by the mass difference between the dark matter particles. This study demonstrates that analyzing the annual modulation of both the event rate and the electron recoil energy provides crucial additional data to differentiate among competing theoretical interpretations. We first generalize the formalism of annual modulation to include electronic recoils and inelastic dark matter scattering. Subsequently, we examine a specific theoretical framework involving two Dirac fermions and a dark photon, incorporating all pertinent cosmological and experimental constraints. Applying this model to both XENON1T and XENONnT data with realistic thresholds, efficiencies, and energy resolutions, we fit the key physical parameters: the mass splitting and the electron scattering cross-section. We then illustrate the enhanced discriminatory power of utilizing the annual variation in both signal rate and recoil energy using a simplified model based on these parameters for XENONnT. This more sensitive approach, which surpasses time-only modulation analyses, offers a template applicable to other dark matter scenarios with varying candidates, mediators, and cosmological assumptions. Specifically, for the $U(1)$ model with two Dirac fermions that accommodates the XENON1T excess under XENONnT conditions, accounting for the annual variation in both rate and recoil energy enables a more rapid and precise determination of the model's free parameters.

We examine the incompressible 2D Navier-Stokes equations under periodic boundary conditions, subject to both deterministic time-periodic forcing and degenerate stochastic forcing. Our analysis demonstrates that the system admits a unique ergodic periodic invariant measure that exhibits exponential mixing within a Wasserstein metric. Furthermore, we establish the weak law of large numbers for the continuous-time inhomogeneous solution process. Additionally, when restricting this process to periodic times, we derive both the weak law of large numbers and the central limit theorem. These findings remain valid regardless of noise intensity and apply to any viscosity value exceeding a lower bound $
u_1$, which is defined by the Grashof number $G_1$ linked to the deterministic forcing. In the laminar regime, a higher viscosity threshold $
u_2$ emerges, characterized by the Grashof number $G_2$ associated with both deterministic and random forcings. For this laminar case, we prove that the system exhibits trivial dynamics for any viscosity greater than $
u_2$ by showing the existence of a unique globally exponentially stable random periodic solution that underpins the unique periodic invariant measure.

This work examines countably infinite Markov decision processes (MDPs) featuring transition rewards. The $\limsup$ and $\liminf$ threshold objectives aim to maximize the probability that the $\limsup$ or $\liminf$ of the infinite sequence of transition rewards, respectively, remains non-negative. We delineate the full landscape of strategy complexity for these goals, defining both upper and lower bounds on the memory needed by $\varepsilon$-optimal and optimal strategies. Furthermore, we leverage these findings to resolve two open questions from [Sudderth, Decisions in Economics and Finance, 2020] regarding the memory requirements for optimal strategies in expected $\limsup$ and $\liminf$ payoff scenarios.

The presence of adversarial attacks raises significant concerns regarding the security of machine learning (ML) models. In numerous safety-critical domains, including financial forecasting, fraud detection, and anomaly identification, datasets often consist of mixed-type data containing both numerical and categorical features. However, generating adversarial examples for such mixed-type data remains underexplored. This paper introduces M-Attack, a novel algorithm capable of effectively creating adversarial examples within mixed-type datasets. Using M-Attack, adversaries can subtly perturb both numerical and categorical features to deceive targeted classification models. Furthermore, by incorporating specific regularizations, the generated examples can bypass potential detection mechanisms, rendering the attacks particularly stealthy. Extensive empirical studies confirm the method's effectiveness and efficiency while assessing the robustness of current classification models against this threat. The results underscore the feasibility of generating adversarial examples in real-world ML applications.

Domain adaptation seeks to utilize labeled data from a source domain to train a classifier for an unlabeled target domain that follows a distinct distribution. While earlier techniques primarily align distributions through global or class-specific methods, global alignment often fails to achieve fine-grained class-to-class overlap, and pseudo-label-supervised class alignment cannot ensure reliability. To address these issues, we introduce the Cycle Label-Consistent Network (CLCN), a simple yet efficient approach that leverages the cycle consistency of classification labels. By employing dual cross-domain nearest centroid classification, CLCN generates a robust self-supervised signal to enhance discrimination within the target domain. The proposed cycle label-consistent loss function strengthens the alignment between ground-truth and pseudo-labels from source samples, thereby promoting statistically similar latent representations across both domains. This loss can be integrated into any existing classification architecture with negligible computational cost. Extensive experiments on MNIST-USPS-SVHN, Office-31, Office-Home, and Image CLEF-DA benchmarks demonstrate that our method mitigates the adverse effects of erroneous pseudo-labels and learns more discriminative features. Consequently, the approach achieves absolute performance gains of 9.4% on Office-31 and 6.3% on Image CLEF-DA compared to using the source domain alone.

Recent findings indicate that supermassive black holes likely reside at the centers of numerous galaxies, and intermediate-mass black holes (IMBHs) within globular clusters have similarly been theorized. This study examines gravitational lensing as a novel method for investigating these objects. It is established that the mass distribution of a self-gravitating system, such as a globular cluster, varies significantly depending on whether a central massive object exists. By evaluating potential mass distributions for a Milky Way globular cluster, we estimate that an IMBH would produce a gravitational lensing separation angle in the range of milliarcseconds.

This study introduces a novel approach to determining the accessibility of stochastic partial differential equations (SPDEs) influenced by additive pure jump noise. A key innovation lies in permitting the driving noises to be degenerate. Leveraging this framework, we achieve, for the first time, the accessibility of a specific class of SPDEs driven by degenerate pure jump noise, encompassing 2D stochastic Navier-Stokes equations, stochastic Burgers-type equations, singular stochastic p-Laplace equations, stochastic fast diffusion equations, and others. Furthermore, we prove the ergodicity of singular stochastic p-Laplace equations and stochastic fast diffusion equations under additive pure jump noise, noting that these driving noises may include Lévy processes characterized by heavy tails.

Traditional image-based feature descriptor design relies on iterative scanning of image patches to extract local information, resulting in significant computational overhead. To circumvent these scanning procedures, we introduce matrix multiplication-based local feature descriptors: the Matrix projection based Local Binary Pattern (M-LBP) and the Matrix projection based Histogram of Oriented Gradients (M-HOG). Furthermore, we propose an integrated M-LBP-HOG formulation that computes both descriptors simultaneously in a single step. Evaluated on a publicly available mammogram dataset, the proposed methods demonstrate promising results regarding both classification accuracy and computational efficiency.

Parameter identifiability refers to the ability to derive specific parameter values from the equations of a given differential model. Understanding whether a system is globally or locally identifiable enables the design of more effective practical experiments for extracting parameters from experimental data. This paper introduces a web-based software tool designed to address specific identifiability inquiries. Specifically, the toolbox assesses the identifiability of individual model parameters and identifies all functions of those parameters (known as identifiable combinations) that can be determined from single or multiple experiments. The program is freely accessible at https://maple.cloud/app/6509768948056064.

The study of isolated systems under Floquet engineering typically relies on an effective time-independent Floquet Hamiltonian, which governs the stroboscopic dynamics of periodically driven quantum systems in intervals of the driving period and is commonly derived analytically via high-frequency expansions. Extending these principles to open quantum systems governed by a Markovian Lindblad-type master equation proves challenging. Specifically, even for a simple two-level system, two distinct phases emerge: one where the effective time-independent Floquet generator remains a Markovian Lindblad operator, and another where it does not. Although numerical methods confirm the existence of a Lindbladian Floquet generator (Floquet Linbladian) in the high-frequency limit, standard analytical high-frequency expansions fail to capture this behavior accurately. We demonstrate that a valid Floquet Lindbladian can indeed be derived from high-frequency expansions by employing a suitably selected rotating frame. Using this framework, we further characterize the transition to a lower-frequency phase where a Floquet Lindbladian ceases to exist, revealing that the resulting non-Markovianity of the Floquet generator stems entirely from the micromotion of the driven open system.

Dissolved manganese (Mn) serves as a biologically critical element, with its oxidized form playing a key role in eliminating trace constituents from ocean waters. As part of the GEOTRACES initiative, recent efforts have yielded highly precise Mn measurements across the Atlantic, Indian, and Arctic Oceans. This study aims to integrate these novel data points with advanced modeling to clarify the primary sources and redistribution mechanisms of Mn globally. To achieve this, we employed a global circulation model to simulate dissolved Mn distribution, incorporating simplified parameterizations for realistic sources, processes, and sinks. While the model accounts for oxidation, (photo)reduction, aggregation, and settling, it currently excludes biological uptake. The simulation successfully replicates observational data and yields the following findings:

*   Elevated surface Mn levels result from the interplay between photoreduction and upper-ocean sources, with dust being the dominant contributor, followed by sediments and, locally, rivers.
*   In the Atlantic, surface Mn descends into the North Atlantic Deep Water; however, intense removal rates prevent its southward propagation.
*   Most of the deep ocean exhibits a relatively uniform background dissolved Mn concentration ranging from 0.10 to 0.15 nM. The model replicates this pattern via a 25 pM threshold for manganese oxides, indicating that a minimum Mn concentration is required before aggregation and removal processes become effective.
*   Distinct hydrothermal signals observed in data are reproduced by assuming both high Mn sources and vigorous removal rates in the immediate vicinity of hydrothermal vents.

Log-loss, or cross-entropy loss, is a standard metric in machine learning for evaluating classification algorithms. This paper explores the challenge of deducing dataset labels solely from one or more log-loss scores, without direct access to the data itself. Surprisingly, we demonstrate that for any finite set of classes, it is possible to accurately reconstruct the dataset labels from a single, carefully designed prediction vector's log-loss score, provided arbitrary precision arithmetic is permitted. Furthermore, we introduce label inference algorithms (attacks) that remain effective even when noise is added to the scores or when arithmetic precision is limited. These methods leverage concepts from number theory and combinatorics and do not require model training. We validate the practicality and ease of executing these attacks through experimental simulations on real-world datasets.

We examine priority-based school choice scenarios involving farsighted students. We demonstrate that the singleton set containing the matching generated by the Top Trading Cycles (TTC) mechanism constitutes a farsighted stable set. Conversely, the matching resulting from the Deferred Acceptance (DA) mechanism may not belong to any farsighted stable set. Consequently, the TTC mechanism yields an assignment that is both Pareto efficient and farsightedly stable. Furthermore, anticipating three steps ahead is sufficient to stabilize the TTC matching.

Recent advancements have successfully applied Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) to classify diabetic retinopathy (DR) fundus images. However, the deeper representations within these networks often capture high-level semantics while sacrificing spatial resolution. To generate clinically actionable predictions for ophthalmologists, this study employs Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM), a post-attention technique applied to the penultimate layer of deep learning models, to create coarse localization maps. This approach highlights discriminative regions, offering evidence that supports ophthalmologists in diagnosis and potentially saves lives through early detection. Specifically, the research utilizes pre-trained weights from four state-of-the-art models—VGG16, ResNet50, InceptionV3, and InceptionResNetV2—to generate and compare localization maps for DR fundus images. Results indicate that InceptionV3 delivers the superior performance, achieving a test classification accuracy of 96.07%, while also localizing lesions more effectively and rapidly than the other models.

We demonstrate strengthened versions of the Birkhoff Ergodic Theorem applicable to weakly and strongly mixing measure-preserving systems. Our pointwise results for weakly mixing systems are shown to be strictly more powerful than the Wiener-Wintner Theorem. Furthermore, these theorems for weakly and strongly mixing systems uniquely characterize their respective classes of systems.
