Additionally, the techniques employed in this work enable the derivation of an enhanced pointwise ergodic theorem for other tiers of the ergodic hierarchy, including ergodicity and mild mixing, though not for K-mixing. The author intends to incorporate these further pointwise ergodic theorems into his thesis.

This paper examines Brown's definition of the probabilistic zeta function for finite lattices as an extension of the concept applied to finite groups. We introduce a more suitable alternative for non-atomistic lattices. While the probabilistic zeta function retains a general Dirichlet series form, this series is not necessarily ordinary, distinguishing it from the group case. We calculate the function across various finite lattice examples, revealing a link to Stirling numbers of the second kind specifically for the divisibility lattice. Additionally, we investigate which lattices yield ordinary Dirichlet series when transitioning from groups to lattices, focusing on partition lattices and $d$-divisible partition lattices. Applying the prime number theorem, we demonstrate that the probabilistic zeta functions for these latter structures generally do not result in ordinary Dirichlet series.

This paper addresses the network utility maximization problem within a load-coupled heterogeneous network, incorporating diverse user priorities by jointly optimizing user association, load distribution, and power control. To manage the inherent nonconvexity, we first derive a closed-form optimal resource allocation strategy and characterize the ideal base station load distribution pattern. These insights are crucial for simplifying the original challenge and enabling the transformation of the nonconvex load distribution and power control subproblems into a convex form through exponential variable substitution. Consequently, we propose a low-complexity iterative algorithm to generate a suboptimal solution for the joint optimization. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm outperforms conventional methods.

Estimating 3D motion, encompassing scene flow and point cloud registration, has gained significant attention. Building on 2D flow techniques, recent approaches utilize deep neural networks to build cost volumes for precise 3D flow calculation. However, these methods face limitations due to the difficulty of defining search windows on point clouds caused by their irregular structure. This paper addresses this challenge with a straightforward yet effective strategy. We split the problem into two interconnected phases: first optimizing 3D flows point-by-point, and then applying global regularization through a recurrent network. Consequently, the recurrent network processes only regular point-wise data as input. Experiments evaluate our approach on both 3D scene flow and point cloud registration tasks. For scene flow, we compare results on the standard FlyingThings3D and KITTI datasets. For registration, we assess data pairs featuring large poses and partial overlaps from ModelNet40, following prior methodologies. Our findings demonstrate that the proposed method surpasses existing techniques, achieving new state-of-the-art results in both tasks and highlighting the effectiveness of this zero-order approach for irregular point cloud data.

The success of quantum information technology relies on controlling large ensembles of qubits with high precision. Quantum dots represent a promising avenue because they align well with semiconductor fabrication processes. While individual qubits have demonstrated operation fidelities exceeding 99.9%, performance drops to 98.67% when two qubits are driven at once. This study reports single-qubit randomized benchmarking across a two-dimensional array of spin qubits, testing configurations with one, two, and four simultaneously driven qubits. By meticulously optimizing qubit parameters, we achieved native gate fidelities of 99.9899(4)%, 99.904(4)%, and 99.00(4)% for these respective configurations. Additionally, we observed that cross-talk between next-nearest neighbors generates errors often too small to detect within current error margins, suggesting that such cross-talk is highly localized. These findings regarding single-qubit gate quality and simultaneous operation capabilities are vital for scaling up germanium-based quantum technologies.

Play-to-earn represents a promising sector within decentralized applications, merging blockchain technology with engaging games and financial incentives to draw diverse participants. Despite significant capital investment, this emerging crypto niche remains controversial, causing the traditional gaming industry to remain cautious about adopting blockchain solutions. Furthermore, systematic research into these projects is currently scarce. This paper examines play-to-earn initiatives through the lenses of economic and governance models, as well as their implementation, evaluating how blockchain enhances these projects via system robustness, transparency, composability, and decentralized governance. We start by identifying key participants and characterizing tokens as outcomes of composability. Next, we outline the project roadmaps and governance structures to demonstrate a shift from centralized to decentralized control. Additionally, we categorize project implementations based on varying degrees of robustness and transparency. Finally, we address future research challenges regarding security and societal impacts, including potential attacks, token economics, and governance issues.

Hollow-core anti-resonant fibers (HC-ARFs) have garnered significant interest within the fiber optics community because of their exceptional light-guiding capabilities and wide-ranging applications. Notably, nested HC-ARFs have recently achieved competitiveness with standard fibers and, in some aspects, surpassed them. Their effectiveness relies on a precisely engineered geometry, which makes their optical properties highly sensitive to even minor structural variations. During fabrication, these variations occur, resulting in geometric imperfections that degrade fiber performance. In this study, we present, to our knowledge, the first statistical modeling and analysis of how these imperfections affect propagation loss using a Monte-Carlo simulation. We examined random fluctuations in the thickness of outer and nested tube walls, as well as random offsets in tube angles. Our results indicate that loss increases caused by perturbed tube angles are roughly an order of magnitude greater than those from varying wall thicknesses for fundamental modes (FM) and two orders of magnitude greater for higher-order modes (HOM) at a wavelength of 1.55 $\mu$m. Additionally, the higher-order-mode-extinction-ratio (HOMER) scales with the intensity of structural variations, suggesting an improvement in the fiber's "single-modeness." Furthermore, bending conditions drastically amplify the combined loss contribution of these effects, reaching +50% at a 4 cm bend radius compared to +5% in a straight fiber. We believe this research aids in predicting the performance of realistic HC-ARFs post-fabrication.

Constructing a robust Machine Learning (ML) model for a specific dataset is a complex process involving multiple stages, with comparing numerous generated models to identify the optimal one for deployment being particularly critical. This comparison becomes increasingly difficult when dealing with a dynamic set of features. Evaluations extend beyond mere performance metrics; users also seek to understand the relationships between features and model outcomes, such as feature importance for interpretability. To address this, this paper introduces the RadialNet Chart, a new visualization technique designed to compare ML models trained with varying feature counts while exposing implicit dependencies. In this visualization, ML models are depicted as lines and features as arcs, with lines generated via a recursive function. The structural layout encodes the dependency of models on dynamic features, making connections between models and their associated features immediately apparent through line relationships. Additionally, model performance is represented through color and line width. Consequently, feature importance can be directly discerned from the chart's structure, facilitating effective ML explanations.

If n is divisible by 4, a square with side length n can be tiled using T-tetrominos through a standard construction. When n is even but not a multiple of 4, there is also a well-established method to tile such a square with T-tetrominos and exactly four monominos. Conversely, Walkup demonstrated that tiling a square with only T-tetrominos is impossible. Turning to the case where n is odd, Zhan proved that a single monomino is insufficient for tiling. Hochberg further established that no more than nine monominos are ever required. We provide a construction for every odd n that utilizes exactly five monominos, thus settling this problem.

XGBoost remains a leading machine learning model in the industry, valued for its high accuracy and efficiency. Addressing data isolation challenges within big data contexts, the development of a secure and efficient Federated XGBoost (FedXGB) system is essential. Current FedXGB approaches often suffer from data leakage or are limited to two-party scenarios with significant computational and communication costs. This paper introduces a secure, lossless multi-party federated XGB framework that modifies the split criterion calculation under secret sharing and resolves leaf weight computation through distributed optimization. Furthermore, the study provides a comprehensive security analysis and presents numerical results demonstrating the proposed FedXGB's superiority over state-of-the-art models on benchmark datasets.

Data-efficient image classification with deep neural networks, particularly in scenarios with limited labeled data, has become a prominent research focus recently. However, objectively comparing existing methods is challenging due to inconsistent evaluation datasets and frequent comparisons against untuned baselines with default hyperparameters. To address this, we have established a benchmark for data-efficient image classification featuring six diverse datasets across various domains—including natural images, medical imagery, and satellite data—and data types such as RGB, grayscale, and multispectral. Leveraging this benchmark, we re-evaluated the standard cross-entropy baseline alongside eight data-efficient deep learning methods published between 2017 and 2021 at prestigious venues. To ensure a fair and realistic assessment, we meticulously tuned the hyperparameters for every method on each dataset. Surprisingly, we discovered that optimizing the learning rate, weight decay, and batch size on a separate validation split yields a highly competitive baseline. This tuned baseline surpasses all but one specialized method and remains competitive with the remaining one.

Adaptive User Interfaces (UIs) aim to automatically modify interfaces to better assist users in their tasks, with the core challenge lying in inferring user intent from input to select appropriate adaptations. Designing effective online UI adaptations is difficult because it often depends on laboriously hand-crafted rules or the collection of high-quality user data. To address these issues, we model UI adaptation as a multi-agent reinforcement learning problem. In this framework, a user agent learns to interact with the UI to complete a task, while an interface agent simultaneously learns adaptations to maximize the user agent's performance. The interface agent remains agnostic to the specific goal, instead learning the task structure from the user agent's behavior to provide support. We demonstrate that this approach significantly reduces the number of required actions in a simulated photo editing task. Additionally, user studies confirm that our interface agent generalizes effectively from simulated users to real users.

This work introduces a data-driven framework for space-time adaptive processing (STAP) radar that integrates classical radar methods, computer vision, and deep learning. We constructed a comprehensive dataset of received radar signals by simulating targets with varying strengths within a specific area using RFView, a site-specific radio frequency modeling tool from ISL Inc. For every sample in this region, we produced heatmap tensors representing the output power across range, azimuth, and elevation for a minimum variance distortionless response (MVDR) beamformer, which can also serve as a test statistic. These tensors function as stacked images; in airborne contexts, the moving radar generates a sequence of these time-indexed stacks, effectively creating a video. Our objective is to leverage these visual representations for target detection and localization, mirroring computer vision techniques such as the Faster Region-Based Convolutional Neural Network (Faster R-CNN). While Faster R-CNN utilizes a proposal network for regions of interest, a regression network for anchor box positioning, and a classification algorithm optimized for natural images, our current research aims to develop analogous tools tailored for radar heatmap images. We plan to create a large, representative adaptive radar signal processing database for training and evaluation, conceptually similar to the COCO dataset for natural imagery. As an initial demonstration, this paper presents a regression network designed to estimate target locations, highlighting the viability and substantial performance gains offered by our data-driven methodology.

This work investigates the hydrodynamic and large-scale dynamics of a two-species generalization of the TASEP (2-TASEP), where two particle types move in opposing directions and exchange positions. We calculate the shock and rarefaction solutions for the model's hydrodynamic equations, demonstrating that the system belongs to the Temple class. Furthermore, we fully resolve the Riemann problem and validate our theoretical findings against Monte Carlo simulations.

The concept of "weather regimes" in mid-latitude atmospheric circulation has long been recognized as regions within phase space characterized by higher-than-average density and/or prolonged persistence. Meteorologists and climatologists have extensively investigated these regimes because they offer a way to significantly simplify the complex and chaotic dynamics of the mid-latitudes. Various well-known, simple non-linear dynamical systems have served as toy models to illustrate and understand such regime behavior. However, the literature lacks a universally accepted, precise definition of a "regime." In this work, we propose an approach that links the existence of regimes in a dynamical system to the presence of non-trivial topological structures within the system's attractor. Using persistent homology—a computational tool from topological data analysis—we demonstrate that this method is both computationally feasible and practically insightful, successfully identifying regime structures across a variety of examples.

While current face anti-spoofing (FAS) techniques demonstrate high accuracy within intra-domain settings, their performance deteriorates significantly in cross-domain contexts due to inadequate generalization. Although recent approaches like domain generalization and representation disentanglement have been investigated, their efficacy remains constrained by two primary challenges: first, the difficulty of mapping all faces into a unified feature space, where unknown domains failing to align with known regions lead to erroneous predictions; and second, the inability to fully account for diverse spoof artifacts during disentanglement. To address these limitations, we introduce a Feature Generation and Hypothesis Verification framework. Notably, this work pioneers the use of feature generation networks to produce hypotheses for both genuine faces and known attacks. Following this, two verification modules are employed to determine if an input face originates from the real-face space and adheres to the real-face distribution. Additionally, we provide an analysis linking our framework to Bayesian uncertainty estimation, offering theoretical backing for robust defense against unknown domains. Experimental evaluations across multiple public datasets confirm that our approach yields promising results and surpasses state-of-the-art methods.

The facility known as RHIC, or the "isobar run," was originally intended to compare observables from collisions of $^{96}_{40}Zr$ and $^{96}_{44}Ru$ to identify effects dependent on atomic number ($Z$). However, STAR data revealed with exceptional precision that these two nuclides differ more significantly than anticipated, generating effects exceeding those attributable solely to charge. Although numerous studies have attempted to quantify these discrepancies in relation to various observables, there remains a general consensus that the differences stem from nuclear structure, specifically the properties of the lowest excited states. Despite this, the exact link between low-energy and high-energy nuclear physics remains undefined. This paper proposes such a connection through the concept of thermal density matrices for "preheated" nuclei, where the effective temperature determines the set of excited states included in the calculations. Furthermore, I suggest employing a semiclassical "flucton" method at finite temperatures to compute these thermal density matrices.

This paper introduces a numerical approach for solving a multiscale model of surfactant sorption kinetics around an oscillating bubble. Particle evolution is described by a convection-diffusion equation for surfactant concentration $c$, subject to boundary conditions on the bubble surface that account for short-range attractive and repulsive potentials \cite{multiscale_mod}. Within the fluid domain, particles are advected by flow induced by bubble oscillations. The proposed solution method employs a finite-difference scheme on a uniform Cartesian grid, applicable to both 2D and 3D axisymmetric domains. A level-set function delineates the bubble region, while a ghost-point technique discretizes boundary conditions to ensure second-order accuracy at curved interfaces. The resulting sparse linear system is resolved using a geometric multigrid method tailored specifically to this problem. Accuracy tests confirm second-order convergence in both space and time. Fluid dynamics are modeled using the Stokes equations via a second-order monolithic approach that solves momentum and continuity equations simultaneously. Given the small amplitude of oscillations, a simplified model is utilized where the computational bubble remains stationary, with oscillations represented solely through time-dependent boundary conditions. Numerical comparisons with a moving domain model validate that this simplification is appropriate for the investigated problem class.

Large pre-trained models tend to degrade over extended deployments due to shifting input distributions, evolving user needs, or newly identified knowledge gaps. While recent model editors allow behavior modification by adjusting weights during deployment, these methods often cause performance decay on original data and forget previous corrections when applied repeatedly. We introduce a new Lifelong Model Editing framework where streaming errors are detected and corrected without affecting unrelated inputs, all without access to training edits, external datasets, or upstream data. To address this, we propose General Retrieval Adaptors for Continual Editing (GRACE), which learns to store activations from a selected layer in an adaptive codebook as edits arrive, keeping the original model weights frozen. This enables GRACE to perform thousands of sequential edits using only streaming errors while minimally impacting unrelated inputs. Experimental results demonstrate that GRACE outperforms recent model editors and generalizes effectively to unseen data. The code is available at https://www.github.com/thartvigsen/grace.

We develop planar black hole solutions within AdS gravity minimally coupled to a scalar field possessing an even, super-exponential potential. Our analysis reveals that the black hole interior evolves through an infinite series of Kasner epochs, driven by the scalar field oscillating back and forth within its potential. We derive an analytic expression for the transitions, or `bounces,' between these epochs and provide an explicit formula for their timing and magnitude at late interior times, thereby completely describing the interior dynamics. Consequently, we demonstrate that the interior geometry converges toward the Schwarzschild singularity at late times, despite the scalar field ascending further up its potential with each successive bounce.

We present advancements in computing the spin-orbit interaction for the HD$^+$ molecular ion, which remains the primary source of theoretical uncertainty in determining the hyperfine structure of rovibrational transition lines. We have derived and numerically evaluated corrections of order $m\alpha^7\ln(\alpha)$. Furthermore, we compare the resulting theoretical hyperfine intervals with experimental data and address the noted discrepancies.

This study introduces an ensemble forecasting method utilizing randomized neural networks. Enhanced randomized learning refines the fitting capabilities of individual models by deriving network parameters directly from data and target function characteristics. By employing a pattern-based representation for time series, the approach is particularly effective for handling data with multiple seasonalities. We present six distinct strategies to regulate the diversity among ensemble members. Empirical evaluations across four real-world forecasting tasks confirm the method's efficacy and superior performance. The proposed approach outperforms both traditional statistical models and current state-of-the-art machine learning techniques regarding forecasting accuracy. Key benefits include rapid and straightforward training, a simple architecture, ease of implementation, high precision, and the capacity to address nonstationarity and complex seasonal patterns in time series.

This study details photometric and spectral observations of the symbiotic star ZZ CMi, revealing intranight variability characterized by both smooth fluctuations and flickering in the U band with an amplitude of approximately 0.10–0.20 mag. Variability in the B band is significantly lower, remaining under 0.03 mag. Additionally, we observed variability in the H-alpha and H-beta emission lines, suggesting an outflow with velocities between 120 and 150 km/s. These findings classify ZZ CMi as an accretion-powered symbiotic system featuring an M4–M6 III cool component and a white dwarf similar to those found in recurrent novae and jet-ejecting symbiotic stars. The data can be accessed at www.astro.bas.bg/~rz/ZZCMi/ZZCMi.tar.gz.

This paper adapts recently developed algorithms for quadratic forms over number fields (arXiv:1304.0708) to apply to global function fields of odd characteristics. Initially, we introduce an algorithm to determine whether a given non-degenerate quadratic form is isotropic or hyperbolic. Subsequently, we devise a method for calculating the dimension of the anisotropic component of a quadratic form. Finally, we present algorithms that compute two specific field invariants: the level and the Pythagoras number.

Although neural conversation models are widely used, they still fail to demonstrate natural chat capabilities with humans. This study investigates user inputs as causes and model-generated responses as effects, operating on the principle that variations in causes should yield distinct effects. To explore this further, we created and expanded the CausalDialogue dataset via crowd-sourcing, which features multiple cause-effect pairs organized within a directed acyclic graph (DAG). Our analysis indicates that standard loss functions often fail to effectively integrate DAG structures, prompting us to introduce a causality-enhanced technique named Exponential Maximum Average Treatment Effect (ExMATE). This method aims to strengthen the influence of causality at the utterance level during the training of neural conversation models. To assess this approach, we developed a comprehensive benchmark using the CausalDialogue dataset with large-scale pre-trained language models, evaluating performance through both human judgment and automatic metrics for coherence, diversity, and agility. Our results demonstrate that existing methods cannot adequately handle conversational DAGs, whereas ExMATE improves the diversity and agility of conventional loss functions without compromising coherence.

We present $\mu$BERT, a mutation testing tool that leverages a pre-trained language model (CodeBERT) to generate mutants. This process involves masking a token within an input expression and employing CodeBERT to predict the original token; consequently, mutants are created by substituting the masked tokens with these predictions. Our evaluation of $\mu$BERT on 40 real faults from Defects4J demonstrates that it detects 27 faults, slightly outperforming the baseline tool PiTest, which detects 26. Furthermore, we find that $\mu$BERT is twice as cost-effective as PiTest when analyzing an equivalent number of mutants. We also assess the utility of $\mu$BERT's mutants for program assertion inference techniques, revealing their potential to enhance specification generation. Finally, we examine the quality and naturalness of several notable mutants produced by $\mu$BERT during our experimental analysis.

This paper extends and consolidates the approaches and findings of Benson, Liardet, Evetts, and Evetts & Levine to demonstrate that rational sets within a virtually abelian group $G$ possess rational (relative) growth series relative to any generating set of $G$. We demonstrate equivalences among the structural frameworks employed in existing literature and confirm the rationality of significant set classes in $G$, including definable sets, algebraic sets, conjugacy representatives, and coset representatives for any fixed subgroup, among others. Additionally, we establish that any rational set, expressed as words over $G$'s generating set, admits multiple EDT0L representations.

This brief tutorial introduces Case Management Model and Notation (CMMN) version 1.0. Designed for readers with foundational knowledge of process or workflow modeling, it comprehensively covers the CMMN notation using a simple complaints process as an example. By the end, readers will be equipped to understand and construct CMMN models, with an appendix providing a reference summary of the notation.

Establishing semantic connections between users and items is a core challenge in the matching phase of industrial recommender systems. Recent progress in this area relies on multi-channel retrieval to efficiently gauge user interest within vast candidate pools. However, current methods predominantly depend on predefined retrieval channels—such as User-CF (U2U), Item-CF (I2I), and Embedding-based Retrieval (U2I)—which restricts access to correlations derived solely from partial latent interaction information. This paper introduces MIC, a model-agnostic integrated cross-channel approach designed for large-scale recommendation. MIC aims to maximize inherent multi-channel mutual information to improve matching performance. Specifically, it robustly models correlations within user-item, user-user, and item-item dimensions using a universal schema based on latent interactions. For each channel, MIC aligns semantically similar pairs while distinguishing others through a more uniform anisotropic representation space. Unlike state-of-the-art methods that demand specific architectural designs, MIC intuitively treats all channels as a unified whole by facilitating complete information flow among users and items, making it easily adaptable to other retrieval recommender systems. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MIC enhances the performance of several state-of-the-art models on two real-world benchmarks. Furthermore, the successful deployment of MIC on industrial online services empirically validates its scalability and flexibility.

The Analog Ensemble (AnEn) method has proven effective across various weather challenges. Unlike traditional analogs that rely on broad spatial domains and extended timeframes, AnEn restricts both space and time, generating independent results for each grid point within a brief window. This approach identifies similar historical forecasts to produce accurate and calibrated ensemble predictions. At its core, AnEn employs a similarity metric to rank historical data against a new target forecast, with Euclidean distance being a common choice. However, this metric presents a significant challenge: defining appropriate weights for all parameters typically requires feature selection and exhaustive weight optimization. This paper introduces a novel definition of weather analogs using a Machine Learning (ML)-based similarity metric. This approach utilizes trained neural networks to identify analogs, allowing the inclusion of all variables without the need for prior feature selection or weight tuning. Experiments applying this metric to wind speed and solar irradiance forecasts demonstrate that it generally outperforms the traditional Euclidean method. Specifically, the ML metric shows superior capability in correcting large errors and leveraging larger search repositories. Furthermore, spatial predictions generated by the learned metric reveal an ability to define effective latent features that are transferable to other locations.

We establish the stabilization of the full Arthur-Selberg trace formula for metaplectic coverings of symplectic groups defined over a number field. This achievement yields a decomposition of the invariant trace formula for these metaplectic groups, which captures data regarding the genuine $L^2$-automorphic spectrum, into a linear combination of stable trace formulas associated with products of split odd orthogonal groups through endoscopic transfer. Drawing upon methods developed by Arthur and Moeglin-Waldspurger in the linear context, the proof relies on an extensive induction procedure that integrates local and global, as well as geometric and spectral, information. Additionally, as a secondary result, we achieve the stabilization of the local trace formula for metaplectic groups over any local field of characteristic zero.

This study presents neutron depolarization data revealing the suppression of long-range ferromagnetism and the onset of magnetic irreversibility and spin freezing in CePd$_{1-x}$Rh$_x$ near $x^*\approx0.6$. By monitoring neutron depolarization across temperature and field histories, we identify distinct signatures: long-range Ising ferromagnetism below a Curie temperature $T_{\rm C}$ for $x=0.4$, and spin freezing of minute ferromagnetic clusters below a freezing temperature $T_{\rm F1}$ for $x>x^*$. Under zero-field-cooling and field-heating protocols where $x>x^*$, the neutron depolarization exhibits a reentrant temperature dependence between $T_{\rm F2}<T_{\rm F1}$ and $T_{\rm F1}$, which microscopically aligns with the thermally activated expansion of cluster size. Furthermore, the evolution of depolarization and the reentrant behavior as a function of Rh concentration support the formation of a Kondo-cluster glass below $T_{\rm F1}$ situated near a ferromagnetic quantum phase transition at $x^*$.

The volume of digital text on the internet is growing continuously, making the classification of vast and diverse data collections increasingly difficult; this necessitates advanced information processing techniques for effective text organization. A prevalent strategy for managing large corpora is hierarchical text classification, which structures textual data within a hierarchy. Although numerous methods have been suggested for text classification, the majority of existing research focuses on the English language. This paper introduces a deep learning model designed for hierarchical text classification of Urdu news, utilizing a dataset comprising 51,325 sentences sourced from eight online news portals across three genres: Sports, Technology, and Entertainment. The study pursues two primary objectives: first, to construct a substantial human-annotated dataset for Urdu news hierarchical classification, and second, to implement a hierarchical classification of Urdu news using a proposed LSTM-based model termed Hierarchical Multi-layer LSTMs (HMLSTM). The architecture comprises two modules: a Text Representing Layer that employs Word2vec embeddings to convert words into vectors, and an Urdu Hierarchical LSTM Layer (UHLSTM), which is an end-to-end fully connected deep network for automatic feature learning, with one LSTM layer dedicated to each level of the class hierarchy. Extensive experiments were conducted on the custom-created Urdu News Dataset for Hierarchical Text Classification (UNDHTC). The results demonstrate that the proposed method is highly effective for hierarchical text classification, significantly outperforming baseline approaches and yielding competitive results compared to other deep neural models.

This work establishes lower bounds for communication within memory hierarchies or across processors for nested bilinear algorithms, including Strassen's method for matrix multiplication. We extend an existing framework that determines communication limits by analyzing the rank expansion—the minimum rank of any fixed-size column subset—for the three matrices representing a bilinear algorithm. This approach yields bounds applicable to any implementation of a bilinear algorithm, covering a broader range than those restricted to specific dependency graphs. Nested bilinear algorithms encompass fast recursive techniques for convolution, matrix multiplication, and symmetric tensor contractions. Such algorithms are formed by nesting two bilinear methods via the Kronecker product of their encoding matrices. Our primary contribution is a lower bound on the rank expansion of a matrix generated by a Kronecker product, derived from the rank expansion bounds of its operands. To demonstrate this, we map a subset of columns from a submatrix to a two-dimensional grid, condense them into a dense grid, expand the grid, and utilize the resulting grid size to limit the number of linearly independent columns. Applying these rank expansion bounds, we derive new communication lower bounds for nested Toom-Cook convolution, Strassen's algorithm, and efficient algorithms for partially symmetric contractions.

Audio-visual correlation learning seeks to identify key correspondences and comprehend natural relationships between audio and video. As deep learning advances rapidly, this emerging field has garnered significant attention. Over recent years, numerous datasets and methodologies have been introduced for this purpose, inspiring this comprehensive survey. This paper reviews state-of-the-art models designed to learn audio-visual correlations while also examining related tasks, definitions, and paradigms within AI multimedia. Furthermore, we analyze common objective functions used to optimize these models and explore how audio-visual data is leveraged during the optimization process. Most critically, we offer an extensive comparison and summary of recent advancements in state-of-the-art audio-visual correlation learning, alongside a discussion of future research directions.

This study presents the inclusive differential production cross-section of photons across six pseudorapidity intervals: 6.1 < $\eta$ < 6.5, 6.5 < $\eta$ < 7.0, 7.0 < $\eta$ < 7.5, 7.5 < $\eta$ < 8.0, 8.0 < $\eta$ < 8.5, and $\eta$ > 8.5. These measurements were obtained using the RHICf experiment during pp collisions at $\sqrt{s}$ = 510 GeV in June 2017. Furthermore, cross-sections were calculated for three $x_F$-$p_T$ phase space regions matching the coverage of LHCf results at $\sqrt{s}$ = 7 and 13 TeV for comparison. After accounting for uncertainties, the findings align with both the Feynman scaling law and the predictions of EPOS-LHC, QGSJET-II-04, Sibyll 2.3d, and DPMjet-III 2019.1, despite some models showing weak dependencies on collision energy.

For a compact Riemannian manifold $X$ with dimension two or three, and a chosen point $P \in X$, we establish comparison formulas that link the zeta-regularized determinant of any self-adjoint extension of the (symmetric) Laplace operator to that of the self-adjoint Laplacian on $X$. The domain of this extension consists of smooth functions with compact support that exclude the point $P$.

Learning from demonstration (LfD) offers a highly effective method for transferring human skills to robots. Historically, LfD has focused on replicating Cartesian and joint positions, velocities, and forces. While this traditional method succeeds in certain applications, many complex tasks require acquiring skills involving orientation, impedance, and manipulability, which possess distinct geometric properties. Accurately encoding these skills necessitates accounting for the underlying geometric structure of the skill manifold and ensuring that constraints derived from this structure are satisfied throughout both the learning and execution phases. However, standard models like Dynamic Movement Primitives (DMPs) are restricted to Euclidean data and struggle to correctly embed quantities subject to geometric constraints. This paper introduces a novel, mathematically rigorous framework leveraging Riemannian geometry to enable DMPs to properly incorporate these geometric constraints. The resulting formulation is capable of handling data sampled from any Riemannian manifold, such as unit quaternions and symmetric positive definite matrices. Extensive evaluations on both simulated environments and real-world robot experiments demonstrate that the proposed approach retains key DMP advantages, including convergence to target goals and the ability to modify goals dynamically during operation.

Many applications involve observing data in matrix form with inherent temporal dependencies, a domain where matrix-variate time series modeling is an emerging area of econometrics. Despite well-documented stylized facts across various fields, current models fail to capture non-abrupt regime switches within matrix dynamics. This paper extends linear matrix-variate autoregressive frameworks by developing a regime-switching model designed to handle smooth transitions, termed the matrix smooth transition autoregressive model. We detail the estimation procedures and validate the model's asymptotic properties using both simulated and real-world data.

We apply a two-mode approximation to a system of interacting one-dimensional spinless soft-core bosons and half-spin fermions confined in a double-well potential featuring a substantial central barrier. This model incorporates all on-site repulsive contact interactions—boson-boson, fermion-fermion, and boson-fermion—represented by delta functions, and corresponds to bosonic and fermionic isotopes of ytterbium ($^{170}\text{Yb}$ and $^{171}\text{Yb}$). Using this approximation, we observe that when the boson-fermion interaction strength $U_{BF}$ exceeds the boson-boson strength $U_{BB}$, the system enters an immiscible phase; conversely, when $U_{BB} \geq U_{BF}$, a miscible phase emerges, defined by the temporal overlap of bosonic and fermionic probability densities. Furthermore, we report that the Bose-Fermi interaction leads to an apparent suppression of collapse-revival oscillations in the boson density probability within the investigated parameter ranges.

Due to lattice mismatch between graphene and hexagonal boron nitride (hBN), a graphene/hBN (G/hBN) heterostructure exhibits a long-period moiré superstructure. This periodic potential modulates the system's electronic properties. In this study, we numerically compute the optical conductivity of G/hBN under circularly polarized light. The absence of spatial inversion symmetry in G/hBN gives rise to valley polarization. Notably, in the absence of doping, this polarization peaks in the infrared and terahertz regimes when the twist angle approaches zero; however, for hole-doped systems, the valley polarization remains largely insensitive to variations in the twist angle. These findings offer valuable insights for designing valleytronic devices based on G/hBN.

Recent developments in audio codecs utilizing discretized neural autoencoders have demonstrated significantly higher compression ratios for speech of comparable quality. However, these models are heavily dependent on specific speech content and tend to generate unintended outputs when exposed to noise. By building upon VQ-VAE autoencoders paired with WaveRNN decoders, we introduce compressor-enhancer encoders and their corresponding decoders, which function effectively even in noisy environments. Furthermore, our observations indicate that a compressor-enhancer model outperforms a standard compressor trained exclusively on clean speech when processing clean audio inputs.

This study presents a comprehensive analysis of all regimes governing the propagation of optical dispersive shock waves (DSWs) in nematic liquid crystals. Originating from step initial conditions in the optical field, these DSWs exhibit resonance because linear diffractive waves synchronize with the DSW, creating a resonant linear wavetrain that propagates ahead of it. The analysis identifies six distinct regimes, each necessitating unique solution methods. Previous research applied a single solution method across all regimes, failing to achieve full agreement with numerical results; notably, the standard DSW structure vanishes for sufficiently large initial jumps. Utilizing asymptotic theory, approximate methods, or Whitham modulation theory tailored to specific regimes, the derived solutions align excellently with numerical solutions of the nematic equations across all cases. Furthermore, the resonant wavetrain is found to be unstable for small initial jumps but stabilizes once the jump height exceeds a critical threshold. Additionally, the DSW is generally unstable, with stability only occurring in two specific scenarios: at small jump heights where no resonance exists, and at large jump heights where the standard DSW structure is absent.

Mega-constellations in Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellite networks (SatNets) are poised to be pivotal in delivering comprehensive future internet and communication services. These networks will ensure extensive coverage while enhancing service continuity, availability, and scalability. To facilitate the convergence of terrestrial Fifth Generation (5G) systems with satellite networks, the satellite industry has actively engaged in 3rd Generation Partnership Project (3GPP) standardization efforts. This paper examines these 3GPP activities concerning SatNet integration within 5G and beyond, highlighting specific use cases and summarizing the requirements needed to achieve them. It further discusses affected New Radio (NR) domains alongside potential solutions, outlines anticipated management and orchestration needs for SatNets in a 5G context, and explores future standardization paths aimed at fully integrating SatNets into Sixth Generation (6G) to achieve ubiquitous global connectivity.

When cloud cover obscures photovoltaic (PV) panels, their power output fluctuates quickly. Consequently, to ensure grid stability and meet demand, utility companies depend on reserve power sources, often fossil fuels, which contribute to environmental pollution. Accurate short-term PV power forecasting allows operators to maximize PV energy harvest and safely minimize the reliance on polluting fossil fuel reserves. Although various machine learning models have been created to predict solar irradiance at specific facilities, few address short-term global-scale irradiance modeling. Additionally, existing models are frequently proprietary, lack transparent architectures, or depend on computationally intensive Numerical Weather Prediction (NWP) systems. In this study, we introduce a Convolutional Long Short-Term Memory Network that frames solar nowcasting as a next-frame prediction task. This approach is more efficient than NWP models and features a simple, reproducible architecture. Our model predicts solar irradiance across North America for up to three hours in under 60 seconds on a single machine without a GPU, achieving a Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) of 120 W/m² when evaluated on two months of data.

The rheological behavior of a dilute binary mixture of inertial suspensions under simple shear flow is investigated using the Boltzmann kinetic equation. The influence of the surrounding viscous gas on solid particles is modeled through a deterministic viscous drag force and a stochastic Langevin-like term based on the environmental temperature $T_\text{env}$. By applying Grad's moment method, the temperature ratio and pressure tensor are derived as functions of the coefficients of restitution, concentration, component masses and diameters, and $T_\text{env}$. These analytical findings are validated against event-driven Langevin simulations for hard-sphere mixtures with matching mass densities [$m_1/m_2=(\sigma_1/\sigma_2)^3$, where $m_i$ and $\sigma_i$ denote the mass and diameter of species $i$]. The theoretical predictions align with simulations across various size ratios $\sigma_1/\sigma_2$ and collision types (elastic and inelastic) within a broad parameter range. Notably, both the temperature ratio $T_1/T_2$ and the viscosity ratio $\eta_1/\eta_2$ (where $\eta_i$ represents the partial contribution of component $i$ to the total shear viscosity $\eta=\eta_1+\eta_2$) exhibit discontinuous changes at a specific shear rate as the size ratio increases; this phenomenon, anticipated in the thermodynamic limit, remains elusive in simulations due to finite system sizes. Furthermore, a Bhatnagar--Gross--Krook (BGK)-type kinetic model tailored for mixtures of inelastic hard spheres is solved exactly when $T_\text{env}$ is significantly lower than the kinetic temperature $T$. Finally, the velocity distribution functions derived from Grad's method, the BGK model, and simulations are compared.

Despite the rich phenomenology of radio pulsar polarization properties, the rotating vector model (RVM), established half a century ago, remains the superior method for determining beam geometry. Applying the RVM to a sample of 854 MeerKAT-observed pulsars allows us to draw conclusions about the broader population. The primary findings are that (i) the geometric interpretation of position angle traversal holds for most pulsars, (ii) cases where the RVM fails are associated with a higher ratio of circular to linear polarization, (iii) emission heights derived via both geometric and relativistic approaches indicate that most pulsars emit below 1000 km regardless of spin period, and (iv) orthogonal mode jumps appear in the position angle traverse for approximately one-third of the population. These results exhibit only a weak dependence on pulsar spin-down energy.

We examine the Dirichlet eigenvalues of the Laplacian within a Poissonian distribution of hard spherical obstacles of constant radius inside large boxes in $\mathbb{R}^d$ for $d \ge 2$. In a box of side-length $2l$ centered at the origin, the lowest eigenvalue is typically of order $(\log l)^{-2/d}$. We demonstrate that as $l \to \infty$, with a probability approaching $1$, the spectral gap remains larger than $\sigma (\log l)^{-(1 + 2/d)}$, where the small positive constant $\sigma$ reflects the desired closeness of this probability to unity. Notably, the scale $(\log l)^{-(1+ 2/d)}$ is anticipated to accurately represent the gap's magnitude. Our findings rely on establishing novel deconcentration estimates. By merging this lower bound on the spectral gap with the work of Kerner, Pechmann, and Spitzer, we deduce a type-I generalized Bose-Einstein condensation in probability for a Kac-Luttinger system of non-interacting bosons amidst Poissonian spherical impurities. Specifically, when the density surpasses the critical threshold, there is a sole macroscopic occupation of the one-particle ground state.

The creation of heavy quarks (charm and beauty) offers distinctive perspectives on the transport characteristics of the Quark-Gluon Plasma (QGP) within heavy-ion collisions. Experimentally, the nuclear modification factor ${{R}_{\rm AA}}$ and the azimuthal anisotropy coefficient ${v}_{\rm 2}$ of heavy-flavor mesons serve as potent observables for investigating medium-induced phenomena, such as energy loss and collectivity, affecting heavy quark propagation during QGP evolution. Recent measurements of prompt and non-prompt open heavy-flavor hadrons enable a systematic comparison of the transport dynamics associated with charm and beauty quarks. Using a newly developed framework, this study undertakes such an analysis. Through a quantitative examination of ${{R}_{\rm AA}}$ and ${v}_{\rm 2}$, we find that both charm and beauty quarks act as effective probes of QGP dynamical features, specifically the mass hierarchy governing energy loss and azimuthal anisotropy, which are faithfully transmitted to various $D/B$-meson species. Furthermore, our calculations successfully reproduce both ${{R}_{\rm AA}}$ and ${v}_{\rm 2}$ data for prompt and non-prompt $D^{0}$ mesons in central ($0-10\%$) and semi-central ($30-50\%$) Pb--Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}=5.02~{\rm TeV}$. Additionally, we provide predictions for $B$-meson observables suitable for future experimental tests, extending down to the low momentum region.

Unlike conventional media, social platforms typically offer quantified data on user engagement for each piece of content. While some argue that these visible cues facilitate the spread of misinformation, this study investigates their causal impact on user behavior. Through an experiment involving 628 Americans on a custom newsfeed interface, we systematically manipulated the presence and intensity of these social cues. Our findings indicate that displaying cues signaling high engagement from others increases the likelihood of users liking and sharing posts. Specifically, compared to a control group without such cues, the presence of social cues led to a greater increase in the sharing of true news relative to false news. Additionally, these cues make it harder to accurately predict a post's popularity. Collectively, our results suggest that, contrary to concerns about distraction or the promotion of low-quality content, social cues can, under certain conditions, enhance the ability to discern truth and reduce the dissemination of misinformation. This work highlights the critical role social cues play in shaping attention and engagement, urging platforms to understand these effects before altering how cues are displayed.

In our paper, we established that for a compact space $X$, the inclusion $I_{f}(X)$ belongs to $ANR$ if and only if $X$ itself is in $ANR$. Furthermore, we demonstrated that the functor $I_{f}$ preserves the property of a compact space being a $Q$-manyfold or a Hilbert cube, as well as the property of map layers being $ANR$-compact, compact $Q$-manyfolds, or Hilbert cubes (defined as finite sums of Hilbert cubes).

The emergence of rapid numerical solvers has driven a swift transition toward iterative methods in various fields, particularly computational mechanics, driven by the growing need to resolve large-scale linear systems. However, most conventional solvers are heavily reliant on specific problem geometries and discretizations, often failing when these parameters vary. To address this, the Hybrid Iterative Numerical Transferable Solver (HINTS) integrates a standard solver with a neural operator to enhance performance, initially targeting a single geometry. This study investigates the "T" in HINTS, specifically its geometry transferability capabilities. We first demonstrate the direct application of a HINTS model trained on one geometry to a related, different geometry without modifications. Furthermore, we introduce operator-level transfer learning combined with HINTS to further accelerate convergence on new geometries and discretizations. Numerical experiments involving Darcy flow and plane-strain elasticity problems confirm that both the direct application and the transfer learning-enhanced HINTS accurately solve these challenges across varying geometries. Notably, the transfer learning approach enables HINTS to achieve machine-zero convergence even more rapidly than direct application.

Determining how classical and quantum correlations influence work extraction is a fundamental thermodynamic issue. We address this by recognizing that in closed quantum systems, the maximum cyclic work obtainable corresponds to ergotropy. Consequently, we seek to identify and analyze the contributions of various initial correlation types—specifically total, classical, discord, and entanglement correlations—to ergotropy. Through this process, we have developed and examined ergotropy-based correlation quantifiers. Our findings indicate that discord correlations invariably provide a positive contribution to work extraction, whereas total, classical, and entanglement correlations may diminish it.

The multi-particle spring system serves as a crucial and extensively applied physical model; however, as the particle count rises, determining the kinematic trajectories of these particles becomes increasingly challenging. The core solution to this issue depends on the feasibility of developing a dynamic model for multi-particle spring systems that facilitates numerical computation. In this study, by introducing a novel physical quantity, the spring action $\mathcal{K}$, we investigate and rebuild the dynamic models for two prevalent types of multi-particle spring systems. The findings indicate that our constructed multi-particle spring dynamic model offers significant advantages when calculating systems with a high number of particles. This approach provides vital theoretical foundations for applying multi-particle spring systems to engineering and scientific challenges.

Consistent with Pomeau's conjecture regarding the role of directed percolation (DP) in the onset and decay of turbulence within wall-bounded flows, we introduce a minimal stochastic model designed to explain the spatially intermittent regimes seen in channel flow prior to its transition back to laminar conditions. Numerical simulations reveal that a regime characterized by bands drifting obliquely in two stream-wise symmetrical directions bifurcates into an asymmetrical state before finally decaying into laminar flow. Formulated as a probabilistic cellular automaton evolving von Neumann neighborhoods with probabilities derived from detailed analysis of simulation data, the model incorporates band propagation along with two primary local mechanisms: longitudinal splitting of bands sharing the same orientation, and transversal splitting that generates a daughter band with an opposite orientation to its parent. The final decay stage, which exhibits one-dimensional DP characteristics within a two-dimensional geometry, is interpreted as a consequence of lateral spreading becoming irrelevant in the single-orientation regime. Furthermore, the model replicates the bifurcation that restores symmetry when the probability associated with transversal splitting is varied, thereby facilitating an investigation into the critical properties of this bifurcation, analogous to thermodynamic phase transitions.

Should neutrinos be Dirac fermions, new physics beyond the Standard Model must exist to explain their minute masses. This paper systematically investigates a general mechanism utilizing two extra scalars and a heavy intermediate fermion to naturally produce tiny Dirac neutrino masses at both tree and one-loop levels. For tree-level scenarios, we prioritize models where additional scalars acquire small vacuum expectation values without fine-tuning. In one-loop cases, we examine models featuring dark matter candidates protected by $Z_2^D$ symmetry. Across both approaches, we focus on $SU(2)_L$ scalar multiplets with no more than five components, deriving the full set of viable models. We also briefly address phenomenological implications, including lepton flavor violation, leptogenesis, and potential LHC signatures.

High-sensitivity, high-velocity resolution neutral hydrogen (HI) spectral lines were observed toward the high-mass star-forming region G176.51+00.20 using the central seven beams of the Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical radio Telescope (FAST) in its 19-beam tracking mode. This pilot study investigates narrow-line self-absorption (HINSA) in regions with detected bipolar molecular outflows. Two HINSA components were identified across all seven beams: a strong CO emission region (SCER) at approximately $-$18 km s$^{-1}$ and a weak CO emission region (WCER) at approximately $-$3 km s$^{-1}$. The SCER detected in Beam 3 is likely better classified as a WCER. Within the SCER, HINSA appears linked to the molecular material traced by CO, whereas in the WCER (including Beam 3's SCER), HINSA is likely associated with CO-dark or CO-faint gas rather than CO clouds. The fractional HINSA abundance varies from $\sim 1.1 \times 10^{-3}$ to $\sim 2.6 \times 10^{-2}$. Notably, Beam 1 exhibits lower HINSA abundance compared to the surrounding beams (2 and 4–7); this potential ring structure may result from HI ionization or rapid conversion of HI to H$_2$ in the denser inner region.

The conventional supervised learning paradigm relies on the assumption that training and test data originate from the same distribution. Domain generalization (DG) techniques aim to develop models capable of generalizing to unseen domains after being trained on data from various existing domains. We expand upon DG by addressing a more complex scenario where the label space of the target unseen domain may also shift. We term this challenge Zero-Shot Domain Generalization (ZSD), representing, to our knowledge, the inaugural attempt to address generalization across both new domains and new classes within them. We present a straightforward approach that leverages semantic class information to modify current DG methods to satisfy ZSD requirements. Our evaluation on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, F-MNIST, and PACS datasets establishes a robust baseline to encourage further exploration in this emerging research area.

We conduct a thorough computer simulation study of the phase structure and semiclassical effective action within (2+1)-dimensional Causal Dynamical Triangulations (CDT) quantum gravity. This investigation explores two main directions: first, systematically relaxing simplicial manifold constraints to expand the ensemble of triangulations, and second, examining CDT geometries with spatial topologies other than the sphere or torus. By analyzing multiple triangulation ensembles and spatial topologies, we find that the phase structure remains qualitatively unchanged under these generalizations. Additionally, we calculate the effective action for spatial volumes across varying conditions and topologies. Where sufficient statistical data was available, the resulting effective actions aligned with minisuperspace actions derived from continuum Einstein gravity. Overall, our findings suggest that 1) partially relaxing simplicial conditions or altering the spatial genus does not impact the continuum limit of 3D CDT, and 2) increasing the spatial genus likely has no effect on the leading-order terms of the emergent effective action.

A graph $G$ possesses the Perfect-Matching-Hamiltonian (PMH) property if every one of its perfect matchings can be paired with another perfect matching such that their union forms a Hamiltonian cycle. Originating in the 1970s through the work of Las Vergnas and Häggkvist, the investigation of graphs with the PMH-property integrates three fundamental graph concepts: matchings, Hamiltonicity, and edge-colourings. This study focuses on cubic graphs, aiming to characterize those where every perfect matching aligns with a specific colour in a proper 3-edge-colouring. We demonstrate that this condition is equivalent to the graphs being even-2-factorable (E2F), meaning all their 2-factors consist exclusively of even cycles. While bipartite cubic graphs trivially satisfy the E2F property, our analysis is restricted to non-bipartite cubic graphs. Although the PMH-property provides a sufficient (though not necessary) condition for a cubic graph to be E2F, the primary objective of this work is to define an infinite family of non-bipartite, E2F cubic graphs parameterized by two variables, which we term "papillon graphs." We further determine the specific parameter values under which these papillon graphs exhibit the PMH-property or are merely E2F, and we prove that papillon graphs with distinct parameters are never isomorphic.

The surge in complex machine learning techniques, especially deep learning, has significantly accelerated human activity recognition, with notable applications in healthcare. Within broader body sensor network systems, analyzing faces and full-body movements has become a prevalent method for assessing health status. However, utilizing intricate models to process private or sensitive data raises valid concerns regarding the potential leakage of identifiable information. This study specifically examines a deep neural network trained on individual facial images, utilizing video recordings of 493 participants undergoing neurological evaluation via eye-tracking. Various inputs, including outputs, gradients, intermediate layer activations, loss values, and labels, were fed into a deep network equipped with a support vector machine emission layer to detect whether specific faces from the training set were present. The results of the inference attack and accompanying mathematical analysis suggest a low probability of unintended memorization of facial features within the model. Consequently, the research demonstrates that this named model maintains the integrity of the training data with reasonable confidence, and this methodology can be adapted for similar scenarios involving different models.

Building on the findings by Shor [Comm. Math. Phys. 246(3), 453 (2004)] and Hastings [Nature Phys. 5, 255 (2009)], it is established that the strong superadditivity of entanglement of formation does not generally hold. This paper establishes specific conditions under which strong superadditivity applies and uses these to define classes of states that exhibit this property.

This study presents a measurement of the inelastic proton-proton cross section using the CMS detector at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s} = 13$ TeV. The analysis utilizes events characterized by energy deposits in forward calorimeters spanning pseudorapidities from -6.6 to -3.0 and +3.0 to +5.2. For events where the masses of the diffractive dissociation systems at negative and positive pseudorapidities ($M_\mathrm{X}$ and $M_\mathrm{Y}$) exceed 4.1 GeV and 13 GeV, respectively, an inelastic cross section of $68.6 \pm 0.5$ (syst) $\pm 1.6$ (lumi) mb is determined. These findings are compared against results from other experiments and predictions derived from high-energy hadron-hadron interaction models.

This article investigates the freeness of hyperplane arrangements, focusing particularly on the extensively studied graphic arrangements. While Stanley established that a graphic arrangement is free precisely when its corresponding graph is chordal, and Dirac characterized chordal graphs as those formed by "gluing" complete graphs, we extend Dirac's construction to simple matroids featuring modular joins, as defined by Ziegler. We demonstrate that every arrangement whose associated matroid arises from this specific construction is divisionally free. Furthermore, we apply these findings to arrangements linked with gain graphs and those defined over finite fields.

We present a numerical strategy for addressing nonlinear eigenproblems. Our method relies on approximating a vector-valued function that serves as the solution to a non-homogeneous form of the eigenproblem. This approximation is achieved using the minimal rational interpolation technique. A key feature is the use of an adaptive sampling scheme: the costly data required for approximation is collected at optimally selected locations, guided by a greedy error indicator. This ensures that computational resources are focused exclusively on regions where the most significant information regarding unapproximated eigenvalues resides. Subsequently, the desired eigenvalues and eigenvectors are extracted through post-processing of the resulting surrogate model. Numerical examples are provided to demonstrate the method's efficacy.

For decades, space physics, solar physics, and plasma physics have utilized the concept of energetic particle reservoirs, which relies on deterministic assumptions of outer reflecting boundaries or magnetic mirrors rather than stochastic diffusion within magnetic turbulence. Through simulations using a five-dimensional time-dependent Fokker-Planck transport equation, this study demonstrates that these so-called reservoirs are naturally explained and quantitatively reproduced by diffusion processes in turbulent magnetic fields, eliminating the need for hypotheses regarding reflecting boundaries. Consequently, our findings strongly indicate that the term "reservoir," rooted in deterministic structures, should be replaced with "flood," reflecting a stochastic diffusion mechanism. This linguistic shift symbolizes a fundamental change in perspective and pragmatic approach for studying energetic particles and related plasma phenomena in heliophysics and astrophysics.

The FAIR principles (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable), originally established for scientific data, are equally applicable to digital entities like research software and scientific workflows that process such data. These guidelines extend not only to the data itself but also to the essential infrastructure, processes, and software required to define and execute workflows. Designed as flexible guidelines rather than rigid rules, the FAIR framework accommodates varying community standards and levels of compliance. However, practical factors such as existing policies, traditions, and technological limitations often constrain the degree of FAIRness achievable. Consequently, obstacles frequently arise throughout the workflow lifecycle, stemming directly from incomplete implementations of these principles. This paper details specific, anonymized cases where data and workflows were Findable yet fell short in other critical areas expected by modern FAIR methodologies, tools, and users. By describing how these challenges were successfully resolved, we illustrate the motivation behind advancing systems and approaches toward fully FAIR workflows.

The interaction between topological properties and valley degrees of freedom has garnered significant attention due to its potential for novel phenomena and applications. Utilizing first-principles calculations, we reveal an intrinsic valley-polarized quantum anomalous Hall effect in the monolayer ferrovalley material Janus VSiGeN4, characterized by edge states that exhibit chiral spin-valley locking. Furthermore, applying small tensile or compressive strain can induce a phase transition from the valley-polarized quantum anomalous Hall state to a half-valley-metal state. As strain increases, the material transforms into a ferrovalley semiconductor displaying the valley anomalous Hall effect. This phase transition originates from the sequential inversion of V d orbitals at the K valley. Additionally, we observe that these transitions reverse the sign of Berry curvature, leading to distinct polarized light absorption across different valley states. Consequently, our study offers an optimal material platform for investigating the interplay among topology, spintronics, and valleytronics for both practical applications and experimental research.

Multidimensional heterogeneity and endogeneity characterize a broad category of econometric models. This paper examines models with heterogeneous coefficients where the outcome is expressed as a linear combination of known treatment functions and these varying coefficients. By employing control variables, we derive identification results for average treatment effects. Specifically, within a triangular framework utilizing discrete instruments, we demonstrate that average treatment effects remain unidentified if the number of support points is less than or equal to the number of coefficients. A key sufficient condition for identification is that the second moment matrix of the treatment functions, conditional on the controls, is nonsingular with probability one. Finally, we connect this condition to the identification of average treatment effects in contexts involving multiple treatments.

We conduct a Bayesian analysis of small-field inflation models, utilizing the latest data from Planck 18, ACTPol, and BICEP3. Instead of relying on proxy slow-roll parameters, we employ Artificial Neural Networks (ANN) to analyze the model coefficients directly. These networks link the models to their projected scalar index $n_s$ and running $\alpha$, offering a more accurate alternative to the Lyth-Riotto expressions. Our investigation identifies the most probable coefficients for a sixth-degree polynomial inflationary potential, resulting in a tensor-to-scalar ratio of $r\lesssim 0.03$. This analysis is performed for individual datasets as well as the combined Planck and ACTPol sets, with BICEP3 data incorporated into all three scenarios. We demonstrate that these models are viable with coefficients tuned to approximately $\Delta\gtrsim 1/60$. Notably, we observe a significant tension between the ACTPol and Planck datasets and attempt to address this discrepancy.

This study investigates the formation of an inverse-S sigmoid structure driven by the magnetic non-potential features of a rotating sunspot within Active Region (AR) 12158. Data from the Helioseismic Magnetic Imager (HMI) and Atmospheric Imaging Assembly (AIA) indicate that the erupting sigmoid originated at the sunspot's location. The sunspot exhibited a rotation rate of 0–5°/h, initially increasing before declining. Temporal variations in various non-potential parameters closely aligned with this rotational behavior. The magnetic evolution of the active region was modeled as a sequence of force-free equilibria, where the Non-Linear Force-Free Field (NLFFF) configuration around the sunspot reproduced the observed sigmoid. Magnetic field lines originating from the sunspot's periphery formed the sigmoid's body, while interior lines overlaid it, resembling a flux rope. Two significant Coronal Mass Ejection (CME) events occurred during the sunspot's rotation. In the first event, coronal current concentrations intensified, whereas they diminished in the second, correlating with changes in photospheric net vertical current; however, magnetic energy was released in both instances. The findings suggest that the sigmoid's magnetic connectivity was driven by the sunspot's slow rotation, which evolved into a highly twisted flux rope under dynamic conditions. Ultimately, an excessive critical twist within the flux rope likely caused a loss of equilibrium, triggering the dual eruptions.
We demonstrate that specific Tate–Shafarevich groups are unramified, allowing us to establish an obstruction to the Hasse principle for torsors under tori defined over p-adic function fields.

Primordial black holes (PBHs) may originate from various early-universe mechanisms, with one specific pathway linking them to inflation by invoking amplified primordial curvature perturbations at small scales. This study re-evaluates how the evolution of the primordial power spectrum influences PBH formation, specifically regarding the resulting PBH mass function. We detail the rapid transitions of the background across different Hierarchy parameters, which must stem from a consistent derivative expansion of the background inflaton field. Furthermore, we address artifacts related to matching calculations and underscore the robustness of the previously identified $k^4$ steepest growth rate for single-field inflation, even with conservatively smoothed transitions, alongside constraints on the maximum allowable growth of the power spectrum amplitude. Our findings indicate that the mass function is largely unaffected by the steepness of the power spectrum's growth and decay, relying instead primarily on the peak amplitude and the existence of plateaus spanning more than an e-fold. While the power spectrum's shape can be restricted by other observational tracers, determining the physical boundaries of its form remains a relevant inquiry.

This paper introduces an Adaptive Model Predictive Control (AMPC) strategy to guide a two-wheeled mobile robot with unknown inertia toward a target position and orientation. The robot is modeled as a knife-edge or skate subject to nonholonomic kinematic constraints, with its dynamical equations derived via the Lagrangian method. At each time step, control inputs are generated using Model Predictive Control (MPC) based on nominal parameters that are continuously updated through a recursive least squares algorithm. The proposed algorithm's effectiveness is validated through numerical simulations presented at the conclusion of the study.

We examine electroweak phase transition dynamics within a newly proposed baryogenesis framework featuring CP violation from the dark sector. This model incorporates a complex scalar singlet coupled to the Higgs via a portal, a $U(1)_l$ gauge symmetry for leptons mediated by a $Z^\prime$ boson, and a fermionic dark matter candidate. Our analysis reveals a unique thermal evolution for the scalar sector: a $Z_2$-breaking singlet vacuum in the early universe, triggered by dark Yukawa interactions, drives a one-step, strongly first-order electroweak phase transition. We investigate the parameter space capable of reproducing the observed baryon asymmetry and dark matter density while satisfying limits from electric dipole moments, collider experiments, and direct dark matter detection. The complex singlet, produced through the Higgs portal, decays into Standard Model particles after traversing a specific distance. We assess the sensitivity of the $\mathcal{L}=\unit[139]{fb^{-1}}$ $\sqrt{s}=\unit[13]{TeV}$ Large Hadron Collider to long-lived singlet scalars and determine their impact on the model's viable parameter space. Finally, accounting for existing theoretical uncertainties, we project gravitational wave signals potentially observable by future detectors.

This study examines various Riemannian metrics and evolution equations within the framework of diffeomorphic shape analysis. Following a brief overview of different methodologies for constructing Riemannian shape spaces, with particular emphasis on the foundations of the large deformation diffeomorphic metric mapping algorithm, the discussion shifts to elastic metrics and the growth models derived from them. Within this latter context, a novel class of metrics based on optimizing a growth tensor is proposed, and several of its characteristics are investigated.

Gun violence represents a significant public safety issue in the United States. In 2006, California introduced the Armed and Prohibited Persons System (APPS), a distinctive firearm monitoring initiative designed to combat gun violence. The program operates by first identifying firearm owners who subsequently become legally prohibited from possessing guns, followed by the confiscation of their weapons. This study aims to evaluate APPS's impact on California's murder rates by analyzing annual, state-level crime data from across the U.S. spanning the years before and after the program's implementation. To achieve this, we adapt a non-parametric Bayesian method known as multitask Gaussian Processes (MTGPs) for panel data. MTGPs provide flexible and parsimonious models that encompass various existing approaches, offering direct control over temporal and cross-unit dependencies alongside natural uncertainty quantification. We further extend this methodology to handle non-Normal outcomes, auxiliary covariates, and multiple outcome series, all of which are crucial for our specific application. Additionally, we demonstrate that this approach possesses favorable Frequentist properties, notably functioning as a weighting estimator with distinct weights for different units and time periods. Our analysis reveals that the heightened monitoring and enforcement under APPS significantly reduced homicides in California. Furthermore, the reduction in murders was driven exclusively by a decline in gun-related homicides, with no detectable impact on non-gun murders. The estimated cost per murder avoided is markedly lower than conventional valuations of a statistical life, indicating a highly favorable benefit-cost ratio for this enforcement strategy.

Although broadband, coherent light sources carrying optical angular momentum hold significant promise for both classical and quantum communication, currently available options are scarce. This study investigates the generation of supercontinua within a ring configuration of coupled optical fibers. When short pulses possessing discrete angular momentum enter this system, they experience soliton fission, a process that spontaneously breaks azimuthal symmetry. Consequently, a pulse train is produced featuring a broadband frequency spectrum alongside a complex angular momentum distribution. These spatio-temporal solitary waves, confined to individual fiber cores, emit a unique type of resonant radiation. Remarkably, this radiation can occur even without intrinsic higher-order dispersion, driven instead by the lattice dispersion inherent to the ring array. Furthermore, we examine how inter-core coupling influences the resulting supercontinuum, demonstrating that a slight twist in the array can effectively modulate its angular momentum content and resonant frequencies via the induced Peierls phase.

In Machine Translation evaluation, pairwise comparisons are used to determine the superior system, requiring experimenters to allocate a budget for Direct Assessment (DA) judgments. We present a cost-effective method for utilizing this budget, yet demonstrate that standard budget sizes often fail to support robust comparisons. Viewing statistical significance as the foundation of a solid comparison, we analyzed the statistical power (the probability of achieving significance) across a large set of pairwise DA comparisons. Due to the inherent nature of statistical estimation, distinguishing differences smaller than 1–2 DA points yields low power, and achieving a meaningful increase in power necessitates at least 2–3 times more samples. Since variance reduction alone cannot deliver these improvements, we must accept the reality of undetectable differences and increased costs.
