In response, we propose interim testing—an "early stopping" data collection strategy that maximizes power per judgment by adaptively directing the budget toward pairs that are borderline significant. This approach can deliver up to a 27% efficiency improvement when spending triple the current budget, or achieve 18% cost savings while maintaining the existing evaluation power.

This letter explores causality within string field theory by employing pp-wave light-cone gauge string field theory. We extend the Ramsey scheme to the context of string field theory to analyze relevant processes, constructing an explicit characteristic function for interactive string field theory based on this approach. Utilizing this characteristic function, we derive the average difference between the initial and final values of any operator in string field theory. Furthermore, we apply quantum information theoretic methods, specifically those rooted in quantum Fisher information, to extract insights regarding these string field theoretical processes.

Following the recent high-precision measurement of the Standard Model $W$ boson mass by the CDF II detector, we calculate the contributions to the oblique parameters $S$, $T$, and $U$ arising from two extra Higgs doublets (one inert and one hidden), hidden neutral dark gauge bosons, and additional heavy fermions within the gauged two-Higgs-doublet model (G2HDM). Although the impacts of the hidden Higgs doublet and new heavy fermions are negligible, a hidden gauge sector defined by $SU(2)_H \times U(1)_X$ with a coupling strength $\gtrsim 10^{-2}$ and a gauge boson mass $\gtrsim 100$ GeV can account for the $W$ boson mass anomaly; however, such a scenario is ruled out by dilepton high-mass resonance searches at the Large Hadron Collider. Conversely, updated global fits incorporating the new $W$ boson mass measurement yield significant effects on the mass splitting and mixing angle of the inert Higgs doublet in G2HDM. Furthermore, we examine the implications for the diphoton signal strength of the 125 GeV Higgs boson ($h \to \gamma \gamma$) and the potential observability of the $h \to Z \gamma$ process at the High-Luminosity Large Hadron Collider. Our analysis also incorporates existing constraints on the dark matter candidate $W^\prime$, including limits from dark matter relic density, direct detection experiments, and invisible Higgs decays.

We demonstrate that each intermediate $\beta$-transformation is topologically conjugate to a greedy $\beta$-transformation featuring a hole at zero, while also presenting a counterexample showing this correspondence is not bijective. Leveraging this characterization, we (1) establish a Krieger embedding theorem for intermediate $\beta$-transformations, thereby complementing the findings of Li, Sahlsten, Samuel, and Steiner [2019], and (2) derive novel metric and topological insights into survivor sets of intermediate $\beta$-transformations with a hole at zero, building upon the work of Kalle, Kong, Langeveld, and Li [2020]. Additionally, we develop a technique to compute the Hausdorff dimension of these survivor sets and investigate specific bifurcation sets. Furthermore, by considering unions of survivor sets from intermediate $\beta$-transformations, we identify a significant class of sets within metric number theory: sets of badly approximable numbers in non-integer bases. Assuming the underlying symbolic space is of finite type, we prove that these sets of badly approximable numbers are winning in Schmidt games and possess the countable intersection property, thus extending the results of Hu and Yu [2014], Tseng [2009], and Färm, Persson, and Schmeling [2010].

Numerous numerical investigations have demonstrated that geminal-based approaches offer a promising avenue for modeling strongly correlated systems with minimal computational expense. To address missing dynamical correlation effects, various strategies have been developed, often utilizing \textit{a posteriori} corrections to handle correlation arising from broken-pair or inter-geminal states. This study evaluates the accuracy of the pair coupled cluster doubles (pCCD) method augmented by configuration interaction (CI) theory. We benchmark multiple CI models, including those limited to double excitations, against selected coupled cluster (CC) corrections and standard single-reference CC methods, while also testing a simple Davidson correction. The performance of these pCCD-CI schemes is assessed on difficult small systems, specifically the \ce{N2} and \ce{F2} dimers, as well as various di- and triatomic actinide compounds. Overall, the proposed CI methods significantly enhance spectroscopic constants relative to the conventional CCSD approach, particularly when a Davidson correction is incorporated. However, their accuracy falls between that of the linearized frozen pCCD and the frozen pCCD variants.

The youngest known Galactic supernova remnant, G1.9+0.3, likely originating from a Type Ia event, exhibits unexpected irregularities in the spatial and velocity distribution of its ejecta. Notably, high-velocity shocked iron appears in multiple distant locations, sometimes extending beyond prominent silicon and sulfur emissions, strongly indicating a highly asymmetric explosion. This study presents high-resolution hydrodynamic simulations in two and three dimensions, modeling the evolution of two asymmetric Type Ia models from 100 seconds to several hundred years within a uniform medium. At the estimated age of G1.9+0.3 (approximately 100 years), our 2D simulations reveal almost no iron shocked to the point of X-ray visibility; significant iron shock only occurs in much higher-density environments where the expansion speed contradicts observations. Conversely, our 3D model, utilizing the most asymmetric Type Ia model from Seitenzahl et al. (2013), displays features resembling G1.9+0.3. We analyze this model's evolution through images of three compositional classes: carbon and oxygen, intermediate-mass elements, and iron-group elements. Between 13 and 1800 years, we track how the initially highly asymmetric remnant evolves as explosion-driven asymmetries diminish, replaced by those caused by hydrodynamic instabilities. Around the 100-year mark, the 3D model shows comparable shocked masses for C+O, IMEs, and IGEs, each approximately 0.03 solar masses. The rapid nature of these evolutionary changes suggests that continued monitoring with the Chandra X-ray Observatory could reveal significant variations.

Surface acoustic waves (SAW) can gather micro-particles into droplets within seconds, yet the underlying mechanism remains unclear, with current theories falling short by several orders of magnitude. This study investigates how fluid viscosity and particle size influence SAW-driven collective dynamics in droplets. Contrary to expectations of aggregation, our experiments typically show particles avoiding the droplet center to form "black holes." We demonstrate that these black holes result from steric hindrance: poloidal streamlines intended to drive particles toward the center approach the solid wall too closely, causing particles to contact the wall at the black hole's edge before reaching the center. The size of these black holes correlates with the size of aggregates found in less viscous droplets, suggesting a shared formation mechanism. In the case of black holes, particles touching the solid are washed away by the flow, whereas in aggregate formation (white dwarfs), particles remain in contact with the solid, roll to the center, and accumulate. Additionally, we examine the stability conditions of aggregates at the droplet's bottom and apply the concept of hydrodynamic shielding to concentrate 1 $\mu$m particles using 10 $\mu$m beads as shields.

RDF2vec is a knowledge graph embedding approach that generates random walks to extract sequences from the graph, which are then processed by the word2vec algorithm to derive vector representations for entities. This poster presents two novel walk extraction methods, termed e-walks and p-walks, which prioritize either the structural context or the neighborhood of an entity, respectively, enabling the creation of embeddings that emphasize similarity or relatedness. We evaluate a preliminary set of 12 RDF2vec variants by combining these walk strategies with both order-aware and classic approaches alongside CBOW and skip-gram word2vec models.

Classic research on causal emergence has demonstrated that certain Markovian dynamical systems exhibit significantly stronger causal links at higher-level descriptions compared to their lower-level counterparts, provided the system states are coarse-grained appropriately. However, detecting this emergent causality from data remains an unsolved challenge because identifying the correct coarse-graining strategy is difficult. This paper introduces a general machine learning framework, the Neural Information Squeezer, which automatically derives the effective coarse-graining strategy and macro-state dynamics to directly identify causal emergence from time series data. By breaking down coarse-graining into information conversion and information dropout, the framework allows for precise control over the width of the information channel and enables the analytical derivation of key properties, including the exact formula for macro-dynamics effective information. Furthermore, we demonstrate how this approach extracts dynamics across various levels and identifies causal emergence in several example systems.

The identification of topological superconductivity in doped Bi$_2$Se$_3$ has rendered this material class pivotal for condensed matter physics, yet the structural basis of its superconducting state has remained obscure despite extensive recent investigation. By employing scanning tunneling microscopy and normal incidence x-ray standing wave (NIXSW) techniques, we have determined the vertical location of dopants—a critical factor for elucidating topological superconductivity—in Sr$_{x}$Bi$_2$Se$_3$. Utilizing a novel methodology that incorporates the inelastic mean free path of photoemitted electrons into the analysis of NIXSW data, we successfully differentiate between symmetry-equivalent sites. Our findings indicate that Sr atoms do not reside within the van der Waals gap separating the Bi$_2$Se$_3$ quintuple layers; instead, they are located within the quintuple layer, positioned near the outer Se planes.

Qualitative causal relationships offer a concise representation of the direction, dependencies, temporal limits, and monotonicity rules governing discrete or continuous interactions. Whether in common or scholarly discourse, we describe interactions involving quantities (such as sleep reducing stress), discrete events or entities (like one protein inhibiting another's transcription), or intentional and functional elements (such as patients praying to alleviate pain). This paper introduces a transformer-based NLP framework that simultaneously identifies and extracts (1) variables or factors mentioned in text, (2) qualitative causal links between these variables, and (3) qualifiers and magnitudes that define these causal relationships. We validate this method and present encouraging outcomes from two applications: analyzing text from academic papers, news reports, and social media.

This study investigates monotonic statistical complexity measures—specifically those analogous to Rakhmanov's probability density for hypergeometric orthogonal polynomials (HOPs) in a continuous real variable—extending beyond the Cramér-Rao bound. Each measure quantifies two configurational aspects of spreading. The Fisher-Shannon and LMC (López-Ruiz-Mancini-Calvet) complexity metrics, both comprising two entropic components, are derived analytically as functions of the polynomial degree and the parameters of the orthogonality weight. Furthermore, the asymptotic behavior of these dual-spreading measures is analyzed for Laguerre and Gegenbauer HOP families where the weight parameter approaches infinity. This analysis relies on the asymptotics of Rényi and Shannon entropies, which are intrinsically linked to the $\mathfrak{L}_{q}$-norms of these polynomials. These asymptotic properties of the algebraic norms govern the radial and angular charge and momentum distributions in various multidimensional physical systems featuring spherically symmetric quantum-mechanical potentials, particularly in high-energy (Rydberg) and high-dimensional (quasi-classical) states. This connection arises because the wavefunctions for these states, defined in both position and momentum spaces, are represented using Laguerre and Gegenbauer polynomials.

Named Entity Recognition (NER) involves identifying and categorizing entity spans within a text, a task that becomes "nested NER" when these spans overlap. While span-based approaches are commonly employed to address nested NER, most existing methods generate an $n \times n$ scoring matrix (where $n$ represents sentence length) without accounting for the spatial relationships between spans. This paper introduces a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) to model these spatial relations within the score matrix. Despite its simplicity, our approach outperforms several recent methods using identical pre-trained encoders across three standard nested NER datasets. Additional analysis indicates that incorporating CNNs aids in identifying more nested entities. Furthermore, we observed that inconsistent sentence tokenization across studies for these datasets hampers direct comparison; therefore, we provide a pre-processing script to standardize evaluations in future research.

We demonstrate that for any finite set $A$ and any $\varepsilon>0$, there exists a $k=k(\varepsilon)$ such that the higher energy ${\mathsf{E}}_k(A)$ does not exceed $|A|^{k+\varepsilon}$, unless $A$ possesses a highly specific structure. As a consequence, we establish that every finite subset of the real numbers or the prime field must contain either an additive Sidon-type subset of cardinality $|A|^{1/2+c}$ or a multiplicative Sidon-type subset of cardinality $|A|^{1/2+c}$.

This study aims to evaluate the reliability of solutions derived from the linear ordering problem (LOP), which ranks $M$ objects based on pairwise comparisons. We employ a probabilistic framework, modeling comparison outcomes as Bernoulli variables with a shared parameter estimated from observed data. Since brute-force enumeration of this parameter incurs prohibitive $O(M!)$ complexity, we reformulate the task by introducing Slater's spectrum—a generalization of Slater's index—and develop an efficient algorithm to compute it, reducing the complexity to $O(M^2 2^M)$, which is feasible for moderate-sized LOPs. Additionally, a slight adjustment to this algorithm enables the identification of all LOP solutions. We present numerical results using both synthetic and real-world datasets, and the Python implementations of these algorithms are made publicly available.

State representation learning focuses on deriving concise representations from raw data within robotics and control domains. Current methods include auto-encoders, forward and inverse dynamics modeling, and leveraging generic priors regarding state properties. Despite the variety of applications and techniques, the field currently lacks standardized evaluation benchmarks, metrics, and tasks. This paper introduces a comprehensive suite of environments, data generators, robotic control scenarios, metrics, and tools designed to support iterative state representation learning and assessment in reinforcement learning contexts.

Observations of hot-Jupiter atmospheres reveal significant variability in both hot spot location and the amplitude of spectral features. Previous atmospheric flow simulations, utilizing standard forcing and initialization methods, typically yielded a single, stationary hot region situated eastward of the substellar point at a pressure level of approximately $3\!\times\! 10^{-3}$ MPa. In contrast, this study employs high-resolution (up to T682) pseudospectral simulations that successfully resolve small-scale eddies and waves intrinsic to hot-Jupiter atmospheres due to ageostrophic effects. These models demonstrate that the atmospheres host numerous intense storms across a broad spectrum of scales, ranging from planetary to smaller dimensions. These planetary-scale storms govern the large-scale spatial arrangement and temporal fluctuations of both hot and cold regions. Furthermore, these major storms display quasi-periodic life cycles within multiple equilibrium states, all of which are detectable in the disk-integrated temperature flux time series.

Parameterized Quantum Circuits (PQCs) hold significant promise for achieving quantum advantage on near-term hardware, yet their performance on real devices suffers severe degradation due to substantial quantum noise. For instance, in Quantum Neural Network (QNN) models applied to MNIST-4 classification on the IBMQ-Yorktown device, the accuracy gap between noise-free simulations and noisy results exceeds 60%. While existing noise mitigation strategies are general and fail to exploit PQC-specific traits, current PQC research often overlooks noise effects entirely. To address this, we introduce QuantumNAT, a framework designed for PQC-specific noise-aware optimization during both training and inference to enhance robustness. Our experiments reveal that the impact of quantum noise on PQC measurement outcomes can be modeled as a linear map involving scaling and shifting relative to noise-free results. Leveraging this insight, we propose post-measurement normalization to align feature distributions between noisy and noise-free scenarios. Additionally, we enhance robustness by injecting noise into the training process through the insertion of quantum error gates based on realistic hardware noise models. Finally, we implement post-measurement quantization to convert outcomes into discrete values, effectively denoising the data. Extensive testing across eight classification tasks on six quantum devices shows that QuantumNAT boosts accuracy by up to 43%, achieving 94% accuracy for 2-class, 80% for 4-class, and 34% for 10-class problems on real quantum computers. The code for constructing and training PQCs with noise awareness is accessible via the TorchQuantum library.

We examine energy distribution and quantum thermodynamics in periodically driven polaritonic systems within their stationary state at room temperature. Specifically, we analyze a strongly coupled exciton interacting with a harmonic oscillator, quantifying energy reorganization and interaction effects as functions of coupling strength, driving force, and detuning. By deriving a quantum master equation for the polariton density matrix under weak environmental interactions, we calculate the dissipative time propagator and the long-term evolution of arbitrary initial states. This methodology offers direct access to the stationary state, bypassing numerical challenges associated with weakly damped quantum systems near resonance, while also generating polariton lineshape maps. Subsequently, we evaluate thermodynamic performance during harmonic modulation, showing that peak efficiency arises at resonance. Furthermore, we present an expression for the irreversible heat rate based on the polariton's effective temperature—defined as the proportionality factor between heat and von Neumann entropy rates—and numerically confirm that this aligns with thermodynamic laws.

The Hausa language, part of the Afroasiatic phylum, is the most widely spoken native language in sub-Saharan Africa, with over 100 million speakers primarily located in Nigeria and Niger. Although it is one of the most spoken Chadic languages and is well-documented linguistically, it is currently classified as a low-resource language in the field of natural language processing (NLP) due to a scarcity of available data. This scarcity is a common challenge across many African languages, making it essential to develop richer resources to accelerate downstream NLP tasks and meet modern societal needs. While existing datasets from news outlets and religious texts offer some utility, they lack sufficient diversity. To address this, we present an extensive collection of curated Hausa datasets encompassing both formal and informal registers sourced from reputable websites and social media platforms. This corpus represents the largest and most diverse set of Hausa social media data to date, capturing unique linguistic features. Additionally, the collection includes a parallel dataset suitable for machine translation and the detection of harmful or inciting online content. The paper outlines the data curation process, including collection and preprocessing methods, and suggests potential research problems that can be tackled using these resources.

This work offers a straightforward, physically based derivation of the conservation equation governing gravitational radiation propagation. The approach is exact and yields a result that mirrors the intuitive structure of a Poynting equation, linking the outward flux of stress-energy to the volumetric radiation reaction force exerted back on the sources, including their purely gravitational components. When averaged, the resulting gravitational radiation pseudotensor matches precisely with those obtained through significantly more complex methods.

Precise calculation of fluid-fluid interface curvature is vital for the effectiveness of Volume of Fluid (VOF) techniques in flows dominated by surface tension. This research utilizes artificial neural networks featuring a deep multilayer perceptron (MLP) structure to derive interfacial curvature from volume fraction data on regular grids. By applying input normalization, odd-symmetric activation functions, and bias-free neurons, we developed an economical MLP model that maintains the inherent symmetries of curvature fields. Integrated into the OpenFOAM flow solver, this symmetry-preserving MLP was evaluated against established methods. The results demonstrate that the symmetry-preserving model outperforms standard MLPs and matches the accuracy and convergence of leading conventional approaches, even while utilizing a smaller stencil.

This study generalizes the Four Color Theorem by defining $H(d,k)$ as the collection of all $k$-uniform hypergraphs that admit a linear embedding into $\mathbb{R}^d$. The paper examines both lower and upper bounds for the maximum weak and strong chromatic numbers within these hypergraphs. Specifically, it is demonstrated that for dimensions $d>2$, there exist hypergraphs in $H(2d-3,d)$ with $n$ vertices exhibiting a weak chromatic number of $\Omega(\log n / \log \log n)$. In contrast, the weak chromatic number for $n$-vertex hypergraphs in $H(d,d)$ is bounded above by $O(n^{(d-2)/(d-1)})$ when $d>2$.

This note introduces efficient, deterministic methods for dimensionality reduction tailored to a specific class of subspace approximation tasks. Given a set $P$ of $M$ points in $\mathbbm{R}^N$, these techniques identify an $O(n \log M)$-dimensional subspace that is guaranteed to encompass a near-optimal $n$-dimensional hyperplane $\mathcal{H}$ for $P$. The optimality is measured by the cumulative projection error $(\sum_{{\bf x} \in P} \| {\bf x} - \Pi_\mathcal{H} {\bf x} \|^p_2)^{1/p}$, valid for any $p > 2$. The deterministic approach executes in $\tilde{O}(MN^2)$ time; alternatively, a randomized variant achieves $\tilde{O}(MNn)$ time while preserving error guarantees with high probability. Specifically for $p = \infty$, these methods integrate with algorithms for computing the John ellipsoid to yield an $n$-dimensional subspace that minimizes the maximum $\ell_2$-distance from any point in the convex hull of $P$ to the subspace, maintaining an $\tilde{O}(MNn)$ runtime. Furthermore, the proposed dimensionality reduction techniques can be integrated with other existing subspace approximation algorithms for $2 < p \leq \infty$, such as those relying on convex programming relaxations for higher accuracy, to accelerate their execution times.

Most machine learning systems apply a uniform model to both simple and complex tasks, unlike humans who utilize the dual-process theory of mind by switching between fast (instinctive) and slow (analytical) thinking based on problem difficulty. We introduce FLOWGEN, a graph-generation model inspired by this cognitive framework that builds large graphs incrementally. At each step, the system routes generation to either a fast (weaker) or a slow (stronger) model depending on the current difficulty. Although these modules share identical architectures, they differ in parameter count and generative capability. Experiments on real-world graphs demonstrate that FLOWGEN can produce graphs comparable to those from a single large model while achieving up to 2x speedup.

High costs and time requirements for data labeling and model training act as significant bottlenecks when training deep neural networks on extensive datasets. Strategies such as active learning, which focus on selecting smaller, representative data samples, offer a solution to these challenges. While previous research in NLP active learning has highlighted sampling biases inherent in uncertainty-based querying and proposed expensive fixes, our large-scale empirical study reveals that active set selection based on the posterior entropy of deep models like FastText.zip (FTZ) is resilient to such biases and less sensitive to algorithmic variations in query size and strategy compared to traditional findings. Furthermore, FTZ-based queries generate sample sets comparable to those produced by more complex methods, such as ensemble networks. We validate the efficacy of these selected samples by constructing small, high-quality datasets that enable the rapid and cost-effective training of large models. Consequently, we introduce a straightforward baseline for deep active text classification that surpasses current state-of-the-art performance. This work aims to provide valuable insights for dataset compression and active, semi-supervised, or online learning scenarios. The associated code and models can be accessed at: https://github.com/drimpossible/Sampling-Bias-Active-Learning

This paper examines how dependence influences the detection of a specific class of structured signals within Ferromagnetic Ising models. Prominent instances of this class encompass Ising Models defined on lattices, as well as Mean-Field variants such as dense Erd\H{o}s-R\'{e}nyi and dense random regular graphs. Our findings establish sharp detection thresholds for each scenario, precisely delineating the connection between the detection problem and the underlying dependence structure, while also illustrating methods to remain agnostic regarding the intensity of dependence across these models.

Driven by the growing interest in the Lie algebraic and geometric structures emerging from tensor products of division algebras and their significance in high-energy theoretical physics, this work examines generalized bioctonionic projective and hyperbolic planes. Following a Veronese representation of the complexified Cayley plane $\mathbb{O}P_{\mathbb{C}}^{2}$, we introduce a new, explicit construction of the bioctonionic Cayley-Rosenfeld plane $\left( \mathbb{C}\otimes \mathbb{O}\right) P^{2}$, also utilizing Veronese coordinates. We explore the isometry groups of these generalized bioctonionic planes, recovering all complex and real forms of the exceptional groups $F_{4}$ and $E_{6}$, while characterizing the planes as symmetric and Hermitian symmetric spaces. The paper concludes with a discussion of potential physical applications.

KETEK-manufactured prototype SiPMs featuring 4384 pixels of $15 \times 15~\mu $m$^2$ were subjected to reactor neutron irradiation across eight fluence levels ranging from $10^9$ to $5\times 10^{14}$ cm$^{-2}$. Subsequent measurements—including capacitance-voltage, admittance-frequency, forward and reverse current-voltage, and charge-voltage tests, conducted both with and under sub-nanosecond laser illumination—were carried out over a temperature span of $-30~^\circ $C to $+30~^\circ $C. Various analytical methods were employed to determine how electrical parameters, breakdown voltage, activation energy for current generation, dark-count rate, and light-pulse response depend on neutron fluence and temperature. Finally, the outcomes derived from these distinct analysis approaches were compared.

This article introduces GSEIM, a novel simulation package designed to solve systems of ordinary differential equations. The program's structure is visualized through a block diagram, and its various functionalities are examined. Two methods for integrating new components into GSEIM—specifically as templates or subcircuits—are detailed using a concrete example. Finally, simulation cases are presented to demonstrate the package's capabilities.

Using a variational approach within the non-relativistic quark model, we analyze the spectrum and decay rates of low-lying charmonium states. This investigation combines a Coulomb-like potential from perturbative one-gluon exchange, a linear confining potential, and a potential derived from the instanton vacuum to address hyperfine mass splitting. We calculate radiative (E1, M1), two-photon, leptonic, and two-gluon decay rates for these states, achieving overall consistency between our predicted masses and decay widths and experimental observations.

Handling missing data and incomplete time series is a tedious, unavoidable, and labor-intensive challenge when working with real-world data. Effective spatio-temporal representations could enable imputation techniques to fill gaps in temporal data by leveraging information from sensors across various locations. However, conventional methods fail to capture the nonlinear temporal and spatial dependencies inherent in networks of interconnected sensors and do not fully utilize the often robust relational information available. Specifically, most current deep learning-based imputation approaches do not explicitly model relational aspects and lack processing frameworks capable of adequately representing structured spatio-temporal data. In contrast, graph neural networks (GNNs) have recently gained popularity as expressive and scalable tools for processing sequential data with relational inductive biases. This work presents the first evaluation of GNNs for multivariate time series imputation. We introduce GRIN, a novel GNN architecture designed to reconstruct missing data across different channels of a multivariate time series by learning spatio-temporal representations through message passing. Empirical results demonstrate that our model surpasses state-of-the-art methods on relevant real-world benchmarks, achieving mean absolute error improvements frequently exceeding 20%.

Wavelet Monte Carlo simulations investigate the movement of passive particles within microswimmer environments, incorporating both typically neglected thermal fluctuations and the hydrodynamic flows produced by the swimmers. Despite utilizing high Péclet numbers, our findings indicate that thermal motion significantly influences particle dynamics; it can be modeled as a decorrelation factor in velocity autocorrelation functions, where the decay time scales with the Péclet number. Comparable decorrelation effects arise from swimmer rotational behaviors, such as run-and-tumble motion, impacting both entrainment and far-field loop contributions. Consequently, for small tracer-like particles at Péclet numbers relevant to *E. coli* at room temperature, active diffusivity exhibits a weak apparent power law scaling close to $Pe^{0.2}$. Conversely, large particles display a diminished hydrodynamic response to nearby forces, resulting in a corresponding decrease in active diffusivity. The interplay of these factors produces a non-monotonic relationship between active diffusivity and particle size, offering insights into experimental observations reported by Patteson et al.

Research into model checking procedural programs has significantly advanced the development of temporal logics designed for context-free structures. Prominent examples include logics for Nested Words, such as CaRet and NWTL. More recently, the logic OPTL was proposed, built upon the more expressive class of Operator Precedence Languages (OPL). We introduce a new OPL-based logic called POTL, demonstrate its first-order (FO) completeness, and outline a corresponding model checking algorithm. POTL enhances NWTL by allowing the specification of requirements involving pre/post-conditions and stack inspection, even when exception-like constructs are present. Furthermore, POTL surpasses OPTL by achieving FO-completeness and offering more straightforward expression of stack inspection and function-local properties.

Nonlinearity operating at the mean-field level can generate self-intersecting energy band structures in momentum space, giving rise to nonlinear Dirac cones as a notable outcome. This paper employs the Qi-Wu-Zhang model augmented with power-law nonlinearity to systematically investigate the Aharonov-Bohm phase resulting from an adiabatic process in momentum space, specifically examining two paths that encircle a single nonlinear Dirac cone. Remarkably, the Aharonov-Bohm phase exhibits a $\pi$-jump exclusively at the critical nonlinearity where the Dirac cone emerges or vanishes when the interaction follows a Kerr nonlinearity; for all other nonlinearity powers, the phase varies continuously with the strength of the nonlinearity. These findings could facilitate the experimental characterization of power-law nonlinearities and encourage further fundamental research into geometric phases and adiabatic following within nonlinear systems.

Geostationary satellites provide a distinct advantage for analyzing the diurnal cycle of the Earth's Radiation Budget at the top of the atmosphere (TOA), a critical component for climate research. However, the continuous temporal coverage of geostationary orbits is limited by a fixed viewing geometry. Consequently, inaccuracies in the angular distribution models (ADMs) utilized during radiance-to-flux conversions, or residual errors in converting narrowband to broadband data dependent on viewing angles, can introduce systematic biases in estimated radiative fluxes. This study examines clear-sky reflected TOA observations by comparing overlapping views from Meteosat Second Generation satellites positioned at 0° and 41.5°E longitude, allowing for the quantification of viewing-angle-dependent variations. Utilizing SEVIRI data, we identify primary sources of discrepancies and demonstrate that these can be substantially reduced to the level of one month. For each satellite, this is accomplished through a masking procedure followed by a pixel-level empirical fit incorporating all clear-sky data for every daily timeslot throughout November 2016. When applied to each month of 2017, the method yields a quadratic mean albedo root-mean squared difference across the dual-view region that remains consistent month-to-month, with an average 2017 value of 0.01. Identified sources of error include the challenge of estimating flux near the limb over sunglint oceans, the absence of specific angular distribution models for aerosols over oceans in the data processing, and an observer-dependent diurnal asymmetry artifact influencing clear-sky albedo dependence on solar zenith angle, particularly over land.

Bi-stochastic normalization of kernelized graph affinity matrices offers an efficient alternative normalization strategy for graph Laplacian methods in data analysis, computable via Sinkhorn-Knopp (SK) iterations. This study establishes the convergence of the bi-stochastically normalized graph Laplacian to the manifold (weighted-)Laplacian, including convergence rates, when $n$ data points are independently and identically distributed (i.i.d.) samples from a general $d$-dimensional manifold embedded in a potentially high-dimensional space. Under the joint limit where $n \to \infty$ and kernel bandwidth $\epsilon \to 0$, the paper proves that the point-wise convergence rate of the graph Laplacian operator (in the 2-norm) is $ O(n^{-1/(d/2+3)})$ for large finite $n$, up to logarithmic factors, achieved with the scaling $\epsilon \sim n^{-1/(d/2+3)}$. Furthermore, when manifold data are contaminated by outlier noise, theoretical analysis demonstrates point-wise consistency of the graph Laplacian matching the rate for clean data, modulo an additional error term proportional to the boundedness of the mutual inner-products of the noise vectors. The analysis indicates that, within this framework, approximate bi-stochastic normalization yields the same consistency rate as the exact version. Inspired by these findings, we introduce an approximate, constrained matrix scaling problem solvable by SK iterations with early stopping, applied to simulated clean and noisy manifold data. Numerical experiments validate our theoretical claims and confirm the robustness of the bi-stochastically normalized graph Laplacian against outlier noise.

This study investigates near-field image transmission and error vector magnitude (EVM) measurements within a metal enclosure characterized by a rich scattering environment. We analyze how loading the enclosure impacts the performance of software-defined radio (SDR)-based near-field communication links. By examining critical receiver parameters, we assess the link's behavior under conditions of rich scattering and when the enclosure is loaded with RF absorber cones. Performance evaluation involved transmitting wideband OFDM-modulated packets carrying image data. Our results indicate that loading the metal enclosure with RF absorbers enhances the performance of wideband OFDM-based near-field communication, specifically improving the near-field EVM. Furthermore, loading the enclosure increases the coherence bandwidth; conversely, an empty enclosure exhibits frequency selectivity, implying a coherence bandwidth narrower than the signal bandwidth.

Training Reinforcement Learning (RL) agents for high-stakes applications is often too costly due to the dangers inherent in exploration, forcing agents to rely exclusively on data gathered by safe policies in the past. Although prior research has focused on optimizing average performance using offline data, we concentrate on optimizing a risk-averse metric, specifically Conditional Value at Risk (CVaR). We introduce the Offline Risk-Averse Actor-Critic (O-RAAC), a model-free RL algorithm capable of learning risk-averse policies entirely within an offline framework. Our results demonstrate that O-RAAC achieves higher CVaR than risk-neutral methods across various robot control tasks. Moreover, adopting risk-averse criteria ensures the distributional robustness of average performance against specific distribution shifts. Empirically, we show that when natural distribution shifts occur, O-RAAC successfully learns policies that maintain strong average performance.

Bers and Finn established a renowned theorem asserting that isolated singularities in solutions to the non-parametric minimal surface equation are removable. This paper demonstrates that the theorem holds true even when the area functional is substituted with a general linear growth functional dependent on the gradient's modulus. It is important to note that Serrin ([1]) had previously proven singularity removability on sets with $(n-1)$-dimensional Hausdorff measure zero within an even broader framework. Our primary objective is to extend comparison principles, such as those detailed in Section 10 of [2], beyond the specific geometric constraints of minimal surfaces. In doing so, we find that generalized catenoids provide a suitable instrument for establishing our findings.

This paper investigates the 't Hooft expansion of $d=4$ $\mathcal{N}=4$ supersymmetric Yang-Mills (SYM) theory with gauge groups $SO(N)$ or $Sp(N)$. Specifically, we analyze the $1/N_5$ expansion under the condition of fixed $g_sN_5$, where $g_s$ represents the string coupling in bulk type IIB string theory defined on $AdS_5\times\mathbb{RP}^5$, and $N_5$ corresponds to the RR 5-form flux through $\mathbb{RP}^5$. Notably, $N_5$ deviates from $N$ due to a shift arising from the RR charge of the O3-plane. As a case study, we examine the $1/N_5$ expansion of the free energy for $\mathcal{N}=4$ SYM on $S^4$ and $1/2$ BPS circular Wilson loops in the fundamental representation of $SO(N)$ or $Sp(N)$. Our results indicate that the $1/N_5$ expansion exhibits behavior more akin to a "closed string" expansion compared to the standard $1/N$ expansion.

Sparse computations are prevalent in scientific simulations, where performance critically depends on optimizing sparse code. However, irregular computation patterns and compact data structures in sparse matrix operations pose significant challenges to vectorization. Existing methods primarily target regular regions within the code or incur costs to reorganize data and computations to create more regular areas. This paper introduces a novel polyhedral model known as partially strided codelets (PSC), which facilitates vectorization of regions with irregular data access while enhancing data locality in sparse computations. Our DDF inspector-executor framework efficiently identifies PSC codelets by mining memory accesses using an access function differentiation technique. This framework generates vectorized code for the sparse matrix multiplication kernel (SpMV), which features parallel outer loops, and for kernels with carried dependencies, such as the sparse triangular solver (SpTRSV). We evaluated the performance of DDF-generated code on 60 large and small matrices containing between 0.05M and 130M nonzeros. Results show that DDF outperforms the highly specialized MKL library with average speedups of 1.93x for SpMV and 4.5x for SpTRSV. Furthermore, on the same dataset, DDF surpasses the state-of-the-art inspector-executor framework Sympiler by up to 11x for SpTRSV and the work by Augustine et al. by up to 12x for SpMV.

This study investigates the electronic, magnetic, and optical characteristics of the double perovskite Sr$_2$CoIrO$_6$ (SCIO) subjected to biaxial strain using density functional theory (DFT) that incorporates a Hubbard $U$ term and spin-orbit coupling (SOC), alongside absorption spectroscopy data from epitaxial thin films. Although SrIrO$_3$ acts as a semimetal with suppressed spin and orbital moments, and bulk SrCoO$_3$ behaves as a ferromagnetic metal with spin and orbital moments of 2.50 and 0.13 $\mu_{B}$ respectively, the SCIO double perovskite manifests as an antiferromagnetic Mott insulator. In SCIO, Co and Ir planes align antiparallel along the [110] direction; Co displays a spin moment of approximately 2.35–2.45 $\mu_{B}$ and an enhanced orbital moment of 0.31–0.45 $\mu_{B}$, while Ir surprisingly develops significant spin and orbital moments of 1.21–1.25 $\mu_{B}$ and 0.13 $\mu_{B}$. Orbital occupation analysis reveals an electronic reconstruction driven by substantial charge transfer from minority to majority spin states in Ir and from Ir to Co, indicating an Ir$^{4+\delta}$, Co$^{4-\delta}$ configuration. Applying biaxial strain ranging from -1.02% (on NdGaO$_3$) to 0% (on SrTiO$_3$) and 1.53% (on GdScO$_3$) notably affects the orbital polarization of $t_{2g}$ states, resulting in a non-monotonic variation of the band gap between 163 and 235 meV. The absorption spectrum exhibits a two-plateau feature arising from transitions from the valence band to the lower, narrow $t_{2g}$ and higher, broader $e_{g}$ bands. Furthermore, accounting for many-body effects, specifically excitonic interactions via the Bethe-Salpeter equation (BSE), widens the calculated band gap by approximately 0.2 eV and better aligns the theoretical results with experimental spectra, particularly regarding the second peak's position at roughly 2.6 eV.

Time crystals represent a genuine non-equilibrium quantum phase characterized by the breaking of time-translational symmetry. While experimental realizations have successfully achieved time crystals in non-equilibrium closed systems, it remains an open question whether such phases persist when systems interact with an environment. Although coupling to a bath can stabilize time crystals through dissipation in certain regimes, incoherent noise may alternatively destroy the crystalline order. Consequently, the stabilization mechanisms for time crystals in open versus closed systems are not necessarily identical. In this work, we propose a method to identify open system time crystals using a single metric: the Floquet propagator. Utilizing this framework, we demonstrate time-crystalline behavior in an explicitly short-range interacting open system and highlight the critical influence of decay process characteristics.

The standard model's Higgs sector can be augmented by adding an $SU(2)_L$ Higgs triplet, $\Delta$, to facilitate the generation of minimal neutrino masses through the type-II seesaw mechanism. This paper investigates the pair production of this triplet at future $e^{-}p$ colliders. We predict the production cross sections for this process via vector boson fusion at the FCC-ep and ILC$\otimes$FCC, noting that the production of a pair of doubly charged Higgs bosons is the dominant channel. This dominance allows us to examine the collider phenomenology of the triplet. The decay modes of the doubly charged Higgs depend on the magnitude of the triplet's vacuum expectation value, resulting in either pairs of same-sign charged leptons or pairs of same-sign $W$ bosons. To assess the discovery potential of the doubly charged Higgs at these future $e^{-}p$ colliders, we analyze both decay scenarios in detail and present the respective detection sensitivities for the mass of the doubly charged Higgs.

This paper presents an exploratory study of plagiarism patterns within mathematical literature, based on an analysis of editorial notes from zbMATH. Although the majority of instances examined involved straightforward copying of prior work, we also uncovered various forms of disguised plagiarism. We conducted a detailed investigation of 11 specific cases to assess the effectiveness of existing plagiarism detection systems in identifying such occurrences. Additionally, we outline the procedural steps necessary for uncovering these cases and those that may remain undetected in the future.

Measuring the mixing-induced CP-violating phase phi_s in Bs decays is crucial for investigating new physics. This study selects 7421 +/- 105 signal events from the predominantly CP-odd final state J/\psi pi+ pi- within 1/fb of proton-proton collision data recorded at sqrt{s} = 7 TeV using the LHCb detector. A time-dependent analysis of the data produces a phi_s value of -0.019^{+0.173+0.004}_{-0.174-0.003} rad, which aligns with Standard Model predictions, and no indication of direct CP violation is observed.

This paper investigates a hyperbolic variant of the Navier-Stokes equations, derived through the relaxation approximation of the Euler system within a thin strip domain. Our primary objective is to establish the existence and uniqueness of global solutions for these equations, given analytic initial data in the tangential variable and subject to a uniform smallness condition. Furthermore, we validate the transition from the anisotropic hyperbolic Navier-Stokes system to the hydrodynamic hyperbolic Navier-Stokes system under the assumption of small analytic data.

Multilingual users frequently alternate between languages on social media, often adopting a shared script for convenience even when native scripts exist. This practice results in code-mixed content that adheres to diverse grammatical rules within a single script, presenting significant challenges for natural language processing, particularly in sentiment analysis. This study presents experimental results from a dataset of movie reviews featuring code-mixing between English and Bengali, both written in Roman script. We evaluated several machine learning algorithms trained exclusively on English features, with the Naive Bayes model achieving the highest accuracy of 59.00%. Additionally, models trained on both code-mixed data and English features were assessed, yielding a peak accuracy of 72.50% using a Support Vector Machine (SVM). The analysis concludes with an examination of misclassified examples and a discussion of the hurdles required to improve future accuracy.

Foraminifera are single-celled marine organisms that create shells which persist as fossils within marine sediments. These fossils are crucial for paleo-oceanographic and climatological studies. Nevertheless, identifying and counting them has remained a manual, labor-intensive, and time-consuming process since the 19th century. This study introduces a deep learning-based instance segmentation model designed to classify, detect, and segment microscopic foraminifera. Built upon the Mask R-CNN architecture, the model utilizes weights pre-trained on the COCO detection dataset. We employed a fine-tuning strategy to adapt these parameters to a new dataset comprising over 7,000 images of microscopic foraminifera and sediment grains. The model achieved a COCO-style average precision of $0.78 \pm 0.00$ for classification and detection, and $0.80 \pm 0.00$ for segmentation. When excluding challenging images containing sediment grains, performance improved to $0.84 \pm 0.00$ for detection/classification and $0.86 \pm 0.00$ for segmentation. We provide both quantitative and qualitative analyses of the prediction results. Based on these findings, we suggest future research directions and conclude that this model represents a significant step toward automating the identification and counting of microscopic foraminifera.

This research investigates an iterative method for solving coupled algebraic Riccati equations within the context of general two-player closed-loop Nash differential games over an infinite horizon. Furthermore, we introduce a practical algorithm designed to identify positive definite solutions. Specifically, the study includes multiple numerical examples related to matrix Riccati equations across various dimensions.

We examine the formation of topological valley Hall and kink states within a two-dimensional topolectrical (TE) framework, driven by the breaking of chiral and reflection symmetries. This TE architecture comprises two distinct segments, each supporting unique topological states characterized by opposite valley Hall indices, which are joined by a heterojunction. In actual circuit implementations, the valley Hall index across these segments can be inverted by adjusting the onsite potentials at sublattice nodes. The introduction of resistive coupling, which renders the system non-Hermitian, results in both gapped and gapless valley and kink states appearing in the admittance spectra. These topological modes are identifiable through electrical impedance measurements that correspond to the admittance spectra. Furthermore, we validate the stability of these valley Hall and kink states using realistic LTspice simulations that account for component tolerances and parasitic effects. Our findings highlight the utility of TE circuit networks as a viable platform for implementing and controlling valley-dependent and kink topological phenomena.

Diam-mean equicontinuity serves as a valuable dynamical concept in investigating non-periodic order. By employing a specific "local" skew product involving a shift and an odometer within a cellular automaton (CA), we demonstrate the existence of a CA that is almost diam-mean equicontinuous yet fails to be almost equicontinuous (and consequently, not almost locally periodic). As an application, we establish that Kurka's dichotomy does not apply to diam-mean analogues of sensitivity and equicontinuity.

This paper examines the approximation of optimal control problems for the Navier-Stokes equation using Dynamic Programming. These problems, prevalent in various industrial applications, pose significant numerical challenges because their semi-discretized dynamics result in high-dimensional systems of ordinary differential equations. Conventional methods typically rely on the Pontryagin maximum principle, which formulates the solution as a two-point boundary value problem. In contrast, we propose an alternative strategy centered on the value function and the resolution of a Bellman equation, a task notably difficult in high dimensions. To address the curse of dimensionality, we employ a recent multilinear approximation of the dynamics integrated with a dynamic programming algorithm structured on a tree. Furthermore, we address key implementation details of this novel approach and provide numerical examples to demonstrate its efficacy on standard control problems found in existing literature.

The phase space for a gyrostat with a fixed point and a heavy top corresponds to the Lie-Poisson space $\textbf{e}(3)^*\cong \mathbb{R}^3\times \mathbb{R}^3$, which is the dual of the Lie algebra $\textbf{e}(3)$ associated with the Euclidean group $E(3)$. Within this space, three distinct Poisson submanifolds are identified: (i) a dense open submanifold $\mathbb{R}^3\times \dot{\mathbb{R}}^3$ containing all $4$-dimensional symplectic leaves (where $\vec{\Gamma}^2>0$); (ii) a $5$-dimensional Poisson submanifold within $\mathbb{R}^3\times \dot{\mathbb{R}}^3$ defined by the condition $\vec{J}\cdot \vec{\Gamma} = \mu ||\vec{\Gamma}||$; and (iii) another $5$-dimensional Poisson submanifold in $\mathbb{R}^3\times \dot{\mathbb{R}}^3$ defined by $\vec{\Gamma}^2 = \nu^2$. Here, $\dot{\mathbb{R}}^3$ represents $\mathbb{R}^3$ excluding the origin, $(\vec{J}, \vec{\Gamma})$ are elements of $\mathbb{R}^3\times \mathbb{R}^3$, and $\nu < 0$ and $\mu$ are fixed real constants. Utilizing the $U(2,2)$-invariant symplectic structure of Penrose twistor space, we derive full and complete $E(3)$-equivariant symplectic realizations for these submanifolds, resulting in $8$-dimensional spaces for case (i) and $6$-dimensional spaces for cases (ii) and (iii). Consequently, the Hamiltonian systems on $\textbf{e}(3)^*$ lift to these symplectic realizations. This approach allows us to lift integrable cases of the fixed-point gyrostat and the heavy top, thereby generating a broad family of integrable Hamiltonian systems on the phase spaces defined by these realizations.

Deep neural network (DNN) based speech enhancement models have garnered significant interest due to their superior performance, yet their deployment in real-time scenarios is hindered by high computational costs. Conventional compression techniques like pruning and quantization fail to effectively exploit data-specific characteristics. This paper presents the integration of a Skip-RNN strategy into speech enhancement architectures featuring parallel RNNs. By allowing RNN states to update intermittently while maintaining continuous output mask updates, this approach substantially lowers computational demands without introducing noticeable audio artifacts. Furthermore, to maximize the distinction between voice and noise, we refine the skipping mechanism using voice activity detection (VAD) guidance, achieving even greater efficiency. Experimental results on the high-performance dual-path convolutional recurrent network (DPCRN) demonstrate that our method outperforms alternatives such as network pruning or training smaller models directly. Additionally, we confirm the strategy's generalizability by validating it across two other leading speech enhancement models.

This study fully characterizes the four scenarios in which the Hitchin fibration on a 2-dimensional moduli space of irregular Higgs bundles over $\mathbb{C}P^{1}$ possesses exactly one singular fiber. We provide a detailed examination of the case where the fiber at infinity is of type $I_0^*$, offering constructions for all potential configurations of singular curves within such elliptic fibrations.

A subset of vertices $S$ in a graph $G$ constitutes a geodesic transversal if it includes at least one vertex from every maximal geodesic within $G$. This study identifies the smallest such transversals for specific interconnection networks, including mesh of trees, and notable chemical architectures like silicate networks and carbon nanosheets. Additionally, several practical general bounds for this graph invariant are derived throughout the analysis.

Scalar field dark matter presents a compelling alternative to the conventional WIMP framework, where astrophysical and cosmological simulations play a crucial role in constraining the particle's mass, especially at low masses where its wave-like behavior becomes apparent on astrophysical scales. While these simulations typically rely on a classical field approximation, this study investigates the extension of such models to incorporate quantum corrections. We examine how significant corrections alter predictions and determine the timescales over which they become dominant. Specifically, these corrections tend to suppress density fluctuations and enhance the impact of "quantum pressure." During collapse, these effects grow exponentially, becoming significant within approximately 30 dynamical times. Consequently, the outcomes of classical field simulations may diverge from those including quantum corrections for systems characterized by short dynamical times.

This work investigates the maximum geometric independent set and clique problems within the streaming model. In this setting, geometric objects arrive sequentially in an insertion-only stream, and the objective is to identify a subset where every pair of objects is either disjoint or intersecting. We demonstrate that finding a maximum set of independent segments or 2-intervals requires a linear number of bits; no constant factor approximation algorithm exists without such memory usage. Notably, our lower-bound proof applies even to segments whose intersection graphs are interval graphs. This highlights a significant contrast with intervals, for which a 2-approximation for independent sets is achievable using only $O(\alpha(\mathcal{I})\log |\mathcal{I}|)$ bits, where $\alpha(\mathcal{I})$ denotes the size of the largest independent set. Conversely, we prove that no constant-factor approximation for the geometric clique problem is possible with sublinear memory, even when restricted to unit intervals. On the constructive side, we establish that the maximum geometric independent set of axis-aligned unit-height rectangles can be approximated within a factor of 4 using $O(\alpha(\mathcal{R})\log |\mathcal{R}|)$ bits.

Upcoming far-infrared space missions depend heavily on high-sensitivity spectroscopy as a key diagnostic method. However, these systems are vulnerable to straylight because of their use of ultra-sensitive few-mode detectors, a challenge highlighted by the Herschel mission that disrupts spectral measurement and calibration. To achieve the scientific objectives of future endeavors, it is essential to comprehend complex modal behavior and establish suitable verification and calibration protocols. This paper introduces a modal framework designed to address these challenges, utilizing Herschel-SPIRE as a case study, and illustrates how this technique can facilitate the design and verification of spectrometers for subsequent far-infrared missions.

We determined the parallax of the James Webb Space Telescope through nearly simultaneous observations conducted by the Lulin One-meter Telescope and the GROWTH India Telescope, which are positioned approximately 4,214 kilometers apart. This experiment effectively illustrates the concept of parallax typically introduced in basic astronomy curricula.

The primary approach to analyzing program complexity involves extracting and solving a recurrence relation that defines running time based on input size. We introduce a technique that automatically derives these recurrences from the syntax of higher-order recursive functional programs. The generated recurrences, formulated within a call-by-name language featuring recursion, explicitly calculate execution time as a function of input magnitude. To ensure a uniform method applicable to both call-by-name and call-by-value strategies, we employ Call-by-Push-Value (CBPV) as an intermediate language. Finally, we apply domain theory to construct a denotational cost semantics for the derived recurrences.

The asymptotic safe gravity framework is applied to examine the modified Newtonian dynamics (MOND) paradigm. We calculate the quantum corrections to the logarithmic potential, a feature recognized for maintaining the constant circular velocity $v$ observed in spiral galaxies, and subsequently establish reasonable limits for $v$.

This study introduces a framework for product quality inspection utilizing deep learning. Initially, we classify various deep learning models suitable for inspection systems and provide a comprehensive guide on constructing such systems. Subsequently, we examine connection schemes that efficiently integrate these models into the inspection infrastructure. Furthermore, we propose a robust method to maintain and improve the deep learning models, ensuring the system's stability and ease of maintenance. All proposed techniques are consolidated into a unified framework with detailed explanations for each component. To validate the system's effectiveness, we conducted comparative performance analyses across diverse test scenarios.

I introduce a web service designed to query entity embeddings within the Wikidata knowledge graph. This embedding is generated using Gensim's Word2Vec algorithm and a basic graph walk approach applied to a Wikidata dump. The service features a REST API that, when combined with the Wikidata API, provides access to a multilingual dataset covering over 600,000 Wikidata items and properties.

This study investigates the cooperative edge caching problem within fog radio access networks (F-RANs). To reduce content transmission latency, we formulate a cooperative caching optimization problem aimed at determining the globally optimal caching strategy. Acknowledging the non-deterministic polynomial hard (NP-hard) nature of this challenge, we propose a Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) framework for cooperative caching. This approach utilizes a Double Deep Q-Network (DDQN) at each fog access point (F-AP) and incorporates a communication mechanism within the multi-agent system. Specifically, every F-AP maintains a record of the historical caching strategies of its peer F-APs to serve as observations for the communication protocol. Through the exchange of these observations, the F-APs collaborate to achieve the globally optimal caching strategy. Simulation outcomes demonstrate that the proposed MARL-based scheme significantly outperforms benchmark methods in minimizing content transmission delay.

This research examines the physics of sheath formation within a collisional plasma featuring two electron temperatures and an oblique external magnetic field. Initially, a comparative analysis was conducted among the fluid, Boltzmann, and nonextensive electron models to determine an appropriate range for the nonextensive parameter $q$. The study subsequently focuses on a collisional two-temperature plasma where both hot and cold electron densities follow the non-extensive distribution, while cold ions are modeled using fluid equations. Sheath properties were analyzed across various collisional regimes by adjusting the non-extensive parameter $q$, as well as the ratios of hot-to-cold electron densities and temperatures. The magnetic field inclination angle was varied within the range of $1^\circ \leq \alpha \leq 5^\circ$. Findings indicate that the electron distribution deviates significantly from the Boltzmann distribution when the magnetic field is nearly parallel. Additionally, a notable discovery is that collisional flux deposition is enhanced in highly magnetized conditions. These results aim to improve the understanding of plasma-matter interaction processes involving multiple electron groups under near-parallel magnetic fields.

Text-to-Speech (TTS) systems generate speech from text using various methods, such as concatenative synthesis, Hidden Markov Model (HMM) approaches, or Deep Learning (DL) architectures with multiple components. This paper introduces an end-to-end Deep Learning-based Bangla speech synthesis system. The implementation utilizes only three primary modules—an Encoder, a Decoder, and a Post-processing network for waveform synthesis—with minimal human annotation. Notably, it operates without requiring a frontend preprocessor or a Grapheme-to-Phoneme (G2P) converter. Trained on 20 hours of phonetically balanced single-speaker audio, the model achieved a Mean Opinion Score (MOS) of 3.79 out of 5.0 in subjective testing and a Perceptual Evaluation of Speech Quality (PESQ) score of 0.77 (on a scale of -0.5 to 4.5) in objective testing. These results demonstrate that the system outperforms all existing non-commercial state-of-the-art Bangla TTS systems in terms of naturalness.

In magnetized plasmas operating at scales significantly larger than ion kinetic scales, a constant-magnitude magnetic field combined with parallel Alfvénic flows constitutes a nonlinear solution within an isobaric, constant-density environment. These structures, referred to as spherically polarized Alfvén waves, are commonly observed in the solar wind and are believed to originate from the amplification of small-amplitude fluctuations as they travel outward through the corona. This study introduces a computational approach to generate such solutions of arbitrary amplitude and general multi-dimensional complexity, alongside an exploration of their characteristics. The primary challenge involves calculating a zero-divergence, constant-magnitude magnetic field, which restricts the solution to a single quasi-free function while imposing stringent constraints on individual field components. Inspired by the mechanism of wave growth in the solar wind, our method addresses this by initiating from low-amplitude Alfvénic fluctuations dominated by a strong mean field and subsequently "growing" magnetic perturbations into the large-amplitude regime. We provide example solutions exhibiting nontrivial structures in one, two, and three dimensions, revealing a distinct propensity to develop extremely sharp gradients or discontinuities, except in one-dimensional cases. Beyond serving as a valuable input for further computations, particularly regarding parametric decay, these findings offer a natural explanation for the highly abrupt field discontinuities seen in magnetic switchbacks within the low solar wind.

A thorough investigation into drain current dispersion in $\beta$-Ga$_2$O$_3$ FETs was conducted using DC, pulsed, and RF measurement techniques. The virtual gate effect within the gate-drain access region and interface traps beneath the gate are identified as the primary causes for the observed pulsed current dispersion and high-temperature threshold voltage shifts, respectively. Unpassivated devices exhibit substantial differences between DC and pulsed IV characteristics due to a gate lag effect, characterized by time constants ranging from 400 to 600 $\mu$s. Analysis of temperature-dependent Arrhenius plots yielded an activation energy of 99 meV. The slow transient response of the drain current over time is attributed to variable range hopping-mediated slow transport alongside shallow trap levels. These traps are likely introduced during the reactive ion etching phase of fabrication. However, their impact can be mitigated through surface passivation, such as the application of Silicon Nitride, which notably enhances both current dispersion and RF cutoff frequency. Ultimately, this study highlights how traps negatively influence current dispersion, thereby restricting the high-frequency performance of the device.

Koopman decomposition represents a non-linear extension of eigen-decomposition and is increasingly employed in the study of spatio-temporal dynamics. Established methods like dynamic mode decomposition (DMD) and its linear counterparts approximate the Koopman operator and have been widely applied to various fluid dynamics challenges. Although nonlinear variants of DMD, such as extended/kernel dynamic mode decomposition (EDMD/KDMD), offer a richer set of nonlinear observables, they are rarely used for large-scale problems mainly because identifying the Koopman invariant subspace is difficult when faced with thousands of resulting eigenmodes. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a multi-task feature learning framework designed to extract the most informative Koopman invariant subspace by eliminating redundant and spurious Koopman triplets. Specifically, we implement a pruning procedure that penalizes deviations from linear evolution, effectively treating these algorithms as sparsity-promoting extensions of EDMD/KDMD. Additionally, we generalize KDMD to a continuous-time context and establish connections between our method, sparsity-promoting DMD, and an empirical criterion through the lens of non-convex optimization. The efficacy of our approach is validated across simple dynamical systems, two-dimensional cylinder wake flows at varying Reynolds numbers, and three-dimensional turbulent ship air-wake flows. The latter scenarios are engineered to exhibit strong nonlinear transients, necessitating precise Koopman operator approximations. We analyze the underlying physical mechanisms, focusing on transient dynamics characterization, and compare our findings with existing theoretical frameworks and numerical approximations.

The text demonstrates a method for calculating the instability rates of double-periodic solutions to the cubic nonlinear Schrödinger (NLS) equation using Lax linear equations. These solutions are characterized by a wave function modulus that is periodic in both space and time, effectively generalizing standing waves which exhibit time-independence and spatial periodicity. Like other waves within the NLS framework, these double-periodic solutions are spectrally unstable; this instability corresponds to bands in the Lax spectrum that lie outside the imaginary axis. A straightforward numerical approach is employed to determine the unstable spectrum and to compare the instability rates of these double-periodic solutions against those of standing periodic waves.

Mathematical modeling is a crucial component for analyzing the transient behavior of dynamical systems and conducting engineering tasks like optimization and control. While dynamic models can be constructed using first-principles and expert insight, this process is often prohibitively difficult for complex systems found in fields such as biology, chemical engineering, neuroscience, and finance. Consequently, data-driven modeling has emerged as a compelling alternative, facilitated by rapid progress in sensor and measurement technologies. Specifically, the operator inference framework offers a data-driven approach that models dynamic processes by assuming a specific structure for the nonlinear terms. This work proposes integrating operator inference with certain deep neural network techniques to deduce unknown nonlinear dynamics, leveraging recent deep learning advances and any available prior knowledge. We also outline several extensions and benefits of this methodology. Finally, we demonstrate that the proposed approach successfully addresses dynamics in neural systems and the glycolytic oscillator.

This study investigates charmonium-like states by analyzing the regularity of energy level differences and the behavior of leptonic decay widths for excited charmonia. Using a phenomenological Martin-like confinement potential, we examine spectroscopic states and calculate di-leptonic decay widths based on their radial wave functions. Observed deviations from expected patterns suggest these states are admixtures of nearby S and D states. Our analysis strongly supports $\psi(3686)$ as a mixture of $c\bar{c}(2S)$ and a $c\bar{c}g$ (4.1 GeV) hybrid, while identifying $\psi(4040)$ and $\psi(4160)$ as charmonium (3S, 3D) admixtures with mixing angles of $11^\circ$ and $45^\circ$, respectively. We classify the $Y(4260)$ as a pure $c\bar{c}(4S)$ state, predicting a leptonic decay width of 0.65 keV, and note that $X(4630)$ is closer to the $c\bar{c}(6S)$ state. Finally, the nature of $\psi(4415)$ remains uncertain as it does not conform to either a pure or admixture state profile.

We introduce a theoretical framework comprising two Higgs doublets and multiple $SU(2)$ scalar singlets, governed by a global non-Abelian flavor symmetry $\mathcal{Q}_6\times\mathcal{Z}_2$. This discrete symmetry successfully reproduces the observed fermion mass hierarchies and mixing angles post-symmetry breaking. Within this setup, only the third fermion generation acquires mass via Standard Model (SM) mechanisms, while lighter fermions gain mass through a seesaw-like process. To achieve this, the model extends the particle spectrum with electrically charged vector-like fermions (VLFs), right-handed Majorana neutrinos, and various SM scalar singlets. We investigate LHC-accessible processes involving these VLFs, specifically analyzing double production channels for both vector-like leptons (VLLs) and vector-like quarks (VLQs), alongside single production topologies for VLLs. By employing genetic algorithms to optimize neural networks, we calculate the statistical significance of potential discoveries in future LHC runs. Our findings indicate that VLLs with masses exceeding $200~\mathrm{GeV}$ cannot be definitively excluded. For VLQs, we demonstrate that the high-luminosity LHC phase could probe masses up to 3.8 TeV, while Run-III data alone would allow us to exclude VLQs up to $3.4~\mathrm{TeV}$. Furthermore, we illustrate how the model's predicted VLL masses provide a viable explanation for the muon anomalous magnetic moment.

Adiprasito, Avvakumov, and Karasev recently achieved a breakthrough by constructing a triangulation of the $n$-dimensional real projective space using a subexponential number of vertices. Their approach involved reducing the problem to identifying a small downward closed set-system $\cal F$ on an $n$-element ground set that meets a specific criterion: for any two disjoint sets $A, B\in\cal F$, there must exist elements $a\in A$ and $b\in B$ such that either ($B\cup\{a\}\in\cal F$ and $A\cup\{b\}\setminus\{a\}\in\cal F$) or ($A\cup\{b\}\in\cal F$ and $B\cup\{a\}\setminus\{b\}\in\cal F$). Letting $f(n)$ denote the minimum cardinality of such a family, they established the upper bound $f(n)<2^{O(\sqrt{n}\log n)}$ and posed the question of finding a nontrivial lower bound. It is demonstrated that their construction is nearly optimal, with the bounds $2^{(1.42+o(1))\sqrt{n}}\le f(n)\le 2^{(1+o(1))\sqrt{2n\log n}}$. Additionally, a variant of this problem is examined where the condition is strengthened: for any disjoint $A, B\in\cal F$ with $|A|>|B|$, there must be an $a\in A$ such that $B\cup\{a\}\in\cal F$. For this stricter requirement, the size of the minimal $\cal F$ is shown to lie between $2^{\Omega(\sqrt{n}\log n)}$ and $2^{O(n\log\log n/\log n)}$.

The nature of quantum critical phenomena in the quasi-one-dimensional limit remains unresolved. This study investigates the impact of uniaxial stress on the quasi-1D Kondo lattice CeCo$_2$Ga$_8$ through electric transport and AC heat capacity measurements. It is hypothesized that CeCo$_2$Ga$_8$ resides near, but on the quantum-disordered side of, a quantum critical point. Compressing the $c$ axis, which aligns with the Ce-Ce chains, enhances the onset of the coherent Kondo effect. Conversely, elongating the intra-chain distance via compression along the $a$ or $b$ axes results in a more rapid divergence of electronic specific heat at low temperatures. These findings indicate that tensile intra-chain strain ($\varepsilon_c > 0$) drives CeCo$_2$Ga$_8$ closer to a quantum critical point, whereas compressive intra-chain strain ($\varepsilon_c < 0$) likely pushes it away. This work offers a unique example of manipulating a quasi-1D Kondo lattice near a quantum critical point using uniaxial stress, thereby facilitating further exploration of quantum criticality's distinctive features in the quasi-1D regime.

Let $A$ denote an expansive dilation on $\mathbb{R}^n$, and let $p(\cdot):\mathbb{R}^n\rightarrow(0,\,\infty)$ be a variable exponent function satisfying the globally log-H\"{o}lder continuous condition. We consider the variable anisotropic Hardy space $\mathcal{H}^{p(\cdot)}_A({\mathbb {R}}^n)$, defined through the non-tangential grand maximal function. In this study, the authors demonstrate that for any $f\in \mathcal{H}^{p(\cdot)}_A({\mathbb {R}}^n)$, its Fourier transform corresponds to a continuous function $F$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ within the framework of tempered distributions. Building on this result, the authors establish a higher-order convergence property of $F$ at the origin and derive a modified version of the Hardy-Littlewood inequality tailored to anisotropic Hardy spaces with variable exponents.

Majorana zero modes in condensed matter systems have garnered significant attention recently due to their unique non-Abelian exchange statistics and their potential for topological quantum computation, drawing interest from both experimentalists and theorists. It is widely accepted that breaking time-reversal symmetry is essential for creating these modes in quasi-one-dimensional topological insulators. However, conventional methods such as applying magnetic fields or coupling with ferromagnets often produce detrimental side effects, including the degradation of superconductivity and the emergence of sub-gap states, which have historically hindered their direct experimental observation. This review examines several proposals that utilize the control of the superconducting order parameter's phase as either the primary mechanism for breaking time-reversal symmetry or as an auxiliary tool to minimize the required magnetic field. These strategies offer practical advantages for enhancing Majorana formation and provide deeper insights into the physics governing topological superconducting states.

Real-world epidemic spreading processes often interact cooperatively, competitively, or asymmetrically, necessitating a description grounded in coevolutionary dynamics. While complex behaviors like discontinuous outbreak transitions and hysteresis can emerge, a comprehensive understanding of these phenomena across the parameter space remains elusive. We introduce a theoretical framework for interacting spreading dynamics on complex networks utilizing spectral dimension reduction. Specifically, by deriving a two-dimensional system of macroscopic variables from microscopic quenched mean-field equations, we enable the analytical determination of a complete phase diagram. This diagram forecasts previously identified critical phenomena—such as the relationship between discontinuous transitions and hysteresis, along with the emergence and significance of tricritical points—which were formerly accessible only through numerical simulations.
