Additionally, two less-explored issues at IACTs involve a) classifying different primary nuclei within CCR events and b) identifying anomalous events potentially triggered by Beyond Standard Model particles, which may produce shower signatures distinct from standard gamma ray or CCR patterns. These tasks—categorizing the initiating primary particle or tagging anomalous showers in a model-independent manner—are ideally addressed using machine learning (ML). Conventional research on gamma ray/CCR separation relies on multivariate analysis of derived shower properties, which discards significant information compared to full shower images. Our work tackles these challenges by employing ML architectures trained on complete simulated shower images rather than limited derived properties. We demonstrate binary and multi-category classification using convolutional neural networks and introduce the use of autoencoders for anomaly detection in VHE gamma ray experiments. Using the H.E.S.S. experiment as a case study, we apply these methods. However, the broader impact of these techniques lies in their applicability to any IACT, including the upcoming Cherenkov Telescope Array (CTA), and their potential adaptation for CCR experiments.

This research investigates fundamental reachability issues within pseudo-orbits of linear dynamical systems. Pseudo-orbits serve as a computational model characterized by limited precision, with pseudo-reachability representing a robust counterpart to classical reachability. Leveraging the $o$-minimality of $\reals_{\exp}$, we establish the decidability of the discrete-time pseudo-reachability problem for diagonalisable linear dynamical systems, accommodating arbitrary semialgebraic targets. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our methodology allows the reduction of the continuous-time pseudo-reachability problem to the (classical) time-bounded reachability problem, which is recognized as conditionally decidable.

Recent advancements in comprehending the semirelativistic excitation of atomic hydrogen through electron impact have emerged from the integration of polarized electron beams and powerful laser fields. This paper reviews relativistic theoretical frameworks for laser-assisted electron scattering, with a specific focus on spin-related phenomena. It further explores various spin configurations within inelastic electron-atom collisions, highlighting the laser field's pivotal role in uncovering new details about collision dynamics. Furthermore, modern theoretical studies of these relativistic, laser-assisted interactions underscore the critical necessity of experimental data to evaluate the precision of computational models.

This paper introduces an analytical framework designed for channel estimation and data detection in massive MIMO uplink systems equipped with 1-bit analog-to-digital converters (ADCs) under independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) Rayleigh fading conditions. Initially, we derive closed-form expressions for the mean squared error (MSE) of channel estimation, evaluating both the state-of-the-art linear minimum MSE estimator and scaled least-squares estimators. Regarding data detection, we provide closed-form formulas for the mean and variance of estimated symbols when using maximum ratio combining; these metrics facilitate efficient minimum distance detection and aid in optimizing transmit symbol sets. Our analytical results explicitly rely on critical system parameters, including signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), the count of user equipments, and pilot length, thereby allowing for a precise characterization of estimation and detection performance in 1-bit ADC environments. Furthermore, the proposed analysis reveals a fundamental SNR trade-off, indicating that operating at an optimal noise level substantially improves system performance.

Pharmaceutical companies receive millions of unsolicited medical inquiries annually, which are hypothesized to be a rich source of information about medicinal products and treatments. However, the sheer volume and specialized content of these inquiries make it challenging to conduct timely, recurrent, and comprehensive analyses. This study proposes a machine learning framework utilizing natural language processing and unsupervised learning to automatically identify key topics within real-world customer medical inquiries. This method operates without the need for ontologies or annotations. Medical information specialists have validated that the discovered topics are both meaningful and medically relevant, confirming that unsolicited inquiries serve as a valuable source of customer insights. Consequently, this work establishes a foundation for machine-learning-driven analysis of medical inquiries in the pharmaceutical sector, with the ultimate goal of enhancing patient care.

For practitioners accustomed to syntactic methods, semantic proof strategies like reducibility, realizability, and logical relations often appear mysterious, yet their efficacy is undeniable. This raises the question of their underlying mechanism and where the core logical effort occurs. To cultivate an intuitive grasp of these proofs, we implemented a normalization argument for the simply-typed lambda-calculus with sums by encoding it as a program within a dependently-typed meta-language. The specific technique examined is Krivine's classical realizability, which offers a proof-relevant formulation of reducibility arguments akin to unary logical relations. While reducibility attaches a predicate to every type, realizability assigns a set of realizers—abstract machines that integrate first-class contexts with lambda-terms. Normalization follows directly from an adequacy theorem, or "fundamental lemma," asserting that every well-typed term translates into a realizer for its type. By expressing this adequacy theorem as a dependent program, we demonstrate that it functions as an evaluation procedure. Specifically, a weak normalization proof explicitly computes the reduction sequence from an input term to its normal form. Notably, the definitions of reducibility predicates, including truth and falsity witnesses for each connective, dictate the evaluation order, causing each datatype constructor to operate either lazily or strictly. Although these concepts are well-known among experts, our dependently-typed functional program offers an accessible entry point for a broader audience, serving as a gentle introduction to abstract machine calculi that have recently become powerful tools in research.

This study presents a theoretical investigation into potential $\Lambda^0_b(5912)$ and $\Lambda^0_b(5920)$ pentaquark states within the $\gamma{}p\to{}\Lambda_b^{0(*)}B^+$ reactions, utilizing an effective Lagrangian framework. The analysis incorporates contributions from the $s$-channel nucleon pole, $t$-channel $\bar{B}^{{*}-}$ exchange, and contact terms. Grounded in chiral unitary theory, where these resonances are dynamically generated, we calculate the total and differential cross sections using coupling constants for the $\Lambda^0_b(5912)$ and $\Lambda^0_b(5920)$ interactions with $\bar{B}p$ and $\bar{B}^{*}p$ channels derived from the same theory. Our results indicate that the cross sections for the $\gamma{}p\to{}\Lambda_b^{0}(5912)B^{+}$ and $\gamma{}p\to{}\Lambda_b^{0}(5920)B^{+}$ reactions are approximately 0.0164 nb and 0.00527 nb, respectively. Future measurements at facilities such as the China Electron-Ion Collider (EicC) or the US-EIC could detect these total cross sections and specific angular distribution characteristics, providing a means to verify the molecular nature of these states as pentaquarks.

We present an open-source, hardware-based contact tracing device constructed from accessible components for under $20. This project addresses the need for a privacy-preserving alternative to mobile phone-dependent contact tracing solutions. By utilizing Bluetooth Low Energy on an ESP32 microcontroller, the system enables direct, peer-to-peer exchange of health data between nearby individuals without requiring a smartphone or application. Designed for individual assembly and configuration within minutes, this device offers a strictly decentralized approach to contact tracing.

By combining Gaia EDR3 cross-matched data with the 2MASS Point Source Catalog, we identified a sample of Red Clump (RC) stars exhibiting parallax uncertainties below 20% to map the local spiral structure formed by old stellar populations. The resulting density map of RC stars reveals an arc-like overdensity spanning longitudes from approximately $90^\circ$ to $243^\circ$, which passes in close proximity to the Sun. This feature likely represents a segment of a spiral arm traced by old stars, thereby reflecting the gravitational potential of the Galaxy near our location. When compared with spiral arms identified through young objects, significant offsets are observed between the two components. Specifically, the arm traced by RC stars exhibits a larger pitch angle, resulting in a more loosely wound configuration.

Advancements in high-throughput molecular biology now enable the analysis of complex, multivariate phenotypes alongside high-dimensional genomic and omics data, a challenge addressed through high-dimensional multi-response regression where response variables often exhibit strong correlations. To address this, we previously developed various multivariate Bayesian variable and covariance selection models, including Bayesian estimation techniques for sparse seemingly unrelated regression (SUR) to handle both variable and covariance selection. These implementations feature several variable selection priors, notably the hotspot detection prior for latent variable inclusion indicators, which facilitates sparse selection of associations between predictors and multiple phenotypes. Additionally, we propose an alternative approach utilizing a Markov random field (MRF) prior to integrate prior knowledge regarding the dependence structure of inclusion indicators. The computational feasibility of inferring Bayesian SUR via Markov chain Monte Carlo methods is achieved through the factorization of the covariance matrix among response variables. This paper introduces BayesSUR, an R package that enables users to easily configure and execute a diverse range of Bayesian SUR models implemented in C++ for enhanced efficiency. The package features a modular design, allowing users to independently select priors for variable and covariance selection. We evaluate the performance of sparse SUR models employing both the hotspot prior and a spike-and-slab MRF prior using synthetic and real datasets, including examples from eQTL and mQTL studies as well as in vitro anti-cancer drug screening applications.

We identify eight nearby active galactic nuclei (AGNs) that are likely Compton-thin along the line of sight, based on prior research. Using the MYTORUS model, we analyze broadband X-ray spectra from 20 individual $Suzaku$ observations, self-consistently incorporating Fe K$\alpha$ line emission and both direct and scattered continuum from material with finite column density and solar iron abundance. This modeling approach enables us to distinguish the global, out-of-line-of-sight equivalent hydrogen column density from that within the line of sight. We find that for 5 of the 20 observations (spanning 3 AGNs), the global column density exceeds $\gtrsim 1.5 \times 10^{24}$cm$^{-2}$, indicating that the distant scattering matter is Compton-thick. Additionally, for a fourth AGN, 2 out of 5 observations suggest a Compton-thick nature, albeit with significant uncertainties. Although some of these AGNs have previously been reported to host relativistically broadened Fe K$\alpha$ emission, our modeling shows that the Fe K$\alpha$ line is unresolved in all but two $Suzaku$ observations, and the data are well-fitted by models containing only a narrow Fe K$\alpha$ line.

We revisit the standard DFT$+U$ approach applied to non-collinear magnets. Although numerous studies either omit the exchange correction parameter \textit{J} or deem its precise value insignificant, we demonstrate that for non-collinear magnetic calculations, \textit{J} profoundly influences the magnetic ground state. By examining trends in the lithium orthophosphate series LiMPO$_4$ (M = Fe, Ni) and the difluorite series MF$_2$ (M = Mn, Fe, Co, Ni), we highlight the significant dependence of magnetic canting and magnetocrystalline anisotropy on \textit{J}. These findings are explained by extending conventional DFT$+U$ equations into the spinor framework, where \textit{J} directly impacts the off-diagonal elements responsible for spin canting.

Deformation twinning serves as a primary mechanism for permanent deformation, particularly in low-symmetry crystals like hexagonal close-packed (hcp) metals. Given the growing utilization of hcp metals, such as magnesium, in structural, automotive, and armor sectors due to their superior strength-to-weight ratios, a thorough understanding of twinning and its interplay with dislocation slip is essential. While significant progress has been made at the microscopic level via atomistic simulations of dislocation-twin boundary interactions and at the macroscopic level by approximating twinning as "pseudo-slip" while neglecting morphology, these approaches often overlook the collective formation of twins across multiple grains with complex shapes that dictate bulk behavior. These mesoscale dynamics remain underexplored and constitute the primary focus of this study. We introduce a unified model capable of describing twin and slip morphology, their evolution, and mutual interactions at a scale spanning several grains to investigate their macroscopic implications. This approach integrates a phase-field model of twinning with a crystal plasticity model of slip and leverages parallel computing on graphic processing units to ensure rapid simulations.

This work investigates the convergence of the spectral shift function when finite interval restrictions of a pair of full-line Schrödinger operators, defined on intervals $(-\ell,\ell)$ with coupled boundary conditions, are considered as $\ell\to \infty$. The analysis specifically addresses the scenario where these restrictions are relatively prime to those satisfying Dirichlet boundary conditions. By employing a Krein-type resolvent identity, we demonstrate that the spectral shift function for these finite interval restrictions converges weakly to the corresponding function for the pair of full-line Schrödinger operators as the interval length increases without bound.

**Aims:** This study sought to classify gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) with minimal supervision by utilizing cutting-edge techniques derived from graph theory. **Methods:** Various graph-based classification approaches, specifically leveraging different versions of the $k$-nearest neighbour graph, were employed across multiple GRB datasets within the duration-hardness ratio parameter space to determine the optimal partitioning. **Results:** Generally, both two and three groupings were found to be viable, although results became increasingly ambiguous as the sample size grew. **Conclusions:** While the methodology does not provide clear evidence for a third class of GRBs, it cannot definitively exclude this possibility. Furthermore, there is no indication of the existence of more than three distinct classes.

Prior research indicates that pre-trained masked language models (MLMs), including BERT, can yield competitive results in extracting factual knowledge from certain datasets, suggesting their potential as dependable knowledge sources. This paper presents a rigorous investigation into the mechanisms driving MLM predictions across various extraction frameworks. Our analysis reveals that previously observed strong performance largely stems from biased prompts that overfit to dataset artifacts. Moreover, we demonstrate that integrating illustrative examples and external context enhances knowledge prediction primarily through entity type guidance and leakage of golden answers. These findings clarify the underlying mechanisms of MLM prediction and significantly challenge the earlier assertion that current MLMs can reliably function as factual knowledge repositories.

Recent advancements in sampling algorithms, which utilize piece-wise deterministic Markov processes (PDMPs) to simulate continuous-time stochastic processes, have demonstrated significant potential. Nevertheless, these techniques often encounter difficulties when sampling from distributions characterized by multiple modes or heavy tails. This work demonstrates how tempering strategies can enhance the mixing performance of PDMPs in such scenarios. We propose an extended distribution defined over both the posterior state and an inverse temperature parameter; this parameter interpolates between a tractable distribution at zero and the target posterior at one. The marginal distribution of the inverse temperature comprises a mixture of a continuous distribution on [0,1) and a point mass at 1. Consequently, while samples obtained at an inverse temperature of one represent draws from the posterior, the algorithm also explores lower-temperature distributions to facilitate improved mixing. We detail the implementation of PDMPs, specifically the Zig-Zag sampler, to sample from this extended distribution. The resulting method is straightforward to implement and empirical results indicate that it can surpass existing PDMP-based samplers when addressing challenging multimodal posteriors.

A Banach space is defined as locally almost square if, for each element $y$ on its unit sphere, there exists a sequence $(x_n)$ on the unit sphere such that $\lim\|y\pm x_n\|=1$. If this sequence is additionally required to be weakly null, the space is termed weakly almost square. Although these two concepts are distinct, this study explores whether local almost squareness entails a weaker form of the second property by substituting the sequence with a net. Focusing specifically on Banach lattices, we strengthen the definition of local almost squareness by mandating that the sequence resides within the lattice's positive cone. Utilizing this characterization, we demonstrate that this positive variant of local almost squareness ensures that every relatively weakly open subset of the unit ball possesses a diameter of 2, a condition known as the diameter two property. Consequently, this result enables the construction of new examples of Banach spaces that exhibit the diameter two property.

Gaseous outflows seem to be a universal characteristic of both type-1 and type-2 active galactic nuclei (AGN). The primary diagnostic tool is the presence of emission features shifted to higher frequencies via the Doppler effect, indicating that the emitting gas is approaching the observer. However, aside from this blueshift, the observational signatures of outflows often remain ambiguous, and no established criteria currently exist to isolate outflow contributions within the integrated, single-epoch spectra of type-1 AGN. Emission spectra obtained using typical apertures for long-slit spectroscopy or fiber optics encompass a broad range of spatial scales, complicating the analysis of line profiles to distinguish between different kinematic components. Nevertheless, the hundreds of thousands of quasar spectra available at moderate resolution require a rigorous analysis of line profiles to accurately model the dynamics of the emitting regions. In this brief study, we examine several profiles of the HI Balmer line H$\beta$ from both composite and individual optical spectra of sources radiating at moderate Eddington ratios (Population B, following Sulentic et al. 2000). We detect features and profile shapes attributable to outflows from narrow-line region gas across a wide range of luminosities.

Topological materials hold significant promise for quantum technologies. While non-interacting systems like topological insulators and superconductors are well-classified by fundamental symmetries, the impact of interactions on topological properties remains only partially understood. In this work, we present a model where topology arises from the quantum interference between single-particle dynamics and global interactions. The system consists of soft-core bosons interacting through correlated hopping across a one-dimensional lattice. The emergence of quantum interference triggers a spontaneous breaking of translational symmetry, resulting in a phase analogous to the nontrivial states of the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. Similar to the fermionic Peierls instability, this newly formed quantum phase manifests as a topological insulator at half-filling. Originating from quantum interference, this topological phase is confirmed by exact density-matrix renormalization group calculations but is completely missing from mean-field approaches. We propose that these dynamics can be implemented in current experimental platforms, such as cavity quantum electrodynamics setups, where the topological characteristics can be detected via light emitted from the resonator.

In an ever-changing world, automatically identifying differences between two images of the same scene holds significant practical value across many fields. This paper addresses the challenge of detecting "object-level" alterations within image pairs, even when viewpoint and lighting conditions vary. To achieve this, we present four key contributions: (i) a scalable approach to generate a large-scale change detection training dataset by utilizing existing object segmentation benchmarks; (ii) a novel co-attention-based architecture capable of implicitly establishing correspondences between image pairs and identifying changes through bounding box predictions; (iii) four new evaluation datasets spanning diverse domains and transformations, including synthetic changes, real-world 3D surveillance footage, and synthetic 3D scenes with camera motion; and (iv) an evaluation of our model on these datasets that demonstrates generalization capabilities for zero-shot and beyond-training transformations.

The construction of hybrid atomic orbitals is suggested as a method to identify approximate common eigenstates of finite first-moment matrices, where their hybridization and orientation can be tuned a priori based on anticipated local environments. Corresponding Wannier functions, derived from Kohn-Sham single-particle states, form an orthonormal multi-orbital tight-binding basis that mimics hybrid atomic orbitals anchored to their immediate atomic neighbors while spanning the Kohn-Sham state subspace. This proposed basis enables the derivation of predominantly single tight-binding parameters from first principles for nearest-neighbor bonds involving up to two orbitals, regardless of orientation, and facilitates the transfer of these parameters across isostructural systems simply by mapping neighborhoods and projecting orbital charge centers. Using hybridized 2s, 2p, and 3s, 3p valence electrons, the spatial extent of self-energy correction (SEC) applied to TB parameters is found to be localized primarily within the third-nearest neighborhood. This localization allows for the effective transfer of self-energy-corrected TB parameters from smaller reference systems to larger target systems with minimal additional computational cost beyond the explicit calculation of SEC in the reference systems. Ultimately, this approach offers a cost-effective means to estimate the quasi-particle structure of large covalent systems with acceptable accuracy.

Ytterbium mode-locked fiber lasers represent complex dynamical systems capable of exhibiting various pulsed operating modes contingent upon external parameters like pump power, making their systematic experimental analysis a significant challenge. This study investigates single-pulse regimes within such lasers by examining the impact of nonlinear amplitude modulation on intracavity pulses. To comprehensively capture the system's dynamics, researchers conducted average power measurements reflecting the slow time scale alongside simultaneous time-resolved measurements for the fast time scale. By quantifying the average nonlinear transmission induced by amplitude modulation, the study successfully correlates transitions between different dynamical regimes with the underlying system nonlinearity.

Time-lapse photography is utilized in cinema and promotional content because it compresses the passage of time and enhances visual appeal; however, the necessity for prolonged durations and stable shooting makes it a significant challenge for photographers. This paper introduces a time-lapse photography system integrating both virtual and real robots. To enable efficient shooting, we parameterize the process and propose an optimization method that leverages various aesthetic models, including image and video quality assessment networks, to determine optimal parameters. We also develop an interface allowing users to view and adjust these parameters while utilizing virtual robots for photography within a 3D environment. Furthermore, the system exports these parameters to guide real robots in capturing time-lapse footage in the physical world. Additionally, we present a method for automatically evaluating the aesthetic quality of time-lapse videos. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach efficiently generates time-lapse videos. A user study further confirms that our system achieves effects comparable to professional photographers while offering greater efficiency.

We present a metric termed "width" to quantify nondeterminism within automata. This concept extends the definition of good-for-games (GFG) automata, which are equivalent to NFAs with a width of 1 and allow for the on-the-fly construction of accepting runs on any accepted input. We detail an incremental determinisation method for NFAs that may outperform standard full powerset determinisation, with its efficiency contingent upon the input NFA's width. This approach extends to infinite words and is especially effective for coBüchi automata. For coBüchi automata, the procedure enables the computation of either a deterministic or a GFG automaton, yielding greater algorithmic efficiency in the latter scenario. We substantiate this by demonstrating that verifying whether a coBüchi automaton is determinisable via pruning is NP-complete. Furthermore, we establish that determining the width of an automaton is EXPTIME-complete for both finite and infinite words, a result that implies EXPTIME-completeness for multipebble simulation games on NFAs.

This study examines the Lefschetz standard conjecture regarding degree $2$ cohomology for hyper-K\"ahler manifolds that admit a covering by Lagrangian subvarieties. Specifically, when a Lagrangian fibration is present, we demonstrate that the Lefschetz standard conjecture follows from the SYZ conjecture, which characterizes divisor classes linked to such fibrations. In dimension $4$, we address the broader scenario of a fourfold $X$ covered by Lagrangians, establishing the Lefschetz standard conjecture in degree $2$ under the conditions that $\rho(X)=1$ and $X$ is general within its moduli space. Furthermore, we explore connections between Lefschetz cycles and the rational equivalence of points alongside Bloch-Beilinson type filtrations, offering a comprehensive interpretation of a recent notable result by Marian and Zhao.

Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have emerged as a leading method for decoding EEG signals, serving as the standard benchmark for motor imagery Brain-Computer Interface (BCI) tasks. Nevertheless, training CNNs across multiple subjects remains difficult, as it often leads to a decline in individual performance due to the "negative transfer" problem. This issue arises when learning from dissimilar data distributions causes the network to misrepresent individual subjects rather than capturing a more comprehensive representation, thereby preventing CNNs from directly leveraging multi-subject data to improve performance. To overcome this challenge, we extend deep transfer learning strategies to multi-subject EEG training by introducing the Separate-Common-Separate Network (SCSN). This architecture utilizes a multi-branch design that splits feature extractors for each individual subject. Additionally, we investigate the integration of Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) into the SCSN framework (SCSN-MMD) to enhance the alignment of feature distributions across subjects. Evaluations on both the BCI Competition IV 2a dataset and our own online recorded dataset demonstrate that the proposed SCSN (achieving 81.8% and 53.2%) and SCSN-MMD (achieving 81.8% and 54.8%) significantly outperform the benchmark CNN (73.4% and 48.8%) when utilizing data from multiple subjects. These results indicate that our networks offer a promising solution for training EEG decoders on large multi-subject datasets without succumbing to negative transfer effects.

This work investigates the dimensional reduction of general relativity to a single null dimension. The resulting theory comprises six scalar fields subject to three constraints and possesses an infinite-dimensional symmetry that extends the Geroch group. To define a local action of this symmetry on the solution space, an infinite series of new fields and constraints must be introduced. This symmetry resembles a hyperbolic Kac-Moody algebra, though certain defining relations are verified only "order by order" across the infinite tower of fields. This Lie algebra remains enigmatic, lacking a known geometric interpretation and posing challenges in basis enumeration. By analyzing the algebra's action on solution space, we uncover a compelling link to the representation theory of the symmetric group. Furthermore, this symmetry may hold relevance for understanding gravitational dynamics near spacelike singularities.

Building on a relative Wu theorem within \'etale cohomology, we examine how Steenrod operations align between Chow groups and \'etale cohomology. Leveraging the obstructions to algebraicity derived from this compatibility, we develop novel instances of non-algebraic cohomology classes across diverse fields ($\mathbb{C}$, $\mathbb{R}$, $\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p$, $\mathbb{F}_q$). Furthermore, we apply Steenrod operations to analyze mod $2$ cohomology classes of a compact $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$ manifold $M$ that are algebraizable, meaning they remain algebraic on some real algebraic model of $M$. Our work provides fresh examples of both algebraizable and non-algebraizable classes, thereby addressing inquiries posed by Benedetti, Ded\`o, and Kucharz.

El Niño serves as a quintessential example of an atmosphere-ocean coupling, yet it remains uncertain whether quantitative correlations between relevant climate events can adequately describe it. To address this, we constructed a machine learning model for El Niño prediction utilizing climate index time series. By converting these multidimensional time series into path signatures, the model effectively captures the order and nonlinearity of climate events, resulting in robust forecasting performance (a mean square error of 0.596 for a 6-month lead time). Furthermore, the approach reveals the sequence of climate events likely to influence future NINO3.4 sea surface temperatures. Forecasting trials identified fluctuations in the North Pacific Index and various NINO indices as critical precursors. These findings indicate that El Niño exhibits a degree of predictability grounded in the correlation of climate events.

The constituent quark model, enhanced with relativistic corrections, is employed to examine the decay characteristics of multi-strangeness $\Xi$ and $\Omega$ baryon resonances. Calculations of strong decay widths for various $\Xi$ and $\Omega$ states are used to verify internal quark arrangements, thereby determining their spin-parity ($J^P$) quantum numbers and internal structures. Our results indicate that Roper-like resonances within the multi-strangeness sector exhibit large decay widths, similar to their counterparts in the light and heavy baryon sectors. Furthermore, we calculated the decay ratio for $\Omega(2012)$ as $\Gamma{(\Omega\to \Xi \bar{K} \pi)} / \Gamma{(\Omega\to \Xi \bar{K})}=4.5\%$, which aligns with experimental observations when assigned a $J^P=3/2^-$ state. This suggests that the $\Omega(2012)$ can be naturally interpreted as a three-quark state within the quark model. A systematic analysis of the decays of other low-lying $\Xi$ and $\Omega$ resonances is also presented, offering valuable insights for future experiments aimed at revealing the structures of these resonances.

Particulate matter pollution ranks among the most lethal forms of air contamination globally, significantly affecting both human health and the environment. Among these, PM2.5 is a critical component for calculating the Air Quality Index (AQI). However, traditional monitoring stations rely on expensive, cumbersome, energy-intensive, and slow instruments. Additionally, constraints in data availability and scalability prevent these conventional systems from delivering real-time monitoring with high spatial and temporal resolution. To address these limitations, this study introduces an analytical equation-based prediction method for PM2.5 utilizing an Artificial Neural Network (ANN). Because the derived equations can be executed on low-cost processing tools or Wireless Sensor Nodes (WSN), the approach proves highly practical. The research also analyzes correlations between PM2.5 and other pollutants to identify optimal predictors, leveraging a large, authenticated dataset from the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) online stations in India. Using eight predictors, the proposed method achieved an RMSE of 1.7973 µg/m³ and an R² of 0.9986, while utilizing only three predictors yielded an RMSE of 7.5372 µg/m³ and an R² of 0.9708. These results confirm that the proposed approach offers a promising solution for monitoring PM2.5 without relying on power-hungry gas sensors or bulky analyzers.

This paper investigates one-point statistics of spiral turbulent pulsations occurring within a three-dimensional coherent vortex. Under the assumption that the helical flow originates from a statistically axially symmetric random force with broken mirror symmetry, we first compute the mean velocity-vorticity. Subsequently, for an electrically conducting fluid, we analyze the $\alpha$-effect. The components of the $\alpha$-matrix are shown to depend heavily on the relationship between the Rossby number ($\operatorname{Ro}$) and the magnetic Prandtl number ($Pr_m$) in the region where $\operatorname{Ro}\lesssim 1$ and $Pr_m \lesssim 1$. Finally, we derive criteria for these numbers that determine when the $\alpha$-effect induces instability in large-scale magnetic fields.

Colloids function effectively as "large atoms," serving as excellent models for atomic and molecular systems. Consequently, colloidal hard disks provide a robust representation of two-dimensional (2D) materials; while their phase behavior is well understood, their rheological properties have been less explored. This study utilizes a new, particle-resolved experimental setup alongside complementary computer simulations to investigate the shear rheology of quasi-hard-disk colloids under extreme confinement. Specifically, quasi-2D hard disks are trapped within a circular "corral" formed by 27 particles held in optical traps. This confinement, combined with shear, inhibits the hexagonal ordering typically seen in bulk systems, resulting in a layered fluid structure. Rheological measurements are obtained by balancing driving and drag forces across each layer. Despite the severe confinement, the system displays rheological characteristics strikingly similar to unconfined 2D and 3D hard particle systems, featuring a dynamic yield stress and shear-thinning of comparable intensity. By analyzing particle motion perpendicular to the shear direction, we demonstrate that increasing the shear rate causes particles to become more tightly bound to their respective layers without a corresponding rise in density. Therefore, shear thinning arises from reduced dissipation due to weakened inter-layer interactions as the shear rate increases. We successfully replicated these experimental findings using Brownian Dynamics simulations that incorporate Hydrodynamic Interactions (HI) via the Rotne-Prager tensor. The necessity of including HI to match experimental results underscores their critical role in momentum transmission throughout the system.

Automatically generated object bounding boxes in video sequences often contain noisy and unrepresentative frames, posing significant hurdles for learning discriminative representations in video re-identification (Re-ID). While most current approaches address this issue by evaluating frame importance based solely on local part alignments or global appearance correlations, they fall short due to the diverse and unknown noise sources that frequently coexist in captured video data. This work proposes a joint optimization of both local alignments and global correlations, enhancing their mutual reinforcement to better integrate complementary discriminative Re-ID information across all relevant frames within video tracklets. Specifically, we simultaneously optimize a Local Aligned Quality (LAQ) module to assess frame quality based on local alignments and a Global Correlated Quality (GCQ) module to estimate global appearance correlations. By utilizing a local-assembled global appearance prototype, we link LAQ and GCQ to leverage their complementary strengths. Extensive experiments on five Re-ID benchmarks—MARS, Duke-Video, Duke-SI, iLIDS-VID, and PRID2011—demonstrate that the proposed model outperforms state-of-the-art methods.

Community detection serves as a core function in many graph-based applications, identifying natural groupings in real-world networks without predefined size or count constraints. Although highly applicable, large-scale parallel computing support for this task remains limited due to the irregular and sequential characteristics of existing heuristics. This paper introduces parallelization strategies for rapid community detection, utilizing the Louvain method as a serial baseline. Developed by Blondel et al. in 2008, the Louvain method is an iterative approach to modularity optimization that is widely adopted for its speed and memory efficiency in finding high-modularity partitions. However, its inherent sequential nature restricts scalability. We identify specific properties of the method that hinder parallelization and propose heuristics designed to overcome these sequential bottlenecks. Our implementation uses OpenMP multithreading and evaluates performance on real-world graphs from diverse domains, including the internet, citations, and biology. Compared to the standard serial Louvain version, our parallel approach achieves higher modularity for most inputs within comparable or fewer iterations, delivering speedups of up to 16x with 32 threads.

This work establishes two "master" convolution theorems concerning multivariate determinantal polynomials. The proofs rely on fundamental characteristics of a newly defined "minor-orthogonal" ensemble alongside the properties of matrix mixed discriminants. Furthermore, the paper presents several applications, such as providing an alternative derivation of Barvinok's result regarding the computation of the permanent for low-rank matrices, as well as identifying a polynomial convolution associated with the unitarily invariant addition of generalized singular values.

Building an $A_{\infty}$-structure on a loop space within the category of diffeological spaces presents two minor challenges. First, path concatenation in this category requires a specific technical workaround (referencing P.~I-Zemmour \cite{MR3025051}), which seemingly limits the number of times concatenation can be iterated. Second, there is no natural decomposition of an associahedron into a smooth simplicial or cubical complex. By overcoming these obstacles, we demonstrate that the smooth loop space of a well-behaved diffeological space constitutes a h-unital smooth $A_{\infty}$-space.

Alchemy is a novel meta-learning framework that balances sufficient complexity to support meaningful abstractions with the simplicity required for detailed analysis. Additionally, it offers an optional symbolic interface that facilitates meta-RL research even with limited computational resources. This study initiates the application of Symbolic Alchemy to pinpoint design choices that allow deep-RL agents to acquire various abstraction types. By employing diverse behavioral and introspective analyses, we examine how trained agents utilize and encode abstract task variables, uncovering notable parallels with the neuroscience of abstraction. Finally, we outline future directions for leveraging meta-RL and Alchemy to deepen our understanding of how the brain represents abstract variables.

Object pose estimation serves as a fundamental perceptual skill for robotics. We introduce a fully convolutional adaptation of the PoseCNN architecture designed to densely forecast object translations and orientations. This approach offers multiple benefits, including enhanced spatial resolution for orientation estimates—particularly valuable in cluttered environments—a substantial decrease in parameters by eliminating full connectivity, and accelerated inference speeds. Furthermore, we propose and analyze various aggregation strategies for dense orientation predictions that function as post-processing steps, such as averaging and clustering. Our results show that the method matches PoseCNN's accuracy on the difficult YCB-Video dataset, supported by a comprehensive ablation study of different configurations. Finally, we demonstrate that model performance can be further enhanced by incorporating an iterative refinement module within the network to ensure prediction consistency.

In its scholarly data initiatives, the Internet Archive (IA) has launched the first iteration of the refcat citation graph dataset, which is derived from academic publications and supplementary sources. This dataset aggregates information from the fatcat cataloging project (the foundation of IA Scholar), large-scale web crawls focused on both primary and secondary scholarly works, along with metadata from the Open Library and Wikipedia. The initial version of this graph contains more than 1.3 billion citations. Distributed under a CC0 Public Domain Dedication via the Internet Archive, the dataset's source code—which includes logic for both exact and fuzzy citation matching—is available under an MIT license. This report aims to briefly outline the dataset's current composition and its derivation process.

Utilizing the chiral quark-soliton model alongside heavy quark symmetry, we characterize the spectra of beauty and charm baryons. These heavy baryons are categorized based on the SU(3) representations of their light quark components. We propose that the recently observed $\Xi_b$ states correspond to negative parity excited anti-triplets or sextets, whereas the $\Sigma_b$ states represent negative parity sextets. Furthermore, we examine the implications of these assignments for decay modes and provide mass predictions for the unobserved members of the sextet.

A primary limitation in deploying Monte Carlo and variational inference algorithms is the requirement to cheaply and exactly compute the marginal densities of proposal distributions and variational families. This constraint excludes many promising approaches, including those relying on complex simulations or stochastic optimization. This paper expands the design space by introducing a framework for applying these inference methods even when proposal densities lack exact evaluations. We propose Recursive Auxiliary-Variable Inference (RAVI), which approximates necessary densities through meta-inference—an additional layer of Monte Carlo or variational inference targeting the proposal rather than the model. RAVI unifies and generalizes several existing methods for inference with expressive approximating families, demonstrating that these correspond to specific meta-inference algorithm choices, while also offering new theoretical insights into their bias and variance. We validate the RAVI framework and its theorems by analyzing and enhancing Salimans et al.'s Markov Chain Variational Inference and by creating a novel sampler for Dirichlet process mixtures. This sampler achieves state-of-the-art performance on a standard astronomy benchmark and a difficult data-cleaning task involving Medicare hospital data.

Derived from conventional ABO$_3$ perovskites, A-site ordered perovskites such as CaCu$_3$B$_4$O$_{12}$ display diverse electronic and magnetic characteristics. This study focuses on the specific influence of copper by investigating CaCu$_3$Ti$_4$O$_{12}$ and CaCu$_3$Zr$_4$O$_{12}$, elucidating the mechanism behind the crystallization of A-site ordered structures from their conventional counterparts and explaining the stabilization of the non-trivial, experimentally observed G-type antiferromagnetic (G-AFM) order. First-principles electronic structure calculations, supported by phonon analysis, indicate that the formation of these ordered perovskites is driven by Jahn-Teller distortions within the CuO$_{12}$ icosahedra. Furthermore, crystal orbital Hamiltonian population analysis combined with spin dimer-based magnetic exchange interactions reveals that nearest-neighbor (J$_1$) and next-nearest-neighbor (J$_2$) couplings are direct and weakly ferromagnetic, while the third-neighbor interaction (J$_3$) is exceptionally strong and antiferromagnetic, arising from an indirect superexchange mechanism. Structural analysis demonstrates that G-AFM stabilization necessitates the conditions J$_1$ < 2J$_2$ and J$_1$ < 2J$_3$. The close agreement between theoretical and experimental Néel temperatures at an on-site Coulomb interaction $U$ of approximately 7 eV underscores the significance of strong electron correlation. Additionally, the magnetic ordering proves to be robust against variations in pressure and strain.

We present the detection and analysis of a planet associated with the microlensing event OGLE-2018-BLG-0799. Detected by multiple ground-based telescopes, the planet-host mass ratio is determined to be $q = (2.65 \pm 0.16) \times 10^{-3}$. While ground-based data constrain the angular Einstein radius $\theta_{\rm E}$, the microlensing parallax vector $\vec{\pi}_{\rm E}$ is primarily restricted by Spitzer observations. However, systematics identified in the 2019 Spitzer baseline introduce ambiguity regarding the parallax magnitude. Our preferred model, derived from a full Bayesian analysis incorporating a Galactic model, suggests a system consisting of a $M_{\rm planet} = 0.26_{-0.11}^{+0.22}~M_{J}$ planet orbiting a host star of $M_{\rm host} = 0.093_{-0.038}^{+0.082}~M_{\odot}$ at a distance of $D_{\rm L} = 3.71_{-1.70}^{+3.24}$ kpc. An alternative interpretation shifts the minima localization along the arc-shaped parallax constraints, resulting in a more massive host with a median mass of $0.13~M_{\odot}$ located 6.3 kpc away. This study validates the robustness of the osculating circles formalism while highlighting the need for further research to understand how photometric systematics influence the specific localization of the microlens parallax vector and the resulting physical parameter estimates.

We introduce a framework for constructing an extended two-component Bose-Hubbard model utilizing a polariton condensate within an optical microcavity. Unlike the standard two-component Bose-Hubbard model, which relies solely on Kerr nonlinearity, our approach incorporates a nonlinear tunneling term that is contingent upon the difference in particle numbers between the two modes. Under a mean-field approximation, this system corresponds to a nonrigid pendulum with a variable length whose sign can also be altered. We investigate both the dynamic and ground state characteristics of this model, demonstrating that a first-order phase transition occurs as the nonlinear tunneling rate is adjusted. Additionally, we outline a method for extracting the polariton condensate wave function.

We re-examine the quantitative analysis of the ultrafast magneto-acoustic experiment conducted by Kim and Bigot [1] on a freestanding nickel thin film using our recently developed method for decomposing magnetic and acoustic eigenmodes, proposed by Vernik et al. [2]. By applying this modeling framework to time-resolved reflectivity data, we achieve unprecedented accuracy in determining the amplitudes and lifetimes of standing perpendicular acoustic phonon resonances. Our findings indicate that acoustic damping follows a $\propto\omega^2$ scaling for frequencies up to 80~GHz, with peak amplitudes reaching $10^{-3}$. The observed magnetization dynamics across various external magnetic field orientations align closely with numerical solutions of magneto-elastically driven magnon harmonic oscillators. Furthermore, symmetry-based selection rules for magnon-phonon interactions derived from our model enable clear distinction between spatially uniform and non-uniform modes, a result validated by comparing resonantly enhanced magneto-elastic dynamics measured simultaneously on opposite sides of the film. Finally, the separation of time scales associated with the early rise and late decay of precession amplitudes allows for the simultaneous extraction of both magnetic (Gilbert) and acoustic damping parameters from a single measurement.

Segmenting, classifying, and quantifying nuclei in Haematoxylin & Eosin-stained histology images facilitates the extraction of interpretable cell-level features suitable for downstream explainable models in computational pathology. The Colon Nuclei Identification and Counting (CoNIC) Challenge is designed to advance research and innovation in automatic nuclei recognition within this field. This report outlines the method we submitted for the CoNIC challenge. Our approach utilizes a multi-task learning framework that executes both panoptic segmentation and regression tasks. For the panoptic segmentation component, we employ encoder-decoder deep neural networks that predict both a segmentation map and a direction map, allowing for the separation of adjacent nuclei into distinct instances.

The Inert Doublet Model (IDM) extends the Standard Model by adding a second Higgs doublet, which generates four new scalar particles; the lightest among them is stable and serves as a viable dark matter candidate. Researchers evaluated the potential for discovering these IDM scalars at the Compact Linear Collider (CLIC), a proposed next-generation electron-positron collider at CERN, specifically for two high-energy operating modes at center-of-mass energies of 1.5 TeV and 3 TeV. Using full detector simulations via GEANT4, the study examined the CLIC sensitivity to pair-produced charged IDM scalars within selected high-mass benchmark scenarios and semi-leptonic final states. To extend these findings across a broader range of benchmarks, the CLIC detector model within the DELPHES fast simulation framework was adjusted to account for beam-induced $\gamma\gamma \rightarrow$ had. backgrounds. The analysis concludes that heavy charged IDM scalars could be detected at CLIC across most considered scenarios, reaching mass scales of approximately 1 TeV.

We re-examine how the covering factor (CF) of the dust torus in active galactic nuclei (AGNs) depends on their physical properties, specifically by incorporating AGN polar dust emission. The CF is derived from the ratio of infrared (IR) luminosity attributed to the AGN dust torus ($L_{\rm IR}^{\rm torus}$) to the AGN bolometric luminosity ($L_{\rm bol}$), utilizing a non-linear relationship between this luminosity ratio and the intrinsic CF. Our study utilizes a sample of 37,181 type 1 quasars at redshifts $z < 0.7$ from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey Data Release 16 quasar catalog. Physical parameters, including $L_{\rm bol}$, black hole mass ($M_{\rm BH}$), and Eddington ratio ($\lambda_{\rm Edd}$), are obtained through spectral fitting with QSFit. We perform spectral energy distribution decomposition using X-CIGALE with clumpy torus and polar dust models to estimate $L_{\rm IR}^{\rm torus}$ while isolating it from contributions by stellar and AGN polar dust. For the 5,720 quasars with securely determined physical quantities, we analyze correlations between the CF and (i) $L_{\rm bol}$, (ii) $M_{\rm BH}$, and (iii) $\lambda_{\rm Edd}$. Our results confirm anti-correlations between the CF and all three parameters. Furthermore, including AGN polar dust emission strengthens these anti-correlations compared to analyses that exclude it, suggesting that polar dust winds, driven by AGN radiative pressure, are a critical factor in regulating the obscuring material of AGNs.

An isospin-symmetry-related combined amplitude analysis examines the decays $B^0 \rightarrow \overline{D}^0 D^+_s\pi^-$ and $B^+\rightarrow D^- D^+_s\pi^+$ using data from the LHCb detector, collected in proton-proton collisions at center-of-mass energies of 7, 8, and 13$\,\rm{TeV}$ with an integrated luminosity of 9$\,\rm{fb^{-1}}$. Two new resonant states are identified: one with a mass of $2.908\pm0.011\pm0.020\,\rm{GeV}$ and width of $0.136\pm0.023\pm0.011\,\rm{GeV}$ decaying to $D^+_s\pi^+$, representing the first observation of a doubly charged open-charm tetraquark with minimal quark content $[c\bar{s}u\bar{d}]$; and another decaying to $D^+_s\pi^-$, identified as a neutral tetraquark with $[c\bar{s}\bar{u}d]$ quarks. Both states exhibit a spin-parity of $0^+$, and their consistent resonant parameters indicate they form an isospin triplet.

This study introduces a model describing a single classical nova outburst cycle, utilizing self-consistent, optically thick winds driven by radiation pressure gradients. Using a Henyey code, we simulated the evolution of a $1.0~M_\odot$ white dwarf accreting at a rate of $5 \times 10^{-9}~M_\odot$ yr$^{-1}$, where the outer hydrogen-rich envelope transitions into a steadily moving layer during wind phases. Our results confirm the absence of internal shock waves during the thermonuclear runaway. The wind mass loss rate peaks at $1.4 \times 10^{-4}~M_\odot$ yr$^{-1}$ coinciding with maximum photospheric expansion, at which point the photospheric temperature drops to $\log T_{\rm ph} = 3.90$ K. Nearly all accreted material is subsequently ejected via the wind. The energy released by hydrogen burning is distributed primarily as photon emission (64%), gravitational potential energy gained by lifting the wind against gravity (35%), and a negligible fraction as wind kinetic energy (0.23%). We predict that the nova will exhibit significant brightness in the far-UV (100–300 Å) band approximately one day after the runaway begins, roughly 25 days prior to the optical maximum. During the decay phase, the envelope structure closely resembles a steady-state solution.

We develop a family of four-dimensional noncommutative deformations of $U(1)$ gauge theory based on a general framework recently introduced in JHEP 08 (2020) 041 for specific coordinate-dependent noncommutative algebras. This framework encompasses $\mathfrak{su}(2)$, $\mathfrak{su}(1,1)$, and angular (or $\lambda$-Minkowski) noncommutative structures. We observe that introducing a fourth, commutative coordinate $x^0$ introduces significant new features in the deformed field strength expression compared to the three-dimensional counterpart. The resulting field theoretical models function as Poisson gauge theories, representing the semi-classical limit of fully noncommutative gauge theories. Our derived expressions for deformed gauge transformations, field strength, and classical action possess flat commutative limits and are exact, incorporating all orders of the deformation parameter. Furthermore, we examine the relationship between this formalism and the $L_{\infty}$ bootstrap along with symplectic embeddings, subsequently deriving the underlying $L_{\infty}$-algebra for our model.

This work introduces a non-distributive two-sorted hypersequent calculus named \textbf{PDBL}, along with its modal extension \textbf{MPDBL}, specifically designed for pure double Boolean algebras and pure double Boolean algebras with operators, respectively. A relational semantics for \textbf{PDBL} is developed, interpreting every formula as a semiconcept within a context. For \textbf{MPDBL}, the semantics relies on Kripke contexts, where formulas are likewise treated as semiconcepts of the base context. Both systems are proven to be sound and complete relative to these relational frameworks. By incorporating specific sequents into \textbf{MPDBL}, one can derive logics grounded in Kripke contexts that are reflexive, symmetric, or transitive; notably, one such system serves as a logic for topological pure double Boolean algebras. Furthermore, \textbf{PDBL} is shown to adequately express fundamental concepts and relations of conceptual knowledge, enabling inferences that involve negations. Establishing a link with rough set theory, the paper defines lower and upper approximations of context semiconcepts. It is then demonstrated that the modal operators and associated sequents in \textbf{MPDBL} successfully capture these approximation operators along with their properties.

Moons in close orbits around rocky exoplanets undergo rapid tidal evolution, leading to either a merger with their host planet or a state of dynamical instability within a Hubble time. This review examines the conditions under which moons become unbound, specifically analyzing how atmospheric tides influencing planetary spin affect these outcomes. Our findings indicate that such tides can shift the final result from a merger to an escape, though this occurs only within a restricted range of parameters. We further trace the evolution of these ejected moons, demonstrating that the most probable long-term fate is a return collision with the original planet. The debris from such an impact is projected to create dust clouds with optical depths near 0.001, temperatures in the hundreds of Kelvin, and a duration of several thousand years. These characteristics suggest this mechanism could explain transient warm dust clouds observed around middle-aged main sequence stars. Additionally, a late-stage collision between a planet and a moon on a hyperbolic trajectory could sterilize a potentially habitable world.

Understanding ubiquitous phenomena such as thermal conductivity, displacive phase transitions, and heat transport requires time-resolved mapping of lattice dynamics in both real and momentum spaces. Typically, this is achieved using time-resolved diffraction and microscopy within a pump-probe setup to visualize induced lattice movements. This study demonstrates that inelastic scattering methods, supported by theoretical simulations, can yield comparable insights to those from time-resolved imaging. To validate the approach, simulated lattice dynamics in germanium showed excellent agreement with time-resolved x-ray diffuse scattering data obtained via an x-ray free-electron laser. This method proves robust for reconstructing in-situ lattice dynamics across varying environmental conditions, including temperature, pressure, and magnetic fields. Furthermore, it offers significant advantages in scenarios where pump-probe diffraction is impractical, such as in inelastic neutron scattering experiments.

This study introduces a new training protocol for encoder-decoder deep neural networks that consolidates an $N \times M$ architecture into a unified model, allowing for dynamic selection of encoder and decoder layer counts during inference. Conventional methods typically feed the final output of an $N$-layer encoder into an $M$-layer decoder and apply softmax loss only to the decoder's last layer. In contrast, our approach calculates a combined loss comprising $N \times M$ individual losses, where each of the $M$ decoder layers is evaluated against the output of each of the $N$ encoder layers using softmax loss. This single model supports decoding with arbitrary, reduced numbers of encoder and decoder layers. Practically, this method (a) accelerates decoding with negligible impact on translation quality and (b) eliminates the requirement to train separate $N \times M$ models, thus reducing storage requirements. We demonstrate these benefits through a case study on neural machine translation and provide a corresponding cost-benefit analysis.

This study introduces an efficient method for developing a foundational video-text model capable of handling tasks such as open-vocabulary video classification, text-to-video retrieval, video captioning, and video question-answering. We propose VideoCoCa, which adapts a pretrained image-text contrastive captioner (CoCa) to video-text applications with minimal additional training. Unlike prior approaches that rely on complex cross-frame fusion modules and extensive fine-tuning on video data, we discovered that the generative and contrastive attentional pooling layers within the image-text CoCa architecture are immediately adaptable to "flattened frame embeddings," providing a robust zero-shot transfer baseline for numerous video-text tasks. Specifically, the frozen image encoder of a pretrained image-text CoCa processes each of the $T$ video frames to generate $N$ token embeddings per frame. These $N \times T$ tokens are flattened into a long sequence representing the frozen video, upon which CoCa's pooling layers are applied. Crucially, all model weights, including the pooling layers, are directly loaded from the pretrained image-text CoCa without any video or video-text data. Consequently, VideoCoCa's zero-shot baseline achieves state-of-the-art performance on zero-shot video classification benchmarks like Kinetics 400/600/700, UCF101, HMDB51, and Charades, as well as zero-shot text-to-video retrieval on MSR-VTT and ActivityNet Captions. Furthermore, we investigate lightweight fine-tuning of VideoCoCa, yielding strong results in video question-answering (iVQA, MSRVTT-QA, MSVD-QA) and video captioning (MSR-VTT, ActivityNet, Youcook2). Ultimately, our approach establishes a simple yet effective baseline for future research in video-text modeling.

We present a new data-driven framework for designing targeted gene panels to estimate exome-wide biomarkers in cancer immunotherapy. First, we develop a generative model capturing mutation profiles across the exome, accounting for gene- and variant-type-specific mutation rates. Building on this, we propose a novel procedure to estimate biomarkers such as tumor mutation burden and tumor indel burden. Our method enables practitioners to either select a targeted panel of a predetermined size and construct a corresponding estimator, apply the approach to an existing panel for prediction, or expand a panel to a specific size. We validate the superior performance of our approach using data from three non-small cell lung cancer studies and six additional cancer types.

The growing intricacy of infrastructure systems has created vital interdependencies among various networks, where communication relies on electricity and power grids depend on communication. This mutual reliance has spurred extensive research into coupled multilayer networks, often assuming a "hard" interdependence where a failure in one network triggers cascading failures in another. Although empirical proof of such direct hard coupling is scarce, the recovery of a network inherently demands resources provided by other networks, creating well-documented interdependencies driven by the recovery process itself; without functional support networks, recovery is significantly delayed. This study gathered data on the recovery times of millions of power grid outages, revealing evidence of universal nonlinear behavior following major disruptions. We constructed a theoretical framework to examine recovery coupling, which predicts quantitative signatures distinct from those of multilayer cascading failures. By utilizing controlled natural experiments, we isolated the impact of recovery coupling from other factors like resource constraints, providing direct proof of its effect on system functionality. These findings extend beyond infrastructure, offering valuable perspectives on the fragility and aging processes within biological systems.

This study investigates the mass spectra of all-charm tetraquark states with the [cc][$\bar{c}\bar{c}$] configuration, employing a Coulomb plus linear potential alongside the relativistic mass correction term $\mathcal{O}(\frac{1}{m})$. To establish the fitting parameters for these tetraquarks, we initially computed the mass spectra and decay constants ($f^{2}_{P/V}$) of charmonia [c$\bar{c}$]. Our analysis estimated the masses of tetraquark states in both ground and radially excited configurations, incorporating spin-spin, spin-orbital, and tensor interactions. The resulting charmonia mass spectra align well with existing experimental data and theoretical predictions, while the tetraquark spectra agree with prior theoretical models. Furthermore, we propose that the recently observed LHCb state X(6900), with a mass range of 6.2–6.9 GeV, corresponds to the P-wave of all-charm tetraquarks and possesses quantum numbers of $0^{-+}$, $1^{-+}$, or $2^{-+}$.

A wide range of communication and sensing systems depend on detecting signals amidst noisy and interference-laden conditions. While signal processing theory offers methods like the generalized likelihood ratio test (GLRT) for detection based on linear observation models, many real-world scenarios involve nonlinearities in the received signal that severely degrade GLRT performance. This study introduces a neural network classifier placed before the GLRT detector to identify specific nonlinear time samples within a received signal. We demonstrate that pre-processing nonlinear signals with our trained classifier to filter out excessively nonlinear samples (i) enhances GLRT detection performance on nonlinear data and (ii) maintains the theoretical guarantees of the GLRT for accurate signal detection in linear observation models.

Neutron stars are hypothesized to be encircled by belts of asteroids, debris, and gas. Kozai-Lidov perturbations, driven by a distant yet gravitationally bound companion, can cause these orbiting bodies to fall toward the central compact object. Such processes might generate fast radio bursts (FRBs), potentially through magnetic wake fields induced by asteroids within the compact object's wind. It is suggested that a few percent of binary neutron star systems—encompassing configurations with main sequence stars, white dwarfs, other neutron stars, or black holes—could explain the observed rates of non-repeating FRBs. Notably, our findings indicate that close companion orbits produce repeating sources, while wide orbits yield non-repeating ones. This dynamic allows for a calculated ratio between repeating and non-repeating sources of approximately a few percent, aligning closely with observational data. Our scenario offers three testable predictions for the coming years: first, most repeaters should cease activity within 10 to several decades as their asteroid belts deplete; second, some non-repeaters might occasionally repeat if we observe the short-period tail of the FRB distribution; and third, electromagnetic counterparts to binary neutron star mergers could manifest as series of short, sub-Jansky-level radio bursts.

Speaker verification (SV) is essential for securing voice-driven technologies and enabling access control on billions of devices. As a biometric method, SV must be unbiased, delivering consistent and reliable results regardless of a speaker's demographic, social, or economic background. However, current evaluation practices fail to adequately assess bias because they are oversimplified, aggregate users in ways that do not reflect real-world scenarios, and ignore the consequences of errors. This paper introduces design guidelines for building SV evaluation datasets that overcome these limitations. We propose a schema for grading the difficulty of utterance pairs and an algorithm for creating inclusive SV datasets. Experimental validation on the VoxCeleb1 dataset confirms that both the number of utterance pairs per speaker and the assigned difficulty levels significantly impact evaluation performance and variability. Ultimately, this work advances the development of more inclusive and fair practices for evaluating speaker verification systems.

This research investigates the effectiveness of kernels within complex Langevin simulations designed to model quantum real-time dynamics along the Schwinger-Keldysh contour. We present multiple instances where a systematic approach identifies kernels that ensure the proper convergence of complex Langevin methods. These strategies integrate existing knowledge about the system with the requirements for convergent complex Langevin dynamics to construct the necessary kernels. Consequently, we successfully simulated up to $1.5\beta$ on the real-time Schwinger-Keldysh contour for a $0+1$ dimensional anharmonic oscillator with parameters $m=1,\lambda=24$, a result that was previously impossible to achieve using the complex Langevin equation alone.

We develop a quantum mechanics framework grounded in the hypothesis of compact extra dimensions, specifically for a particle seeking to detect them. By introducing a probability function, we model the particle's transition into an additional two-dimensional window. We analyze the general properties of this function and establish a specific length scale governing the occurrence of the particle within this extra window. From a novel perspective, we propose that this new length scale serves as an additional quantum criterion for quantization, complementing the Planck constant. Utilizing the canonical quantization of second-class constrained systems, we construct the desired quantum mechanics, where the probability function is integrated into the structure of these constraints. This approach effectively incorporates extra-dimensional phenomena into three-dimensional quantum mechanics. We discuss certain aspects of this effective double quantum theory, which may be further investigated to explore extra dimensions quantum mechanically, contrasting with field-theoretic approaches. Specifically, we attempt to derive solutions for the wave function and spectrum of a free particle using the Frobenius method for solving linear differential equations. In this context, the length scale of the extra dimension characterizes the singularity of the wave equation at the boundary of the tiny extra window connected to 3D space.

This wordless proof establishes that a regular triangular grid with $n$ vertices per side contains $\binom{n+2}{4}$ equilateral triangles by defining a mapping from four-element subsets of $\{1,2, \dots, n+2\}$ to the set of these triangles. Specifically, we demonstrate the triangle associated with the subset $\{4,5,8,11\}$ under this bijection for the case where $n = 10$.

The Hellmann-Feynman (HF) theorem allows for the direct calculation of forces from electron density, facilitating efficient force computations for large systems via machine learning (ML) models of that density. However, the widespread adoption of the HF method with atom-centered basis sets is hindered by the Pulay force; neglecting it typically introduces errors exceeding 10 eV/Ang. This study demonstrates that employing a suitably augmented Gaussian basis set for density functional calculations can suppress the Pulay force, enabling HF forces to match the accuracy of analytical forces derived from state-of-the-art basis sets. Consequently, geometry optimization and molecular dynamics can now be reliably executed using HF forces. These findings establish a robust pathway for accurately and efficiently simulating large systems through the combination of ML densities and the HF theorem.

Cooperative interactions are ubiquitous across diverse many-body systems, including ecological communities, social groups, and economic networks. This study examines the dynamics of a two-species population (A and B) governed by symmetric cooperative interactions. In an isolated setting, we calculate the probability of fixation—where only one species survives—as a function of initial concentrations and time, noting that the time to fixation grows exponentially with population size. However, introducing migration at rate $\lambda$, where members enter and replace random individuals, generates complex dynamics. Although the population appears to reach a steady state, its distribution undergoes a transition from unimodal to trimodal as the migration rate drops below a critical threshold $\lambda_c$. In this low-migration regime ($\lambda < \lambda_c$), the state is not static but strongly fluctuates between near-fixation conditions dominated by either species A or B. The characteristic time for these fluctuations diverges as $\lambda^{-1}$, meaning that despite the cooperative nature of the interactions, a typical observation will show a population consisting almost entirely of one species.

This paper examines sequential bargaining interactions between a proposer and a veto player who both possess single-peaked preferences, though the proposer faces uncertainty regarding the veto player's ideal point. Since the proposer cannot commit to future proposals, patient players can sometimes reach equilibria featuring Coasian dynamics, where the veto player's private information significantly diminishes the proposer's bargaining leverage. However, our primary finding demonstrates that equilibria also exist where the proposer achieves the high payoff associated with having commitment power. This outcome is driven by the veto player's single-peaked preferences, which allow the proposer to employ a "leapfrog" strategy: securing agreement early from low-surplus types to credibly extract surplus from high-surplus types later. Methodologically, our approach leverages the link between sequential bargaining and static mechanism design.

Estimating the count of species or unobserved classes within a random sample drawn from a larger population is a pervasive challenge in statistics. While traditional approaches typically deal with small sample sizes, emerging technologies like high-throughput DNA sequencing now enable the analysis of massive, heterogeneous populations at unprecedented scales. This shift necessitates new algorithms that leverage data volume to address heterogeneity while maintaining computational speed and scalability. We introduce a non-parametric, moment-based estimator that is both computationally efficient and flexible enough to handle variations in underlying population abundances. This method extends a well-known moment-based lower bound (Chao, 1984), originally proposed by Harris (1959), which was previously impractical due to the absence of cost-effective algorithms for solving the required system of nonlinear equations. By applying principles from the classical moment problem, we demonstrate how to obtain solutions efficiently, resulting in estimators that are simultaneously conservative and more informative. This capability is vital for modern genomic research, where numerous large-scale experiments demand robust species estimation. We illustrate the utility of our estimator through applications in estimating T-cell receptor repertoires and dropout rates in single-cell RNA-seq experiments.

Although Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have advanced significantly, explaining their predictions remains an unresolved challenge. Current leading methods focus on generating local explanations—such as identifying important subgraph structures and node features—to interpret individual instances like single nodes or graphs. Consequently, these explanations are highly instance-specific, preventing a holistic understanding of the GNN model, which limits generalizability and hinders application in inductive settings. Furthermore, because these methods are designed for single instances, they struggle to naturally explain sets of instances, such as graphs belonging to a specific class. To address these limitations, this study introduces PGExplainer, a parameterized explainer for GNNs. By utilizing a deep neural network to parameterize the explanation generation process, PGExplainer facilitates the collective explanation of multiple instances. Compared to existing approaches, PGExplainer demonstrates superior generalization capabilities and is readily applicable in inductive settings. Experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets reveal highly competitive performance, achieving up to a 24.7% relative improvement in AUC for graph classification tasks over the leading baseline.

We present an interpolation technique to estimate the spectral gap for Brownian motion on general domains, where the process exhibits sticky-reflecting boundary diffusion linked to the first nontrivial eigenvalue of the Laplace operator under Wentzell-type boundary conditions. For manifolds, our proofs utilize new applications of the renowned Reilly formula.

To investigate the application of proof assistants in logic research, we formalized the model and proof system for multi-agent modal logic S5 incorporating PAL-style dynamic modalities using the Lean theorem prover. This work includes formal proofs for the reduction axiom of public announcements, as well as the soundness and completeness of modal logic S5, all of which are type-checked with Lean 3.19.0. The full proof is currently accessible via Github.

This study aims to develop a revised theory of gravity that incorporates the back-reaction of Quantum Electrodynamics (QED) within curved spacetime. Recognizing that vacuum fluctuations naturally generate interactions between gravity and photons, we employ an effective action for electromagnetism to capture these quantum effects. This approach yields a set of modified Maxwell's equations and a novel Lagrangian governing gravitational dynamics. By enforcing Cauchy predictability on these equations, we derive a new effective metric, enabling the calculation of the gravity Lagrangian. Consequently, this new Lagrangian depends not only on higher-order derivatives of the metric tensor but also on photon polarization. This dependency gives rise to phenomena such as gravitational birefringence and the existence of black holes featuring event horizons that vary with polarization.

It has been hypothesized that for a finite $p$-group with $p \geq 5$, if the product of two faithful irreducible characters contains more than $(p+1)/2$ distinct irreducible constituents, then the number of such constituents must be at least $p$. This paper presents a counterexample to that conjecture.

Accurate state estimation is crucial for numerous robotics applications. This study focuses on improving state estimation accuracy for robotic systems by refining the dynamics models employed within estimation algorithms.
