A key outcome of this study is the analysis of non-coincident correlators predicted by a complete field-theoretic approach and their relationship with those derived using the stochastic formalism. Our findings reveal a discrepancy between stochastic predictions and field-theoretic results in the regime where significant sub-Hubble correlators are expected; however, this inconsistency can be resolved by incorporating a reduced speed of sound for the scalar field. Furthermore, we explore an alternative stochastic method based directly on the evolution of probability distributions. While both approaches yield identical results for the field's 2-point functions, they diverge regarding 4-point functions essential for density correlators, leading us to discuss the behavior of both methods in the context of Wick's theorem.

We build microstates for 3d black holes within the Hilbert space of tensionless null strings that possess non-zero winding numbers in the direction transverse to the horizon. This combinatorial structure aligns with the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy and incorporates its semiclassical logarithmic corrections.

This paper explores the utility of knotoids for modeling knots within open curves and introduces novel knotoid invariants. We demonstrate that these invariants effectively yield robust metrics for quantifying the degree of knotting in open curves. Furthermore, we define biframed planar knotoids and develop new invariants for them that allow for polynomial-time computation. Applying these invariants, we refine the classification of planar knotoids containing up to five crossings by distinguishing several pairs of prime knotoids previously conjectured to be distinct by Goundaroulis et al.

Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) ranks as one of the most prevalent chronic conditions globally and stands as the third leading cause of death worldwide. It is frequently underdiagnosed or remains undetected until the disease has progressed. While spirometry remains the diagnostic gold standard for COPD, it is often difficult to administer, particularly in resource-limited settings. In contrast, chest X-rays (CXRs) are widely accessible and could serve as an effective screening method to identify candidates for further testing. To date, no research has employed deep learning (DL) algorithms utilizing extensive multi-site, multi-modal datasets to detect COPD while assessing fairness across demographic groups. Our study utilizes three CXR datasets: CheXpert for pre-training, MIMIC-CXR for model development, and Emory-CXR for validation. We specifically selected CXRs from early-stage COPD patients not requiring mechanical ventilation for training and validation. We visualized Grad-CAM heatmaps for true positive cases on the base model using both the MIMIC-CXR and Emory-CXR test sets. Additionally, we proposed two fusion strategies: (1) model-level fusion employing bagging and stacking with MIMIC-CXR data, and (2) data-level fusion incorporating multi-site data from MIMIC-CXR and Emory-CXR, as well as multi-modal data combining MIMIC-CXR and MIMIC-IV electronic health records, to enhance overall performance. A fairness analysis was conducted to determine if these fusion methods introduced performance disparities among different demographic groups. Results indicate that DL models can successfully detect COPD using CXRs, thereby facilitating early screening, particularly in low-resource regions where CXRs are more available than spirometry. Furthermore, the multi-site data fusion approach improved the model's generalizability on the Emory-CXR test data. Future research should explore the use of CXRs or other modalities for predicting COPD.

Astrophysical plasmas are pervaded by turbulence, a factor crucial to both magnetic reconnection and the acceleration processes within it. This study examines particle acceleration occurring during rapid three-dimensional turbulent reconnection, where the turbulence itself is driven by the reconnection process. Particles oscillate between reconnection-driven inflows through mirror reflection and the convergence of intense magnetic fields. Through repeated head-on collisions, the kinetic energy of these inflows is transformed into the energy of accelerated particles. Turbulence governs the inflow velocity and creates diverse angles between the inflows and the local turbulent magnetic fields. Since both the energy gained by particles and their likelihood of escaping rely on the inflow speed, the spectral index of the resulting particle energy distribution is not constant; it falls within the range of approximately 2.5 to 4. The steepest spectra are anticipated under conditions of a strong guide field, corresponding to a small angle between the total incoming magnetic field and the guide field. Furthermore, in the absence of scattering diffusion required to confine particles, reconnection acceleration can be highly efficient when the inflow speed is high and the guide field is weak.

This study introduces a deep learning-optimization framework designed to address dynamic mixed-integer programs. We propose a bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) architecture capable of processing temporal information in both directions to derive optimal solutions for sequential decision-making tasks. The framework is applied to the single-item capacitated lot-sizing problem (CLSP), utilizing binary variables to indicate production status per period. Given the dynamic characteristics of the CLSP, it is modeled as a sequence labeling task, allowing a recurrent neural network to effectively capture temporal dependencies. Computational experiments indicate that our LSTM-Optimization (LSTM-Opt) framework substantially decreases solution times for benchmark CLSP instances with negligible impacts on feasibility and optimality. For instance, predictions at the 85% confidence level cut average CPLEX solution times by a factor of nine across over 240,000 test cases, maintaining an optimality gap below 0.05% and infeasibility under 0.4%. Furthermore, models trained on shorter planning horizons can accurately predict optimal solutions for instances with longer horizons. On the most challenging dataset, 25% confidence LSTM predictions reduced solution times from 70 CPU hours to under two CPU minutes for a specific case, achieving a 0.8% optimality gap with zero infeasibility. The LSTM-Opt framework surpasses classical machine learning methods like logistic regression and random forest in solution quality, and exceeds exact approaches, including ($\ell$, S) and dynamic programming-based inequalities, regarding solution speed improvements. This machine learning strategy holds promise for solving other sequential decision-making problems akin to the CLSP that require rapid, frequent, and repetitive resolution.

Language, as a fundamental element of our culture, is deeply intertwined with human migration. To investigate how and if migration affects language formation, we analyzed the naming game model incorporating migrating agents. First, when all agents are permitted to migrate, the system develops an effective surface tension that drives coarsening; this behavior is highly robust across various agent densities and migration rates. Conversely, when only multilingual agents can migrate, monolingual islands typically emerge. In this scenario, if the migration rate is high enough, the majority of agents converge on a single common language that arises spontaneously, without the surface-tension-driven coarsening observed in the previous case. Furthermore, the slow coarsening seen in dense, static populations is extremely fragile; even a negligible migration rate can shift the system toward the rapid formation of monolingual islands. Our findings indicate that while migration significantly impacts language formation, precise characterization of this influence requires considering additional factors such as agent density and mobility.

This study details the development of high-performance, silica-based integrated two-dimensional lens assisted beam-steering (LABS) arrays, marking the first instance of point-to-multipoint optical frequency transfer. Each LABS unit incorporates $N$ antennas and can generate an arbitrary number of output beams at distinct angles with minimal control complexity. We demonstrate that the LABS supports 16 scanning angles, enabling access for up to 16 simultaneous user nodes. The monolithic transceiver design, featuring a coaxial configuration for light transmission and reception, significantly reduces out-of-loop phase noise. Furthermore, we present non-blocking, point-to-multipoint indoor free-space optical frequency transfer links utilizing LABS with free-space distances of 24 m and 50 m. Following compensation for the 50 m free-space link, fractional frequency instabilities of $4.5\times10^{-17}$ and $7.7\times10^{-20}$ are achieved at averaging times of 1 s and 20,000 s, respectively. This work confirms the viability of 2D LABS for free-space optical time-frequency transfer and offers guidance for the creation of chip-scale optical time-frequency transfer systems.

The excitonic insulator represents a rare electronic state characterized by a correlated excitonic ground state. Materials displaying this phase are anticipated to possess fascinating attributes, including high-temperature excitonic superconductivity, yet definitive experimental confirmation remains absent. In this work, we theoretically introduce two-dimensional semiconductor hybrids functionalized with organic molecules as viable excitonic insulator prototypes, specifically highlighting the WS$_2$-F6TCNNQ system. This material system demonstrates an excitonic insulating phase at room temperature, driven by a ground state condensate of interlayer excitons. Addressing practical experimental conditions, we compute the phase diagram for key variables: temperature, gap energy, and dielectric environment. Additionally, to assist in future experimental identification, we outline methods for characterizing distinct electronic phases using far-infrared to terahertz (THz) spectroscopy.

This study introduces a generic, feature-driven navigation framework for autonomous vehicles that leverages a soft-constrained Particle Filter. By incorporating selected map features, such as road and landmark positions, alongside vehicle states, the system designs adaptive soft constraints. Following the extraction of mapped landmark features from instance-based segmented images generated by a monocular camera, vehicle-to-landmark distances are estimated using Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) models within a mixture-of-experts architecture. The framework utilizes both the mean and variance outputs from these GPR models to enforce adaptive constraints. Experimental findings demonstrate that integrating image segmentation features significantly enhances distance prediction accuracy and that the proposed soft-constrained method ensures reliable vehicle localization, even when facing a limited number of landmarks and noisy observations.

We demonstrate that, modulo local equivalences, a specific truncation of the involutive knot Floer homology for a knot in $S^3$ and the involutive bordered Heegaard Floer theory of its complement are mutually determining. Specifically, for any two knots $K_1$ and $K_2$, we show that the $\mathbb{F}_2[U,V]/(UV)$-coefficient involutive knot Floer homology of $K_1 \sharp -K_2$ is $\iota_K$-locally trivial, provided that $\widehat{CFD}(S^3 \backslash K_1)$ and $\widehat{CFD}(S^2 \backslash K_2)$ meet a particular condition interpretable as the bordered analogue of $\iota_K$-local equivalence. Furthermore, we derive an explicit algebraic formula for calculating the hat-flavored truncation of the involutive knot Floer homology of a knot using the involutive bordered Floer homology of its complement. Consequently, we establish an algebraic satellite operator acting on the local equivalence group of knot Floer chain complexes, which can be explicitly computed up to a suitable truncation.

Solving for the ground state of multi-orbital Hubbard models is essential for understanding strongly correlated electron systems, but current techniques face difficulties in achieving both zero temperature and infinite system size simultaneously. The prevailing approach involves approximating a finite-dimensional model with its $d=\infty$ counterpart, which is formally addressed using dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT); however, this method is constrained by the limitations of unbiased impurity solvers regarding zero temperature and multiple orbitals. A novel alternative is the recently introduced variational discrete action theory (VDAT), which solves the $d=\infty$ Hubbard model using a variational ansatz governed by an integer parameter $\mathcal{N}$, converging monotonically toward the exact solution as computational resources increase. This work presents a decoupled minimization algorithm to apply VDAT to the multi-orbital Hubbard model in the $d=\infty$ limit, specifically investigating $\mathcal{N}=2$ to $4$. At $\mathcal{N}=2$, VDAT rigorously recovers the multi-orbital Gutzwiller approximation, aligning with established results. At $\mathcal{N}=3$, the method accurately captures the interplay between Hubbard $U$, Hund $J$, and crystal field $\Delta$ across the entire parameter space of the two-orbital model with minimal computational expense. We demonstrate that for sufficiently large $U/t$ and $J/U$, the parameter $\Delta$ induces a first-order transition within the Mott insulating phase. Furthermore, in the limit of large orbital polarization with finite $J/U$, interactions exert nontrivial effects even at small $U/t$. These findings suggest that VDAT will significantly advance the understanding of multi-orbital Hamiltonians and strongly correlated electron materials.

Automatic discourse processing, which facilitates understanding of how sentences interconnect, is currently constrained by data limitations. Existing discourse formalisms require labor-intensive annotation involving complex taxonomies of relations, rendering them unsuitable for non-expert annotators. In contrast, this study utilizes the Questions Under Discussion (QUD) framework for discourse analysis to automatically derive QUD structures. By treating each sentence as a response to a question prompted by the preceding context, we represent sentence relationships as free-form questions rather than relying on rigid, fine-grained taxonomies. We present the inaugural QUD parser capable of generating question dependency structures across entire documents, trained on the large-scale DCQA question-answering dataset, which is annotated in alignment with the QUD framework. Crucially, data collection for this paradigm is easily crowdsourced. Human evaluations demonstrate that this approach yields a parser with robust performance. We further illustrate the distinctions between our QUD structures and RST trees and highlight the utility of QUD analysis for document simplification. These results indicate that QUD parsing represents a promising alternative for automatic discourse processing.

We define and analyze Certificate Game complexity, a metric derived from the winning probability of a zero-communication game where two players receive inputs with differing function values and must identify an index $i$ such that $x_i \neq y_i$. We establish upper and lower bounds for strategies involving private coins, public coins, shared entanglement, and non-signaling protocols, highlighting specific separations between them. Specifically, public coin complexity is shown to be upper-bounded by Randomized Query and Certificate complexity, while also being lower-bounded by fractional and randomized certificate complexity; this positions it as a promising tool for deriving strong lower bounds on randomized query complexity. Furthermore, private coin complexity is lower-bounded by zero-error randomized query complexity.

The quantum variant reveals a striking divergence between classical and quantum query models. While public coin certificate game complexity does not exceed randomized query complexity, quantum certificate game complexity can surpass quantum query complexity by a quadratic factor. Leveraging non-signaling concepts from quantum information, we demonstrate a lower bound of $n$ for the quantum certificate game complexity of the $OR$ function, despite its quantum query complexity being $\Theta(\sqrt{n})$. This "non-signaling bottleneck" is further shown to apply to all functions exhibiting high sensitivity, block sensitivity, or fractional block sensitivity.

Finally, we examine the single-bit version of certificate games, where player inputs have a Hamming distance of 1. We prove that the single-bit certificate game complexity with shared randomness equals sensitivity up to constant factors, offering a novel characterization of sensitivity. Additionally, the single-bit version with private randomness corresponds to $\lambda^2$, where $\lambda$ represents spectral sensitivity.

We examine the scalar sector of the most comprehensive multi-Higgs doublet model that adheres to an exact symmetry. We demonstrate that such a model displays decoupling if and only if the vacuum state also respects this symmetry. This universal principle is further verified independently and explicitly for three-Higgs doublet models by thoroughly analyzing all symmetry-constrained configurations and their potential vacua. Additionally, we explore specific features of various decoupling patterns.

We present a novel implicit shape representation termed Primary Ray-based Implicit Function (PRIF). Unlike prevailing methods that rely on signed distance functions (SDF) to process spatial coordinates, PRIF functions on oriented rays. It is specifically designed to directly output the surface intersection point for any input ray, bypassing costly sphere-tracing procedures. This approach facilitates efficient shape extraction and differentiable rendering. Furthermore, we show that neural networks trained to encode PRIF successfully perform diverse tasks, such as representing individual shapes, generating shapes within specific categories, completing shapes from sparse or noisy data, estimating camera poses through inverse rendering, and performing neural rendering with color.

This study employs first-principles calculations to examine how Cobalt (Co) substitution influences the structural and magnetic characteristics of Mn$_3$Ga. In its pure form, the ferrimagnetic Heusler compound Mn$_3$Ga adopts a tetragonal structure. Upon substituting with Co, the preferred crystal phase depends on the concentration $x$: the material remains tetragonal for $x \leq 0.5$ and transitions to a cubic phase for $x \geq 0.5$. Notably, ferrimagnetism remains stable across all concentrations and phases. While the magnetic moments of the two Mn atoms show little variation with $x$, the Co magnetic moments behave differently in the two phases, causing distinct trends in the total magnetic moment ($M_{tot}$). Specifically, in the tetragonal phase ($x \leq 0.5$), the Co moment is nearly negligible, leading to a decline in $M_{tot}$ as $x$ increases. Conversely, in the cubic phase ($x \geq 0.5$), the Co moment is approximately $1\mu_B$, driving an increase in $M_{tot}$. The electronic structure was further analyzed using partial density of states for various $x$ values. To explain the unexpectedly low Co moment in the tetragonal regime, the magnetic exchange interaction was investigated, revealing that the exchange coefficient between Co and Mn is significantly smaller when $x \leq 0.5$ compared to when $x \geq 0.5$.

This study explores the "statite" (or static-satellite) concept, which utilizes a solar sail to enable an artificial satellite to hover stationary. The goal is to establish a dynamic orbital slingshot mechanism designed to intercept Interstellar Objects (ISOs) as they traverse our solar system. ISOs present a rare scientific chance to address core questions regarding the sources of solar system volatiles, the makeup of exo-solar systems, and the exchange rates of material between different systems. Nevertheless, current satellite propulsion systems face significant challenges in visiting ISOs due to their rapid heliocentric speeds and limited warning time. This research applies the statite concept to ISO missions and outlines potential configurations optimized for flybys and rendezvous operations.

Despite the extensive utility of sketch-to-photo retrieval, acquiring paired, richly labeled ground truth is expensive, whereas photo retrieval datasets are readily available. Consequently, prior research involves pre-training models on abundant photo retrieval data (the source domain) and subsequently fine-tuning them on scarce sketch-to-photo data (the target domain). However, this approach risks forgetting source domain knowledge during fine-tuning, while simple co-training may lead to negative transfer due to significant domain discrepancies. Furthermore, because the identity label spaces of source and target data are typically disjoint, standard category-level Domain Adaptation (DA) cannot be directly applied. To overcome these challenges, we introduce an Instance-level Heterogeneous Domain Adaptation (IHDA) framework. We employ a fine-tuning strategy for identity label learning to transfer instance-level knowledge inductively. Simultaneously, we select labeled attributes from the source data to create a shared label space for both domains. Guided by these shared attributes, DA techniques bridge cross-dataset and heterogeneous domain gaps, facilitating transductive transfer of instance-level knowledge. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves a new state-of-the-art on three sketch-to-photo retrieval benchmarks without requiring additional annotations, paving the way for more effective models on limited-labeled heterogeneous image retrieval tasks. The related code is accessible at https://github.com/fandulu/IHDA.

In this work, we detail the development of NJet, an open-source C++ library designed for precise computations of high-multiplicity one-loop amplitudes. As a key application, we provide the first comprehensive next-to-leading order (NLO) calculation of the five-jet cross section at hadron colliders.

This paper demonstrates that for a cut-and-project scheme $(G, H, \mathcal{L})$ and a compact window $W \subseteq H$, the natural projection establishes a bijection between Fourier transformable measures supported within the strip $\mathcal{L} \cap (G \times W)$ on $G \times H$ and those supported inside $\oplam(W)$. We employ this formula to connect the Fourier transforms of these measures and illustrate how this relationship allows for the re-derivation of established results concerning the Fourier analysis of measures with Meyer set support.

Graph convolutional networks (GCNs) facilitate the learning of topologically informed node embeddings, aiding tasks like classification and link prediction. However, their inherent design lacks positional sensitivity and struggles to model long-range dependencies without additional layers, which causes over-smoothing and escalates computational and spatial complexity. Moreover, intricate node dependencies complicate mini-batching, restricting their utility on large-scale graphs. This paper introduces the Scalable Multi-resolution Graph Representation Learning (SMGRL) framework, designed to efficiently generate multi-resolution node embeddings. As a model-agnostic approach, SMGRL integrates with any existing GCN architecture. It significantly lowers training expenses by operating on a coarsened, lower-dimensional version of the graph before leveraging self-similarity to extend results across multiple resolutions. Furthermore, inference for these embeddings can be distributed across multiple machines to further minimize memory and computational demands. By aggregating these multi-resolution embeddings, the framework produces high-quality representations that capture both short- and long-range node dependencies. Experimental results indicate that this approach enhances classification accuracy without imposing substantial computational overhead.

We establish an approximate max-multiflow min-multicut theorem specifically for graphs with bounded treewidth. Specifically, for any graph with treewidth $r$, we demonstrate that if a fractional multicommodity flow of value $f$ and a multicut of capacity $c$ exist, then $f \leq c \leq \mathcal{O}(\ln (r+1)) \cdot f$. Since it is established that the multiflow-multicut gap on $r$-vertex expander graphs with constant degree can reach $\Omega(\ln r)$, our result is tight up to constant factors. Our approach is constructive, yielding a polynomial-time algorithm that achieves an $\mathcal{O}(\ln (r+1))$-approximation for the minimum multicut problem on treewidth-$r$ graphs. This algorithm operates by rounding the optimal fractional solution derived from the natural linear programming relaxation of the multicut problem. Furthermore, we propose innovative adjustments to the standard region-growing algorithm to enable this rounding process, ensuring that the loss in treewidth remains logarithmic.

Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) have emerged as a prevalent remote sensing tool, playing a pivotal role in developing smart cities. Nevertheless, the intricate nature of urban environments poses significant challenges to secure and precise data acquisition, complicating 3D modeling and scene updates. Consequently, determining optimal UAV flight paths and ensuring accurate onboard camera data collection are non-trivial tasks in urban modeling. This research introduces the concept of optimized views photogrammetry, demonstrating its precision and applicability for large-scale 3D reconstruction. Unlike traditional oblique photogrammetry, this method utilizes rough models to generate and refine UAV trajectories by accounting for model point reconstructability and viewpoint redundancy. The study first analyzes the precision of 3D models generated via optimized views photogrammetry using UAV imagery and subsequently validates its engineering potential through a large-scale case study in Qingdao, China. Utilizing Ground Control Points (GCPs) for orientation precision assessment and Terrestrial Laser Scanning (TLS) point clouds for model quality evaluation, the results indicate that optimized views photogrammetry can establish stable image networks and achieve orientation accuracy comparable to existing methods. Furthermore, the accurate image acquisition strategy notably enhances mesh model quality, particularly in areas with severe occlusions, where accuracy improves by 3 to 5 times. The Qingdao case study confirms that optimized views photogrammetry serves as a reliable and potent solution for large-scale 3D modeling within complex urban settings.

Handling statistical modeling and inference tasks where the sample size is significantly smaller than the number of covariates presents significant challenges. Chakraborty et al. (2012) addressed this issue by conducting a comprehensive hierarchical Bayesian analysis of nonlinear regression using relevance vector machines grounded in reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS); however, they failed to establish the theoretical properties underlying their approach. The current study re-examines this problem, proposes a novel class of global-local priors distinct from those previously used, and delivers findings regarding posterior consistency and posterior contraction rates.

Recent inconsistencies between experimental data and theoretical predictions in multi-lepton plus $b$-jet analyses for the $t\bar{t}W^\pm$ process, as reported by ATLAS, suggest a need for higher-precision observables and theoretical models to effectively constrain various new physics scenarios in this channel. Addressing this, we utilize NLO QCD calculations incorporating full off-shell top quark effects to predict the cross-section ratio ${\cal R}=\sigma_{t\bar{t}W^+}/\sigma_{t\bar{t}W^-}$ at the LHC with $\sqrt{s}=13$ TeV. By applying different transverse momentum cuts on $b$-jets, we achieve a theoretical precision of $2\% -3\%$ for ${\cal R}$, offering enhanced sensitivity to new physics effects that may only become apparent with sufficiently precise Standard Model predictions. Motivated by these discrepancies, we also re-evaluate the charge asymmetry of top quarks and their decay products within the $t\bar{t}W^\pm$ production mechanism. Since these asymmetries are uniquely sensitive to the chiral characteristics of potential new physics, we attain theoretical uncertainties below $15\%$. Finally, we examine the influence of top quark decay modeling by explicitly comparing our results with those derived under the narrow-width approximation.

In Orthogonal Time Frequency Space (OTFS) modulation, data symbols exist within the delay-Doppler (DD) domain. This domain offers a significant advantage: channels that are time-frequency dispersive in high-mobility scenarios appear time-invariant when observed in the DD domain. This time-invariance facilitates the development of efficient equalizers for such dispersive channels. This paper introduces an OTFS system utilizing the discrete Zak transform. The proposed formulation streamlines OTFS implementation and simplifies both the derivation and analysis of the input-output relationship for time-frequency dispersive channels within the DD domain.

This paper introduces the concept of a super n-Lie algebra and demonstrates its construction from a binary super Lie algebra endowed with a supertrace analog. Applying this method to the super Lie algebra derived from a Clifford algebra with an even number of generators, we utilize a matrix representation defined on a spinor supermodule to generate a sequence of super 3-Lie algebras indexed by positive even integers.

This study introduces CATCH, a newly developed proton detector system tailored for the $\Sigma$p scattering experiment at J-PARC (E40). Designed as a cylindrical apparatus surrounding an inner target, CATCH measures the trajectory and energy of protons emitted from the target to facilitate kinematic identification of $\Sigma$p scattering events. The system consists of three coaxially arranged components: an inner cylindrical fiber tracker (CFT), a bismuth germanate (BGO) calorimeter, and an outer plastic scintillator hodoscope (PiID). The CFT comprises 5,000 scintillation fibers organized into two cylindrical layers with straight and spiral configurations. Surrounding the CFT are 24 BGO crystals dedicated to measuring the recoil proton's kinetic energy, while the PiID verifies whether the proton has been stopped within the calorimeter. To assess CATCH's performance, proton-proton (pp) and proton-carbon (pC) scattering experiments were conducted using an 80 MeV proton beam. Following energy calibrations for both the CFT and BGO calorimeter, the system achieved a total recoil proton energy resolution of 2.8 MeV ($\sigma$) across the full angular range. Additionally, the CFT demonstrated an angular resolution of 1.27 degrees ($\sigma$) for protons and a time resolution exceeding 1.8 ns ($\sigma$). We also established an analysis method to derive the pp scattering cross section using CATCH. The resulting relative differential cross section for pp elastic scattering aligned with reliable partial wave analysis, with systematic errors kept below 10%. These performance metrics confirm that CATCH meets the requirements for a robust detection system for the upcoming $\Sigma$p scattering experiment at J-PARC.

This paper investigates the divergent basic hypergeometric series, a $q$-analog of the divergent hypergeometric series. While this series formally satisfies a linear $q$-difference equation, we provide an explicit solution that admits the basic hypergeometric series as its $q$-Gevrey asymptotic expansion. This solution is derived through $q$-Borel summability, the $q$-analog of classical Borel summability. Our findings demonstrate a $q$-analog of the Stokes phenomenon. Furthermore, we show that taking the limit $q\to1$ in our result yields the Borel sum of the classical hypergeometric series. Although a similar problem was previously examined by Dreyfus, we emphasize that our outcome differs significantly from his.

Recent theoretical investigations into model-based deep learning have focused on the convergence of gradient descent within shallow ReLU networks derived from generative models featuring sparse hidden layers. Inspired by the effectiveness of architectures enforcing structured sparsity, we propose and examine a group-sparse autoencoder designed to accommodate various generative models. This architecture employs a group-sparse ReLU activation function to ensure that non-zero units within a specific layer appear in contiguous blocks. For clustering applications, inputs activating the same group of units are classified into the same cluster. We analyze the gradient dynamics of a shallow version of this autoencoder when trained on data conforming to a group-sparse generative model. Theoretically, we demonstrate that the network parameters converge to a neighborhood of the generating matrix in this context. Numerical experiments validate our model, revealing that networks utilizing group-sparse ReLUs outperform those with standard ReLUs in both sparse coding and parameter recovery. Furthermore, real-world data experiments support these simulation findings and underscore the clustering potential of structured sparsity models.

We introduce CluSTAR-ND, a rapid hierarchical galaxy/(sub)halo identifier that generates {\bf Cl}ustering {\bf S}tructure via {\bf T}ransformative {\bf A}ggregation and {\bf R}ejection in {\bf N}-{\bf D}imensions. This tool aims to enhance Halo-OPTICS—a method for automatically extracting significant astrophysical clusters from the 3D spatial coordinates of simulation particles—by reducing execution time, enabling metric adaptivity, and supporting datasets with varying feature dimensions. Our direct comparison reveals that CluSTAR-ND yields equally robust clustering structures while operating at least $3$ orders of magnitude faster. To optimize its performance, we calibrated $4$ of the $7$ CluSTAR-ND parameters; if not explicitly defined by the user, these are automatically selected optimally based on the input data. Ultimately, we conclude that CluSTAR-ND is a reliable astrophysical clustering algorithm suitable for identifying stellar satellite groups within large synthetic or observational datasets.

The quantum strategy (or quantum combs) framework serves as a valuable tool for analyzing interactions between entities that process and exchange quantum information across multiple rounds. We establish a time-reversal property for a specific class of linear functions, defined on quantum strategy representations within this framework, which correspond to the set of rank-one positive semidefinite operators on a particular space. This property asserts that the maximum value attained by such a function over all valid quantum strategies remains the same when the function's temporal direction is reversed, even though the strategies themselves are typically not time-reversible. One application of this result is an alternative derivation of a known relationship between the conditional min- and max-entropy of bipartite quantum states, as well as broader generalizations of that relationship.

Numerous challenges confronting modern reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms—including robustness, generalization, transferability, and computational efficiency—are intrinsically linked to compression. While previous research has effectively established the benefits of minimizing information in supervised learning, standard RL approaches lack a dedicated compression mechanism. The RL domain is distinct due to two factors: (1) its sequential structure enables agents to leverage historical data to bypass future observations, and (2) agents can optimize their strategies to favor states requiring minimal bits for decision-making. Leveraging these attributes, we introduce RPC, a method for acquiring concise policies. This approach integrates concepts from information bottlenecks, model-based RL, and bits-back coding into a streamlined, theoretically grounded algorithm. Our technique jointly refines a latent-space model and policy to ensure self-consistency, steering the policy away from states where the model exhibits inaccuracy. We show that our method attains significantly tighter compression than previous techniques, yielding up to 5x higher rewards compared to standard information bottlenecks. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the policies learned by our method exhibit enhanced robustness and superior generalization to novel tasks.

Because quantum systems exhibit strong correlations, classical machine learning techniques such as stochastic gradient descent are frequently inadequate for training neural network quantum states (NQSs). These challenges can be addressed using physics-inspired methods, with stochastic reconfiguration (SR)—which emulates imaginary time evolution—being the most widely adopted. In this work, we investigate an alternative optimization approach for complex-valued NQSs based on the linear method (LM), providing its explicit formulation using complex parameters. Beyond the theoretical framework, we offer numerical proof that the LM can effectively optimize complex-valued NQSs, marking the first known application of this method in this context. When compared to the state-of-the-art SR algorithm, we find that the LM achieves convergence in up to ten times fewer iterations, though each epoch incurs a higher computational cost. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the LM becomes the superior training strategy when sampling costs are high; however, this efficiency gain is accompanied by increased variance.

Healthcare information is naturally multimodal, encompassing electronic health records (EHR), medical imaging, and multi-omics data. Integrating these diverse sources enhances our understanding of human health and facilitates optimal personalized care. Recent advancements in artificial intelligence (AI), especially machine learning (ML), allow for the fusion of these modalities to generate multimodal insights. Consequently, this scoping review synthesizes and analyzes literature utilizing AI to fuse multimodal medical data across various clinical applications. Specifically, the review examines studies that exclusively combine EHR with medical imaging to develop AI methods for clinical use. We provide a comprehensive analysis of fusion strategies, associated diseases and clinical outcomes, the ML algorithms employed for each application, and available multimodal datasets. The study adhered to PRISMA-ScR guidelines, with relevant studies retrieved from Embase, PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar. Data were extracted from 34 studies meeting the inclusion criteria. The analysis revealed a typical workflow involving raw data input, fusion of modalities via conventional ML or deep learning (DL) algorithms, and evaluation through clinical outcome predictions. Early fusion was the predominant technique, appearing in 22 of the 34 studies. Furthermore, multimodal fusion models demonstrated superior performance compared to traditional single-modality models for the same tasks. From a clinical perspective, disease diagnosis and prediction were the most frequent outcomes, reported in 20 and 10 studies, respectively.

We examine a non-reciprocally coupled two-field Cahn-Hilliard system known to exhibit oscillatory dynamics, suppress coarsening, and support localized states. Following the model's introduction, we briefly assess the linear stability of homogeneous states, demonstrating that all instability thresholds match those of a corresponding Turing system (a two-species reaction-diffusion system). Subsequently, we explore interactions between linear modes, focusing on the "Hopf-Turing" resonance through a weakly nonlinear analysis of the associated amplitude equations. The resulting states are then compared against fully nonlinear simulations of a specific conserved amended FitzHugh-Nagumo system. The study concludes with a discussion on the constraints inherent to the weakly nonlinear approach.

With the growing size of dairy herds, there is increasing interest in automated health monitoring for cows. Since lameness is a common issue, it is often identified by analyzing gait, which can be tracked in video footage using pose estimation models capable of automatically locating anatomical landmarks. While most existing animal pose estimation models are static—processing videos frame-by-frame without leveraging temporal context—this study extends a static deep-learning model to incorporate information from previous frames. We evaluated the performance of both static and temporal models using a dataset of 1,059 samples comprising four consecutive frames at 30 fps from 30 different dairy cows walking through an outdoor corridor. Given that farm settings often involve occlusions, we assessed the robustness of both approaches by introducing artificial occlusions into the videos. Results indicated that on non-occluded data, both methods achieved a Percentage of Correct Keypoints (PCKh@0.2) of 99%. However, on occluded data, the temporal model outperformed the static model by up to 32.9%, demonstrating the advantage of temporal data for pose estimation in environments prone to occlusion. Furthermore, we assessed the generalization capabilities of the temporal model by testing it on videos of unknown cows not included in the training set. The model achieved an average PCKh@0.2 of 93.8% on known cows and 87.6% on unknown cows, indicating strong generalization to new individuals and ease of fine-tuning for new herds. Finally, we found that for more challenging tasks involving occlusions and unknown subjects, a deeper architecture provided greater benefits.

The connection between thermodynamics and the Lloyd bound regarding holographic complexity in black holes has garnered significant attention. This study examines $D$-dimensional anti-de Sitter black holes featuring hyperbolic geometry, alongside those with momentum relaxation that exhibit minimum values for both mass and temperature. We demonstrate that the singularities in the thermodynamic curvature of these black holes align precisely with the zero points of action and volume complexity at the Lloyd bound. Specifically, for black holes possessing a single horizon, volume complexity vanishes at minimum mass, while action complexity vanishes at minimum temperature; in both cases, the thermodynamic curvature diverges. Given the behavior of action complexity and thermodynamic curvature at minimum temperature, we suggest that action complexity serves as an order parameter for these black holes within thermodynamic frameworks. Furthermore, we derive the critical exponent associated with thermodynamic curvature across various dimensions.

A novel characterization of free massless superfields with arbitrary superspin $Y$ (where $Y > 1/2$) is introduced. Adopting a first-order approach, we relax certain constraints—specifically reality conditions and gauge redundancies—on the unconstrained higher-spin prepotentials to construct invariants of first and half order. These invariants facilitate the formulation of trivially invariant actions. Furthermore, additional auxiliary superfields, functioning as spin connections, are employed to establish a new local symmetry that recovers the necessary degrees of freedom.

Parametric instabilities have been investigated across diverse physical domains, including fluids, mechanical systems, and inflationary cosmology, over the last two centuries. However, only in recent decades did this subharmonic instability emerge as a pivotal mechanism for the thermalization of the Early Universe within the framework of preheating theory. This study examines a parametrically driven two-fluid interface to replicate essential features of inflationary preheating via the emergence of nonlinear Faraday waves. We provide a comprehensive analysis of the effective field theory governing interfacial waves by leveraging the factorization of higher-order correlations. Although the system is a complex, highly interacting hydrodynamical environment subject to damping, we demonstrate that the scattering of large-amplitude Faraday waves corresponds to the widening of primary resonance bands and the development of secondary instabilities, as anticipated in preheating dynamics.

We present a method for deriving provably optimal control sequences for quantum systems subjected to time-correlated multiplicative control noise. Leveraging the circuit-level noise model from [Phys. Rev. Research 3, 033229(2021)], we demonstrate that identifying such sequences can be formulated as a convex optimization problem, ensuring guaranteed optimality through the problem's inherent convexity. Furthermore, we show that this technique accommodates more general off-axis time-correlated dephasing noise. Although this extension sacrifices provable optimality, numerically optimized sequences still yield nearly optimal performance when control noise dominates the dephasing effects. This approach facilitates the creation of optimal quantum logic gates in environments where amplitude drift noise is significant compared to dephasing, such as in ion-trap based quantum computers or under conditions of rapid control.

The motion averaging (MA) algorithm has been widely investigated as an effective approach for multi-view registration, with numerous variants developed to recover global motions from relative ones and mitigate accumulated errors through information redundancy. However, existing methods typically rely on the Gauss-Newton technique to solve least squares problems for global motion increments, often resulting in limited efficiency and weak robustness against outliers. To address these limitations, this paper introduces a novel MA framework for multi-view registration that integrates a Laplacian kernel-based maximum correntropy criterion (LMCC). By combining the Lie algebra motion framework with correntropy measures, we define a new cost function that incorporates all constraints from relative motions, where the correction of global motions is formulated as an optimization problem maximizing this cost. Using quadratic techniques, this optimization is decomposed into two subproblems: calculating weights for each relative motion based on current residuals and solving a second-order cone program (SOCP) to determine motion increments for the next iteration. Additionally, we present a new strategy for kernel width selection that ensures efficient exploitation of redundancy from relative motions even in the presence of significant outliers. Experimental comparisons with other MA-based methods on both synthetic and real datasets confirm that our approach outperforms existing techniques in terms of efficiency, accuracy, and robustness.

We calculate the one- and two-loop renormalization group flows for integrable $\sigma$-models possessing Poisson-Lie symmetry. These models are defined by a twist function featuring $2N$ simple poles or zeros alongside a double pole at infinity. This setup unifies numerous known integrable deformations within a framework that admits a geometric interpretation as surface defects in a 4D Chern-Simons theory. Our findings indicate that these models are renormalizable at the one-loop level and yield a remarkably concise formula for the twist function's flow. However, at the two-loop level, renormalizability is restricted exclusively to models where $N$=1. When applied to the $\lambda$-deformation on a semisimple group manifold, our results successfully reproduce established $\beta$-functions found in existing literature.

Neural Ordinary Differential Equations (NODEs), which represent a continuous-depth neural network framework, have demonstrated exceptional efficacy across various representative datasets. To address limitations in the original NODE framework, recent advancements have introduced augmented models. In this work, we introduce a novel class of continuous-depth networks incorporating delay mechanisms, termed Neural Delay Differential Equations (NDDEs). To compute the necessary gradients, we employ the adjoint sensitivity method to derive the delayed dynamics of the adjoint variable. Because delay differential equations constitute infinite-dimensional dynamical systems with richer behaviors, NDDEs exhibit superior capacity for nonlinear representation compared to NODEs. We analytically prove that NDDEs function as universal approximators and further extend the framework by constraining the initial function to satisfy ordinary differential equations (ODEs). Through illustrative examples, we demonstrate the outstanding capabilities of both standard NDDEs and those with ODE-based initial values. Specifically, (1) we successfully model delayed dynamics where trajectories in lower-dimensional phase spaces intersect—a scenario where traditional NODEs fail without modification—and (2) we achieve reduced loss and higher accuracy on both synthetically generated data from complex models and real-world image datasets, including CIFAR10, MNIST, and SVHN. Our findings indicate that thoughtfully integrating dynamical system elements into network architecture significantly enhances performance.

We present a novel implementation of a broad-band soft X-ray polarimeter, largely derived from an earlier design. This system, known as the Pioneer Soft X-ray Polarimeter (PiSoX), is a SmallSat mission developed in response to NASA's Astrophysics Pioneers solicitation, targeting small-scale platforms such as CubeSats, balloon experiments, or SmallSats. Similar to the REDSoX Polarimeter, the grating configuration is optimized for polarimetry using broad-band focusing optics by aligning the spectrometer channels' dispersion with laterally graded multilayers (LGMLs). The instrument achieves polarization modulation factors exceeding 90%. For PiSoX, the optical system utilizes lightweight silicon mirrors arranged in a one-bounce parabolic setup. High-efficiency, blazed gratings sourced from opposite sectors are oriented to disperse light onto an LGML, creating a channel that spans wavelengths from 35 to 75 Angstroms (165 – 350 eV). As the satellite rotates, the intensities of the dispersed spectra, following reflection and polarization by the LGMLs, yield the three Stokes parameters required to calculate a source's linear polarization fraction and orientation. Furthermore, the design is scalable to higher energies as LGML technology advances, and we illustrate potential scientific outcomes from instruments utilizing this architecture.

This study presents a general investigation into the properties of a specific class of locally symmetric embedded hypersurfaces within spacetimes that allow for a $1+1+2$ decomposition. These hypersurfaces, which correspond to constant-time slices, are defined by the form of the Ricci tensor relative to the induced metric. First, we derive the Ricci tensor form for general hypersurfaces and outline the conditions under which this general case simplifies to constant-time slices. We then characterize these hypersurfaces, utilizing key physical spacetime quantities to determine their local geometry. Additionally, we examine scenarios where these hypersurfaces possess a Ricci soliton structure, specifically analyzing cases where the associated vector fields are Killing or conformal Killing fields. Finally, within the context of spacetimes exhibiting local rotational symmetry, we demonstrate that only those with vanishing rotation and spatial twist can support the considered hypersurface types, resulting in necessarily flat hypersurfaces. In such instances, if a Ricci soliton structure exists, it must be steady, with the soliton field components remaining constant.

This article introduces a novel information-theoretic quantity, termed \textit{balanced partial entanglement} (BPE), applicable to any bipartite mixed state $\rho_{AB}$. Defined as a subregion integral of the entanglement contour subject to specific balance constraints, the BPE relies on the chosen purification and is therefore not intrinsic; however, it offers a valuable framework for classifying purifications. We examine the entropy relations obeyed by the BPE, noting their strong resemblance to those of the entanglement of purification. In the context of holographic CFT$_2$, we demonstrate that the BPE corresponds to the entanglement wedge cross section (EWCS) area divided by $4G$. Notably, under canonical purification, the BPE equals half the reflected entropy, which also correlates directly with the EWCS. Consequently, the BPE serves as a generalization of reflected entropy for arbitrary purifications of $\rho_{AB}$. Finally, we interpret the link between the BPE and the EWCS through the holographic perspective of the entanglement contour.

Algorithm selection (AS) involves identifying the most appropriate algorithm from a predefined pool for a specific problem instance, such as picking SAT solvers. While typical AS benchmark suites include candidate sets of only a few dozen algorithms, scenarios combining AS with hyperparameter optimization result in an intractable number of candidates. This explosion in complexity hinders the learning of effective meta-models and necessitates expensive online performance evaluations. Consequently, we introduce the extreme algorithm selection (XAS) framework, which operates with fixed sets of thousands of candidate algorithms to enable meta-learning. We evaluate how current state-of-the-art AS methods perform within the XAS context and propose new approaches utilizing a dyadic feature representation that describes both problem instances and algorithms. Our results demonstrate that this dyadic representation significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art solutions across multiple metrics.

In recent years, legged robots have gained significant popularity and power due to their ability to advance autonomous mobility. This study introduces a deep reinforcement learning method utilizing Proximal Policy Optimization to develop a robust, Lidar-driven locomotion policy within a partially observable setting. To actively navigate difficult terrains through visual perception, we propose a new learning approach called the Dynamic Reward Strategy (DRS). This strategy acts as an effective heuristic for training a versatile gait via a neural network without relying on historical data. Furthermore, evaluations conducted in a modified OpenAI Gym environment demonstrate a success rate exceeding 90% across all tested challenging terrains.

Dyck paths are presented as a combinatorial framework modeling the representation category of Dynkin type An quivers. Specifically, a bijection is established between certain Dyck paths and the perfect matchings of associated snake graphs. This methodology enables the derivation of formulas for cluster variables in Dynkin type An cluster algebras using Dyck paths.

More than 5% of the global population, amounting to 466 million individuals, suffers from disabling hearing loss, including 4 million children who may be hard of hearing or completely deaf. Those classified as deaf typically experience profound hearing loss, meaning they have little to no auditory perception. Consequently, deaf individuals worldwide often rely on sign language, which utilizes hand gestures and facial expressions as a fully developed natural language complete with its own grammar and vocabulary. This necessitates the development of translation models capable of converting between sign languages and spoken text. This study focuses on translating Modern Standard Arabic (MSAr) into sign language. To achieve this, we created a gloss representation from MSAr that isolates the essential features required for generating animated signs. Our methodology identifies the most relevant features within the input Arabic sentence to ensure the preservation of meaning during translation.

Reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RIS) are poised to be pivotal in next-generation wireless communication systems. Typically, these surfaces utilize reflection beamforming codebooks to direct signals toward intended receivers. However, previous research has predominantly focused on static, pre-defined codebooks that fail to adapt to environmental or hardware constraints, resulting in substantial beam training overhead. This study introduces a novel deep reinforcement learning framework designed to efficiently construct RIS reflection beam codebooks. By employing a multi-level design that facilitates learning transfer across multiple RIS subarrays, the proposed method accelerates convergence and significantly lowers computational complexity, even for large-scale RIS surfaces. The approach is versatile, supporting both co-located and distributed RIS configurations with arbitrary geometries and accommodating both stationary and non-stationary channel conditions. Furthermore, the solution operates without explicit channel knowledge, dynamically adjusting codebook beams to match the surrounding environment, user distribution, and hardware specifics. Simulation results demonstrate that the learning framework can derive optimized interaction codebooks within a reasonable number of iterations. Notably, a learned codebook using only six beams surpasses the performance of a 256-beam DFT codebook, thereby drastically reducing beam training overhead.

We present a general mechanism for generating topological flat minibands by restricting massive Dirac fermions within a periodic moiré potential, a setup realizable in transition metal dichalcogenide heterobilayers. We demonstrate that this topological phase is safeguarded by the symmetry of the moiré potential and persists even with arbitrarily large Dirac band gaps. Using the MoTe$_2$/WSe$_2$ heterobilayer as a case study, we show that the topological phase can be controlled via a vertical electric field. By mapping the Coulomb interaction onto these topological fat minibands, we identify a correlated Chern insulator at half-filling and a quantum valley-spin Hall insulator at full-filling, thereby providing a theoretical explanation for the topological states observed experimentally in MoTe$_2$/WSe$_2$. This work highlights the critical role of Dirac structures in forming topological minibands and reveals a versatile strategy for designing topological moiré materials.

This study presents a liquid scintillator containing an enriched lithium chloride aqueous solution, achieving a 0.40% Li-6 concentration, along with its optical properties and neutron response performance. Utilizing capture-gated coincidence techniques, the light output spectra from 2.5 MeV, 14.1 MeV, and Cf-252 neutrons were recorded after the scintillator was integrated into a fast neutron spectrometer. Additionally, the spectrometer was run in non-coincidence mode to measure thermal neutrons, with potential enhancements to spectrometer performance also discussed.

RowHammer is a DRAM vulnerability that induces bit errors in a victim row by rapidly accessing adjacent rows. Recent research indicates that newer DRAM devices are increasingly susceptible to RowHammer, with numerous studies highlighting system-level attacks aimed at privilege escalation or data leakage. Building on two key insights regarding RowHammer's behavior—specifically that the induced bit error rate fluctuates consistently with temperature changes and that certain vulnerable cells trigger errors only at specific thermal levels—this paper introduces SpyHammer. This novel attack exploits these characteristics to monitor the temperature of critical infrastructure, including industrial manufacturing, automotive systems, and medical devices. SpyHammer represents the first practical method for spying on DRAM temperature, achieving an accuracy of within 2.5°C at the 90th percentile across 12 real DRAM modules from four major manufacturers.

Deep Neural Networks have proven effective for hyperspectral image classification; however, existing research predominantly utilizes generic architectures that overlook inherent image characteristics, such as physical noise generation. This oversight limits the ability of these models to extract discriminative features and achieve superior classification results. To address this, we propose a novel deep learning framework incorporating a noise-inclined module and a denoising structure. Initially, we characterize the spectral signatures of hyperspectral images using a physical noise model to account for high intraclass variance and significant interclass overlap. Subsequently, the noise-inclined module captures physical noise within objects, which is then eliminated through the denoising framework. Ultimately, a Convolutional Neural Network integrating these components is developed to derive discriminative features and deliver robust classification performance. Experiments on two standard real-world datasets confirm the efficacy of the proposed approach. The code for our method and comparative techniques is available at https://github.com/shendu-sw/noise-physical-framework.

The international Future Circular Collider (FCC) study focuses on designing proton-proton, electron-positron, and electron-proton colliders situated within a proposed 100 km tunnel in the Geneva area. The FCC-ee component, intended as an electroweak, Higgs, and top factory, will facilitate collisions across a center-of-mass energy spectrum ranging from 90 GeV (Z-pole) to 365 GeV (t$\bar{t}$), delivering unprecedented integrated luminosities that generate vast datasets and present major data processing hurdles. This essay examines the storage and CPU requirements across the project's various phases, highlighting potential solutions primarily derived from models established for the HL-LHC.

By integrating the classical theory of motives with the recent framework of noncommutative motives, this article establishes that two quadrics (or more broadly, two involution varieties) sharing the same Grothendieck class necessarily possess identical even Clifford algebras and signatures. Furthermore, as a practical application, we demonstrate across various scenarios—such as when the base field is local or global—that for two quadrics (or involution varieties), having the same Grothendieck class is equivalent to being isomorphic.

Capturing scintillation light generated by liquid Argon and Xenon following molecular excitations from charged particles remains a significant challenge. This study introduces an initial design for a device capable of collecting sufficient luminosity to reconstruct the trajectories of ionizing particles. The approach utilizes masks to encode light signals in conjunction with single-photon detectors, enabling the detection of tracks over focal distances spanning tens of centimeters. Numerical simulations indicate that complex signals can be successfully decoded and identified using a relatively small number of acquisition channels. This innovative technique holds great promise for next-generation detectors aimed at neutrino physics and dark matter research. Specifically, the integration of coded masks with SiPM detectors is proposed for a liquid-Argon target within the Near Detector of the DUNE experiment.

Depth estimation and semantic segmentation are fundamental to scene understanding, with current state-of-the-art approaches utilizing multi-task learning to jointly model both tasks at the pixel level. These existing methods typically rely on sharing common features or concatenating feature maps from separate branches, yet they often neglect the deep correlation between geometric cues and scene parsing. This paper introduces the concept of "semantic objectness" to leverage the geometric relationship between these tasks through an analysis of the imaging process, subsequently proposing the Semantic Object Segmentation and Depth Estimation Network (SOSD-Net) based on this objectness assumption. To our knowledge, SOSD-Net is the first network to apply geometric constraints for simultaneous monocular depth estimation and semantic segmentation. Furthermore, by recognizing the mutual implicit relationship between the two tasks, we incorporate an iterative training strategy inspired by the expectation-maximization algorithm to enhance network performance. Extensive experiments on the Cityscapes and NYU v2 datasets demonstrate the superior efficacy of this proposed approach.

This paper introduces novel approaches for learning Chinese word representations by leveraging the rich semantic information contained within graphical components. Since Chinese learners often derive word meanings from these components, our proposed models enhance word representations by integrating character glyph features. These features are extracted directly from character bitmaps using a convolutional auto-encoder (convAE), subsequently refining word embeddings that are already enriched with character-level information. Additionally, this work contributes to the field by establishing and publicly releasing several evaluation datasets for traditional Chinese.

Most nuclear many-body approaches determine observables by explicitly utilizing many-body wave functions, with the variational two-particle reduced density matrix (2-RDM) method being a notable exception. This technique allows for the calculation of ground-state energies in both open-shell and closed-shell nuclear systems by minimizing a constrained linear functional of the 2-RDM. Despite this potential, the method has rarely been applied in nuclear theory because early results indicated that nuclear ground states were significantly overbound compared to those of atoms and molecules. To address this, we adapted new constraints from the recently developed atomic and molecular variational 2-RDM method for use in nuclear physics. Our calculations demonstrate that this refined approach accurately describes nuclear systems containing only valence neutrons. However, for systems where both neutrons and protons are active, the method still yields overbound energies. We will discuss the likely causes of these discrepancies and propose solutions.

We provide a geometric proof regarding persistence properties for a bi-Hamiltonian system describing shallow water waves, covering both periodic and non-periodic scenarios. A fundamental element of our method involves one of the system's Hamiltonians. Consequently, our findings refine recent studies on unique continuation properties for shallow water equations and offer a new approach to demonstrating that the only compactly supported solution to the system is the trivial zero function.

Quantizing weights and activations is a primary strategy for minimizing the computational burden of training Deep Neural Networks (DNNs). Although existing techniques support 4-bit quantization during the forward pass, this covers merely one-third of the training workflow. To significantly reduce the overall computational footprint, it is necessary to quantize neural gradients—specifically, the loss gradients relative to the outputs of intermediate layers. This study investigates the necessity of unbiased quantization in training quantized networks, detailing how to preserve it. Consequently, we propose a \textit{logarithmic unbiased quantization} (LUQ) method that applies 4-bit quantization to both forward and backward phases, delivering state-of-the-art performance without additional overhead. For instance, on ResNet50 trained on ImageNet, LUQ yields a degradation of only 1.1\%. Furthermore, applying three epochs of high-precision fine-tuning alongside a variance reduction technique lowers this degradation to 0.32\%, with both enhancements incurring overhead comparable to prior methods.

This study introduces an automatic algorithm designed to categorize nocturnal audio recordings from obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) patients into three groups: OSA-related snoring, simple snoring, and other sounds. Recent research suggests that understanding OSA-related snoring can help pinpoint the location of airway collapse. Audio signals were captured using a ceiling microphone simultaneously with full-night polysomnography. Time and frequency features of these signals were extracted to distinguish between the three sound categories. Two algorithms were developed to identify OSA-related snoring, grounded in the hypothesis that such snoring patterns reveal the site of upper airway collapse. An unbiased nested leave-one-patient-out cross-validation method was employed to select an optimal feature set from the available options. The results demonstrated an 87% accuracy in identifying snore events from audio recordings and a 72% accuracy in specifically detecting OSA-related snores among those events. A direct approach using a multi-class LDA classifier achieved 64% accuracy with the selected feature set. These findings clearly indicate that OSA-related snore events can be successfully extracted from nocturnal sound recordings, offering a potential new tool for determining the site of airway collapse based solely on audio data.

Following the COVID-19 outbreak, numerous nations enacted containment strategies to curb disease spread, with digital data confirming significant reductions in individual mobility across various regions. Yet, it was uncertain whether these drops in movement triggered profound structural shifts within mobility networks and how such shifts would influence dynamic network processes. This study analyzes mobile phone user data from Germany to reveal that lockdowns not only drastically lowered mobility but also induced substantial, long-term structural transformations in the mobility network. Specifically, long-distance travel was curtailed disproportionately, resulting in a more localized, clustered network structure and a dampening of the "small-world" phenomenon. We demonstrate that these architectural changes significantly impacted epidemic dynamics by flattening the infection curve and postponing the spread to remote geographical areas.

Gating modules have been extensively studied in dynamic network pruning to lower the runtime computational expenses of deep neural networks without compromising feature representation. Despite these advancements, current methods often overlook the consistency between feature and gate distributions, potentially causing distortion in gated features. To address this, we introduce a Feature-Gate Coupling (FGC) approach designed to align the distributions of features and gates. FGC operates as a plug-and-play module executed through an iterative self-supervised process involving two stages. In the first stage, FGC employs the $k$-Nearest Neighbor method within the feature space to identify instance neighborhood relationships, treating them as self-supervisory signals. In the second stage, FGC applies contrastive learning to regularize gating modules using these generated signals, thereby aligning neighborhood relationships across both feature and gate spaces. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed FGC method significantly outperforms baseline approaches and state-of-the-art techniques, offering a superior accuracy-computation trade-off. The code is publicly accessible.

This work summarizes recent findings on single and double soft theorems for two distinct particles: the dilaton, which serves as the Nambu-Goldstone boson in spontaneously broken conformal field theories, and the massless scalar particle found in closed string theories. The discussion highlights both the similarities and differences between the soft theorems of these particles, as well as their relationships to the underlying symmetries of their respective theories.

This study introduces a Jacobian-free inversion technique designed to enhance the efficiency of Electrical Resistivity Tomography (ERT) for characterizing shallow aquifers. While the adjoint state method is commonly used to compute Jacobians efficiently, it requires intrusive modifications to forward model code and often lacks scalability when handling the numerous observations typical of 3D ERT surveys with dense multi-electrode arrays. To address these challenges, the Principal Component Geostatistical Approach (PCGA)—a rapid and scalable Jacobian-free inverse modeling method—is employed to tackle this high-dimensional, data-intensive problem. By linking PNNL's E4D simulation software with the Python interface pyPCGA, the approach was implemented without any intrusive code changes, and the example code is available in a public repository. The results demonstrate that high-resolution 3D subsurface characterization is computationally viable, indicating significant potential for practical application.

Dialogue systems offer transformative potential for human-machine interaction, yet their performance relies heavily on the quality of training data. Consequently, creating effective annotation tools is crucial to enhancing both the speed and accuracy of dialogue data labeling. Addressing this need, we present LIDA, an annotation platform specifically engineered for conversation data. To our knowledge, LIDA is the inaugural system capable of managing the complete dialogue annotation workflow, converting raw text (such as output from transcription services) into structured conversation data. Additionally, LIDA allows for the integration of arbitrary machine learning models as annotation recommenders and includes a specialized interface for resolving inter-annotator disagreements, particularly following crowdsourced labeling efforts. The tool is fully open source, well-documented, and publicly accessible at [https://github.com/Wluper/lida].

This paper derives approximate bound state solutions for the $N$-dimensional time-independent fractional Schrödinger equation under a generalized pseudoharmonic potential defined as $V(r^{\alpha})=a_1r^{2\alpha}+\frac{a_2}{r^{2\alpha}}+a_3$, where the parameter $\alpha$ (with $0<\alpha<1$) governs the fractional behavior of the spatial variable $r$. The investigation utilizes Jumarie-type derivatives alongside the Laplace transform method. Consequently, the approximate bound state solutions are expressed using Mittag-Leffler functions and fractionally defined confluent hypergeometric functions. This work serves as a generalization of prior studies on the topic when $\alpha=1$ for arbitrary $N$. Numerical results for energy eigenvalues and eigenfunctions are presented for a representative diatomic molecule across various values of $\alpha$ near unity. Finally, the study correlates its findings with the Cornell potential model, specifically the case where $\alpha=\frac{1}{2}$ and $a_3=0$, to predict approximate quarkonia mass spectra.

This study investigates Grad-Avg, an optimizer designed for error functions, proving mathematically that its iterates converge to a minimizer under boundedness conditions. We apply Grad-Avg alongside common optimizers to regression and classification problems. In regression, Grad-Avg exhibits behavior nearly identical to Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD), a finding supported by mathematical justification. For classification tasks, performance improves when parameters are appropriately scaled. Experimental results on two benchmark datasets demonstrate that Grad-Avg converges more rapidly than other state-of-the-art optimizers.

We introduce ScotoZee, a singly charged scalar extension of the Scotogenic framework, which simultaneously addresses recent anomalies in the $W$ boson mass and the lepton $g-2$. This model accommodates either scalar or fermionic dark matter candidates while naturally generating small radiative neutrino masses. The approximately 100 GeV mass splitting among inert doublet fields, necessitated by the $W$ boson mass shift, can be circumvented through mixing with a singlet scalar, a mechanism also crucial for resolving the $(g-2)_\ell$ anomaly within $1\sigma$. We demonstrate that this framework remains consistent with dark matter relic abundance limits, charged lepton flavor violation constraints, direct detection bounds, and collider data. Furthermore, the model yields testable predictions for lepton flavor violating $\tau\to\ell\gamma$ decays in forthcoming experiments.

Scientific literature frequently contains novel or rare vocabulary, posing a significant challenge for word embedding models to generate high-quality vectors for these infrequent or emerging terms. This study demonstrates how Latent Semantic Indexing (LSI) can resolve this issue by inferring embeddings for domain-specific words from current knowledge graphs, such as the MeSH graph, while maintaining the integrity of the original word embedding model without retraining. By evaluating the enhanced model on a biomedical word-pair similarity task, we show that LSI effectively generates reliable embedding vectors for rare and out-of-vocabulary terms within the biomedical domain.

This paper examines multilinear operators that are multiple almost summing and introduces a novel definition of type and cotype for such operators. We investigate the criteria under which this new framework recovers the classical concepts of type and cotype for multilinear operators. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these classes constitute Banach multi-ideals and prove their coherence and compatibility with the associated homogeneous polynomials.

We introduce a new deep learning framework designed for resequencing animation videos. Our approach generates novel video sequences by minimizing the perceptual distance between images derived from an original animation clip. To quantify this perceptual distance, we leverage convolutional neural network activations and train a dedicated network using human perceptual judgments to learn the metric. We demonstrate that combining this perceptual metric with graph-based manifold learning enables our framework to produce smooth and visually engaging animation results across various styles. Unlike prior resequencing methods, our system handles a broad spectrum of image styles without relying on hand-crafted feature extraction, background subtraction, or feature correspondence. Furthermore, we illustrate that this framework is also applicable to arranging unordered image collections in an aesthetically pleasing manner.

This study expands sampling theory on graphs by developing a framework that leverages the structural properties of product graphs to enable efficient sampling and recovery of bandlimited signals defined on them. Product graphs, which are formed by combining smaller graph atoms, offer a versatile and practical approach for modeling complex, multi-modal data classes. While prior research has established sampling theories for bandlimited signals on graphs, our proposed framework notably reduces both sample complexity and computational complexity.

In 2018, CERN executed a test run in the North Area, operating parasitically downstream of the COMPASS spectrometer. The primary objective was to examine elastic interactions between muons and atomic electrons using an experimental setup akin to that proposed for the MUonE project, which intends to conduct highly precise measurements of the differential cross-section for such elastic interactions.
