Specifically, we found that monolingual models pretrained and fine-tuned on various languages perform competitively against those sharing the same target language. Notably, performance remains consistent across tasks regardless of the pretraining language; for instance, models trained on distant languages like German and Portuguese exhibit comparable results on English tasks.

This paper presents a framework for polynomial approximation of solutions to initial value problems in differential equations. Originally designed for ordinary differential equations, this framework is subsequently expanded to handle constant delay differential equations. Within this structure, various relevant classes of Runge-Kutta methods can be derived.

This paper introduces a straightforward, easy-to-implement Bayesian hypothesis test designed to detect an association, quantified by Kendall's \tau coefficient, between two variables measured on at least an ordinal scale. Since likelihood functions for the data are unavailable, we utilize the asymptotic sampling distributions of the test statistic as proxy likelihoods. We further define a truncated normal prior on the noncentrality parameter of the alternative hypothesis, yielding a Bayes factor that is available in closed form via the cumulative distribution function of the standard normal distribution. By examining the asymptotic properties of this Bayes factor, we identify the necessary prior conditions to ensure consistency regardless of which hypothesis holds true. The efficacy of the proposed Bayes factor is demonstrated through simulation studies and a real-data application. Notably, this method is suitable for inclusion in undergraduate and graduate nonparametric statistics courses, with a focus on fostering students' Bayesian thinking in data analysis.

Temporal action localization is a critical yet difficult research area driven by its wide-ranging applications. Given the high labor costs associated with frame-level or segment-level annotations for untrimmed videos, research has increasingly focused on weakly-supervised action detection. However, most current frameworks depend on Class Activation Sequence (CAS) to localize actions by minimizing video-level classification loss; while this approach highlights the most discriminative parts of actions, it often overlooks minor regions. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel weakly-supervised framework utilizing adversarial learning between two modules. The first module is a Seeded Sequence Growing (SSG) Network, engineered to progressively expand seed regions—highly reliable areas initialized by a CAS-based framework—to their anticipated boundaries. The second module is a specialized classifier tasked with mining trivial or incomplete action regions, trained on shared features after the seed regions activated by SSG are erased. Consequently, the entire network comprising these two modules operates through adversarial training. The objective of this adversary is to identify features that are challenging for the action classifier. Specifically, the erasure performed by SSG compels the classifier to uncover minor or even previously undetected action regions within the input feature sequence, while the classifier simultaneously guides the seeds to grow further in an alternating fashion. Ultimately, precise action locations and categories are derived from the well-trained SSG and classifier. Extensive evaluations on two public benchmarks, THUMOS'14 and ActivityNet1.3, demonstrate that our proposed method achieves impressive performance compared to state-of-the-art approaches.

CRESST stands as a leading direct detection experiment for sub-GeV/c$^2$ dark matter particles, distinguished by its ability to utilize a diverse range of nuclides in its target material. This study specifically examines dark matter interactions with the protons and neutrons of $^{6}$Li, made feasible by recent calculations of nuclear matrix elements for this isotope. To demonstrate the utility of $^{6}$Li, we analyzed data from a prior CRESST prototype composed of LiAlO$_2$, which was operated in an above-ground facility at the Max-Planck-Institut für Physik in Munich, Germany. Incorporating $^{6}$Li into the limit calculations significantly enhances the constraints on spin-dependent neutron interactions across the entire mass spectrum. Specifically, for dark matter masses below 1 GeV/c$^2$, this inclusion yields an improvement of more than two orders of magnitude compared to limits previously established using the same dataset.

We establish improved lower bounds for additive spanners and emulators, which serve as lossy compression methods for undirected graphs, along with new bounds for shortcut sets that decrease the diameter of directed graphs. Specifically, we demonstrate that no $O(n)$-sized shortcut set can reduce the diameter below $\Omega(n^{1/6})$, and no $O(m)$-sized set can achieve a diameter lower than $\Omega(n^{1/11})$, surpassing Hesse's [Hesse03] previous limit of $\Omega(n^{1/17})$. By integrating these constructions with the edge-splitting technique from Abboud and Bodwin [AbboudB17], we derive additive stretch lower bounds of $+\Omega(n^{1/11})$ for $O(n)$-sized spanners and $+\Omega(n^{1/18})$ for $O(n)$-sized emulators, thereby exceeding the $+\Omega(n^{1/22})$ bounds set by Abboud and Bodwin.

Whenever an individual sits before a television or monitor, their face is exposed to dynamic, time-varying light patterns. This paper introduces a method to leverage these patterns for synthetic face relighting under arbitrary illumination conditions. Drawing inspiration from Debevec et al.'s Light Stage, which enabled relighting in controlled environments, we show that useful data can be captured using standard displays rather than costly, room-sized spherical gantries typically found only in specialized labs. Instead of forcing users to endure rapid, uncomfortable flashing lights, our approach utilizes images of the user viewing regular content like YouTube videos. By training a deep network on a specific user's face images paired with corresponding monitor light patterns, the system learns to predict how that user would appear under any target lighting condition. Experimental results confirm that our technique generates realistic relighting outcomes, with video demonstrations available at http://grail.cs.washington.edu/projects/Light_Stage_on_Every_Desk/.

We present a measurement of the inclusive $J/\psi$ production cross sections in the reaction $e^+e^-\rightarrow {J}/\psi{\rm X}$, utilizing 3.21 fb$^{-1}$ of data collected by the BESIII detector at the BEPCII collider across an energy range of 3.645 to 3.891 GeV. The energy-dependent lineshape derived from these cross sections is not adequately modeled by two Breit-Wigner (BW) amplitudes corresponding to the expected decays $\psi(3686)\rightarrow {J}/\psi{\rm X}$ and $\psi(3770)\rightarrow {J}/\psi{\rm X}$. Instead, a superior fit is achieved using three BW amplitudes associated with the decays $\psi(3686)\rightarrow {J}/\psi{\rm X}$, $R(3760)\rightarrow {J}/\psi{\rm X}$, and $R(3790)\rightarrow {J}/\psi{\rm X}$, identifying two distinct structures, $R(3760)$ and $R(3790)$. Based on this model, we determined their masses, total widths, and the product of leptonic width and branching fractions as follows: $M_{R(3760)}= {3761.7\pm 2.2 \pm 1.2}$ MeV/$c^2$, $\Gamma^{\rm tot}_{R(3760)}= {6.7\pm 11.1 \pm 1.1}$ MeV, $\Gamma^{ee}_{R(3760)}\mathcal B[R(3760)\rightarrow {J}/\psi {\rm X}]=(4.0\pm 4.3\pm 1.2)$ eV, $M_{R(3790)} = {3784.7\pm 5.7 \pm 1.6}$ MeV/$c^2$, $\Gamma^{\rm tot}_{R(3790)} = {31.6 \pm 11.9 \pm 3.2}$ MeV, and $\Gamma^{ee}_{R(3790)}\mathcal B[R(3790)\rightarrow {J}/\psi {\rm X}]=(18.1\pm 10.3\pm 4.7)$ eV, where the first uncertainties represent statistical errors and the second systematic errors.

This study investigates global dynamics within a monetary framework featuring overlapping generations of finite-horizon agents and a binding lower bound on nominal interest rates. Debt-based targeting rules heighten the risk of self-fulfilling liquidity traps, as agents anticipate austerity measures following deflationary recessions. In contrast, activist yet sustainable fiscal policies—specifically those implementing intertemporally balanced tax reductions and/or transfer hikes in response to disinflationary trends—can prevent liquidity traps and steer the economy toward a globally stable inflationary path converging on the target. However, if last-resort fiscal stimulus is excessively aggressive, it may induce spiral dynamics around the liquidity-trap steady state, resulting in global indeterminacy.

Spin defects in silicon carbide (SiC) have gained significant attention because of their superior optical and spin characteristics, making them valuable for quantum information applications. This study systematically examines how the spin properties of divacancy defects in implanted 4H-SiC vary with temperature. We analyzed the zero-field splitting parameter ($D$), inhomogeneous dephasing time ($T_2^{*}$), coherence time ($T_2$), and depolarization time ($T_1$) across a temperature range of 5 to 300 K. Two samples, implanted with nitrogen molecule ions ($\rm{N_2}^{+}$) at fluences of $1\times 10^{14}/\rm cm^{2}$ and $1\times 10^{13}/\rm cm^{2}$, were evaluated; while both exhibited similar temperature-dependent spin behaviors, the sample with the lower ion fluence demonstrated longer $T_2$ and $T_1$ values. We offer theoretical explanations for these observed temperature-dependent dynamics. This research enhances our understanding of spin property variations in solid-state systems, potentially aiding the development of wide-range thermometers utilizing established semiconductor materials.

High-mass gamma-ray binaries serve as potent nonthermal galactic sources, often containing a pulsar whose relativistic wind collides with an inhomogeneous stellar wind. Previous modeling efforts have relied on either simplistic analytical methods or computationally intensive numerical simulations, neither of which effectively explores a parameter space that is both realistic and broadly applicable. By integrating various semi-analytical tools, this study examines the dynamics and high-energy radiation resulting from a pulsar wind interacting with a stellar wind of varying inhomogeneity levels to determine observable consequences. We utilized a Monte Carlo method alongside a phenomenological clumpy-wind model to calculate the arrival of wind clumps at the interaction site, while a semi-analytical approach was employed to simulate the dynamics of clumps penetrating deep into the pulsar wind zone. This methodology enables the characterization of the shocked pulsar wind region's evolution over timescales significantly shorter than the orbital period. Leveraging this three-dimensional data on the emitting structure, we applied analytical adiabatic and radiative models to calculate variable high-energy emission across binary scales. We find that an inhomogeneous stellar wind drives stochastic variations on an hour-timescale within the geometry of the two-wind interaction structure. Depending on the degree of inhomogeneity, we predict X-ray and gamma-ray variability at the 10–100% level on an hourly scale, with peak variations occurring approximately once per orbit. These results, derived from a comprehensive framework, indicate that current X-ray and future very-high-energy instruments will be capable of detecting the impact of a clumpy stellar wind on shocked pulsar wind emission in gamma-ray binaries.

Since Knowledge Graphs (KGs) function as symbolic structures, specialized methods are required to align them with data mining approaches. RDF2Vec is an unsupervised method that generates task-independent numerical embeddings for KG nodes by adapting successful language modeling techniques. Although the initial approach introduced the Weisfeiler-Lehman (WL) kernel to enhance representation quality, we demonstrate both theoretically and experimentally that this kernel offers minimal improvement for walk embeddings within a single KG. Instead of relying on the WL kernel, we introduce five distinct strategies designed to extract information complementary to standard random walks. By evaluating these approaches across multiple benchmark datasets, we find that the \emph{n-gram} strategy yields the best average performance for node classification tasks, and that optimizing the walk strategy can lead to superior predictive outcomes.

Astrophysical black holes are thought to be encircled by luminous accretion flows, a feature essential for imaging them. This paper examines how quintessence dark energy influences the shadow images of a Hayward black hole within static and infalling spherical accretion environments. We analyze the impacts of magnetic charge and the quintessence state parameter on the event horizons, photon sphere, and impact parameter of this black hole. Furthermore, we investigate the observed specific intensity, as well as the shadow and photon ring luminosities, for the quintessence Hayward black hole across two distinct spherical accretion models. A comparison between a spherically accreting Hayward black hole with and without quintessence reveals that the presence of quintessence dark energy leads to an increase in the radii and luminosity of the shadow and photon rings, while simultaneously decreasing the observed specific intensity of the shadow.

This paper presents the `logitr` R package, designed for rapid maximum likelihood estimation of multinomial and mixed logit models featuring unobserved heterogeneity. By allowing parameters to vary randomly across individuals based on a selected distribution, the package outperforms similar tools like `mlogit`, `gmnl`, `mixl`, and `apollo` in speed. It supports utility models defined in either "preference space" or "willingness to pay (WTP) space," facilitating the direct estimation of marginal WTP. This direct approach avoids the unreasonable WTP distribution issues often found when calculating WTP post-estimation from preference space models. The paper discusses the implications of each parameterization on WTP estimates, outlines the design features driving `logitr`'s performance, and presents a benchmarking study against comparable packages. Additionally, it emphasizes features tailored for WTP space models, such as a unified interface for specifying models in either space and a parallelized multi-start optimization loop. This loop is especially valuable for navigating non-convex log-likelihood functions to identify different local minima.

Social media platforms like Facebook and Instagram are notorious for monitoring user behavior for commercial purposes. Currently, the only way to ensure privacy on these services is to stop using them entirely, yet many users hesitate to do so due to convenience or social and professional obligations. This study introduces a method to balance privacy and convenience on Facebook through obfuscation. We developed MetaPriv, a tool that simulates user interactions with the platform. By injecting noisy interactions into user accounts, MetaPriv confuses Facebook's profiling algorithms, resulting in inaccurate assessments of user interests and habits. Extensive experiments conducted on both a dummy account and two real user accounts demonstrated the tool's efficacy, showing that a significant increase in privacy can be achieved within a few weeks. We envision that MetaPriv can be expanded to support other social media platforms, enabling users to reclaim their privacy without sacrificing convenience. To uphold the principles of open science and reproducible research, the source code is publicly accessible online.

This overview explores the known and unknown aspects of the Kepler-Heisenberg problem, an intriguing dynamical system. The core concept involves reformulating the classical planetary motion problem within a sub-Riemannian framework. This approach yields a system that is both surprisingly rich and beautiful, characterized by a blend of mystery and manageability, thereby presenting numerous questions that appear non-trivial yet solvable.

We examine a rough differential equation featuring a drift component driven by a Gaussian geometric rough path. Assuming natural constraints on the rough path, specifically non-determinism, and uniform ellipticity of the diffusion coefficient, we establish path-by-path well-posedness even for irregular drifts. For fractional Brownian motion $B^H$ where $H>\frac14$, we demonstrate that the drift can be $\kappa>0$ H\"older continuous and bounded, provided $\kappa>\frac32 - \frac1{2H}$. This outcome is achieved by employing a flow transformation of the equation alongside Malliavin calculus tailored for Gaussian rough paths.

Cloud applications are progressively evolving from large monolithic architectures into intricate networks of loosely coupled microservices. Although this shift offers significant benefits, it also brings about challenging, cascading Quality of Service (QoS) violations that are hard to identify and remediate. We introduce Sage, an interactive root cause analysis system for cloud microservices powered by machine learning. Sage utilizes unsupervised learning to avoid the overhead associated with trace labeling, identifies the root causes of unpredictable performance in real-time, and implements corrective measures to restore system efficiency. Experimental results on both local dedicated clusters and large Google Compute Engine environments demonstrate that Sage delivers high accuracy in detecting root causes and ensures predictable performance.

Sentiment Analysis involves identifying the emotional tone of a sentence and categorizing it as positive, negative, or neutral. Recently, India has experienced a significant surge in active social media users, resulting in a vast amount of unstructured text data. Given that the Indian population is typically fluent in both Hindi and English, they frequently produce code-mixed Hinglish content, which combines Hindi expressions written in Roman script with English words. Effectively understanding the sentiments within these texts is essential. Our team, rns2020, participated in Task 9 of SemEval2020 with the goal of developing a system for sentiment analysis of this code-mixed social media text. We propose a framework called NITS-Hinglish-SentiMix designed to effectively perform sentiment analysis on such Hinglish data, achieving an F-Score of 0.617 on the test dataset.

The fundamental identity of Dark Matter remains a primary enigma in contemporary physics. Certain theoretical frameworks suggest a massive gauge boson, known as a "dark photon" ($A^\prime$), could facilitate interactions between Dark Matter particles and those in the Standard Model. Ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions generate intensely Lorentz-contracted electromagnetic fields with energy densities high enough to potentially produce light dark photons. This paper presents constraints on dark photon parameters by searching for anomalous $e^+e^-$ pair production arising from $\gamma A^\prime$ and $A^\prime A^\prime$ fusion in ultra-peripheral $\rm{Au}+\rm{Au}$ collisions. The analysis leverages STAR measurements of the Breit-Wheeler process ($\gamma\gamma \rightarrow e^+e^-$), focusing specifically on polarization-dependent azimuthal asymmetries in the final-state $e^+e^-$ pairs. These results provide valuable insights for future investigations in ultra-peripheral heavy-ion collisions and help constrain upcoming theoretical models of the dark photon mechanism.

Computational methods for optimizing partial differential equation (PDE)-constrained systems under uncertainty frequently rely on various approximations, including finite-dimensional representations of control and state spaces, sample average estimates for risk and reliability metrics, smooth substitutes for nonsmooth functions, and penalty methods for handling constraints. This paper evaluates the performance of controls derived from such approximation-based algorithms and concurrently develops estimates for optimality gaps in general optimization problems defined over metric spaces. Assuming mild conditions, we prove that limiting controls can achieve arbitrarily small optimality gaps as the errors inherent in these approximations diminish. The analysis covers a wide range of problems involving multiple expectation, risk, and reliability functions that depend on PDE solutions and appear within both objective functions and constraints. Specifically, we examine problems featuring buffered failure probability constraints approximated using an augmented Lagrangian approach. We validate this framework through an application to an elliptic PDE characterized by a random coefficient field and a distributed control variable.

Minimizing sensor needs without compromising optimal control performance is essential for industrial applications aiming to develop robust, cost-effective, and computationally efficient controllers. However, standard feature selection methods from machine learning struggle to apply to control systems characterized by changing dynamics. This paper introduces a new framework called Dual-world embedded Attentive Feature Selection (D-AFS), which efficiently identifies the most pertinent sensors for systems under dynamic control. Unlike most Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) algorithms that rely on a single environment, D-AFS operates in both a real world and a virtual counterpart featuring twisted features. By evaluating the DRL agent's performance across these two worlds, D-AFS quantitatively determines the importance of specific features for control tasks. The proposed method is evaluated using a classic active flow control problem, specifically cylinder drag reduction. Results demonstrate that D-AFS successfully identifies an optimized layout of five probes, achieving 18.7% drag reduction compared to the state-of-the-art solution using 151 probes, and 49.2% improvement over a five-probe layout designed by human experts. Additionally, the approach was applied to four OpenAI classical control benchmarks, where D-AFS achieved sensor configurations that were equal to or superior to the original solutions. These findings suggest a novel pathway for creating efficient and optimal sensor designs for both experimental and industrial systems. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/G-AILab/DAFSFluid.

It is a well-known phenomenon that helicopters descending rapidly can enter the Velocity Ram Airspeed (VRS) region, where blade lift deviates significantly from standard conditions, potentially causing instability; consequently, this area is typically avoided by increasing horizontal speed. This study investigates the VRS phenomenon specifically within small-scale quadcopters, identifying the corresponding region through a combination of first-principles modeling and wind tunnel experiments. Furthermore, we argue that quadcopters should also avoid the Wake Blowdown (WBS) or autorotation region, a constraint not always applicable to helicopters. We propose a model detailing the velocity constraints required to evade these hazardous zones and address the challenge of designing optimal time-efficient descent trajectories that circumvent both VRS and WBS. Finally, these optimal trajectories are implemented on a quadcopter, with flight tests demonstrating that adherence to these paths enables a significantly faster descent compared to purely vertical trajectories that also avoid these regions.

Although multi-vessel maritime collisions are uncommon, 2017 saw a series of fatal at-sea incidents involving United States Navy ships that claimed the lives of seventeen service members. This paper introduces an experimental shipboard collision-avoidance system designed to address these tragedies. Our proposed solution utilizes video image processing to ensure the safe navigation and stationing of maritime vessels. Specifically, we employ a convolutional neural network trained on synthetic maritime data to identify nearby vessels, analyze their headings, and issue alerts when inbound ships are detected. Furthermore, we introduce the Navigational Hazards - Synthetic (NAVHAZ-Synthetic) dataset, which contains one million annotated images of ten different vessel classes captured from both virtual vessel-mounted cameras and human "Topside Lookout" viewpoints. This dataset features diverse sea states, lighting conditions, and optical degradations, including fog, sea-spray, and salt accumulation. Our results demonstrate that synthetic imagery can effectively support computer vision-based collision-warning systems, yielding promising performance.

Bicycle-sharing systems (BSS) are now a daily necessity for many residents in larger, affluent cities within developed regions. However, designing the layout of these stations typically demands costly data collection, travel behavior surveys, trip modeling, and subsequent optimization of station placement. Smaller towns and cities, particularly in developing areas, often struggle to fund such initiatives, and the planning process is inherently time-consuming. Nevertheless, as the pandemic demonstrated, municipalities must rapidly adapt to shifting mobility patterns, including a surge in citizens switching from public transport to cycling. Consequently, the ability to quickly deploy bike-sharing infrastructure will be crucial to meeting rising demand. This paper tackles the challenges of cost and time in BSS layout design by proposing a new approach to streamline planning through spatial embedding techniques. Utilizing only publicly available OpenStreetMap data and station configurations from 34 European cities, the study developed a method to segment cities into micro-regions using the Uber H3 discrete global grid system. Furthermore, it identifies optimal locations for new stations by leveraging transfer learning from existing systems across different cities. Ultimately, this work provides a mechanism to assist planners in making informed decisions regarding station layouts by allowing them to select reference cities for comparison.

Over the last decade, the practicality of computational materials discovery has expanded significantly thanks to advancements in computing capabilities and crystal structure prediction algorithms (CSPA). Nevertheless, the high computational expense of the *ab initio* calculations inherent to CSPA restricts its application to small unit cells, thereby limiting the range of compositional and structural possibilities it can investigate. Previous research has mitigated this issue by employing machine learning to forecast formation energy and assess material stability, thereby avoiding numerous unnecessary *ab initio* computations. Among these methods, graph neural networks (GNNs) demonstrate exceptional accuracy in predicting formation energy. Conventionally, GNNs are trained on extensive datasets comprising relaxed structures. However, candidate structures generated by CSPA are often unrelaxed and geometrically distinct from their relaxed counterparts, resulting in poor predictions that impede the model's capacity to filter out energetically unfavorable candidates before *ab initio* evaluation. Our findings indicate that while prediction error on relaxed structures decreases with training, the error on unrelaxed structures rises, revealing an inverse relationship between the accuracy of predictions for the two structure types. To address this, we introduce a simple, physically grounded, and computationally efficient perturbation technique that augments training data, dramatically enhancing predictions for unrelaxed structures. Testing this approach on a dataset of 623 Nb-Sr-H hydride structures using a crystal graph convolutional neural network, we observed that incorporating our augmentation method reduced the mean absolute error (MAE) of formation energy predictions by 66% compared to models trained solely on relaxed structures. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this reduction in error accelerates CSPA by significantly improving the model's ability to accurately exclude energetically unfavorable structures.

Homochirality serves as a defining characteristic of all biochemical life, making the fractional circular polarization it generates a promising and distinct biosignature. Although high-quality circular polarimetric spectra are readily and rapidly acquired in laboratory settings, obtaining precise measurements in the field remains difficult due to significant variations in lighting and target motion. This study presents field measurements taken with the specialized TreePol circular spectropolarimeter over distances of several kilometers, demonstrating that photosynthetic life can be easily differentiated from non-living matter. We highlight the utility of circular polarization signals as a remote method for characterizing and monitoring terrestrial vegetation, with applications in agriculture and forestry. Furthermore, we explore the potential of using circular polarization for the remote detection of life beyond Earth.

The weak splitting number $wsp(L)$ of a link $L$ is defined as the smallest number of crossing changes required to transform $L$ into a split union of knots. We outline criteria determining when specific $\mathbb{R}$-valued link invariants provide lower bounds for $wsp(L)$. These findings are utilized to derive novel bounds for $wsp(L)$ based on the multivariable signature and to re-establish existing lower bounds involving the $\tau$ and $s$-invariants. Furthermore, we introduce new obstructions derived from link Floer homology and employ these techniques to calculate $wsp$ for all prime links with nine or fewer crossings, except for two cases.

Online learning to rank (OLTR) interactively selects item lists from a large pool based on click models that reflect user behavior. While recent research primarily addresses stochastic environments where item attractiveness remains constant, many real-world scenarios involve dynamic or arbitrarily shifting conditions. This study examines OLTR within both stochastic and adversarial settings using the position-based model (PBM). We introduce a method grounded in the follow-the-regularized-leader (FTRL) framework with Tsallis entropy, alongside a novel self-bounding constraint tailored for PBM. We demonstrate that the proposed algorithm achieves $O(\log{T})$ regret in stochastic environments and $O(m\sqrt{nT})$ regret in adversarial ones, where $T$ represents the number of rounds, $n$ the number of items, and $m$ the number of positions. Furthermore, we establish a lower bound of $\Omega(m\sqrt{nT})$ for adversarial PBM, which aligns with our upper bound and surpasses previous state-of-the-art lower bounds. Experimental results indicate that our algorithm effectively learns across both environment types and performs competitively against existing methods designed for single environments.

We introduce a zero-temperature three-flavor Polyakov-Nambu-Jona-Lasino (PNJL) model, designated PNJL0, by incorporating a traced Polyakov loop ($\Phi$) dependence into the scalar, vector, and 't Hooft interaction strengths. Our analysis of the model's thermodynamics focuses on the first-order confinement/deconfinement phase transition, utilizing $\Phi$ as the order parameter. In the symmetric quark matter scenario, we observe a significant decrease in the constituent strange quark mass ($M_s$) at the chemical potential corresponding to the deconfinement point. Furthermore, the inclusion of $\Phi$ promotes chiral symmetry restoration even for strange quarks. We also examine a charge-neutral system of quarks and leptons under weak equilibrium conditions. Applying these findings, we construct a hadron-quark phase transition by coupling a density-dependent hadronic model with the SU(3) PNJL0 model, where the quark sector consists of deconfined particles. This framework is employed to generate mass-radius profiles consistent with recent observations from the Neutron Star Interior Composition Explorer (NICER) mission.

A locally repairable code (LRC) is termed Singleton-optimal when it meets the Singleton-type bound, making it a subject of significant theoretical interest within the LRC domain. Recent years have seen extensive research into this area, with a primary challenge being the determination of the maximum length of a q-ary Singleton-optimal LRC for specific locality and minimum distance parameters. Unlike classical Maximum Distance Separable (MDS) codes, the maximum length of Singleton-optimal LRCs is highly sensitive to both minimum distance and locality, rendering their investigation more complex and difficult. While prior literature has addressed this problem, most studies focus on specific parameter regimes—particularly small minimum distances and locality—and depend on the constraints that $(r+1)$ divides $n$ and that recovery sets are disjoint, where $r$ denotes locality and $n$ denotes code length. This paper examines the problem across a broader spectrum of parameters, including scenarios where the minimum distance is proportional to the length. Additionally, we establish new upper bounds for the maximum length of Singleton-optimal LRCs with small minimum distances by eliminating the aforementioned constraints. Our results demonstrate that even without these constraints, superior upper bounds are achieved for codes with small locality and distance compared to existing findings. Furthermore, by combining our derived upper bounds for small-distance and locality cases with a newly proposed propagation rule, we generate additional upper bounds for codes featuring relatively large distances and locality, under the assumption that $(r+1)$ divides $n$ and recovery sets remain disjoint.

A primary limitation of current state-of-the-art (SOTA) named-entity recognition (NER) systems is their inability to generalize to unseen domains, a critical issue given the high cost and time required to gather labeled data for new domains. To address this, we introduce ZERO, a model designed for zero-shot and few-shot NER that leverages pre-existing semantic word embeddings to adapt to unfamiliar domains. ZERO utilizes the LUKE model to generate contextualized word representations, which are then dimensionality-reduced and directly compared against external knowledge embeddings to train the system on recognizing unseen entities. Our findings indicate that ZERO achieves strong performance on unseen domains with an average macro F1 score of 0.23, surpasses LUKE in few-shot scenarios, and remains competitive in in-domain settings. Furthermore, we observe that performance across source-target domain pairs is inversely proportional to their KL divergence.

Wireless interconnections for sensors, actuators, and controllers offer superior flexibility, reduced installation and maintenance expenses, and enhanced robustness in extreme environments compared to wired alternatives. Nevertheless, to enable wireless communication within cyber-physical systems (CPS), their functional and non-functional characteristics must align with established wired architectures. Consequently, we introduce Time-Triggered Wireless (TTW), a wireless framework designed for multi-mode CPS that ensures reliable communication with guaranteed end-to-end latency for distributed applications running on inexpensive, low-power embedded hardware. This is accomplished by leveraging the high reliability and deterministic nature of a synchronous transmission stack we developed, alongside coupling distributed task execution timings with message exchanges across the wireless network through a new co-scheduling algorithm. Although certain TTW concepts have existed previously and the system has been successfully applied to feedback control and the coordination of multiple mechanical systems with closed-loop stability guarantees, this paper details the underlying algorithmic, scheduling, and networking mechanisms along with their experimental validation, which have not been previously disclosed. TTW is available as open source and ready for deployment at ttw.ethz.ch.

We introduce EdiTTS, a ready-to-use speech editing framework grounded in score-based generative modeling for text-to-speech applications. This approach enables precise, granular adjustments to audio content and pitch without requiring additional training, task-specific optimization, or changes to the underlying model architecture. Specifically, EdiTTS achieves desired outcomes by applying coarse perturbations within the Gaussian prior space to guide the diffusion model, while utilizing masks and softening kernels to restrict iterative edits strictly to the intended regions. Validation through listening tests and speech-to-text back-transcription demonstrates that EdiTTS surpasses current baselines, generating robust outputs that effectively meet user-defined constraints.

This study establishes a geometrically exact framework for analyzing the coupled bending and torsional deformation of a one-dimensional filament adorned with angled, stiff, fish-scale-like protrusions. By integrating a Cosserat kinematic formulation with specific scale contact constraints, the model overcomes the limitations of standard finite element methods when dealing with large deflections. For the first time, the derived structure-property relationships elucidate the combined influence of bending and twisting on a slender, fish-scale-inspired substrate. While this model encompasses existing theories for pure bending and twisting, it also uncovers previously unseen phenomena resulting from the interaction of these loads. These discoveries include a novel interpretation of kinematic locking, various contact regimes, asymmetric sensitivity between curvatures, and abrupt transitions in nonlinear moment-curvature and torque-twist responses, all of which reflect the intricate patterns of scale engagement.

This paper presents a convolutional architecture designed for learning tasks where data resides on multigraphs. By leveraging algebraic signal processing (ASP), we establish a convolutional signal processing model specifically for multigraphs (MSP). Building on this, we introduce multigraph convolutional neural networks (MGNNs), which are structured as stacked layers that process information according to the MSP framework. Furthermore, we devise a method for the efficient calculation of filter coefficients within MGNNs and a computationally inexpensive approach to minimize the dimensionality of data passed between layers. Finally, we evaluate the performance of MGNNs relative to other learning architectures in the context of optimal resource allocation for multi-channel communication systems.

The OSSS inequality, originally established by O'Donnell, Saks, Schramm, and Servedio at FOCS'05, provides an upper bound on the variance of a function $f$ dependent on independent 0-1 random variables. This bound is expressed through the influences of these variables and the computational complexity of a randomized algorithm evaluating $f$. Duminil-Copin, Raoufi, and Tassion later extended this inequality to monotonic measures, yielding new insights into Potts and random-cluster models. Their extension prompts the question of whether the inequality applies to other measure types. We address this by deriving a version of the OSSS inequality for non-monotonic $k$-out-of-$n$ measures, which involve selecting $k$ elements uniformly from a set of size $n$. As an illustration, we apply this inequality to analyze the probability of an occupied horizontal crossing in an $R \times R$ box on the triangular lattice within the site percolation model where exactly half of the vertices are occupied.

This research estimates equilibrium isotope effects (EIEs) during evaporation into various organic solvents—specifically bromobenzene, dibromomethane, ethanol, methanol, and trichloromethane—within their pure phases. The calculations utilize Kohn-Sham Density Functional Theory (KS-DFT) combined with both full Hessian vibrational analysis (FHVA) and partial Hessian vibrational analysis (PHVA). Both methods qualitatively predict compound EIEs; for weakly interacting systems (bromobenzene, dibromomethane, and trichloromethane), FHVA and PHVA yield identical EIE values. Conversely, in strongly interacting systems (ethanol and methanol), PHVA calculates slightly lower EIEs than FHVA. Furthermore, applying Symmetry-Adapted Perturbation Theory (SAPT) alongside the Independent Gradient Model (IGM) allowed researchers to determine how minor fluctuations in interaction energy influence carbon and bromine EIEs in dibromomethane. Additionally, SAPT and IGM demonstrated that seemingly negligible intermolecular interactions in ethanol significantly alter carbon position-specific isotope effects, underscoring the critical role of solvent effects in strongly interacting compounds. These findings offer crucial insights into understanding and characterizing non-covalent interactions within EIE predictions and serve as a rigorous validation test for PHVA.

The hippocampal-entorhinal complex is believed to facilitate domain-general processing and representation of structural knowledge within arbitrary state, feature, and concept spaces. Specifically, it allows for the creation and navigation of cognitive maps, which significantly support overall cognition. It has been suggested that multi-scale successor representations explain the computations performed by place and grid cells. This study introduces a neural network approach to learn these representations, applying it across various scenarios: a spatial exploration task using supervised learning, a spatial navigation task using reinforcement learning, and a non-spatial task involving the inference of linguistic structures from sample sentences. In every scenario, the neural network successfully learned and approximated the underlying structure by constructing successor representations. Moreover, the resulting neural firing patterns closely resemble those experimentally observed in place and grid cells. We conclude that cognitive maps and neural network-based successor representations of structured knowledge offer a promising pathway to address certain limitations of deep learning in the pursuit of artificial general intelligence.

The finite element method (FEM) is extensively employed across numerous simulation domains. However, simulations involving regions with highly varying spatial extents become computationally prohibitive due to the excessive number of degrees of freedom, a challenge exemplified by the cables within particle accelerator magnets. To address translationally invariant domains, this study introduces a quasi-3D approach that integrates a 2D FEM with a nodal basis in the cross-section alongside a spectral method utilizing a wavelet basis longitudinally. Additionally, an adaptive, time-dependent spectral method with a wavelet basis is presented. All proposed techniques are validated, and the method's efficacy is demonstrated through a successful simulation of hot-spot propagation resulting from a quench in Rutherford cables.

The operator-product expansion (OPE) allows for the derivation of the lowest-order, nonlocal quark scalar condensate component within the gluon vacuum polarization. Specifically, this nonlocal quark scalar condensate is computed by solving the Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) Dyson-Schwinger Equation (DSE). Subsequently, the field-theoretic properties of the gluon vacuum polarization and the nonperturbative gluon propagator are examined under the Landau gauge of Lorentz gauge fixing. The resulting gluon propagator remains finite in the infrared region, enabling the determination of the single gluon mass, $m_g$. Our calculated ratio of $m_g/\Lambda_{QCD}$, ranging from 1.33 to 1.39, aligns with prior determinations. Furthermore, the analytic structure of the gluon propagators derived from the OPE is investigated. Numerical analysis of the gluon's Schwinger function provides clear evidence of positivity violations within the gluon propagator. Additionally, a novel approach for determining the chemical potential dependence of both the gluon vacuum polarization and the dressed gluon propagator is introduced.

Pseudo-Hermitian matrices are defined as those that are Hermitian with respect to an indefinite metric. Conceptually, they arise from truncating pseudo-Hermitian operators, defined on a Krein space along with their metric, down to a finite-dimensional subspace. Consequently, within the framework of random matrix theory, these matrices serve as models for chaotic or disordered PT-symmetric quantum systems, as well as their gain-loss-balanced classical counterparts, specifically in the phase of broken PT-symmetry. Their eigenvalues are either entirely real or appear in complex-conjugate pairs. This paper presents a family of pseudo-Hermitian random matrix models that vary parametrically with their metric. Utilizing the diagrammatic method, we derive the averaged resolvent and eigenvalue density as explicit functions of the metric in the large-$N$ limit. As a specific example, we select a simple set of metrics corresponding to an ensemble of elements from a non-compact unitary Lie algebra and calculate the resolvent and eigenvalue density in closed form. The resulting spectrum features a finite proportion of complex eigenvalues distributed uniformly across two two-dimensional regions symmetric about the real axis, alongside a complementary fraction of real eigenvalues condensed into a finite segment with a known non-uniform density. The counts of complex versus real eigenvalues are determined by the metric's signature, specifically the number of its positive and negative eigenvalues. Furthermore, we conducted extensive numerical analysis for these specific metrics, demonstrating that the numerical results converge rapidly to the asymptotic analytical expressions derived for large $N$.

A graph is defined as vertex-transitive when its automorphism group acts transitively on its vertices, and it is a Cayley graph if that group contains a subgroup acting regularly on them. This paper classifies tetravalent, vertex-transitive, non-Cayley graphs of order $6p$ for every prime $p$.

We demonstrate that for any $d$ linearly independent functions mapping a set into a $d$-dimensional vector space over any field, the collection of zero sets formed by all non-trivial linear combinations of these functions possesses both VC-dimension and Littlestone dimension equal to $d-1$. Furthermore, we identify the conditions under which such families achieve the maximum possible VC-dimension of $d-1$ and provide a sufficient criterion for them to be maximal regarding Littlestone dimension $d-1$.

In this presentation, I provide a concise overview of the precision test concerning the unitarity of the first row of the CKM matrix, with a primary focus on the determination of $V_{ud}$ and $V_{us}$ through pion, kaon, neutron, and superallowed nuclear beta decays. I will examine the present state of key Standard Model theoretical inputs required for these processes and highlight the necessity for future enhancements.

This research investigates the three-dimensional equilibrium form of a shell created by deploying an accordion-like origami structure, constructed from an elastic sheet featuring parallel creases intersected by a single central longitudinal fold. Surprisingly, although the imprinted crease pattern lacks intrinsic geodesic curvature, the resulting structure displays an effective curvature generated by the deformation of the central fold. Both finite element simulations and experiments with manually fabricated mylar prototypes reveal a robust empirical correlation between the dimensions of the crease network and the resulting apparent curvature. A thorough analysis of this geometric relationship identifies three characteristic elastic deformations that drive three distinct forms of morphogenesis. We detail the kinematics of these crease network deformations and establish their phase diagram. Leveraging the frustration arising from the competition between crease stiffness and the network's deformation kinematics, we offer a new methodology for designing curved origami structures governed by stringent geometric constraints.

We analyze the pion-nucleon $\sigma$-term, $\sigma_{\pi N}$, utilizing six ensembles of 2+1+1-flavor highly improved staggered quark action provided by the MILC collaboration. The primary systematic challenge in lattice computations of nucleon correlation functions arises from excited-state contributions. By employing chiral perturbation theory ($\chi$PT), we estimate these effects and demonstrate that the dominant contributions to the isoscalar scalar charge originate from N$\pi$ and N$\pi\pi$ states. Consequently, we perform two distinct analyses of the lattice data to eliminate excited-state contamination: a conventional method and a novel approach incorporating N$\pi$ and N$\pi\pi$ states. The standard analysis yields $\sigma_{\pi N} = 41.9(4.9)$ MeV, aligning with prior lattice results, whereas our preferred $\chi$PT-inspired analysis produces $\sigma_{\pi N} = 59.6(7.4)$ MeV, consistent with phenomenological values derived from $\pi$N scattering data. Our data from a single physical pion mass ensemble were essential in revealing this discrepancy; thus, further calculations on additional physical mass ensembles are required to validate our findings and reconcile the tension between lattice QCD and phenomenology.

This study investigates a fractal universe model proposed by Calcagni [JHEP{\bf03}(2010)120] for a power-counting renormalizable field theory within a fractal spacetime. By adopting a timelike fractal profile, we derived the corresponding field equations to examine structure formation and expansion history. Numerical analyses utilizing matter power spectra indicate enhanced structure growth in fractal cosmology, contradicting local galaxy survey data. Furthermore, Hubble parameter evolution suggests a decreasing Hubble constant, which conflicts with low-redshift $H_0$ measurements. Consequently, these initial numerical findings imply that fractal cosmology fails to resolve tensions between local and global observational probes. To achieve greater accuracy, we subsequently constrained the model using observational datasets including Planck CMB, weak lensing, supernovae, baryon acoustic oscillations (BAO), and redshift-space distortions (RSD). The resulting limits on the fractal dimension $\beta$ reveal no significant deviation from the standard cosmological model.

We recently released WeNet, a production-focused end-to-end speech recognition toolkit featuring a unified two-pass (U2) framework and an integrated runtime capable of handling both streaming and non-streaming decoding within a single model. To further enhance ASR performance and meet diverse production needs, this paper introduces WeNet 2.0, which includes four key advancements. (1) We introduce U2++, a unified two-pass framework utilizing bidirectional attention decoders; by incorporating future contextual information via a right-to-left attention decoder, it strengthens the shared encoder's representational capacity and boosts rescoring performance. (2) We integrate an n-gram language model and a WFST-based decoder into WeNet 2.0, enabling the utilization of extensive text data in production environments. (3) We develop a unified contextual biasing framework that leverages user-specific contexts, such as contact lists, to deliver rapid adaptation capabilities for production use and enhance ASR accuracy in both scenarios with and without language models. (4) We establish a unified input-output interface designed to support large-scale datasets for efficient model training. In conclusion, the newly launched WeNet 2.0 delivers up to a 10% relative improvement in recognition performance across various corpora compared to the original version, while offering several essential production-oriented features.

The robotics revolution is advancing through the widespread adoption of robots across diverse commercial applications. Despite the vast variety of environments and use cases, these systems rely on a shared set of components, including modular and scalable architectures, sensing, planning, mobility, and autonomy. While the Robot Operating System (ROS) played a crucial role in the previous era by accelerating research with its open-source, modular framework, ROS 1 lacked essential features required for production environments. In contrast, ROS 2 and its associated projects have been rebuilt from the ground up to address the demands of modern robotic systems operating in new and exploratory domains at all scales. This review examines the philosophical and architectural shifts driving ROS 2's evolution in this new chapter. Furthermore, through case studies, we demonstrate how ROS 2 adoption is propelling real-world robotic systems toward reliable deployment in complex and challenging settings.

This study presents search results for supersymmetry within proton-proton collisions at the LHC, focusing on final states characterized by photons and missing transverse momentum. Using the CMS detector, an integrated luminosity of 35.9 fb$^{-1}$ was analyzed at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV. The findings are interpreted using gauge-mediated supersymmetry breaking models to establish production cross-section limits for gluino and squark pairs. At a 95% confidence level, gluino masses are excluded below 1.86 TeV, and squark masses are excluded below 1.59 TeV.

This study initially details efforts to develop an automated model for detecting bias in Bing and Google search results using cutting-edge methodologies. Secondly, the paper aims to examine YouTube video search outcomes regarding perceived gender bias, specifically focusing on the narrator's gender as interpreted by the viewer. However, experimental findings reveal that the F1-scores of our best model are inadequate for establishing a reliable automated bias analysis system. Consequently, manual annotations are employed to evaluate YouTube video search results for perceived gender bias.

This study theoretically examines the emergent phases of strongly correlated spin-1/2 Fermi gases composed of Rydberg-dressed atoms within a one-dimensional optical lattice. Under weak coupling conditions, a bosonization approach reveals the capacity to induce alternating quantum phase transitions among distinct Luttinger liquids. Conversely, at strong coupling, the ground state exhibits complex phase separation characterized by Luttinger liquid "puddles" divided by magnetic domain walls, arising from the interaction between incommensurate filling and the Rydberg core length scale. Such phases are observable in ultracold Rydberg atom ensembles utilizing $^6$Li.

Precise distance measurements (<10%) for Galactic star clusters enable accurate determination of the physical properties of any physically linked Planetary Nebula (PN), as well as its central star (CSPN) and progenitor. The progenitor's mass correlates with the PN's chemical composition and contributes essential data to the widely utilized white dwarf (WD) initial-to-final mass relation (IFMR), which is vital for understanding carbon and nitrogen evolution across entire galaxies. Currently, only one PN (PHR1315-6555) has been confirmed as physically associated with a Galactic open cluster (ESO 96-SC04), featuring a turn-off mass of approximately 2 M$_{\odot}$. We employed deep HST photometry to search for the CSPN of this currently unique PN, and in this work, we present our findings.

This paper introduces an efficient Federated Distillation Learning System (EFDLS) designed for multi-task time series classification (TSC). The system comprises a central server and multiple mobile users, each potentially executing distinct TSC tasks. EFDLS incorporates two innovative components: a feature-based student-teacher (FBST) framework and a distance-based weights matching (DBWM) scheme. Within each user device, the FBST framework facilitates knowledge transfer from a teacher's hidden layers to a student's hidden layers through distillation, utilizing models with identical architectures. Periodically, the student model's hidden layer weights are uploaded to the server for each connected user. The DBWM scheme operates on the server, employing least square distance to assess weight similarity between models. This method identifies a partner for every connected user by selecting the partner whose weights exhibit the minimal distance to the user's uploaded weights. Consequently, the server facilitates an exchange of these weights between the user and its partner, which are then loaded into the respective teachers' hidden layers. Experimental evaluations on selected UCR2018 datasets demonstrate that the proposed EFDLS achieves superior top-1 accuracy.

This study introduces a proximal bundle (PB) framework utilizing a general bundle update scheme to address hybrid convex composite optimization (HCCO) problems, deriving a unified iteration-complexity bound applicable to all variants within this framework. Consequently, it establishes, for the first time and in a cohesive manner, iteration-complexity bounds for three PB variants grounded in distinct bundle update schemes within the HCCO setting. Among these, two variants are universal, meaning their implementations do not depend on parameters specific to the HCCO instance, whereas the third, a newly proposed variant, lacks universality but offers the benefit of generating simple, one-cut bundle models. Furthermore, the paper details a universal adaptive PB variant based on one-cut models (which falls outside the main framework) and demonstrates that its iteration-complexity matches that of the two aforementioned universal PB variants.

Grasping the implicit biases inherent in training algorithms is vital for elucidating why overparametrised neural networks succeed. This paper investigates the impact of label noise on the training dynamics of a quadratically parametrised model by analyzing its continuous-time formulation. We explicitly characterize the solution selected by the stochastic flow and demonstrate that it effectively solves a Lasso program. To finalize our analysis, we establish nonasymptotic convergence guarantees for these dynamics along with conditions necessary for support recovery. Furthermore, we present experimental results that validate our theoretical assertions. Our findings underscore that structured noise can enhance generalisation, offering a theoretical explanation for the superior performance of stochastic dynamics observed in practical applications.

Driven by the neutron decay anomaly, we re-examine the model for neutron decay into three new particles, $n \rightarrow \chi\chi\chi$, where $\chi$ serves as dark matter. By precisely calculating the $\bar{\chi} n \rightarrow \chi\chi$ reaction rate, we determine that accommodating the anomaly within all existing constraints requires two distinct "generations" of the $\chi$ particle.

Our research demonstrates that a network-structured metapopulation of cooperators, defectors, and destructive agents engaging in the public goods game with mutations can achieve either global synchronization or chimera states. Global synchronization manifests as a unified, periodic surge in cooperation, while chimera states indicate a fragmentation into clusters exhibiting both synchronous and incoherent bursts of cooperative behavior. Numerical simulations reveal that the system's dynamics oscillate between these two steady states via a first-order transition. Furthermore, depending on the parameters governing dynamical and topological characteristics, various chimera configurations with differing counts of coherent and incoherent clusters are observed. These findings constitute the first systematic investigation into the occurrence and characterization of chimera states within evolutionary game theory, offering significant insights into their mechanisms and broadening their applicability to both natural and social systems.

Blind image deblurring aims to simultaneously infer the blur kernel and the underlying latent image from a single blurred input. Since this is an ill-posed problem, it necessitates imposing constraints on either the latent image or the blur kernel. Unlike recent approaches that focus on priors for the latent image, this study regulates the architecture of the blur kernel itself. We introduce a kernel mixture model that utilizes a Gaussian kernel as its foundation. By structurally combining multiple Gaussian kernels with varied scales and centers, this mixture can effectively model the nearly non-parametric nature of blur. Furthermore, a data-driven strategy for determining the number of base kernels enhances the model's flexibility. This method is applied to a remote sensing task to reconstruct images from blurry satellite captures. The results demonstrate that regulating the blur kernel structure yields superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods that rely on regulating the latent image.

An effective model describing the valence band of hexagonal manganese telluride (NiAs-structure) near the A-point of the Brillouin zone has been developed. The study demonstrates that although band splitting at the A-point remains minimal under standard antiferromagnetic ordering (with magnetic moments aligned in the basal plane), rotating these moments out of the plane significantly amplifies the splitting, reaching approximately 0.5 eV. We suggest extending recent experimental work by Moseley et al. (Phys. Rev. Materials 6, 014404), which observed this inversion of magnetocrystalline anisotropy in Li-doped MnTe, to further validate the semiconductor band structure's unique sensitivity to magnetic configuration.

Neural networks have demonstrated high efficiency across various practical domains, including image recognition and detecting phase transitions in quantum physics. This study explores their application to state classification within single-shot quantum measurements. By utilizing dispersive readout of a superconducting transmon circuit, we show enhanced assignment fidelity for both two-state and three-state classification tasks. Crucially, our approach enables real-time data processing without requiring additional overhead or substantial data transfer to storage. Furthermore, we illustrate the ability of neural networks to adapt to experimental imperfections, such as local oscillator phase drift in heterodyne detection setups.

We demonstrate that the shortest and closest lattice vector problems in any norm admit a constant-factor approximation computable within $2^{0.802\, n}$ time. This result stands in contrast to the corresponding $2^n$ time lower bounds derived from (gap)-SETH, which hold even for small constant approximations. For both the Shortest Vector Problem (SVP) and the Closest Vector Problem (CVP), we reduce the general case to the Euclidean norm. A pivotal technical component of this reduction is an adaptation of Milman's construction of an $M$-ellipsoid; this approach approximates any symmetric convex body $K$ with an ellipsoid $\mathcal{E}$ such that $2^{\varepsilon n}$ translates of a constant scaling of $\mathcal{E}$ suffice to cover $K$, and conversely.

This paper analyzes and counts permutations consisting exclusively of 3-cycles that avoid specific patterns, specifically addressing all six patterns of length 3. Our findings reveal that the count of such permutations with $n$ 3-cycles avoiding the pattern 231 (or equivalently 312) equals $3^{n-1}$. Furthermore, the generating function for permutations with $n$ 3-cycles avoiding the pattern 132 (or equivalently 213) is expressed through a formula utilizing the generating functions for Catalan and Motzkin numbers. Finally, we characterize the number of permutations with $n$ 3-cycles that avoid the pattern 321 as a weighted sum based on statistics derived from Dyck paths of semilength $n$.

Large pretrained language models have recently dominated the field of natural language processing. While BERT popularized masked language modeling, the T5 model introduced a more versatile sequence-to-sequence training objective. This approach encompasses masked language modeling but is better suited for generative tasks like machine translation, summarization, open-domain question answering, text simplification, and dialogue systems. Although monolingual T5 variants have primarily been developed for well-resourced languages, the massively multilingual T5 supports 101 languages. In contrast, this study trained two T5-type sequence-to-sequence models of different sizes for Slovene, a morphologically rich language with limited resources, and analyzed their performance. Regarding classification tasks, the SloT5 models generally underperform compared to the monolingual Slovene SloBERTa model, though they remain a viable option for generative tasks.

This work provides an algorithmic proof of the General Néron Desingularization theorem for one-dimensional local rings and implements it in Singular, alongside a theorem that restates Greenberg's strong approximation theorem within the same context.

Although Group Testing (GT) was initially proposed by Dorfman in 1943 to address blood testing issues, the concept has since been widely applied across various domains. Among the numerous binomial GT methods developed over time, Yao and Hwang introduced the Pairwise Testing Algorithm (PTA) in 1990, proving it to be the sole optimal nested GT procedure when contamination probability falls within the interval $\left[1-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},\frac{3-\sqrt{5}}{2}\right]$. Despite the foundational importance of this finding, the PTA has garnered limited attention in academic literature, leaving even its elementary probabilistic characteristics unexamined. This paper addresses that deficiency by offering a comprehensive characterization of the probabilistic properties of the PTA.

Conducting playtests is a critical phase in game design, where feedback informs iterative refinements. To streamline this, designers often utilize procedural personas to automate testing; however, this paper introduces two novel enhancements to that process. First, we advocate for "developing personas," which can evolve toward varying objectives, unlike traditional procedural personas that remain fixed to a single goal. Second, while human testers naturally adapt by exploring new paths after testing known ones, standard Reinforcement Learning (RL) agents often ignore prior exploration. We propose the Alternative Path Finder (APF), a methodology trained on historical paths and integrated into RL training. APF adjusts the environment's reward structure without altering the agent's ultimate goal, thereby encouraging the generation of novel trajectories that still achieve the objective. Using the GVG-AI and VizDoom frameworks with a Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) agent, our experiments demonstrate that developing personas yield deeper insights into diverse player behaviors compared to procedural ones. Furthermore, we illustrate the distinct alternative paths discovered by APF and explain why conventional RL agents fail to learn them.

Diverse fields, including sensing and stealth technology, demand ultrawide-angle electromagnetic wave absorbers that also possess superior mechanical properties. This study introduces a novel 3D reconfigurable metamaterial absorber (MMA) constructed from honeycomb structures and VO2 films. Simulation results indicate that this MMA achieves strong absorptivity exceeding 90% for both TM- and TE-polarized oblique incidences within the yoz-plane, maintaining performance up to an incident angle of 87°. Under normal incidence, when the VO2 films are in their insulating state, the absorber demonstrates high efficiency across the 1-4 THz frequency band. As the temperature of the entire structure rises, VO2 undergoes a phase transition from insulating to metallic. The analysis reveals that under oblique incidence, ohmic losses in the VO2 films—particularly those aligned parallel to the incident electric field—are the primary mechanism driving absorption in this MMA. To elucidate the underlying physical processes, the study examines the induced electric fields and power loss densities within the structure. Additionally, it is demonstrated that the VO2-based honeycomb absorber maintains full-coverage angular characteristics for TM-polarized waves propagating in the xoz-plane. Given its exceptional ultra-wide-angle absorption (angular stability) and mechanical robustness, this MMA is anticipated to be suitable for applications such as camouflage, electromagnetic interference mitigation, imaging, and sensing. To the best of the authors' knowledge, this configuration represents the widest reported incident angle range for absorptivity.

The fluxonium qubit, benefiting from extended coherence times and robust anharmonicity at the half-flux-quantum sweet spot, holds significant promise for achieving high-fidelity quantum gates. Nevertheless, existing two-qubit gate implementations often degrade these coherence properties by necessitating either transient occupation of non-computational states or detuning the magnetic flux from the optimal point. In this work, we implement a rapid all-microwave cross-resonance gate between two capacitively coupled fluxoniums, ensuring that qubit dynamics remain strictly within the computational subspace. We successfully execute a direct CNOT gate in 70 ns, achieving a fidelity of $\mathcal{F}=0.9949(6)$, even accounting for constraints imposed by imperfect measurement techniques and device coherence. These findings suggest a viable route to lowering two-qubit error rates below $10^{-4}$ using current technology.

Recent advancements in neuroimaging have significantly enhanced our comprehension of the human mind. Among these, functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) is the most prevalent technique, yet its application for identifying individual differences is often hindered by high costs and challenges in data acquisition from specific groups, such as infants and children. While surrogate markers that correlate with fMRI findings could be practically valuable, few stand-alone predictors currently exist. This study addresses this gap by employing machine learning models and data augmentation to predict established fMRI markers of human cognition from multivariate patterns of functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS). fNIRS is a portable, cost-effective optical neuroimaging method. We recruited 50 participants who completed two cognitive tasks—the stop signal task and the probabilistic reversal learning task—with neural activation recorded via either fNIRS or fMRI during two separate visits. Our results demonstrate that fMRI markers related to response inhibition and prediction error signals can be accurately predicted from 48-channel fNIRS activation in the prefrontal cortex using these methods. These findings indicate that fNIRS can serve as a viable surrogate for fMRI activation, potentially expanding our ability to study diverse populations, including infants.

Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have reached human-level accuracy in difficult object recognition tasks and serve as the primary quantitative models for predicting neural and behavioral responses in visual recognition. However, a common criticism suggests that, unlike newborn animals which learn quickly and efficiently, CNNs are "data-hungry," needing vast datasets to achieve accurate object recognition. This critique undermines the viability of using CNNs to model visual development. In this study, we directly compared the data requirements of CNNs and newborn animals through parallel controlled-rearing experiments involving chicks and neural networks. We raised chicks in strictly regulated visual environments and replicated these conditions virtually by creating an animal chamber within a video game engine. An agent navigating this virtual space captured visual images used to train the CNNs. When provided with training data comparable to that of the chicks, the CNNs successfully solved the same challenging view-invariant object recognition tasks. Consequently, CNNs were not more data-hungry than animals; both successfully developed robust object models from training data consisting of a single object.

Ground-based detectors can detect gravitational waves from various astrophysical origins, ranging from binary coalescences to isolated rotating neutron stars. Among these, the most promising yet undetected signals are long-duration, quasi-monochromatic Continuous Waves (CWs). The PyFstat package offers a suite of tools for CW data analysis, centering on the F-statistic—a matched-filter technique that has served as a standard for LIGO-Virgo CW searches for twenty years. Built upon LALSuite's established routines but enhanced with a modern Python interface, PyFstat allows for flexible design of new search strategies. Consequently, it fulfills two primary roles: (i) it democratizes LALSuite's CW capabilities via an accessible Python environment, aiding both new users and developers in exploring innovative methods; and (ii) it delivers production-ready search classes for scenarios absent in LALSuite, particularly for MCMC-based follow-up of candidates identified in wide-parameter-space searches.

We present a geometric framework for understanding phase transitions (PTs) in Hamiltonian systems within the microcanonical ensemble. This approach reformulates Bachmann's classification of PTs for finite systems by expressing them through the geometric characteristics of energy level sets (ELSs) linked to the Hamiltonian. By defining microcanonical entropy as the logarithm of the ELS volume, weighted by an appropriate metric tensor, we demonstrate an exact correspondence between thermodynamics and geometry. Specifically, we show that derivatives of entropy with respect to energy correspond to specific combinations of geometric curvature structures of the ELSs, which themselves are precise functions of the potential's derivatives. This establishes a direct link between the microscopic Hamiltonian description and the emergent collective behavior during a PT. Furthermore, we examine the geometry of ELSs in the thermodynamic limit, revealing that non-analyticities in energy derivatives of entropy arise from corresponding non-analyticities in specific geometric properties of the ELSs near the transition point. The validity of this theory is confirmed by analyzing PTs in $\phi^4$ and Ginzburg-Landau-like models.

Conventional web search requires developers to exit their development environments to find solutions via browsers, a process that frequently ignores the specific context of programming issues. This constant switching between the browser and the IDE is both time-wasting and distracting, while traditional keyword-based searches often fail to aid problem resolution effectively. This paper introduces an Eclipse IDE-integrated web search tool that aggregates data from three search engines (Google, Yahoo, Bing) and a programming Q&A platform (Stack Overflow). The system displays search results directly within the IDE, factoring in the selected error content, problem context, result popularity, and search engine recommendations. Testing with 25 runtime errors and exceptions demonstrated that this method surpasses keyword-based approaches, achieving a recommendation accuracy of 96%. Additionally, a user study with five participants yielded a result agreement rate of 64.28%. Although these preliminary findings are encouraging, further validation with a broader range of errors and a larger user group is necessary to fully establish this as a robust IDE-based web search solution.

Thanks to advancements in deep neural networks, Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have become prevalent across various applications. The initial GAN framework relied on the non-parametric assumption of infinite network capacity, yet it remains unclear whether GANs can accurately model target distributions without prior information. This overconfident assumption leaves critical training challenges unresolved, including non-convergence, mode collapse, and vanishing gradients. To stabilize training and enhance discrimination, regularization and normalization are frequently used to introduce prior information. While numerous specific regularization and normalization techniques have been introduced for GANs, no comprehensive survey exists that primarily addresses the objectives and evolution of these methods, aside from a few limited studies. This work presents a thorough review of regularization and normalization techniques from multiple angles of GAN training. We first systematically outline different training perspectives to identify distinct objectives for these methods, subsequently proposing a novel taxonomy. Additionally, we evaluate the performance of mainstream approaches across various datasets and examine their frequent application in state-of-the-art GANs. Finally, we outline potential future research directions in this field. All related code and studies on GAN regularization and normalization are available at https://github.com/iceli1007/GANs-Regularization-Review.

The enumeration $d_k(n)$ of $k$-elongated plane partition diamonds has arisen as an extension of the classical integer partition function $p(n)$. This paper presents an extensive investigation into congruence families for $d_k(n)$ modulo powers of 5, considering cases where $n$ and $k$ follow linear progressions. Specifically, we establish an infinite family of congruences for $d_k(n)$ modulo powers of 5. This family defies proof via classical methods, such as those employed for Ramanujan's congruence families for $p(n)$. Instead, our proof relies on the recently developed localization method and exploits a remarkable internal algebraic structure previously unseen in any congruence family proofs. We contend that this finding holds significant implications for future research in partition congruences.

Quantum entanglement stands as a pivotal concept within quantum physics. This review examines recent advancements in understanding entanglement within many-body systems, specifically through large-$N$ solvable models such as the Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev (SYK) model and its extensions. We analyze entanglement entropy in the original SYK model via three distinct methods: exact diagonalization, the eigenstate thermalization hypothesis, and the path-integral formalism. In coupled SYK systems, entanglement entropy exhibits linear growth followed by saturation at the thermal limit, a phenomenon linked to replica wormholes in gravitational theories. Furthermore, we investigate the steady-state entanglement entropy of quantum many-body systems subjected to repeated measurements, where symmetry breaking in the expanded replica space induces a measurement-induced entanglement phase transition.

Assume $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are positive real numbers. Let $F(x)$ be a Hahn series belonging to $K[[x^\Gamma]]$. We demonstrate that if $F(x)$ satisfies both $\alpha$-Mahler and $\beta$-Mahler properties, it necessarily reduces to a rational function, $F(x) \in K(x)$, provided that certain non-degeneracy conditions are met by $\alpha$ and $\beta$.
