Launched on December 25, 2021, the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) is the subject of this document, which details a simulated Near Infrared Spectrograph (NIRSpec) observation of the Orion Bar within the Early Release Sciences (ERS) program "PDRs4all." The data generation process utilizes a direct forward model of the instrument applied to a synthetic representation of the Orion Bar, combined with format matching to output data in the JWST pipeline standard. A publicly available 3D cube for a single order is provided, compatible with STScI tools like Cubeviz and the science products created by the PDRs4all team. This cube serves as a template for proposers seeking NIRSpec observations of extended sources using JWST.

This study presents the development of a deep Artificial Neural Network (ANN) designed to accurately localize simulated gravitational wave signals across the sky. The sky was modeled as a sphere segmented into 18, 50, 128, 1024, 2048, and 4096 sectors, with source direction estimated by classifying signals into these sectors based on their right ascension and declination. We generated training data by injecting simulated binary black hole signals, with component masses uniformly distributed between 30 and 80 solar masses, into Gaussian noise, utilizing whitened strain values as input features. The ANN was fed features derived from raw time-domain strain data and analytical versions obtained via Hilbert transformation, including arrival time delays, phase differences, and amplitude ratios measured at the Hanford, Livingston, and Virgo detectors. Results demonstrate that the model achieves very high accuracy (>90%) in classifying unseen gravitational wave samples into correct sectors for coarse resolutions (18, 50, and 128 sectors). Furthermore, we evaluated the model's performance on test samples corresponding to published LIGO binary black hole merger events (GW150914, GW170818, and GW170823) using 1024, 2048, and 4096 sectors, comparing outcomes against BAYESTAR and Parameter Estimation (PE) methods. Additionally, our model localizes a single GW signal in approximately 0.018 seconds when running on 14 Intel Xeon CPU cores.

Conventional methods for acquiring 3D scene data typically necessitate capturing multiple 2D images from various angles. In contrast, this study presents a reconstruction of 3D information via ray-tracing using quantum-correlated photon pairs. By employing time-tagging cameras to record both photons in separate image planes and leveraging their inherent correlations in position, momentum, and time, the propagation path of the photons can be determined. Utilizing these trajectory details for each photon pair, we successfully demonstrated capabilities such as refocusing, depth-of-field control, and parallax visualization of three-dimensional scenes. As camera technology advances, this approach could surpass conventional methods in momentum resolution, thereby offering an extended depth of field and broader viewing angles. Furthermore, the combination of high photon correlation and low photon flux inherent to quantum sources makes this technique particularly ideal for imaging light-sensitive samples.

We introduce the concept of an associative (BiHom-)Yang-Baxter pair with weight $(\lambda,\gamma)$, which yields solutions for the double curved Rota-Baxter (BiHom-)system. Equivalent characterizations for (quasitriangular) covariant BiHom-bialgebras are established. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the associative BiHom-Yang-Baxter equation with weight $-1$ arises from the unitary quasitriangular covariant BiHom-bialgebra. Finally, we outline two methods for constructing (BiHom-)pre-Lie modules starting from Rota-Baxter (BiHom-)paired modules.

This paper introduces two foundational concepts regarding elementary particle motion: internal "spin motion" or *Zitterbewegung* and the particle as concentrated energy. First, the particle undergoes random motion within a confined quantum-sized volume, behaving like a vibrating system that diffuses when absorbing or emitting quantized energy. This quantum volume acts as a carrier amplitude, while the particle's vibrational motion, characterized by specific frequency and amplitude, functions as a modulating signal. The diffusion current within this volume gives rise to the spin phenomenon, evidenced by the presence of Clifford algebra. Second, the particle is defined as pure energy concentrated on the surface of a three-dimensional spherical form (a 2-manifold without boundary). By establishing the particle's mass as an invariant quantity based on these two ideas, we derive both the diffusion constant within the quantum volume ($\beta = \hslash/2m$) and the Schrödinger equation. Additionally, by positing that the particle's vibrational motion within the quantum volume serves as the fundamental unit of time interval (proper time or particle clock), we demonstrate that the particle's relativistic effects must correspond to atomic processes.

We consider Bartnik data, defined by a specified metric and mean curvature, on a 2-sphere that represents a minor perturbation of the data associated with the standard unit sphere in Euclidean space. We calculate the mass of the unique (up to diffeomorphism) asymptotically flat static vacuum extension to second order in the perturbation magnitude; this extension is a slight deviation from the flat metric on the exterior of the unit ball and generates the prescribed boundary data. As an application, we derive a novel upper bound for the Bartnik mass of small metric spheres, accurate to fifth order in the radius.

Active forces disrupt the conventional framework of statistical mechanics, rendering the standard derivation of stationary state probabilities inapplicable. Furthermore, it remains unclear how distinct forms of dissipation, such as curl forces or coupling to multiple temperature baths, influence microscopic state probabilities. This manuscript demonstrates that a single microscopic response function dictates the reaction of stationary probabilities to non-equilibrium perturbations in an overdamped system, covering two distinct types of non-equilibrium: differential heat baths and deterministic non-conservative forces. This function is calculable via a path integral within the unperturbed system. While an analytic form exists for harmonic systems, drawing parallels with quantum theory reveals that microscopic state probabilities correspond to the total dissipation across all paths originating from that state. We derive simple analytic expressions for harmonic systems, showing that these two non-equilibrium regimes exhibit divergent behaviors in the original system's mode space. Additionally, we explore extending these findings to anharmonic systems, suggesting a general principle where dissipative processes most significantly impact the soft modes of the equilibrium state. Our theoretical predictions are validated through simulations of active polymers.

Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) utilized in practical scenarios, including autonomous driving, have demonstrated susceptibility to manipulation attacks like poisoning and fine-tuning. Consequently, guaranteeing the integrity and authenticity of these models is critical, as compromised versions may generate erroneous results or act maliciously. This paper introduces DeepiSign, a self-contained tamper-proofing mechanism designed to safeguard CNN models against such threats. By leveraging fragile invisible watermarking, DeepiSign securely embeds a secret and its corresponding hash directly into the model. Verification is achieved by extracting the secret, recalculating its hash, and comparing it against the embedded value. To mitigate the impact of the embedded secret on model performance, the method employs a wavelet-based approach to shift weights into the frequency domain, embedding the secret within less significant coefficients. Theoretical analysis indicates that DeepiSign can conceal up to 1KB of data per layer with negligible accuracy loss. Experiments conducted on four pre-trained architectures (ResNet18, VGG16, AlexNet, and MobileNet) across three datasets (MNIST, CIFAR-10, and ImageNet) against three attack vectors (targeted input poisoning, output poisoning, and fine-tuning) confirm that DeepiSign maintains verifiable integrity without degrading classification accuracy and remains robust against representative CNN manipulation attacks.

Gradient inversion attacks pose a significant threat to data privacy in federated learning (FL) by allowing the reconstruction of training samples from model updates. While previous research has introduced defenses based on differential privacy and heuristic gradient compression—particularly the latter, which maintains model accuracy while substantially reducing attack success—this work challenges the validity of those findings. We demonstrate that current protective measures are vulnerable to a straightforward adaptive attack. By training a model on auxiliary data to learn gradient inversion techniques, this new approach successfully compromises existing defenses across both vision and language tasks, indicating that the perceived privacy risk in FL remains underestimated.

Dense retrievers utilize pre-trained language models to encode queries and documents into an embedding space, requiring high-dimensional embeddings to capture training signals and ensure retrieval effectiveness. However, such high dimensions result in increased index storage and retrieval latency. To address this, we propose a Conditional Autoencoder (ConAE) that compresses these high-dimensional embeddings while preserving their distribution and enhancing the recovery of ranking features. Experimental results demonstrate that ConAE effectively reduces embedding dimensions, achieving ranking performance comparable to the teacher model while improving system efficiency. Further analysis reveals that ConAE can mitigate embedding redundancy in dense retrieval using merely a single linear layer. All code for this project is available at https://github.com/NEUIR/ConAE.

Although substantial research has been conducted, genuine quantum advantages remain rare in algorithms designed for classical optimization, largely due to prohibitive circuit depths and nonconvex optimization landscapes. To address these hurdles, we propose a novel variational quantum algorithm enhanced by multi-basis graph encodings and nonlinear activation functions. This approach yields superior optimization performance, doubles the effective quantum resources, and reduces measurement complexity by a quadratic factor. While simulating many qubits using conventional quantum formalism is infeasible because of exponential scaling, we overcome this barrier by employing exact circuit representations based on factorized tensor rings. Specifically, the combination of shallow circuits enabled by our method and efficient tensor-based simulation allows us to optimize the MaxCut problem for nonlocally connected graphs with 512 vertices from the DIMACS library using only a single GPU. By enhancing quantum optimization performance while minimizing resource requirements and utilizing shallower, more fault-tolerant circuits, we demonstrate meaningful advancement in the field of variational quantum optimization.
We demonstrate the rigidity of the tangent bundle associated with a manifold of K3^[2]-type.

A defining characteristic of non-Hermitian systems is the existence of two distinct topological categories: one that extends Hermitian topological phases and another, unique to non-Hermitian contexts, known as line-gap and point-gap topology, respectively. While the bulk-boundary correspondence is a foundational principle in line-gap topology, its function within point-gap topology remained ambiguous until now. This work establishes the bulk-boundary correspondence for point-gap topology in non-Hermitian systems. By identifying the necessary conditions for point-gap topology under open boundary conditions, we demonstrate that the bulk point-gap topology in such open systems can differ from that in periodic boundary conditions. Furthermore, we provide a comprehensive classification of open boundary point-gap topology incorporating symmetry and show that non-trivial open boundary topology gives rise to robust and exotic surface states.

Precise management of a laser beam's shape and polarization is crucial for fields including high-resolution imaging, optical manipulation, and optical communications. This study introduces an inverse design approach for monolithic whispering-gallery nanolasers that emit axially with customized beam profiles and polarization states. We successfully designed and experimentally validated three distinct sub-micron cavities, each generating a unique radiation mode: an azimuthally polarized doughnut beam, a radially polarized doughnut beam, and a linearly polarized Gaussian-like beam. The measured output beams demonstrated field overlaps of 92%, 96%, and 85% with their respective target modes for the azimuthal, radial, and linear cases, confirming the method's versatility in creating ultra-compact lasers with tailored emission characteristics.

"Civilian self-defense groups have displaced the influential Knights Templar drug cartel from various towns in Michoacán. This militia movement has gained significant traction on social media, especially through the 'VXM' ('Courage for Michoacán') Facebook page, which boasts over 170,000 followers. While prior research on the Drug War has noted social media's role in reporting violent incidents in real time, VXM distinguishes itself by adopting a pro-militia propagandist stance that facilitates two-way engagement with its audience. This study offers a descriptive analysis of VXM and its user base, examining nine months of activity from the page's inception until May 2014. This period included 6,000 posts by administrators and over 108,000 comments from followers. The analysis outlines primary conversation themes, posting frequency, connections to offline events and public figures, and the behavior of the most active audience members. The findings illustrate VXM's online mobilization tactics and demonstrate how the audience contributes to shaping the narrative of this armed conflict. Finally, the paper discusses potential applications of these insights for the development of future communication technologies."

This study investigates the application of artificial neural networks to determine the geographical origin of clove buds by analyzing their metabolite profiles. While large datasets are typically essential for precise machine learning identification, the clove industry is constrained by the high cost of extraction and the scarcity of metabolite composition data, resulting in the use of smaller datasets. Despite these limitations, the results demonstrate that both backpropagation and resilient propagation algorithms, configured with one or two hidden layers, can accurately identify clove bud origins. Specifically, the backpropagation model with a single hidden layer achieved 99.91% accuracy on training data and 99.47% on testing data. Meanwhile, the resilient propagation model utilizing two hidden layers attained 99.96% accuracy for training and 97.89% for testing.

This study introduces an efficient numerical approach for seismic blind deconvolution within a multichannel context. The proposed technique operates through two iterative steps: initially, a wavelet is estimated across all channels, followed by a simultaneous refinement of the reflectivity estimate using sparse deconvolution. The reflectivity update is modeled as a basis pursuit denoising problem, solved via the spectral projected-gradient algorithm to yield a sparse solution while adhering to the recorded noise level. Wavelet re-estimation is achieved through a closed-form solution in the frequency domain by identifying the minimum energy wavelet shared across all channels, requiring no prior knowledge of the wavelet except its duration. Evaluations on both synthetic and real data demonstrate that the method produces sparse reflectivity series and stable wavelet estimates, outperforming existing techniques with substantially reduced computational cost.

NGC 7469 is a prominent Luminous Infrared Galaxy characterized by a circumnuclear star-forming ring with a radius of approximately 830 pc encircling a Seyfert 1 active galactic nucleus (AGN). While prior research identified nuclear winds in X-ray and UV bands, along with an extended biconical outflow traced by infrared coronal lines, this study investigates extended outflows by analyzing the kinematics of the $\mathrm{H\beta}$ and [O III] $\lambda 5007$ optical emission lines using VLT/MUSE integral field spectrograph data. Our analysis reveals two distinct kinematic regimes: a slower outflow spanning most of the star-forming ring, potentially driven by intense star formation, and a faster regime (reaching peak velocities of $-715 \ \mathrm{km \ s^{-1}}$) detected exclusively in [O III] within the western sector between the AGN and the ring's massive star-forming zones, which is likely AGN-driven. These findings demonstrate a scenario where the combined feedback from both the AGN and star formation can be effectively resolved spatially, offering a valuable pathway to better comprehend feedback mechanisms in the central kiloparsec of AGN.

In a varying environment, consider a doubly infinite branching tree where the backward-in-time genealogy of the current generation is uniquely defined by the coalescent point process $(A_i, i\geq 1)$, with $A_i$ representing the coalescence time between individuals $i$ and $i+1$. Generally, this process lacks the Markov property. While Lambert and Popovic (2013) introduced a Markov process of point measures $(B_i, i\geq 1)$ to reconstruct the coalescent point process under constant environmental conditions, we provide a counterexample demonstrating that this process does not possess the Markov property. We define a vector-valued Markov process containing the minimal information necessary to reconstruct the standing population's genealogy and identify it as the Markovian correction to $(B_i, i\geq 1)$. Furthermore, when offspring distributions follow a lineal fractional pattern, we demonstrate that the variables $(A_i, i\geq 1)$ are independent and identically distributed.

The optical colors of quasars are typically explained through two main frameworks: unified models, which link color to the random orientation of the accretion disk relative to the observer, and evolutionary models, which posit a connection between quasar systems and their surrounding environments. To evaluate these theories, we investigated the dark matter halo environments of optically selected quasars across a range of $g-i$ optical colors. This analysis utilized two-point correlation functions for approximately 0.34 million eBOSS quasars and measured the gravitational lensing of cosmic microwave background photons by roughly 0.66 million XDQSO photometric candidates. Neither method revealed a correlation between halo bias and optical color. Consequently, we find that quasars with redshifts between 0.8 and 2.2 reside in halos of a consistent characteristic mass ($M_{h}\sim 3\times 10^{12} \ h^{-1} M_{\odot}$), irrespective of their color. This suggests that a quasar's large-scale environment is not tightly coupled to its observed optical color. Furthermore, by stacking 1.4 GHz FIRST images, we confirmed existing findings that red and blue quasars exhibit fundamentally different radio properties, indicating that these distinctions are not merely due to orientation. Instead, the differences likely originate on nuclear scales, possibly caused by reddening from a dusty nuclear wind. Additionally, we demonstrate that the halo environments of optically selected quasars are independent of their $r-W2$ optical-infrared colors, contrasting with previous studies suggesting that mid-infrared-selected obscured quasars inhabit more massive halos. We conclude by discussing the implications of these results for models of quasar and galaxy co-evolution.
We demonstrate that the formula for the precise irrationality exponent of regular continued fractions also holds true for semi-regular continued fractions under specific conditions.

Although numerous methods exist for identifying depression, they mainly assess the current severity of the condition. This study investigates predicting future depression through machine learning applied to longitudinal socio-demographic data. We demonstrate that factors such as housing status and family environment details offer valuable indicators for anticipating psychiatric disorders. To achieve this, we propose a novel deep multi-task recurrent neural network designed to capture time-dependent depression cues. This model jointly optimizes the depression prediction task with two auxiliary anomaly ranking tasks: contrastive one-class feature ranking and deviation ranking. These auxiliary tasks address two critical challenges: first, the high within-class variance in depression samples, enabling the learning of representations robust to diverse in-class distributions; and second, the scarcity of labeled data, significantly improving sample efficiency and reducing dependence on large, hard-to-collect labeled datasets. Extensive empirical evaluations on large-scale child depression data confirm that our model is highly sample-efficient, accurately predicting depression onset 2–4 years in advance and substantially outperforming eight representative baselines.

The advent of large-scale pretrained language models has significantly enhanced text generation capabilities, with impressive results often achievable through few-shot fine-tuning. However, prior research predominantly relies on random sampling to select these few-shot training examples, largely neglecting the impact of selection strategies on performance. This study investigates instance selection in few-shot neural text generation, focusing on identifying high-value data points for annotation within a constrained labeling budget using only unlabeled data. Guided by the intuition that training instances should be both diverse and representative of the overall data distribution, we introduce a straightforward selection method based on K-means clustering. Our experiments demonstrate that even this basic clustering approach consistently outperforms random sampling across three distinct text generation tasks: data-to-text generation, document summarization, and question generation. We anticipate that this research will draw greater attention to this previously underexplored domain.

Neural network policies developed via Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) are widely recognized as vulnerable to adversarial attacks. This paper examines attacks that introduce perturbations into the observation space controlled by the external environment, which have been demonstrated to severely degrade policy performance. We investigate well-trained deterministic and stochastic neural network policies within continuous control benchmarks, subjecting them to four established observation-space adversarial attacks. To mitigate these threats, we introduce a novel defense mechanism based on a detect-and-denoise framework. In contrast to prior adversarial training methods that necessitate sampling data under attack conditions, our approach eliminates the need for such risky training scenarios. Comprehensive experimental results indicate that our technique achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art adversarial training strategies.
This note introduces a more straightforward approach to demonstrating the compactness of closed intervals within a simply ordered set equipped with the order topology.

This study introduces two random banking data generators built upon migration matrices and scoring rules. These generators offer a novel approach for researchers seeking to validate comparative methods across various credit scoring techniques. The analysis examines how a single cyclic macroeconomic variable affects stability over time regarding client characteristics and account metrics. The data provides significant utility for comprehending the intricacies of banking processes and supports both academic research and student studies. Furthermore, the paper presents compelling insights into crisis behavior, demonstrating that when crises are driven by multiple factors—including both application and behavioral customer traits—it becomes extremely difficult to identify these specific influences within standard scoring analyses, as crisis indicators appear universally across all risk reports.

Drawing inspiration from the European Central Bank's unconventional measures, we propose a specialized class of Multiplicative Error Models (MEM), termed MEM with Asymmetry and Policy effects (MAP), designed to assess how these policies influence stock market volatility. This new modeling framework isolates baseline volatility dynamics from a distinct component that captures policy impacts, characterized by heightened volatility on announcement dates and a subsequent decline as implementation effects unfold. When tested across four Eurozone markets, a Model Confidence Set analysis reveals a notable enhancement in forecasting accuracy following the Expanded Asset Purchase Programme. Furthermore, a multi-step ahead forecasting exercise determines the duration of this impact, while shock simulations on the policy variable quantify the resulting volatility reduction, which proves to be particularly pronounced in debt-troubled nations.

Numerous model-based scientific and engineering techniques, including system identification, sensitivity analysis, optimization, and control, necessitate extensive model evaluations. Specifically, real-time control of urban water systems and online flood warning mechanisms demand rapid predictions of network responses across varying actuation and parameter settings. Consequently, standard urban drainage simulators are often too computationally slow for these purposes. To address this efficiency requirement, fast surrogate models known as emulators offer a viable solution. Emulators are appealing because they trade off unnecessary accuracy for computational speed; however, they require careful tuning to adequately predict system behavior and can struggle to extrapolate beyond their training data. Despite the availability of numerous emulator development strategies, selecting the appropriate approach has historically been subjective. This paper compares the performance of two emulator families applied to open channel flows within urban drainage simulations: mechanistic emulators based on Gaussian Processes that incorporate knowledge of the simulator's equations, and purely data-driven emulators utilizing matrix factorization. Our findings indicate that, for many urban applications, straightforward data-driven emulation surpasses mechanistic approaches. Nevertheless, we identify scenarios where mechanistic emulation may be advantageous, particularly for temporal extrapolation and handling sparse or unevenly sampled data. Additionally, we reference recent advancements in Machine Learning that have yet to be widely adopted by the Bayesian environmental science community.

Formal verification ensures robust software correctness, a necessity for systems where safety or security is paramount. Hoare logic serves as a prevalent formalism for rigorously verifying software against specifications defined by pre- and post-condition assertions. Recent strides in semantic parsing, combined with enhanced computational power, now allow for the accurate extraction of logical forms from natural language text. This paper introduces a formal framework for verifying imperative programs using Hoare logic, driven by logical forms derived from the compositional semantic parsing of natural language assertions. We term this methodology Natural Hoare Logic, which facilitates direct formal verification of software based on safety requirements articulated by domain experts in plain language. The approach addresses both declarative assertions regarding program invariants and state changes, as well as imperative assertions that define commands modifying program state. Furthermore, we explore extensions incorporating domain knowledge and propose practical strategies to mitigate errors arising from semantic parsing.

This article constructs a conjugacy map for a linear difference equation featuring infinite delay and associated nonlinear perturbations. We further demonstrate that this map is injective under certain additional conditions. As an application of our findings, we establish that cases of (uniform) exponential dichotomy are consequences of our result.

When a physical system is driven out of equilibrium, the statistical distribution of its dynamical trajectories reveals key physical properties. A central challenge in nonequilibrium statistical mechanics is characterizing the distribution of dynamical observables, such as entropy production rates or currents. Asymptotically, for a wide range of observables, the distribution follows a large deviation principle under Markovian dynamics, allowing long-time fluctuations to be described via a scaled cumulant generating function. However, calculating this function analytically (and often numerically) remains intractable for complex, interacting systems, necessitating robust numerical methods to investigate nonequilibrium materials. This work introduces an algorithm that reformulates the problem as a variational optimal control task. We determine optimal control forces using neural network ansätze specifically tailored to the target physical systems. Our approach yields accurate and transferable solutions for two systems comprising large numbers of interacting particles.

We introduce a test of the recently proposed $f(\mathcal{R})$ gravity model at galactic scales by analyzing test particles in stable circular orbits around galactic centers. Our investigation employs the Palatini approach within the Weyl transformation framework, which converts the theory from the Jordan frame to the Einstein frame. We derive the rotational velocity expressions for these particles under the new $f(\mathcal{R})$ model and demonstrate that predicted rotation curves align well with observational data from high and low surface brightness galaxies, suggesting the model can account for flat rotation curves. Additionally, we examine the ultra-diffuse galaxy AGC 242019, previously identified as a dark matter-dominated system with a slowly rising rotation curve similar to low surface brightness galaxies, finding that our model's predictions fit its rotation curve accurately. Finally, we analyze the Tully-Fisher relation across the entire galaxy sample, confirming that the model's predictions remain consistent with the data.

Graph-based synset induction techniques, including MaxMax and Watset, rely on global clustering within a synonymy graph. However, these methods are highly sensitive to the graph's structure, where sparsity in the input dictionary can significantly degrade synset quality. This paper introduces two strategies to mitigate the incompleteness of input dictionaries: the first employs pre-processing to insert missing edges, while the second utilizes post-processing to merge similar synset clusters. We evaluate these methods using two Russian language datasets and analyze their impact on synset induction performance. Furthermore, we conduct a detailed error analysis for each approach and discuss leading alternative methods for addressing the issue of sparse synonymy dictionaries.

The sundial serves as a traditional timekeeping instrument, particularly before mechanical clocks were invented. In classical Islamic civilization, the sun's daily trajectory became the primary method for determining prayer times, a function achieved through sundials. This technology likely spread to Indonesia during the era of Islamic acculturation. Since that time, advancements in Indonesian astronomy, technology, art, and architecture have been partially mirrored in the design and use of sundials. Given the scarcity of these historical artifacts in existing literature, there is an urgent need for comprehensive documentation and investigation of Indonesian sundials. Such data collection can be facilitated by the general public through a citizen science initiative. This approach not only satisfies scientific curiosity but also educates the populace by exposing them to scientific concepts. This article discusses the general framework of citizen science and proposes its application to Indonesian sundial research under the "Suryakala-Nusantara" program.

Photonic lattices are extensively employed to simulate quantum physics due to the analogous evolution of paraxial waves and quantum particles; however, nonparaxial wave propagation disrupts this quantum-optical analogy. This study demonstrates that nonparaxiality applies both stretching and compressing forces to the energy spectrum within the renowned Aubry-Andre-Harper model. By investigating mini-gaps arising from the finite size effects of nonparaxiality, we experimentally show that the expansion of one band gap facilitates the adiabatic transfer of boundary states, while the narrowing of the other gap triggers a Landau-Zener transition. In contrast, under the paraxial approximation, identical transport behaviors would be anticipated for both gaps. These findings not only provide a foundation for future research into dynamic state transfer but also suggest applications that utilize nonparaxial transitions as an additional degree of freedom.

Security has become a paramount concern in contemporary society to safeguard critical assets against disclosure, theft, or destruction. While Schneier's informal attack tree model, widely adopted in industry and recommended by the 2008 NATO report for risk assessment, laid the groundwork, subsequent theoretical research has explored various formal approaches, notably through attack-defense trees. Building on M. Audinot et al.'s 2017 introduction of path semantics over transition systems for attack trees, we propose a two-player interpretation of this formalism. In our approach, transition systems are substituted with concurrent game arenas, where semantics are defined by strategies. We demonstrate that while the emptiness problem is NP-complete under the original path semantics, it becomes PSPACE-complete in our two-player framework. Furthermore, we show that the membership problem is coNP-complete for this new interpretation, whereas it reduces to P in the context of path semantics.

We propose a flavor model utilizing the A4 modular group to simultaneously describe quark and lepton parameters, including masses and mixing angles. The light neutrino masses are generated through the inverse seesaw mechanism. For an inverted neutrino mass hierarchy, lepton masses and mixing are derived from Yukawa coupling ratios and the modulus $\tau$ near specific fixed points. The quark sector masses and mixing also emerge at these same $\tau$ values, showing consistency with recent experimental data.

We introduce an enhanced model-fit pipeline for determining stellar parameters of M-type dwarfs, building on our prior research by Hejazi et al. 2020. This pipeline was utilized to analyze low-resolution (R~2000) spectra of 3745 M dwarfs and subdwarfs gathered from the MDM, Lick, Kitt Peak National, and Cerro Tololo Interamerican Observatories. We investigated variations in derived parameter values within the Hertzsprung-Russell (HR) diagram, utilizing Gaia Early Data Release 3 (EDR3) parallaxes and optical magnitudes. Furthermore, we examined the distribution of these stars in the [alpha/Fe] versus [M/H] abundance diagram, assessing changes in metallicity class, effective temperature, surface gravity, and Galactic velocity components (U, V, and W). The study also includes analyses of projected motions in two-dimensional UV, VW, and UW planes, variations in chemical parameters within these planes, and distributions in abundance-velocity diagrams. The accuracy of our pipeline is validated by the distinct stratification of effective temperature and chemical parameters in the HR diagram, the alignment of our stellar distributions in the [alpha/Fe] versus [M/H] and metallicity-velocity planes with previous studies, the detection of substructures in abundance-velocity diagrams, and the observed chemical homogeneity among binary system components.

Effective and safe robotic control relies heavily on robust multi-agent trajectory prediction. A key hurdle lies in efficiently learning a representation that approximates the true joint distribution of contextual, social, and temporal data to facilitate planning. To address this, we introduce "AutoBots," or Latent Variable Sequential Set Transformers, which are encoder-decoder models designed to generate scene-consistent multi-agent trajectories. The encoder utilizes a stack of interleaved temporal and social multi-head self-attention (MHSA) modules that alternately perform equivariant processing across these dimensions. The decoder combines learnable seed parameters with temporal and social MHSA modules, enabling efficient inference over the entire future scene in a single forward pass. AutoBots are capable of predicting either the trajectory of a single ego-agent or the distribution of future trajectories for all agents. In single-agent scenarios, our model achieves top rankings on the global nuScenes vehicle motion prediction leaderboard and strong performance on the Argoverse challenge. For multi-agent settings, we evaluate on the synthetic partition of the TrajNet++ dataset to demonstrate socially consistent predictions. Additionally, we apply the model to general set sequences and illustrate its ability to capture the sequential structure of strokes in Omniglot symbols. A notable advantage of AutoBots is their efficiency, as all models are trainable on a single desktop GPU (1080 Ti) in less than 48 hours.

Vector-like quarks (VLQs) are anticipated in numerous physics models extending beyond the Standard Model (SM) and may serve as significant indicators of new physics at the TeV scale. This study investigates the single production of exotic singlet and doublet vectorlike bottom quarks (VLQ-$B$) at the future Compact Linear Collider (CLIC) through the reaction $e^{+}e^{-}\to B\bar{b}$, specifically analyzing the decay $B\to bZ$ via two channels: $Z\to \ell^{+}\ell^{-}$ and $Z\to \nu\bar{\nu}$. We compute the cross sections for both the signal and pertinent Standard Model backgrounds. Following a rapid simulation of these events, we present the 95\% confidence level exclusion limits and $5\sigma$ discovery potential regarding the VLQ-$B$ mass and coupling strength $\kappa_{B}$, assuming a CLIC center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s}=3$ TeV and an integrated luminosity of 5~ab$^{-1}$.

The spectral energy distribution (SED) spanning millimetre to centimetre wavelengths serves as a valuable method for analyzing dust within protostellar envelopes, alongside free-free emission from the protostar and outflows. Although extensive research covers low- and high-mass protostars, few studies address solar-type protostars in high-mass star-forming regions, which are likely indicative of the conditions during the Solar System's formation. This study examines OMC-2/3 solar-type protostars situated near HII regions, making them susceptible to intense UV radiation. Our objective is to determine if the small-scale structure ($\leq$1000 au) and evolutionary stage of these protostars are influenced by nearby HII regions, similar to how large-scale ($\leq$10$^4$ au) gas chemistry is affected. Utilizing ALMA at 1.3 mm (246.2 GHz), we imaged the continuum of 16 OMC-2/3 solar-type protostars with a resolution of 0.25$''$ (100 au). We supplemented these observations with archival VANDAM survey data at 333 and 32.9 GHz to build dust SEDs, derive dust parameters, and evaluate free-free emission contamination in the centimetre range. Analysis of the mm-to-cm SEDs revealed low dust emissivity spectral indexes ($\beta < 1$) for most sources and detected free-free emission in only 5 of the 16 targets. Furthermore, we were able to verify or adjust the evolutionary classifications of the sample. Ultimately, no correlation was found between dust parameters and the protostars' positions within the OMC-2/3 filament. These findings indicate that the small-scale dust properties of OMC-2/3 protostars remain unaffected by the high UV illumination from adjacent HII regions.

Adaptive gradient techniques are the standard for optimization in machine learning, enabling the training of the most extensive deep models. This paper investigates the challenge of learning a local preconditioner that evolves alongside the data during the optimization process. We introduce an adaptive gradient method that offers provable regret guarantees relative to the best possible local preconditioner. To establish this result, we derive a novel adaptive regret bound for online learning that surpasses existing adaptive methods. Our approach demonstrates robustness in automatically selecting optimal learning rate schedules across popular benchmarks in vision and language tasks. Without requiring manual tuning of the learning rate, our method achieves comparable and stable accuracy to a fine-tuned optimizer within a single execution.

Emerging spintronic technologies utilize magnetic skyrmions as information carriers, making their reliable detection a critical necessity. However, the inherent high mobility of these chiral magnetic structures causes stochastic movement at finite temperatures, complicating the accurate measurement of their topological indices. In this work, we show that artificial neural networks can be effectively trained to reconstruct the skyrmion number from time-integrated, dimensionally reduced data within confined geometries. These findings validate the ability to retrieve topological charges from time-averaged measurements and blurred dynamic skyrmion ensembles, offering significant immediate implications for interpreting experimental data, skyrmion-based computing, and memory architectures.

This paper presents the first fully manually annotated paraphrase corpus for Finnish, comprising 53,572 pairs collected from alternative subtitles and news headlines. Within this dataset, 98% of the pairs are manually verified as paraphrases within their specific contexts, if not universally. Furthermore, we develop a manual candidate selection approach and validate its effectiveness for high-quality paraphrase retrieval, balancing both cost and quality.

Proper nouns pose significant challenges for end-to-end (E2E) automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems because specific names often occur infrequently during training and can be phonetically similar to common words. Unlike traditional ASR models, E2E architectures do not include a dedicated pronunciation model trainable on proper nouns or a language model trained on extensive text-only corpora. Previous approaches have tackled this by integrating extra training data or supplementary models. In contrast, this paper leverages recent advancements in minimum word error rate (MWER) training to introduce two novel loss criteria specifically designed to enhance proper noun recognition. Unlike prior methods, this approach requires neither new training data nor external models during inference. Our experiments demonstrate relative improvements ranging from 2% to 7% across several relevant benchmarks.

High-energy particle collisions serve as an ideal environment for testing non-extensive statistical methods, particularly because these reactions occur far from the thermodynamical limit. In small systems like electron-positron or nuclear collisions, the particle count is orders of magnitude below Avogadro's number, causing finite-size and fluctuation effects to significantly impact final-state single-particle energy distributions. Consequently, the Boltzmann-Gibbs thermodynamical framework, despite its simplicity, fails to adequately describe identified hadron spectra. Instead, these spectra are accurately modeled using Tsallis-Pareto distributions derived from non-extensive thermodynamics. By applying the $q$-entropy formula, we interpret underlying microscopic physics through the Tsallis $q$ and $T$ parameters. This paper examines these parameters across a broad center-of-mass energy range by analyzing identified hadron spectra from recent years. We demonstrate that the fitted Tsallis parameters exhibit dependencies on both center-of-mass energy and particle species (mass). These findings are well described by a QCD-inspired parton evolution model. Based on this comprehensive study, we conclude that both mesonic and baryonic components are non-extensive ($q>1$), in addition to the observed mass-ordered hierarchy in the parameter $T$. Furthermore, we conduct a detailed comparison of theoretically derived parameters against the PYTHIA8 Monte Carlo Generator, perturbative QCD, and quark coalescence models.

Outlier detection is a crucial component of data mining, serving either as a pre-processing step before analysis or as a post-processing measure prior to visualization, depending on the outlier's significance and utility. This technique is widely applied across various domains, including the identification of credit card fraud, network intrusions, machine failures, and potential terrorist activities. Outliers are defined as data points possessing characteristics that significantly diverge from the rest of the dataset; they can introduce noise, inconsistencies, and anomalies during analysis, often necessitating adjustments to the original data. Despite this, there is a prevalent misconception that outliers must always be removed or substituted. In reality, these points can hold substantial value if examined independently, as they may originate from distinct mechanisms and offer critical insights relevant to the research question. This study reviews various outlier detection methods specifically for spatial analysis. Spatial or geospatial data refers to information exhibiting geographic properties, such as location or boundaries, exemplified by weather metrics like temperature, precipitation, and wind velocity collected for specific regions.

Histopathological images (HIs) serve as the definitive standard for diagnosing certain tumors. However, analyzing these images is both time- and resource-intensive, presenting significant challenges even for seasoned pathologists, which often leads to inconsistencies between and within observers. To expedite this process, computer-aided diagnosis (CAD) systems offer a viable solution. This paper reviews machine learning techniques applied to HI analysis, encompassing both shallow and deep learning approaches. Furthermore, it addresses common tasks in HI analysis, such as segmentation and feature extraction, and provides a compilation of both public and private datasets utilized in HI research.

Account security remains a persistent challenge in practice, yet the adoption of Two-Factor Authentication (2FA) remains low across most domains. While 2FA can mitigate security risks, online gaming has pioneered a unique strategy to encourage its use by offering in-game rewards, such as avatar customization, to players who enable it. This paper assesses the efficacy of such incentives and explores their potential application beyond gaming. Our research methodology included two surveys—one targeting gamers and one the general public—along with three focus group interviews designed to evaluate various incentive structures for both contexts. Our findings indicate that while visual modifications are the most favored incentive within gaming, they do not hold the same appeal in non-gaming environments. Nevertheless, our explorations suggest that carefully selected incentives can effectively drive 2FA adoption even outside the gaming sphere.

This paper introduces a new evaluation metric designed for assessing performance in semantic segmentation. Recent research has increasingly focused on training pixel-level classifiers using large-scale image datasets to achieve accurate segmentation, which involves assigning a class label to every pixel within a scene. This task holds significant potential for various computer vision applications, including object detection, classification, scene understanding, and others. To validate the proposed weighted Intersection over Union (wIoU) metric, we evaluated state-of-the-art methods on public benchmark datasets, such as KITTI, using this metric and compared the results against other conventional evaluation measures.

We introduce the inaugural data release from the ALMA-IMF Large Program, focusing on 12m-array continuum calibration and imaging. This program surveys fifteen dense molecular cloud regions at various evolutionary stages to measure the core mass function (CMF). We detail the data acquisition and initial calibration performed by the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA), followed by our subsequent calibration and imaging procedures. The resulting images are composite products derived from multiple 12m array configurations, utilizing a subset of the observed bandwidth processed through multi-term, multi-frequency synthesis imaging and deconvolution. These self-calibrated data products demonstrate significant noise reductions compared to those generated from the delivered data alone. We evaluate various approaches to continuum selection, calibration parameters, and image weighting, illustrating the value and necessity of our enhanced processing. Two versions of continuum selection will be distributed: the "best-sensitivity" dataset, which incorporates the full bandwidth including bright emission lines that may contaminate the continuum, and the "cleanest" dataset, which isolates spectral portions free from line emission. Additionally, we provide a preliminary analysis of continuum spectral indices, confirming that the ALMA products can effectively distinguish between free-free and dust emission, and in certain instances, identify optically thick emission sources. These data products are now made publicly available.

Networks have emerged as essential and widespread frameworks across various disciplines for modeling interactions between entities, ranging from social friendships to biological protein connections. A significant hurdle remains in comprehending the structure and dynamics of these systems. While networks naturally evolve over time, the majority of current graph representation learning techniques are designed exclusively for static networks. Although methods for dynamic network modeling exist, there is a scarcity of efficient continuous-time dynamic graph representation approaches capable of delivering accurate, low-dimensional network characterization and visualization while explicitly incorporating key network traits like homophily and transitivity. This paper introduces the Piecewise-Velocity Model (PiVeM) for representing continuous-time dynamic networks. PiVeM learns dynamic embeddings where node evolution over time is approximated using piecewise linear interpolations derived from a latent distance model featuring piecewise constant, node-specific velocities. The model yields analytically tractable expressions for the associated Poisson process likelihood, enabling scalable inference that remains invariant to the number of events. Furthermore, a scalable Kronecker-structured Gaussian Process prior is applied to the dynamics to account for community structures, temporal smoothness, and optimally learned, disentangled latent embedding dimensions. We demonstrate that PiVeM effectively represents network structure and dynamics within ultra-low two-dimensional spaces, outperforming state-of-the-art methods in downstream tasks such as link prediction. In conclusion, PiVeM facilitates easily interpretable visualizations and characterizations of dynamic networks, thereby enhancing our understanding of the intrinsic dynamics of time-evolving systems.

Conclusive evidence for medium-induced parton energy loss remains absent in both very peripheral heavy-ion and proton-ion collisions. Nevertheless, the standard explanation for azimuthal momentum anisotropies in these systems suggests the occurrence of partonic rescattering. The forthcoming light-ion experiments at the LHC offer a distinctive chance to investigate parton energy loss across systems of comparable dimensions. This work presents predictions for the anticipated parton energy loss signal within charged hadron spectra during a system size scan at the LHC. We evaluate a broad range of model assumptions by analyzing the transverse momentum and centrality dependencies of the charged hadron nuclear modification factor in lead-lead and xenon-xenon collisions. Finally, we strive to derive a model-independent prediction for the charged hadron nuclear modification factor in oxygen-oxygen collisions.

Recent theoretical and experimental studies have examined particle-hole symmetry breaking in the fractional quantum Hall effect (FQHE), with a primary focus on non-Abelian states within the second electronic Landau level. This work presents a theoretical investigation into the breaking of particle-hole symmetry in incompressible FQHE states located in the lowest Landau level, specifically under the realistic influence of finite magnetic field strength. We demonstrate that a finite magnetic field induces mixing between Landau levels and sub-bands, a mechanism known to disrupt particle-hole symmetry at the Hamiltonian level. Our analysis evaluates Haldane pseudopotentials, energy spectra, gaps, and wave functions under these realistic conditions. We observe that while particle-hole symmetry is broken between states related by particle-hole conjugation—as evidenced by energy gaps—it remains largely preserved when assessed through the effective mass of composite fermions. Finally, we relate these findings to recent experimental observations concerning particle-hole symmetry in the lowest Landau level FQHE [Pan et al. Phys. Rev. Lett. 124, 156801 (2020)].

This study establishes a comprehensive framework for evaluating the efficacy of interferometric gravitational wave detector networks. Applying this framework demonstrates that expanding the current LIGO-VIRGO array with future detectors in Japan (LCGT), Australia, and India yields substantial advantages, including significantly higher detection rates than previously estimated. The research identifies a universal probability distribution function (pdf) for detected signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) values, indicating that the most probable SNR for the inaugural detected event will be 1.26 times the search threshold. Furthermore, for binary systems, a universal pdf is derived for detected orbital inclination values after accounting for Malmquist bias, suggesting that gamma-ray bursts linked to detected binary coalescences should occur 3.4 times more frequently than predictions based solely on gamma-ray burst beaming fractions. By utilizing network antenna patterns, three new performance metrics are proposed to characterize the relative capabilities of various networks. The analysis reveals that adding any new observatory to the planned LIGO-VIRGO network can boost the detected event rate by factors of 2 to 4 through coherent data analysis that suppresses spurious instrumental coincident backgrounds. Relocating one LIGO detector to Australia would further enhance direction-finding capabilities by a factor of four or more. Incorporating LCGT into the original LIGO-VIRGO configuration not only improves localization but also increases the detection rate by nearly another factor of two over the gains from adding a single extra site, largely by optimizing the network duty cycle. Ultimately, these expanded advanced networks are projected to detect three to four hundred neutron star binary coalescences annually.

Originally proposed in the context of chiral symmetry, axions are now primarily sought as dark matter candidates. This paper presents a nonabelian counterpart to axions, which also serves as a potential dark matter source. The nonabelian symmetries involved, which extend the Peccei-Quinn symmetry, hold intrinsic interest. Furthermore, a detailed analysis employing fermion measure and zeta function methods demonstrates that these symmetries remain non-anomalous.

Mutation testing is a proven method for evaluating test suite quality by introducing artificial faults into production code. Recently, this technique has been adapted for machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) systems, with researchers developing tools, approaches, and statistical heuristics to assess whether DL mutants are detected. However, this work argues that current DL mutation testing practices may not fully align with the classical interpretation of the technique. We observe that ML development mirrors a test-driven development (TDD) cycle: a training algorithm acts as a "programmer," creating a model that fits data points (test inputs) to labels (implicit assertions) within a specific threshold. When applying the TDD metaphor to existing ML mutation techniques, the boundary between production and test code becomes ambiguous, and the realism of mutation operators is questionable. Furthermore, the fundamental hypotheses of classical mutation testing—the competent programmer hypothesis and the coupling effect hypothesis—do not naturally extend to ML system development. As we demonstrate, drawing valid parallels requires more deliberate scoping and explicit concept mapping. Consequently, based on these findings, we propose several actionable steps to better align ML mutation testing techniques with the paradigms and terminology of classical mutation testing.

This paper investigates the stability of skyrmions (SKYs) arising from the geometric confinement (GC) effect recently observed in nano-domains, where SKYs exist exclusively within boundaries and remain stable under low magnetic fields. Despite this phenomenon, the underlying mechanism of the GC effect remains unclear. Our numerical analysis reveals that this effect does not occur in the standard model, which discretizes Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction (DMI) energy on lattice edges, but is present in a discrete model where DMI energy is defined on lattice volume elements. In this latter model, surface DMI energy becomes negligible compared to that in the interior. Based on this finding, we examined a model with zero DMI energy on surfaces parallel to the external magnetic field, demonstrating that SKY stability is significantly enhanced in the low magnetic field regime.

Molecular simulation technologies offer researchers unprecedented insights into the nanoscale interactions governing physical processes. However, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations are constrained by the need to operate on finite-sized systems to align with computational resources. To mitigate artifacts caused by these finite boundaries, MD simulations typically employ periodic boundary conditions (PBC). Yet, calculating specific physical properties, such as diffusion coefficients via mean square displacements, necessitates continuous particle trajectories where atomic movements remain uninterrupted across cell faces. In such scenarios, unwrapping schemes that modify atomic coordinates to eliminate these jumps are essential post-processing tools. This study applies two established unwrapping methods to 1-microsecond wrapped trajectories of a small water box, revealing that existing schemes can produce spurious diffusion coefficients, generate unrealistically long bonds within unwrapped molecules, and yield inconsistent atomic coordinates upon rewrapping. We find that previous unwrapping approaches fail to account for varying periodic box dimensions. Consequently, we introduce an additional correction term to the displacement unwrapping scheme proposed by von Bulow et al. to rectify these artifacts, resulting in an algorithm that hybridizes existing heuristic and displacement methods. Following treatment with this new scheme, molecular geometries remain accurate even after extended simulations. In preparation for longer MD trajectories, we have developed implementations of this improved scheme across multiple PBC handling tools.

This paper introduces a general optimization-based framework for calculating differentially private M-estimators and proposes a novel approach for building differentially private confidence regions. Initially, we demonstrate that robust statistics, when combined with noisy gradient descent or noisy Newton methods, yield optimal private estimators characterized by global linear or quadratic convergence, respectively. We provide local and global convergence guarantees under conditions of local strong convexity and self-concordance, proving that our private estimators converge with high probability to a near-optimal neighborhood of their non-private counterparts. Secondly, we address parametric inference by developing differentially private estimators for the asymptotic variance of these private M-estimators. This process naturally facilitates the creation of approximate pivotal statistics, enabling the construction of confidence regions and the execution of hypothesis tests. Furthermore, we showcase the efficacy of a bias correction technique that improves small-sample empirical performance in simulations. Finally, we illustrate the advantages of our proposed methods through various numerical examples.

The next-to-minimal supersymmetric standard model can accommodate light neutralino dark matter in the GeV mass range, where the singlino component dominates due to an approximate Peccei-Quinn symmetry. This study examines the viability of such light neutralino dark matter given LHC Run 1 results, alongside the most recent constraints from LUX and Xenon1T experiments. Specifically, we illustrate the sensitivity of the dark matter mass parameter space regarding invisible decays into $Z$ bosons and the Standard Model Higgs.

We establish an extension criterion for codimension one foliations on projective hypersurfaces, relying on the degrees of both the foliation and the hypersurface, and we demonstrate an isomorphism between the respective foliation spaces in specific cases. Additionally, we provide examples of foliations that fail to meet the extension criterion and consequently do not extend.

We present several families of planar graphs that are minor-minimal intrinsically spherical 3-linked. A graph is defined as intrinsically spherical 3-linked if, in every spherical embedding, it contains a non-split 3-link composed of two disjoint cycles ($S^1$s) and two disjoint vertices ($S^0$), or alternatively, a cycle and two pairs of disjoint vertices. We conjecture that the graphs $K_4 \dot{\bigcup} K_4$, $K_{3,2} \dot{\bigcup} K_{3,2}$, and $K_4 \dot{\bigcup} K_{3,2}$ constitute the complete set of minor-minimal intrinsically type I spherical 3-linked graphs, meaning that in any spherical embedding, they possess a non-split link consisting of two cycles and one $S^0$.

Eddington-inspired Born-Infeld gravity represents a significant extension of Einstein's general relativity, capable of producing non-singular cosmological models and preventing final-stage singularities during gravitational collapse. In the Newtonian regime, this framework yields a modified Poisson equation, leading to model-specific adjustments in stellar observables relative to the low-energy predictions of general relativity, which allows for the derivation of astrophysical constraints. This study establishes such a constraint by analyzing observational data from cataclysmic variable binaries, specifically focusing on the tidal disruption threshold of a secondary star by a white dwarf primary. We employ a numerical approach to calculate stellar observables based on the Roche lobe filling condition within the modified gravity context. These theoretical values are then compared against existing observational data using a Monte Carlo error propagation technique, ultimately constraining the theory at the $5\sigma$ confidence level.

Driven by the hypothesis that terrestrial limbless locomotion strategies converge based on interfacial effects, this study demonstrates how 3D gait modifications and adaptations to varied terrains can be interpreted through local friction modulation. Utilizing an "everything-is-friction" modeling framework enhanced by 3D simulations, we systematically explain the emergence and disappearance of diverse natural locomotory behaviors in relation to specific environments. This approach simplifies terrain heterogeneity by treating solid obstacles as high-friction zones, a concept validated by experiments showing snakes "diffracting" around rows of posts [1], analogous to optical waves. Extending this optical analogy, we illustrate phenomena such as snake refraction, reflection, and lens focusing. Leveraging these insights, we engineered surface friction patterns to achieve passive snake navigation within complex topographies. In summary, our research presents a unified perspective linking active and passive 3D mechanics with heterogeneous interfacial effects to account for extensive biological observations and to potentially guide engineering design.

Deductive software verification faces significant hurdles when dealing with pointer aliasing. This paper presents an extension of SPARK, a rigorously defined subset of Ada designed for the formal verification of mission-critical systems, by incorporating pointers. Our approach employs a permission-based static alias analysis technique, drawing inspiration from Rust's borrow-checker and affine types, which enforces a Concurrent Read, Exclusive Write policy. This analysis has been integrated into the GNAT Ada compiler and validated using several complex test cases. The paper provides a formal specification and soundness proof of these analysis rules for a simplified version of SPARK, alongside a discussion of the implementation and a comparative analysis with Rust.

Over the past ten years, quantum information science and technology (QIST) has advanced considerably, transitioning from exclusive research environments to active industrial applications and product development. This burgeoning quantum sector necessitates a skilled workforce proficient in QIST competencies. Consequently, educational institutions must understand the specific job roles available, the relevant skills required, and the appropriate degrees for these positions to effectively support training programs. Simultaneously, students must learn how to align their academic paths with the current demands of the industry. This report presents findings from a survey of 57 quantum companies aimed at identifying the essential jobs, skills, and degrees for this emerging workforce. The results reveal a spectrum of roles, ranging from specialized positions like quantum algorithm developers and error correction scientists to broader categories within business, software, and hardware. While these general roles require diverse skills, most are not strictly quantum-related. Furthermore, beyond the highly specialized positions, employers seek candidates with various levels of education, from bachelor's to master's and doctoral degrees. These insights enable students, faculty, and university administrators to make informed decisions regarding the development of a robust future quantum workforce.

$N$-jettiness subtractions offer a comprehensive framework for conducting fully-differential next-to-next-to-leading order (NNLO) computations. Because this method relies on the physical resolution variable $N$-jettiness, $\mathcal{T}_N$, subleading power corrections in $\tau=\mathcal{T}_N/Q$ (where $Q$ represents the hard interaction scale) can be calculated systematically. This work examines the structure of these power corrections for $0$-jettiness, $\mathcal{T}_0$, specifically within the $gg\to H$ process. Utilizing soft-collinear effective theory, we analytically derive the leading power corrections $\alpha_s \tau \ln\tau$ and $\alpha_s^2 \tau \ln^3\tau$, achieving partial agreement with prior literature, and conduct an extensive numerical analysis of power corrections across the $gg$, $gq$, and $q\bar q$ channels. This analysis entails numerically extracting the $\alpha_s\tau$ and $\alpha_s^2 \tau \ln^2\tau$ terms and investigating their sensitivity to the definition of $\mathcal{T}_0$. Incorporating these power-suppressed logarithms substantially diminishes the magnitude of residual power corrections, thereby enhancing the numerical efficiency of the subtraction technique. Furthermore, gaining a deeper understanding of power corrections for both $q\bar q$ and $gg$ initiated processes yields insights into their universality, shedding light on their behavior in more complex scenarios where analytical calculations are currently unavailable.

The emergence of next-generation radio interferometers, including the Square Kilometer Array (SKA), has created new frontiers for astronomical inquiry. Nevertheless, anthropogenic Radio Frequency Interference (RFI) stemming from human communication and activities drastically degrades data fidelity and diminishes telescope sensitivity. To address this, we developed a robust Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) using machine learning to detect RFI. We constructed three visibility function datasets by superimposing RFI onto SKA1-LOW simulation data; one dataset served for training, while the remaining two were used for validation. Experimental outcomes indicate an Area Under the Curve (AUC) of 0.93, demonstrating satisfactory accuracy and precision. Furthermore, we evaluated the model's efficacy by applying it to real observational data from LOFAR and MeerKAT. The findings confirm that the model performs effectively, achieving overall results comparable to the AOFlagger software and offering improvements over current methods in certain scenarios.

This study examines whether Moran's $I$ statistic can effectively measure spatial-kinematic substructure in young star-forming regions. Detecting such substructure in young clusters would support the hierarchical model of star cluster formation, which posits that systems originate from initially substructured conditions, even if they appear spatially smooth and centrally concentrated. Conversely, its absence would suggest a monolithic formation process. We applied the Moran's $I$ statistic to $N$-body simulations of star clusters featuring various primordial spatial-velocity configurations to track its temporal evolution. Our findings indicate that this statistic reliably quantifies spatial-kinematic substructure and can help determine whether the spatial-kinematic characteristics of regions younger than approximately 6 Myr align better with hierarchical or monolithic formation models. Furthermore, the statistic can definitively rule out initial conditions lacking kinematic substructure, such as those predicted by the monolithic model, in regions up to and potentially beyond 10 Myr old. Consequently, this offers a kinematic signature of the star cluster formation process that remains observable for many millions of years, long after any initial spatial structure has been dissipated.

Data centers are vital to modern commercial and social operations yet remain significant electricity consumers. To reduce their environmental footprint, it is essential to enhance their energy efficiency without compromising service quality (QoS). Addressing this, we propose an analytical model grounded in queueing theory to assess data center QoS. Building on this model, we introduce a specialized evolutionary optimization framework that employs a custom solution representation and a constraint-aware initialization operator. This framework determines the optimal placement of virtual network functions to balance multiple conflicting objectives regarding energy usage and QoS, and it can be seamlessly integrated with any existing evolutionary multi-objective optimization algorithm. Comprehensive experiments confirm both the accuracy and efficiency of our QoS model, as well as the effectiveness of our tailored algorithms for virtual network function placement across various scales.

Large pretrained models can undergo private fine-tuning to reach performance levels nearly matching those of non-private counterparts. A recurring insight from these findings is the unexpected ability of high-dimensional models to achieve beneficial privacy-utility trade-offs. This observation appears to conflict with established theories regarding model-size dependence in differentially private convex learning, prompting the question: under what circumstances does the performance of differentially private learning remain stable as model size increases? We determine that the magnitudes of gradients projected onto specific subspaces are a critical determinant of performance. To rigorously characterize this phenomenon in private convex learning, we propose a condition called \emph{restricted Lipschitz continuity} and derive enhanced bounds for excess empirical and population risks that are independent of dimensionality under certain conditions. Empirically, we demonstrate that in the private fine-tuning of large language models, gradients are predominantly governed by a limited number of principal components. This behavior mirrors the conditions required for obtaining dimension-independent bounds in convex scenarios. Collectively, our theoretical and empirical findings offer a plausible explanation for recent advancements in large-scale private fine-tuning. The code to replicate our results is available at \url{https://github.com/lxuechen/private-transformers/tree/main/examples/classification/spectral_analysis}.

Core-collapse supernovae (CCSNe) represent a primary origin of gravitational waves, with their characteristic frequencies making them ideal candidates for detection by current advanced ground-based observatories. Identifying these events could elucidate the fundamental explosion mechanisms via waveform analysis, a capability previously demonstrated using the Supernova Model Evidence Extractor (SMEE; Logue et al. 2012), which employs principal-component analysis and Bayesian model selection. This study introduces a complementary method relying on supervised dictionary learning, proving its ability to reconstruct and categorize CCSN signals based on their morphological features. The waveform data utilized were derived from (a) two public catalogs of numerical simulations for neutrino-driven (Mur) and magneto-rotational (Dim) explosions, and (b) a third simulated catalog of sine-Gaussian (SG) waveforms. These signals were embedded in colored Gaussian noise to mimic Advanced LIGO's broadband background and adjusted to user-defined signal-to-noise ratios (SNR). Our methodology successfully classified signals from all three dictionaries; notably, at SNR levels between 15 and 20, it achieved perfect matches for Dim and SG signals and approximately 85% accuracy for Mur signals. These findings align closely with SMEE results for the same CCSN signals when injected into a single LIGO detector. Finally, we examine the primary constraints of this approach alongside potential avenues for enhancement.

Self-interactions within dark matter produce unique signatures in the characteristics of Milky Way satellite galaxies by influencing tidal stripping, ram pressure, and gravothermal collapse. We map the parameter space of self-interacting dark matter—defined by interaction cross-section and velocity scale—to identify where each mechanism prevails, demonstrating how relative mass loss varies based on a satellite's initial mass, density profile, and orbital path. By analyzing Milky Way satellites with exceptionally high central densities and small pericenter distances, we derive novel, conservative constraints within this parameter space. Our findings, when combined with limits from galaxy clusters, support velocity-dependent cross-section models that induce gravothermal core collapse in the most dense satellites.

This paper introduces a stochastic optimization algorithm designed to efficiently identify Bayesian experimental designs that maximize expected information gain. Since the gradient of this gain with respect to design parameters involves a nested expectation, standard Monte Carlo methods with a fixed number of inner samples produce biased estimators. By adapting randomized multilevel Monte Carlo (MLMC) techniques, we develop an unbiased Monte Carlo estimator for this gradient that possesses a finite expected squared $\ell_2$-norm and a finite expected computational cost per sample. This unbiased estimator integrates effectively with stochastic gradient descent, enabling the proposed optimization strategy to locate optimal Bayesian experimental designs. Numerical experiments demonstrate the algorithm's efficacy on both a simple test case and a more complex pharmacokinetic application.

Temporal action detection (TAD) remains a critical yet difficult challenge in video understanding, requiring the simultaneous prediction of action semantic labels and their temporal boundaries within untrimmed videos. While most current approaches rely on a head-only learning strategy—pre-training a video encoder for action classification and optimizing only the detection head for TAD—the impact of end-to-end learning has not been rigorously evaluated, nor has the efficiency-accuracy trade-off in this context been thoroughly investigated. This paper provides an empirical analysis of end-to-end TAD, demonstrating its superiority over head-only methods with performance gains of up to 11%. Furthermore, we examine how various design choices, such as the detection head architecture, video encoder, and input resolution, influence both accuracy and speed. Leveraging these insights, we developed a mid-resolution baseline detector that achieves state-of-the-end performance among end-to-end methods while operating more than four times faster. We hope this work guides future research in end-to-end learning, and our code and models are accessible at \url{https://github.com/xlliu7/E2E-TAD}.

Recent years have seen growing inconsistencies in measurements of the universe's current expansion rate ($H_0$) and matter clustering estimates ($S_8$). Utilizing the latest cosmological observations, we re-evaluate a novel model designed to resolve these tensions, wherein cold dark matter decays into dark radiation. This decay process is governed by the rate $Q = \alpha \mathcal{H} ho_{m ddm}$, with $\alpha$ representing a dimensionless constant that defines the mechanism's strength, $\mathcal{H}$ denoting the conformal Hubble rate in a spatially flat Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker universe, and $ho_{m ddm}$ being the energy density of the decaying cold dark matter. Analysis of the most recent 2018 Planck temperature and polarization data reveals no evidence for $\alpha 
eq 0$ and indicates that this model fails to alleviate the $H_0$ tension by more than $3\sigma$, contradicting findings from the 2015 Planck data analysis. We further explore two extensions where the dark energy equation-of-state parameter deviates from $-1$ ($w
