Reports of aluminium monoxide in exoplanetary atmospheres have emerged, with high-resolution spectroscopic studies poised to detect it strongly provided that high-precision laboratory data is available. This study applies a \textsc{marvel} (measured active rotational-vibrational energy levels) analysis to existing spectroscopic data for $^{27}$Al$^{16}$O, utilizing 22\,473 validated transitions to derive 6\,485 distinct energy levels. These empirically determined levels yield a spectroscopically refined version of the ExoMol ATP line list for $^{27}$Al$^{16}$O. Simultaneously, the accuracy of line lists for the isotopically substituted species $^{26}$Al$^{16}$O, $^{27}$Al$^{17}$O, and $^{27}$Al$^{18}$O is enhanced by applying consistent level corrections. These updated line lists can be accessed via the ExoMol database at http://www.exomol.com.

Biopsy specimen data regarding structure and composition plays a vital role in diagnosing and monitoring diseases. This information can theoretically be derived from Raman and infrared (IR) hyperspectral images (HSIs), which capture the spatial arrangement of a sample's constituent molecules. Although each tissue component is characterized by a distinct combination of spectral and spatial features, the high dimensionality of HSI datasets makes the extraction and utilization of these features for image segmentation a complex challenge. This study demonstrates how deep convolutional autoencoder (CAE)-based networks can address this task end-to-end. The approach involves first detecting and compressing relevant features from HSI patches into low-dimensional latent vectors, followed by a clustering step that groups patches with similar spatio-spectral characteristics. We highlight the benefits of this end-to-end spatio-spectral segmentation method compared to i) a non-end-to-end version of the same technique and ii) a method relying solely on spectral features (spectral k-means), using simulated HSIs of porcine tissue as test cases. Furthermore, we evaluate the potential strengths and constraints of three distinct CAE architectures: a generic 2D CAE, a generic 3D CAE, and a 2D CNN architecture modeled after the UwU-net, which is specialized for HSI feature extraction. Performance was assessed using IR HSIs of real colon samples. Our findings indicate that all architectures successfully generated segmentations that closely align with hematoxylin and eosin (HE) stained adjacent tissue slices, serving as approximate ground truths, thereby demonstrating the robustness of the CAE-driven approach for segmenting biomedical HSI data. Additionally, we emphasize the necessity for more precise ground truth data to rigorously compare the specific advantages provided by each architecture.

We introduce a model-agnostic search strategy for physics beyond the standard model (BSM) at the LHC, utilizing a new application of neural density estimation for anomaly detection. Our method, termed Classifying Anomalies THrough Outer Density Estimation (CATHODE), posits that BSM signals are localized within a specific signal region (such as one defined by invariant mass). By training a conditional density estimator on features external to this region, interpolating it into the signal region, and sampling from the result, we generate a set of events that mimic the background model. We then employ a classifier to differentiate between the actual data and these sampled background events, thereby achieving performance close to the optimal anomaly detector. Using the LHC Olympics R&D dataset, we show that CATHODE nearly reaches the theoretical performance limit and substantially surpasses other methods designed to improve bump hunts, such as CWoLa Hunting and ANODE. Furthermore, we demonstrate that CATHODE remains highly robust against feature correlations, maintaining near-optimal performance even in these more complex scenarios.

Foundational theories like the Condorcet Jury Theorem suggest that aggregating individual decisions significantly boosts accuracy; however, these premises often fail when individuals can adjust their choices after observing others. In sequential settings, rational agents treat others' selections as informational cues, generating strong correlations that breach the theorem's independence requirement. This paper demonstrates how such dependencies arise when rewards are based solely on individual accuracy and analyzes the resulting effect on group performance. Furthermore, it illustrates how a straightforward competitive reward mechanism—where agents earn more for selecting options that few others have chosen—can encourage independent decision-making and restore collective accuracy to optimal levels. Finally, the study shows that this scheme is robust, enhancing group accuracy across a broad spectrum of competition intensities, indicating its potential for effective real-world application to bolster collective wisdom.

This article examines the physics principles and methodologies underpinning Fermilab's Muon g-2 Experiment, presenting the eagerly awaited outcomes from Run-1. Designed to address discrepancies between the Standard Model and prior data from Brookhaven National Laboratory, the experiment yielded a muon magnetic anomaly value of $a_\mu(FNAL)=116592040(54)\times10^{-11}$. This finding aligns closely with Brookhaven's earlier results. The updated world average, $a_\mu(Exp)=116592061(41)\times10^{-11}$, deviates from the Standard Model's theoretical prediction, $a_\mu(SM)=116591810(43)\times10^{-11}$, by 4.2 standard deviations, providing a strong indication of physics beyond the Standard Model. The study necessitates the concurrent measurement of muon precession frequency, magnetic field strength, and muon distribution within the field. These three measurements, along with primary systematic corrections and uncertainties, will be analyzed in detail.

In this paper, we establish Vogan's conjecture regarding local Arthur packets for irreducible Arthur parameters of $p$-adic general linear groups—specifically those that are irreducible as representations of $W_F \times SL_2(\mathbb{C}) \times SL_2(\mathbb{C})$. Our findings demonstrate that such packets can be uniquely characterized by the properties of simple perverse sheaves defined on a moduli space of Langlands parameters.

A pseudoscalar "axionlike" field, denoted as $\phi$, could account for the $3\sigma$ indication of cosmic birefringence found in the cosmic microwave background (CMB) polarization's $EB$ power spectrum. Determining whether $\phi$ functions as dark energy or dark matter requires a tomographic analysis. Since the effective mass of the dark energy field driving current cosmic acceleration must be below $m_\phi \simeq 10^{-33}$ eV, a mass $m_\phi \gtrsim 10^{-32}$ eV would cause $\phi$ to evolve prior to reionization. This would result in varying levels of birefringence across low ($l\lesssim 10$) and high multipoles in the $EB$ spectrum; detecting such variation via a full-sky satellite mission would disprove the hypothesis that $\phi$ is dark energy. Conversely, if $m_\phi \gtrsim 10^{-28}$ eV, $\phi$ would begin oscillating during recombination, producing a unique signature in the high-multipole $EB$ power spectrum that ground-based CMB instruments can measure with high precision. This tomographic method, which depends on the spectral shape, offers reduced sensitivity to errors in polarization angle calibration.

We introduce a convolutional neural network designed to classify responses derived from correlation filters. This proposed method enhances classification accuracy and ensures invariance to both image classes and parameters.

We introduce a generalized quantum scattering circuit capable of executing non-invasive quantum measurements on NMR qubits, a capability essential for testing temporal non-contextual inequalities. Leveraging this circuit, we experimentally confirm the violation of the Peres-Mermin inequality—the temporal counterpart to the Klyachko-Can-Binicioglu-Shumovsky (KCBS) inequality—using a three-qubit NMR quantum information processor. Additionally, we demonstrate the violation of a transformed Bell-type inequality, which serves as the spatial equivalent of the temporal KCBS inequality, and establish that its Tsirelson bound matches that of the temporal KCBS inequality. In the temporal KCBS scenario, the contextual bound remains strictly lower than both the quantum temporal and nonlocal bounds.

Using the complex scaling method, we investigate two-body resonance states with $J^{\pi}=0^{+}, 1^{+}$, and $2^{+}$ for systems comprising $Y_{c}$ ($\Lambda_{c}$, $\Sigma_{c}$, or $\Sigma_{c}^{*}$) and $N$, utilizing the $Y_{c}N$-CTNN potentials introduced in our prior work. This analysis yields four resonances situated near the $\Sigma_{c}N$ and $\Sigma_{c}^{*}N$ thresholds. Based on an examination of the binding energies within partial channel systems, we identify these states as Feshbach resonances. Furthermore, by comparing our findings with $Y_{c}N$ resonance states in the heavy quark limit—where $\Sigma_{c}N$ and $\Sigma_{c}^{*}N$ thresholds become degenerate—we observe that they constitute two pairs of heavy-quark doublets, consistent with heavy quark spin symmetry.

The potential for charge-to-spin conversion through Rashba spin-orbit effects offers exciting prospects for advancing nanoscale spintronics. In this study, we employ first-principles calculations to investigate the electronic and spintronic characteristics of the Tl$_2$O/PtS$_2$ heterostructure, confirming its dynamical stability through positive phonon frequencies. We observe an unexpectedly high binding energy of -0.38 eV per unit cell, indicating robust interlayer interactions between Tl$_2$O and PtS$_2$. Notably, we identify significant Rashba spin-splitting with a large $\alpha_R$ value in the valence band of Tl$_2$O, arising from interfacial spin-orbit coupling induced by PtS$_2$. Furthermore, utilizing electron localization function and atomic orbital projections, we analyze the impact of van der Waals binding on orbital rearrangements, providing a detailed explanation of the electronic dispersion near the Fermi level. We also clarify the unique band structure alignment within momentum space alongside real-space separation in the Tl$_2$O/PtS$_2$ system. Given that 2D Tl$_2$O remains unverified experimentally, we present, for the first time, the calculated Raman spectra for both pristine Tl$_2$O and the heterostructure, discussing peak positions associated with atomic vibrational modes. These results suggest a promising pathway for exploring spin physics and potential spintronic applications using 2D heterostructures.

The oscillation between ordinary neutrons ($n$) and their dark mirror counterparts ($n'$) can gradually convert a standard neutron star into a hybrid object containing a portion of mirror dark matter. The consequences of the reverse process occurring within mirror neutron stars rely on the sign of the baryon asymmetry in the mirror sector. Specifically, if this asymmetry is negative, as suggested by specific baryogenesis models, then $\bar{n}'-\bar{n}$ transitions would generate a core of gravitationally trapped antimatter inside the mirror star. The annihilation of accreted gas against such an antimatter core could account for $\gamma$-ray source candidates with spectra consistent with baryon-antibaryon annihilation, recently spotted in the Fermi LAT catalog. Furthermore, antimatter escaping following the merger of mirror neutron stars could contribute to the flux of cosmic antihelium and heavier antinuclei sought by the AMS-02 experiment.

Gopalakrishnan, Islam, and Knap utilized a perturbative method to study transport in localized systems interacting with non-Markovian dephasing noise, specifically within the deeply localized regime where single-particle hopping represents the minimal energy scale. Although their analytical and numerical work is strictly confined to this deeply localized context, they frequently applied their approximation beyond its valid range in most of their findings, rendering those results incorrect. We identify these erroneous outcomes and suggest specific adjustments to the parameter values required to achieve accurate results.

The Large Sky Area Multi-Object Fiber Spectroscopic Telescope (LAMOST) serves as a key instrument for conducting spectroscopic surveys focused on galaxy evolution and cosmology. The seventh data release of the LAMOST ExtraGAlactic Survey (LEGAS) is now accessible, providing redshift measurements for 193,361 galaxies distributed across approximately 11,500 square degrees of the sky, with significant overlap with other imaging (SDSS, HSC) and spectroscopic (BOSS) projects. With an estimated depth of $r\sim17.8$, high signal-to-noise ratios, and a spectral resolution of $R=1800$, LAMOST spectra are well-suited for measuring galaxy velocity dispersions, which are crucial for understanding galaxy structure, formation, and central dark matter content. This study presents the first central velocity dispersion estimates for roughly 86,000 galaxies within the LAMOST footprint. Utilizing a wrap-up procedure for spectral fitting with \textsc{pPXF}, we derived these velocity dispersion measurements. Statistical uncertainties were evaluated by comparing LAMOST results with those from SDSS and BOSS over a shared sample of about 51,000 galaxies. The datasets demonstrate strong agreement within statistical limits, particularly after correcting velocity dispersion values to a 1 effective radius aperture. Additionally, we provide a preliminary Mass-$\sigma$ relation that aligns with prior analyses based on local galaxy samples. These initial findings indicate that LAMOST spectra are appropriate for measuring galaxy velocity dispersions to supplement existing northern hemisphere catalogs of galaxy internal kinematics. Future work will extend this analysis to subsequent LAMOST data releases.

Mixture models serve as a fundamental statistical approach for analyzing data derived from heterogeneous populations. This study addresses the enduring discussion between finite and infinite mixtures by unifying these strategies, demonstrating that a finite mixture can be viewed as a specific realization of a point process. Adopting a Bayesian nonparametric framework, we propose a novel class of priors known as Normalized Independent Point Processes and examine their probabilistic characteristics. Additionally, we develop a conditional algorithm for finite mixture models with a stochastic number of components, which bypasses the complexities typically encountered with Reversible Jump methods and recent marginal algorithms. Finally, we apply this model to real-world data and explore a significant application within the field of population genetics.

For any compact convex domain $K$ in the Euclidean plane, the mixed area $A(K,-K)$ satisfies the upper bound $1/(6\sqrt{3})L(K)^2$, where $L(K)$ denotes the perimeter of $K$. This inequality, established by Ulrich Betke and Wolfgang Weil in 1991, achieves equality for polygons if and only if $K$ is a regular triangle. We confirm their conjecture that among all convex domains, equality holds exclusively for the regular triangle. This result is derived by proving a stronger stability version of the geometric inequality $6\sqrt{3}A(K,-K)\le L(K)^2$.

Amidst the vast data landscape of the big data era, the current generation struggles to locate relevant information within the immense volumes of data hosted on online platforms. Consequently, there is a critical demand for information filtering mechanisms to assist users in retrieving their desired content. Recently, the field of recommender systems has gained prominence due to its extensive real-world applications. This paper examines the various techniques and advancements within recommender systems across sectors such as e-commerce, e-tourism, e-resources, e-government, e-learning, and e-libraries. By analyzing recent scholarly work, the study offers a comprehensive overview of current developments and highlights existing challenges in recommendation technologies. Ultimately, the findings provide practitioners and researchers with essential guidance and insights regarding recommendation systems and their practical applications.

Humans construct sophisticated mental models of their surroundings, encompassing both geometric and semantic details across various levels of abstraction, from objects to entire buildings, while tracking static and dynamic entities and their interrelations. Conversely, current robotic internal representations often offer only a fragmented view, typically limited to sparse or dense sets of geometric primitives or isolated objects. This paper aims to bridge the perception gap between humans and robots by proposing a new 3D Dynamic Scene Graph (DSG) that seamlessly integrates metric and semantic information within dynamic environments. A DSG functions as a layered graph where nodes denote spatial concepts at different abstraction levels, and edges define their spatio-temporal relationships. Our second contribution, Kimera, is the first fully automatic system for constructing DSGs from visual-inertial data; it incorporates state-of-the-art methods for visual-inertial SLAM, metric-semantic 3D reconstruction, object localization, human pose and shape estimation, and scene parsing. The third contribution involves a thorough evaluation of Kimera across real-world datasets and photorealistic simulations, featuring the newly released uHumans2 dataset, which simulates crowded indoor and outdoor scenarios. Results demonstrate that Kimera achieves state-of-the-art performance in visual-inertial SLAM, generates accurate real-time 3D metric-semantic meshes, and constructs DSGs for complex indoor environments containing dozens of objects and people within minutes. Additionally, we illustrate how DSGs enable real-time hierarchical semantic path planning. The core components of Kimera are available as open-source software.

We introduce a deep learning approach for multivariate regression that leverages pattern recognition to facilitate rapid learning from sensor data. By converting sensor inputs into images, we utilize Computer Vision architectures and training protocols. Furthermore, we investigate advanced models to produce regression outputs predicting continuous agricultural crop yield data. Our results, benchmarked against top performers from MLCAS2021, demonstrate that a straightforward training process yields an MAE of 4.394, an RMSE of 5.945, and an R² of 0.861.

The structure of the unbound $^{15}$F nucleus was examined through the inverse kinematics resonant scattering of a radioactive $^{14}$O beam onto a CH$_2$ target. By analyzing the $^{1}$H($^{14}$O,p)$^{14}$O and $^{1}$H($^{14}$O,2p)$^{13}$N reactions, researchers confirmed a previously identified narrow $1/2^{-}$ resonance situated near the two-proton decay threshold and discovered two additional narrow resonances with spins of $5/2^{-}$ and $3/2^{-}$. These newly detected levels decay via 1p emission to the ground state of $^{14}$O and through sequential 2p emission to the ground state of $^{13}$N, passing through the $1^-$ resonance of $^{14}$O. A Gamow shell model (GSM) analysis of the experimental results indicates that the wave functions associated with the $5/2^{-}$ and $3/2^{-}$ resonances are likely collectivized due to continuum coupling with adjacent 2p- and 1p- decay channels. Furthermore, the unified GSM framework successfully reproduces both the observed excitation function for $^{1}$H($^{14}$O,p)$^{14}$O and the resonance spectrum of $^{15}$F.

This study presents a non-existence theorem for $\alpha$-harmonic mappings and establishes a direct link between $\alpha$-harmonic and harmonic maps through conformal deformation. Second, it examines the instability of non-constant $\alpha$-harmonic maps concerning the Ricci curvature conditions of the target manifold. The research then explores the notion of $\alpha$-stable manifolds and their physical applications. Finally, it investigates the $\alpha$-stability of compact Riemannian manifolds that possess a non-isometric conformal vector field, as well as Einstein Riemannian manifolds, under specific assumptions regarding the smallest positive eigenvalue of the Laplacian operator on functions.

Tensor factorization models have demonstrated significant potential in knowledge graph completion (KGC), yet they are frequently hindered by severe overfitting. Although various regularizers, including those based on squared Frobenius and tensor nuclear norms, have been developed to mitigate this issue, their restricted applicability hampers practical deployment. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a new regularizer called DUality-induced RegulArizer (DURA). This approach not only effectively boosts the performance of current models but also remains broadly applicable across different methods. The core innovation of DURA stems from the insight that for any existing tensor factorization-based KGC model (the primal), there is often a closely related distance-based KGC model (the dual). Experimental results indicate that DURA delivers consistent and substantial improvements on standard benchmarks.

This study details measurements of the groomed jet radius and momentum splitting fraction from proton-proton collisions at $\sqrt{s}=5.02$ TeV, utilizing the ALICE detector at the Large Hadron Collider. Inclusive charged-particle jets were reconstructed at midrapidity using the anti-$k_{\rm{T}}$ algorithm for transverse momentum values between 60 and 80 GeV/$c$. The analysis presents findings derived from two distinct grooming techniques: soft drop and, notably, dynamical grooming for the first time. To investigate the influence of collinear radiation on these jet substructure observables, various configurations for each grooming algorithm were employed. These experimental results are contrasted with perturbative calculations that incorporate the resummation of large logarithms to all orders in the strong coupling constant. The study demonstrates satisfactory agreement between the theoretical predictions and the experimental data across all examined grooming settings.

Humans possess the ability to recognize and classify new combinations of familiar concepts. Compositional Zero-Shot Learning (CZSL) aims to learn how primitive concepts, such as objects and states, combine, enabling the zero-shot classification of even unseen compositions. This work operates without assuming prior knowledge about which novel compositions are feasible, addressing an open-world setting where impossible combinations vastly outnumber possible ones. We introduce the Compositional Variational Graph Autoencoder (CVGAE), which learns variational embeddings for primitive concepts as nodes and evaluates the feasibility of their combinations through edges. This modeling strategy ensures CVGAE is scalable for real-world applications, unlike the current state-of-the-art method, CGE, which is computationally prohibitive. For instance, on the C-GQA benchmark dataset, CGE necessitates 394,000 nodes, whereas CVGAE achieves the task with only 1,323 nodes. The method maps graph and image embeddings into a shared space using a deep metric learning approach, training a similarity metric via bi-directional contrastive loss between projected embeddings. We validate our approach's efficacy across three benchmark datasets and further demonstrate through an image retrieval task that the representations learned by CVGAE are superior for compositional generalization.

**Motivation:** Identifying cancer driver genes, which are the genomic factors responsible for cancer, is a cornerstone of biomedical research. Since these genes propel cancer development and progression, pinpointing them and understanding their regulatory mechanisms is vital for designing effective treatments and interventions. Leveraging advancements in computer and data science, numerous computational approaches have emerged to analyze diverse genomic data types for uncovering cancer drivers and the underlying mechanisms of disease progression. Given the intricate nature of how cancer genes drive disease and the rapid evolution of this field, a comprehensive review of existing computational methodologies for detecting various cancer driver types is essential.

**Results:** This survey examines computational strategies for identifying cancer drivers from genomic data, classifying them into three categories: methods for single driver identification, methods for detecting driver modules, and methods for personalized cancer driver discovery. We also present a case study comparing the performance of current methods, analyze their respective strengths and limitations, and discuss future challenges and directions. Furthermore, we explore resources for discovering and validating cancer drivers to offer a centralized reference of tools that facilitate driver discovery. Ultimately, the paper aims to equip researchers with a robust foundational understanding to advance further work in this domain.

Active screening serves as a prevalent strategy for managing the propagation of recurring infectious illnesses like tuberculosis and influenza. Under this method, health personnel periodically identify a specific segment of the population for testing. However, due to the scarcity of health workers, only a limited fraction of individuals can be reached within any specific timeframe. Considering the disease's repetitive cycle and rapid transmission rate, the primary objective is to reduce the total number of infections over an extended period. This process can be modeled as sequential combinatorial optimization across a network of individuals and their interactions. The primary computational hurdles in this formulation include the problem's combinatorial complexity, the necessity for sequential planning, and the uncertainty regarding the infectious status of the population. Existing active screening research struggles to scale effectively to long time horizons while fully accounting for the future impact of current interventions. This paper introduces a novel Deep Q-Network (DQN) based reinforcement learning (RL) approach featuring several innovative modifications to tackle these issues. Firstly, we employ Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) to model the Q-function, leveraging correlations within the underlying contact network. Secondly, to bypass the need for solving a combinatorial optimization problem at every time step, we break down node selection into a sub-sequence of decisions and establish a two-level RL framework to address the problem hierarchically. Lastly, to accelerate the slow convergence of RL caused by sparse rewards, we integrate concepts from curriculum learning into our hierarchical RL system. We validate our RL algorithm using various real-world networks.

Recent advancements in reconstructing 3D scenes from multiple viewpoints have largely relied on matching isolated features, intensity variations, or curved structures. However, in general scenarios lacking controlled data, rich texture, specific geometric models, or simple scene complexity, most techniques yield unorganized outputs like point clouds, meshes, or voxels, with a few exceptions generating unstructured 3D curve fragments. Ideally, many applications demand structured representations of curves, surfaces, and their spatial relationships. This paper advances this goal by proposing a method that integrates 2D image curves into a set of 3D curves, encoding their topological connectivity within a 3D graph. The outcome is a "3D drawing," which complements surface models much like a 3D scaffold supports a tent stretched across it. We validate our approach using both synthetic and real-world datasets.

This paper employs a dynamic game-theoretic framework to examine pollution control strategies within Russia's Eastern Siberia region, utilizing actual numerical parameter values for the analysis. The findings demonstrate that collaboration among primary polluters yields advantages not only for the environment but also for the involved companies.

We present a toy model of the ten-point elliptic double-box, originally identified in arXiv:1712.02785, formulated using elliptic polylogarithms. This specific case represents an unphysical limit of the full elliptic double-box, depending solely on three dual conformal cross-ratios. Although the diagram exhibits complete permutation symmetry with respect to these cross-ratios in this limit, neither of the two elliptic polylogarithm formalisms employed to describe it makes this symmetry obvious. We note that the resulting function is a pure elliptic polylogarithm, a conclusion derived from nontrivial identities among elliptic integrals that rely on the conformal cross-ratios.

This study addresses the massive random access challenge within MIMO quasi-static Rayleigh fading channels. We establish achievability and converse bounds for the minimum energy-per-bit needed for each active user to send $J$ bits over a blocklength $n$ with power $P$, subject to a per-user probability of error (PUPE) constraint, considering scenarios with and without \emph{a priori} channel state information at the receiver (CSIR and no-CSI). In the no-CSI scenario, we analyze both cases where the count of active users $K_a$ is known and where it is not. Our achievability bounds are based on the design of a "good region." Numerical results indicate that the gap between achievability and converse bounds remains below 2.5 dB for CSIR and under 4 dB for no-CSI across most regimes. When the distribution of $K_a$ is known, the performance difference between knowing and not knowing the specific value of $K_a$ is minimal. For instance, with $n=1000$, $J=100$, $\epsilon=0.001$, and $L=128$ antennas, the additional energy-per-bit required when $K_a$ is unknown and follows a $\text{Binom}(K,0.4)$ distribution is less than 0.3 dB on the converse side and 1.1 dB on the achievability side compared to the known $K_a$ case. Spectral efficiency scales roughly linearly with $L$ in the CSIR setting, whereas this growth rate diminishes in the no-CSI setting. Additionally, we evaluate a pilot-assisted scheme, which proves suboptimal particularly when $K_a$ is large. Leveraging non-asymptotic results, we derive scaling laws for the scenario where all users are active and $J=\Theta(1)$: with no-CSI, reliable service for $K=\mathcal{O}(n^2)$ users is achievable when $L=\Theta(n^2)$ and $P=\Theta(1/n^2)$; under mild conditions with CSIR, the PUPE constraint is met if and only if $\frac{nL\ln KP}{K}=\Omega(1)$.

This study presents first-principles calculations on the electronic and mechanical characteristics of few-layer borophene, incorporating interlayer van der Waals (vdW) forces. The anisotropic metallic nature remains consistent from monolayer to few-layer configurations. In bilayer borophene, the energy splitting near the Fermi level at the $\Gamma$ point is approximately 1.7 eV, significantly exceeding the 0.5–1 eV range typical of other layered semiconductors, which points to stronger vdW interactions in this metallic system. Notably, critical strains increase with layer count, granting the material greater flexibility compared to its monolayer form. Due to the buckled atomic arrangement, out-of-plane negative Poisson's ratios are maintained as the number of layers grows. Conversely, in-plane negative Poisson's ratios vanish in layered borophene, a stark contrast to puckered black phosphorus. Expanding the interlayer distance to 6.3 $\mbox\AA$ restores the negative Poisson's ratio, suggesting that the shift in Poisson's ratio behavior stems from the robust interlayer vdW interactions inherent to layered borophene.

This paper examines the loop quantum cosmological model derived from the ADM Hamiltonian, specifically focusing on a spatially flat, homogeneous FRW universe. The resulting modified Friedmann equation retains the same structure as the APS LQC model; however, the critical matter density required for the bounce is reduced to one-quarter of that in the APS framework, expressed as $\rho_{cL}=\frac{\rho_c}{4}$. This reduction is significant because a lower critical bounce density implies that quantum gravitational effects become relevant at earlier stages compared to the previous LQC model. Furthermore, this lower threshold suggests that detecting quantum gravity effects will be more feasible than in the earlier model.

This study investigates whether high-mass star formation parallels or diverges from solar-mass star formation by analyzing new molecular line data and modeling the accretion flow around the massive protostar IRAS20126+4104. We synthesized recent VLA observations of NH3(1,1) and (2,2), new SMA data on CHCN(13-12), prior VLA measurements of NH(3,3) and NH(4,4), and earlier Plateau de Bure results for C34S(2-1), C34S(5-4), and CHCN(12-11) to create a comprehensive dataset of molecular lines spanning excitation energies from 15 to 419 K. These observations were compared with simulated spectra generated from a high-mass star formation model that scales up the standard disk-envelope paradigm used for low-mass accretion flows. Our findings indicate that, consistent with the standard paradigm, the data necessitate both a warm, dense, rapidly rotating disk and a cold, diffuse infalling envelope. Consequently, this research suggests that accretion mechanisms around 10 solar mass stars are comparable to those around solar mass stars.

High-performance computing environments are characterized by a continuous rise in core counts, necessitating a renewed focus on performance and scalability analysis, as well as established speedup laws like Amdahl's and Gustafson's, particularly regarding asymptotic behavior. Grasping the speedup and efficiency dynamics of algorithmic parallelism is vital for optimizing system operations, forecasting execution times, and analyzing asymptotic properties to establish speedup limits. However, existing literature is fragmented, displaying significant heterogeneity among speedup models and laws. This diversity complicates efforts to survey these models and their interrelations, pinpoint performance determinants within specific algorithmic contexts, and assess the applicability of these models to particular parallel computing scenarios. This work introduces a generic speedup and efficiency model tailored for homogeneous computing environments. Our method generalizes numerous prominent models from the literature, demonstrating that they can be viewed as special cases of this unified framework. By parameterizing the generic speedup model, we identify six distinct asymptotic speedup scenarios and eight asymptotic efficiency scenarios. Combining these scenarios yields eleven scalability cases, which form the basis of a scalability typology. Researchers can utilize this typology to categorize their speedup models and ascertain asymptotic behavior as the number of parallel processing units grows. Furthermore, our findings offer a foundation for exploring various extensions of this setting.

This study attempts emotional style transfer within audio by investigating the MelGAN-VC architecture for diverse emotion-to-emotion conversions. Subsequently, an LSTM-based emotion classifier analyzes the generated audio. Our findings indicate that "sad" audio is synthesized more effectively than "happy" or "anger" audio, likely because human expressions of sadness share greater similarities.

The approach to topological renormalization in anti-de Sitter (AdS) gravity involves introducing a topological term into the action to ensure finiteness and establish a well-defined variational problem. Applying this framework, we analyze the thermodynamics of asymptotically locally anti-de Sitter (AlAdS) spacetimes, specifically examining the physical characteristics of the Misner strings within the Taub-NUT-AdS and Taub-Bolt-AdS solutions. We calculate the Misner string's contribution to entropy by uniformly addressing both the AdS and AlAdS sectors. Since topological renormalization accurately captures physical quantities in the parity-preserving sector, we further explore the holographic implications of incorporating the Chern-Pontryagin topological invariant into the bulk action, with a focus on the emergence of parity-odd terms in the boundary stress tensor.

Over recent years, Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) have sparked a technological revolution, finding diverse applications across military, civilian, and commercial sectors. The rise of autonomous drones has introduced significant challenges, particularly regarding the maintenance of safe operations during missions. Ensuring UAV safety remains a critical and sensitive issue, as any unexpected drone behavior or hazard could result in severe risks. This work proposes a methodology for safety assurance within the Internet of Drones (IoD). The safety analysis employs two complementary approaches: (1) a qualitative method and (2) a quantitative method. The qualitative approach leverages international standards, specifically ISO 121200 and ISO 13849, to evaluate drone mission safety through qualitative assessment techniques. This process begins with hazard identification, proceeds to risk assessment and mitigation, and concludes with safety recommendations tailored to a drone delivery use case. The quantitative approach utilizes Bayesian Networks (BN) for probabilistic modeling, incorporating data from the qualitative phase to model safety risks associated with UAV flights. An illustrative UAV crash scenario serves as a case study to demonstrate the proposed method's applicability. Together, these qualitative and quantitative analyses enable all stakeholders to detect, explore, and address UAV flight risks, thereby assisting the industry in better managing UAV safety concerns.

The one-body reduced density matrix, denoted as $\gamma$, is essential for characterizing and forecasting quantum properties of bosonic systems, including Bose-Einstein condensation. Recent advancements in reduced density matrix functional theory for bosonic ground states confirm the existence of a universal functional $\mathcal{F}[\gamma]$ capable of precisely recovering quantum correlations. Leveraging a new decomposition of $\gamma$, we have created a methodology to construct dependable approximations for these universal functionals. Our findings indicate that for translationally invariant systems, the constrained search framework of functional theories can be converted into an unconstrained problem by parametrizing an Euclidean space. This streamlined search procedure enables the application of conventional machine-learning techniques to efficiently calculate both $\mathcal{F}[\gamma]$ and its functional derivative. Furthermore, we provide a comparative analysis of our approach against Quantum Monte Carlo simulations within the context of the Bose-Hubbard model.

Rank-constrained spatial covariance matrix estimation (RCSCME) is designed to handle scenarios where directional target speech and diffuse noise are mixed. While traditional RCSCME employs independent low-rank matrix analysis (ILRMA) as a preprocessing step, we introduce an approach utilizing independent deeply learned matrix analysis (IDLMA), a supervised extension of ILRMA. This method leverages deep neural networks (DNNs) to separate target speech from noise. Specifically, we incorporate the Denoiser, a single-channel speech enhancement DNN, within IDLMA to estimate both the target speech and the noise. Furthermore, we propose noise self-supervised RCSCME, which estimates noise-only time intervals based on Denoiser outputs to construct a prior distribution for the noise spatial covariance matrix. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed methods outperform conventional approaches across various noise conditions.

Directly imaged planets are self-luminous companions orbiting pre-main sequence and young main sequence stars at wide distances ($\sim10\mathrm{s}-1000\mathrm{s}$~AU), typically possessing greater masses than close-in planets ($\lesssim 10$~AU). Characterizing the host stars of these expansive systems is crucial for understanding different planet formation and evolution pathways. This study provides stellar parameters and metallicity ([Fe/H]) for a subsample of 18 stars with planets detected via direct imaging. By retrieving high-resolution spectra from public archives and applying synthetic spectral fitting combined with Bayesian analysis, we determined stellar properties uniformly. Metallicities were reported for the first time for eight of these sources, while results for the remaining stars align with previous estimates. Our analysis indicates that stars hosting directly imaged planets have near-solar metallicities, with a mean [Fe/H] of $-0.04\pm0.27$~dex. The significant scatter in metallicity implies that a metal-rich environment is not a prerequisite for forming massive planets at large orbital distances. Furthermore, we find that the relationship between planet mass and host star metallicity for these wide-orbit massive planets closely mirrors that observed in the well-studied population of short-period ($\lesssim 1$~yr) super-Jupiters and brown dwarfs around main-sequence stars.

Research indicates that hybrid hadron-quark equations of state supporting a third family of stable compact stars are consistent with the LIGO-Virgo observation of GW170817. These stable objects are termed hybrid hadron-quark stars, existing on a branch separated from the stable neutron star sequence by a gap of unstable hybrid configurations. The ultimate fate of these unstable states remains unexplored, yet it holds significance for understanding "twin stars"—hybrid stars sharing the same mass as neutron stars but possessing different radii. To ensure a well-defined initial value problem for general relativistic hydrodynamic equations, we adjusted existing hybrid equations of state featuring a first-order phase transition. We then utilized three-dimensional simulations within full general relativity to analyze the dynamics of non-rotating and rotating unstable twin stars. Our findings demonstrate that unstable twin stars naturally evolve toward the hadronic branch. Prior to settling into this hadronic state, the stars exhibit quasi-radial oscillations on a dynamical timescale as their cores alternate between the two phases. Consequently, our study implies that forming stable twin stars is challenging if the phase transition involves a significant jump in energy density, suggesting astrophysical hybrid hadron-quark stars are more likely to have masses exceeding the twin star range. Furthermore, we investigated the minimum-mass instability in hybrid stars, discovering that, unlike neutron stars, these configurations do not explode. Finally, our results propose that oscillations between the two Quantum Chromodynamic phases could generate gravitational wave signatures linked to phase transitions during core-collapse supernovae and white dwarf-neutron star mergers.

A locally maximally entangled (LME) state in a multipartite quantum system is defined as one where every elementary subsystem achieves maximal entanglement with its complement. This work follows arXiv:1708.01645, which established necessary and sufficient conditions for the existence of LME states based on subsystem dimensions $(d_1, d_2, \dots, d_n)$ and calculated the dimension of the space ${\cal H}_{LME}/K$ representing LME states modulo local unitary transformations for all non-empty configurations. The current paper offers a pedagogical overview and physical interpretation of the mathematical foundations behind these findings, alongside a broad set of explicit LME state constructions. Specifically, we derive all LME states for tripartite systems with dimensions $(2,A,B)$ and present a general representation-theoretic method for constructing a specific class of stabilizer LME states, which unifies many previously known examples. Furthermore, our results determine the dimension of the SLOCC equivalence class space for states with "generic" entanglement across all multipartite systems, noting its equivalence to ${\cal H}_{LME}/K$. Finally, we compute the dimension of the stabilizer subgroup $S$ within $SL(d_1, \mathbb{C}) \times \cdots \times SL(d_n, \mathbb{C})$ for generic states in arbitrary multipartite systems and identify all instances where this stabilizer is trivial.

The multi-Banana configuration $\widehat{F}_{mb}$ constitutes a local Calabi-Yau threefold of Schoen type. Specifically, it represents a conifold resolution of the fiber product $\widehat{I}_v \times_{\bf{D}} \widehat{I}_w$, where the map $\widehat{I}_v \to {\bf{D}}$ defines an elliptic surface over a formal disc ${\bf{D}}$ featuring an $I_v$ singularity on its central fiber. Building upon methods introduced in our prior work, we extend the approach to calculate genus 0 Gopakumar-Vafa invariants for specific fiber curve classes. We provide an explicit calculation for the cases $v=1$ and $v=w=2$. The derived partition function can be formulated using either the elliptic genera of $\bf{C}^2$ or classical theta functions, depending on the context.

Numerous extensions of the Standard Model propose a parallel sector governed by a new U(1) symmetry, resulting in hidden photons that serve as potential candidates for cold dark matter. These particles are anticipated to undergo kinetic mixing with ordinary photons, generating a minute, oscillating electric field associated with the dark matter. When interacting with a conductive surface, such dark matter can be converted into photons emitted nearly perpendicular to that surface, with the resulting frequency determined by the hidden photon's mass. This contribution reports preliminary findings from a search for hidden photons within the visible and near-UV spectrum, utilizing a large 14 m² spherical metallic mirror, and outlines future investigations into the eV and sub-eV ranges using various electromagnetic radiation detectors.

We present CALAMITY, a high-precision bandpass calibration technique designed for radio interferometry. This method determines direction-independent gains with complex, arbitrary frequency structures to the accuracy needed for 21 cm cosmology, requiring only minimal information about antenna beams or foregrounds and operating without any redundancy. We achieved this through two primary innovations: first, we model foregrounds on each baseline independently using a flexible, highly efficient set of basis functions that minimize overlap with 21 cm modes while enforcing spectral smoothness in the calibrated foregrounds. Second, we leverage an off-the-shelf, GPU-accelerated API (TensorFlow) to simultaneously solve for per-baseline foregrounds and per-frequency antenna gains within a single optimization loop. GPU acceleration is essential for efficiently solving the large number of foreground and gain parameters across all frequencies for interferometers with $\gtrsim 10$ antennas in a reasonable timeframe. This paper provides an overview of our technique, supported by realistic simulations, and demonstrates its capability to identify and remove pathological gain structures to the level required for measuring fluctuations in the 21 cm emission field from hydrogen gas during the Cosmic Dawn and Reionization. For those wishing to begin using CALAMITY immediately, a tutorial notebook is available at https://github.com/aewallwi/calamity/blob/main/examples/Calamity_Tutorial.ipynb.

Given the widespread occurrence of Alzheimer's disease (AD), developing robust detection strategies is critical. This study evaluates the performance and generalizability of three speech-based AD detection methods on the recent ADReSSo challenge dataset: 1) conventional acoustic features, 2) novel pre-trained acoustic embeddings, and 3) a hybrid approach combining both features and embeddings. Our findings indicate that while feature-based methods achieve higher precision, classification models utilizing pre-trained embeddings demonstrate superior and more balanced cross-validated performance across multiple metrics. Additionally, embedding-only approaches exhibit greater generalizability. Ultimately, our top-performing model surpassed the acoustic baseline by 2.8% in the challenge.

Cross-modal retrieval demands precise models to fetch pertinent results across different modalities like text, images, and video. This paper advances prior research by addressing the challenge of rapidly and effectively evaluating models both qualitatively and quantitatively. We introduce DIME (Dataset, Index, Model, Embedding), a modality-agnostic utility designed to manage multimodal datasets, trained models, and preprocessing steps, thereby facilitating easy model comparison via a web-based graphical interface. By natively supporting the creation of modality-independent queryable indexes and the extraction of relevant feature embeddings, DIME also serves as a powerful, efficient instrument for exploring and searching through datasets.

This review examines recent literature concerning quantum plasmas with any degree of degeneracy, contrasting this with the common assumption of complete degeneracy in dense environments. The core methodology involves adjusting the numerical coefficient of the Bohm potential term in quantum fluid models to align with linear wave predictions from quantum kinetic theory within the long-wavelength limit. Furthermore, the equation of state for an ideal Fermi gas is applied across all degeneracy levels. This framework facilitates the rapid derivation of weakly nonlinear equations using reductive perturbation theory, yielding quantum Korteweg-de Vries and quantum Zakharov-Kuznetsov equations alongside criteria for bright and dark soliton propagation. The study also derives quantum ion-acoustic waves in both magnetized and unmagnetized plasmas, as well as magnetosonic waves, for arbitrary degeneracy. Finally, it delineates the specific physical conditions under which these models are applicable and identifies scenarios involving mixed dense-dilute systems.

Human conduct arises from planning that involves breaking down complex tasks into goals, subgoals, and basic actions. This paper proposes and tests a normative framework for this decomposition, grounded in the premise that individuals structure tasks to minimize planning costs without compromising performance. By analyzing 11,117 graph-based planning tasks, we demonstrate that our framework validates several existing decomposition heuristics and generates unique predictions distinct from two other normative theories. Furthermore, we conducted a behavioral study with 806 participants using a diverse set of 30 randomly selected graphs—larger and more varied than any prior study in this domain. Our findings indicate that human behavior aligns more closely with our proposed framework and specifically supports the betweenness centrality heuristic, which our approach justifies. Collectively, these results offer novel theoretical insights into the computational mechanisms driving the intelligent organization of goal-directed actions.

Non-contrastive self-supervised learning techniques, including BYOL and SimSiam, achieve impressive practical results by minimizing the distance between two augmented views of the same image, yet their theoretical foundations remain underdeveloped. While Tian et al. (2021) clarified why representations avoid collapsing to zero, the mechanism behind feature learning remained unclear. This work demonstrates that within a linear network setting, non-contrastive methods successfully learn an optimal projection matrix and lower sample complexity for downstream tasks. Our analysis reveals that weight decay functions as an implicit threshold, filtering out features with high variance under augmentation while retaining those with low variance. Building on these insights, we propose DirectCopy, a simpler and more computationally efficient algorithm that eliminates the eigen-decomposition step found in the original DirectPred method from Tian et al. (2021). Experimental results on STL-10, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet show that DirectCopy matches or exceeds the performance of DirectPred.

We provide a comprehensive characterization of the highly dusty main-sequence star TYC 8830 410 1. This system contains an inner planetary dust belt at a temperature of approximately 300 K, exhibiting a fractional infrared luminosity of roughly 1%. Mid-infrared spectroscopy identifies a prominent, mildly crystalline solid-state emission feature. TYC 8830 410 1, classified as a G9V star, is co-moving and co-distant with an M4-type companion located at a separation of 49.5 arcseconds; we estimate the system's age to be around 600 million years. Additionally, the star undergoes "dipper"-like dimming events observed by ASAS-SN and TESS, with further details provided by LCOGT. These recurring eclipses indicate the presence of at least one star-sized dust cloud orbiting the star, alongside various smaller dust structures. The extreme nature of the material surrounding TYC 8830 410 1 suggests dramatic dust-production mechanisms, potentially involving a giant-impact event similar to the one that created the Earth-Moon system, occurring hundreds of millions of years after such processes are believed to have ended in our solar system. Ultimately, TYC 8830 410 1 offers significant potential for advancing our understanding of the origin, structure, and evolution of extremely dusty inner planetary systems.

We reveal a new mechanism for the superscattering of subwavelength resonators, one deeply rooted in the physics of bound states in the continuum. Our findings show that superscattering arises from constructive interference governed by the Friedrich-Wintgen mechanism, allowing the cross-section within a single open scattering channel to surpass existing theoretical limits. By constructing a non-Hermitian model to analyze the interference of quasi-normal mode resonances, we demonstrate that this phenomenon is exclusive to scatterers lacking spherical symmetry, meaning it cannot be anticipated using classical Mie theory. These results expose unique physical behaviors in non-Hermitian systems, offering significant insights for the design of functional metadevices.

Human-in-the-loop machine learning is extensively utilized in artificial intelligence to obtain labels from experts or to refine predictions through feedback, often by abstracting away the nuances of an expert's decision-making process. This study introduces a method that additionally elicits imperfect decision rules from experts to capture their reasoning. These rules provide supplementary information that can generalize to new distributions, thereby enhancing performance in scenarios involving distribution shifts, such as domain adaptation. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach in lifelong learning and domain adaptation tasks, while also exploring its potential in other AI domains like knowledge acquisition for expert systems. Empirical results from both simulated and real-user studies confirm that eliciting decision rules not only improves domain adaptation but also effectively transfers expert knowledge to AI models.

Magic-angle twisted trilayer graphene (MATTG) has recently been identified as a new moiré material characterized by intense electronic correlations and non-conventional superconductivity. Despite this, spectroscopic investigations into its electronic behavior are scarce, leaving the specific nature of its superconductivity and order parameter unclear. This study utilizes high-resolution scanning tunneling microscopy and spectroscopy on MATTG to uncover extensive areas of atomic reconstruction that prefer mirror-symmetric stacking. Within these zones, we detect a series of symmetry-breaking electronic transitions and doping-sensitive band structure distortions akin to those found in magic-angle bilayers, a phenomenon theoretically anticipated due to the presence of flat bands. Notably, in a density range corresponding to two to three holes per moiré unit cell, clear signs of superconductivity appear as significant dips in tunneling conductance at the Fermi level, featuring coherence peaks that diminish under higher temperatures and magnetic fields. The observed doping-dependent evolution of conductance aligns with a gate-controlled shift from a gapped to a nodal superconductor; theoretically, this supports a sharp transition from Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer (BCS) to Bose-Einstein condensation (BEC) superconductivity with a nodal order parameter. Furthermore, within this doping window, we identify peak-dip-hump structures indicating that superconductivity arises from strong coupling to bosonic modes in MATTG. These findings facilitate deeper insights into superconductivity and correlated states in graphene-based moiré systems beyond twisted bilayers, where unconventional superconductivity and nodal pairing have previously been documented.

Stochastic optimization challenges frequently arise when data distributions shift in response to the chosen decision variables. A prime example occurs when population members alter their features to game a deployed classifier, thereby increasing their probability of receiving a positive label. Recent research into performative prediction has proposed an intriguing approach: identifying the decision that is optimal relative to the static distribution it creates. Extending this research, we demonstrate that standard stochastic algorithms—typically engineered for static scenarios—can be directly applied to locate such equilibria with minimal efficiency loss. This is because the primary effect of the distributional shift is to introduce a bias into these algorithms that diminishes linearly as the solution is approached. Leveraging this insight, we establish rigorous convergence guarantees for widely used methods, including stochastic gradient descent, clipped gradient, proximal point, and dual averaging (along with their accelerated and proximal variants). In practical settings, executing a decision rule is often far costlier than sampling data. We present modifications to these algorithms that preserve their sample efficiency while limiting the number of decision rule deployments to a logarithmic scale.

Smart agriculture represents a transformative trend in the agricultural sector, utilizing embedded plant sensors to gather essential data for informed decision-making, thereby enhancing crop quality and mitigating threats like pests and diseases. In Saudi Arabia, where palm cultivation is paramount, there is a growing demand for smart agricultural technologies to boost date production and curb disease outbreaks. A particularly devastating threat is the red palm weevil, an insect capable of inflicting severe damage and wiping out extensive palm groves. The primary challenge lies in the fact that weevil damage remains invisible to the human eye until the infestation reaches an advanced stage, necessitating advanced technological solutions for early detection and prevention of spread. To address this, this project presents an IoT-based smart palm monitoring prototype as a proof-of-concept that enables (1) remote palm surveillance via smart sensors and (2) the early identification of red palm weevil infestations. Farmers can utilize web or mobile applications to manage their farms and receive alerts regarding potential infestations. The Elm IoT platform was employed to bridge the sensor and user layers, while accelerometer data was collected and analyzed using signal processing and statistical methods to establish a unique infestation fingerprint.

Quantum hardware operations, including gates and measurements, are inherently prone to imperfections that cause errors. Effectively mitigating these unavoidable errors is essential for fully harnessing the capabilities of quantum systems. This paper introduces a unified framework designed to reduce gate and measurement errors when calculating quantum expectation values using the truncated Neumann series. The core concept involves approximating the inverse of quantum errors by linearly combining errors of various orders generated through sequential device applications, utilizing specifically selected coefficients to neutralize error effects. Notably, the estimation error decreases exponentially with the truncated order, while the mitigation overhead remains independent of system size, provided the device exhibits moderate noise resistance. Numerical evaluations across different error types demonstrate a significant enhancement in computational accuracy. The proposed framework offers several key benefits: it addresses both gate and measurement errors within a single approach, requires no assumptions about error structure or complete error characterization via tomography, and is highly scalable. These attributes make the framework efficient and practical, thereby expanding the utility of near-term quantum devices for real-world applications.

Building on the foundational work of Feynman and Deutsch, we formally introduce the theory of physical computability and its corresponding physical complexity theory. To accomplish this, we outline a framework capable of assessing nearly all computational forms across diverse physical mechanisms. This paper primarily utilizes this framework to revisit the theory of Quantum Computation. Additionally, as a preliminary exploration of broader issues, we present several examples of other physical mechanisms within this study.

We numerically integrate the equations of motion for active nematics, coupled with a Turing reaction-diffusion model, to investigate how active nematic flow influences stripe patterns generated by Turing instability. When activity is uniform throughout the system, these patterns dissociate once the flux from active advection counterbalances the reaction-diffusion flux. Conversely, if activity is linked to Turing morphogen concentrations and neighboring stripes exhibit equal but opposite activity, the system self-organizes into shearing flows; in this state, stripes tend to fracture and slip laterally to connect with adjacent ones. We examine the role of active instabilities in governing the transition between these regimes, with our findings holding relevance for mechanochemical coupling in biological contexts.

We examine the target space theory for bosonic and heterotic strings, compactified to three dimensions and expanded to first order in $\alpha'$, utilizing a formulation that is explicitly invariant under T-duality via ${\rm O}(d,d,\mathbb{R})$, where $d=23$ for the bosonic case and $d=7$ for the heterotic case. Although two-derivative supergravity displays an enhanced U-duality symmetry of ${\rm O}(d+1,d+1)$, this continuous group is reduced to ${\rm O}(d,d,\mathbb{R})$ by the leading $\alpha'$ correction. We re-examine this phenomenon by calculating the complete effective actions in three dimensions to first order in $\alpha'$ through the dualization of vector gauge fields. By introducing a vector compensator, we construct a formulation that is formally ${\rm O}(d+1,d+1)$ invariant and identify a chiral structure that permits the reconstruction of the bosonic action from the heterotic one. Additionally, integrating out the external $B$-field yields a specific massive deformation, which generates a new Chern-Simons term derived from composite connections; notably, this term remains ${\rm O}(d+1,d+1)$ invariant to leading order in the deformation parameter.

A Kavli Foundation-sponsored workshop titled \emph{Petabytes to Science} took place in Las Vegas from February 12th to 14th, 2019. The primary objective was to examine emerging trends and technologies that could advance astronomy, while also addressing strategies for developing the future workforce, education, and public engagement. This document was co-authored during the event and refined in the subsequent weeks, encapsulating the discussions and highlighting key recommendations generated by the workshop. Moving forward, portions of this document will be distilled to formulate potential white papers for the decadal survey.

This paper reports on the luminosity measurements obtained by the CMS detector at the LHC's interaction point 5, utilizing proton-proton collisions at $\sqrt{s} =$ 13 TeV during the 2015 and 2016 runs. The absolute luminosity scale for individual bunch crossings was determined using beam-separation scans via the van der Meer technique, achieving relative precisions of 1.3% and 1.0% for 2015 and 2016, respectively. The primary sources of uncertainty stem from residual discrepancies between measured and operational beam positions, the assumption of factorizable proton bunch spatial density functions transverse to the beam, and the modeling of electromagnetic interactions among protons within colliding bunches. When the van der Meer calibration is applied to the full run periods during which CMS was fully operational, the resulting integrated luminosities are 2.27 and 36.3 fb$^{-1}$ for 2015 and 2016, with relative precisions of 1.6% and 1.2%, respectively. These results represent some of the most precise luminosity measurements ever achieved at a bunched-beam hadron collider.

We examine second sound across different states of matter using non-equilibrium effective field theory (EFT). Specifically, we demonstrate that at finite temperature, each state of matter admits at least two qualitatively distinct EFTs—often more—ensuring that for any given system, there is always one formulation supporting a propagating second-sound wave and another that does not. To facilitate the construction of these theories, we apply the coset method tailored for non-equilibrium systems. Our findings indicate that the presence or absence of second-sound modes stems from differing selections of a novel type of inverse Higgs constraint. Furthermore, we show that relying on these new inverse Higgs constraints is unnecessary if EFTs are formulated on a specialized manifold; this manifold resembles the standard fluid worldvolume but features reduced gauge symmetries.

Role discovery involves partitioning graph nodes into categories based on structural similarity. Contemporary approaches to this task generally utilize graph embedding techniques to detect intricate local patterns. Nevertheless, interpreting or validating the roles identified by these methods becomes challenging when applied to large-scale, real-world networks. Drawing inspiration from recent progress in explainable artificial intelligence (XAI), this study introduces a novel framework for elucidating role assignments in extensive graphs by leveraging small, representative subgraph structures called graphlets. We apply our approach to a substantial, multidisciplinary citation network, successfully uncovering significant citation patterns that mirror interdisciplinary research trends.

Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a developmental condition marked by substantial challenges in social interaction, communication, and behavior. Individuals with autism and associated intellectual or developmental disabilities (AUIDD) generally necessitate sustained care and specialized therapeutic instruction. Effective management of AUIDD depends on precise behavioral monitoring conducted by trained applied behavioral analysts (ABAs). Nevertheless, this task places a heavy burden on clinicians, who must gather and interpret data, pinpoint problematic behaviors, perform pattern analysis to forecast outcomes, hypothesize treatment efficacy, and assess intervention impacts. The convergence of digital technologies in clinical workflows and progress in automated decision-making via Artificial Intelligence (AI) underscores the value of enhancing teaching and therapy through advanced algorithms and high-fidelity sensors. This article introduces an AI-Augmented Learning and Applied Behavior Analytics (AI-ABA) platform designed to deliver customized treatment and learning strategies for AUIDD individuals. By establishing systematic experiments alongside automated data collection and analysis, AI-ABA can foster self-regulatory behaviors through reinforcement-based augmented or virtual reality and mobile applications. Consequently, AI-ABA can enable clinicians to concentrate on making accurate, data-driven choices, thereby elevating the quality of individualized interventions for those with AUIDD.

Recent years have witnessed significant advancements in learned image compression, with Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) and Multi-Scale Structural Similarity (MS-SSIM) emerging as the primary evaluation metrics. However, since these metrics capture only partial aspects of human perception, existing approaches typically optimize two separate models using each metric as an independent loss function. This strategy is suboptimal and complicates the selection of a model that excels in both visual quality and overall performance. To address this limitation, we introduce Harmonize optimization metrics in Learned Image Compression (HLIC), which employs reinforcement learning to adapt the loss function online. This approach effectively combines the strengths of both PSNR and MS-SSIM, resulting in superior visual quality and higher VMAF scores. To the best of our knowledge, this work represents the first exploration of automatic loss function adaptation for harmonizing optimization metrics in low-level vision tasks such as learned image compression.

Prior research suggests that the peak of quarkonium entropy at the deconfinement transition correlates with the entropic force responsible for heavy quarkonium dissociation. This study investigates such entropic forces within a rotating, hot, and dense medium via the AdS/CFT correspondence. We find that introducing angular velocity amplifies the entropic force, thereby promoting quarkonium dissociation, a result mirrored by the inclusion of chemical potential. Additionally, our findings indicate that quarkonium dissociates more readily in a rotating medium than in a static one.

This article introduces two discretization techniques for planar linear elasticity rooted in isogeometric analysis (IGA). The first approach employs the established ansatz of weakly imposed symmetry for the stress tensor to derive a well-posed mixed formulation; while similar modified mixed problems have been explored previously, our focus lies on leveraging IGA to effectively manage curved boundary geometries. The second approach addresses the more complex scenario of strong symmetry by discretizing the mixed weak form derived from the Hellinger-Reissner variational principle. We demonstrate the existence of appropriate approximate fields that result in an inf-sup stable saddle-point problem. Furthermore, convergence proofs are provided for both methods, and for the weak symmetry case, several numerical experiments illustrate the approximation behavior.

Semantic parsing remains difficult because of the structural and semantic disparities between natural language utterances and their corresponding logical forms. This paper introduces an unsupervised method called Synchronous Semantic Decoding (SSD), which addresses both gaps by integrating paraphrasing with grammar-constrained decoding. We reframe semantic parsing as a constrained paraphrasing task: for any given utterance, the model concurrently produces a canonical version of the sentence and its meaning representation. During this synchronous decoding process, utterance paraphrasing is restricted by the logical form's structure, allowing for controlled generation of the canonical utterance. Simultaneously, semantic decoding is directed by the semantics of this canonical utterance, enabling the unsupervised generation of the logical form. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that SSD is a viable and effective approach, achieving competitive performance on various datasets without supervision.

HarmonicBalance.jl is an open-source Julia package built to streamline the analysis and resolution of periodic, time-dependent nonlinear ordinary differential equations. It employs the harmonic balance method to model system time-dependence, approximating behavior through harmonic terms with slowly changing amplitudes. Within this framework, all potential steady-state responses are derived by solving a polynomial system. HarmonicBalance.jl integrates harmonic balance with modern symbolic algebra tools and the homotopy continuation method to numerically identify every steady-state solution along with their fluctuation dynamics. To facilitate the investigation of complex steady-state topologies, the package includes an intuitive graphical user interface for custom solution observables and phase diagrams. This free software can be accessed at https://github.com/NonlinearOscillations/HarmonicBalance.jl.

This study examines the properties of a recently proposed conserved charge in general relativity across the inflationary, matter-dominated, and radiation-dominated epochs of the expanding universe. We demonstrate that during inflation, this charge manifests as Bekenstein-Hawking entropy, whereas in the matter and radiation eras, it corresponds respectively to matter and radiation entropy; notably, the charge remains conserved throughout. These findings are qualitatively supported by a numerical analysis of a model incorporating a scalar field and radiation. The results presented herein offer additional evidence for the interpretation that the conserved charge in general relativity represents entropy.

A reconfiguration problem involves determining a sequence of valid transformations that connects two feasible solutions, ensuring every intermediate state remains feasible. This paper examines the distributed spanning tree reconfiguration problem by introducing a novel operation known as $k$-simultaneous add and delete. In this operation, each node may add or remove at most $k$ edges, provided no two nodes modify the same edge simultaneously. First, we observe that for rooted spanning trees, reconfiguration between two inputs can be achieved in a single round within the CONGEST model using one $1$-simultaneous add and delete step. Consequently, we focus on unrooted spanning trees, demonstrating that transforming one unrooted tree into another via a single $1$-simultaneous add and delete step necessitates $\Omega(n)$ rounds in the LOCAL model. Furthermore, we establish that performing such a transformation with a single $2$-simultaneous add and delete step is achievable in $O(\log n)$ rounds within the CONGEST model.

Recognizing scenes is a core component of robotic perception. While humans excel at this task due to their extensive knowledge of real-world objects, leveraging human-derived object priors for scene recognition remains underutilized. This paper proposes utilizing meaningful object representations to enhance indoor scene understanding. Initially, we establish a baseline using an Improved Object Model (IOM) that enriches object knowledge by integrating a scene parsing algorithm pretrained on the ADE20K dataset, which features a wide variety of indoor object categories. To better analyze object co-occurrences and pairwise relationships, we reframe the IOM from a Bayesian standpoint as the Bayesian Object Relation Model (BORM). Furthermore, we integrate this BORM with PlacesCNN to create the Combined Bayesian Object Relation Model (CBORM) for scene recognition. On the reduced Places365 and SUN RGB-D datasets, CBORM significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods without requiring retraining, demonstrating the method's strong generalization capabilities. The code is available at https://github.com/hszhoushen/borm.

Modeling and simulating intelligent, adaptive behaviors within spatially explicit individual-based models remains a persistent challenge for researchers. Although real-world behavioral data are increasingly abundant, few methods exist to quantify and formalize how key individual behaviors evolve across space and time. Consequently, standard agent decision-making frameworks, such as event-condition-action rules, are often limited to modeling only a narrow spectrum of behaviors. We contend that these traditional frameworks frequently fail to mirror real-world scenarios and cannot adequately capture how behaviors develop in response to stimuli. Recently, there has been growing interest in Machine Learning methods for simulating intelligent adaptive behaviors, with Reinforcement Learning (RL) emerging as a promising approach. This paper investigates the application of RL to generate emergent agent behaviors within a simple predator-prey Agent-Based Model (ABM). Through a series of simulations, we demonstrate that agents trained using the novel Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) algorithm exhibit behaviors characteristic of real-world intelligent adaptation, including hiding, evading, and foraging.

This research aims to systematically mine unstructured data from hacker forums, where posts often lack formal writing standards. While various security initiatives and commercial organizations utilize publicly available information, they predominantly rely on structured sources. Our study addresses the challenge of identifying malicious IP addresses reported within these forums. We propose an automated method designed to detect these threats without depending on external resources. A primary innovation involves using matrix decomposition to extract latent behavioral features from users, which are then integrated with textual data from related posts. A significant advantage of our approach is its adaptability across different language forums, as it avoids the need for complex Natural Language Processing; instead, it requires only a few keywords in the target language alongside specific user behavior features. Additionally, we have created a tool to automate data collection from security forums, using which we gathered approximately 600,000 posts from three distinct sources. Our method demonstrates high classification accuracy, achieving a precision rate exceeding 88% for identifying malicious IPs across all three forums. We contend that our solution offers substantially richer insights, uncovering up to three times more potentially malicious IP addresses than the VirusTotal reference blacklist. As cyber conflicts intensify, gaining early access to actionable intelligence is crucial for neutralizing hackers' first-move advantage, making this work a meaningful step in that direction.
For each countable ordinal $\xi$, we define a metric space $X_{\xi}$ such that both its transfinite asymptotic dimension and its complementary-finite asymptotic dimension equal $\xi$.

Between 2005 and 2012, the Fermilab Main Injector delivered high-intensity beams of 120 GeV protons for the generation of antiprotons and neutrino beams. Through hardware upgrades and enhanced diagnostics, the facility achieved sustained operation at approximately 400 kW of beam power. While transmission efficiency remained exceptionally high, some beam loss occurred at or near the 8 GeV injection energy, where a 95% transmission rate resulted in roughly 1.5 kW of lost beam. By minimizing and localizing these losses, residual radiation levels decreased while beam power doubled. The lost beam was routed to either the collimation system or the beam abort mechanism. Additionally, critical apertures were expanded, and improved instrumentation enabled the optimal utilization of available space.
