We investigate the dynamics of a finite-dimensional quantum system subjected to frequent, generic quantum operations, modeled as an arbitrary quantum dynamical semigroup. By extending the Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff formula, we recast this pulsed evolution into a continuous framework, uncovering an underlying adiabatic process. Consequently, we derive a generalized form of quantum Zeno dynamics that not only encompasses all established phenomena found in existing literature but also characterizes novel types.

Revenue-optimal mechanisms for multiple items are notoriously intricate, frequently utilizing randomized lotteries for buyers. In the standard single-item purchase framework, optimal mechanisms can generate revenue infinitely greater than any "simple" mechanism—defined as those with a size polynomial in the number of items—even when restricted to just two items and one buyer (Briest et al. 2015; Hart and Nisan 2017). We propose a novel parameterized family of mechanisms termed "buy-$k$" mechanisms, which provide a smooth transition between traditional single-item mechanisms and recently analyzed multi-item mechanisms (Chawla et al. 2019, 2020, 2022). In a buy-$k$ mechanism, a buyer may select up to $k$ options from a menu. We demonstrate that limiting the seller to incentive-compatible buy-$n$ mechanisms eliminates the anomalous infinite revenue characteristics of the single-item model. Specifically, for an additive buyer, the revenue gap relative to bundling—an extremely straightforward mechanism—is bounded by $O(n^2)$ for any arbitrarily correlated distribution $\mathcal{D}$ over $n$ items. Furthermore, our methods establish analogous upper bounds for arbitrary monotone valuations, though with an exponential factor in the approximation.

Conversely, we prove that permitting a buyer to choose only a small number of menu options fails to ensure sub-exponential approximations, even if the benchmark is relaxed to the optimal deterministic buy-$k$ mechanism. If an additive buyer is restricted to purchasing $k = \Theta(n^{1/2-\varepsilon})$ menu options, the revenue gap between the optimal deterministic buy-$k$ mechanism and bundling can be exponential in $n$. Consequently, no "simple" mechanism can achieve a sub-exponential approximation within this regime.

Unlike natural languages, understanding source code relies heavily on the grammatical connections between tokens, independent of their specific identifiers. Graph-based representations, such as Abstract Syntax Trees (AST), can uncover token relationships that are not immediately apparent in the raw code. We introduce GN-Transformer, a novel approach designed to learn end-to-end from a combined sequence and graph modality termed the Syntax-Code-Graph (SCG). By extending the Graph Networks (GN) framework with self-attention mechanisms, GN-Transformer leverages SCG, which results from the early fusion of source code snippets and their AST structures. Through experiments analyzing SCG structure, model design ablations, and hyper-parameter tuning, we demonstrate that the performance gains stem from this fused representation. The proposed method achieves state-of-the-art results on two code summarization datasets across three metrics: BLEU, METEOR, and ROUGE-L. Furthermore, an expert-user study evaluating human-perceived quality confirms that our model surpasses existing state-of-the-art approaches in both accuracy and perceived quality.

The study examines nuclear binding energies using two versions of the Skyrme model: the first substitutes the conventional Skyrme term with a sixth-order derivative term, while the second incorporates a potential quartic in pion fields. It is demonstrated that solitons in the first model diverge substantially from previously assumed ans\"atze in the literature. Binding energies derived from both models are lower than those from the standard Skyrme model, with the results from the second model aligning closely with experimental values.

This paper investigates the asymptotic properties of the smallest eigenvalue, $\lambda_{N}$, of the Hankel (or moments) matrix $\mathcal{H}_{N}=\left(\mu_{m+n}\right)_{0\leq m,n\leq N}$, defined under the weight function $w(x)=x^{\alpha}{\rm e}^{-x^{\beta}}$ for $x\in[0,\infty)$, where $\alpha>-1$ and $\beta>\frac{1}{2}$. Building upon prior work by Szeg\"{o}, Chen, and others, we derive an asymptotic expression for the orthonormal polynomials $\mathcal{P}_{N}(z)$ as $N\rightarrow\infty$ corresponding to $w(x)$. Leveraging this result, we establish specific asymptotic formulas for $\lambda_{N}$. Furthermore, by utilizing the parallel algorithm developed by Emmart, Chen, and Weems, we generate numerous numerical results for $\lambda_{N}$ that align with our theoretical findings.

An equivariant minimal surface in $\mathbb{CH}^n$ is defined as a minimal map from the Poincaré disc into $\mathbb{CH}^n$ that connects two actions of the fundamental group of a closed surface $\Sigma$: a Fuchsian representation on the disc and an irreducible isometric action on $\mathbb{CH}^n$. The moduli space of such surfaces is analyzed by linking it to the nilpotent cone within the moduli space of $PU(n,1)$-Higgs bundles over the associated conformal surface. This article establishes a necessary condition for the smoothness of points on this cone, demonstrating that the moduli space is smooth everywhere except at points corresponding to branched minimal immersions or $\pm$-holomorphic immersions. This reasoning can be readily extended to show that the entire space of (unbranched) immersions in $\mathbb{RH}^n$ is smooth. For $\mathbb{CH}^2$, the connected components of the moduli space of minimal immersions are characterized by the Toledo invariant and the Euler number of the normal bundle. This classification is achieved by examining the limit points of the $\mathbb{C}^\times$-action on the nilpotent cone; specifically, limits as $t \to 0$ yield only branched minimal or $\pm$-holomorphic immersions. Consequently, the Euler number of the normal bundle can only change when passing through branched minimal maps.

Let $\mathfrak{u}_\zeta^\vee$ represent the small quantum group linked to a simple Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}^\vee$ and a root of unity $\zeta$. Building on the geometric description of the center of $\mathfrak{u}_\zeta^\vee$ found in [8], we employ a combinatorial approach to establish a formula for the dimension of a specific subalgebra within the $G^\vee$-invariant component of the center $Z(\mathfrak{u}_\zeta^\vee)^{G^\vee}$. This subalgebra is conjectured to be identical to the entire $G^\vee$-invariant center. Furthermore, when $G=SL_n$, we investigate a refinement of this dimension formula determined by two gradings with geometric origins.

In the last ten years, 3D graphics have evolved to achieve high realism, significantly increasing in size and complexity. However, application-specific and hardware-related limitations often require these models to be simplified or lossily compressed, which can compromise visual fidelity. Consequently, evaluating visual quality is crucial for optimizing the Quality of Experience (QoE) by balancing data size against perceptual quality to guide compression strategies. This study focuses on assessing the subjective and objective quality of textured 3D meshes. We introduce a large-scale dataset comprising 55 source models characterized by geometric, color, and semantic complexity, which have been distorted using five types of compression artifacts applied to geometry, texture mapping, and texture images, resulting in over 343,000 distorted stimuli. From this collection, we identified a challenging subset of 3,000 stimuli for a massive crowdsourced experiment involving over 4,500 participants, yielding 148,929 quality ratings. Utilizing this subjectively rated dataset, we developed a learning-based quality metric for 3D graphics. This metric achieves state-of-the-art performance on our textured mesh dataset and on a separate dataset of distorted meshes with vertex colors. Finally, we demonstrate the utility of our metric and dataset in investigating how distortion interactions and content characteristics affect the perceived quality of compressed textured meshes.

We demonstrate that for any prime $p>2$, where $q=p^\nu$ is a power of $p$ and $n\ge p$, there exists a Galois extension $K/\mathbb F_q(T)$ that is ramified exclusively at $\infty$ with $\mathrm{Gal}(K/\mathbb F_q(T))=G$, provided $G$ is the symmetric group $S_n$ or the alternating group $A_n$. This result holds with the sole exception of $G=S_{p+1}$ when $\mathbb F_q\supset \mathbb F_{p^2}$. Consequently, this validates Abhyankar's conjecture for symmetric and alternating groups over finite fields of odd characteristic, subject to the aforementioned exception regarding $S_{p+1}$ and the condition $\mathbb F_q\supset\mathbb F_{p^2}$.

Building on the spherically symmetric black hole (BH) derived from the quadratic $f(T)$ theory in \cite{Bahamonde:2019zea}, we compute its energy, curvature invariants, and torsion, showing that higher-order torsion contributions weaken the singularity relative to the Schwarzschild BH in general relativity (GR). We also analyze the thermodynamic properties to highlight the impact of these higher-order terms. Consequently, we construct a new spherically symmetric BH based on the cubic form $f(T)=T+\epsilon\Big[\frac{1}{2}\alpha T^2+\frac{1}{3}\beta T^3\Big]$, with $\epsilon<<1$ and $\alpha, \beta$ as constants. This solution is defined by the parameters $\alpha$, $\beta$, and $\epsilon$, reducing to GR when $\epsilon=0$. We investigate the physics of these new solutions using the same methodology applied to the quadratic case, demonstrating that the higher-order torsion term, $\frac{1}{2}\alpha T^2+\frac{1}{3}\beta T^3$, can yield intriguing physical phenomena.

This paper investigates the shape optimization problem concerning the first eigenvalue of the $p$-Laplace operator under mixed Neumann-Dirichlet boundary conditions on multiply-connected domains within hyperbolic space. Specifically, we demonstrate that among all such domains with a fixed volume and a specified $(n-1)$-th quermassintegral for the convex Dirichlet (inner) boundary, the concentric annular region maximizes the first eigenvalue. Furthermore, we establish a Nagy-type inequality applicable to outer parallel sets of a convex domain in hyperbolic space.

We present more than 13 years of optical and near-ultraviolet spectropolarimetric data concerning P Cygni, a renowned Luminous Blue Variable (LBV). As a pivotal transitional stage for the most massive stars, LBVs exhibit the highest mass-loss rates among stellar groups. By employing spectropolarimetry, we investigate the geometry of the near circumstellar environment around P Cygni and derive insights into LBV mass-loss mechanisms. Utilizing data from the HPOL and WUPPE spectropolarimeters, we quantify the interstellar polarization contribution to P Cygni's signal, examine polarization variability within the H$\alpha$ emission line, and search for periodic signals. Additionally, we introduce a novel statistical method for identifying preferred position angles in deviations from spherical symmetry, a technique new to astronomy. Our results align with prior studies, indicating free-electron scattering from clumps uniformly distributed around the star. However, this picture is complicated by variations in the percent-polarization of the H$\alpha$ line and the discovery of several previously unobserved periodicities.

We introduce $\text{POINT}^2$, a Point-Of-Interest Network designed for tracking and triangulation, to address the challenge of multiview 2D/3D rigid registration in medical interventions. $\text{POINT}^2$ establishes 2D point-to-point correspondences between pre- and intra-intervention images by tracking random points of interest (POIs), subsequently estimating the 3D pose of the pre-intervention volume through a triangulation layer. By integrating the POI tracker and triangulation layer into a unified framework, the method jointly learns discriminative 2D features and estimates 3D poses. Unlike previous approaches, $\text{POINT}^2$ achieves reliable 2D/3D registration with only a single forward pass. Additionally, the shift-invariant nature of the POI tracker enhances robustness against variations in the initial 3D pre-intervention pose. Extensive experiments on a large-scale clinical cone-beam CT (CBCT) dataset demonstrate that $\text{POINT}^2$ surpasses existing learning-based methods in accuracy, robustness, and execution speed. Moreover, when employed as an initial pose estimator, the method boosts the robustness and speed of state-of-the-art optimization-based techniques by a factor of ten.

We examine a straightforward lattice model possessing local symmetry, constructed from a crossed module of finite groups. The dynamical variables in this framework are linked to both the edges and faces of a four-dimensional lattice. Under specific conditions, the model converges to established topological quantum field theories. This study concentrates on the system's dynamics, investigating them through both analytical methods and Monte Carlo simulations. We establish a factorization theorem that simplifies the calculation of correlation functions for local observables by relating them to simpler, known models. By integrating this theorem with standard Kramers-Wannier dualities, we propose a comprehensive phase diagram, a structure subsequently validated by numerical simulations. Additionally, we detail the model's topological charges, symmetries, and symmetry breaking mechanisms. The associated order parameters include the Polyakov loop and its extension, termed the Polyakov surface. The latter is notably significant because it falls outside the applicability of the factorization theorem. Numerical results indicate that the expectation value of the Polyakov surface can identify all phase transitions and exhibits sensitivity to the magnitude of the topological charge.

This study introduces an iterative learning control (ILC) framework designed for continuously operating repetitive systems lacking an initial condition reset. To achieve this, we construct a lifted system representation that incorporates the impact of initial conditions on system dynamics and projects these dynamics across multiple future iterations. Furthermore, we formulate an economic cost function and corresponding update law that evaluates performance over an extended future horizon, enabling a prediction range beyond the immediate next iteration. The convergence of the iteration, accounting for varying initial conditions and applied inputs, is rigorously proven and validated through a simulated servo-positioning system.

Integrating deep neural networks into robotics presents a significant hurdle: the absence of uncertainty metrics for their predictions. Although recent studies have attempted to estimate uncertainty in deep object detectors, these efforts have achieved limited success primarily because 1) information is lost during the non-maximum suppression (NMS) stage, and 2) the approach fails to address the multitask, many-to-one characteristics of anchor-based detection. To address these issues, we propose BayesOD, a method that reimagines both standard detector inference and NMS through a Bayesian lens. Evaluations across four standard object detection datasets demonstrate that BayesOD generates uncertainty estimates with stronger correlation to detection accuracy, resulting in a substantial decrease of 9.77%–13.13% in minimum Gaussian uncertainty error and 1.63%–5.23% in minimum categorical uncertainty error. The source code will be made available at {\url{https://github.com/asharakeh/bayes-od-rc}}.

This paper addresses the challenge of measuring and testing joint independence across a set of multivariate random variables. Leveraging the developing theory of optimal transport (OT) and multivariate ranks, we introduce a distribution-free test for multivariate joint independence. Central to this approach is the concept of rank joint distance covariance (RJdCov), a higher-order extension of the renowned distance covariance metric designed to capture dependencies within all variable subsets. RJdCov can be readily estimated from data without requiring moment assumptions, and the associated joint independence test is universally consistent. Calibration of the test is achievable without prior knowledge of the (unknown) marginal distributions, valid both asymptotically and in finite samples. Beyond its distribution-free nature and universal consistency, the proposed test demonstrates statistical efficiency, evidenced by non-trivial asymptotic (Pitman) efficiency. We validate this by calculating the limiting local power against mixture and joint Konijn alternatives. Furthermore, we utilize the RJdCov metric to develop an independent component analysis (ICA) method that is straightforward to implement and robust against outliers and contamination. Extensive simulations compare the proposed test's performance against other existing methods. Finally, we apply the test to uncover higher-order dependence structures among various US industries using stock price data.

This paper examines a variant of D. Price's bibliographic network growth model, wherein each iteration assigns a fixed number of citations through a weighted mix of uniform (accidental) and preferential (rich-get-richer) mechanisms. Rather than employing the standard master equation method, we analyze and resolve the problem using the rank-size distribution. Our findings demonstrate that this process asymptotically converges to a Pareto-type 2 distribution with a highly interpretable parameterization. Furthermore, we establish that the Price model's solution in terms of rank-size distribution aligns with the expected values of order statistics from an independent Paretian sample. We also evaluate the bias and mean squared error of three robust estimators for the model's parameters. An empirical study of a vast collection of academic papers reveals an excellent fit across the entire distribution range, not merely in the tail as is typical for power-law frameworks. Notably, the estimated models suggest a greater degree of preferential attachment and a reduced proportion of randomness compared to prior research.

Rapidly addressing patients showing signs of impending clinical decline is a fundamental principle of healthcare, leading to the development of the Rapid Response System (RRS). This approach involves immediately evaluating and treating patients who meet specific criteria for deterioration, aiming to halt the decline and avoid ICU transfer, cardiac arrest, or mortality. Despite widespread adoption, systematic reviews have not consistently demonstrated the effectiveness of RRS. Typically, RRS relies on simple, consensus-based rules that detect significant physiological deviations or clinical observations. If predictive patterns can be identified in patient data prior to the onset of physiological instability indicated by current criteria, intervention strategies could be significantly improved. This study applies machine learning to electronic medical records to predict the risk of clinical deterioration. Our models demonstrate higher sensitivity and provide earlier warning times compared to the rule-based systems currently used in hospitals. These findings justify further clinical validation; if successful, hospitals can integrate this approach into their IT infrastructure to utilize model-generated alerts for preventing adverse outcomes or reducing ICU length of stay.

Eclipsing systems are fundamental for studying stellar and binary system characteristics. These systems gain additional value when their components pulsate, as they offer precise constraints on physical properties and a complementary technique for identifying pulsation modes, which is vital for accurate asteroseismology. Space missions designed to detect exoplanets by generating high-precision light curves for thousands of stars have simultaneously advanced our understanding of variable stars and renewed focus on binary systems. This progress has been especially beneficial for identifying eclipsing binaries with pulsating components, a field that is rapidly evolving. This review highlights recent findings from such systems using data from the {\it Kepler} and TESS missions. We examine various configurations, including semi-detached binaries in (near-)circular orbits, non-synchronized binaries with chemically peculiar components, systems exhibiting the heartbeat phenomenon, and detached, eccentric double-lined systems, all containing one or more pulsators. Covering a wide range of pulsating star types, we discuss unevolved or slightly evolved stars of spectral types B, A, and F, as well as red giants displaying solar-like oscillations. Several systems also present additional complexities, such as tidal interactions, angular momentum exchange, mass transfer, and magnetic activity. Investigating how these phenomena and orbital evolution influence the excited pulsations in these components provides a new avenue for understanding pulsation physics.

An epidemiological analysis of mortality data from twelve nations examined during the initial phase of the COVID-19 pandemic is presented. These selected countries experienced significant impacts early on, resulting in daily death counts that closely mirror the dynamics predicted by basic SIR equations. The SIR model was solved parametrically, treating proper time as the variable, to investigate general characteristics of its solutions, including asymmetry and time-scaling. Furthermore, Gumbel functions were employed as approximations to the SIR solutions due to their similar behavioral patterns. By extracting and comparing the parameters of both the SIR model and the Gumbel functions across the various nations, it was determined that ten of the countries are accurately described by the SIR model, with estimated basic reproduction numbers ranging from 3 to 8.

We utilized angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy to investigate the interplay between Fermi surface topology and charge-density waves (CDW) in epitaxial VTe2 films. Our findings indicate that the two-dimensional triangular Fermi pocket observed in monolayer (1ML) VTe2 transforms into a highly warped quasi-one-dimensional (1D) surface in the 6ML sample, a change likely driven by the 1T-to-1T' structural phase transition. Furthermore, we identified a metallic Fermi edge across the entire surface in 6ML at low temperatures, contrasting with the anisotropic pseudogap seen in 1ML; this distinct CDW behavior is corroborated by first-principles band-structure calculations. These results underscore the necessity of concurrently regulating both structural phases and Fermi surface characteristics to effectively tune CDW properties in ultrathin transition-metal dichalcogenides.

This paper investigates the existence of fixed points in nonnegative neural networks, defined as systems that process nonnegative input vectors using nonnegative parameters. By demonstrating that these networks function as monotonic and (weakly) scalable functions within nonlinear Perron-Frobenius theory, we establish existence conditions for their fixed points that are less restrictive than those derived previously via convex analysis. Additionally, we prove that the fixed point set for such networks typically forms an interval, which collapses to a single point in scalable networks. These findings enhance the understanding of autoencoders, as their fixed point sets correspond exactly to perfectly reconstructible inputs, and offer insights into loop-unrolling techniques viewed as fixed-point search algorithms. Theoretical conclusions are validated through numerical simulations involving an autoencoder that compresses angular power spectra in massive MIMO systems and subsequently reconstructs the original input spectra from the compressed data.

Building on the work of Iwaniec, Luo, and Sarnak (2000), we apply one-level density theorems to determine the proportion of non-vanishing $L$-functions within a family at low-lying heights along the critical line, relative to the analytic conductor. To address the resulting Fourier optimization challenges, we introduce a unified framework grounded in the theory of reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces of entire functions, with a distinct space for each symmetry type, and provide explicit formulas for their reproducing kernels. Additionally, we revisit the estimation of the height of the first low-lying zero in a family, a problem previously addressed by Hughes and Rudnick (2003) and Bernard (2015). In this context, we resolve the corresponding Fourier optimization issue by linking it to de Branges spaces of entire functions and leveraging their explicit reproducing kernels. Finally, the appendix examines the related question of identifying sharp embeddings between the Hilbert spaces corresponding to the five symmetry types and the classical Paley-Wiener space.

Current deep learning architectures often lack robustness and fail to generalize effectively when faced with distributional shifts. Although significant progress has been made to mitigate these issues, there remains a lack of systematic research regarding how different optimizers impact out-of-distribution generalization. This study investigates the performance of common first-order optimizers within both empirical risk minimization and invariant risk minimization frameworks across various types of distributional shifts. Utilizing DomainBed, WILDS, and the Backgrounds Challenge as benchmarks for out-of-distribution testing, we analyzed image and text classification tasks. By evaluating over 20,000 models with an extensive search of hyperparameters, we assessed both in-distribution and out-of-distribution classification accuracy. Our key findings are: (i) contrary to established beliefs, adaptive optimizers like Adam underperform compared to non-adaptive methods such as standard SGD and momentum-based SGD; and (ii) the relationship between in-distribution and out-of-distribution performance varies by dataset, exhibiting three distinct patterns: linear returns, increasing returns, and diminishing returns. We believe these insights will assist practitioners in selecting appropriate optimizers and anticipating their behavior.

We analyze the Benjamin-Ono equation featuring a slowly varying potential $u_t + (Hu_x - Vu + \tfrac12 u^2)_x = 0$, where $V(x) = W(hx)$ with $0 < h \ll 1$, $W \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R})$, and $H$ representing the Hilbert transform. The soliton solution is defined as $Q_{a,c}(x) = cQ(c(x-a))$, with $Q(x) = \frac{4}{1+x^2}$, and parameters $a \in \mathbb{R}$, $c > 0$. Assuming the initial condition $u_0(x)$ is close to $Q_{0,1}(x)$ in the $H_x^{1/2}$ norm, we demonstrate that the corresponding solution $u(x,t)$ stays close to a soliton profile $Q_{a(t),c(t)}(x)$ within the same norm, while explicitly determining the evolution of the parameters $(a,c)$ over an $O(h^{-1})$ time scale.

Distributed monitoring is essential for managing cloud datacenter operations. While system administrators have traditionally utilized tools like Nagios and Ganglia to track status on desktop machines, the rise of mobile devices has driven the development of monitoring solutions tailored for smartphones. This work outlines the key characteristics required for smartphone-based monitoring, quantifies the limitations of applying existing solutions directly to this domain, and presents a design that mitigates these issues. We also share results from an early prototype named MAVIS, which analyzed one month of monitoring data from roughly 3,000 machines managed by Purdue's central IT organization.

When the $S$-action is trivial, the negative cyclic homology of a differential graded algebra over the rational field contains the Hochschild homology as a direct summand. Leveraging this property, we demonstrate that for a BV exact manifold, the Chas-Sullivan string bracket simplifies to the composition of the loop product and the BV operator on loop homology. This reduction stems directly from the equivalence between BV exactness and the triviality of the $S$-action. Additionally, we establish that the Lie bracket on the loop cohomology of the classifying space of a connected compact Lie group undergoes the same reduction. Utilizing these findings, we examine the non-triviality of string brackets. A significant result is that simply-connected spaces with positive weights are BV exact. Finally, we explore higher BV exactness in the context of the cobar-type Eilenberg-Moore spectral sequence.

This paper presents a novel generalization of Leibnitz numbers, achieved by applying the Beta function to modify Bernstein basis functions. Additionally, we explore properties of these numbers using generating functions derived from the Volkenborn integral on the set of $p$-adic integers. We also introduce new identities and relations connecting Leibnitz numbers with Daehee numbers, Changhee numbers, inverse binomial coefficients, and combinatorial sums. Furthermore, we provide a computational formula for these generalized Leibnitz numbers implemented in Mathematica 12.0, presenting calculated values and corresponding tables. Finally, by applying the Volkenborn integral to Mahler coefficients, we derive several new formulas involving the Leibnitz numbers.

We demonstrate that various nonlinear equations, such as symmetric and asymmetric $\phi^4$, modified Korteweg de Vries (MKdV), mixed KdV-MKdV, nonlinear Schr\"odinger (NLS), quadratic-cubic NLS, and higher-order neutral scalar field theories, along with higher-order KdV-MKdV and quadratic-cubic NLS models, support superposed periodic kink and pulse solutions. Furthermore, several of these equations also allow for superposed hyperbolic kink solutions.

This work establishes a functional framework using direct integral expansions to analyze the spectra of specific periodic block-operator Jacobi matrices, including general second-order 2D partial difference operators. We derive an optimal upper bound for the Lebesgue measure of these spectra and provide examples demonstrating operators with multiple spectral gaps.

Existing literature typically assesses volatility roughness using realized volatility derived from high-frequency data; however, some researchers argue this approach yields biased estimates and may not accurately reflect the roughness of the underlying volatility process. In this study, we aim to quantify the roughness of implied volatility for short-term options and the VIX index, evaluating whether these metrics serve as more suitable proxies for instantaneous volatility.

This paper establishes a limiting absorption principle for high-order Schrödinger operators across a broad class of potentials, extending findings by A. Ionescu and W. Schlag. The core approach involves addressing boundary operators through the restriction theorem of the Fourier transform. Two primary tools employed are the Stein--Tomas theorem within Lorentz spaces and a refined trace lemma attributed to S. Agmon and L. H\"ormander.

Mobile networks (MN) promise to revolutionize human interaction by enabling novel connected experiences. However, their increasing complexity, driven by intricate configurations and expanding service demands, creates substantial hurdles in deployment, management, operation, optimization, and maintenance, necessitating a comprehensive understanding of the MN landscape. Artificial Intelligence (AI), known for simulating intelligent computer behavior, has proven highly effective across various domains, indicating its potential to comprehend MN states and facilitate smart decision-making. This paper introduces an AI-driven mobile network architecture, addressing challenges related to cognitive complexity, high-dimensional decision spaces, and self-adaptation to dynamic system changes. It further explores AI-based solutions and proposes a deep learning method that directly maps MN states to perceived Quality of Service (QoS), thereby unifying cognition with decision-making. This approach empowers operators to make more intelligent choices to ensure QoS. The efficacy and benefits of the proposed method are validated using a real-world dataset covering 31,261 users across 77 stations over a five-day period.

LiDAR-based place recognition serves as a critical element for SLAM and global localization in robotics and autonomous driving. The application of deep learning (DL) to extract meaningful data from 3D LiDAR has significantly enhanced place recognition, improving re-localization and loop-closure detection, especially under varying environmental conditions. Despite these advancements, generating descriptors from 3D LiDAR data that remain invariant to changes in orientation and environment remains an open challenge. To tackle this, we introduce AttDLNet, a novel deep learning framework that employs a range-based proxy representation for point clouds and an attention network with stacked layers to prioritize long-range context and inter-feature relationships. Evaluated on the KITTI dataset with an accompanying ablation study, the results demonstrate that incorporating attention mechanisms boosts performance, enabling efficient loop closures and surpassing existing 3D LiDAR-based methods. The ablation study further reveals that middle encoder layers yield the highest mean performance, whereas deeper layers exhibit greater robustness to orientation variations. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/Cybonic/AttDLNet.

A group is defined as capable when it serves as the central factor of another group. This paper presents, among other findings, a characterization of capable groups with order $p^2q$ for any distinct primes $p$ and $q$, thereby extending Theorem 1.2 by S. Rashid, N. H. Sarmin, A. Erfanian, and N. M. Mohd Ali in their work "On the non abelian tensor square and capability of groups of order $p^2q$" published in *Arch. Math.* 97 (2011), 299–306. Additionally, the authors calculate the count of distinct element centralizers for both finite and infinite groups possessing a central factor of order $p^3$, which generalizes Proposition 2.10 from the paper by S. M. Jafarian Amiri, H. Madadi, and H. Rostami titled "On $F$-groups with the central factor of order $p^4$" in *Math. Slovaca* 67 (5) (2017), 1147–1154.

Neural Architecture Search (NAS) has proven effective at discovering efficient Transformer designs that surpass manually crafted ones for natural language applications, such as neural machine translation (NMT). Current NAS techniques typically explore dense architecture spaces where all sub-architecture weights are active for every input. Inspired by recent breakthroughs in sparsely activated models like Mixture-of-Experts (MoE), we integrate sparse architectures with conditional computation into the NAS search space. Since this expressive space encompasses previously dense architectures, we present AutoMoE, a new framework designed to identify efficient, sparsely activated sub-Transformers. Models generated by AutoMoE achieve (i) a 3x reduction in FLOPs compared to manually designed dense Transformers and (ii) a 23% reduction in FLOPs over state-of-the-art NAS-generated dense sub-Transformers, all while maintaining comparable BLEU scores on NMT benchmark datasets. The AutoMoE framework involves three training stages: (a) designing a heterogeneous search space comprising both dense and sparsely activated Transformer modules (determining the number of experts, their placement, and sizes); (b) training a SuperNet via weight-sharing to jointly train multiple subnetworks sampled from the extensive search space; and (c) conducting an evolutionary search to find the architecture that best balances task performance with computational constraints like FLOPs and latency. The AutoMoE code, data, and trained models can be accessed at https://github.com/microsoft/AutoMoE.

This work investigates the asymptotic expansion of the determinant of the graph Laplacian for discretizations of half-translation surfaces equipped with a flat unitary vector bundle. Through this analysis, we establish a connection between the asymptotic behavior of spanning tree counts and the weighted sums of cycle-rooted spanning forests (using the monodromy of the bundle's connection) and their respective zeta-regularized determinants. As an application, and by integrating our findings with recent results from Kassel and Kenyon, we derive an explicit formula for the limit of the probability that a uniformly sampled cycle-rooted spanning forest with non-contractible loops on discretizations converging to a specific surface induces a given lamination via its cycles. Additionally, we compute explicit values for the limits of certain topological observables within the associated loop measures.

This paper provides a comprehensive overview of Unidirectional Loop Metamaterial (ULM) structures and their applications. By simulating electron spin precession in ferrites through loops equipped with unidirectional loads—typically transistors—the ULM displays all the essential characteristics of ferrite materials and stands as the sole existing magnetless ferrimagnetic medium. We offer an expanded explanation of ULM physics alongside a unified description of its component and system-level applications.

Modeling porous materials under shock conditions presents a significant complexity, which this study addresses using the recently developed material-point method. The primary focus lies on the impacts of shock intensity and porosity dimensions, specifically examining mean-void-size variations for a constant porosity level. The findings identify local turbulence mixing and volume dissipation as critical mechanisms driving the conversion of kinetic energy into heat. In scenarios with minimal porosity, the shocked region may reach a dynamic steady state, while voids in the downstream area reflect rarefactive waves, causing minor oscillations in mean density and pressure. For identical porosity values, larger mean-void-sizes result in higher mean temperatures. Conversely, when porosity is substantial, hydrodynamic properties fluctuate throughout the shock-loading process: following the initial phase, mean density and pressure decline, whereas temperature rises at an accelerated rate. Distributions of local density, pressure, temperature, and particle velocity generally exhibit non-Gaussian characteristics and temporal variability, with changing rates dependent on porosity magnitude, mean-void-size, and shock strength. Notably, stronger shocks amplify porosity effects. This research supplements experimental data for rapid processes and uncovers fundamental mechanisms regarding energy and momentum transport.

Previous research modeled the perturbed distribution of circulating electrons as adiabatic when analyzing the dispersion relation of electrostatic geodesic acoustic modes (GAM). This study introduces the electron geodesic current (FEGC) flow to adjust that adiabatic distribution. Utilizing drift kinetic theory, the findings indicate that FEGC significantly enhances the frequency magnitude of standard GAMs while simultaneously lowering their damping rate. The frequency increase is attributed to FEGC's contribution to radial flow. The reduction in damping occurs because, when FEGC effects are included, the new resonant velocity exceeds the ion thermal velocity associated with a Maxwellian equilibrium distribution, contrasting with the unmodified Landau resonant velocity. Notably, FEGC alters the behavior of low-frequency GAM frequency and damping rate as functions of the safety factor $q$.

Scientific machine learning has emerged as a vital instrument for addressing high-dimensional differential equations and creating surrogates for intricate physical systems. This study introduces a deep learning-driven numerical approach to solve elliptic partial differential equations (PDEs) featuring random coefficients. By applying the direct method of calculus of variations, we clarify the stochastic variational formulation of the problem. This framework enables the transformation of the random coefficient PDE into a stochastic optimization task, which is then resolved through an integration of Monte Carlo sampling and deep learning approximation. The proposed method proves to be both straightforward and highly effective. Numerical experiments are conducted to validate the method's efficiency and precision.

Guided by the principle that "copying is simpler than memorizing," this paper presents GNN-LM, an extension of standard neural language models (LMs) capable of leveraging similar contexts from the entire training corpus. We construct a directed heterogeneous graph linking an input context with its semantically related neighbors drawn from the training data, where nodes represent tokens in both the input and retrieved contexts, and edges denote their connections. Graph neural networks (GNNs) are then built on this structure to aggregate information from analogous contexts for token decoding. This approach offers direct access to reference contexts, thereby enhancing the model's generalization capabilities. Extensive experiments confirm GNN-LM's efficacy: it achieves a new state-of-the-art perplexity of 14.8 on WikiText-103 (a 3.9-point improvement over the vanilla LM) and demonstrates significant gains on the One Billion Word and Enwiki8 datasets compared to strong baselines. Furthermore, detailed ablation studies were conducted to elucidate the underlying mechanisms of GNN-LM. \footnote{The code is available at https://github.com/ShannonAI/GNN-LM}

Interest in polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) extends across many disciplines, with infrared spectroscopy typically serving as the primary tool for analyzing their molecular structures. While theoretical studies often rely on either quantum calculation methods or empirical potentials to determine vibrational frequencies, combining the high accuracy of the former with the low computational cost of the latter remains a significant challenge. This study utilized machine learning techniques to construct a potential energy surface and dipole mapping using an artificial neural network (ANN) architecture. Trained exclusively on 11 small PAH molecules, the resulting ANNs successfully reproduced the infrared spectra of these training molecules and, more critically, of 8 large PAHs not included in the training set, thereby demonstrating the transferability of this approach.

Natural Language Processing (NLP) systems employ pre-trained Masked Language Models (MLMs) like BERT, which are trained on vast datasets such as Wikipedia to generate language representations. Because these models learn from unlabeled text, they risk embedding the cultural and social biases present in their source material. This study utilizes the StereoSet tool to evaluate biases in both general-purpose and medical-specific MLMs. Results indicate that general-purpose models exhibit significant overall bias, with RoBERTa scoring 61 and BERT scoring 57. Gender bias represented the strongest category for these models, yielding scores of 73 for RoBERTa and 63 for BERT, while biases related to race, religion, and profession aligned closely with their overall scores. Conversely, medical MLMs demonstrated higher bias levels across most categories compared to their general-purpose counterparts, with the exception of SciBERT, which achieved a superior race bias score of 55 compared to BERT's 53. Medical models also displayed elevated gender and religious biases (ranging from 54–58 and 46–54, respectively, versus 63–73 and 58 for general models). Ultimately, the evaluation of four medical MLMs revealed inferior performance regarding stereotyped assessments of race, gender, religion, and profession compared to general-purpose models. These disparities likely stem from the distinct training data sources used for medically focused models, which directly influence the bias ratings observed by the StereoSet tool.

Deep generative models are increasingly employed across scientific and industrial sectors for diverse applications, yet a persistent hurdle remains in accurately capturing the data's probability density, whether explicitly or implicitly. Recent approaches have proposed leveraging classifier weights to enhance the learned density of these models. We generalize this concept to encompass all generative model types and demonstrate that refining the latent space through iterated generative modeling can overcome topological barriers and boost precision. This method is also effective for scenarios involving non-differentiable target models with numerous internal latent dimensions that require marginalization prior to refinement. We validate our Latent Space Refinement (LaSeR) protocol across various examples, with a specific focus on integrating Normalizing Flows and Generative Adversarial Networks.

A conventional informal technique for determining a program's asymptotic complexity involves deriving a recurrence relation based on input size and subsequently calculating a closed-form upper bound. We provide a formal treatment of this approach for functional programs within a higher-order language featuring let-polymorphism. The process comprises two stages: first, a monadic translation generates a cost-annotated version of the source program; second, this extracted program is evaluated within a specific model. A defining characteristic of the second stage is that distinct models represent different definitions of size. This flexibility manifests in various scenarios, such as when analyzing functions with inductive type arguments, where the appropriate size metric may vary. Furthermore, for polymorphic functions, our method allows for a formal characterization of argument size based on the data shared across all type instances of the domain. We illustrate the utility of this approach with several examples of different models that validate various informal cost analyses.

Personalized Internet of Things (IoT) systems modify their operations in response to contextual cues, including user habits and location. However, this adaptability creates a side-channel vulnerability that inadvertently exposes private user data. Consequently, this study investigates how effectively a malicious eavesdropper can observe IoT system actions to deduce sensitive information. Specifically, we demonstrate two practical instances of a novel spyware category, termed Context-Aware Adaptation Based Spyware (SpyCon), within mobile and smart home environments. Experimental results indicate that SpyCon can forecast user daily routines with 90.3% accuracy. The remainder of this paper introduces VindiCo, a software framework designed to identify and counteract SpyCon. Since SpyCon is a new form of malware lacking known signatures or established behavioral patterns, traditional detection methods relying on code signatures or application behavior are insufficient. Therefore, VindiCo employs a novel information-centric detection engine alongside various mitigation strategies to limit SpyCon's capacity to extract private data. Because VindiCo utilizes general detection and mitigation mechanisms, it remains independent of the specific inference algorithms employed by SpyCon. Our findings demonstrate that VindiCo lowers SpyCon's inference accuracy from 90.3% to baseline random-guess levels with minimal performance overhead.

We demonstrate that the action of the Kauffman bracket skein algebra of a surface $\Sigma$ on the skein module of the handlebody bounded by $\Sigma$ is faithful precisely when the quantum parameter is not a root of unity.

This study investigates optical forces acting on parity-time (PT) symmetric heterostructures when subjected to normal incidence from either a single or two counter-propagating plane waves. Our approach utilizes a generalized parametric space derived from PT-symmetry conditions and the Lorentz reciprocity theorem. Within this framework, we comprehensively map various PT phases and extraordinary wave phenomena, while simultaneously determining the directionality and magnitudes of the resulting optical forces. Under single-wave illumination, the system exhibits a symmetric pushing effect in the exact symmetry phase, uni-directional null (UNF) and bi-directional null (BNF) forces at the exceptional point (EP), and flipped pulling-pushing forces in the broken symmetry phase, with BNF occurring at the pushing-pulling transition point. When illuminated by two counter-propagating waves, both the magnitude and directionality of the resultant force can be adjusted via the relative phase of the incident waves. Notably, we identify a null force region within the broken symmetry phase and at the EP that remains independent of the relative phase. Furthermore, we present several PT-symmetric heterostructure examples to validate these findings. These results hold promise for applications in PT optomechanics and force rectification.

Delivering high-quality video streams, whether via Video-On-Demand (VOD) or live broadcasting, typically necessitates transcoding to align with the specific capabilities of end-user devices, such as supported formats or spatial resolutions. Given the substantial computational demands of transcoding and the rapid growth in streaming consumption, Streaming Service Providers (SSPs) increasingly depend on cloud infrastructure to ensure Quality of Service (QoS). Cloud platforms provide a heterogeneous array of Virtual Machines (VMs) with varying performance characteristics and pricing structures. Efficiently leveraging these cloud resources for video transcoding demands a comprehensive performance evaluation across different VM types. This research presents, for the first time, an in-depth analysis of video stream transcoding performance on heterogeneous cloud VMs. Such analysis is essential for accurately predicting transcoding durations on diverse VMs and for developing scheduling algorithms optimized for video tasks. Building on these findings and accounting for cost disparities among VM types, this study also introduces a model to assess the suitability of each VM type for specific transcoding operations. This model equips resource provisioning strategies with precise data on performance and cost trade-offs, enabling the efficient utilization of cloud services for video streaming.

Advancements in traffic forecasting hold significant potential for enhancing urban mobility. The traffic4cast competition addresses short-term traffic prediction with exceptional granularity, providing high-resolution data on speed and volume at five-minute intervals. To enhance generalization across unfamiliar cities, as demanded by the 2021 extended challenge, we suggest predicting small, quadratic city segments instead of processing entire city rasters simultaneously. During inference, decomposing test data into spatially cropped, overlapping patches boosts the stability and robustness of final predictions, as multiple patches covering a single cell can be handled independently. Experimental results on both the traffic4cast test set and a validation set confirm that this patch-wise approach improves accuracy. Additional performance gains are achievable through the adoption of a Unet++ architecture and by increasing the number of patches processed per sample at test time. We conclude that our snippet-based methodology, when integrated with other high-performing network architectures from the competition, significantly leverages model performance, especially on unseen cities. The complete source code is accessible at https://github.com/NinaWie/NeurIPS2021-traffic4cast.

Exponentially-localized Wannier functions form a basis for the Fermi projection of a Hamiltonian, characterized by rapid exponential decay in space. For periodic insulators in two and three dimensions, it is established that such functions exist if and only if an orthonormal basis for the Fermi projection possesses a finite second moment (meaning all basis elements satisfy $\int |\boldsymbol{x}|^2 |w(\boldsymbol{x})|^2 \,\text{d}{\boldsymbol{x}} < \infty$). This study extends a comparable result to non-periodic insulators in two dimensions. Specifically, we demonstrate that if an orthonormal basis for the Fermi projection exists with a finite moment of order $5 + \epsilon$ (where $\epsilon > 0$, i.e., $\int |\boldsymbol{x}|^{5 + \epsilon} |w(\boldsymbol{x})|^2 \,\text{d}{\boldsymbol{x}} < \infty$), then an orthonormal basis exhibiting exponential spatial decay also exists. This finding provides evidence supporting the Localization Dichotomy Conjecture for non-periodic systems, recently formulated by Marcelli, Monaco, Moscolari, and Panati.

Motivated by the recent LHCb discovery of the $P_{cs}(4459)$, we explore its production via $\Xi_b$ decay within a molecular framework employing an effective Lagrangian method. By assigning various $J^P$ quantum numbers to the $P_{cs}(4459)$, we estimate the branching fraction for the $\Xi_b \to P_{cs}(4459) K$ process, finding values around $10^{-4}$. Combined with the particle's decay characteristics, these predictions offer opportunities for verification through high-precision experiments, thereby advancing our comprehension of molecular models and the determination of the $P_{cs}(4459)$'s $J^P$ quantum numbers.

Stance detection involves identifying the attitude of a text regarding a particular topic or claim. Although significant research has been conducted on this topic in recent years, the majority of efforts have centered on English, primarily because annotated data for other languages is scarce. The TW-10 Referendum Dataset, introduced at IberEval 2018, was an earlier attempt to supply multilingual stance-annotated data for Catalan and Spanish. However, the Catalan subset within TW-10 suffers from severe class imbalance. This paper tackles these challenges by introducing a novel multilingual dataset for stance detection on Twitter, specifically for Catalan and Spanish, designed to support research in multilingual and cross-lingual contexts. The dataset features annotations regarding stance on the topic of Catalan independence. Additionally, we present a semi-automatic annotation method grounded in a classification of Twitter users. We evaluate the new corpus using various supervised techniques, ranging from linear classifiers to deep learning models. Comparing our balanced dataset against the TW-10 corpus highlights the advantages of well-balanced data for multilingual and cross-lingual stance detection studies. Finally, we achieve new state-of-the-art results on the TW-10 dataset for both Catalan and Spanish.

Non-Gaussian states are fundamental to numerous optical quantum technologies, and the optical quantum state synthesizer (OQSS)—which utilizes Gaussian inputs, linear optics, and photon-number resolving detectors—represents a promising avenue for preparing these states. However, a critical and unavoidable challenge lies in the computational complexity of simulating state preparation on classical computers, which hinders the generation of advanced non-Gaussian states essential for quantum information processing. To address this, an efficient design methodology for OQSS circuits is urgently needed. Our proposed solution employs a backcasting strategy, dividing the OQSS circuit into sublayers and simulating the process backward from the final to the initial layers. Furthermore, our findings indicate that each detector registers at most two photons, substantially lowering the demands placed on photon-number resolving detectors. Given its capacity to prepare a diverse range of non-Gaussian states, the proposed OQSS framework stands as a vital component for general optical quantum information processing.

This study examines the evolution of specific geometric quantities on a compact Riemannian manifold $M^n$ under a Yamabe soliton metric, utilizing these findings to establish bounds for the soliton constant. We demonstrate that the commutator of two soliton vector fields sharing the same metric within a specific conformal class yields a Killing vector field. Furthermore, we prove that a soliton vector field constitutes a geodesic vector field if and only if the manifold possesses constant curvature.

We provide a criterion for the local solvability of a hyperelliptic curve $C$ defined over a local field $K$, assuming $C$ achieves semistable reduction following a tame extension of $K$ and the residue field $k$ is large enough relative to the curve's genus. This criterion is formulated using the cluster picture of $C$, a combinatorial structure that governs much of the curve's local arithmetic behavior.

The $\mu PT$ ensemble within statistical ensemble theory characterizes equilibrium systems that exchange energy, particle number, and volume with their surroundings. This work derives general, model-independent properties regarding the statistics of volume and particle number. The discussion examines non-analytic points of the partition function in relation to divergent fluctuations and ensemble equivalence. Furthermore, examples illustrating these concepts include quantum and classical ideal gases, as well as a mean-field interacting Bose gas model.

This paper introduces the BigEarthNet-MM benchmark, a multi-modal archive containing 590,326 paired image patches from Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 to facilitate deep learning research in multi-modal, multi-label remote sensing retrieval and classification. Each patch pair is annotated with multi-labels derived from the 2018 CORINE Land Cover (CLC) map, utilizing its most detailed Level-3 class nomenclature. Initial findings indicate that accurately describing certain CLC classes is difficult when relying solely on single-date BigEarthNet-MM imagery. To address this, the study proposes an evolved class nomenclature consisting of 19 classes, created by interpreting and reorganizing the original CLC Level-3 labels based on the specific properties of the dataset. Experiments utilizing several state-of-the-art deep learning models demonstrate the archive's potential for multi-modal retrieval and classification tasks. Furthermore, models trained from scratch on BigEarthNet-MM outperform those pre-trained on ImageNet, particularly for complex categories such as agriculture and various vegetated or natural environments. All data and deep learning models are made publicly available at https://bigearth.net, serving as a vital resource for advancing research in remote sensing image scene classification and retrieval.

The magnetic evolution of late-type dwarfs remains uncertain because predicting activity levels for M dwarfs of specific masses and ages is challenging. We present findings from a spectroscopic survey of M dwarfs located within the Southern Continuous Viewing Zone (CVZ) of the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS). Since the TESS CVZ overlaps with that of the James Webb Space Telescope, our targets serve as a legacy sample for future research on nearby M dwarfs. We obtained at least one optical spectrum with a resolution of $R\approx 2000$ for 122 stars to measure chromospheric $\mathrm{H}\alpha$ emission, which acts as an indicator of magnetic field strength. The proportion of active stars aligns with expectations for field M dwarfs; consistent with prior studies, we observe that late-type M dwarfs maintain activity longer than their early-type counterparts. Although TESS light curves for approximately 20% of our targets display modulations indicative of rotation, current systematics are insufficient for confidently determining rotation periods ($P_{\mathrm{rot}}$) exceeding half the duration of an observing sector. We report rotation periods for 12 stars where $P_{\mathrm{rot}} {\lower0.8ex\hbox{$\buildrel <\over\sim$}}$ 15 days or where literature values confirm TESS-derived periods. Our combined sample of 21 rotation periods, including those from existing literature, suggests our targets are spun-down field stars. Finally, we analyzed the $\mathrm{H}\alpha$-to-bolometric luminosity distribution. While two stars rotate rapidly enough to be magnetically saturated, they do not exhibit corresponding emission, implying that fast rotators might appear inactive in $\mathrm{H}\alpha$.

Simultaneous detection and recognition of skin lesions remain difficult due to inter-class homogeneity and intra-class heterogeneity, which often limit the generalization capabilities of single Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) trained on small datasets. To address this, we introduce Dermo-DOCTOR, an end-to-end deep CNN framework designed for joint lesion detection and recognition. This system employs two encoders whose feature maps are channel-wise fused to create a Fused Feature Map (FFM). In the detection sub-network, the FFM aids in decoding by concatenating outputs from both encoders with corresponding decoder layers at each stage, thereby recovering spatial information lost during pooling. For the recognition sub-network, outputs from three fully connected layers—integrating features from both encoders and the FFM—are aggregated to determine the final lesion class. We evaluated Dermo-DOCTOR using two public benchmarks, ISIC-2016 and ISIC-2017. On these test sets, the model achieved mean Intersection over Union (IoU) scores of 85.0% and 80.0% for segmentation, respectively. Additionally, the framework demonstrated strong performance in recognition, yielding Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve (AUC) values of 0.98 and 0.91 for the respective datasets. Experimental results indicate that Dermo-DOCTOR surpasses existing literature methods for skin lesion analysis. Given its superior performance on diverse test sets despite limited training data, Dermo-DOCTOR serves as a promising computer-aided tool for dermatologists.

Rare event probabilities are inherently difficult and costly to compute, with their estimates being highly sensitive to the distributional assumptions made about model parameters. Consequently, it is essential to understand how these probabilities respond to changes in the hyper-parameters that define those distributions. This study demonstrates that by (i) accelerating rare event probability calculations using subset simulation and (ii) approximating the outcomes via polynomial chaos expansion, one can analyze global sensitivity through a double-loop sampling strategy. The proposed method is both conceptually straightforward and computationally efficient, with its effectiveness demonstrated through a subsurface flow case study and an analytical example.

Observing gravitational waves at frequencies under 10 Hz is essential for maximizing the potential of gravitational wave astronomy. One proposed method involves using space-based laser interferometers equipped with Fabry-Perot optical cavities; however, practical implementation faces significant hurdles. Specifically, the need for precise cavity length control and the mitigation of laser phase noise could hinder the development of a viable detector. To address these issues, we introduce a novel interferometer configuration called the back-linked Fabry-Perot interferometer. This design eliminates the requirement for high-precision length controls and allows for an offline subtraction technique to handle laser phase noise. This paper outlines the fundamental concept and performs sensitivity analysis, demonstrating that a strain sensitivity of $7\times 10^{-23}$ Hz$^{-1/2}$ could be achieved in the deci-Hertz range, even with additional noise sources. Further technological advancements and research are necessary to enable the practical realization of this system.

We examine the necessary forms for time-dependent Rabi frequencies within a protocol designed to shield quantum gate operations on an atomic qutrit by continuously decoupling the system from environmental noise via external fields. Multiple simulations are conducted to safeguard various quantum gate models, including randomly selected ones. We contend that current experimental capabilities can satisfy the requirements for these Rabi frequencies. Furthermore, we analyze the transition between successive gate operations, including the protection of a qutrit memory state. Finally, we apply this methodology to defend a noise-vulnerable algorithm against decoherence, specifically one that distinguishes the parity of permutations among three elements.

In recent years, rewriting theory has been adapted and expanded to establish systematic coherence proofs for strict higher categories. This work extends that approach to Gray categories—structures equivalent to tricategories—by developing a rewriting framework within the domain of precategories. Precategories encompass Gray categories as specific instances and are optimized for mechanized computation. We demonstrate that finite rewriting systems in this setting possess a finite, efficiently calculable number of critical pairs. Furthermore, we generalize Squier's theorem to our context, proving that a convergent rewriting system ensures coherence; specifically, any two parallel 3-cells are necessarily equal. Leveraging this, we derive coherence results for several prominent structures within Gray categories, including monoids, adjunctions, and Frobenius monoids.

We establish moderate deviation bounds for the lower tail of odd cycle counts in $\calG(n, m)$ random graphs. Specifically, we demonstrate that reducing triangle density by $t^3$ occurs with probability $\exp(-\Theta(n^2 t^2))$ when $n^{-3/4} \ll t^3 \ll 1$. For $k \ge 5$, an identical estimate applies to the probability of decreasing $k$-cycle density by $t^k$, though within the broader range $n^{-1} \ll t^k \ll 1$. In cases where $m \ge \frac 12 \binom n2$, we also determine the leading coefficient of the exponent. These findings extend the work of Goldschmidt et al., who established that for $n^{-3/2} \ll t^k \ll n^{-1}$, the probability follows $\exp(-\Theta(n^3 t^{2k}))$. Consequently, deviations smaller than $n^{-1}$ exhibit small deviation behavior, whereas deviations exceeding $n^{-3/4}$ (for triangles) or $n^{-1}$ (for $k \ge 5$) display large deviation characteristics. Regarding triangles, we hypothesize a sharp transition between these regimes at deviations of size $n^{-3/4}$, attributed to a single large negative eigenvalue of the adjacency matrix driving the majority of the cycle deficit. Ultimately, our results reflect finite size effects associated with phase transitions in constrained random graphs.

This study mapped the kinetic temperature structure of two massive star-forming regions, N113 and N159W, within the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC). Utilizing $\sim$1.6" ($\sim$0.4 pc) resolution observations of the para-H$_2$CO $J_{\rm K_aK_c}$ = 3$_{03}$--2$_{02}$, 3$_{22}$--2$_{21}$, and 3$_{21}$--2$_{20}$ transitions near 218.5 GHz, we constrained RADEX non-LTE models to determine physical conditions. Gas kinetic temperatures, derived from the line ratios 3$_{22}$--2$_{21}$/3$_{03}$--2$_{02}$ and 3$_{21}$--2$_{20}$/3$_{03}$--2$_{02}$, span 28–105 K in N113 and 29–68 K in N159W. The spatial distributions of dense gas traced by para-H$_2$CO align with 1.3 mm dust and *Spitzer* 8.0 $\mu$m emission but show no significant correlation with H$\alpha$ emission. In both regions, high kinetic temperatures ($T_{\rm kin} \gtrsim$ 50 K) in the dense gas appear linked to embedded infrared sources and/or young stellar objects (YSOs), whereas lower temperatures ($T_{\rm kin} <$ 50 K) are found at the peripheries of the H$_2$CO distributions. This suggests that the kinetic temperatures of this dense gas are only weakly influenced by external sources of H$\alpha$ emission. Furthermore, non-thermal velocity dispersions of para-H$_2$CO correlate well with gas kinetic temperatures in N113, implying that the elevated temperatures traced by para-H$_2$CO are associated with turbulence on a $\sim$0.4 pc scale. Dense gas heating appears dominated by internal star formation activity, radiation, and/or turbulence. Consequently, the mechanism heating dense gas in these LMC star-forming regions seems consistent with that in Galactic massive star-forming regions located in the Galactic plane.

Asymmetric Doppler shifts observed in CMB data indicate the rotation of galactic objects. Molecular hydrogen clouds at virial temperatures could constitute part of the galactic halo's dark matter and may explain the rotational asymmetry seen in these halos. We introduce a technique to constrain the parameters of these virial clouds, assuming they behave as a single fluid, with the potential for future extension to multi-fluid systems.

We introduce Camelira, a web-based platform for morphological disambiguation of Arabic across four primary dialects: Modern Standard Arabic, Egyptian, Gulf, and Levantine. Designed with a user-friendly interface, Camelira enables researchers and language learners to investigate linguistic details including part-of-speech tags, morphological features, and lemmas. The system further includes a feature that automatically selects the most suitable dialect-specific disambiguator by utilizing a dialect identification component. Camelira is available to the public at http://camelira.camel-lab.com.

At the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), the interaction of various phenomena—such as intrabeam scattering (IBS), synchrotron radiation, longitudinal beam manipulations, two-beam effects (including beam-beam interactions and e-clouds), and machine non-linearities—alters the population of the beam's core and tails. This leads to non-Gaussian beam distributions at different stages of the beam cycle. Utilizing generalized distribution functions reveals that these modified non-Gaussian profiles independently influence beam emittance evolution and, consequently, collider luminosity. This study concentrates on estimating changes in beam distributions and the resulting root-mean-square (rms) beam size caused by the combined effects of IBS and synchrotron radiation, using the SIRE Monte-Carlo simulation code. SIRE is capable of tracking 3D generalized particle distributions. The code is initially validated against classical semi-analytical IBS theories and subsequently compared with LHC measurements taken at injection and collision energies, along with projections for the high-brightness regime of the High-Luminosity LHC (HL-LHC). Finally, the paper examines how the shape of the distribution affects the evolution of bunch characteristics and overall machine performance.

The necessity for formally defining the fundamental principles of mathematics emerged in the previous century. The expanding scale and intricacy of mathematical disciplines, coupled with the discovery of paradoxes, highlighted the risks of error propagation across various theories. While Gödel's incompleteness theorems demonstrate that no single formal system can simultaneously be complete and consistent in describing all phenomena, they have spurred the development of practical logical fields, notably the theory of automated theorem proving. This field encompasses techniques for mechanically verifying mathematical assertions through logical deduction. Furthermore, these methods are applicable to complex engineering challenges, such as establishing the security properties of software systems or algorithms. This paper evaluates two prominent automated theorem proving tools, Isabelle/HOL and Coq, based on their expressiveness, limitations, and usability. Consequently, it begins with a concise overview of formal systems and automated deduction theory, addressing their primary challenges, followed by a detailed comparison of the key features of the selected provers, supported by illustrative proof examples.

We employ hydrodynamical cosmological simulations to examine distinctions between cold dark matter (CDM) and self-interacting dark matter (SIDM) within the mass regime of massive galaxies ($10^{12}M_{\odot}h^{-1}<M<10^{13.5}M_{\odot}h^{-1}$). Two SIDM scenarios are evaluated: one featuring a constant cross-section ($\sigma/m_{\chi}=1\mathrm{cm^2g^{-1}}$) and another with a velocity-dependent cross-section. By analyzing halo density profiles and concentrations, we compare results from dark-matter-only and hydrodynamical simulations across all tested scenarios. We determine best-fit Einasto profiles, compare their parameters with prior research, and establish concentration-mass relations. Our findings indicate that incorporating baryons diminishes the discrepancies between dark matter models compared to dark-matter-only simulations. In SIDM hydrodynamic runs, deviations from CDM density profiles exhibit a weak mass dependence: the most massive systems ($M>10^{13}M_{\odot}h^{-1}$) display cored profiles, whereas the least massive ones ($M<10^{12.5}M_{\odot}h^{-1}$) retain cuspier profiles. Furthermore, we align our simulation predictions with observational data by examining dark matter fractions and the distribution of strong lensing Einstein radii. We observe that in SIDM, dark matter fractions decline more steeply with increasing stellar mass than in CDM, resulting in lower fractions for $M_{*}>10^{11}M_{\odot}$, a unique SIDM signature. Concurrently, the distribution of Einstein radii derived from both CDM and SIDM hydrodynamic runs aligns well with observed samples of strong lenses where $M>10^{13}M_{\odot}h^{-1}$. In conclusion, the interaction between self-interaction and baryons significantly mitigates expected differences between CDM and SIDM at this mass scale, necessitating techniques capable of separating dark and luminous mass in galactic interiors to effectively constrain self-interactions.

Using the screened nonrelativistic quark model alongside the $^3P_0$ model, we examine the mass spectrum and decay characteristics of $B_s$ mesons. Our findings indicate that the recently identified $B_{sJ}(6064)$ and $B_{sJ}(6114)$ states can be attributed to the $B_s(1^3D_3)$ and $B_s(1^3D_1)$ configurations, respectively, while the $B_{s1}(5830)$ serves as a strong candidate for the $B_{s1}(1P)$. Furthermore, we computed the decay properties of other excited $B_s$ mesons with the predicted masses, which may aid future experimental searches.

Identifying promoter regions within DNA sequences is a critical challenge in bioinformatics that has been extensively researched but remains unsolved. While convolutional networks have yielded significant results by automatically extracting features from DNA chains, no universal architecture exists that can generalize across multiple organisms. Consequently, researchers must continually develop new architectures and tune hyperparameters for each specific organism. To address this, we introduce CapsProm, a versatile capsule network-based model capable of accurately detecting promoter sequences in raw DNA data from seven distinct eukaryotic and prokaryotic organisms. This approach facilitates transfer learning between species and broadens the model's applicability. In testing, CapsProm demonstrated competitive performance, surpassing baseline methods in five out of seven datasets based on F1-score. The source code and models are publicly available at https://github.com/lauromoraes/CapsNet-promoter.

The primary interaction between a solid and a plasma is electrical, resulting in the formation of an electric double layer. This structure consists of an electron-rich region attached to the solid surface, known as the wall charge, and an electron-depleted region within the plasma, referred to as the plasma sheath. While the plasma sheath has been extensively researched since the inception of plasma physics, the wall charge has garnered significantly less attention. Specifically, there is a severe lack of knowledge regarding the in-operando electronic structure of solids exposed to plasmas and how this structure influences the spatial and temporal characteristics of the wall charge. This perspective aims to stimulate research into this underexplored area using modern surface physics techniques. By combining our theoretical investigations into electron microphysics at plasma-solid interfaces with a proposal to measure wall charge via infrared reflectivity, we intend to present a compelling case for initiating such studies. These efforts would establish a new research domain at the intersection of plasma and surface physics, fostering both fundamental and applied scientific inquiry.

The Brier score is a standard metric for assessing probability forecasts. In the context of survival analysis involving right-censored event times, this score is often adjusted using inverse probability of censoring weights (IPCW) to maintain its interpretative integrity. Typically, the censoring distribution is estimated via the Kaplan-Meier estimator, despite its assumption of independence between censoring and covariates. This paper examines how censoring estimates influence the Brier score and demonstrates that such estimation can be problematic. Specifically, when censoring times are identifiable from covariates, the IPCW-adjusted score becomes invalid. To address this, we propose an alternative "administrative" Brier score for scenarios where potential censoring times are known for all subjects. This version eliminates the need to estimate the censoring distribution and remains valid even when censoring times depend on covariates.

The fundamental challenge in text-based person retrieval lies in bridging the heterogeneous divide between multi-modal data. Numerous prior methods attempt to learn a latent common manifold through a **cross-modal distribution consensus prediction (CDCP)** framework. However, when projecting features from a specific modality into this shared space, the distribution of the opposing modality remains entirely unobserved. Consequently, achieving cross-modal consensus and aligning multi-modal features within a constructed common manifold relies solely on the model's internal assumptions rather than the actual data reality. This reliance inevitably prevents effective alignment in the common manifold, resulting in sub-optimal retrieval performance. To address this **CDCP dilemma**, we introduce a novel algorithm called LBUL, designed to learn a Consistent Cross-modal Common Manifold (C$^{3}$M) for text-based person retrieval. Inspired by the Chinese idiom "san si er hou xing," our method embodies the principle of **Look Before You Leap (LBUL)**. The LBUL mapping mechanism consists of a "looking" phase and a "leaping" phase. Unlike CDCP-based approaches, LBUL analyzes the distribution characteristics of both visual and textual modalities prior to embedding data from a single modality into the C$^{3}$M. This ensures a more robust cross-modal distribution consensus, leading to superior retrieval accuracy. We evaluate our method on the CUHK-PEDES and RSTPReid datasets. Experimental results confirm that LBUL surpasses existing methods, achieving state-of-the-art performance.

Let $X$ be a connected, non-compact 2-manifold, potentially with boundary, equipped with a foliation $\Delta$ where every leaf $\omega \in \Delta$ is homeomorphic to $\mathbb{R}$ and possesses a trivially foliated neighborhood. W. Kaplan previously investigated such foliations on the plane, providing a topological classification. He demonstrated that the plane decomposes into a family of open strips foliated by parallel lines, which are joined along specific boundary intervals.
