Multi-armed bandits are extensively utilized in domains such as recommender systems, where the primary objective is to optimize click-through rates. However, additional metrics like user retention, growth potential, and experience quality must also be accounted for. This paper frames such challenges as a $K$-armed bandit problem involving multiple loss functions. We introduce a relative loss vector for each arm, where the $i$-th component measures the performance gap between the arm and the optimal one regarding the $i$-th loss metric. We investigate two distinct objectives: (a) identifying the arm with the smallest $\ell^\infty$-norm of relative losses within a specified confidence interval, known as fixed-confidence best-arm identification; and (b) minimizing the $\ell^\infty$-norm of cumulative relative losses, referred to as regret minimization. For objective (a), we establish a problem-dependent lower bound on sample complexity and outline methods to achieve matching algorithms. For objective (b), we demonstrate a regret lower bound of $\Omega(T^{2/3})$ and present an algorithm that matches this bound.

Data from one-shot devices represent a specific instance of interval censoring. Unlike certain units that survive testing and provide additional lifetime information, true one-shot devices are typically destroyed; however, some non-destructive variants allow surviving units to continue testing, offering further insights. Furthermore, because these devices often endure long durations under normal conditions, accelerated life tests (ALTs) are frequently employed for inference. ALTs utilize a log-linear relationship to connect a unit's lifetime distribution with the stress level applied during testing. By increasing stress to reduce mean lifetimes, researchers can easily extrapolate results back to normal operating conditions. Specifically, the step-stress ALT model gradually elevates stress at predetermined intervals, a method particularly beneficial for non-destructive one-shot devices. Nevertheless, with a small number of test units, outlier data can significantly distort parameter estimates. To address this, the present study develops robust restricted estimators based on the density power divergence (DPD) within linearly restricted subspaces for non-destructive one-shot devices with exponential lifetimes subjected to step-stress ALTs. The paper provides a theoretical analysis of the asymptotic and robustness properties of these estimators and validates them through an empirical simulation study.

While previous theoretical studies on rotating Bose-Einstein condensates have primarily addressed quantum vortex formation and condensate properties, this work investigates alternative aspects by analyzing how rotation influences the ground state of weakly interacting bosons in anharmonic potentials. These analyses are conducted using both mean-field theory and, more specifically, many-body theory via the well-established multiconfigurational time-dependent Hartree method for bosons (MCTDHB). We demonstrate how various levels of fragmentation arise from the disintegration of ground state densities within anharmonic traps, even without increasing the potential barrier to induce strong rotation. This density breakup is linked to the condensate's acquisition of angular momentum through rotation. Beyond fragmentation, we examine many-body correlations by calculating variances in many-particle position and momentum operators. Under strong rotation, these many-body variances decrease below their mean-field equivalents, with some scenarios exhibiting opposite anisotropies between the two. Furthermore, we observe that in systems with higher discrete symmetries of order $k$ (specifically three-fold and four-fold), the system fragments into $k$ sub-clouds, resulting in $k$-fold fragmentation. Collectively, this study offers a comprehensive many-body examination of how and which correlations develop when a trapped Bose-Einstein condensate undergoes rotational breakup.

Driven by advancements in distributed deep learning (DDL), there has been a surging need for resource-heavy distributed and parallel computing to handle DDL tasks. To address communication bottlenecks and load balancing challenges inherent in distributed systems, the "ring-all-reduce" decentralized architecture has become increasingly popular for eliminating the reliance on dedicated parameter servers. Despite this adoption, a significant theoretical gap remains regarding how to design resource optimization algorithms for efficiently scheduling ring-all-reduce DDL jobs within computing clusters. To bridge this gap, we introduce a suite of novel resource scheduling designs tailored for ring-all-reduce DDL workloads. Our contributions are three-fold: i) We develop a new analytical model for resource scheduling in ring-all-reduce deep learning, encompassing diverse objectives such as preventing excessive training, enhancing energy efficiency, and ensuring fairness; ii) Leveraging this analytical framework, we devise an efficient scheduling algorithm named GADGET (greedy ring-all-reduce distributed graph embedding technique), which offers a provable strong performance guarantee; iii) Through extensive trace-driven experiments, we validate the effectiveness of the GADGET approach and demonstrate its superiority over existing state-of-the-art solutions.

We examine systematic effects introduced by half-wave plates (HWPs) in cosmic microwave background (CMB) observations through full-sky, time-domain beam convolution simulations. Based on an optical model of a representative spaceborne two-lens refractor telescope, we assess how various HWP setups, optimized for dichroic detectors at 95 and 150 GHz, influence the reconstruction of primordial B-mode polarization. Special focus is placed on biases resulting from the interplay between frequency-dependent HWP imperfections and polarized Galactic dust, as well as the interaction between the HWP and the instrumental beam. To facilitate these simulations, we expanded the functionality of the open-source beamconv code. To our knowledge, this work presents the first time-domain simulations incorporating both HWP non-idealities and realistic full-sky beam convolution. Our findings indicate that specific achromatic HWP configurations can induce significant systematic polarization angle offsets that differ across sky components with varying frequency dependencies. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that when HWP interactions are considered, realistic beam models featuring non-negligible cross-polarization and sidelobes will generate substantial B-mode residuals, necessitating extensive modeling in certain scenarios.

We introduce MSeg, a unified composite dataset that integrates semantic segmentation data from diverse domains. Simply merging these datasets results in suboptimal performance due to conflicting taxonomies and annotation standards. To resolve this, we harmonized the taxonomies and aligned pixel-level annotations by relabeling over 220,000 object masks across more than 80,000 images, a process demanding over 1.34 years of collective annotator effort. This curated dataset allows for the training of a single semantic segmentation model that performs effectively across domains and generalizes to unseen datasets. We utilize zero-shot cross-dataset transfer as a benchmark to systematically assess model robustness, demonstrating that training on MSeg produces significantly more robust models compared to training on individual datasets or naive mixtures. A model trained on MSeg secured the top rank on the WildDash-v1 leaderboard for robust semantic segmentation without any exposure to WildDash data during training. Additionally, we evaluated our models in the 2020 Robust Vision Challenge (RVC) as an extreme generalization test; the RVC evaluation taxonomy is more detailed and differs from the training data, which includes only three of the seven RVC datasets. Surprisingly, our model achieved competitive results, placing second. To assess progress toward the broader goal of robust, efficient, and complete scene understanding, we extended our approach beyond semantic segmentation to train instance and panoptic segmentation models using the same dataset. We also evaluated various engineering design choices and metrics, including resolution and computational efficiency. While our models have not yet fully achieved this grand aim, our comprehensive evaluation is vital for future progress. All models and code are made available to the community.

Delivering healthcare is inherently a collaborative effort that demands tight coordination among networks of specialists. However, in the United States, care is frequently dispersed across disconnected providers—such as primary care physicians and specialists—resulting in fragmented networks that drive up costs and diminish quality. Although this issue is widely recognized, a lack of quantitative tools capable of analyzing care delivery networks at scale hinders a deeper understanding of fragmentation and limits efforts to resolve it. To address this, we performed a large-scale analysis of U.S. care delivery networks using the discrete Hodge decomposition, an emerging method within topological data analysis. This technique breaks down patient flow networks into three orthogonal subspaces: gradient (representing acyclic flow), harmonic (representing global cyclic flow), and curl (representing local cyclic flow). We observed significant variation in the relative prominence of each subspace, indicating systematic differences in how care delivery networks are organized across various markets. Furthermore, we discovered that the weight of each subspace predicts local care costs and quality, with outcomes generally improving as curl flow increases and deteriorating as harmonic flow increases.

Gantt charts are commonly employed to visualize execution traces of large-scale parallel programs in high-performance computing (HPC). In these visualizations, each parallel processor occupies a row representing its computational state at a specific time, with lines connecting rows to indicate inter-processor communication. When equivalent calls are aligned across rows, these connections reveal communication patterns inherent in the executing code. However, although these structural patterns maintain a consistent definition regardless of scale, they become obscured by the high density of lines when visualizing more than a few hundred processors. Consequently, a more scalable visual metaphor is required to assist HPC experts in comprehending communication within large-scale traces. To address this challenge, we first conducted an exploratory study to determine which visual features are essential for identifying structural similarities across different scales. Leveraging these insights, we designed a set of glyphs to represent these structures within dense charts. We then performed a pre-registered user study to evaluate how effectively users interpret communication using our proposed representation compared to traditional dense Gantt chart depictions. Our evaluation results demonstrate that our representation allows users to identify communication patterns more accurately than full renderings of dense charts. Finally, we discuss the evaluation outcomes and implications for designing metaphors for extensible structures.

We introduce a general approach for generating detuning-modulated composite pulses (DMCPs) by applying $N$ rotations to a standard two-state quantum system, resulting in precise and resilient pulses that do not depend on the system's initial state. This framework features minimal pulse overhead and produces pulses stable against amplitude errors well below the $10^{-4}$ threshold, making them suitable for quantum information processing (QIP) within the system's operational lifetime. This family of pulses addresses unavoidable fabrication imperfections in silicon photonics and reduces the requirement for a specific initial light state to ensure accurate light transfer. Additionally, we generalize universal DMCPs to $n$-level systems possessing irreducible SU(2) symmetry, enabling state transfer that remains highly robust to pulse area errors regardless of the starting state.

We introduce TurbuGAN, a self-supervised, self-calibrating method for imaging through atmospheric turbulence that utilizes a multi-shot approach. This technique eliminates the need for paired training data, automatically adapts to turbulence distributions, incorporates domain-specific priors, and scales effectively from tens to thousands of measurements. Built upon an adversarial sensing framework derived from CryoGAN, TurbuGAN employs a discriminator network to align the distributions of captured and simulated data. Our enhancements over CryoGAN include: (1) extending the forward measurement model to support physically accurate and efficient simulations of light propagation through anisoplanatic turbulence, (2) allowing adaptation to slightly inaccurate forward models, and (3) utilizing pretrained generative networks to apply domain-specific prior knowledge when accessible. We demonstrate the efficacy of TurbuGAN through validation on both simulated and experimentally acquired images distorted by anisoplanatic turbulence.

This study examines the resonant Casimir-Polder interaction between an excited alkali-type atom, characterized by a single electric dipole transition, and a Chern insulator. Due to the Chern insulator's nonzero, time-reversal symmetry breaking Hall conductance, an additional term arises in the resonant Casimir-Polder interaction; this term relies on the interplay between the Hall conductance and the circular polarization of the atomic transition. Our results indicate that the resonant Casimir-Polder shift can be substantially amplified when de-excitation frequencies approach the van Hove singularities of the Chern insulator. Moreover, for relatively large atom-surface separations, the resonant Casimir-Polder force may exhibit a monotonic decay and become repulsive under specific conditions: if the atomic transition is right circularly polarized with a Chern number of $-1$, or left circularly polarized with a Chern number of $1$.

Transient noise, known as glitches, impedes the detection of gravitational waves. This study analyzes data from the third observing run of Advanced LIGO detectors to identify new glitch categories. By utilizing training sets derived from both continuous detector monitoring and contributions from citizen-science volunteers, we refined the Gravity Spy machine-learning algorithm for glitch classification. Our findings reveal a newly identified glitch class associated with ground motion at the detector locations, which is particularly common; we further distinguished two subclasses within this category corresponding to different types of ground movement. After reclassifying the data using the updated model, we determined that 27% of all transient noise at LIGO Livingston falls into this new class, establishing it as the most frequent source of transient noise at that facility. These results illustrate how glitch classification can highlight potential detector improvements and demonstrate that citizen-science volunteers can uncover significant insights within large datasets when provided with a suitable framework.

The Ablowitz-Ladik lattice has been derived from the constrained discrete KP (cdKP) hierarchy. Using gauge transformations, Wronskian solutions for the Ablowitz-Ladik lattice have been obtained. The $u_1$ component of the cdKP hierarchy exhibits a Y-type soliton solution at odd gauge transformation steps but transitions to a dark-bright soliton solution at even steps. The influence of the discrete variable $n$ on the profile of $u_1$ is also examined.

We present specific adaptations of the BFGS algorithm tailored for inherently sequential functions, leveraging SIMD capabilities. Additionally, we offer an updated LBFGS\texttt{++} library that incorporates these enhancements along with AAD, featuring an interface that automatically utilizes the modified library for AAD users. Two case studies demonstrate the performance improvements: the revised library achieves up to 3.8-fold speedup in calibrating European Swaption curves within ORE (a non-parallelizable task) and a 1.4-fold speedup when calibrating the LMM model using a set of European options.

This study examines tidal forces within multidimensional, spherically symmetric spacetimes. By analyzing the geodesic deviation equation in both the Schwarzschild-Tangherlini metric and its electrically charged counterpart, we demonstrate that radial geodesics can be solved explicitly as quadratures across dimensions of any size. Specifically, in five, six, and seven dimensions, these solutions are expressed via elliptic integrals, while asymptotic behavior is derived for higher-dimensional spacetimes. Our findings indicate that near the physical singularity, radial tidal stretching intensifies as spatial dimension increases, whereas transverse tidal compression stabilizes in its leading order once a certain dimension is reached. Furthermore, for non-radial geodesics, the black hole's electric charge does not significantly alter the leading-order transverse compressive force. Finally, we investigate the local characteristics of geodesic deviation equation solutions near the singularity for non-radial paths possessing non-zero angular momentum.

Grasping the nucleosynthetic sources of nitrogen and the evolutionary trajectory of the N/O ratio within the interstellar medium is essential for a holistic understanding of high-redshift galaxy chemical evolution, given that most observational metallicity (O/H) estimates inherently rely on the N/O ratio. Observations at high-redshift reveal a generally constant N/O ratio relative to O/H, despite significant scatter. We demonstrate that these previously unexplained characteristics are accounted for by pre-supernova wind yields from rotating massive stars ($M\gtrsim 10 \, \mathrm{M}_\odot$, $v/v_{\rm{crit}} \gtrsim 0.4$). Our models successfully reproduce both the observed N/O plateau and the scatter at low O/H levels, attributing the latter to variations in star formation efficiency. In contrast, models relying on supernova-dominated yields fail to match the observed N/O at low O/H. This distinct abundance pattern at low O/H indicates that dwarf galaxies are likely devoid of supernova contributions and are instead primarily enriched by pre-supernova wind abundances.

We examine the evolution of a cyclic universe within the holographic dark energy (HDE) framework, utilizing two distinct Infrared (IR) cutoffs to avoid the Big-Rip singularity. Our findings indicate that, even without mutual interaction between cosmic sectors, the HDE model employing the Hubble radius as the IR cutoff behaves like a cosmological constant in cyclic cosmology. Furthermore, we observe that when the Granda-Oliveros (GO) cutoff is selected for the HDE energy density, both interacting and non-interacting universes can undergo a sequence of contraction and expansion cycles.

Images often contain text elements paired with bounding boxes, such as text recognized via optical character recognition on digital screens or labeled objects within natural scenes. We introduce an end-to-end trainable architecture designed to integrate information from both these elements and the image itself to segment or identify the specific image regions referenced by natural language expressions. This method involves calculating an embedding for each element and projecting it onto the corresponding location within the image feature map. Our results demonstrate that this approach outperforms methods relying solely on the image or other techniques incorporating element data in resolving referring expressions. We validate these findings with experimental results on referring expression datasets derived from COCO and a new webpage image dataset we created.

While ethical considerations in social Virtual Reality (VR) are not novel, the intense focus on the Metaverse has elevated "safety" concerns to a critical level. For instance, reports indicate that nearly 50% of female-identifying VR users have experienced at least one incident of virtual sexual harassment. Feeling secure is a fundamental human right, applicable equally to both physical and virtual environments. This paper aims to investigate the gap between user safety concerns and the current design implementations in social VR. We begin by examining safety concerns through an analysis of Twitter data, followed by a synthesis of protective measures employed by four leading social VR platforms. We contend that future research and platform development must prioritize designs grounded in boundary-awareness.

Parallel corpora are essential for training neural machine translation (NMT) systems, yet they are often absent or limited for many language pairs. In such scenarios, pivot-based NMT offers a viable alternative by utilizing intermediate languages for which parallel data exists between the source-pivot and pivot-target pairs. However, translation quality using a single pivot typically lags behind that achievable with a substantial direct parallel corpus. This deficit becomes more pronounced in real-time simultaneous translation, where the necessity to generate output as soon as a few source words are available further degrades performance. To address this challenge, we introduce multi-pivot translation adapted for simultaneous translation environments. Our method involves concurrently translating the source into multiple pivot languages, which are then simultaneously translated into the target language using a multi-source NMT approach. Experimental results in a low-resource context, employing the N-way parallel UN corpus for Arabic-to-English translation via French and Spanish pivots, demonstrate that utilizing two pivot languages in a simultaneous pivot NMT framework can yield improvements of up to 5.8 BLEU points.

Aditya-L1 marks the Indian Space Research Organization's (ISRO) maiden space-based solar observatory. Deployed at the first Lagrangian point, the spacecraft will house seven payloads to ensure continuous solar monitoring. Its suite includes four remote sensing instruments—specifically a coronagraph capturing visible and infrared light, a Near Ultra-Violet (NUV) full-disk imager, and dual full-sun integrated spectrometers for soft and hard X-rays—alongside three instruments designed for in-situ measurements, such as a magnetometer to analyze magnetic field fluctuations during energetic events. As a dedicated mission for multi-messenger solar astronomy, Aditya-L1 aims to deliver comprehensive solar observations across the entire electromagnetic spectrum, featuring broad-energy in-situ data and magnetic field measurements at L1.

This study explores the advantages and challenges of a robot bartender capable of tailoring interactions to users' preferences regarding drinks, music, and hobbies. We posit that a personalized human-robot interaction enhances user engagement, yet this requires individuals to disclose various personal details. Consequently, this paper outlines our research focus and methodology for assessing user perceptions and privacy concerns in such contexts. Through a within-subject experiment, participants engaged with the robot twice: initially without any prior user data, and subsequently with full knowledge of their preferences. Our findings indicate that fewer than 60% of participants expressed concern about sharing personal information with the robot.

This study reports a search for a heavy W' boson decaying into a single vector-like quark (either B or T) alongside a bottom or top quark, respectively. Utilizing 2016 proton-proton collision data from the CMS detector at the LHC, the analysis covers an integrated luminosity of 35.9 fb$^{-1}$ at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV. Both decay pathways yield a final state comprising a top quark, a Higgs boson, and a b quark, all carrying substantial energy. The investigation focuses on scenarios where both the Higgs boson and the top quark undergo all-hadronic decays. Jet substructure techniques are employed to select final-state jets—some of which arise from merged decay products of a boosted top quark and Higgs boson—thereby reducing standard model backgrounds. A potential W' signal would manifest as a narrow peak within the invariant mass distribution of these jets. No significant discrepancy between the observed data and standard model background predictions was found. Consequently, upper limits on the W' production cross section for this specific decay mode have been established across various W' mass hypotheses, spanning from 1.5 to 4.0 TeV and ranging from 0.01 to 0.43 pb. These represent the first constraints for W' boson production in this channel.

This study reports ATLAS measurements of long-range ($|\Delta\eta|>2$) dihadron angular correlations in $pp$ collisions at $\sqrt{s}=8$ and 13 TeV involving a $Z$ boson. The analysis utilizes 19.4 $\mathrm{fb}^{-1}$ of data from $\sqrt{s}=8$ TeV (Run 1) and 36.1 $\mathrm{fb}^{-1}$ from $\sqrt{s}=13$ TeV (Run 2). Two-particle correlation functions are evaluated across relative pseudorapidities of $2<|\Delta\eta|<5$ as a function of relative azimuthal angle, segmented by charged-particle multiplicity and transverse momentum intervals. Corrections are applied for background charged particles arising from simultaneous collisions between proton bunches, and hard-process contributions are subtracted via template fitting. A sinusoidal modulation in the correlations is identified and characterized by the second Fourier coefficient, $v_{2,2}$, which yields the single-particle anisotropy coefficient $v_{2}$. The $v_{2}$ values in $Z$-tagged events, integrated over $0.5<p_{\mathrm{T}}<5$ GeV, show no dependence on multiplicity or $\sqrt{s}$ and align with previous inclusive $pp$ collision results within uncertainties. Furthermore, $Z$-tagged and inclusive $v_{2}$ values remain consistent within uncertainties across charged-particle $p_{\mathrm{T}}$ for $p_{\mathrm{T}}<3$ GeV.

Automatic annotation of temporal expressions represents a significant challenge within information extraction research. The scarcity of gold-standard temporally-annotated datasets hampers progress, and evolving standards over the last decade have resulted in inconsistent data formats. To address these issues, we substantially expand the availability of human-annotated temporal resources by converting legacy formats to TimeML/TIMEX3, a complex task given the variation in annotation methodologies. We introduce a robust conversion tool and a new, extensive temporal expression resource. Leveraging this resource as training data for an existing TimeML annotation tool, we evaluate our conversion process, achieving an F1 score of 0.87, which outperforms all systems in the TempEval-2 timex recognition task.

We present a novel approach to establishing upper bounds on the growth of finitely generated groups and constructing groups with intermediate growth through graphs derived from their actions. These bounds, expressed as $\exp(n^\alpha)$ where $\alpha < 1$, represent the inaugural examples of such estimates for simple groups exhibiting intermediate growth.

At low momentum transfer, the quark-gluon scattering cross section, d{\sigma}/dt, exhibits a power-law divergence in the backward scattering regime, where the outgoing quark travels nearly collinear with the incoming gluon. Within the Regge limit defined by |t|<< s, the dominant behavior of the 2 2 amplitude is characterized by the exchange of Glauber quarks. In Soft-Collinear Effective Theory (SCET) at leading power, this exchange is represented by five non-local Glauber quark operators, with only a single operator arising at tree-level. This study demonstrates that the QCD amplitude for one-loop quark-gluon backscattering at leading power is precisely reproduced by SCET utilizing the tree-level Glauber operator. The consistency between QCD and SCET regarding ultraviolet, infrared, and rapidity divergences, as well as all logarithms, Glauber phases, and finite components across all external gluon polarizations, serves as a robust validation of the effective theory. Furthermore, the analysis reveals that the entire one-loop matching correction vanishes; no modification is required for the tree-level operator, and the coefficients of the remaining four operators stay zero at the one-loop order. These findings imply that SCET incorporating Glauber operators offers a systematically improvable framework for exploring novel facets of Regge physics.

This study examines a free boundary problem involving the one-dimensional compressible Navier-Stokes equations, demonstrating the asymptotic stability of viscous shock waves under specific smallness constraints through an elementary energy estimate.

This paper tackles the challenge of learning low-dimensional entity representations within relational databases composed of multiple tables. These embeddings capture database semantics and support diverse applications, including table auto-completion, fully neural processing of relational joins, and handling missing values. However, existing approaches are limited to single tables or rely on pretrained embeddings from external corpora, rendering them unsuitable for real-world multi-table scenarios. We propose a method leveraging attention-based models to learn entity embeddings directly from relational databases, drawing inspiration from BERT-style pretraining techniques to explore their adaptability for structured data. Our evaluation on relational database auto-completion demonstrates performance improvements over standard baselines.

We examine Hodge theory through several canonical examples in mirror symmetry, focusing specifically on aspects intrinsic to the A-model and highlighting intriguing open problems. Specifically, we demonstrate the creation of a quantum Z-local system on the cohomology of the total space of the canonical bundle over P^2, proposing its connection to the higher algebraic cycles analyzed in our 2011 CNTP publication, "Algebraic K-theory of toric hypersurfaces."

Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) remain susceptible to intentionally engineered adversarial examples. Recent years have seen significant research into query-optimization attacks targeting both white-box and black-box DNNs, alongside the development of defensive countermeasures. This study investigates a previously unexplored vulnerability: DNNs under Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) attacks. From an MitM adversary's perspective, traditional adversarial attacks become impractical; they require multiple queries to obtain model outputs before execution, which is difficult in a MitM scenario, and they are one-off attacks that lack generalizability to new data, reducing the attacker's efficiency. Conversely, generating adversarial examples on the fly using generative models addresses these limitations. However, the adversarial potential of generative models, such as Variational Auto-Encoders (VAEs), remains under-researched. Consequently, we examine using a VAE decoder to either convert benign inputs into adversarial ones or decode outputs from benign VAE encoders into adversarial examples. This approach significantly enhances the capabilities of MitM attackers. Our evaluations demonstrate that the proposed attack achieves a success rate exceeding 95% on both MNIST and CIFAR10 datasets, performing as well as or better than state-of-the-art query-optimization methods, while operating 104 times faster.

This paper investigates various pointwise recurrence concepts for linear dynamical systems through the lens of Ergodic Theory. We demonstrate that for an adjoint operator $T$ acting on a separable dual Banach space $X$, any reiteratively recurrent vector $x_0$ can be used to construct a $T$-invariant probability measure with $x_0$ in its support. This result enables us to prove equivalences between certain strong pointwise recurrence notions that are typically distinct. Specifically, within our framework, we show that reiterative recurrence is equivalent to frequent recurrence. Furthermore, for complex Hilbert spaces, uniform recurrence is equivalent to the existence of a spanning family of unimodular eigenvectors, a property that also holds for power-bounded operators on complex reflexive Banach spaces. These findings, which may seem unexpected, extend naturally to product and inverse dynamical systems, revealing connections to corresponding hypercyclicity concepts. Finally, we analyze the prevalence of operators possessing a non-zero reiteratively recurrent vector using Baire category theory.

This paper investigates infinite-dimensional port-Hamiltonian systems subject to in-domain actuation using two distinct approaches: one grounded in Stokes-Dirac structures and the other leveraging an underlying jet-bundle framework. Within both methodologies, we develop a dynamic controller utilizing the energy-Casimir method to stabilize specific equilibria. Additionally, we introduce distributed-parameter observers derived through damping injection applied to the observer error. Finally, we validate the equivalence of the resulting control schemes by applying them to an in-domain actuated vibrating string and comparing the outcomes.

We present an efficient and precise technique for transforming Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov wave functions into matrix product states (MPSs). These wave functions, referred to as Bogoliubov vacua, possess a distinctive entanglement structure wherein the eigenvectors of the reduced density matrix are themselves Bogoliubov vacua. By leveraging this key property, we achieve an optimal MPS approximation and establish an explicit formula for the associated MPS matrices. Our method's efficacy is validated through benchmarks on the Kitaev chain and the Majorana-Hubbard model defined on a honeycomb lattice. This approach enhances the utility of Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov wave functions and is particularly well-suited for integration with the density-matrix renormalization group method.

The surging bandwidth and energy requirements of neural networks have driven significant interest in innovative neuromorphic hardware, such as photonic integrated circuits. While optical waveguides theoretically support hundreds of channels with terahertz bandwidth, the actual channel capacity of photonic systems is constrained by the embedded devices. In WDM-based photonic neural networks, synapses (network interconnections) are usually implemented using microring resonators (MRRs), where the number of WDM channels (N) is limited by the MRRs' free-spectral range (FSR). For standard silicon MRRs, we estimate N is capped at approximately 30 within the C-band. This limitation restricts the overall neural network throughput and renders applications requiring high input dimensions impractical. Conversely, we experimentally show that synapses based on photonic crystal nanobeams can operate without an FSR constraint in the C-band, thereby removing the limit on channel count. This advancement boosts data throughput and facilitates high-dimensional tasks such as natural language processing and high-resolution image processing. Furthermore, the compact physical size of photonic crystal nanobeam cavities provides superior tuning energy efficiency and compute density compared to MRRs. Consequently, nanophotonic cavity-based synapses present a viable pathway to achieving highly scalable photonic neural networks.

This study addresses the regulation of rotor speed tracking error for wind turbines operating in the full-load region through an efficient robust-adaptive control strategy. The proposed controller mitigates uncertainties arising from pitch actuator faults, unmeasurable wind disturbances, and model nonlinearities affecting control input effectiveness. Due to the multi-layer architecture of wind turbines, where high-level structures are nonlinearly coupled via aggregated low-level control authorities, the design process is bifurcated into two phases. Initially, an $\mathcal{L}_2$ controller is implemented to dampen the impact of wind disturbance fluctuations on rotor speed. Subsequently, a low-level controller utilizing a novel adaptation mechanism is developed to counteract actuator faults. Theoretical analysis confirms that the high-level closed-loop equilibrium for rotor speed tracking error dynamics achieves finite-gain $\mathcal{L}_2$ stability, while the low-level error dynamics are globally asymptotically stable. Furthermore, simulation outcomes demonstrate that the developed controller substantially lowers the root mean square of rotor speed errors compared to established methods, even under significantly fluctuating wind conditions and time-varying uncertainties in control input effectiveness.

In magnetoelectric multiferroics, which exhibit both electric and magnetic dipole moments, electrical manipulation of magnetization or magnetic control of polarization introduces an additional degree of freedom. Research has identified polycrystalline microstructures that enhance overall polarization and magnetization, outperforming single-crystalline counterparts. Furthermore, characterizing the local fields within these polycrystalline configurations highlights the significant, non-trivial role of randomness in facilitating improved cross-coupling through anisotropic and asymmetric strains.

A defining trait of collective and particle-hole excitations in neutron-rich nuclei is their strong coupling to unbound neutrons in continuum single-particle orbits. The continuum random phase approximation (cRPA) serves as a robust many-body framework for describing these excitations and calculating transition strengths from the ground state. To address radiative neutron capture, this study develops an extended cRPA scheme capable of modeling gamma-decays from excited states to both low-lying excited levels and the ground state. This is accomplished by incorporating a non-local one-body operator that induces transitions to low-lying excited states and analyzing the corresponding density-matrix response. As a demonstration, we perform numerical calculations on dipole, quadrupole, and octupole excitations in $^{140}$Sn, examining E1 and E2 transitions decaying to the $2^{+}_{1,2}$ and $3^{-}_{1}$ states. The findings indicate scenarios where the branching ratio to low-lying states is comparable to or exceeds that to the ground state. Finally, we highlight the critical roles of collectivity and continuum orbits in both the initial and final states.

Accurate segmentation of the hippocampus in MRI scans is critical for diagnosing, treating, and researching neuropsychiatric conditions. While automatic segmentation via deep learning is a rapidly evolving field, most state-of-the-art models are trained exclusively on public datasets containing healthy individuals or those with Alzheimer's disease. This limitation prompts a crucial inquiry: can these methods effectively identify the hippocampus in a distinct domain, specifically epilepsy patients who have undergone hippocampal resection? This paper introduces a state-of-the-art, open-source, ready-to-use deep learning framework for hippocampus segmentation. The approach employs an extended 2D multi-orientation strategy featuring automatic pre-processing and orientation alignment. Developed and validated on the HarP public Alzheimer's dataset, the methodology was evaluated against other recent deep learning techniques across two domains: the HarP test set and an internal epilepsy dataset with hippocampal resections named HCUnicamp. Our results demonstrate that, despite being trained solely on HarP, this method outperforms existing literature in both datasets based on Dice scores. Furthermore, we provide separate analyses of training and testing on HCUnicamp volumes, comparing cross-domain performance between epilepsy and Alzheimer's data. Although current methods, including ours, achieve Dice scores exceeding 0.9 on HarP, all tested approaches generated false positives within HCUnicamp resection areas, indicating that further improvements are necessary for segmentation tasks involving resections.

The rise of Web 2.0 has established tag recommenders as essential instruments designed to assist users in identifying appropriate tags for their saved resources. While existing algorithms often achieve high prediction accuracy, they typically rely on data-driven methods that fail to fully account for the cognitive mechanisms involved in human tagging behavior. This thesis seeks to model these cognitive dynamics within social tagging to enhance recommendation quality and deepen our understanding of the underlying processes. As an initial step toward this goal, we developed a novel tag recommender algorithm that integrates individual micro-level processes (such as resource categorization or temporal evolution) with collective macro-level processes (such as imitating other users' tags). Preliminary evaluations using datasets from BibSonomy, CiteULike, and Delicious indicate that our approach surpasses current state-of-the-art methods, including Collaborative Filtering, FolkRank, and Pairwise Interaction Tensor Factorization. We conclude that recommender systems can be significantly improved by incorporating principles derived from human cognition.

On a finite graph, we establish that the trace of holonomies defines an intertwining relationship between merge-and-split generators acting on ensembles of geodesic loops and Casimir operators associated with unitary connections. Furthermore, by incorporating a deformation component into the loop generator, this finding is generalized to a modified Casimir operator that is self-adjoint relative to the Yang-Mills measure.

Numerous bacterial species, such as the common pathogen *H. pylori*, exhibit a helical structure. Driven by recent experimental findings indicating non-uniform cell wall synthesis in *H. pylori*, this study explores how elastic heterogeneity might induce helical cell shapes. Through both theoretical modeling and experimental validation, we demonstrate that pressurizing an elastic cylinder reinforced with helical lines can generate helical morphogenesis. The resulting helix properties are strongly influenced by the initial angle of these reinforcements. Our results reveal that steep reinforcement angles produce crooked helices that surprisingly exhibit a reduced end-to-end distance when pressurized. This research offers insights into the mechanisms underlying helical cell morphology generation and could inspire the development of new pressure-controlled helical actuators.

We report a simultaneous determination of the strong coupling constant $\alpha_s$ and the top-quark pole mass $m_t$, utilizing top-quark pair production data from the ATLAS and CMS experiments at the 8 TeV LHC. This study marks the first application of differential NNLO theoretical predictions, calculated for varying top-quark masses, to four specific kinematic distributions: the mean transverse momentum, mean rapidity, and the pair's invariant mass and rapidity. By employing fastNLO tables, we enable swift computation of these differential predictions across various PDF sets. We analyze the single-differential distributions provided by the experiments individually and jointly to achieve the optimal theoretical fit. Our resulting values are $\alpha_s=0.1159^{+0.0013}_{-0.0014}$ and $m_t=173.8^{+0.8}_{-0.8}$ GeV, which align with prior extractions based on top-quark measurements. Furthermore, the derived $m_t$ value is consistent with the Particle Data Group's world average.

The collision of two neutron stars generates gravitational waves, creates a compact object within a dense, magnetized environment, and launches a relativistic, collimated jet that culminates in a short gamma-ray burst (SGRB). Research indicates that the jet's interaction with its surroundings significantly influences the outflow's structure and the resulting gamma-ray emission. This study introduces a series of 2.5-dimensional RMHD simulations tracking the evolution of a relativistic, non-magnetized jet penetrating media with varying degrees of magnetization, as expected post-neutron star merger. Our findings reveal that a magnetized ambient medium primarily suppresses jet instabilities and inhibits the formation of collimation shocks. Consequently, internal shocks become less efficient, leading to bursts with lower-luminosity prompt emission. Conversely, the jet-head velocity and the magnetization induced within the jet remain largely unaffected by the ambient medium's magnetization. Further numerical investigations utilizing larger computational domains are required to derive light curves and spectra, thereby enhancing our understanding of the impact of magnetized environments.

These notes explore derived algebraic geometry through the lens of animated rings. Specifically, we revisit Toën-Vaquié's proof demonstrating that the derived stack of perfect complexes is locally geometric when expressed using $\infty$-categories. In doing so, we review essential concepts in derived commutative algebra and derived algebraic geometry. Furthermore, we examine deformation theory and quasi-coherent modules within the framework of derived stacks.

Neural ranking models (NRMs) are now a cornerstone of information retrieval (IR). Because labeled relevance data is scarce, training these models depends heavily on negative sampling using unlabeled data. While machine learning research generally indicates that using hard negatives—samples similar to positives—improves performance, our empirical study in IR reveals the opposite. When we sampled top-ranked results (excluding known positives) from a stronger retriever as negatives, the NRM performance degraded. Our investigation attributes this superficially to a higher concentration of false negatives (unlabeled positives) in the top results of a stronger retriever, which harms training. The root cause, however, is pooling bias in dataset construction, where annotators only label a small subset of samples retrieved by basic methods. Consequently, we can frame the false negative problem in NRM training as learning from datasets affected by pooling bias. To address this, we introduce a novel Coupled Estimation Technique (CET) that jointly learns a relevance model and a selection model to correct for this bias. Experiments across three retrieval benchmarks demonstrate that NRMs trained with CET achieve significant improvements in ranking effectiveness compared to other baseline strategies.

This paper presents calculations regarding the jumps of ramification groups for certain finite non-abelian Galois extensions over complete discrete valuation fields of positive characteristic $p$ with perfect residue fields, where the Galois group has an order of $p^{n+1}$ and $2\leq n\leq p$.

Virtual reality (VR) video applications demand high bandwidth, low latency, and significant computational resources, creating challenges for current resource-limited wireless and edge networks to support on-demand VR delivery. To address this, we introduce a joint horizontal and vertical collaboration architecture within mobile edge computing (MEC)-enabled small-cell networks. In this framework, multiple MEC servers collaboratively offer edge caching and viewpoint computation services to VR head-mounted devices (HMDs), with computation tasks alternatively executed at the HMDs or the cloud. The design integrates power allocation at base stations (BSs) with both horizontal and vertical MEC server collaboration to minimize end-to-end latency. Consequently, a joint optimization problem involving caching, power allocation, and task offloading is formulated, solved by a discrete branch-reduce-and-bound (DBRB) algorithm based on monotone optimization principles. Simulation results confirm that the proposed architecture and algorithm outperform existing solutions.

This study investigates various metrics for quantum correlations and teleportation within the Heisenberg XY model, analyzing two distinct scenarios: one without PT-symmetric operations and another incorporating them. Initially, we examine quantum correlation measures in thermally entangled states absent of PT-symmetry. While violations of Bell's inequality and concurrence fail to detect non-local correlations in these states, the entangled states that exhibit no such correlation according to these metrics remain valuable for teleportation. Subsequently, we integrate non-unitary PT-symmetric time evolution into the model to identify measures confirming the presence of correlations. Our findings demonstrate that this model serves as an efficient resource for teleportation, achieving maximum fidelity under non-unitary time evolution.

The quest to detect life on exoplanets is driven by the potential for life to alter its planetary surroundings, with atmospheric gases like oxygen and methane serving as prime indicators due to the evolutionary advantages of their biological production. Yet, distinguishing these gases as biological in origin from geochemical or astrophysical sources demands a deep comprehension of planetary context, specifically the anticipated atmospheric evolution of lifeless worlds. This study evaluates our current knowledge of this context regarding several candidate biosignatures and their future detectability. We examine the framework for oxygen and outline how hypothetical abiotic oxygen scenarios can be tested. Conversely, our understanding of how planetary context regulates non-biological methane (CH$_4$) production remains limited, despite the potential for CH$_4$ biosignatures in anoxic atmospheres to be easily detected by the James Webb Space Telescope. We assess the environmental context for CH$_4$ and conclude that abundant atmospheric methane coexisting with CO$_2$, where the CO:CH$_4$ ratio is much less than 1, suggests biological origins, though exact thresholds rely on stellar conditions and are constrained by poorly defined abiotic methane scenarios. A similar contextual framework is applied to alternative or non-specific biosignatures. Regardless of how life is distributed across the universe, observing terrestrial exoplanets in the coming decades will yield a quantitative grasp of atmospheric evolution on lifeless worlds. This insight will guide future instrument design to either verify the presence of extraterrestrial life or confirm its absence.

The rise of deep learning has substantially enhanced the quality of generated media. Yet, as synthetic content becomes increasingly photorealistic, it is becoming nearly indistinguishable from authentic material, thereby sparking serious concerns regarding the proliferation of fake or manipulated information online. Consequently, there is a pressing need to create automated tools capable of reliably and promptly identifying synthetic media. This study examines current state-of-the-art techniques for detecting synthetic images, emphasizing the critical components of the most effective approaches and evaluating their performance across various generative architectures. Special focus will be placed on realistic and challenging scenarios, such as content shared on social networks or produced by novel, unseen architectures, to analyze how appropriate augmentation and training strategies influence a detector's ability to generalize.

According to the Gliner vacuum perspective, the first law of mechanics for regular black holes is refined by removing specific deformations. In this framework, the mass-related deformation is incorporated into enthalpy or internal energy, while the parameter-related deformation forms a natural $V$-$P$ term. This revised first law restores the structural similarity to thermodynamic systems, thereby re-establishing the correspondence between mechanical and thermodynamic variables. Notably, the linear relationship between entropy and horizon area for regular black holes remains intact. Building upon this modified thermodynamic law, we construct a self-consistent theory of Ruppeiner geometry and derive a universal attractive characteristic for the microstructure of regular black holes. Furthermore, the repulsive and attractive interactions occurring both inside and outside regular black holes are examined in detail.

The text presents Lieb's convex formulation of density-functional theory in a pedagogical style, focusing on its links to both Hohenberg-Kohn and Levy's constrained-search theories. It examines the Hohenberg-Kohn and Lieb variation principles, underscoring the reciprocal relationship between ground-state energy and the universal density functional. Furthermore, it reviews applications of the Lieb variation principle, illustrating its utility in computing Kohn-Sham potentials for atoms and molecules, analyzing the exchange-correlation functional and adiabatic connection via high-precision many-body techniques, and determining exchange-correlation holes and energy densities for atomic and molecular systems.

The classical three-spin Heisenberg system serves as a fully integrable mechanical model. This paper details the explicit computation of thermodynamic properties, including the density of states, specific heat, susceptibility, and spin autocorrelation functions. These results are derived through (semi-)analytical methods and validated against corresponding Monte Carlo simulations. Specifically, for the long-time autocorrelation function, we observe that under certain coupling constant conditions, the decay approaches constant values via a $1/t$ damped harmonic oscillation, for which we provide a theoretical explanation.

We experimentally verify that next-nearest-neighbor (NNN) coupling within a waveguide array can inherently be negative. This is achieved by fabricating dielectric zig-zag waveguide arrays using direct laser writing (DLW). By adjusting the zig-zag angle, one can modulate the ratio between nearest and next-nearest-neighbor couplings from positive to negative, enabling the suppression of NNN-coupling to zero at a specific angle. We detail the derivation of appropriate higher-order coupling constants for tight-binding models using non-orthogonal coupled mode theory. Our experiments confirm the presence of negative NNN-couplings and demonstrate the enhanced precision of this refined model, particularly when higher-order terms become significant. These findings are also relevant to other discrete systems where the tight-binding model is frequently applied.

Rotor walks in directed graphs function as a deterministic counterpart to Markov Chains, where a pebble traverses vertices according to a specific rule until it reaches a sink. The ARRIVAL problem, introduced by Dohrau and colleagues, involves identifying which specific sink the walk will ultimately reach. Although the number of steps in such a walk can grow exponentially, the problem resides in the complexity class NP $\cap$ co-NP, though its status in P remains unknown. Research has also explored variants involving one or two players, creating deterministic equivalents to stochastic frameworks like Markovian decision processes and stochastic games by substituting random transitions with rotor-routing rules. The decision problems associated with these variants concern the existence of strategies that guarantee specific outcomes regarding the final sink; these are established as NP-complete for a single player and PSPACE-complete for two players. This work introduces a specific class of directed graphs called tree-like multigraphs, which structurally resemble undirected trees. We demonstrate that reachability problems for these graphs, whether involving zero, one, or two players, can be resolved in linear time, despite the rotor walks themselves potentially requiring an exponential number of steps. This efficiency is achieved through a newly defined concept of "return flow," which quantifies the frequency with which the pebble rebounds within the graph's subtrees.

This study reports the initial direct investigation into exotic Higgs boson decays of the form H $\to$ $\mathcal{A}\mathcal{A}$, where $\mathcal{A}$ $\to$ $\gamma\gamma$, utilizing events containing two photon-like objects. The hypothetical particle $\mathcal{A}$ is theorized to be a low-mass spin-0 entity that decays immediately into a merged diphoton system, which is reconstructed as a single photon-like object. The analysis utilizes data from the CMS experiment acquired at $\sqrt{s}$ = 13 TeV, with an integrated luminosity of 136 fb$^{-1}$. No significant excess over the predicted background was observed. Consequently, upper limits on the branching fraction $\mathcal{B}$(H $\to$ $\mathcal{A}\mathcal{A}$ $\to$ 4$\gamma$) were established at 95% confidence level, ranging from (0.9-3.3) $\times$ 10$^{-3}$ for $\mathcal{A}$ masses between 0.1 and 1.2 GeV.

This study introduces the Facial Identity Controllable GAN (FICGAN), a model designed to produce high-quality, de-identified face images that guarantee privacy while offering precise control over attribute retention to improve data utility. Addressing an underexplored yet critical aspect of face de-identification, we focus on two key challenges: achieving robust privacy protection without sacrificing image quality, and analyzing the balance between de-identification intensity and the preservation of source attributes to enhance utility. Consequently, we developed FICGAN, an autoencoder-based conditional generative model capable of disentangling identity-related attributes from non-identity ones within facial images. By employing the manifold k-same algorithm to enforce k-anonymity, our approach strengthens security and privacy. Extensive experiments confirm that our model surpasses existing methods across various face de-identification scenarios.

RRT* is a highly efficient sampling-based motion planning algorithm; however, in the absence of leveraging accessible environmental data, such algorithms often suffer from sampling failures, the generation of redundant nodes, and an inability to explore narrow passages. To address these limitations and enhance search efficiency by better exploiting environmental information, this paper introduces a novel improvement to RRT*. The proposed method achieves this by: 1) quantifying local obstacle knowledge during the neighbor rewiring phase through directional visibility, 2) accumulating environmental data throughout the search process, and 3) adjusting the sampling strategy to bias selections toward nodes near obstacles once an initial solution is identified. This resulting algorithm, termed RRT* by Local Directional Visibility (RRT*-LDV), effectively utilizes local known information and implements an innovative weighted sampling strategy. Experimental results demonstrate that the accelerated RRT*-LDV surpasses standard RRT* in both convergence speed and success rates for locating narrow passages, even within high Degree-Of-Freedom scenarios.

PPSZ currently stands as the most efficient algorithm for solving (d,k)-CSP problems across a wide range of parameter values. The standard approach processes variables in a random sequence, assigning each a color from the available d options while excluding any colors eliminated by examining local constraints. We introduce and evaluate an enhanced variant termed "impatient PPSZ," which immediately assigns a random valid color to a variable the moment only two options remain. Our analysis demonstrates that this modified algorithm achieves an exponential improvement over the original PPSZ for all values of k and d ≥ 3 when applied to formulas with a unique satisfying assignment.

The Bondi-van der Burg-Metzner-Sachs (BMS) group, which uniquely characterizes the symmetries of asymptotic infinity and the gravitational waves traveling through it, has grown increasingly vital for precise waveform modeling. Specifically, existing waveform frameworks—including post-Newtonian (PN) expansions, numerical relativity (NR), and black hole perturbation theory—yield results defined in distinct BMS frames. Therefore, constructing a comprehensive model for compact object mergers that ideally integrates these three approaches requires a rapid and reliable technique to resolve BMS ambiguities. In this study, we introduce the first method capable of fixing the full BMS freedom of NR waveforms to align with the frames used in PN or black hole perturbation theory. We accomplish this by identifying specific BMS transformations that adjust particular charges in a predetermined manner, such as applying a center-of-mass transformation to set the center-of-mass charge to zero. Our findings indicate that this new charge-based approach is twenty times faster and more accurate when mapping to the superrest frame compared to prior optimization-based techniques. Additionally, while developing this frame-fixing method, we derived the PN expression for the Moreschi supermomentum up to 3PN order without spins and 2PN order with spins. This supermomentum corresponds effectively to energy flux or null memory contributions at future null infinity ($\mathscr{I}^{+}$). Leveraging this PN calculation, we also identified oscillatory ($m \neq 0$ modes) and spin-dependent memory terms that were previously unrecognized or absent from strain expressions in the post-Newtonian literature.

A novel event reconstruction algorithm utilizing a maximum likelihood approach has been created for Super-Kamiokande. This advancement enhances kinematic and particle identification, allowing for the examination of atmospheric neutrino data within a detector volume 32% greater than prior studies, thereby increasing sensitivity to the neutrino mass hierarchy. Analysis of 253.9 kton-years of Super-Kamiokande IV atmospheric neutrino data shows a weak indication favoring the normal hierarchy, while the inverted hierarchy is disfavored at the 74% confidence level based on the analysis's best-fit oscillation parameters.

Radiation pressure-driven solar sails facilitate space missions that are beyond the reach of chemical rockets alone. A sail capable of deflecting sunlight at a large average angle could provide significant propulsion for missions like a solar polar orbiter. This study examines the momentum transfer efficiency of sunlight diffracted by a sun-facing sail made of periodic sawtooth prism elements. The results show that when the grating period is significantly longer than the peak of the solar spectrum, the spectrally averaged efficiency approaches that of a monolithic prism. This idealized diffraction analysis predicts a higher transverse radiation pressure force than an idealized reflective sail. With advancements in modern optical design and fabrication, diffractive solar sails may eventually replace reflective sails.

Data science exploration typically relies on computational notebooks and dataframe APIs like pandas, which offer flexible tools for cleaning, transforming, and analyzing data. However, visually inspecting dataframes remains a laborious process that demands significant coding for visualization and considerable cognitive effort to decide on subsequent analytical steps. We introduce Lux, an always-on framework designed to expedite the discovery of visual insights within dataframe workflows. When a user prints a dataframe in their notebook, Lux automatically suggests visualizations to highlight key patterns and trends while proposing promising directions for further analysis. Additionally, Lux provides a high-level language for generating visualizations on demand, fostering rapid experimentation with the data. Our results show that through careful design and three specific system optimizations, Lux incurs an overhead of no more than two seconds compared to pandas for over 98% of datasets in the UCI repository. We assessed Lux's usability through a controlled first-use study and interviews with early adopters, confirming that it effectively addresses data scientists' need for visualization support integrated into their dataframe workflows. The framework has already gained traction among practitioners, boasting over 3.1k stars on GitHub.

A significant emerging challenge in climate change communication is the widespread presence of conspiracy theories. This study examines prominent climate-related conspiracy theories identified within a substantial Twitter dataset. Utilizing advanced stance detection techniques, we determine whether these theories are more prevalent among climate change skeptics or believers. Furthermore, we investigate which specific theories garner the most traction and how their popularity varies according to belief levels. Our results indicate that climate change disbelievers are the primary drivers behind the dissemination of messages containing conspiracy-related keywords, with the sharing of different theories varying in frequency. Finally, we explore the implications of these findings for effective climate change communication strategies.

M. Bhargava and P. Harron previously demonstrated that for $n=3,4,5$, the shapes of rings of integers in $S_n$-number fields of degree $n$ exhibit equidistribution within the space of shapes as the fields are ordered by discriminant. Rather than focusing solely on shapes, this work associates grids with each number field to retain more comprehensive data; the space of grids constitutes a fiber bundle over the space of shapes. This paper strengthens the Bhargava-Harron theorem by establishing that the grids corresponding to the rings of integers of these $S_n$-number fields become equidistributed in the space of grids.

The magnetic moments ($a_\gamma$) and weak magnetic moments ($a_W$) of charged leptons and quarks are highly sensitive to quantum effects arising from new physics heavy resonances. Within the framework of effective field theory, these moments are generated by two independent operators; consequently, measuring both $a_\gamma$ and $a_W$ is essential for gaining insights into new physics. While the $a_W$ values of Standard Model fermions have been measured at LEP, this study examines the contributions from both magnetic and weak magnetic moment operators in the processes $pp\to H \gamma$ and $gg\to H \to \tau^+ \tau^- \gamma$ at the High-Luminosity Large Hadron Collider. We show that these two processes can probe a significant portion of the parameter space that remains inaccessible to LEP.

We have gathered significant spectroscopic data from various surveys concerning star-forming galaxies in the local Universe. To constrain our models, we selected objects displaying a rich spectrum of lines from multiple elements, with a specific focus on relatively weak lines such as [OIII]4363, HeII4686, HeI4471, and HeI5876. We modeled these spectra in detail by considering the combined effects of stellar photoionization and shocks. Our findings indicate that the abundances of most elements relative to hydrogen are lower than solar levels but not as depleted as those derived from direct strong-line and $T_e$ methods. Sulfur, detected via [SII]6717, 6731, and [SIII]6312 lines, shows no depletion, pointing to a substantial contribution from the interstellar medium (ISM). We expanded the sample to include optical-UV spectra of local low-metallicity dwarf galaxies, incorporating CIV/Hb and CIII]/Hb line ratios to precisely determine C/H relative abundances. The results reveal sub-solar He/H ratios in certain objects and suggest that the geometrical thickness of clouds influences HeII/Hb line ratios. We attribute the low He/H values to the mixing of winds from star-forming regions with ISM clouds.

Mental health issues significantly affect the quality of life for millions globally, yet diagnosing these disorders remains difficult, often relying on subjective patient self-reports of behavioral patterns. Consequently, there is a pressing need for innovative diagnostic strategies. The emergence of body-area networks featuring accurate sensors in smartwatches and smartphones, combined with deep neural networks (DNNs), offers a promising solution. However, diagnosing diseases using wearable medical systems (WMSs) and DNNs, particularly when deployed on edge devices, continues to pose challenges. To address this, we introduce MHDeep, a framework that leverages commercially available WMSs and efficient DNN models to diagnose three key mental health conditions: schizoaffective disorder, major depressive disorder, and bipolar disorder. MHDeep processes eight distinct categories of data from sensors embedded in smartwatches and smartphones. Given the scarcity of real-world data, the framework incorporates a synthetic data generation module to augment real datasets with synthetic samples drawn from the same probability distribution. These synthetic datasets are used to pre-train the DNN models, establishing a weight prior. Additionally, a grow-and-prune DNN synthesis approach is employed to simultaneously learn the network architecture and weights during training. The models were evaluated using three different data partitions based on data collected from 74 individuals, with assessments conducted at both the data instance and patient levels. MHDeep achieved average test accuracies of 90.4%, 87.3%, and 82.4% for distinguishing healthy instances from those with schizoaffective, major depressive, and bipolar disorders, respectively. At the patient level, the MHDeep DNNs attained accuracies of 100%, 100%, and 90.0% for the three disorders, respectively.

This research examines the polar collective dynamics of Janus colloidal particles driven by an alternating current electric field. At sufficiently high densities, polar interactions between the particles create an orientationally ordered state that mirrors the Vicsek model, displaying characteristics like genuine long-range order and massive number fluctuations. By independently measuring single-particle polarity and velocity, we analyzed the dynamics within this ordered phase. We identified statistical properties of this state that had not been theoretically addressed, including an asymmetric relationship between polarity and velocity, rotational diffusion that is enhanced relative to the disordered state, and an algebraic auto-correlation of polarity. These experimental results, situated at the intersection of Vicsek physics and Active Brownian Particle physics, illuminate the previously unexplored physics resulting from the interplay between polarity and velocity.

This paper aims to enhance object detection by leveraging the relationships between objects. Instead of depending on predefined, labeled graph structures, we derive a graph prior from object co-occurrence statistics. Our central approach involves modeling object relations based on initial class predictions and co-occurrence priors to construct an image graph, thereby improving classification and bounding box regression. Furthermore, we learn the joint distribution of object relations using energy-based modeling. By sampling from this distribution, we generate a refined graph representation that boosts detection performance. Experiments on the Visual Genome and MS-COCO datasets show that our method is detector-agnostic, fully trainable end-to-end, and particularly effective for rare object classes. Additionally, we achieve consistent improvements over detectors such as DETR and Faster-RCNN, as well as state-of-the-art techniques for modeling object interrelationships.

Ad hoc teamwork (AHT) involves developing an agent capable of collaborating with unfamiliar teammates in the absence of prior coordination. Current AHT approaches are often classified as type-based, necessitating a predefined set of teammates for training. The challenge of designing these teammate types significantly influences how well agents generalize to types encountered only during deployment. This study introduces a method to uncover diverse teammate types by optimizing best response diversity metrics. We demonstrate that our approach generates teammate types that demand a broader spectrum of responses from the learner during collaboration, thereby potentially enhancing the learner's robustness in AHT scenarios compared to other methods.

This research investigates the configurations of ribbon or ladder polymers situated in poor solvents. The interplay between anisotropic bending rigidity and surface tension drives these ribbon polymers to spontaneously form highly anisotropic condensates. In contrast to standard flexible polymers, these condensates exhibit multiple distinct layering transitions dependent on chain length or solvent quality, while their size varies non-monotonically with chain length. Furthermore, we demonstrate that condensate fluctuations are generally minimal, indicating overall stability.

We investigate the production of a large power spectrum, required for primordial black hole formation, using the effective theory of single-field inflation. Our analysis examines mechanisms such as a transition to a ghost-inflation-like phase and scenarios involving a temporarily activated exponentially growing mode. In these cases, the amplification of the power spectrum arises from either a rapid shift in effective couplings or an alteration of the perturbation dispersion relation, with the background evolution remaining approximately de Sitter and unchanged throughout inflation. The stability of our findings is ensured by a weakly broken Galileon symmetry, which safeguards the effective couplings from significant quantum corrections. We further explore the relationship between power spectrum enhancement and the energy scale of operators exhibiting weak Galileon invariance, while also analyzing constraints imposed by strong coupling and the validity of the perturbative expansion.

Signed link prediction is a critical task with wide-ranging applications, involving the binary classification of edges as either positive or negative. Because of fundamental differences, methods designed for unsigned networks cannot be directly adapted to signed link prediction, which also requires adhering to specific structural constraints such as the structural balance property. While recent approaches typically utilize either generative or discriminative models to create node representations, we introduce SigGAN, a novel framework inspired by the success of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). SigGAN integrates the discriminator and generator architecture to address unique challenges in signed networks, including the incorporation of negative edge information, the significant disparity between positive and negative edges, and the principles of structural balance theory. Experimental results on various real-world datasets demonstrate that SigGAN outperforms state-of-the-art techniques, confirming its effectiveness.

Volcanism serves as a significant, enduring source of volatile elements like carbon and hydrogen for Earth's atmosphere, likely for Venus, and potentially for exoplanets. Atmospheric models often rely on one of two assumptions: either that atmospheric composition is dictated by the high-temperature equilibrium of volcanic eruptions, or that volcanic gases thermally re-equilibrate to the cooler surface temperature. The latter scenario has been proposed to generate false-positive biosignatures, such as the simultaneous presence of CO2 and CH4 without CO. This study tests these foundational assumptions by using chemical kinetic calculations to determine the relaxation timescales of volcanic atmospheres. We find that assuming thermochemical equilibrium is valid only for planets with atmospheric temperatures exceeding approximately 700 K. At lower temperatures, slow chemical kinetics prevent redox-sensitive species like CH4, CO, and NH3 from reaching low-temperature equilibrium. Consequently, volcanic atmospheres on exoplanets with temperatures at or below those of Venus will be "quenched," retaining chemical signatures from the high-temperature volcanic source. This quenching at temperatures ≤700 K eliminates the possibility of generating CO2+CH4 false-positive biosignatures through thermochemistry alone, thereby supporting the utility of these signatures for life detection. However, because quenched volcanic gases exhibit speciation characteristic of a more oxidized atmosphere in equilibrium, this process complicates the interpretation of atmospheric data regarding planetary interior properties.

Kernel methods derived from tree ensembles, such as Random Forests (RF) and Gradient Boosted Trees (GBT), have proven competitive with their direct ensemble counterparts, especially in high-dimensional settings. However, the efficacy of these kernel algorithms is contingent upon the alignment between the kernel and the target variable. While this relationship is established for other contexts, the specific kernel-target alignment in tree-ensemble-based kernel learning remains unexplored, which is the primary focus of this study. Through eigenanalysis of the kernel matrix, we establish that for continuous targets, high performance in tree-based kernel learning correlates with robust kernel-target alignment. Furthermore, we demonstrate that successful kernels are defined by strong target-aligned components, manifested as scalar products between the kernel matrix's eigenvectors and the target. This indicates that when such learning succeeds, the relevant information for the supervised task is concentrated within a lower-dimensional manifold spanned by these aligned components. The persistence of these components is further validated through sensitivity analysis using landmark learning. In addition to a thorough simulation study, we present experimental results from multiple real-world datasets that corroborate our simulation findings.

This study addresses an infinite-horizon stochastic linear-quadratic (LQ) optimal control problem featuring regime switching, random coefficients, and cone constraints on the control. To solve this, the authors introduce two novel extended stochastic Riccati equations (ESREs) defined over an infinite horizon. By analyzing a sequence of ESREs on finite horizons, they establish the existence of nonnegative solutions for both standard and singular cases. Leveraging these findings alongside approximation methods, the paper derives explicit expressions for the optimal state feedback control and the corresponding optimal value. Ultimately, these theoretical results are applied to resolve a lifetime portfolio selection problem aimed at tracking a specific wealth level, incorporating regime switching and portfolio constraints.

Graph artificial intelligence has demonstrated significant efficacy in modeling intricate systems, spanning from biological dynamic networks to physical interacting particle systems. Yet, the growing heterogeneity of graph data necessitates multimodal approaches capable of integrating diverse inductive biases—the underlying assumptions algorithms employ to generalize to unseen inputs. Learning from multimodal graph datasets introduces fundamental hurdles, as inductive biases often differ across modalities, and graphs may not always be explicitly provided. To overcome these obstacles, multimodal graph AI techniques synthesize various data types by exploiting cross-modal relationships.
