Instead, its primary utility lies as an instructional tool to elucidate fundamental renormalization group concepts. This paper begins by introducing a model for electrons in graphene and preparing it for renormalization group treatment through the introduction of its Grassmann representation and scale decomposition. Subsequently, we define the hierarchical graphene model and examine its renormalization group flow. From the perspective of renormalization group theory, graphene exhibits notable simplicity due to its super-renormalizable nature. To demonstrate the analysis of a more complex system, we also apply these methods to the Kondo model, a strongly coupled system characterized by a non-trivial fixed point.

We introduce ARC-DA, a direct-answer ("open response," "freeform") variant of the ARC (AI2 Reasoning Challenge) multiple-choice benchmark. Although ARC has significantly influenced the field, its multiple-choice structure fails to reflect real-world queries and is prone to specific artifacts. To address these limitations, ARC-DA transforms questions into direct-answer formats through a hybrid approach involving crowdsourcing and expert validation. The final collection comprises 2,985 questions with 8,436 valid answers, noting that most questions admit multiple correct responses. As one of the earliest direct-answer datasets featuring natural questions that demand reasoning without obvious decompositions, ARC-DA details the conversion methodology, suitable evaluation metrics, and several high-performing models. Despite strong results (81% GENIE, 61.4% F1, 63.2% ROUGE-L), substantial room for improvement remains. Furthermore, the dataset offers a fertile ground for research into explanations, given the reasoning required to formulate answers. We anticipate that ARC-DA will catalyze further progress in complex question-answering within the community and is accessible at https://allenai.org/data/arc-da.

This research evaluates various convolutional neural network architectures and hardware acceleration tools for detecting breast cancer in microscopic sentinel lymph node images. Using an off-the-shelf deep learning framework, models with varying depths were trained and assessed on a public dataset exceeding 300,000 lymph node images across four different hardware cards. The study also examined the effects of transfer learning, data augmentation, and hyperparameter fine-tuning. Results indicate that hardware acceleration can reduce training time by five to twelve times, whereas increasing model depth extends training duration by four to six times, depending on the specific hardware. While deeper models significantly enhance performance, data augmentation and transfer learning did not yield improvements. However, fine-tuning hyperparameters notably boosted results, with the top-performing model achieving accuracy comparable to state-of-the-art solutions.

A theoretical framework integrating atomic-scale interfacial details has been developed to account for the electronic structure of buried interfaces and model charge carrier behavior in heterostructures under finite interfacial broadening. When applied to ultrathin heteroepitaxial (SiGe)m/(Si)m superlattices, this model forecasts localized energy levels within the band structure caused by sub-nanometer broadening, creating new pathways for electron-hole recombination. Experimental results at varying superlattice thicknesses and periodicities confirm these predicted interfacial electronic transitions and their associated absorptive effects. By mapping the energy of critical points, optical transitions are identified in the 2 to 2.5 eV range, thereby extending optical absorption to lower energies. This phenomenon allows for a simple, non-destructive method to probe atomic-level broadening in heterostructures.

We establish novel findings regarding the additive Galois module structure of specific wildly ramified, finite, non-abelian extensions of Q. Specifically, for a Galois extension K/Q where the Galois group G is isomorphic to A4, S4, or A5, we provide necessary and sufficient criteria for the ring of integers of K to be free over its corresponding order within the rational group algebra Q[G].

This study focuses on achieving global exponential attitude tracking for spacecraft despite gyroscopic measurements affected by bias. Initially, an exponentially convergent nonlinear observer is developed using contraction analysis to estimate the gyro bias. Leveraging this estimator and the quaternion logarithm to represent the tracking error, a globally exponentially convergent controller is formulated. This controller ensures the unique equilibrium of the closed-loop system, defined by the unit quaternion tracking error. To improve energy efficiency and robustness against measurement noise, a hysteretically switching variable, as referenced in [1], is integrated into the control loop, resulting in an unwinding-free globally exponentially convergent tracking controller. Numerical simulations were conducted to assess performance regarding tracking accuracy, energy consumption, and robustness to measurement noise and time-varying gyro biases.

A primary difficulty in characterizing 2-D topographies lies in concisely describing the dominant nature of their local configurations. In a 2-D grid of bistate units, this involves identifying characteristic configuration variables, such as nearest-neighbor pairs and triplet combinations. The 2-D cluster variation method (CVM) offers a theoretical basis for linking a set of these variables to just two parameters within a system at free energy equilibrium. This study introduces a technique to identify the most appropriate two-parameter set for a specific 2-D topography, utilizing approaches from variational inference.

This research specifically addresses topographies where the activation enthalpy parameter ($\epsilon_0$) is zero, ensuring an equiprobable distribution between the two states. This constraint is applied because equiprobability yields an analytic solution for configuration variables as functions of the $h$-value, defined by the interaction enthalpy parameter ($\epsilon_1$) as $h = \exp(2\epsilon_1)$. Consequently, computationally derived configuration values can be compared against analytically predicted values for a given $h$.

The methodology is demonstrated using four patterns derived from three distinct naturally occurring black-and-white topographies, all satisfying the equiprobability condition. The results align with expectations: as patterns transition from fewer like-near-like nodes to greater like-near-like masses, the $h$-values of the corresponding free energy-minimized models increase. Additionally, the configuration variable values of these optimized model patterns show approximate alignment with the analytically predicted values.

Over the past few years, multimodal AI has experienced significant growth as researchers combine diverse data types, including text, images, and speech, to enhance modeling outcomes. This project utilizes multimodal AI alongside matrix factorization for representation learning, processing both textual and visual data concurrently by applying established methods from Natural Language Processing (NLP) and Computer Vision. The resulting representations are assessed through downstream classification and regression tasks. Furthermore, the proposed methodology is adaptable beyond this specific project, as it incorporates Auto-Encoders for unsupervised representation learning.

Rotation leads to an increase in both the mass and equatorial radius of a neutron star. While the absolute values of mass and radius are highly sensitive to the unknown equation of state (EOS) of cold, dense matter, the rotational enhancements themselves are nearly independent of the EOS. This EOS independence forms the basis of neutron star universality. In this study, we calculate sequences of rotating neutron stars with constant central density and employ a set of randomly generated EOS to derive simple correction factors for mass and radius, based on hydrostatic equilibrium calculations for non-rotating stars. These correction factors rely solely on the non-rotating star's mass and radius and are almost EOS-independent, making it computationally efficient to incorporate rotating neutron star observations into EOS inference codes. Additionally, we develop a mapping from the measured mass and radius of a rotating neutron star to its non-rotating counterpart, enabling the construction of a zero-spin mass-radius curve if masses and radii are measured for numerous neutron stars with varying spins. We further demonstrate that changes in polar and equatorial radii are symmetric: the polar radius contracts at the same rate that the equatorial radius expands. This symmetry correlates with the observation that equatorial compactness (the mass-to-radius ratio) remains nearly constant along one of the constant-density sequences.

Digital mammography remains the primary modality for breast cancer screening. While its advantages for detection exceed the risks of x-ray exposure, it is essential to minimize radiation doses without compromising diagnostic image quality. Numerous studies have explored using deep neural networks to reconstruct low-dose images, emphasizing that the selection of training data and loss functions critically influences outcomes. This study proposes a modified ResNet architecture featuring hierarchical skip connections to restore low-dose digital mammography images. We compared these restored images against standard full-dose references and assessed various loss functions. For training, 256,000 image patches were extracted from a dataset of 400 retrospective clinical exams, where simulated dose variations created low- and full-dose pairs. To validate the model in a realistic setting, real low-dose and full-dose images were acquired using a commercial mammography system and an anthropomorphic breast phantom, then processed by the trained network. An existing analytical restoration model served as a benchmark. Objective evaluation utilized the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and mean normalized squared error (MNSE), broken down into residual noise and bias components. The results indicate that the perceptual loss function (PL4) achieves noise levels comparable to full-dose acquisitions while producing significantly lower signal bias than other loss functions.

We present a theoretical framework explaining absorption and emission line systems in classical novae using a fully self-consistent explosion model. Our findings indicate that a reverse shock forms well beyond the photosphere ($\gtrsim 10^{13}$ cm) due to collisions between faster, later-ejected mass and earlier material. During the period near optical maximum, optically thick winds blow continuously at a rate of $\sim 10^{-4} ~M_\odot$ yr$^{-1}$; however, wind velocity decreases approaching the maximum and rises afterward, meaning the shock develops only after the peak brightness. The nova ejecta is partitioned by this shock into three components—the outermost expanding gas (pre-maximum wind), the shocked shell, and the inner fast wind—which correspond to pre-maximum, principal, and diffuse-enhanced absorption/emission line systems, respectively. Most of the ejecta eventually remains confined within the shocked shell. The emergence of the principal system aligns with the development of this shock, which is sufficiently intense to account for thermal hard X-ray emissions. The shocked layer reaches a high temperature of $k T_{\rm sh} \sim 1$ keV $\times ((v_{\rm wind} - v_{\rm shock})/{\rm 1000 ~km~s}^{-1})^2$, where the velocity term represents the difference between the diffuse-enhanced ($v_{\rm d}$) and principal ($v_{\rm p}$) systems. Finally, we compare a $1.3 ~M_\odot$ white dwarf model with the observational characteristics of the GeV gamma-ray emitting classical nova V5856 Sgr (ASASSN-16ma) to discuss the conditions under which novae can generate GeV gamma-ray emissions.

This research examines multiple facets of the quantum architecture within the minimal, potentially realistic, renormalizable $\mathrm{SO}(10)$ Higgs framework, where $\mathbf{45}\oplus \mathbf{126}$ scalars trigger symmetry breaking to the Standard Model gauge group $\mathrm{SU}(3)_{c}\times \mathrm{SU}(2)_{L}\times \mathrm{U}(1)_{Y}$. Leveraging comprehensive one-loop corrections to scalar masses and the corresponding beta functions for scalar self-couplings, we delineate the parameter space regions allowing for a perturbative treatment, alongside refined constraints derived from SM vacuum stability and gauge coupling unification. Our analysis reveals that the model remains fully consistent and potentially viable only within extremely narrow parameter domains associated with intermediate symmetry breaking chains featuring well-defined $\mathrm{SU}(4)_{C}\times \mathrm{SU}(2)_L\times \mathrm{U}(1)_R$ or $\mathrm{SU}(3)_{c}\times \mathrm{SU}(2)_L\times \mathrm{SU}(2)_R\times \mathrm{U}(1)_{B-L}$ structures, showing a distinct preference for the former. Absent accidental fine-tunings in the scalar sector, this leads to a precise prediction for the unification scale and its associated gauge coupling, with significant consequences for the phenomenology of grand unified theories built upon this specific symmetry structure.

Prior phenomenological research and measurements indicate that weighted angular moments calculated from jet constituents capture the color connections between the initiating partons that generate the jets. This study reports measurements of two such distributions—the jet-pull angle and jet-pull magnitude—both derived from the jet-pull angular moment. The analysis focuses on $t\bar{t}$ events featuring one leptonically and one hadronically decaying $W$ boson, utilizing $36.1$ fb$^{-1}$ of $pp$ collision data at $\sqrt{s} = 13$ TeV collected by the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider. These observables are examined for two dijet systems: those corresponding to the color-connected daughters of the $W$ boson and the $b$-jets resulting from top-quark decays. To facilitate comparison with color model predictions, the measured distributions are unfolded to the stable-particle level, with corrections applied for experimental detector effects. Although certain predictions align well with the data for specific observable combinations, no single prediction adequately describes the data across all observables.

Coded Distributed Computing (CDC) lowers communication overhead in distributed systems by leveraging redundant computation and multicasting. While the optimal tradeoff between computation and communication has been extensively analyzed for homogeneous systems—with some findings for heterogeneous ones—current approaches often rely on precise data placement and output function assignment. Such requirements are impractical in scenarios lacking central server orchestration, where nodes retrieve data autonomously. This paper addresses general heterogeneous distributed systems where data placement and output functions are arbitrary and pre-defined. To mitigate communication load in this setting, we introduce two schemes: One-Shot Coded Transmission (OSCT) and Few-Shot Coded Transmission (FSCT). Both methods cluster nodes and split transmissions into multiple rounds, designing coded strategies within each round to maximize multicast efficiency. The primary distinction lies in their decoding mechanisms: OSCT employs a one-shot approach where each encoded message is independently decodable by target nodes, whereas FSCT enables nodes to jointly decode multiple received symbols to potentially achieve greater multicast gains. Supporting these proposals with theoretical converse proofs, we establish sufficient conditions for the optimality of both OSCT and FSCT. These results not only align with known optimality findings for homogeneous and 3-node systems but also demonstrate scenarios where our schemes are optimal while existing methods fall short.

The gravitational field associated with an idealized plane-wave solution to the Maxwell equations admits a closed-form description. Following an examination of this specific solution to the Einstein-Maxwell equations, the motion of neutral test particles—responding solely to the gravitational background—is investigated. Subsequently, the dynamics of neutral fields within this particular Einstein-Maxwell setting are analyzed, covering scalars, Majorana spinors, and abelian vector fields in turn.

Zeckendorf demonstrated that every positive integer possesses a unique representation as a sum of non-consecutive Fibonacci numbers, defined by the sequence $F_1 = 1, F_2 = 2$, and $F_{n+1} = F_n + F_{n-1}$. Inspired by this theorem, Baird, Epstein, Flint, and Miller introduced the two-player Zeckendorf game, in which participants alternate moves on a multiset of Fibonacci numbers summing to $N$. The game ends when no further moves are possible, with the last player to move declared the winner. Specifically examining random games where available moves are selected uniformly, they hypothesized that as $N$ approaches infinity, the distribution of game lengths converges to a Gaussian.

This work establishes that the sum of certain move counts remains constant and derives a lower bound for the number of shortest games on input $N$ using Catalan numbers. While Baird et al. and Cuzensa et al. previously identified strategies for achieving the minimum and maximum possible game lengths for a given $N$, we prove that the set of all achievable game lengths forms a continuous interval of natural numbers; that is, any length between the shortest and longest is attainable.

We also advance the analysis of probabilistic properties in random Zeckendorf games by investigating two probability measures on the space of all games for a fixed $N$: the uniform measure and the measure resulting from selecting moves uniformly at each step. Under both measures, we show that as $N \to \infty$, each player wins with probability $1/2$. Additionally, we identify natural partitions of the collection of games for a fixed $N$ that exhibit weak convergence to a Gaussian in the limit. The paper concludes with a discussion of numerous open problems.

Since its introduction, Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) has achieved significant milestones, notably the capability to process raw visual data. Nevertheless, training agents to execute tasks using image feedback remains a difficult hurdle. This challenge involves processing vast quantities of data from high-dimensional observation spaces frame-by-frame, with actions determined by end-to-end deep neural network policies. Pre-processing images serves as an effective strategy to reduce these high-dimensional spaces, remove irrelevant scene information, and facilitate feature extraction and representation within the agent's neural network. Modern video games exemplify this challenge for DRL algorithms due to their visual intricacy. In this paper, we introduce a low-dimensional observation filter that enables a deep Q-network agent to successfully play in the visually complex and modern video game, Neon Drive.

Perturbative supersymmetry breaking within the string vacuum landscape is anticipated to generate large soft terms following a power-law or logarithmic distribution, though this is moderated by an anthropic veto against vacua that fail to satisfy the atomic principle or produce a weak scale that is excessively large. Consequently, statistical analyses of these vacua predict a light Higgs mass of approximately 125 GeV, with superpartners (except perhaps light higgsinos) typically lying beyond the LHC's detection range. Conversely, models featuring dynamical supersymmetry breaking (DSB), where a hidden sector gauge coupling is uniformly scanned, result in gaugino condensation and a logarithmic uniform distribution of soft parameters. In this scenario, soft terms follow a $m_{\rm soft}^{-1}$ distribution that favors small values; however, scanning these parameters generally yields a Higgs mass significantly below 125 GeV and sparticle masses usually accessible to the LHC. Therefore, the DSB landscape scenario appears ruled out by current LHC data, suggesting instead that the exponential suppression of the weak scale is established anthropically on the landscape through the atomic principle.

**Objective:** While brain networks are increasingly viewed as promising biomarkers in mental health research, few methods exist to effectively utilize their complexity for precise classification. This study aims to create a new Bayesian Support Vector Machine (SVM) framework that treats high-dimensional networks as covariates, addressing the shortcomings of current penalized techniques. **Methods:** We introduce a Bayesian SVM model utilizing a novel Dirichlet process mixture of double exponential priors on coefficients. This approach enables feature selection and uncertainty quantification by unsupervisedly pooling edge information to identify differential sparsity levels. We developed variations of this model to incorporate both static and dynamic connectivity features, alongside an integrative analysis combining data from multiple scanning sessions. The model was tested on resting-state fMRI data from the Human Connectome Project (HCP) for intelligence level classification and a second task for classifying Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD). **Results:** The proposed method demonstrated significantly higher classification accuracy compared to state-of-the-art alternatives. Notably, the multi-session analysis yielded the highest accuracy in the HCP dataset. **Conclusion:** Our findings provide robust evidence that the new Bayesian SVM offers an automated, unsupervised solution for network-based classification, delivering substantial improvements over both penalized methods and parametric Bayesian approaches. **Significance:** This work stands among the first to definitively showcase the benefits of Bayesian SVMs for classifying mental health outcomes using networks and underscores the critical value of multi-session network analysis.

Thermal excitations in finite quantum systems are of particular interest because they lack phase transitions and cause the BCS theory to fail. This study investigates a four-particle pairing Hamiltonian at finite temperatures using both a quantum simulator and a superconducting quantum computer. We employ the variational quantum deflation (VQD) method to determine excited states and apply error-mitigation techniques to enhance accuracy in noisy conditions. By running the same circuits at zero temperature to simulate thermal excitations, we observe a smooth temperature-dependent transition, which contrasts with the spurious phase transition produced by the finite-temperature BCS (FT-BCS) approach.

We present an explicit formula for the Gromov width of symplectic toric manifolds derived from simple graphs. As a consequence, we demonstrate a non-squeezing theorem adapted to the inclusion of connected graphs.

We introduce a novel interstellar dust model featuring large grains as a unified composite material termed "astrodust," alongside distinct nanoparticle varieties such as polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs). We contend that a single-composition framework for grains exceeding $\sim0.02\,\mu$m best accounts for the observed independence of the far-infrared (FIR) polarization fraction from frequency and the specific ratio between optical and FIR polarization. Furthermore, we establish a size distribution and alignment function for 1.4:1 oblate astrodust grains; when combined with PAHs, this model successfully replicates the mean wavelength dependence and polarization characteristics of Galactic extinction and diffuse interstellar medium emission, all while adhering to constraints on solid-phase abundances. Complete model data and Python-based interfaces are now publicly accessible.

This paper investigates the characterization of a newly defined submersion, termed semi-invariant conformal $\zeta^{\perp}$-Riemannian submersion, which maps from almost contact metric manifolds to Riemannian manifolds. This concept serves as a generalization of several established submersions on Riemannian manifolds. We establish significant and sufficient conditions under which these submersions are totally geodesic and harmonic. Additionally, several examples are analyzed, specifically focusing on submersions equipped with a horizontal Reeb vector field.

In 2020, we monitored the Episodically Active Asteroid (6478) Gault using telescopes across Asia and North America and determined that it has ceased activity following its outbursts at the turn of 2018–2019. This dormant phase enabled us to derive its absolute magnitude as $H_r = 14.63 \pm 0.02$ and $G_r = 0.21 \pm 0.02$ through secular phasecurve observations. Furthermore, time-series photometric lightcurves collected over 17 hours across multiple days in August, September, and October 2020 allowed us to constrain Gault's rotation period. These lightcurves display a repeating feature with an amplitude of $\lesssim 0.05$ magnitude, indicating a rotation period of approximately 2.5 hours and a semi-spherical or top-like morphology, similar to the Near-Earth Asteroids Ryugu and Bennu. This ~2.5-hour period aligns closely with the critical rotation limit for an asteroid of Gault's physical properties, suggesting that its multi-epoch activity resulted from surface mass shedding driven by rapid rotation, which was likely spun up by the Yarkovsky-O'Keefe-Radzievskii-Paddack (YORP) effect.

Reconstructing 3D scenes—defined by object shapes and spatial arrangements—from 2D images is a critical task for robotics and graphics. Although recent progress has been made in inferring 3D geometry and layout from single images, most existing methods depend on expensive-to-acquire 3D ground truth for training. To address this, we introduce a method capable of predicting 3D shape and layout without any 3D supervision; instead, it utilizes multi-view images with only 2D labels, which are far easier to collect at scale. Extensive evaluations on the 3D Warehouse, Hypersim, and ScanNet datasets demonstrate that our approach effectively scales to large collections of realistic imagery and performs competitively against methods reliant on 3D ground truth. Furthermore, on Hypersim and ScanNet, where reliable 3D annotations are unavailable, our method surpasses supervised approaches trained on smaller, less diverse datasets.

The study of chiral-odd gluon transversity distributions offers a potential window into novel aspects of hadron physics. While recent advancements have significantly improved our understanding of quark transversity, no experimental data currently exists for gluon transversity. This phenomenon is absent in spin-1/2 nucleons but present in spin-1 deuterons; consequently, measuring it in deuterons allows physicists to probe hadronic physics beyond the simple proton-neutron bound state, as direct nucleon contributions are excluded. This discussion outlines how gluon transversity can be measured at hadron accelerators like Fermilab and NICA, alongside charged-lepton scattering experiments, using the cross sections of the proton-deuteron Drell-Yan process as a illustrative example.

Although communication aids coordination, excessive uncertainty can cause it to break down. I examine a scenario where vagueness-induced uncertainty prevents the public sharing of beliefs. I demonstrate that asserting an epistemic modal claim, such as "Might p," can expose a speaker's uncertainty, thereby enhancing coordination prospects even without a shared epistemic foundation. This offers a game-theoretic justification for epistemic modality. The proposed account integrates standard relational semantics for epistemic modality, Stalnaker's view of assertion as an informative update, and a Bayesian framework for handling uncertainty.

This study examines state preparation through postselected weak measurements within a three-wave mixing process. The analysis assumes the signal input mode is initialized as a vacuum, coherent, or squeezed vacuum state, while the idler input mode is a weak coherent state passing through a medium with second-order nonlinear susceptibility. Results demonstrate that detecting a single photon in one output channel of the idler beam prepares the signal output channel in a single-photon Fock state, a single-photon-added coherent state, or a single-photon-added squeezed vacuum state with high fidelity, contingent upon the initial signal states and adjustable parameters. Furthermore, the properties of these weak-measurement-based output states—including squeezing, signal amplification, second-order correlations, and Wigner functions—are analyzed. The proposed scheme offers a promising alternative and effective method for generating useful nonclassical states for quantum information processing.

Gravitational wave backgrounds introduce correlated noise into spatially separated detectors. This correlation causes statistical efficiency losses in real detector networks compared to idealized systems with independent noise. Assuming an isotropic background, we analyze these losses specifically regarding angularly averaged sensitivity curves, deriving straightforward formulas based on overlap reduction functions and the ratio of background noise power to instrumental noise. Furthermore, for future triangular interferometers like ET and LISA, we explore optimal network configurations designed to minimize these potential statistical penalties.

We introduce the inaugural coreset designed for clustering points in $\mathbb{R}^d$ that contain multiple missing coordinates, a capability absent in prior constructions which were limited to handling only a single missing coordinate. The primary difficulty in this scenario arises because objective functions, such as $k$-Means, are computed solely on the available (non-missing) coordinates, which differ from point to point. An $\epsilon$-coreset is defined as a compact, reweighted subset of a large dataset that approximates the clustering objective within a factor of $(1+\epsilon)$ for any potential set of cluster centers. Our proposed coresets for $k$-Means and $k$-Median clustering achieve a size of $(jk)^{O(\min(j,k))} (\epsilon^{-1} d \log n)^2$, where $n$ represents the number of data points, $d$ is the dimensionality, and $j$ denotes the maximum number of missing coordinates per point. Additionally, we present an algorithm capable of constructing these coresets in near-linear time, thereby enhancing a recent quadratic-time PTAS for $k$-Means with missing values [Eiben et al., SODA 2021] to near-linear efficiency. We empirically validate our importance sampling-based coreset construction, which is straightforward to implement, across various real-world datasets. Our approach demonstrates a flexible balance between coreset size and accuracy, consistently surpassing uniform-sampling baselines, and notably accelerates Lloyd's-style heuristics for $k$-Means involving missing values.

A ring possesses the $2$-nil-sum property when every element that is neither central nor a unit can be expressed as the sum of two nilpotents. We demonstrate that a ring has this property if and only if it is either a simple ring with the $2$-nil-sum property or a commutative local ring featuring a nil Jacobson radical, and we present an example of a non-commutative simple ring that satisfies the $2$-nil-sum property. Additionally, we establish that a simple right Goldie ring has the $2$-nil-sum property if and only if it is a field.

Real scalar fields exhibiting attractive self-interactions can form self-bound entities known as oscillons. These dense structures are prevalent in prominent theories regarding dark matter and inflation, with a specific focus on long-lived oscillons that persist beyond 14 billion years, providing significant astrophysical clues to the present era. We present a novel formalism for calculating oscillon properties with enhanced precision, utilizing it to examine their internal architecture and pinpoint the mechanisms driving their extended lifespans. Specifically, we demonstrate that applying realistic boundary conditions naturally favors a near-minimally radiating solution, with oscillon longevity emerging from its geometric configuration. Additionally, we establish a natural terminology for oscillon stability to forecast novel aspects of their evolution. This framework enables the development of efficient algorithms to investigate whether long-lived oscillons require fine-tuning and to what degree. Ultimately, we construct a set of potentials capable of supporting ultra-long-lived oscillons, with lifetimes exceeding $10^{17}$ years.
We present numerous examples of closed complex surfaces with diffeomorphism groups that are not simply-connected and include loops that are not homotopic to loops of symplectomorphisms.

Capturing depth information is critical for three-dimensional imaging, a field seeing rapid growth in applications such as autonomous driving and smartphone auto-focus. While Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) using Single-Photon Avalanche Diode (SPAD) arrays is an emerging high-speed depth imaging technology, it typically suffers from lower spatial resolution compared to conventional intensity cameras. To overcome this limitation, we propose a specialized deep network that leverages multiple features derived from camera histogram data to enhance the native resolution of depth images. Designed for dual-mode SPAD cameras that alternate between high-resolution intensity and low-resolution depth capture at high frame rates, this system requires no additional sensors. The network utilizes the captured intensity images and features extracted from downsampled histograms to guide the upsampling of depth data. Our approach delivers significant denoising and resolution improvements across diverse signal-to-noise ratios and photon levels. When applied to various 3D datasets, the method achieves a four-fold increase in depth resolution alongside effective noise reduction.

Visual place recognition (VPR) involves identifying previously visited locations based on visual data, a task for which numerous performance-enhancing methods have been proposed. Recently, multi-process fusion has gained traction as a strategy where various VPR techniques operate in parallel, merging their outputs to improve results. However, currently, there is no established standard for selecting and integrating these diverse methods from the broad array of available options. To our knowledge, this study is the first to systematically analyze the complementarity among state-of-the-art VPR approaches to determine which pairings yield superior performance. We introduce a defined framework that serves as a validation tool, employing a McNemar's test-like method to assess the complementarity between any two techniques. This framework calculates upper and lower bounds for complementarity alongside an estimate of the maximum achievable VPR performance. Using this approach, we present results from testing eight leading VPR methods across ten common datasets, demonstrating the potential of specific technique combinations to enhance overall performance.

The Daala project aims to rival the most advanced patent-encumbered video codecs by offering a royalty-free solution. A key component of our strategy involves substituting conventional codec components with alternative methods that prioritize perceptual quality over simple metrics like PSNR. This paper outlines our findings on the efficacy of these tools, detailing which succeeded and which failed. Additionally, we assess their compatibility with traditional codec architectures and present performance results within the Alliance for Open Media codec framework.

We have derived the full and independent sets of effective operators for mass dimensions 5 through 9 within both the $
u$SMEFT framework (Standard Model Effective Field Theory with light sterile right-handed neutrinos) and the $
u$LEFT framework (low-energy Effective Field Theory with light sterile neutrinos). These models offer systematic descriptions of all Lorentz-invariant physical effects involving Majorana or Dirac neutrinos, encompassing scenarios with or without lepton number violation. Specifically, in $
u$SMEFT, the counts of independent operators including sterile neutrinos are 2 (18), 29 (1614), 80 (4206), 323 (20400), and 1358 (243944) for dimensions 5, 6, 7, 8, and 9, respectively, corresponding to one (or three) fermion generations. In contrast, the $
u$LEFT theory yields 24, 5223, 3966, 25425, and 789426 independent operators for the same dimensions.

This study investigates faint, diffuse extended X-ray emission linked to radio lobes and the hot intracluster medium (ICM) gas within a sample of radio galaxies. Utilizing shallow archival Chandra observations (approximately 10 ks) for 60 radio galaxies—comprising 7 FR I and 53 FR II types with redshifts ranging from 0.0222 to 1.785 selected from the 3CR catalog—we applied Bayesian statistics to detect asymmetries in X-ray emission between regions containing radio lobes and those containing ICM gas. In the Chandra broadband range (0.5–7.0 keV), characterized by the highest detected flux and signal-to-noise ratio, we determined that non-thermal X-ray emission from radio lobes dominates the thermal emission from the surrounding environment for roughly 77% of the sources. Additionally, we observed that the relative intensity of on-axis non-thermal emission from the lobes increases with redshift compared to off-axis thermal emission from the environment. These findings suggest that the primary mechanism for non-thermal X-ray emission in radio lobes is inverse Compton upscattering of cosmic microwave background (CMB) seed photons by relativistic electrons; this process yields an observed flux that remains roughly constant with redshift because the increasing CMB energy density offsets the effects of distance.

We examine the general characteristics of thermal relic freezeout. By providing analytic estimates for relic abundance across arbitrary freezeout scenarios, we identify the conditions under which instantaneous freezeout applies and detail corrections for slow freezeout processes. These findings extend the relationship between dark matter mass and coupling required to match observed abundance, encompassing established cases like WIMPs, SIMPs, coannihilation, coscattering, inverse decays, and forbidden channels while generalizing beyond them. Consequently, we derive an approximate perturbative unitarity bound on dark matter mass for any thermal freezeout. We demonstrate that extending beyond the maximal masses permitted by dark matter self-annihilation (WIMP-like scenarios where $m_{\rm DM}\gg\mathcal{O}(100~\rm TeV)$) implies the existence of nearly degenerate states and generic metastability for dark matter. Furthermore, we show that thermal relic freezeout mechanisms can accommodate dark matter masses as high as the Planck scale.

This study examines the linear evolution of matter perturbations using a specific projected massive gravity model that eliminates the Boulware-Deser ghost and maintains global Lorentz symmetry. Our results indicate that at subhorizon scales, alterations to linear growth are significantly suppressed, even in the absence of nonlinear screening for extra forces. Furthermore, by analyzing distance and redshift space distortion data, we derive observational limits and identify a parameter space that satisfies both theoretical requirements and empirical constraints.

This paper introduces an automated approach for generating training datasets tailored to deep convolutional neural networks designed for playing card detection. The method eliminates the need for time-intensive manual image collection and object labeling. When the YOLOv4 network was trained on this synthetically generated dataset, it achieved a detection accuracy of 99.8%. This proposed solution is a component of a broader initiative to automate the broadcasting of duplicate bridge tournaments using computer vision and neural networks.

This study examines video streaming within telecommunication networks, considering the significant shift toward network virtualization. It will illustrate the significance and potential of volumetric media delivery through specific examples. Subsequently, the paper will address the optimal design for management platforms supporting volumetric media, along with associated challenges and potential solutions. Finally, an overview of current research hurdles and prospects will be provided to foster future collaborative efforts in this domain.

This study investigates the impact of stochastic resetting to random locations on the first passage times and Shannon entropy of a Brownian particle. We examine distinct entropy regimes, specifically the \textit{externally-driven}, \textit{zero-entropy}, and \textit{Maxwell demon} scenarios, demonstrating that the minimum mean first passage time (MFPT) can occur within any of these. We introduce a new analytical approach to calculate the MFPT, the mean first passage number of resets (MFPNR), and the mean first passage entropy (MFPE) when the particle resets to positions drawn from \textit{a priori} known distributions. Our analysis highlights the interaction between the second moment of the reset position distribution and the reset rate, detailing their influence on both MFPT and MFPE. Furthermore, we propose a mechanism where the entropy per reset falls into either the \textit{Maxwell demon} or \textit{externally driven} category, while the total mean first passage entropy aligns with the \textit{zero-entropy} regime. We also identify an overlap between the dynamic phase space and the entropy phase space. Applying this method to a generalized Evans-Majumdar model, we assume random resets sampled from a Gaussian distribution and explore \textit{toggling resets}, where the reset position depends on the reset parity. All findings are consistent with numerical simulations.

Medical imaging datasets often suffer from domain shift caused by differences in scanner manufacturers and imaging protocols, which undermines the generalization capabilities of machine learning models. Domain generalization (DG), designed to train models on multiple source domains for effective performance on unseen test domains, holds significant promise for the medical imaging field. To achieve DG, recent model-agnostic meta-learning (MAML) has been adopted to transfer knowledge from prior training tasks to aid in learning new testing tasks. However, clinical settings typically provide only a limited number of annotated source domains, restricting the diversity of training tasks and heightening the risk of overfitting within this framework. This paper introduces a novel DG approach for medical image classification that combines episodic training with task augmentation. Leveraging meta-learning, we establish a paradigm where knowledge transfer occurs from simulated episodic training tasks to real-world DG testing tasks. Addressing the scarcity of source domains in practical medical deployments, we specifically target task-level overfitting and propose task augmentation to increase variety during training task generation, thereby mitigating this issue. Furthermore, utilizing the proposed learning framework, we introduce a new meta-objective to regularize the deep embeddings of training domains. To demonstrate the efficacy of this method, we conduct experiments on both histopathological and abdominal CT images.

This paper presents seven continued fraction formulae, derived using the MC-algorithm, each consisting of products and quotients of three gamma functions with three parameters; one of these extends Entry 34 from Chapter 12 of Ramanujan's second notebook. Rigorous proofs for five of these results are established via the Bauer-Muir transformation, a process that critically relies on applying the transformation twice with distinct nonlinear modifying factors.

This study explores the behavior of the trailing digits of tetration with a general base. Specifically, the final digits stabilize after a certain hyper-exponent, and determining them involves calculating expressions modulo $10^n$. Surprisingly, though unproven, I conjecture that this repetition relies on the base's residue modulo 10 and a specific representation of that base. The following discussion presents results, tables, and examples to substantiate this hypothesis. We are close to proving a formula that identifies the minimum hyper-exponent $u$ for a generic base $q$, such that the last $n$ digits of the tetration remain constant from the $u$-th level onward.

On August 17, 2017, the LIGO-Virgo Collaboration (LVC) identified an extraordinary gravitational-wave (GW) event that occurred within approximately 1.7 seconds of the GRB 170817A detected by Fermi-GBM and INTEGRAL. This event aligns with a neutron star-neutron star (NS-NS) merger, which was later followed by a radio/optical/X-ray transient. This study presents the primary findings from the AGILE satellite's observations of the GW170817 localization region and its electromagnetic counterpart. At the moment of LVC detection ($T_0$), the Earth blocked the view of the GW170817 localization region; however, the AGILE instrument gathered valuable data both before and after the event due to its spinning observation mode, which scans sources multiple times hourly. The first exposure of the region by the gamma-ray imaging detector (GRID) commenced roughly 935 seconds post-$T_0$. Across repeated exposures spanning minutes, hours, and days surrounding the GW170817 event, no significant X-ray or gamma-ray emission was detected from the region, even when incorporating data from the Mini-calorimeter and Super-AGILE instruments. These measurements represent some of the earliest space-based observations of GW170817 and offer critical constraints on the precursor and delayed emission characteristics of the NS-NS coalescence. With high confidence, we rule out the presence of an X-ray/gamma-ray emitting magnetar-like object possessing a large magnetic field of $10^{15} \, \rm G$. Our findings hold particular significance for understanding the early evolutionary phase of the electromagnetic remnant.

Fiber nonlinearities cause crosstalk in wavelength division multiplexed (WDM) systems, thereby restricting system capacity as transmitted power rises. In a WDM network, a user is defined as an entity operating at a specific optical wavelength. Conventionally, WDM channel capacity is evaluated by assuming various signal models for other users and treating their resulting interference as noise. This paper, however, adopts a multiuser information-theoretic perspective, modeling the dispersion- and cross-phase modulation-impaired optical WDM system as an interference channel. We derive an outer bound on the capacity region of simultaneously achievable rate pairs using a simplified K-user perturbative model and genie-aided techniques. Additionally, we obtain an achievable rate region through time-sharing among specific single-user strategies. Results demonstrate that this time-sharing approach yields superior rate tuples compared to treating nonlinear interference as noise. Specifically, for a single-polarization, single-span system with a launch power 4.4 dB above the optimum, treating nonlinear interference as noise achieves a rate of 1.67 bit/sym, whereas time-sharing achieves 6.33 bit/sym.

Hyperentangled Bell state analysis (HBSA) serves as a critical component for specific hyper-parallel quantum information processing tasks. We introduce a fully deterministic and complete HBSA protocol utilizing the spatial and polarization degrees of freedom of a two-photon system, enhanced by a fixed-frequency entangled resource and a time interval degree of freedom. In this scheme, parity information from both spatial and polarization hyper-entanglement is distinguished via distinct photon pair time intervals, while phase information is identified through detection signatures. Unlike prior approaches, incorporating the time interval degree of freedom reduces the number of required auxiliary entanglements from two to one. Furthermore, the added frequency and time interval degrees of freedom exhibit greater resilience against collective channel noise.

Condensed matter physics involves both fermionic and bosonic quasiparticles. However, due to the constraints of the Fermi level, ideal electronic materials exhibiting emergent particles with higher-dimensional degeneracy manifolds, such as nodal lines or surfaces, have yet to be discovered. This study reveals that first-principles calculations and symmetry analysis confirm that the realistic ternary nitride Li$_6$WN$_4$ possesses ideal, nearly flat nodal-surface and nodal-line structures within its phonon spectra. These degeneracies exhibit a lantern-like geometry, a feature guaranteed by nonsymmorphic symmetry. The associated topological phonon surface state occupies precisely half of the surface Brillouin zone, distinguishing it from the states found in conventional nodal-line and nodal-surface semimetals. Consequently, these findings establish the presence of ideal lantern-like phonons in actual materials, thereby expanding the classification of topological quantum phases and offering a robust foundation for exploring the interplay between nodal-line and nodal-surface phonons within a single substance.

Real-time PCR, also known as quantitative PCR (qPCR), serves as a robust method for quantifying nucleic acids. However, due to the complexity of the reaction system and its thermal cycling, accurately deriving initial nucleic acid concentrations from fluorescence data has long been a source of confusion. Despite numerous proposed algorithmic improvements, the classical threshold method remains the standard for routine applications. In this study, we first reconstruct the PCR process using stochastic simulations to demonstrate the origin of the linear relationship between the threshold value and the logarithm of the initial nucleic acid quantity. Subsequently, we introduce a novel method for the absolute quantification of nucleic acids via qPCR. By tracking fluorescence signal fluctuations at every stage of the thermal cycle, we calculate a representation of step-wise efficiency variations. This represents the first work to determine PCR efficiency changes directly from fluorescence signals, bypassing the need for curve fitting or complex analysis. Our findings indicate that efficiency fluctuations during PCR are intricate and cannot be adequately modeled by simple monotonic functions. Utilizing the calculated efficiency, we present a new absolute qPCR analysis technique for precise nucleic acid determination, which entirely circumvents the efficiency problem.

We investigate an entanglement harvesting scheme involving two Unruh-deWitt detectors existing in quantum superpositions of static paths within both static de Sitter and thermal Minkowski spacetimes. For the first time, we show that placing each detector in a spatial superposition enables entanglement extraction from the quantum field in scenarios where it remains impossible for detectors following classical trajectories. Remarkably, for detectors on sufficiently delocalized paths immersed in a thermal bath, the harvested entanglement increases with field temperature, thereby contradicting the no-go theorem established by Simidzija et al. (Phys. Rev. D 98, 085007). Additionally, we identify intriguing phenomena regarding mutual information harvesting, which exhibits a strong dependence on the nonlocal correlations between the superposed trajectories of the respective detectors.

We examine how spatially correlated noise influences the velocities of self-propelled particles. While correlations in random forces acting on these particles can trigger directed collective motion, such as swarming, strong correlations in fluctuations can locally align velocities even when repulsive coupling favors disorder, resulting in a macroscopic, turbulent velocity field. Conversely, although this noise aligns velocities locally, the transition to globally directed swarming is suppressed when the noise correlation length is nonzero but smaller than the system size. We investigate this swarming transition in $d$-dimensional space using a mean-field model of globally coupled velocity vectors.

Consider the polynomial ring $S=K[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ over a field $K$. A $t$-spread lexsegment ideal $I$ is defined as a monomial ideal generated by a $t$-spread lexsegment set. This study identifies all $t$-spread lexsegment ideals possessing a linear resolution through the utilization of Betti splittings. As practical applications, we derive explicit formulas for the Betti numbers of this specific class of ideals and characterize all incompletely $t$-spread lexsegment ideals that exhibit linear quotients.

This work presents a theoretical investigation into the collective quantum dynamics of interacting superconducting qubit arrays (SQAs) subject to frequency disorder. Interactions are mediated either by mutual inductive coupling between neighboring qubits (short-range Ising interaction) or via coupling to a low-dissipation resonator (long-range exchange interaction). Without interactions, the Fourier transform of the temporal correlation function of the total polarization (the dynamic susceptibility, $C(\omega)$) exhibits a series of sharp, low-magnitude resonances corresponding to individual qubit transitions. We demonstrate that even weak inter-qubit interactions can surpass the effects of disorder, leading to the simultaneous emergence of collective excited states. This collective phenomenon appears as a single, prominent resonance in $C(\omega)$. When a weak, non-resonant microwave photon field is present in the resonator, the locations of the dominant resonances shift depending on the photon number, illustrating the collective AC Stark effect. Furthermore, coupling an SQA to a transmission line facilitates direct experimental observation of these collective states through microwave transmission and enables the use of SQAs as sensitive single-photon detectors.

Dissemination of misinformation and fake news poses a worldwide threat that hinders advancements in democracy and public health. While previous studies have primarily targeted the semantic content and media sources of such news, our research focuses on identifying individuals prone to sharing fake news by analyzing the language of various participants within the fake-news ecosystem, including sharers, fact-checkers, and random users, to build a linguistic profile. We found that both fake-news and fact-check sharers utilize significantly more high-arousal negative emotions; however, fake-news sharers uniquely exhibit higher existentially-based needs. Integrating these psycholinguistic cues, derived from their tweets, into a model based on socio-demographic factors substantially enhances the accuracy of classifying fake-news sharers. This study demonstrates that while fake-news sharers differ from other ecosystem actors regarding existential needs, they share similarities in other areas, such as anger levels, underscoring the necessity of examining the entire ecosystem to improve identification and prediction accuracy. Ultimately, our approach can assist in mitigating the spread of fake news by allowing platforms to proactively screen posts from potential sharers.

We re-examine total variation denoising by investigating an augmented framework that incorporates an available estimate of the image gradient. Our findings demonstrate that this approach enhances reconstruction quality, revealing that the resulting model aligns with total generalized variation (TGV) denoising, thereby offering a novel justification for its use. Additionally, we introduce a constrained denoising model and develop a variational framework that is essentially parameter-free, meaning all parameters are derived directly from the noisy input. Furthermore, we apply Chambolle-Pock's primal-dual algorithm and the Douglas-Rachford method to these new models; the latter requires solving large-scale discretized partial differential equations. To address this, we propose an inexact solution strategy using the preconditioned conjugate gradient method and derive corresponding preconditioners. Numerical experiments confirm that the proposed method exhibits effective denoising performance and that preconditioning substantially accelerates convergence. Finally, we analyze the duality gap across various TGV denoising formulations to establish a straightforward stopping criterion.

Identifying the cutting edge of research remains a persistent hurdle across all disciplines; without consensus on what constitutes the state-of-the-art, reviewers cannot be satisfied and educators cannot effectively teach the forefront of their field. We introduce a new method to ascertain this state-of-the-art using a novel crowdsourced "reuse graph" approach. Compared to other community monitoring techniques, such as artifact tracks or citation-based searches, our reuse graphs are significantly easier to construct and validate. An analysis of 170 papers from 2020 software engineering conferences revealed more than 1,600 instances of reuse, demonstrating that it is pervasive in SE research. Previous skepticism regarding the scarcity of reuse in this field likely stemmed from employing inappropriate methods to measure irrelevant metrics.

We examine the indistinguishability of single photons extracted from collective Rydberg excitations within cold atomic ensembles. These Rydberg spin waves are generated via either off-resonant two-photon excitation to the Rydberg state or through Rydberg electromagnetically induced transparency (EIT). To evaluate photon indistinguishability, we conduct Hong-Ou-Mandel interference experiments, comparing the single photons against weak coherent states. Our analysis of indistinguishability across various detection windows reveals that photons produced by off-resonant excitation achieve high indistinguishability, ranging from 89% for the full waveform to 98% with narrow detection windows. Similarly, we present the first investigation into the indistinguishability of photons generated via Rydberg EIT, finding that their values are lower than those obtained from off-resonant excitation. These findings are significant for the application of Rydberg atoms as nodes in quantum networks.

This study introduces a generalized natural inflation (GNI) framework to investigate axion-like particle (ALP) inflation and dark matter (DM). Distinct from standard natural inflation, the GNI model incorporates two extra parameters, $(n_1, n_2)$, which enhance its generality. Specifically, $n_1$ establishes a link between GNI and other ALP inflation models, while $n_2$ regulates the inflaton's mass. By adhering to constraints from cosmic microwave background and other cosmological observations, the model demonstrates that small-field inflation is feasible across a broad mass spectrum, and within specific parameter regions, the ALP inflaton can act as a viable dark matter candidate.

Recent systematic studies have established that model checking for Halpern and Shoham's interval temporal logic (HS) is decidable under three different semantics. This paper specifically examines the trace-based semantics, where infinite execution paths derived from finite Kripke structures serve as the primary semantic units. In this framework, intervals correspond to finite segments of traces, and a proposition is valid over an interval only if it holds for every state within it (the homogeneity assumption). We propose parametric HS (PHS), a quantitative extension of HS over traces that enables the expression of parametric timing constraints regarding interval durations. We demonstrate that both model checking—determining if a Kripke structure satisfies a PHS formula under some parameter valuation—and satisfiability—verifying if a PHS formula has a trace model under the homogeneity assumption—are decidable. Furthermore, we identify a fragment of PHS that encompasses parametric LTL, for which both model checking and satisfiability are proven to be EXPSPACE-complete.

The ability to slow or halt electromagnetic (EM) waves has garnered significant research interest due to its promising applications in energy storage, optical buffering, and nonlinearity enhancement. Nevertheless, conventional EM wave trapping methods often fail to achieve true confinement because of unavoidable reflections. This paper introduces a novel metal-semiconductor-semiconductor-metal (MSSM) structure and demonstrates, through theoretical analysis and numerical simulations, a genuine rainbow trapping effect within a tapered MSSM model operating at terahertz frequencies. Furthermore, functional devices including optical buffers, switches, and filters are realized based on this truly trapped rainbow phenomenon. Leveraging the one-way propagation characteristic of these structures, the resulting high-performance optical devices are anticipated for integration into optical circuits.

Irrotational flow is characterized by the second-order elliptic partial differential equation $E^2\psi=0$, where $\psi$ represents the function to be determined and $E^2$ denotes the Stokes operator. This paper derives solutions for this equation within three axisymmetric coordinate systems: parabolic, tangent sphere, and cardioid. We demonstrate that while the Stokes equation allows for variable separation in parabolic coordinates, it undergoes R-separation in the tangent sphere and cardioid systems. Finally, the manuscript summarizes all established results regarding the 0-eigenspace of $E^2$ across these axisymmetric coordinate frameworks.

Although node embeddings are highly effective for network analysis, their full application to node clustering remains underutilized. Most current state-of-the-art methods for signed networks prioritize link sign prediction, and existing clustering approaches typically do not utilize graph neural networks (GNNs). To address this, we present SSSNET, a novel GNN framework designed for semi-supervised clustering of signed networks. SSSNET employs a new probabilistic balanced normalized cut loss to train nodes and operates as an end-to-end system that integrates embedding generation and clustering without intermediate steps, prioritizing node clustering while accounting for polarization effects. Our primary innovation reinterprets social balance theory for signed network embeddings; whereas standard heuristics assume that "an enemy's enemy is a friend," our approach maintains a neutral stance on this relationship. Experiments across various datasets—including synthetic signed stochastic block models, polarized variations, and real-world data at different scales—demonstrate that SSSNET achieves performance comparable to or better than state-of-the-art spectral clustering methods across diverse noise and sparsity levels. Furthermore, SSSNET enhances existing methodologies by enabling the incorporation of exogenous information, such as node-level features or labels.

This study examines the $f$-mode oscillations of hyperon stars containing dark matter using the relativistic Cowling approximation. Macroscopic properties are derived from relativistic mean-field equations of state, assuming dark matter resides within the stellar interior. We compute $f$-mode frequencies for the $l=2$ mode using four distinct neutron star equations of state. Furthermore, we analyze the impacts of various configurations—specifically those with hyperons alone, dark matter alone, or both—on $f$-mode oscillations by varying astrophysical parameters such as mass ($M$), radius ($R$), compactness ($M/R$), surface redshift ($Z_s$), mean density ($\bar{\rho}$), and dimensionless tidal deformability ($\Lambda$). Our results reveal significant variations in $f$-mode frequencies depending on the presence of hyperons and/or dark matter. Additionally, we identify strong correlations between canonical frequencies and $\Lambda$ ($f_{1.4}-\Lambda_{1.4}$) as well as between maximum frequencies and the canonical $\Lambda$ ($f_{max}-\Lambda_{1.4}$).

This paper revisits the identification strategy proposed by Kirkeboen et al. (2016), which demonstrates how combining instruments for multiple unordered treatments with individual treatment rankings can yield identification even in the presence of observed and unobserved heterogeneity in treatment effects. We demonstrate that the core assumptions of their identification argument have testable implications and provide a new characterization of the bias resulting from assumption violations. Collectively, these findings enable researchers to test underlying assumptions and assess whether any resulting biases are economically significant. Motivated by these insights, we estimate and compare the earnings returns to post-secondary fields of study in Norway and Denmark. In both countries, we apply Kirkeboen et al.'s (2016) identification strategy using data on individual field rankings and field-specific instruments derived from admission system discontinuities. We empirically investigate the nature and causes of differences in field payoffs across the two nations. Our results reveal a strong cross-country correlation in field payoffs, particularly after excluding fields that violate the assumptions required for identification.

This study establishes a novel, robust Gaussian approximation bound for sums of independent random vectors. By leveraging optimal transport theory, the method provides \textit{explicit} relationships regarding both the dimensionality $p$ and the sample size $n$. These dependencies define a new fundamental threshold for practical applications within statistical learning theory. Specifically, utilizing this bound, we demonstrate distributional approximation for the maximum norm in high-dimensional scenarios where $p > n$.

Considering two Riemannian manifolds $(B,g_B)$ and $(F,g_F)$, we establish harmonicity criteria for vector fields on the Riemannian warped product $B\times_fF$, where $f:B \longrightarrow ]0,+\infty[$, by employing a specific variational condition. Subsequently, we apply these results to the scenario where $B=\mathbb{R}$ and $F$ is a three-dimensional connected Riemannian Lie group $G$ endowed with a left-invariant metric, aiming to identify harmonic vector fields on $\mathbb{R}\times_fG$. We present examples of harmonic vector fields on $G$ that are not left-invariant and characterize harmonic vector fields on $\mathbb{R}\times_fG$. Finally, we provide instances of vector fields on $\mathbb{R}\times_fG$ that function as harmonic maps.

We introduce and investigate two novel forms of "effective resistance" derived from hubs-biased models of network navigation, specifically those where hubs attract or repel the traversal. We demonstrate that these resistance measures correspond to squared Euclidean distances between graph vertices and can be formulated using the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse of the respective hubs-biased Laplacian matrices. Furthermore, we define analogues of Kirchhoff indices based on these new resistance distances and establish several theorems regarding them through the spectral properties of the associated Laplacians. Following extensive computational analysis, we conjecture an ordering of Kirchhoff indices: the one based on hubs-repelling resistance is greater than or equal to that based on standard resistance, which in turn is greater than or equal to the one based on hubs-attracting resistance. Additionally, we note that in real-world brain and neural systems, standard random walks exhibit efficiency comparable to hubs-attracting schemes, whereas infrastructure and modular software networks appear optimized for navigation via their hubs.

Twinkle represents the inaugural entry in a cost-effective series of small satellites managed and funded by Blue Skies Space Ltd., emphasizing the use of commercial off-the-shelf parts. Built upon a highly proven Airbus platform, the satellite hosts a 0.45-meter telescope and a spectrometer capable of capturing simultaneous spectral data across the 0.5–4.5 $\mu$m range. Airbus Stevenage leads as the prime contractor for the spacecraft, with the telescope developed by Airbus Toulouse and the spectrometer by ABB Canada. Designed to enter a thermally stable, sun-synchronous low-Earth orbit, Twinkle is scheduled to commence scientific operations in 2025 with a minimum operational lifespan of seven years. During its initial three-year phase, the mission will execute two major survey programs: one targeting Solar System objects and the other focusing on exoplanets. This paper outlines the mission's architecture, highlights refinements in the design methodology, and explores key scientific themes related to the extrasolar survey.

This paper provides a comprehensive review of observations regarding the stellar longitudinal (effective) magnetic field ($B_e$) and its characteristics. It further examines current perspectives on the genesis, development, and internal structure of $B_e$.

We present BiLQ, an iterative approach for solving general square linear systems $Ax = b$ that utilizes the Lanczos biorthogonalization process grounded in least-norm subproblems, serving as a natural counterpart to BiCG and QMR. While the iterates generated by BiCG, CGS, and BiCGSTAB may fail to exist if the tridiagonal projection of $A$ is singular, BiLQ remains reliable for compatible systems even when $A$ is ill-conditioned or rank-deficient. Similar to the symmetric case, the BiCG residual is typically smaller than the BiLQ residual, and an inexpensive transfer to a BiCG iterate is feasible when it exists. Although the Euclidean norm of the BiLQ error is generally non-monotonic, it exhibits monotonicity in a specific norm determined by the Lanczos vectors; a comparable property is established for the QMR residual. BiLQ integrates with QMR to leverage two initial vectors, enabling the simultaneous solution of a system and its adjoint at a computational cost similar to applying either method individually. We also derive analogous combinations of USYMLQ and USYMQR based on the orthogonal tridiagonalization process, resulting in methods named BiLQR and TriLQR, which can estimate integral functionals involving both primal and adjoint solutions. When compared against Minres-qlp on a related augmented system that demands comparable work and storage, our experiments demonstrate that BiLQR achieves earlier termination than both TriLQR and MINRES-QLP regarding the residual and error for both the primal and adjoint systems.

A prevalent method in semantic parsing involves enhancing sequence-to-sequence models by incorporating retrieved training samples, known as exemplars. However, the efficacy of this technique is constrained by the capacity to identify informative exemplars that facilitate accurate parsing, a challenge that intensifies in low-resource scenarios. While current retrieval strategies typically rely on input similarity between queries and exemplars, we introduce GandR, a procedure that selects exemplars based on the similarity of their outputs. GandR operates in two stages: it first produces a preliminary prediction using input-based retrieval, then retrieves exemplars with outputs similar to this prediction to generate a final result. This approach establishes a new state-of-the-art performance across several low-resource semantic parsing tasks.

Heterogeneity has long been a defining characteristic of distributed computing. However, with the rising adoption of accelerators like GPUs and TPUs, alongside domain-specific computing through ASICs and FPGAs, managing and leveraging this diversity has become an increasingly critical challenge. While harnessing heterogeneity is a well-established problem in distributed systems, empirically evaluating heterogeneous machines using real-world infrastructure from public cloud providers is often prohibitively expensive and time-consuming due to the need to test various applications, objectives, and workload intensities. To address this, we present E2C, an open-source simulation tool designed to enable researchers and practitioners to analyze diverse heterogeneous computing systems and assess their performance across different configurations. E2C features an intuitive graphical user interface (GUI) that allows users to rapidly and cost-free explore system-level solutions such as scheduling, load balancing, and scalability within a controlled environment. Key capabilities of E2C include: (i) simulating heterogeneous computing environments; (ii) integrating and testing new scheduling algorithms; (iii) tracking energy consumption and other performance metrics; and (iv) providing robust visualization to facilitate learning for students. This tool is intended for undergraduate and graduate students in computer science and engineering, as well as researchers and industry professionals.

Recent research has highlighted interpretable transformations within the latent spaces of generative adversarial networks (GANs) that reliably alter generated images. However, current methods for discovering these transformations depend on either a static set of predefined visual concepts or unsupervised disentanglement approaches, the latter of which lack a known alignment with human perceptions of salience. This paper presents a novel method for constructing open-ended vocabularies of primitive visual concepts embedded in a GAN's latent space. The approach integrates three key components: (1) automatically detecting perceptually salient directions through their layer selectivity; (2) having humans annotate these directions using free-form, compositional natural language; and (3) decomposing these annotations into a visual concept vocabulary comprising distilled directions labeled with single words. Experimental results demonstrate that the concepts derived via this method are both reliable and composable, generalizing across various classes, contexts, and observers while facilitating fine-grained manipulation of image style and content.

The proliferation of deepfake media is driven by accessible tools and mobile applications capable of producing realistic videos and images without demanding technical expertise. As this technology advances, both the volume and quality of deepfakes are projected to increase, potentially transforming them into a potent vehicle for spreading misinformation. Consequently, detection mechanisms have become essential. This study introduces a novel hybrid transformer network for deepfake video detection that incorporates an early feature fusion strategy. The architecture leverages two distinct CNNs—XceptionNet and EfficientNet-B4—as feature extractors, which are trained alongside the transformer in an end-to-end fashion using the FaceForensics++ and DFDC benchmarks. Despite its relatively simple design, the model achieves performance comparable to more complex state-of-the-art methods on these datasets. Furthermore, we introduce novel face cut-out and random cut-out augmentation techniques, demonstrating that they enhance detection accuracy and mitigate overfitting. Finally, we show that the proposed model can effectively learn from limited datasets.

This letter explores how non-Hermitian driving influences quantum coherence within a bipartite system. We find that dynamical localization, which is typically suppressed by Hermitian interactions, reappears under non-Hermitian driving, serving as proof that such driving restores quantum coherence. Furthermore, as the strength of non-Hermitian driving increases, entanglement between the two subsystems diminishes; this counterintuitive decay provides additional evidence that non-Hermitian driving protects quantum coherence. The underlying physics stems from the dominance of the quasieigenstate with the largest imaginary quasieigenvalue in governing the dynamics of non-Hermitian systems. This discovery outlines a restoration mechanism for quantum coherence in interacting, dissipative quantum systems, with significant relevance to experimental research spanning many-body physics to quantum information.

This work examines image sets associated with differentially $d$-uniform maps over finite fields. We establish a lower bound for the size of these image sets and analyze their preimage distributions by adapting techniques previously applied to planar maps. These findings are utilized to investigate $d$-uniform Dembowski-Ostrom polynomials, with particular attention given to APN maps defined on binary fields. We demonstrate that APN maps possessing the minimal possible image size necessarily exhibit a highly specific preimage distribution. Furthermore, we prove that for even $n$, the image sets of various well-known families of APN maps achieve this minimum. We also establish connections between the image sets of specialized maps and their Walsh spectra, specifically showing that the classical Walsh spectrum observed in several large classes of APN maps can be attributed to the minimality of their image sets. Finally, we provide upper bounds regarding the image size of APN maps.

Solving Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (POMDPs) remains notoriously difficult. Current state-of-the-art online solvers primarily rely on Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS), which quickly identifies the most promising branches of the belief tree while bypassing suboptimal areas. However, most of these algorithms assume direct access to state rewards and treat belief-dependent rewards merely as the expected value of state rewards. Consequently, they fail to address the more complex and critical scenario of belief-dependent rewards, such as differential entropy approximated via weighted belief particles. This information-theoretic reward structure imposes a heavy computational load. To address this, we integrate a simplification paradigm into MCTS by introducing the Simplified Information-Theoretic Particle Filter Tree (SITH-PFT). This novel variant handles information-theoretic rewards without requiring their full calculation. Instead of computing these expensive rewards directly, we employ adaptive upper and lower bounds that are computationally inexpensive and tightened only as needed by the algorithm. Crucially, our method guarantees that the resulting belief tree and solution are identical to those produced by standard MCTS using explicit reward calculations. Furthermore, our approach is highly general; any algorithm capable of converging to these reward bounds can be easily incorporated to achieve significant speedups without sacrificing performance.

Time reversal symmetry allows for a non-linear Hall effect in systems lacking inversion symmetry, with Weyl semimetals serving as key candidates for observing these signals. This study examines the Berry curvature-induced second and third-order Hall effects in multi-Weyl semimetals characterized by topological charges $n = 1, 2, 3$. Utilizing low-energy effective models, we derive general analytical expressions and identify a significant Berry curvature dipole within these materials.
