Additionally, our analysis of a realistic tight-binding lattice model reveals two distinct variations in the Berry curvature dipole as the topological charge increases, stemming from different underlying Berry curvature components. We provide experimental estimates for the second harmonic of the Hall signal in multi-Weyl semimetals and predict the emergence of a third-order Hall signal. By deriving analytical expressions for the Berry connection polarizability tensor via a low-energy model and estimating the resulting measurable conductivity, our work aims to facilitate the experimental discovery of Berry curvature multipole physics in multi-Weyl semimetals.

The paper introduces double groupoids, along with their corresponding double Lie algebroids and characteristic distributions, as a framework for analyzing and describing continuous media endowed with two distinct constitutive or geometric structures. It proposes several metrics to quantify the misalignment and non-uniformity that can emerge when merging two individually uniform structures, while also introducing and demonstrating the notion of coupled symmetries.

Recent experiments have shown that suspended carbon nanotubes can generate coherent mechanical oscillations when driven by an electric current exceeding a specific voltage threshold, a process analogous to lasing. This study examines the phenomenon through the lens of work extraction, modeling the nano-electromechanical system as a quantum flywheel or battery that transforms electrical power into stored mechanical energy. We present a microscopic model that aligns qualitatively with experimental results and calculate the Wigner function for the quantum vibrational mode within its non-equilibrium steady state. Furthermore, we characterize the threshold for self-sustained oscillations using two methods from non-equilibrium quantum thermodynamics: ergotropy and non-equilibrium free energy. Our analysis reveals that ergotropy acts as an order parameter for the phonon lasing transition. The work extraction framework we utilize is general and applicable to a broad range of other mesoscopic quantum devices.

Machine learning has found numerous applications in recent years, yet its role in information and network security is not a new development. Both machine learning and cryptography share significant similarities, most notably in handling vast datasets and navigating extensive search spaces. As a dynamic field with immense application potential, machine learning has been extensively studied. Over the last thirty years, both supervised and unsupervised techniques have been utilized in cryptographic algorithms, cryptanalysis, steganography, and various other data security contexts. This paper offers an updated survey of machine learning applications within cryptography and cryptanalysis, summarizing existing research and proposing directions for future studies.

This paper introduces efficient sampling-based algorithms to forecast the winner of district-based elections, where a voting rule $r$ determines district winners, and the overall election winner is the candidate securing the most districts. Specifically, for plurality voting with a known margin of victory of at least $\varepsilon$ relative to the total population, we propose an algorithm with a sample complexity of $\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{\varepsilon^4}\log \frac{1}{\varepsilon}\log\frac{1}{\delta}\right)$. We also establish a lower bound, proving that any algorithm within a natural class requires at least $\Omega\left(\frac{1}{\varepsilon^4}\log\frac{1}{\delta}\right)$ samples for the same task. These findings are extended to arbitrary voting rules $r$, demonstrating that predicting the district-based winner incurs an additional overhead of $\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{\varepsilon^2}\log\frac{1}{\delta}\right)$ compared to predicting a single-district winner under $r$. Furthermore, we address the scenario where the margin of victory is unknown but only two candidates are present. We also analyze the median voting rule under single-peaked preferences, showing that the winner can be predicted using $\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{\varepsilon^4}\log\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\log\frac{1}{\delta}\right)$ samples, regardless of whether the harmonious orders across districts are known or identical. Finally, we present results on estimating the margin of victory for district-based elections within both additive and multiplicative error bounds.

Steganography algorithms enable secret communication between a source and a destination by embedding messages or data into images and videos without altering their visual appearance. Steganalysis, conversely, is the discipline dedicated to detecting whether such hidden content exists within an image. Given the vast array of steganography methods, each requiring a unique analytical approach, developing an effective detection process is highly complex. Consequently, researchers strive to create a universal steganalysis capable of identifying both known and unknown steganographic techniques in real-time. This universal approach relies on extracting numerous features to differentiate stego images from cover images. However, this surge in features triggers the "curse of dimensionality" (CoD), an NP-hard issue that complicates real-time steganalysis. Furthermore, large feature sets generate extensive datasets that hinder machine learning from producing optimal models, while the time required to train these models renders real-time processing unfeasible for time-sensitive domains like visual computing. Potential remedies for CoD include deep learning and evolutionary algorithms, which can surmount the limitations of traditional machine learning. This study examines existing evolutionary algorithms designed to enhance real-time image processing, positing that they offer the most viable solutions to the CoD challenge.

This study evaluated the efficacy and user acceptance of three external interaction modalities—visual, auditory, and combined visual-auditory—in enhancing communication between automated vehicle systems (AVS) and pedestrians at crosswalks. An online survey involving 68 participants assessed preferences regarding safety, comfort, trust, understandability, usability, and overall acceptance. Findings indicated that the combined visual-auditory modality was the most favored, surpassing the visual-only and auditory-only options. Additionally, testing various specific methods revealed that a "pedestrian silhouette displayed on the front of the vehicle" was the most preferred visual cue. While "Chime" was generally favored over other auditory options, it was notably more popular among middle-aged participants than younger ones. Furthermore, communicating AVS intentions via pedestrians' smartphones was poorly received due to privacy concerns. These insights offer critical design recommendations for optimizing visual and auditory combinations to improve how AVS convey their intentions to pedestrians.

Current research on Intelligent Reflecting Surfaces (IRS) primarily focuses on their deployment in the environment to dynamically adjust wireless channels between base stations (BS) and users. In contrast, this paper introduces a novel integrated IRS-BS architecture by placing IRS units within the BS antenna radome. Because the distance between these integrated IRSs and the BS antenna array is minimal, inter-component path loss is greatly diminished, facilitating easier real-time control of IRS reflections by the BS. However, this proximity creates a significantly distinct near-field channel model. Consequently, we propose an element-wise channel model for the IRS to characterize the channel vector between each user antenna and the BS antenna array, encompassing direct paths as well as single and double IRS-reflected components. We then formulate an optimization problem to maximize the uplink sum rate by adjusting the reflection coefficients of all IRS elements. Addressing two scenarios with and without perfect Channel State Information (CSI) at the BS, the problem is solved efficiently using the successive refinement method and the iterative random phase algorithm (IRPA), respectively. Numerical results confirm that the integrated IRS-BS architecture achieves substantial capacity gains compared to conventional multi-antenna BSs without integrated IRS. Furthermore, the proposed algorithms significantly outperform benchmark schemes in terms of sum rate, and the IRPA without CSI approaches the performance upper bound of perfect CSI as training overhead increases.

Research has suggested that the decay of hypermagnetic helicity during electroweak symmetry breaking could have generated the Universe's observed baryon asymmetry via the chiral anomaly within the Standard Model. While a fully helical magnetic field capable of producing this asymmetry is insufficient to account for the intergalactic magnetic fields detected by the Fermi satellite, a combination of helical and nonhelical primordial fields might simultaneously explain both baryogenesis and these intergalactic fields. However, we demonstrate that this scenario is excluded by constraints on the amplitude of baryon isocurvature perturbations arising from primordial magnetic fields, which would otherwise lead to excessive deuterium production during big bang nucleosynthesis. Furthermore, we show that any mechanism attempting to generate intergalactic magnetic fields prior to electroweak symmetry breaking fails under these constraints, regardless of the specific helicity or baryogenesis process involved.

The substellar triple system VHS J125601.92$-$125723.9 consists of an equal-mass M7.5 brown dwarf binary paired with an L7 low-mass substellar companion. This study seeks to determine the source of radio emission from the central binary of VHS 1256$-$1257 and to explore the mechanisms governing radio emission in ultracool dwarfs (UCDs). Using the Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array, the European VLBI Network, the Enhanced MERLIN, the NOrthern Extended Millimeter Array, and the Atacama Large Millimetre Array, we conducted multi-epoch observations between 2017 and 2019 across frequencies from 5 GHz to 345 GHz. We detected radio emission at 6 GHz and 33 GHz aligned with the predicted location of the central binary, measuring Stokes I flux densities of $73 \pm 4 \, \mu$Jy and $83 \pm 13 \, \mu$Jy, respectively. No circular polarization or pulses were observed. Furthermore, no emission was detected at higher frequencies (230 GHz and 345 GHz) or at 5 GHz using VLBI arrays. The 6 GHz emission remained stable over nearly three years. To account for these detection and non-detection results, we evaluated various scenarios involving thermal and non-thermal processes, as well as differing contributions from each binary component. Our findings are best explained by non-thermal gyrosynchrotron radiation generated in radiation belts characterized by low plasma density ($n_e$ = 300$-$700 cm$^{-3}$), a moderate magnetic field ($B \approx$ 140 G), and an electron energy distribution following a power law ($d N / d E \propto E^{- \delta}$) with $\delta = 1.36$. These radiation belts are hypothesized to exist in both components and be viewed equatorially.

Estimating fetal weight at birth is a critical component of perinatal care, especially for determining the timing and mode of delivery in antenatal management. However, accurately predicting this weight using prenatal ultrasound is difficult; it demands high-quality images of specific fetal regions during late pregnancy, which are often unattainable due to poor image quality caused by insufficient amniotic fluid. Consequently, standard prediction methods frequently result in substantial errors. This paper introduces the Residual Transformer Module, an extension to a 3D ResNet-based network designed to analyze 2D+t spatio-temporal ultrasound video sequences. Our proposed end-to-end system, BabyNet, automatically estimates fetal birth weight from these ultrasound video scans. We evaluated BabyNet on a specialized clinical dataset containing 225 2D fetal ultrasound videos from 75 patients, captured one day before delivery. Experimental findings indicate that BabyNet surpasses several state-of-the-art approaches and achieves birth weight estimation accuracy comparable to that of human experts. Moreover, combining BabyNet's estimates with those from human experts produces the most accurate results, significantly outperforming all other methods. The BabyNet source code is accessible at https://github.com/SanoScience/BabyNet.

This paper details the distribution of rational points on the Hilbert scheme of two points within the projective plane. Specifically, we explicitly define a two-parameter family of height functions, $H_{s, t}$, such that the height function corresponding to any projective embedding is equivalent to some $H_{s, t}$ modulo multiplication by a bounded function. For specific ranges of the parameters $(s, t)$, we derive an asymptotic formula for the count of rational points with bounded height, whereas for other values, we establish an upper bound. The proof relies on reducing the problem to counting lattice points, a task solved through the application of the geometry of numbers.

This study examines shared listings on two South African equity exchanges: the Johannesburg Stock Exchange (JSE) and the A2X Exchange. A2X functions as an alternative platform offering both new and shared listings within South Africa's financial ecosystem. From a scientific standpoint, this setup allows for a comparison of markets trading identical shares under comparable regulatory and economic conditions, yet characterized by significantly divergent liquidity, costs, and business models. Although A2X currently offers competitive transaction and settlement pricing relative to the JSE, the latter benefits from deeper liquidity. To empirically understand how these distinctions influence price response dynamics, we analyze return distributions and auto-correlations across various time scales, compare price impacts and master curves, and evaluate trading costs on each exchange. Our findings indicate that while various stylized facts converge as measurement or sampling time scales increase, the same securities can exhibit vastly different price responses regardless of time scale—a phenomenon attributable to differences in liquidity and order-book resilience. We demonstrate that direct costs dominate overall trading expenses, highlighting the significance of competitively positioning cost ceilings. While universality is essential for meaningful cross-exchange comparisons of price responses, it has not yet emerged meaningfully for A2X due to the exchange's infancy, thereby complicating such comparisons.

Sentiment analysis plays a pivotal role in advancing artificial intelligence (AI), as the ability to comprehend sentiment enables AI to mimic human language and discourse more effectively. By examining how well-trained Customer Service Representatives (CSRs) develop and respond to emotional states, researchers can enhance the intelligence of human-AI interactions. This paper presents a sentiment analysis pipeline applied to real-world multi-party conversations, specifically service calls. Utilizing acoustic and linguistic features derived from the source data, a new aggregated framework for voice sentiment recognition is developed. The study investigates the sentiment patterns of each individual participant during communication, alongside the overall interaction sentiment dynamics among all parties.

A Morse function is termed "strong" when all its critical values are mutually distinct. For a strong function $f$ and a field $\mathbb{F}$, Barannikov defined a pairing of certain critical points, now referred to as a barcode. Each Barannikov pair corresponds (up to a sign) to a non-zero element of $\mathbb{F}$, designated as a Bruhat number. This paper focuses on analyzing these Bruhat numbers. We examine specific scenarios where the product of these numbers (with some raised to the power $-1$) remains invariant regardless of $f$, interpreting this quantity as Reidemeister torsion. Furthermore, within the context of one-parameter Morse theory, we demonstrate that a generic path of functions must satisfy a particular equation modulo 2, a result initially established in \cite{Akhm} under stricter conditions. At the linear-algebraic level, our constructions rely on a variant of the classical Bruhat decomposition for $GL(\mathbb{F})$. A unitriangular matrix is defined as an upper triangular matrix with 1s on the diagonal. By considering all rectangular matrices over $\mathbb{F}$ modulo left and right multiplication by unitriangular matrices, the enhanced Bruhat decomposition provides a canonical representative for each equivalence class.

The effectiveness of generalized linear models (GLMs), a staple in the insurance sector, hinges on the selection of interacting variables. Identifying these interactions is a labor-intensive task, particularly with high-dimensional datasets, and traditionally relies heavily on actuarial expertise and visual performance metrics. Consequently, we propose a method to automate the discovery of interactions that enhance GLM predictive capabilities. Our strategy leverages neural networks combined with a model-specific detection technique that outperforms conventional methods—such as Friedman H-Statistics or SHAP values—in terms of computational speed. We validate this approach through numerical experiments conducted on diverse datasets, including open-source, synthetic, and proprietary data.

This study examines a hybrid atom-optomechanical setup featuring N identical $\Lambda$-type atoms under dual optical and phononic driving forces. By leveraging both linear and quadratic optomechanical interactions, we demonstrate the generation of multiple electromagnetic transparency windows. Additionally, the inclusion of a mechanical pump allows for the control and tuning of these windows; specifically, adjusting the phase of the external mechanical pump introduces new control parameters and enhances absorption and emission profiles. Consequently, this research offers an effective method for manipulating propagating signals within quantum devices based on cavity-optomechanical systems.

High-quality 3D scene reconstruction from 2D image sets can be accomplished via offline or online mapping techniques. This paper investigates active mapping through the lens of implicit representations, which have recently yielded significant results across various domains. Among the most prominent implicit models is the Neural Radiance Field (NeRF), initially showcased for photorealistic rendering using multi-layer perceptrons, with offline 3D reconstruction emerging as a beneficial byproduct. Subsequently, researchers have adapted NeRF for online reconstruction and localization, effectively creating implicit SLAM systems. Nevertheless, research regarding the application of implicit representations to active vision tasks remains scarce. This study focuses on leveraging neural radiance fields for active mapping and planning—tasks that are intrinsically linked within an active system. For the first time, we introduce an RGB-only active vision framework utilizing radiance field representations to perform online active 3D reconstruction and planning. Specifically, we model this joint challenge as an iterative dual-stage optimization process, alternating between refining the radiance field representation and optimizing path planning. Experimental findings indicate that our proposed method achieves performance comparable to other offline approaches and surpasses existing active reconstruction techniques based on NeRFs.

The vertex cover problem is a cornerstone of combinatorial optimization, characterized by an integral linear programming relaxation for bipartite graphs and a half-integral one for general graphs. Consequently, standard rounding techniques yield optimal solutions for bipartite graphs and a 2-approximation for general graphs, prompting inquiry into whether better approximation ratios can be achieved based on a graph's proximity to bipartiteness. This paper introduces a round-and-bipartize algorithm that leverages an induced bipartite subgraph to achieve superior approximation bounds. Specifically, it assumes access to a vertex subset $S$ whose removal renders the graph bipartite. When $S$ forms an independent set, the study establishes an approximation ratio of $1 + 1/\rho$, where $2\rho - 1$ represents the odd girth of the contracted graph $\tilde{\mathcal{G}} := \mathcal{G} / S$ (with $\rho \geq 2$). The authors demonstrate that this bound is tight for all graphs and independent sets by constructing a family of weight functions that achieve it, alongside tight upper bounds for the fractional chromatic number and integrality gap, both contingent on the odd girth. For an arbitrary set $S$, a tight approximation ratio of $\left(1+1/\rho \right) (1 - \alpha) + 2 \alpha$ is proven, where $\alpha \in [0,1]$ signifies the total normalized dual sum of edges within $S$. Algorithmically, the paper shows that any efficiently $k$-colorable graph with $k \geq 4$ admits a bipartizing set where $\alpha \leq 1 - 4/k$. This yields an approximation algorithm achieving a worst-case bound of $2 - 2/k$ (when $\rho = 2$), which is optimal for this context using the standard relaxation.

Recent developments in set theory, as noted by J. Hamkins in [Ham11], reveal numerous distinct concepts of "set," each defined by its own axiomatic system. This paper aims to present a unified class theory capable of examining all set-theoretic universes and their interconnections simultaneously, thereby removing the necessity to step "outside the theory" for operations such as forcing. Furthermore, we investigate multiversal category theory, demonstrating that concerns regarding "largeness" at every stage of categorification are resolved within this framework; specifically, the category of categories associated with a given universe encompasses all large categories within that universe without requiring a larger universe. Utilizing this expanded freedom, we define a category ${\bf Force}$ where objects are universes and morphisms are forcing extensions; a $2$-category $\mathcal{V}\mathfrak{erse}$ whose objects are the categories of sets for each universe, with component categories formed by functors between them; and a tricategory $\mathbb{Cat}$ whose objects are the $2$-categories of categories per universe, with component bicategories consisting of pseudofunctors, pseudonatural transformations, and modifications between these structures.

This study evaluates two graph generative models aimed at designing novel drug candidates against SARS-CoV-2 viral proteins. Driven by urgency, we selected well-validated models with complementary strengths: an autoencoder capable of producing molecules structurally similar to existing anti-SARS drugs, and a reinforcement learning algorithm designed to generate highly novel compounds. Throughout the generation process, we optimized for multiple design targets to balance drug-likeness, synthetic accessibility, and anti-SARS activity, leveraging \icfifty. This generative framework\footnote{https://github.com/exalearn/covid-drug-design} aims to accelerate future pandemic drug discovery by enabling high-throughput generation of targeted therapeutic candidates.

This paper presents the Eval4NLP-2021 shared task focused on explainable quality estimation. For each source-translation pair, participants must generate a sentence-level quality score and justify it by pinpointing specific words that degrade translation quality. We outline the dataset, annotation protocols, and evaluation framework, review the approaches of six participating systems, and discuss the outcomes. To our knowledge, this marks the inaugural shared task dedicated to explainable NLP evaluation metrics. The datasets and results can be accessed at https://github.com/eval4nlp/SharedTask2021.

Pointing involves tracking a target with a pointer and confirming selection via a click once the pointer is over the target. However, little is understood about how users plan and execute these clicks during the tracking phase. This study introduces the Intermittent Click Planning model, which details the mechanism for planning and executing optimal clicks to predict pointing error rates. In two experiments involving stationary and moving targets, the model accurately forecast error rates (R² = 0.992 and 0.985, respectively). Furthermore, the model effectively distinguished cognitive differences among first-person shooter game players.

Current color-guided depth super-resolution (DSR) methods rely on paired RGB-D training sets, utilizing the structural similarity between RGB and depth images to reconstruct degraded depth maps. However, acquiring such paired data for real-world testing scenarios is often costly and limited. To address this, we introduce a novel approach for the first time that learns cross-modality knowledge during training using both RGB and depth inputs, while testing on datasets containing only depth modality. Our core concept involves distilling scene structural guidance from the RGB modality to the single-modal DSR task without altering the underlying network architecture. Specifically, we introduce an auxiliary depth estimation (DE) task that accepts RGB images as input to predict depth maps, training both the DSR and DE tasks jointly to enhance DSR performance. Building on this, we propose a cross-task interaction module to facilitate bidirectional knowledge transfer. Initially, we design a cross-task distillation framework that encourages the DSR and DE networks to learn from one another through a dynamic teacher-student role exchange. Subsequently, we introduce a structure prediction (SP) task that offers additional structural regularization, enabling both networks to acquire more informative structural representations for depth recovery. Comprehensive experiments confirm that our proposed scheme outperforms existing DSR methods.

Contemporary computing architectures predominantly prioritize moving data to where computation occurs, a design that conflicts with three critical trends driving performance, scalability, and energy limitations: (1) data access has become a primary bottleneck as applications grow increasingly data-intensive, while memory bandwidth and energy fail to scale effectively; (2) energy consumption constrains nearly all platforms, particularly servers and mobile devices; and (3) data movement, specifically between off-chip and on-chip domains, incurs significantly higher costs in bandwidth, energy, and latency compared to computation. These issues are acutely felt in today's data-heavy server environments and energy-limited mobile systems. Concurrently, conventional memory technologies face substantial scaling hurdles regarding reliability, energy efficiency, and performance. Consequently, memory system architects are exploring more intelligent and diverse memory organizations, albeit at increased costs. Evidence of this shift includes the rise of 3D-stacked memory integrated with logic, the integration of error-correcting codes in modern DRAM, the diversification of main memory standards for specific use cases (such as graphics, low-power, high-bandwidth, or low-latency applications), and the development of novel solutions to address critical reliability and security threats like the RowHammer effect. This chapter examines recent research facilitating "processing-in-memory" (PIM), an approach that embeds computation units within or near data storage locations (such as inside memory chips, within the logic layers of 3D-stacked memory, or in memory controllers) to minimize or eliminate data transfer between processing units and memory.

Inspired by a 1964 theorem by Finn and Osserman, which established that the Scherk surface spanning the square inscribed in the unit disk is extremal for the Gaussian curvature at the center point $O$ (assuming a horizontal tangent plane), we investigate and resolve the corresponding question regarding the extremality of the "second derivative" of the Gaussian curvature for such minimal graphs, under the condition that the curvature at $O$ vanishes. We demonstrate that these extremals are specific Scherk-type minimal surfaces defined over the regular hexagon inscribed in the unit disk, provided the Gaussian curvature is zero and the tangent plane remains horizontal at the center.

Quantum materials, including complex oxides, topological insulators, and transition-metal dichalcogenides (TMDs), have facilitated the development of devices poised to transform microelectronics and optoelectronics. Nevertheless, heterostructures combining quantum materials from diverse families are currently limited, despite their potential to vastly expand application possibilities. This study presents the large-scale integration of two highly multifunctional material families: perovskite oxides and TMDs. Specifically, we couple BiFeO$_3$, a room-temperature multiferroic oxide, with WSe$_2$, a semiconducting two-dimensional material promising for photovoltaics and photonics. WSe$_2$ is synthesized via molecular beam epitaxy and transferred onto centimeter-scale BiFeO$_3$ films. Through angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy, we map the electronic structure of 1 to 3 monolayers of WSe$_2$, revealing a substantial energy shift of up to 0.75 eV driven by the ferroelectric polarization direction of the underlying BiFeO$_3$. This pronounced shift suggests new avenues for efficiently manipulating TMD properties through proximity effects.

To reduce the computational cost of evaluating sample models, we introduce and analyze algorithms based on sequential likelihood-to-evidence ratio neural estimation. We apply these methods to a supersymmetric framework explaining the anomalous muon magnetic dipole moment within a phenomenological minimal supersymmetric extension of the standard model, successfully identifying non-trivial models within an experimentally constrained theory space. The paper concludes by outlining additional potential applications of these algorithms for future research.

By definition, the $p$-terminal dc-Josephson current depends on the superconducting phase variables of $p$ terminals. In this study, we develop a protocol for the direct detection of the $p$-terminal dc-Josephson effect where $p \ge 3$, utilizing a device with $N$ superconducting leads ($S_1, \dots, S_N$) characterized by phase variables $\varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_N$. The resulting signal, ${\chi}^{(N)}$, is accessible via microwave experiments and represents a higher-order nonlocal inverse inductance. This quantity is derived by differentiating the current $I_1$ flowing through $S_1$ with respect to the $N-2$ independent phase differences among the remaining leads ($\varphi_2-\varphi_N, \dots, \varphi_{N-1}-\varphi_N$). Our findings indicate that terms with $p \le N-2$ do not contribute to ${\chi}^{(N)}$; therefore, a non-zero value (${\chi}^{(N)} \ne 0$) serves as evidence for either $p=N-1$ or $p=N$ terminal dc-Josephson currents. Specifically, for a system with $N=4$ leads, a non-vanishing ${\chi}^{(4)}$ confirms the presence of $p=3$ or $p=4$ terminal effects, regardless of any $p=2$ terminal contribution. Consequently, we offer a method to demonstrate dc-Josephson effects with more than three terminals ($p \ge 3$) in devices containing more than four superconducting leads ($N \ge 4$). The predicted ${\chi}^{(4)}$ provides a definitive "yes or no" answer regarding the existence of $p \ge 3$ effects: a non-zero value indicates their presence, while a zero value indicates their absence. This work extends the concept of $\varphi$-junctions in Andreev molecules to an arbitrary number $N$ of leads, relying on fundamental properties of the dc-Josephson effect rather than on nontrivial topology or Weyl point singularities.

Smart Contract Templates facilitate legally binding agreements by utilizing operational parameters to link legal terms with standardized code. This paper investigates the design landscape for potential formats regarding the storage and transmission of smart legal contracts. We outline essential requirements and present several key design options, envisioning their evolution into standardized formats for defining and manipulating such agreements. This work serves as an initial step toward enabling industry adoption of enforceable smart contracts.

With neural networks increasingly deployed in real-world scenarios, addressing distributional shifts and sequential task learning without forgetting has become essential. While network expansion methods have shown promise by adding capacity for new tasks and mitigating catastrophic forgetting, their computational cost at large scales can be prohibitive. In response, we introduce Efficient Feature Transformations (EFTs), a simple task-specific feature map strategy that offers substantial flexibility for learning new tasks with minimal parameter additions to the base model. We also propose a feature distance maximization approach that enhances task prediction in class-incremental settings without relying on costly generative models. Extensive experiments across discriminative (CIFAR-100, ImageNet-1K) and generative (LSUN, CUB-200, Cats) task sequences demonstrate that EFTs achieve superior efficacy and efficiency. Notably, even with single-digit parameter growth rates, this method outperforms many other continual learning approaches across diverse settings.

When a system reaches equilibrium, external disturbances generate a sequence of non-equilibrium distributions; modern experimental methods now allow access to this data, which holds critical insights. Jinwoo and Tanaka (L. Jinwoo and H. Tanaka, Sci. Rep. 2015, 5, 7832) mathematically demonstrated that the non-equilibrium free energy profile of a system's substates encapsulates Jarzynski's work, which is spontaneously dissipated as molecules execute their functions. This study numerically confirms this finding through a practical case study analyzing a computer simulation of RNA translocation by a ring-shaped ATPase motor. By interpreting the cyclic translocation of the substrate as a sequence of quenching, relaxation, and a second quenching, the theory quantifies the energy levels of individual ATPase motor sub-states at the process's conclusion. Results indicate that while most molecules achieve an RNA translocation efficiency of 48–60%, approximately 12% reach 80–100% efficiency, aligning with existing literature. Consequently, this theoretical framework serves as a valuable instrument for extracting quantitative details regarding molecular non-equilibrium behavior from experimental data.

As enterprises increasingly prioritize process digitization and integration, they simultaneously face escalating cyber threats. While Business Process Management Notation (BPMN) is widely adopted to manage digital workflows internally and across organizational boundaries, other departments often rely on threat modeling and attack graphs to assess security resilience. This paper introduces a novel methodology that applies attack graph simulations directly to processes defined in BPMN. Key contributions include identifying the attack surface within BPMN, mapping its elements to coreLang—a Domain-Specific Language (DSL) grounded in Meta Attack Language (MAL)—and developing a prototype validated through a real-world invoice integration case study. The research demonstrates that non-invasively augmenting BPMN instances with cybersecurity analysis via attack graphs is feasible with minimal human expertise. Consequently, the resulting insights into potential vulnerabilities offer significant value to process modelers.

Using heat kernel techniques, we analyze the $\eta$-invariant of a Dirac operator on a manifold with boundary under local boundary conditions. In even dimensions, we connect this invariant to those of the boundary Dirac operator, whereas in odd dimensions, it is formulated via the index of boundary operators. We emphasize the critical role of the strong ellipticity condition for our methodology. Furthermore, we demonstrate that while Witten–Yonekura boundary conditions are nearly strongly elliptic, they fail to satisfy the strong ellipticity requirement.

This work examines the normal ordering coefficients for strings composed of $V$ and $U$ that obey the relation $UV=qVU+hV^s$, where $s\in\mathbb N$. The analysis is conducted in two frameworks: initially, these coefficients are treated as multiples of sequences fulfilling a generalized recurrence, and secondly, they are interpreted as $q$-analogues of rook numbers under the row creation rule defined by Goldman and Haglund. Various properties are established, including recurrences, relations to other $q$-analogues, and closed-form expressions. Additionally, a Dobinsky-type formula for the associated Bell numbers is provided, along with an extension of Spivey's Bell number formula. Finally, when regarded as rook numbers, these coefficients are generalized to the case $s\in\mathbb R$ through a modified rook model.

Although linear operator-theoretic methods can analyze nonlinear phenomena, the field is rapidly evolving with data-driven techniques like Extended Dynamic Mode Decomposition (EDMD) and its variants, which leverage machine learning to approximate the Koopman operator. Recently, Neural Ordinary Differential Equations (NODEs)—neural networks featuring a continuous layer structure known for high parameter and memory efficiency—have been introduced. This paper presents an algorithm that utilizes NODEs to execute EDMD. Specifically, NODEs identify a parameter-efficient dictionary that yields a robust finite-dimensional approximation of the Koopman operator. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed method achieves superior parameter efficiency.

In mMTC scenarios involving sporadic access attempts from thousands of devices, random access (RA) and resource collisions become critical challenges. A viable solution involves learning mechanisms, particularly Q-learning, enabling devices to identify optimal transmission time slots based on rewards from a central node. This study introduces a distributed packet-based learning approach where the central node's rewards are adjusted to prioritize devices with higher remaining packet counts. Numerical findings demonstrate that this proposed method achieves a superior throughput-latency trade-off compared to both independent and collaborative alternatives in practical settings. Furthermore, the packet-based technique requires fewer payload bits than collaborative Q-learning RA methods to achieve equivalent normalized throughput.

This paper introduces a geometrical framework for modeling entity ratings, treating rating transitions as stochastic differential equations (SDEs) on a Lie group. The study focuses on calibrating the model to both historical rating transition matrices and market CDS quotes, while comparing various change-of-measure techniques to shift from historical to risk-neutral probabilities. Specifically, it demonstrates the application of the classical Girsanov theorem within a Lie group context. Additionally, the authors address limitations in rating agency matrices—typically derived via the cohort method—by employing a novel Deep Learning technique, which enhances the overall scheme's robustness and applicability. Finally, the model is utilized to calculate bilateral credit and debit valuation adjustments for a netting set under a Credit Support Annex (CSA), incorporating thresholds based on the ratings of both counterparties.

Stellar rotation and activity are intrinsically linked within a dynamo mechanism, yet our comprehension of this process is constrained by our ability to deduce the characteristics of stellar turbulent convection. Specifically, the convective turnover time is a critical factor in calculating the stellar Rossby number, defined as the ratio between the rotation period and the convective turnover time. This study introduces a revised calibration of the convective turnover time's dependence on the $(B-V)$ color index, and consequently on the Rossby number. This new calibration relies on stellar structural properties derived from detailed modeling of solar-like pulsators using asteroseismic data. We demonstrate the effects of this calibration in a stellar activity versus Rossby number diagram by applying it to a sample of approximately 40,000 Kepler-observed stars with available photometric activity proxies ($S_\mathrm{\!ph}$) and surface rotation periods. Furthermore, we present a new calibration of the convective turnover time as a function of the $(G_\mathrm{BP}-G_\mathrm{RP})$ color index to facilitate its application within the ESA Gaia photometric bands.

Producing all recommended MRI modalities for effective diagnosis and treatment planning demands significant resources in terms of cost, time, and effort. However, recent breakthroughs in deep learning, particularly regarding generative models, have markedly advanced style transfer and image synthesis capabilities. This study addresses the challenge of creating missing MR modalities from available ones by framing it as an imputation task utilizing style transfer. By employing a multiple-to-one mapping approach, we developed a network capable of incorporating domain-specific styles to generate target images. Furthermore, we examined style diversity both within individual modalities and across different ones. Evaluated on the BraTS'18 dataset, our model achieves visual metrics, including SSIM and PSNR, that match current state-of-the-art performance. Additionally, assessment by two expert radiologists confirms that the proposed model is efficient, extensible, and well-suited for clinical use.
This paper aims to explore significant characteristics of Genocchi, Euler, and Bernstein polynomials through the application of Hermite polynomial orthogonality.

This study introduces a straightforward model to explain the origins of chemotaxis, investigating how directed cellular movement in response to external chemical cues can emerge from purely reaction-diffusion equations that capture internal cellular mechanisms. Drawing inspiration from the established role of the polarity regulator Cdc42, a rho-GTPase particularly prominent in yeast cells, we examine various iterations of this model to clarify its analytical characteristics and establish global regularity in one and two dimensions. Through computer simulations, we show that under specific parameter conditions within this framework, the velocity of directed motion is proportional to the magnitude of the signaling chemical gradient. This finding aligns with the structure of chemical drift found in the widely recognized Keller-Segel mean field model of chemotaxis.

This study employs the concept of negativity to investigate quantum and thermal entanglement in mixed spin-(1/2,$S$) Heisenberg dimers subjected to an external magnetic field. The analysis thoroughly examines the interplay among the spin size $S$, XXZ exchange interactions, and uniaxial single-ion anisotropy to optimize both the magnitude and thermal robustness of pairwise entanglement. Results indicate that, for identical model parameters, antiferromagnetic spin-(1/2,$S$) Heisenberg dimers display superior entanglement levels and higher critical temperatures compared to their ferromagnetic analogues. Furthermore, increasing the spin magnitude $S$ alongside easy-plane uniaxial anisotropy simultaneously boosts both the degree of entanglement and its thermal stability. The research also demonstrates that bipartite entanglement can be further amplified in these mixed spin systems when $S$ takes half-odd-integer values; under these conditions, thermal negativity reaches its maximum value at sufficiently low temperatures, independent of the specific half-odd-integer spin magnitude. Finally, for cases where $S\!>\!1$, the application of a magnetic field triggers successive discontinuous phase transitions, characterized by a remarkable oscillating dependence of negativity on the magnetic field at low temperatures.

This paper revives a cosmological model proposing that the cosmic microwave background (CMB) originates from thermal emission by intergalactic dust rather than serving as a remnant of the Big Bang. In this framework, the local universe is nearly transparent, but it becomes significantly opaque at redshifts $z > 2-3$. While this opacity remains undetectable in Type Ia supernova observations, quasar data confirm its presence. The opacity rises sharply with redshift due to the high proper density of intergalactic dust in earlier epochs. Crucially, the dust temperature scales as $(1+z)$, precisely offsetting the wavelength shifts caused by redshift; consequently, the dust radiation mimics a single-temperature blackbody. The predicted dust temperature is $T^{D} = 2.776 \, \mathrm{K}$, differing from the observed CMB temperature by only 1.9%, and the calculated ratio of total CMB to extragalactic background light (EBL) intensities is 13.4, closely matching the observational value of 12.5. Within this model, CMB temperature fluctuations arise from EBL variations generated by galaxy clusters and voids. Furthermore, the polarization anomalies in the CMB that correlate with temperature anisotropies are attributed to the polarized thermal emission from needle-shaped conducting dust grains aligned by large-scale magnetic fields surrounding these structures. Finally, the observed sharp decline in luminosity density for $z > 4$ is interpreted as a consequence of the universe's high opacity rather than a reduction in global stellar mass density at high redshifts.

This research investigates synchronizing partial deterministic finite automata (DFAs), a concept that generalizes the classical synchronizing complete DFAs and serves as a specific instance of synchronizing unambiguous nondeterministic DFAs. A partial DFA is defined as synchronizing if there exists a reset word that maps a non-empty set of states to a single state, while remaining undefined for all other states. Although determining synchronicity for partial DFAs is generally PSPACE-complete, we demonstrate that for strongly connected partial DFAs, this problem can be efficiently reduced to the corresponding problem for complete DFAs. By employing combinatorial, algebraic, and formal language techniques, we establish connections between key synchronization issues in strongly connected partial DFAs and their complete counterparts. These connections specifically address the Černý and rank conjectures, the search for reset words, and upper bounds on the lengths of the shortest reset words for literal automata derived from finite prefix codes. Ultimately, we conclude that the fundamental synchronization problems pose equal difficulty in both models, as significant advancements in one domain necessarily lead to improvements in the other.

Active learning (AL) was created to address practical needs by lowering label complexity and annotation expenses in supervised learning. Although recent studies highlight the advantages of combining AL with large pre-trained language models (PLMs), they frequently neglect the real-world obstacles that limit AL's feasibility. This work tackles these issues by utilizing representation smoothness analysis to enhance AL effectiveness. We introduce an early stopping method that functions without a validation set—a resource often missing in practical AL scenarios—and demonstrate substantial gains across various datasets and AL techniques. Furthermore, we discover that task adaptation benefits AL, while standard short fine-tuning fails to outperform random sampling. Our research validates the utility of representation smoothness analysis in AL and offers a stopping criterion that effectively reduces label complexity.

We employ the concept of the principal three-dimensional subgroup within a simple Lie group to pinpoint specific subspaces of the Lie algebra, thereby investigating whether these subspaces are calibrated with respect to invariant forms on the group.

Phase-field modeling has emerged as a premier method for simulating realistic fracture, treating cracks as a secondary phase and utilizing gradient terms to diffuse crack surfaces, thereby allowing standard numerical techniques. However, this regularization implies cracks possess a finite volume, which hinders the accurate representation of crack face closure or contact without healing. Specifically, classical models require zero shear traction and zero normal traction during opening, but normal traction identical to the intact material during closure; phase-field approaches fail to reproduce this behavior. This study resolves that limitation by introducing an effective crack energy density that grants the regularized, finite-volume crack the mechanical characteristics of an idealized sharp crack. The methodology employs QR (upper triangular) decomposition of the deformation gradient tensor within the crack basis to clearly distinguish deformation modes. By relaxing modes that incur no energy cost, the resulting effective energy yields an intact response upon crack face closure and zero energy when they open. A key advantage of this framework is its full compatibility with finite deformation theory, facilitating applications to soft materials and scenarios involving large rotations or deformations. The model is utilized to numerically investigate complex loading conditions, such as (1) cyclic loading on a soft solid cavity, demonstrating crack growth and closure under complex stress states, and (2) cyclic shear, revealing intricate crack branching patterns driven by crack closure.

We demonstrate that for any finite arithmetic progression $\mathcal{A}$ within the integers $\mathbb{Z}$, the cardinality of its product set $\mathcal{A} \cdot \mathcal{A}$ adheres to the inequality $|\mathcal A \cdot \mathcal A| \ge \frac{|\mathcal A|^2}{(\log |\mathcal A|)^{2\theta +o(1)} }$, where $2\theta=1-(1+\log\log 2)/(\log 2)$ represents the constant central to the renowned Erd\H{o}s multiplication table problem. This finding validates a conjecture proposed by Elekes and Ruzsa approximately twenty years prior. Furthermore, if $\mathcal{A}$ is generalized to a subset of a finite arithmetic progression in integers exhibiting positive constant density, we establish that $|\mathcal A \cdot \mathcal A | \ge \frac{|\mathcal A|^{2}}{(\log |\mathcal A|)^{2\log 2- 1 + o(1)}}$. This resolves the typical instance of another conjecture by Elekes and Ruzsa regarding the magnitude of the product set for a set $\mathcal{A}$ whose sum set is bounded by $O(|\mathcal{A}|)$. Our derived bounds are optimal up to the $o(1)$ terms in the exponents, and we additionally provide asymmetric extensions of these findings.

This paper introduces a distributed stochastic algorithm incorporating variance reduction for general smooth non-convex finite-sum optimization, a domain with broad applications in machine learning and signal processing. Within a distributed framework, numerous samples are distributed across multiple network agents, each calculating local stochastic gradients and exchanging information with neighbors to locate the global optimum. To address the variance stemming from stochastic gradients, we devise an enhanced variance reduction method. By integrating gradient tracking with variance reduction, we propose the GT-VR algorithm to tackle large-scale non-convex finite-sum optimization over multi-agent networks. Rigorous proofs demonstrate that the GT-VR algorithm converges to first-order stationary points at a rate of $O(\frac{1}{k})$, accompanied by a comprehensive complexity analysis. Under mild conditions, the proposed method achieves a lower gradient complexity of $\mathcal{O}(PM\epsilon^{-1})$ compared to existing first-order approaches. Furthermore, experimental simulations comparing GT-VR with state-of-the-art algorithms confirm the efficiency of our proposed technique.

A critical phase in designing autonomous systems involves assessing the likelihood of failure. In safety-critical environments, this probability is so low that standard Monte Carlo sampling becomes inefficient for policy evaluation. While adaptive importance sampling methods exist for rare event estimation, they often fail to scale effectively for sequential systems with extended horizons. This research introduces two adaptive importance sampling algorithms designed to efficiently estimate rare event probabilities within sequential decision-making frameworks. These algorithms are grounded in minimizing the Kullback-Leibler divergence between a state-dependent proposal distribution and a target trajectory distribution, yet their implementation draws from policy gradient and value-based reinforcement learning techniques. Furthermore, we employ multiple importance sampling to lower estimation variance and mitigate issues arising from the multi-modality of the optimal proposal distribution. Finally, we validate our approach on a control task involving both continuous and discrete action spaces, demonstrating enhanced accuracy compared to several baseline methods.

We introduce a novelty detection framework for Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) sensors named Sensor-Activated Feature Extraction One-Class Classification (SAFE-OCC). This framework facilitates the safe deployment of computer vision sensors within process control systems. In emergent control applications, CNN models translate visual inputs into state signals understandable by controllers; however, integrating these sensors creates a significant vulnerability, as CNNs can produce high prediction errors when encountering novel or abnormal visual data. Identifying such novelties in real-time is challenging. To resolve this, the SAFE-OCC framework utilizes the convolutional blocks of the CNN to construct an effective feature space for novelty detection using one-class classification. This method generates a feature space that aligns directly with the CNN sensor's internal usage, eliminating the necessity to create an independent latent space. The efficacy of SAFE-OCC is validated through simulated control environments.

Results concerning two-player zero-sum games are extended into complex space within a comprehensive, compact framework. In this context, the payoff function corresponds to the real component of the real-valued case, while pure complex strategies are characterized by the extreme points of the convex polytope $S_\alpha^m:=\{z\in\mathbb{C}^m:$ $|argz|\leqq\alpha,\;\sum_{i=1}^{m}z_i=1\}$, where $\alpha$ represents the "strategy argument" in the interval $(0,\frac{\pi}{2})e$. These strategies enable the extension of definitions and findings regarding Nash equilibria, player security levels, and their interrelations to $\mathbb{C}^{m}$. The paper provides a novel constructive proof of the Minimax Theorem for complex space, offering a method for the precise calculation of equilibria in two-player zero-sum complex games. Additionally, a more straightforward solution approach is derived, relying on solving complex linear systems of the form $Bz=b$.

Conformal Carroll symmetry typically emerges on null manifolds and plays a crucial role in the holography of asymptotically flat spacetimes, generic black hole horizons, and tensionless strings. This study concentrates on two-dimensional null manifolds, examining the two-dimensional Conformal Carroll algebra, which is equivalent to the three-dimensional Bondi-Metzner-Sachs (BMS) algebra. By applying Carroll covariance, we construct the most general free massless Carroll scalar field theory and identify three inequivalent actions. While the time-like and space-like versions previously appeared in literature, we introduce a novel third action termed the mixed-derivative theory. As anticipated, all three formulations possess off-shell BMS invariance. Notably, the mixed-derivative theory exhibits a reduced on-shell symmetry consisting of a single Virasoro algebra rather than the complete BMS algebra. We conclude by exploring potential applications to tensionless strings and flat holography.

Iterative Learning Control (ILC) generates a series of feedforward control inputs at each iteration, utilizing partial system models and historical data to guide the system toward a target reference trajectory. This approach is conceptualized as an online learning problem wherein a decision-maker makes sequential choices by solving a series of optimization tasks with incomplete knowledge of the underlying cost functions. By establishing this link, the study evaluates the performance of an online gradient-descent method relying on inexact gradient estimates within the framework of dynamic and static regret, which are standard metrics in online learning. Furthermore, the research examines the inherent limitations of this scheme and its compatibility with adaptation strategies, concluding with numerical simulations on a standard ILC benchmark.

This report presents the observation of Higgs boson production alongside a top quark-antiquark pair, derived from a combined analysis of proton-proton collision data recorded by the CMS detector at the CERN LHC. The dataset encompasses center-of-mass energies of 7, 8, and 13 TeV, with integrated luminosities reaching up to 5.1, 19.7, and 35.9 fb$^{-1}$, respectively. To enhance sensitivity, results from statistically independent searches for Higgs bosons produced with top quark pairs and decaying into W boson pairs, Z bosons, photons, $\tau$ leptons, or bottom quark jets are merged. An event excess is detected with a significance of 5.2 standard deviations relative to the background-only hypothesis, compared to an expected significance of 4.2 standard deviations for a standard model Higgs boson mass of 125.09 GeV. The combined best-fit signal strength, normalized to standard model predictions, is determined to be 1.26 ${^{+0.31}_{-0.26}}$.

Deep learning methods are now ubiquitous in computer vision, particularly for semantic segmentation, which demands extensive datasets and significant computational resources. Continual semantic segmentation (CSS) is an emerging paradigm that involves sequentially updating a model with new classes. However, continual learning techniques are often susceptible to catastrophic forgetting, a problem exacerbated in CSS where previously learned classes are effectively merged into the background during each update. To address this, we introduce Local POD, a multi-scale pooling distillation framework that maintains both short- and long-range spatial dependencies at the feature level. Additionally, we develop an entropy-based pseudo-labeling strategy for the background, relative to predictions from the previous model, to mitigate background shift and prevent the forgetting of old classes. Our proposed approach, PLOP, demonstrates superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods in existing CSS scenarios as well as on newly introduced challenging benchmarks.

At colliders, neutral long-lived particles are identified either via displaced decay products or as missing energy, with the optimal search strategy depending on both the detector characteristics and the particle's decay length. This study examines the complementary nature of these signatures for the Belle II experiment, specifically focusing on axion-like particles ($a$) generated from meson decays. We introduce a novel approach to detect two-body decays characterized by $B^+ \to K^+ a$ followed by $a\to E\!\!\!/$, where $E\!\!\!/$ represents missing energy. Utilizing an integrated luminosity of $50\,$ab$^{-1}$, Belle II is capable of probing light invisible resonances with branching ratios $\mathcal{B}(B^+\to K^+ a) \gtrsim 10^{-7}$ and decay lengths $c\tau_a \gtrsim 1\,$m. For axion-like particles, we anticipate that the sensitivity of the $B^+ \to K^+ E\!\!\!/$ channel to small couplings could improve by up to two orders of magnitude relative to prior searches at fixed-target and collider facilities. Specifically, for sub-GeV particles, the combination of $B^+ \to K^+ E\!\!\!/$ at Belle II and beam-dump experiments offers the greatest sensitivity, whereas for heavier particles, the smallest couplings can be probed through displaced vertex searches at Belle II, long-lived particle studies at the LHC, and future fixed-target experiments.

While the asymptotic behavior of survival or reunion probabilities for vicious walks with short-range interactions is widely understood, many realistic scenarios involve long-range potentials decaying as $r^{-d-\sigma}$ in $d$ dimensions. Using renormalized field theory, we investigate these long-range effects. For the first time, we determine the exponents governing the decay of the survival probability across all values of $\sigma$ and $d$, accurate to first order in the double expansion involving $\epsilon=2-d$ and $\delta=2-d-\sigma$. Our results identify multiple regions within the $\sigma-d$ plane, each characterized by distinct scaling behaviors for survival and reunion probabilities. Additionally, we compute the leading logarithmic corrections for the first time.

Eye-tracking holds promise for capturing detailed behavioral insights into human cognition within ecologically valid settings; however, processing such abundant data remains difficult. Current automated methods are typically limited to simple, artificial stimuli with clearly defined, static regions of interest, whereas analyses involving complex visual inputs, like natural scenes, depend on tedious manual annotation. This study investigates the application of computer vision techniques for "attention decoding," which involves determining the location of a participant's overt visual attention over time. We introduce a publicly accessible Multiple Object Eye-Tracking (MOET) dataset comprising gaze data from users tracking specific objects in crowded real-world videos, complete with labels and bounding boxes, designed to train and evaluate attention decoding algorithms. Additionally, we present two end-to-end deep learning models for this task and compare their performance against existing state-of-the-art heuristic approaches.

This work investigates ELI queries (ELIQs) within ontologies based on the description logic DL-Lite. We demonstrate that for the DL-LiteH dialect, ELIQs possess a frontier—a set of least general generalizations—that is both polynomial in size and computable in polynomial time. Conversely, in the DL-LiteF dialect, frontiers can be infinite; however, we define a specific syntactic constraint that restores polynomial-time computability and size bounds similar to those in DL-LiteH. Leveraging these findings on frontiers, we prove that ELIQs are learnable in polynomial time under Angluin's exact learning framework using only membership queries, provided the ontology adheres to DL-LiteH or the restricted DL-LiteF format.

This study details the development and validation of a MHz frequency domain multiplexing (FDM) system designed to read out arrays of cryogenic transition edge sensor (TES) X-ray microcalorimeters. The proposed FDM method involves AC-biasing individual TESs at distinct resonant frequencies within the low MHz band via a network of high-$Q$ LC resonators, with their current signals subsequently aggregated by superconducting quantum interference devices (SQUIDs). We successfully demonstrated multiplexed readout for 31 pixels utilizing room-temperature electronics, high-$Q$ LC filters, TES arrays from SRON, and SQUID arrays from VTT. A second configuration was tested with 37 pixels. The resulting summed X-ray spectral resolutions at 5.9 keV were measured as $\Delta E_{\rm 31 pix ~MUX}=2.14\pm0.03$ eV and $\Delta E_{\rm 37 pix ~MUX}=2.23\pm0.03$ eV. These findings are on par with other multiplexing techniques. Future work holds promise for enhancing spectral resolution, scaling up the number of multiplexed TESs, and expanding the applicability of TES X-ray microcalorimeters.

(Abridged) While exoplanetary studies have excitingly revealed planets orbiting very low-mass (VLM) stars like TRAPPIST-1 and Proxima Centauri, existing theoretical models fail to predict giant planet formation under these conditions. However, recent high-resolution ALMA observations of the disk around CIDA 1, a VLM star in Taurus, reveal substructures suggesting a massive planet. Our objective is to replicate the dust ring of CIDA 1, detected via ALMA Band 7 (0.9 mm) and Band 4 (2.1 mm) continuum emission, as well as its $^{12}$CO (J=3-2) and $^{13}$CO (J=3-2) channel maps, by assuming these features result from disk-planet interactions. We aim to determine the mass and location of this candidate planet. Using hydrodynamical simulations, we modeled the protoplanetary disk by varying the embedded planet's mass and position. Subsequently, we calculated dust and gas emission through radiative transfer simulations to generate synthetic observations mimicking actual ALMA data. Our models demonstrate that a planet with a minimum mass of $\sim1.4\,\text{M}_\text{Jup}$ at a distance of $\sim 9-10$ au can account for the observed dust ring morphology and location across both bands. Additionally, we successfully reproduced the low spectral index ($\sim 2$) detected within the ring. Our synthetic images also match the morphology of the $^{12}$CO and $^{13}$CO channel maps where cloud absorption permitted detection. By applying an empirical relationship between planet mass and dust gap width, we estimate a maximum planet mass of $\sim4 - 8\,\text{M}_\text{Jup}$. These findings imply the existence of a massive planet around CIDA 1, thereby challenging current understandings of planet formation around VLM stars.

Cold atomic gases provide a platform for simulating early universe physics in a laboratory setting. In their condensed state, these gases are modeled using field theories that share essential characteristics with high-energy particle theory. This study examines a three-level system experiencing a first-order phase transition driven by bubble nucleation. Theoretical analysis reveals that bubbles form in two dimensions at non-zero temperatures. Calculated nucleation rates show strong consistency between the Stochastic Projected Gross-Pitaevskii equation and the non-perturbative instanton method. Furthermore, simulations incorporating an optical box trap demonstrate that bubbles preferentially nucleate near the trap's boundaries.

This study introduces an air mobility index and leverages Apple's newly created driving trend index to assess how COVID-19 affects crude oil prices. Using quantile regression alongside both stationary and non-stationary extreme value models, we analyze these impacts. Our findings indicate that both the air mobility index and the driving trend index significantly affect the lower and upper quantiles, as well as the median, of WTI crude oil prices. Furthermore, the extreme value model suggests that pandemics like COVID-19, characterized by drastic declines in air mobility, could once again drive oil prices into negative territory.

We establish scattering for the radial nonlinear Klein-Gordon equation, $\partial_{tt} u - \Delta u + u = -|u|^{p-1} u$, where $5 > p > 3$, and initial data $(u_{0}, u_{1})$ belonging to $H^{s} \times H^{s-1}$. The required regularity $s$ satisfies $1 > s > 1-\frac{(5-p)(p-3)}{2(p-1)(p-2)}$ when $4 \geq p > 3$, and $1 > s > 1 -\frac{(5-p)^{2}}{2(p-1)(6-p)}$ when $5> p \geq 4$. Our approach begins by proving Strichartz-type estimates within $L_{t}^{q} L_{x}^{r}$ spaces. Utilizing these decay properties, we derive specific local bounds. By integrating these findings with a Morawetz-type estimate and a radial Sobolev inequality, we regulate the variation of an almost conserved quantity over arbitrarily large time intervals. Once this control is achieved, we demonstrate that certain local bounds can be extended to global ones, which suffices to prove scattering. All necessary estimates demand intricate analysis owing to the specific characteristics of the nonlinearity and the absence of scaling invariance.

This study demonstrates that integrating quantum metrology with networking tools can extend the baseline of an interferometric optical telescope, thereby enhancing the diffraction-limited imaging of point source locations. The proposed quantum interferometer utilizes single-photon sources, linear optical circuits, and high-efficiency photon number counters. Remarkably, even with thermal (stellar) sources characterized by low photon counts per mode and significant transmission losses across the baseline, the detected photon probability distribution preserves substantial Fisher information regarding the source position. This enables a notable improvement in point source positioning resolution, achieving approximately 10 {\mu}as. Our proposal is feasible with existing technology and does not necessitate experimental optical quantum memories.

As archetypal complex systems, financial markets display a diverse array of dynamic behaviors arising from their interactions. This study examines the cryptocurrency market—a recently emerged complex system—by analyzing how its cross-correlation structure evolved over a five-year span from 2017 to 2022. By identifying characteristic correlation patterns within this timeframe, we classify the cryptocurrency market into four distinct states.

Estimating species richness in a specific area remains a significant statistical challenge, primarily due to limited sample sizes and errors in species identification. While existing literature mostly focuses on estimators designed to address underestimation caused by small sample sizes, species identification errors are ubiquitous in surveys and severely compromise the accuracy of observed, singleton, and doubleton counts, thereby distorting the performance of richness estimators. Consequently, to achieve accurate richness estimates, data biased by identification errors must be corrected prior to analysis. This manuscript introduces a novel method to rectify such biases. The process begins by using a species inventory from a subplot, collected by the investigator, to calculate the species identification error rate. Subsequently, this rate is applied to adjust the biased observed, singleton, and doubleton richness values derived from the raw sampling data. Finally, standard literature-based richness estimators are applied to this adjusted data to yield more accurate results. To evaluate the method's performance, we conducted simulations using datasets generated from various species models with differing error rates. Additionally, we applied the approach to real-world data from a presence/absence survey of weeds in an organic farm located in Soft Bridge County, northern Taiwan.

High-resolution rotation-vibration transitions for \spec{h212c16o}, the main isotopologue of methanal, have been analyzed using the MARVEL (Measured Active Rotation-Vibration Energy Levels) method. This study expands upon existing literature by incorporating new, highly accurate measurements of pure rotational transitions within the ground state, as well as the $
u_3$, $
u_4$, and $
u_6$ vibrational states. Among the 
bNonRedTr\ non-redundant transitions processed—sourced from 
bSr\ origins including this work—a total of 
bValTr\ were validated, yielding 
bEl\ empirical energy levels for \spec{h212c16o}\ with statistically robust uncertainties. These empirically determined rotational-vibrational energy levels are utilized to enhance the precision of ExoMol's AYTY line list for hot formaldehyde. The compiled experimental transitions, the derived empirical energy levels, and the updated, improved line list are available in the Supplementary Material.

Research in social forensics has increasingly focused on detecting multimodal fake news, with many current methods employing specialized attention mechanisms to fuse unimodal features. Nevertheless, critical aspects remain unresolved, specifically how feature similarity is computed and its impact on decision-making, alongside the underutilized potential of pretrained multi-modal models in this domain. To address these gaps, this paper introduces FND-CLIP, a multimodal fake news detection framework grounded in Contrastive Language-Image Pretraining (CLIP). For targeted multimodal news, the system extracts deep representations using a ResNet-based encoder for images, a BERT-based encoder for text, and two pair-wise CLIP encoders. The resulting multimodal feature is formed by concatenating CLIP-generated features, weighted by the standardized cross-modal similarity between the two modalities. These features undergo redundancy reduction prior to classification. Furthermore, a modality-wise attention module is implemented to adaptively reweight and aggregate the features. Extensive experiments on standard fake news datasets demonstrate that the proposed framework excels at mining critical features for detection. The FND-CLIP model outperforms prior approaches, yielding accuracy improvements of 0.7%, 6.8%, and 1.3% on the Weibo, Politifact, and Gossipcop datasets, respectively. Additionally, the study validates that CLIP-based learning enhances flexibility in multimodal feature selection.

Debiased machine learning serves as a meta-algorithm utilizing sample splitting and bias correction to generate confidence intervals for scalar summaries derived from machine learning models. For instance, an analyst might seek a confidence interval for a treatment effect estimated via a neural network. We present a nonasymptotic theorem for debiased machine learning that applies to any global or local functional of any machine learning algorithm, provided it meets a few straightforward and interpretable criteria. Formally, we establish consistency, Gaussian approximation, and semiparametric efficiency through finite-sample reasoning. The convergence rate achieves $n^{-1/2}$ for global functionals and degrades gracefully for local ones. Our findings result in a concise set of conditions enabling analysts to convert modern learning theory rates into conventional statistical inference. Furthermore, these conditions expose a general double robustness characteristic inherent in ill-posed inverse problems.

A well-known conjecture by Sidorenko and Erdős-Simonovits posits that quasirandom graphs contain asymptotically the fewest copies of any bipartite graph $H$ compared to all graphs sharing the same vertex count and edge density. Over the past ten years, this conjecture has garnered significant attention and has been proven for a wide variety of bipartite graphs. The prevailing pattern suggests that a graph satisfies the conjecture if it can be constructed recursively from basic components like trees. Our work extends beyond this existing framework by demonstrating that the conjecture holds for any bipartite graph $H$ with partition $A \cup B$, provided that the count of vertices in $B$ with degree $k$ meets a specific divisibility requirement for every $k$. Consequently, for every bipartite graph $H$ with partition $A \cup B$, there exists a positive integer $p$ such that the blow-up $H_A^p$—formed by taking $p$ vertex-disjoint copies of $H$ and merging all instances of $A$ at corresponding vertices—satisfies the conjecture. Alternatively, this result implies that for every bipartite $H$, there is a positive integer $p$ for which an $L^p$-variant of Sidorenko's conjecture is valid.

This work presents an ACL2 program implementing the Hebrew calendar and the formal verification of several key properties, notably that the algorithm determining new year placements guarantees every year's length falls within a specific set of admissible values. These properties have been relied upon for centuries despite the subtleties in their original reasoning and the lack of explicit proof. To ensure accessibility for a wider audience, the program is written in Restricted Algorithmic C (RAC), a simplified language using only fundamental C constructs for which an automatic translator to ACL2 logic exists. Although RAC was originally designed for modeling arithmetic hardware, this application serves as a straightforward demonstration of both the language and its translator.

We demonstrate that any translation of a model set remains a model set within a suitably adjusted cut-and-project scheme. When confined to Euclidean direct space, we prove that any translation of an inter model set also constitutes a model set in a modified scheme featuring a second countable internal space. In both scenarios, the window in the revised scheme retains the original window's topological and measure-theoretic characteristics. Furthermore, these findings extend to a broader category than inter model sets, which we designate as almost model sets.

Achieving top-tier performance in modern neural networks relies heavily on selecting an optimal architecture. Neural Architecture Search (NAS) automates the discovery of task-specific structures, typically utilizing supernetworks where subnetworks represent candidate architectures. These subnetworks are trained concurrently, eliminating the need to train each model from scratch and significantly boosting NAS efficiency. Building on the Neural Architecture Transfer (NAT) method—which employs a multi-objective evolutionary algorithm to identify high-quality subnetworks within an ImageNet-pretrained supernetwork for computer vision—we introduce ENCAS (Evolutionary Neural Cascade Search). ENCAS extends this approach by searching across multiple pretrained supernetworks to generate a Pareto front of architectural cascades that maximize accuracy while minimizing FLOPs. Evaluated on standard benchmarks like CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet, ENCAS achieves Pareto dominance over prior state-of-the-art NAS models with up to 1.5 GFLOPs savings. Furthermore, applying ENCAS to a pool of 518 publicly available ImageNet classifiers yields Pareto dominance across all computation regimes, raising the peak accuracy from 88.6% to 89.0% while reducing computational effort by 18% (from 362 to 296 GFLOPs). The project's code is accessible at https://github.com/AwesomeLemon/ENCAS.

The relaxor ferroelectric transition in Cd$_2$Nb$_2$O$_7$ is attributed to the condensation of two $\Gamma$-centered phonon modes, $\Gamma_4^-$ and $\Gamma_5^-$, yet their specific contributions remain contentious. While $\textit{ab initio}$ calculations suggest $\Gamma_4^-$ is the primary driver, global crystal refinements indicate $\Gamma_5^-$ plays that role. This study resolves the discrepancy using x-ray pair distribution function data, revealing that $\Gamma_4^-$ dominates locally while $\Gamma_5^-$ prevails globally. This finding aligns with our own $\textit{ab initio}$ simulations, which show near-degenerate energy surfaces for these distortion modes. Furthermore, our first-principles calculations indicate these surfaces are nearly isotropic, offering an explanation for the material's multiple structural transitions and relaxor characteristics. Our results identify several local structural models, including those exhibiting two-in/two-out Nb displacements within tetrahedra. Although this hints at a charge analog to spin ice in Cd$_2$Nb$_2$O$_7$, our data support a Heisenberg-like description of dipolar fluctuations over an Ising model.
