We hope these findings inspire further experimental research into Nb and Cd dipolar fluctuations and their associated mode dynamics.

Millicharged particles (MCPs) are a prevalent topic in experimental searches and appear in numerous well-motivated extensions of the Standard Model. This study examines how interactions within various media attenuate MCP fluxes generated at accelerator facilities. Using the dedicated MCP search at SLACmQ as a case study, we demonstrate that such attenuation can substantially impact the final sensitivity regarding the MCP parameter space, leaving a significant portion unexplored. By applying our analysis to the SLACmQ experiment [53], we revise their exclusion limits in close agreement with Ref. [54]. Furthermore, we identify that the newly accessible region, encompassing MCP masses between $10^{-4}$ eV and 1 GeV and charges $\gtrsim 10^{-5} e$, can be effectively investigated by the NA64$e$ experiment at the CERN SPS. Regarding production mechanisms, light MCPs are primarily generated through virtual photons during electron-nucleus scattering, whereas heavy MCPs mainly originate from the decays of vector mesons produced when electrons interact with nuclei.

Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) are widely regarded as the gold standard for evaluating causal hypotheses within clinical settings. However, standard statistical methods struggle to investigate prognostic variables along a hypothesized cause-and-effect pathway. To address this, we introduce AutoCI, a novel automated causal inference method grounded in the invariant causal prediction (ICP) framework, designed for re-interpreting clinical trial data causally. When compared to existing approaches, AutoCI efficiently identifies causal variables, demonstrating clear differentiation across two real-world RCTs involving endometrial cancer patients with mature outcomes and extensive clinicopathological and molecular data. This performance is achieved by significantly suppressing the causal probabilities assigned to non-causal variables. Furthermore, ablation studies confirm that AutoCI's assignment of causal probabilities remains consistent even in the presence of confounders. Ultimately, these findings validate the robustness and feasibility of AutoCI for future real-world clinical analyses.

We introduce an augmentation strategy for Contrastive Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) by adapting an existing Salient Image Segmentation method known as Global Contrast based Salient Region Detection. Originally designed for distinct Computer Vision applications, this technique was empirically found to enhance the SSL framework. This insight emerged from our efforts to learn representations of solar panel aerial imagery via SSL, which presents difficult boundary challenges. Following the successful application of this method to our specific domain, we developed a generalized approach and performed a rigorous, systematic evaluation of its impact on various Contrastive SSL algorithms under standard augmentation schemes. Assessments across multiple datasets confirmed that the proposed technique positively influences SSL performance. Furthermore, we hypothesize that salient image segmentation alone could serve as an effective augmentation policy for Contrastive SSL when addressing downstream segmentation tasks.

Although large-scale pre-trained language models excel at producing realistic text, controlling their output remains a significant challenge. Existing techniques, such as prompting, are often inadequate, thereby restricting the practical application of these models. To address this limitation, we introduce "inverse prompting," an innovative approach designed to improve generation control. The fundamental concept involves using the generated text to predict the prompt during beam search, which strengthens the alignment between the prompt and the output while enhancing controllability. We empirically validated this method by pre-training a large-scale Chinese language model and conducting a systematic evaluation through human assessment on open-domain poem generation and long-form question answering. Our findings demonstrate that inverse prompting significantly outperforms baseline methods, with generation quality on certain tasks approaching human-level performance. Researchers can explore our poem generation demo at https://pretrain.aminer.cn/apps/poetry.html and our QA demo at https://pretrain.aminer.cn/app/qa. Additionally, the source code is available for researchers at https://github.com/THUDM/InversePrompting.

In February 2018, the VIX index experienced its most substantial rise on record, causing considerable losses for several major volatility-linked products, though the exact causes remain unidentified. This study examines the linear causality between the VIX index and its derivatives during January and February 2018. Given the limitations of statistical inference within stochastic volatility models, the behavior of the volatility expectation index, VIX, continues to be debated. By utilizing intraday data, we uncover new empirical findings regarding their interaction. Our analysis reveals bidirectional causality between the VIX spot and the implied volatility of S&P 500 options, indicating a volatility feedback mechanism. While the spot index tends to lag its own futures, vector autoregression error correction mechanisms demonstrate a significant mean-reverting equilibrium. These findings align with recent theories suggesting that implied volatility exerts a stronger feedback effect than realized volatility. Ultimately, the paper identifies retroactive information flows and offers fresh insights into the market microstructure of VIX derivatives and their associated S&P 500 options.

This paper investigates the eigenvalues associated with buckling problems on domains within a unit sphere. By incorporating a novel parameter and applying the Cauchy inequality, we refine the inequality previously established by Wang and Xia in [12].

Reinforcement learning constitutes a vital component of artificial intelligence. This paper offers a comprehensive review of model-free reinforcement learning that employs the average reward optimality criterion within an infinite horizon framework. Drawing inspiration from Mahadevan's 1996 solo survey, we provide an updated examination of this domain, expanding the scope to include policy-iteration and function approximation techniques alongside traditional value-iteration and tabular methods. Furthermore, we present a detailed mapping of the existing literature and highlight potential avenues for future research.

This study proposes a distributed coordination algorithm designed to address a hierarchical multi-agent decision-making problem. The main objective is to locate the Nash equilibrium of a noncooperative game, ensuring that no individual player benefits from unilaterally deviating from the equilibrium based on their private goals. Simultaneously, the agents collaborate to minimize the social cost among the available Nash equilibria. This optimal Nash equilibrium challenge can be framed as a distributed optimization problem subject to variational inequality constraints. The research focuses on scenarios where the objective functions for both the base game and the social cost optimization exhibit a specific aggregation structure. Given that each agent possesses only local information and lacks knowledge of all other players' decisions, a distributed approach is essential. By integrating Tikhonov regularization with dynamical averaging tracking, we introduce a distributed coordination algorithm that incorporates an incentive term alongside gradient-based Nash equilibrium seeking. This mechanism adjusts player decisions to enhance overall system efficiency. Theoretical analysis demonstrates the algorithm's convergence to the optimal Nash equilibrium in monotone aggregative games, supported by simulation results.

The search for extraterrestrial life represents a captivating field of study for planetary scientists and astrobiologists. The Earth Similarity Index (ESI) is traditionally calculated as the geometric mean of four physical attributes—radius, density, escape velocity, and surface temperature—yielding a score between 1 (identical to Earth) and 0 (completely dissimilar). This paper redefines the metric by incorporating two additional parameters, revolution and surface gravity, to create the New Earth Similarity Index (NESI). The study primarily focuses on identifying exoplanets capable of sustaining tardigrade life by adjusting the temperature variable within the NESI framework to establish the Tardigrade Similarity Index (TSI), which ranges from 1 (survivable) to 0 (non-survivable). The authors catalog and analyze both NESI and TSI scores for approximately 3,370 confirmed exoplanets.

By integrating recent developments in response theory and nonequilibrium ensemble reweighting, we investigate the dynamic and static correlations responsible for electric field-dependent ionic conductivity in electrolytes. Our analysis covers solutions modeled using both implicit and explicit solvents, varying dielectric properties, and multiple concentrations. Models utilizing implicit solvents at low concentrations and low dielectric constants display strong field-dependent conductivities. When compared to the Onsager-Wilson theory of the Wien effect, our results show qualitative agreement at low concentrations with high static dielectric constants but diverge elsewhere; this discrepancy arises from enhanced ion correlations under those specific conditions. In contrast, explicit solvent effects dampen nonlinear responses, resulting in weakly field-dependent conductivity across physically attainable field strengths. Through the decomposition of relevant time correlation functions, we attribute this field insensitivity to persistent frictional forces exerted by the solvent on the ions. These findings demonstrate the value of nonequilibrium response theory in explaining nonlinear transport phenomena.

This work offers a comprehensive re-examination of the theoretical foundations regarding Coulomb-nuclear interference (CNI), accompanied by a rigorous analysis of the method used to derive the fundamental parameters $\rho^{~pp}$, $\sigma_{tot}^{~pp}$, and $B^{~pp}$ from TOTEM data at $\sqrt{s} = 13$ TeV. By providing a more robust theoretical description of CNI and conducting a detailed statistical examination of the TOTEM data at low momentum transfer, our findings diverge from those previously reported by the TOTEM collaboration.

To address the challenge of selecting $p\geqslant 2$ representative points from the Pareto Front (PF) in bi-objective optimization, this paper investigates $p$-dispersion problems across four standard variants, introducing a new variant called Max-Sum-Neighbor $p$-dispersion specifically for 2d PFs. The study establishes that 2-dispersion and 3-dispersion problems can be solved in $O(n)$ time within a 2d PF. Furthermore, dynamic programming algorithms are developed for three other variants, demonstrating polynomial complexity in this context. Specifically, the Max-Min $p$-dispersion problem is solved in $O(pn\log n)$ time with $O(n)$ memory, the Max-Sum-Min variant in $O(pn^3)$ time and $O(pn^2)$ space, and the novel Max-Sum-Neighbor variant in $O(pn^2)$ time and $O(pn)$ space. The paper concludes by discussing complexity outcomes and parallelization strategies relevant to practical application.

This research investigates the behavior of solitary waves moving through a one-dimensional chain of bistable elements when encountering a localized inhomogeneity, or defect. Numerical simulations demonstrate that the outcome of an interaction—whether the wave is transmitted, captured, or reflected—depends on its initial velocity. The system's dynamics are primarily governed by energy transfer between the wave and a breather mode localized at the defect. We developed a reduced-order, two-degree-of-freedom Hamiltonian model to describe wave-breather interactions and analyzed it using dynamical systems methods. Specifically, lobe dynamics analysis uncovered the intricate phase space structure responsible for the system's complex behavior. Ultimately, this study contributes to establishing a rational framework for defect engineering to control nonlinear waves in mechanical metamaterials.

This study examines thermal entanglement in a system of two superconducting qubits across arbitrary interaction strengths and ground state frequencies, quantifying the phenomenon via concurrence calculations. We propose a configuration featuring an external tunable coupler qubit positioned between the two superconducting qubits to induce entanglement. The analysis of concurrence behavior addresses three distinct scenarios, evaluating the impacts of temperature, effective qubit-qubit coupling strength, and qubit frequencies on thermal entanglement. Notably, achieving maximally entangled states is most effective when the two superconducting qubits share identical frequencies. Furthermore, we observe that for a fixed temperature, thermal entanglement can be adjusted by modifying the internal capacitance and inductance of the qubits.

Simulations of explosive nucleosynthesis in novae forecast the creation of $^{22}$Na, a critical astronomical marker for refining nova models. However, its 1.275 MeV gamma-ray line remains undetected by current space-based gamma-ray telescopes. Additionally, the $^{20}$Ne/$^{22}$Ne ratio in presolar grains, a potential identifier for nova material, relies on $^{22}$Na production. Current uncertainties regarding $^{22}$Na yields in classical novae stem primarily from the reaction rate of $^{22}$Na(p, $\gamma$)$^{23}$Mg. At peak nova temperatures, this reaction is governed by a resonance at E$_{\text{R}}$=0.204 MeV, linked to the $E_x$=7.785 MeV excited state in $^{23}$Mg. Existing measurements of the resonance strengths for this state differ by a factor of ten. To address this, an experiment was conducted at GANIL to determine the lifetime and proton branching ratio of this pivotal state using femtosecond resolution. High-resolution detection systems, including the VAMOS, SPIDER, and AGATA spectrometers, were employed to study the reactions populating $^{23}$Mg states, enabling precise lifetime and branching measurements. This study compares the experimental findings with shell-model calculations, which successfully assigned the spin and parity of the key state. The derived values for reduced $M1$ matrix elements ($|M(M1)|\lesssim 0.5$ $\mu_N$) and proton spectroscopic factors ($C^{2}S_{\text{p}}$<10$^{-2}$) appear to exceed the current accuracy limits of the shell model. Based on the reevaluated $^{22}$Na(p, $\gamma$)$^{23}$Mg rate, future space telescopes show promising prospects for detecting $^{22}$Na and observing it from novae.

Multi-view representation learning is crucial for various multi-view applications, including classification and clustering. Nevertheless, the field faces two significant challenges: first, deriving robust multi-view representations from vast amounts of unlabeled data, and second, effectively balancing view consistency with view specificity. To address these issues, this paper introduces a hybrid contrastive fusion algorithm designed to extract robust, shared representations from unlabeled data. Specifically, we discovered that creating an additional representation space and aligning data within it facilitates the learning of robust view-common features. Concurrently, an asymmetric contrastive strategy was developed to prevent the model from converging to trivial solutions. Empirical results indicate that the proposed approach surpasses twelve state-of-the-art multi-view methods across four real-world datasets in both clustering and classification tasks. The source code will be made available shortly at \url{https://github.com/guanzhou-ke/mori-ran}.

This study presents experimental data on net-proton fluctuation measurements on an event-by-event basis from Pb-Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}$ = 2.76 TeV, recorded by the ALICE detector at the CERN LHC. The primary objective of these measurements is to experimentally validate Lattice QCD (LQCD) predictions regarding the second and higher-order cumulants of net-baryon distributions, thereby investigating critical behavior near the QCD phase boundary. Prior to comparing these results with LQCD predictions, it is essential to account for correlations resulting from baryon number conservation and fluctuations in the number of participating nucleons. Both factors impact experimental observations and are typically omitted in theoretical models. For the first time, this work demonstrates that event-by-event baryon number conservation generates subtle long-range correlations originating from very early stages of the collision interactions.

This paper addresses the multi-target detection challenge of reconstructing a signal from noisy measurements containing multiple unknown instances of that signal. Inspired by structure reconstruction in cryo-electron microscopy, we specifically investigate high-noise environments where detecting signal locations is difficult. While prior research utilized an autocorrelation analysis framework to estimate the signal directly by minimizing a least squares objective against observable autocorrelations—without explicitly identifying signal occurrences—this work extends that approach. We propose a generalized framework that substitutes the standard least squares method with a weighted least squares approach. The optimal weights for this method are derived directly from the data, ensuring advantageous statistical characteristics. Our results demonstrate effective signal recovery from highly noisy data, showing that the proposed weighted framework surpasses traditional autocorrelation analysis across a broad spectrum of parameters.

Quantum computing offers the potential to tackle numerous currently unsolvable physics problems, particularly those involving systems in or near thermal equilibrium. There are two primary methods for calculating thermal expectation values on a quantum computer: constructing a thermal state that mimics these values, or sampling energy eigenstates according to a Boltzmann distribution at a specific temperature. This paper focuses on the latter method, proposing an algorithm that utilizes active cooling to generate the required distribution. Although this approach is broadly applicable to diverse systems, it was specifically designed to simulate thermal configurations in non-Abelian gauge theories like QCD, thereby facilitating the study of quark-gluon plasma produced during heavy-ion collisions.

The human ether-a-go-go (hERG) potassium channel (K$_\text{v}11.1$) is essential for regulating cardiac action potentials, and its inhibition can precipitate fatal conditions or long QT syndrome. Consequently, numerous medications have been recalled due to severe hERG-related cardiotoxicity, making early assessment of hERG blockade activity vital during the initial phases of drug discovery. We specifically focus on evaluating the hERG-cardiotoxicity of compounds within the DrugBank database, given that many are either approved therapies or possess high drug development potential. Machine learning-based *in silico* tools provide a rapid and cost-effective means to virtually screen these DrugBank compounds. We have developed accurate and robust classifiers to distinguish between blockers and non-blockers, alongside regressors to quantify the binding potency of DrugBank compounds to the hERG channel. Molecular sequences are encoded using two natural language processing (NLP) techniques: autoencoders and transformers. Additionally, complementary three-dimensional (3D) molecular structures are represented via two sophisticated mathematical methods: topological Laplacians and algebraic graphs. Utilizing these state-of-the-art tools, we identified 227 potential hERG blockers among the 8,641 DrugBank compounds, highlighting significant drug safety concerns. Our predictions offer valuable guidance for subsequent experimental investigations into the hERG-cardiotoxicity of DrugBank compounds.

This technical report details the mission and lessons learned from a reconnaissance operation conducted at a Berlin industrial facility contaminated with hazardous materials following a major fire. The operation relied exclusively on UAVs and cameras to gather site data. Initially, a geo-referenced 3D model was generated to facilitate entry planning. UAVs were then deployed to navigate the severely damaged interior, capturing imagery via a 360° camera mounted beneath the drone, with a specific focus on areas that were challenging to access. Because the raw dataset included duplicate and blurred images, it was refined using visual SLAM, bundle adjustment, and blur detection to produce a usable 3D model and overviews. However, emergency services found the standard 3D model insufficient for extracting critical information. Consequently, an interactive panorama viewer was developed, featuring links to additional 360° images. These links were determined by the semi-dense point cloud and camera positions derived from the visual SLAM algorithm, enabling emergency responders to effectively visualize their surroundings.

The functional object-oriented network (FOON) serves as a graph-based knowledge representation designed for symbolic task planning. By retrieving information from the FOON, a robot can construct a task tree to generate a sequential plan for manipulation tasks. To assess the quality of these acquired trees, we translate them into recipes and compare them against human-created recipes from the Recipe1M+ dataset through a survey. Our preliminary findings indicate no significant differences between the FOON-generated recipes and the human-authored ones regarding correctness, completeness, and clarity.

Although dark matter (DM) has been confirmed through observations across a wide range of redshifts, the hypothesis of moderate DM particle decay remains viable. This encompasses models featuring extremely long-lived but unstable particles as well as mixed scenarios where only a minor portion of dark matter decays. This study examines the impact of DM decay into radiation on non-linear structure formation, analyzing the power spectrum and its redshift evolution as functions of decay lifetime ($\tau$) and the fraction of decaying DM ($f$). We introduce a fitting function achieving sub-percent accuracy for $k\sim10$ h/Mpc. Utilizing this fit, we forecast the sensitivity of a Euclid-like weak lensing (WL) survey to these parameters, incorporating massive neutrinos and baryonic feedback effects. Our results indicate that WL data alone can exclude decay lifetimes shorter than $\tau=75$ Gyr (at 95% CL) for fully unstable dark matter. This limit tightens to $\tau=182$ Gyr when combined with Planck CMB priors and further extends to $\tau=275$ Gyr if baryonic feedback is constrained by future Sunyaev-Zeldovich or X-ray data, representing a 3.2-fold improvement over CMB-only constraints. For a strongly decaying sub-component with $\tau\lesssim 30$ Gyr, we predict the ability to rule out decaying fractions of $f>0.49$, $f>0.21$, and $f>0.13$ (at 95% CL) under the same respective scenarios. Ultimately, we conclude that upcoming stage-IV weak lensing surveys will substantially enhance current limits on dark matter stability.

This paper establishes that $T_{2}^{1}(R) + WPHP(\square_{1}^{p}(R))$ does not imply $ontoPHP(R)$ using forcing techniques. As a secondary result, we construct a model satisfying $T_{2}^{1}(R) + \forall m \leq n^{1 - \epsilon} (PHP_{m}^{m + 1}(\square_{1}^{p}(R))) + \neg PHP_{n}^{n + 1}(R)$, where $n$ is non-standard and $\epsilon$ is arbitrarily small but standard. This finding represents progress toward an open problem originally raised by M. Ajtai in 1990.

Recent deep learning-based blind super-resolution (SR) techniques have demonstrated remarkable success in upscaling frames with unknown degradation by accurately estimating the downscaling kernel from low-resolution (LR) images to aid restoration. Despite their efficacy, these methods are primarily image-centric and fail to utilize the temporal characteristics of kernels across video sequences. This paper explores the temporal properties of such kernels, emphasizing their critical role in blind video super-resolution. We quantified kernel consistency in real-world footage and demonstrated how estimated kernels fluctuate per frame depending on the scene and object dynamics. Leveraging this insight, we re-evaluated established video SR methods, revealing that the common assumption of applying a fixed kernel throughout restoration often introduces visual artifacts in real-world scenarios. To address this, we adapted existing single-image and video SR strategies to incorporate kernel consistency during both kernel estimation and upscaling. Comprehensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world data confirm significant quantitative and qualitative improvements, establishing a new state-of-the-art for blind video SR and highlighting the benefits of exploiting kernel temporal consistency.

This study introduces a robust three-level time-split high-order Leapfrog/Crank-Nicolson scheme designed to solve the two-dimensional unsteady Sobolev and regularized long wave equations found in fluid mechanics. Stability and error estimates for this method are rigorously analyzed using the $L^{\infty}(0,T;H^{2})$-norm. Provided that the time step meets specific criteria, theoretical findings demonstrate that the numerical scheme is strongly stable (within the $L^{\infty}(0,T;H^{2})$-norm framework), achieves second-order accuracy in time, and exhibits spatial convergence of order $O(h^{\frac{8}{3}})$, where $h$ represents the grid size. These outcomes suggest that the proposed algorithm is faster and more efficient than many other numerical methods commonly cited in the literature for this specific problem. Furthermore, numerical experiments validate the theoretical predictions and highlight the effectiveness and practical utility of the three-level time-split high-order formulation.

Data regarding the energy spectrum and mass composition of ultra-high energy cosmic rays obtained by the Pierre Auger Observatory inform a benchmark scenario for extragalactic accelerator emission mechanisms, energetics, and elemental abundances. Assuming sources are distributed according to stellar mass density, the observed gradual rise in cosmic ray mass number on Earth from approximately 2 EeV to the highest energies implies that nuclei are accelerated to energies proportional to their electric charge and emitted with a hard spectral index. Furthermore, the inferred proton flux extending down to roughly 0.6 EeV necessitates a significantly softer spectral index for this population compared to heavier nuclei. This aligns with in-source interactions that affect the energy production rates of injected charged nuclei differently than those of secondary neutrons escaping confinement. Alongside the derived nuclear abundances, these findings constrain radiation levels within source environments. To account for the all-particle flux in the sub-ankle energy range, an additional component that declines steeply with increasing energy up to the ankle feature is required within this framework.

Tutte established that a graph $G$ is planar precisely when the conflict graph linked to each cycle in $G$ is bipartite. We introduce a signed conflict graph (which may not be unique) corresponding to a maximally planar subgraph of a nonplanar graph, such that if $G$ admits a flat embedding, every potential conflict graph derived from any maximally planar subgraph of $G$ remains balanced. Through this approach, we demonstrate that for any graph $G$ with a flat embedding and a planar subgraph $P$ within it, $P$ resides on a sphere that intersects $G$ exclusively at $P$. Furthermore, we conjecture that $G$ is intrinsically linked if and only if every maximal planar subgraph of $G$ yields an unbalanced conflict graph for all possible instances.

This article serves as a concluding overview and discussion of the author's recent research on the foundations of quantum theory. It demonstrates that quantum mechanics, under specific conditions, emerges from a significantly simpler, distinct model. This model is rooted in the mind of a single observer or the collective minds of communicating observers, relying on conceptual variables where an observer must determine which variable to measure. Furthermore, this framework is broadly connected to a theory of decision-making. The findings are examined from multiple perspectives, including a brief treatment of macroscopic consequences.

Although high-quality public datasets are becoming increasingly accessible, the scarcity of training samples remains a primary hurdle for deep learning in skin lesion analysis. Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have emerged as a promising solution to mitigate this by creating synthetic images that are virtually indistinguishable from real ones, leading to numerous studies applying them in medical contexts. However, rigorous experiments on skin-lesion diagnosis utilizing GAN-based data augmentation yield favorable outcomes exclusively on out-of-distribution test sets. Similarly, in GAN-based data anonymization, where synthetic images substitute real ones, positive results are also confined to out-of-distribution scenarios. Given the costs and risks tied to GAN deployment, these findings indicate that their use in medical applications warrants caution.

This study re-examines phase transitions within Twin Higgs (TH) frameworks, demonstrating that strong first-order phase transitions (FOPTs) are achievable if a suitable source of $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetry breaking exists between the twin and Standard Model (SM) sectors. We identified FOPTs in two distinct model classes: first, those featuring hard $\mathbb{Z}_2$ breaking within the scalar potential, and second, those where $\mathbb{Z}_2$ is broken by enhanced Yukawa couplings of twin leptons. Furthermore, we explored a supersymmetric ultraviolet completion for the latter scenario involving light sleptons. While the gravitational wave signatures from these transitions are generally weak, those arising from FOPTs driven by light twin sleptons may fall within the detection range of the AEDGE and Einstein Telescope experiments. These findings suggest a viable mechanism for generating the SM baryon asymmetry in TH models.

Accurate future forecasts are crucial for real-world applications where online prediction of streaming time series data drives downstream decisions. To function effectively in dynamic environments, models must rapidly adjust to shifting data distributions without succumbing to overfitting. We introduce POLA (Predicting Online by Learning rate Adaptation), a method that automatically tunes the learning rate of recurrent neural networks to accommodate evolving time series patterns. POLA meta-learns the stochastic gradient descent (SGD) learning rate by utilizing a prequential or interleaved-test-then-train evaluation framework for online prediction. Evaluated across two real-world datasets using three standard recurrent neural network architectures, POLA achieves predictive performance that is comparable to or superior to other existing online prediction methods.

The demand for analyzing multiple network datasets is rising, driven by the rapid expansion of applications requiring such techniques. These applications range from neuroscience studies of connectomes to computer science research on human mobility within intelligent display systems, all of which have become feasible thanks to recent technological breakthroughs in data collection. Both domains involve analyzing a diverse population of networks. This paper addresses the challenge of clustering elements within such a network population, where each cluster is defined by a representative network. Leveraging Bayesian methods, we simultaneously infer cluster membership, network representatives, and the community structure of those representatives. Comprehensive simulation studies demonstrate that our model effectively performs both multiple network data clustering and parameter inference.

Recommender systems encounter the cold-start issue when new users join or new items are introduced to the catalog. To tackle item cold-start, we suggest substituting the embedding layer in sequential recommenders with a dynamic storage mechanism that lacks learnable weights and can accommodate an unlimited number of representations. This paper introduces FELRec, a large embedding network that recursively refines user and item representations as fresh data emerges. Unlike comparable methods, our model handles new users and items without requiring side information or time-intensive fine-tuning. During item cold-start scenarios, our approach surpasses similar methods by 29.50% to 47.45%. Additionally, the proposed model demonstrates strong generalization capabilities on previously unseen datasets. The source code is publicly accessible at github.com/kweimann/FELRec.

The formation pathways of black holes (BHs)—determining whether massive stars end as core-collapse supernovae (CCSN) or directly collapse into BHs—significantly influence the nucleosynthetic yields averaged over the initial mass function (IMF) for a stellar population. Extending the research of Sukhbold et al. (2016), we calculate these IMF-averaged yields at solar metallicity across various scenarios, including neutrino-driven engine models with extensive BH formation, simple mass-threshold models for BH formation, and a scenario where all stars between $8-120 \text{M}_{\odot}$ explode. Depending on the assumptions made, total $\alpha$-element yields vary by a factor of three, while shifts in relative yields are more modest, typically ranging from 0.05 to 0.2 dex. Ratios of carbon and nitrogen to oxygen or magnesium serve as effective diagnostics for estimating the overall extent of BH formation. Conversely, abundance ratios involving manganese or nickel are useful for distinguishing between complex, theory-driven formation landscapes and simple mass thresholds, owing to their sensitivity to the progenitor core structures of CCSN. We reaffirm earlier findings of a significant (factor of 2.5–4) mismatch between predicted O/Mg yield ratios and observationally derived values, suggesting that current models either overproduce oxygen or underproduce magnesium. No single formation landscape successfully matches all observed abundance ratios; however, these discrepancies provide empirical insights into missing aspects of massive star evolution or explosion physics. Qualitatively consistent results are obtained using the massive star yields from Limongi & Chieffi (2018). We present tables of IMF-integrated yields for multiple landscape scenarios, and users can implement more flexible, custom models via the publicly available $\texttt{Versatile Integrator for Chemical Evolution}$ ($\texttt{VICE}$; https://pypi.org/project/vice/).

Models leveraging the Koopman operator or generator for nonlinear dynamical systems have emerged as effective tools for forecasting, feature extraction, state estimation, and control. For control-affine systems, these generators exhibit affine dependence on inputs, enabling practical finite-dimensional bilinear approximations of the dynamics. However, two primary challenges currently restrict the application of these approaches to actuated systems. First, the efficacy of existing methods is highly sensitive to the selection of basis functions for approximating the Koopman generator, and no universal selection strategy exists for non-measure-preserving systems. Second, when the full state is unobserved, obtaining a sufficiently rich set of functions to characterize the dynamics becomes difficult because standard time-delayed observable construction fails in the presence of actuation. To address these limitations, this work formulates the dynamics of observables governed by the Koopman generator as a bilinear hidden Markov model, estimating parameters via the expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm. The E-step utilizes a standard Kalman filter and smoother, while the M-step mirrors control-affine dynamic mode decomposition applied to the generator. The method's efficacy is demonstrated across three case studies: recovering a finite-dimensional Koopman-invariant subspace for an actuated system featuring a slow manifold; estimating Koopman eigenfunctions for the unforced Duffing equation; and implementing model-predictive control for a fluidic pinball system using only noisy observations of lift and drag.

We introduce a dynamic algorithm designed to maintain connected and 2-edge-connected components in an undirected graph under edge deletions. This Monte-Carlo randomized approach processes any sequence of deletions within $O(m + n \operatorname{polylog} n)$ total time. It can also answer queries regarding whether two specific vertices belong to the same (2-edge-)connected component in constant time. Our method relies on a general Monte-Carlo randomized reduction that transforms decremental $c$-edge-connectivity into a variant of fully-dynamic $c$-edge-connectivity on a sparse graph. Although Monte-Carlo based, our reduction includes a final self-check mechanism applicable to Las Vegas algorithms for static problems like Unique Perfect Matching.

For non-sparse graphs containing $\Omega(n \operatorname{polylog} n)$ edges, our algorithms for connectivity and 2-edge-connectivity process all deletions in optimal linear total time by leveraging existing fully-dynamic solutions. This advancement surpasses Thorup's [J.Alg. 1999] algorithm, which runs in $O(m \log (n^2 / m) + n \operatorname{polylog} n)$ time and achieves linear performance only for graphs with $\Omega(n^2)$ edges.

The constant amortized cost for edge deletions in decremental connectivity for non-sparse graphs contrasts with the $\Omega(\log n/\log\log n)$ worst-case time lower bound in the decremental setting [Alstrup, Thorup Husfeldt, FOCS'98] and the $\Omega(\log n)$ amortized time lower bound in the fully-dynamic setting [Patrascu and Demaine STOC'04].

This study examines vacuum nonlinear electrodynamics corrections to the radiation and spin-down of rapidly rotating pulsars using a perturbative QED framework, specifically the post-Maxwellian approximation. We derive and analyze an analytical formula for the intensity of the pulsar's radiation.

This study tackles the challenge of identifying scientific references within patents by framing the issue as a sequence labeling problem and evaluating the effectiveness of BERT models on these extended text sequences. Citing scientific literature in patents is crucial for understanding the link between academia and industry, yet previous research has largely relied solely on front-page metadata citations. Building upon earlier efforts that utilized Conditional Random Fields (CRF) and Flair for reference extraction, we enhance the quality of the training dataset and develop three BERT-based architectures (BERT, bioBERT, and sciBERT) using this refined labeled data. Our results demonstrate that improved training data significantly boosts model performance. Furthermore, the BERT models outperform both CRF and Flair, achieving cross-validation recall scores of approximately 97%. Using the top-performing model, we processed a dataset of 33,000 patents to extract citations and match them against the Web of Science database. This approach yielded 50% more references than previous methods, totaling 735,000 citations. These newly established connections between patents and publications will enable future research to investigate which specific types of scientific work drive innovation.

Advancements in molecular techniques now allow for the temporal monitoring of bacterial populations; however, deciphering community dynamics and their relationship to ecosystem function remains difficult given the vast microbial diversity. There is a critical need for conceptual frameworks that can interpret time-series data from taxonomically complex bacterial communities in terms of their ecological roles. A fundamental concept for structuring these ecological functions is the "niche," defined as the suite of strategies that allow a population to persist and determine its environmental impact. This study introduces a framework utilizing manifold learning to organize genomic data into bacterial metabolic niches over time. By applying this method to a long-term time-series dataset from the Linnaeus Microbial Observatory (LMO) in the Baltic Sea, we reconstructed the dynamics of these occupied metabolic niches. The findings indicate that occupied metabolic niches form a relatively low-dimensional space, grouping taxa with similar functional traits. Seasonality was a primary driver of these temporal patterns. Furthermore, the composition of these niches varied by season, with some being dominated by single bacterial taxa while others were shared among multiple taxa. These results demonstrate the utility of manifold learning in elucidating the connections between community composition and function in microbial ecosystems.

Recent advances show generative models surpassing extractive ones in Open Domain Question Answering (ODQA) by utilizing decoders to synthesize information across multiple passages. Despite this success, generative approaches are typically bulkier, slower due to auto-regressive beam search, and prone to hallucinations. To address these issues, we introduce an extension to transformer encoders that enables multi-passage information fusion via global representations for cross-sample attention over all tokens. Additionally, we propose a novel method for calculating answer span probabilities to effectively aggregate scores within the global sample space. Our approach achieves a $2.5$ Exact Match improvement over the state-of-the-art on the Natural Questions dataset while utilizing only $25\%$ of the parameters and $35\%$ of the inference latency; on the WebQuestions dataset, it gains $4.4$ Exact Match. When combined with synthetic data augmentation, it also outperforms larger models on TriviaQA. Given the high computational costs of ODQA models, our method's significant reductions in latency and parameter count make it especially advantageous.

Guarded recursion serves as a potent modal framework for recursion, effectively functioning as an abstract manifestation of step-indexing. Currently, it is widely applied within separation logic to model programming languages featuring advanced capabilities, particularly by resolving domain equations that include negative occurrences. Its multi-clocked variant further enables the programming and reasoning about coinductive types by encoding the productivity constraints necessary for recursive type definitions. This paper introduces the first type theory that integrates multi-clocked guarded recursion with the distinctive features of Cubical Type Theory, alongside a corresponding denotational semantics. By combining Higher Inductive Types (HITs) with guarded recursion, the framework facilitates straightforward programming and reasoning regarding coinductive types—such as finitely branching labelled transition systems—that are traditionally difficult to represent in type theory. Consequently, our findings demonstrate that bisimilarity for these structures implies path equality, allowing proofs to be transported along bisimilarity relations. A key technical contribution is a novel principle of induction under clocks, which permits universal quantification over clocks to commute with HITs up to type equivalence, a requirement essential for encoding coinductive types. While similar commutativity conditions for inductive types have previously been established as axioms in type theories employing multi-clocked guarded recursion, our formulation as an induction principle supports the development of general computation rules.

Open-world compositional zero-shot learning (OW-CZSL) aims to identify combinations of states and objects within images, relying solely on a limited training subset of these primitives without prior knowledge of unseen pairings. In this context, models navigate a vast output space encompassing every possible state-object combination. Unlike previous approaches that jointly learn composition embeddings, this work revisits a basic CZSL baseline by predicting states and objects as independent primitives. To foster primitive-specific feature development, the model equips state and object classifiers with distinct non-linear feature extractors. Additionally, it leverages external knowledge to assess composition feasibility, thereby pruning unfeasible options from the output space. Furthermore, a novel setting termed CZSL under partial supervision (pCZSL) is introduced, where training data may lack either state or object labels; our prior knowledge is utilized to infer these missing labels. The proposed Knowledge-Guided Simple Primitives (KG-SP) model achieves state-of-the-art performance in both OW-CZSL and pCZSL, outperforming recent competitors even when integrated with semi-supervised learning methods. Source code is accessible at: https://github.com/ExplainableML/KG-SP.

Kidney exchange initiatives were established to match incompatible donor-recipient pairs. Conversely, patients lacking a living donor must rely on deceased donor (DD) transplants. In India, deceased donors currently provide kidneys directly to individuals on the waitlist. While some articles and recent implementations in Italy have proposed initiating exchange chains from deceased donors, no mathematical model has previously addressed this integration. This study introduces an integer programming formulation that generates deceased donor-initiated chains by simultaneously considering paired exchange registries and deceased donor allocations. The research also addresses the potential overlap where recipients register in both registries independently. A long-term simulation demonstrates that even with a limited number of deceased donors, these chains can significantly increase the total number of potential transplants. Furthermore, the merged registry shows substantial reductions in waiting times and dropout rates.

We establish a universal limit on the rate at which the transverse field must decrease for quantum annealing to reach the ground state of a general Ising model, treating the process as occurring over infinite time. Our theorem relies on a strict upper bound for excitation probability in this infinite-time limit, serving as a mathematically rigorous alternative to earlier findings that depended solely on the leading-order term of the adiabatic condition's asymptotic expansion. Because our theorem provides a sufficient condition for convergence applicable to any generic transverse-field Ising model, individual specific problems may permit more efficient or faster tuning of the coefficient.

This study centers on the automated quantification of breast density in digital mammograms. By training a model with only categorical image-level labels, we achieve the ability to estimate continuous density percentages and generate pixel-wise support maps for dense areas. Specifically, we introduce a weakly supervised loss function that correlates density percentage with mask size.

This study addresses optimal control problems characterized by purely economic costs, which frequently result in optimal policies exhibiting a (nearly) bang-bang structure. We concentrate on policy approximations utilizing Model Predictive Control (MPC) and apply the deterministic policy gradient method to enhance MPC closed-loop performance under unmodeled stochasticity or model errors. When policies display a (nearly) bang-bang structure, we find that the policy gradient method often fails to generate meaningful updates to policy parameters. To address this challenge, we introduce a homotopy strategy grounded in the interior-point method, which relaxes the policy constraints during the learning process. Through an examination of a specific, well-known battery storage problem, we demonstrate that our proposed approach achieves faster and more homogeneous learning compared to a classical policy gradient method.

Hybrid Question Answering (HQA) focuses on deriving answers from diverse data sources, such as tables and passages connected to specific table cells. This heterogeneous data offers reasoning support at various levels of granularity, including column, row, cell, and link levels. Traditional HQA models typically retrieve either coarse- or fine-grained evidence to facilitate reasoning. Our comparative analysis reveals that while coarse-grained evidence is simpler to retrieve, it offers limited value to the reasoning process, whereas fine-grained evidence presents the inverse trade-off. To leverage the strengths and mitigate the weaknesses of evidence at different granularities, we introduce MuGER$^2$, a Multi-Granularity Evidence Retrieval and Reasoning framework. The retrieval component utilizes a unified retriever to acquire multi-granularity evidence from heterogeneous data, while the reasoning component employs an evidence selector to guide the answer reader toward fine-grained evidence based on the retrieved multi-granularity context. Experiments on the HybridQA dataset demonstrate that MuGER$^2$ substantially improves HQA performance, and ablation studies confirm the efficacy of both the retrieval and reasoning mechanisms.

Humans can decompose tasks into various combinations of attributes, a compositional view essential for rapid learning and adaptation by leveraging past experiences to generalize across new settings. This study aims to enable zero-shot policy generalization in Reinforcement Learning (RL) agents by exploiting task compositionality. We introduce a meta-RL approach featuring a disentangled task representation that explicitly encodes distinct task aspects. Generalization to unseen compositional tasks is achieved by inferring their representations through this disentanglement, eliminating the need for additional exploration. The method is evaluated across three simulated environments and a difficult real-world robotic insertion task. Results confirm that our approach successfully achieves zero-shot policy generalization on unseen compositional tasks.

Equipped with a large effective area for hard X-rays, high time resolution, and co-aligned instruments, AstroSat/LAXPC was designed to initiate a new era in rapid variability studies and wide spectral band measurements of X-ray binaries. Over the past five years, the instrument has largely achieved these scientific objectives. In the coming years, it is poised to make more significant discoveries. This paper highlights the primary achievements of AstroSat/LAXPC in unraveling the behavior of black hole and neutron star systems and discusses the exciting possibilities of the instrument's contribution to future science.

This problem examines a game played on a simple graph $G = (V, E)$ where each node represents a light. Clicking a vertex $v$ flips the state of $v$ and its adjacent neighbors. The objective is to determine a sequence of clicks that turns off all lights starting from a given configuration. While this game, known as *Lights Out*, was popularized by Tiger Electronics on a $5 \times 5$ grid, we focus here on solvable starting states to address the Most Clicks Problem (MCP): determining the maximum number of clicks needed to solve a worst-case initial configuration on $G$. The solution to the MCP is established for graphs with nullity 0, where every configuration is solvable. By extending a method introduced by Scherphius, we derive an upper bound for the MCP on all $(6k - 1) \times (6k - 1)$ grids. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this bound precisely resolves the MCP for all such grids with nullity 2. We conjecture that every nullity 2 grid adheres to the $(6k - 1) \times (6k - 1)$ size, which would imply that we have solved the MCP for all nullity 2 square grids.

Medical imaging examinations, including chest radiography, typically produce a vast array of uncommon findings alongside a limited set of common ones. Although a trained radiologist can master the visual patterns of rare conditions by reviewing a few representative cases, teaching machines to handle such "long-tailed" distributions is significantly more challenging, as conventional approaches tend to favor the most frequent categories. This paper introduces a comprehensive benchmark study addressing the long-tailed learning problem within the specific context of thoracic diseases on chest X-rays. Our goal is to optimize classification accuracy across both prevalent "head" classes and rare but critical "tail" classes using naturally distributed data. To achieve this, we propose a new, challenging benchmark designed to advance research into long-tailed learning methods for medical image classification. This benchmark comprises two chest X-ray datasets tailored for 19-way and 20-way thorax disease classification, featuring class distributions ranging from 53,000 to as few as 7 labeled training images. We evaluate both standard and state-of-the-art long-tailed learning techniques on this benchmark to identify the most effective aspects of these methods and derive insights for future algorithmic design. The datasets, trained models, and source code are accessible at https://github.com/VITA-Group/LongTailCXR.

A strong backdoor for a propositional logic formula $\phi$ within a tractable class $\mathcal{C}$ is a variable set $B$ where fixing every variable in $B$ yields a formula belonging to $\mathcal{C}$. Efficient solutions for the SAT problem arise when these backdoors are small or possess favorable structural properties, such as low backdoor treewidth. This paper introduces the concept of recursive backdoors, motivated by the insight that solving SAT involves independently recursing through components generated by partial variable assignments. The quality of a recursive backdoor is defined by its recursive backdoor depth. Much like backdoor treewidth, recursive backdoors of limited depth can encompass backdoors of arbitrary size that exhibit a treelike structure. Nevertheless, the two concepts are incomparable, and our findings establish novel tractability results for SAT.

This paper introduces a novel methodology to achieve nearly optimal estimates of computational resolution limits for two-dimensional super-resolution problems, as previously defined in *Appl. Comput. Harmon. Anal.* 56 (2022), *IEEE Trans. Inf. Theory* 67(7) (2021), and *Inverse Probl.* 37(10) (2021). The study presents five key contributions: (i) it refines the resolution estimates for detecting numbers and recovering locations in two-dimensional super-resolution to nearly optimal levels; (ii) it establishes a stability result for sparsity-promoting algorithms in two-dimensional super-resolution and Direction of Arrival (DOA) problems, demonstrating their optimal performance; (iii) the proposed techniques provide a foundation for achieving nearly optimal resolution limit estimates in higher-dimensional super-resolution scenarios; (iv) inspired by these methods, a new coordinate-combination-based model order detection algorithm is introduced for two-dimensional DOA estimation, with theoretical proof of its optimal performance; and (v) a new coordinate-combination-based MUSIC algorithm is proposed for super-resolving sources in two-dimensional DOA estimation, which exhibits excellent performance and offers significant advantages over conventional DOA algorithms. The coordinate-combination approach appears to be a promising strategy for multi-dimensional DOA estimation.

Since the 1953 introduction of the Metropolis algorithm, researchers have intensified efforts to develop better sampling techniques for statistical mechanics in physical and chemical contexts. A key challenge remains the characterization of thermally activated rare events occurring between long-lived metastable states, such as protein folding. Fully describing these dynamics requires determining both the finite-temperature canonical distribution function and the reaction current between reactant and product states. This study demonstrates a quantum computing approach to address this issue. By leveraging the link between classical stochastic dynamics and the Schrödinger equation, known as stochastic quantization, we variationally prepare quantum states to achieve unbiased sampling from a Boltzmann distribution. Furthermore, reaction rate constants can be calculated as ground state energies of appropriately transformed operators, utilizing a supersymmetric extension of the formalism. We also propose a hybrid quantum-classical sampling strategy designed to overcome local minima and explore configuration spaces within both real-space and spin Hamiltonians. The construction of these quantum algorithms is detailed without relying on oracles or quantum walk operators, and the potential quantum advantages for these applications are analyzed.

Ultrametric matrices possess a complex internal structure that is not immediately evident from their definition. Specifically, strictly ultrametric matrices serve as covariance matrices for certain weighted rooted binary trees. Due to their potential size and density, these matrices are challenging to store and process. This manuscript leverages the inherent tree structure of such matrices to sparsify them using a similarity transformation grounded in Haar-like wavelets. We demonstrate that, with overwhelming probability, an asymptotically negligible portion of off-diagonal entries in large, random strictly ultrametric matrices remain non-zero after this transformation. Furthermore, we introduce a rapid algorithm to compress these matrices directly from their tree representation. We also characterize the subclass of matrices diagonalized by these wavelets and provide a sufficient condition for approximating the spectrum of strictly ultrametric matrices that fall outside this subclass. Our approach grants computational access to the microbiologists' "Tree of Life" covariance model, which was previously too large to handle, and inspires a new wavelet-based phylogenetic $\beta$-diversity metric. Applying this metric to a metagenomic dataset reveals novel insights into noisy high-dimensional data and identifies speciation events critical for understanding the relationships between environmental factors and microbial composition.

This paper examines the group of endotrivial modules for specific $p$-groups. Although Carlson and Th\'evenaz previously determined these groups via support variety theory, we present new homotopical proofs for cyclic $p$-groups, the quaternion group of order 8, and generalized quaternion groups. These proofs utilize Galois descent and Picard spectral sequences, extending the work of Mathew and Stojanoska, and offer conceptual clarity regarding the classical findings of Carlson and Th\'evenaz.

We examine the genesis of jellyfish galaxies through radiation-hydrodynamic simulations involving gas-rich dwarf galaxies with a multi-phase interstellar medium (ISM). Our findings indicate that ram-pressure-stripped (RPS) ISM constitutes the primary source of molecular clumps in the near wake within 10 kpc of the galactic plane, whereas in-situ formation drives dense gas production in the distant tail of gas-rich galaxies. Although only 20% of near-wake molecular clumps derive from the intracluster medium (ICM), this proportion rises to 50% for clumps situated 80 kpc from the galactic center; this shift occurs because the cooling time of RPS gas shortens significantly ($\lesssim$ 10 Myr) due to ISM-ICM mixing. The tail region displays a star formation rate between $0.001$ and $0.01\,{\rm M_{\odot}\,yr^{-1}}$, with the majority of tail stars forming in the stripped wake within 10 kpc. These stars generate luminous H$\alpha$ blobs in the tail, while fainter H$\alpha$ tails (below $6\times10^{38}\,{\rm erg\,s^{-1}\,kpc^{-2}}$) arise primarily from collisional radiation and heating caused by mixing. Furthermore, stripped tails exhibit intermediate X-ray to H$\alpha$ surface brightness ratios (1.5$\lesssim F_{\rm X}/F_{\rm H\alpha}\lesssim$20), falling between the ratios observed in the ISM ($\lesssim$1.5) and pure ICM ($\gg$20). Consequently, our results imply that jellyfish features develop when strong ram pressure strips ISM from gas-rich galaxies, facilitating its mixing with the ICM and enhancing cooling within the tail.

This paper presents an updated version of an arXiv manuscript that re-examines the author's 2008 proof demonstrating the undecidability of the general tiling problem for the hyperbolic plane. By establishing a slightly stronger result, the author proves this using only a single regular polygon as the fundamental tile shape. This issue was first highlighted by Raphael Robinson in 1971, who provided a simplified proof of the Euclidean plane's undecidable tiling problem, originally established by Robert Berger in 1966. The current construction refines the recent arXiv work by significantly reducing the count of required prototiles.

This paper investigates the equivalence of fifth-order differential operators on a line under general fiber-preserving transformations using Cartan's method of equivalence. We address two distinct versions of this problem: the direct equivalence problem and a variant that establishes the necessary and sufficient conditions for two such operators to be related via a fiber-preserving gauge transformation.

We establish a shape theorem for internal diffusion limited aggregation on mated-CRT maps, a class of random planar maps that approximate Liouville quantum gravity (LQG) surfaces. The limiting shape is an LQG harmonic ball, which was constructed in a related paper. Additionally, we demonstrate a corresponding result for the divisible sandpile.

This work investigates the GKK algorithm applied to mean-payoff games lacking simple zero-weight cycles. We introduce a novel symmetric analysis that reduces Pisaruk's $O(n^2 N)$ iteration upper bound to $N + Ep + Em$, a figure smaller than $nN$, where $n$ represents the vertex count, $N$ the maximum absolute weight, and $Ep$ and $Em$ denote the game's largest finite energy and dual-energy values, respectively. Given that each iteration executes in $O(m)$ time, this approach surpasses the existing state-of-the-art pseudopolynomial runtime bound of $O(mnN)$ established by Brim et al., by leveraging the specific structure of the game graph. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the analysis by Dorfman, Kaplan, and Zwick remains applicable to the GKK algorithm, thereby subjecting it to the current best combinatorial runtime bound of $O(m 2^{n/2})$.

A cycle is defined as $2$-colored when its edges receive a proper coloring using two distinct colors. A graph $G$ is termed $(d,s)$-edge colorable if it is $d$-regular and possesses a proper $d$-edge coloring where each edge belongs to at least $s-1$ such $2$-colored $4$-cycles. For a $(d,s)$-edge colorable graph $G$ equipped with a list assignment $L$ of forbidden colors that meets specific sparsity requirements, we establish that a proper $d$-edge coloring of $G$ avoiding $L$ always exists. Specifically, there exists a proper edge coloring $\varphi$ such that for every edge $e$ in $G$, $\varphi(e)$ is not an element of $L(e)$.
A concise proof of Kneser's theorem using transversals is presented.

Analysis of $9\,\text{fb}^{-1}$ of proton-proton collision data recorded by the LHCb detector investigates seven decay channels of the $B_c^+$ meson into a $J/\psi$ or $\psi(2S)$ meson combined with three charged hadrons (kaons or pions). For the first time, the decays $B_c^+\rightarrow (\psi(2S)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi^+ \pi^-)\pi^+ $, $B_c^+\rightarrow \psi(2S)\pi^+\pi^+\pi^-$, $B_c^+\rightarrow J/\psi K^+\pi^+\pi^-$, and $B_c^+\rightarrow K^+K^+K^-$ are observed, while evidence is presented for $B_c^+\rightarrow \psi(2S)K^+K^-\pi^+$. In these measurements, both $J/\psi$ and $\psi(2S)$ mesons are identified through their dimuon decays. The study also reports branching fraction ratios among the various $B_c^+$ decay modes and the fractions proceeding via intermediate resonances. Overall, the findings strongly support the factorisation approach employed for the theoretical description of these decays.

Although cross-modality interaction is essential for Text-Video Retrieval (TVR), the impact of various factors influencing this interaction on performance remains underexplored. This study conducts an in-depth analysis of interaction paradigms, revealing that computation involves two distinct elements: interaction content at varying granularities and a matching function to identify semantically equivalent pairs. We further note that single-vector representations and implicit intensive functions significantly impede optimization. Addressing these issues, we propose a disentangled framework designed to capture sequential and hierarchical representations. First, leveraging the inherent sequential nature of both text and video, a Weighted Token-wise Interaction (WTI) module decouples content and adaptively utilizes pair-wise correlations, thereby constructing a superior disentangled manifold for sequential data. Second, we introduce Channel DeCorrelation Regularization (CDCR) to reduce redundancy among vector components, facilitating the learning of hierarchical representations. Our experiments demonstrate the efficacy of this disentangled approach across multiple benchmarks, where it significantly outperforms CLIP4Clip, achieving improvements of +2.9%, +3.1%, +7.9%, +2.3%, +2.8%, and +6.5% in R@1 scores on MSR-VTT, MSVD, VATEX, LSMDC, ActivityNet, and DiDeMo, respectively.

This study explores a new anytime control algorithm designed for wireless networked control systems subject to random packet dropouts. The controller generates tentative future control sequences by adapting to time-varying, Markovian computational capabilities. Both the sensor-controller and controller-actuator channels exhibit spatial and temporal correlations, which are modeled as a multi-state Markov process. To mitigate the impact of packet losses, a dual-buffer mechanism is introduced. Furthermore, a novel cycle-cost-based method is developed to derive stability conditions for the nonlinear plant, controller, network environment, and available computational resources.

We present an explanation of dynamical localization within a Bose-Einstein condensate (BEC) optomechanical system, covering both position and momentum domains. The proposed experimentally feasible setup consists of a Fabry-Perot cavity featuring a single movable mirror, driven by a single-mode standing wave. Our analysis examines changes in modulation intensity and the effective Planck constant. Considering current experimental capabilities, we outline a specific set of parameters required to observe this phenomenon in a laboratory setting.

Dynamic mechanism design has recently attracted substantial interest from economists and computer scientists. This framework models complex real-world scenarios by enabling agents to interact with a seller across multiple rounds, where their reward functions can evolve over time and depend on the current state. Typically, these interactions are formalized as a Markov Decision Process (MDP). We investigate the scenario where the MDP's reward and transition functions are unknown beforehand, aiming instead to derive an optimal mechanism from an offline dataset. By employing function approximation to manage large state spaces under mild expressiveness constraints, we develop a dynamic mechanism using offline reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms. The resulting mechanisms approximately satisfy three critical properties: efficiency, individual rationality, and truthfulness. Our approach relies on the pessimism principle and requires only a mild assumption regarding the coverage of the offline data. To our knowledge, this is the first offline RL algorithm for dynamic mechanism design that does not presuppose uniform data coverage.

We introduce a DialGPT-based model designed to generate creative dialogue responses conditioned on specific emotions: anger, disgust, fear, happiness, pain, sadness, and surprise. This model produces contextually appropriate replies based on an input sentence and a target emotion label, achieving an emotion expression accuracy of 0.6. Among the tested categories, neutral, fear, and disgust performed best. Furthermore, when assessing the intensity of the conveyed emotions, the model demonstrates the strongest expression for anger, fear, and disgust.

Phase I oncology trials aim to identify the maximum tolerated dose (MTD) for a drug under a given schedule, a process intended to enhance treatment safety without compromising efficacy. While it is generally accepted that toxicity rises with increasing doses for cytotoxic agents, the connection between toxicity and various scheduling combinations remains unclear. To address this, we introduced DRtox, a Bayesian dose-regimen assessment method that utilizes pharmacokinetics/pharmacodynamics (PK/PD) data to estimate the maximum tolerated dose-regimen (MTD-regimen) at the conclusion of the dose-escalation phase for subsequent phase selection. This approach models binary toxicity as a pharmacodynamic endpoint, deriving the dose-regimen toxicity relationship by integrating a dose-regimen PD model with a PD toxicity model. Specifically, the dose-regimen PD model employs nonlinear mixed-effects models, while the PD toxicity model utilizes two distinct Bayesian frameworks: a logistic model and a hierarchical model. Simulation studies across multiple scenarios assessed the method's operating characteristics, revealing that DRtox surpasses traditional model-based designs in accurately selecting the MTD-regimen. Furthermore, incorporating PK/PD information into DRtox yields more precise estimates of the full dose-regimen toxicity curve, potentially enabling recommendations for alternative, untested regimens for expansion cohorts. The DRtox method is designed for application at the end of the dose-escalation stage of an ongoing trial involving patients with relapsed or refractory acute myeloid leukemia (NCT03594955), pending the collection of all toxicity and PK/PD data.

Titan's upper atmosphere is replenished with volatiles, such as atomic oxygen, originating from cryovolcanic activity on Enceladus. Analogous atmospheric exchanges, where oxygen and ozone from TRAPPIST-1d are transferred to TRAPPIST-1e, could mimic biosignatures. To evaluate this potential false positive, we utilized a coupled 1-D photochemical-climate model (Atmos) to simulate the introduction of external water and oxygen into TRAPPIST-1e's upper atmosphere, thereby predicting atmospheric composition. Furthermore, we generated synthetic spectral data using the Planetary Spectrum Generator to assess detectability across the James Webb Space Telescope, Origins Space Telescope, Habitable Exoplanet Observatory, and Large Ultra-violet/Optical/Infrared Surveyor, specifically in the presence of both biotic and abiotic methane surface fluxes. Our analysis reveals that the influx of material required to produce detectable abiotic O2/O3 signals for any of these observatories exceeds 1E12 molecules/cm²/s, a value that is more than two orders of magnitude greater than what is physically feasible.

Using the oxDNA model, we simulate the assembly of DNA copolymers from two types of short duplexes, each featuring single-stranded overhangs at both ends. We demonstrate that the distribution of chain lengths aligns well with a simple theoretical framework that models particle association into ideal, non-interacting clusters as a reversible chemical reaction. The reaction constants for this process can be derived either from Santalucia's theory or from Wertheim's thermodynamic perturbation theory regarding association in spherical patchy particles. These findings indicate that theories relying on minimal molecular details can effectively predict the broad equilibrium characteristics of copolymerization.

Risk Capital Allocations (RCAs) serve as a vital instrument in quantitative risk management, facilitating tasks such as evaluating business unit profitability, pricing new products, and performing marginal economic capital analysis. However, the concept of RCA often remains overshadowed by the closely related notion of Risk Measures (RMs), which frequently dictate the implementation of RCAs. Since most contemporary RCAs are derived from RMs, their popularity is intrinsically linked. Consequently, the RCA induced by the Conditional Tail Expectation (CTE) RM has dominated both academic literature and practical applications. Although the CTE RM is a robust mathematical construct and a significant regulatory standard, its suitability for profitability analysis and pricing remains debated. This paper investigates whether RCAs derived from the CTE RM can align with alternatives grounded in profit maximization principles. Specifically, we comprehensively characterize all probabilistic model settings where the mathematical and regulatory CTE RM accurately reflects the risk perception of a profit-maximizing insurer.

Investigating the structure and interactions of diverse matter forms usually requires scattering experiments involving various projectile particles. While beams of electrons, muons, pions, kaons, protons, antiprotons, and heavy ions have driven significant scientific advances, generating beams of antineutrons, hyperons ($\Lambda$, $\Sigma$, $\Xi$), and their antiparticles remains challenging. This paper introduces and examines a novel, high-quality source for these particles: a super $J/\psi$ factory capable of accumulating trillions of $J/\psi$ decays annually. In the pertinent decay channels, the target particle is produced alongside other final-state particles that serve as tags. This tagging mechanism allows for the precise determination of the projectile's flux and momentum, facilitating an unprecedentedly precise study of interactions across a wide range of targets. These new, high-statistics sources of baryons and antibaryons, characterized by precisely known kinematics, unlock fresh avenues in particle and nuclear physics. Applications include the study of antinucleon-nucleon interactions, the nonvalence $s\bar{s}$ component of the nucleon, (anti)hyperon-nucleon interactions, OZI violation, (multi-strange) hypernuclei, exotic light hadron spectroscopy, and numerous other areas, as well as the calibration of Monte Carlo simulations for hadronic and medical physics.

We examine the optical characteristics of both monolayer and multi-layered BiI$_3$, uncovering that excitons exist exclusively within the monolayer form. Utilizing time-dependent density functional theory, we assess the energy spectrum of the dielectric function. As an atomic layered semiconductor, bulk BiI$_3$ possesses a band gap aligned with the frequency of visible light. Our numerical findings for the bulk material align with prior experimental data and remain consistent across varying layer counts, with the notable exception of the monolayer. Specifically, we identify excitons emerging beneath the resonant peak linked to inter-band excitation in the monolayer. This distinctive optical feature is observable in optical absorption or differential reflectance spectra, effectively distinguishing the monolayer from stacked BiI$_3$ structures.

This study evaluates the effectiveness of sentence embedding models across various tasks in Russian. Our comparison encompasses multiple-choice question answering, next sentence prediction, and paraphrase identification. We utilize FastText embeddings as a baseline, contrasting them with ELMo and BERT. Two distinct experimental series are conducted, employing both unsupervised methods (relying solely on similarity measures) and supervised approaches. Additionally, we introduce new datasets for Russian multiple-choice question answering and next sentence prediction.

We incorporate a long-period generic spatial modulation into the standard Rice--Mele (RM) model, a representative system for the Thouless pump, to investigate the lattice counterpart of fermion charge in quantum field theory. By deriving a Diophantine equation that connects fermion charge to pumped charge, we establish the one-dimensional (1D) equivalent of the Streda formula known from the quantum Hall effect (QHE). This relationship indicates that adiabatically altering the periodicity of the spatial modulation results in a spatial charge pump where the rightmost charge shifts rightward by an amount determined by the Chern number relative to the leftmost charge. Consequently, the length of the fermion chain changes by an integer, enabling the direct experimental verification of the 1D Streda formula.

Young multiple star systems accumulate the bulk of their final mass within the first few million years of existence, spanning the protostellar and protoplanetary stages. Earlier research indicated that in binary systems, the majority of accreted material falls onto the less massive star, driving the system toward mass equalization. However, young stellar populations frequently consist of more than two stars arranged in hierarchical configurations. Although differential accretion in these hierarchical systems holds significant astrophysical importance, the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. This study investigates whether accretion patterns observed in binaries extend to higher-order multiples. We conducted a series of 3D Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics simulations using the Phantom code, modeling both binaries and hierarchical triples (HTs) embedded within an accretion disc. For the first time, we have identified specific accretion trends in HTs and quantified their deviations from binary behavior. These deviations, resulting from the interaction between the inner binary and infalling material from the circum-triple disc, can be modeled using a semi-analytical prescription. Generally, the smaller binary within an HT accretes more mass than a single star of equivalent mass. We found that if the inner binary is more massive than the third body, the standard differential accretion scenario (where the secondary gains more mass) is suppressed; conversely, if the inner binary is less massive than the third body, this standard scenario is amplified. This unique differential accretion mechanism in HTs is anticipated to influence their mass ratio distribution.

This paper introduces SIA_Track, a method developed by the research team at SI Analytics. Built upon the tracking-by-detection paradigm, the approach utilizes pre-existing detectors and trackers, where the tracker component operates online by associating new detections with current tracks. The central innovation lies in the object detector's training procedure, which relies exclusively on synthetic and unlabeled real data. To optimize performance on real-world data, the method first employs pseudo-labeling to generate imperfect labels for real data using a model trained on synthetic datasets.
