Utilizing these findings, we examine the direct consequences for the mass spectrum of ultra-light scalar (axion-like), vector (dark photon), and tensor (additional spin-2) particles, specifically addressing the previously unexplored parameter range of $10^{-20}-10^{-19}$eV. Considering that self-interactions might inhibit axion instability and explain the lack of observed superradiance, we derive upper limits on the axion decay constant (which correspond to lower limits on self-interaction strength). Furthermore, assuming axions are defined by mass and decay constant, we determine the maximum fraction of dark matter attributable to ultra-light particles, concluding that a single species of axion-like particle can account for no more than $10\%$ of dark matter within the mass interval $10^{-21} < \mu \, (\mathrm{eV}) < 10^{-17}$.

Monolayer graphene serves as an ideal system for investigating fundamental light-field driven interference phenomena, specifically Landau-Zener-Stückelberg interference. Nevertheless, directly visualizing the resulting interference patterns in momentum space has remained elusive; to date, such interference has only been inferred indirectly via optically induced residual currents. In this study, we demonstrate that the transient electron momentum density (EMD)—a quantity readily accessible experimentally—offers a robust description of momentum-resolved charge excitations. Utilizing cutting-edge time-dependent density functional theory, we confirm the strong agreement between EMD and conduction band occupancy by comparing them directly; the latter is derived by projecting the time-evolved wavefunction onto the ground state. Furthermore, even under the most intense laser pulses, electron dynamics are found to be nearly exclusively governed by the $\pi$-band, with transitions to other bands being heavily suppressed. Consequently, simple model-based tight-binding approaches are expected to accurately describe laser-induced electron dynamics in graphene.

Traditionally, verifying if decision-makers adhere to specific axioms based on choice data has followed two distinct methods: the functional approach, which imposes constraints on the complete demand function, and the revealed preference approach, which formulates algebraic inequalities to evaluate finite datasets. Leveraging restrictions identified in \cite{kubler2020identification}, this paper establishes a connection between revealed preference tests and function-based constraints. Specifically, we show that any functional restriction capable of characterizing these axioms can be adapted to create a robust test for finite data. Furthermore, we propose an algorithm to execute this conversion efficiently.

This study extends the definition of $\lambda$-radial contraction to complete Riemannian manifolds and introduces the concept of $p^\lambda$-convex functions. Furthermore, a counterexample is provided to demonstrate that, generally, the $\lambda$-radial contraction of a geodesic does not necessarily result in a geodesic. Additionally, we establish relationships between geodesic convex sets and $p^\lambda$-convex sets, proving their equivalence under specific conditions.

This Letter explores the jet-launching capabilities of Bondi-like accretion flows characterized by zero or minimal specific angular momentum through 3D general relativistic magnetohydrodynamic simulations. To test the potential for magnetic jet generation, we introduce large-scale poloidal magnetic fields into the accretion flow around a rapidly rotating black hole. Our findings indicate that the initial magnitude of gas specific angular momentum is the decisive factor in determining whether the disk can achieve and maintain the magnetically arrested disk (MAD) state, which drives exceptionally powerful jets with energy efficiencies exceeding $\gtrsim 100\%$. We observe that MAD states can form even with trace amounts of specific angular momentum, and episodic jets with an average efficiency of roughly $10\%$ persist even when the gas possesses no initial angular momentum. These results offer viable explanations for the production of jets in diverse astrophysical environments lacking significant gas specific angular momentum, including Sgr A*, wind-fed X-ray binaries, tidal disruption events, and long-duration gamma-ray bursts.

Any ordered family of sets within Euclidean space can be linked to a combinatorial code that documents the spatial regions defined by these sets. When considering two such ordered families, a third family can be constructed where each set is the Cartesian product of the corresponding sets from the original families. We establish a general "product theorem" that describes the code of this resulting family based on the codes of the initial families. Leveraging this theorem, we characterize the codes achievable by axis-parallel boxes and highlight distinctions between these codes and those generated by convex open or closed sets. Furthermore, we apply our theorem to demonstrate that a "monotonicity of open convexity" result by Cruz, Giusti, Itskov, and Kronholm remains valid for closed sets provided certain assumptions are slightly relaxed.

Radiative corrections influencing $B \to D \ell \nu_{\ell}$ decays could significantly affect predictions and measurements of the lepton flavour universality ratios $\mathcal{R}(D^+)$ and $\mathcal{R}(D^0)$. This study compares recent calculations of soft-photon corrections for these ratios against those produced by the commonly used PHOTOS package, while also addressing long-distance Coulomb interactions that PHOTOS does not simulate. Additionally, high-energy photon emission effects are investigated via pseudo-experiments within an LHCb-like setting. Results indicate that misestimating these emissions can introduce a bias in $\mathcal{R}(D)$ of up to 7%, though this bias varies across specific analyses. Consequently, achieving future high-precision measurements necessitates a rigorous and accurate assessment of these QED corrections.

The LIGO Scientific Collaboration employs the FINDCHIRP algorithm for matched-filter searches targeting gravitational waves from merging compact binaries. This approach implements optimal filtering with specific enhancements designed to handle uncertain signal parameters and enhance performance against detector data containing nonstationary and non-Gaussian noise. We present detailed information regarding the application of FINDCHIRP in searches for subsolar mass binaries, binary neutron stars, neutron star-black hole binaries, and binary black holes.

This presentation outlines recent experimental findings on $C\!P$ violation within the $B^0$ and $B^\pm$ meson sectors, published by the Belle, Belle II, and LHCb collaborations over the past two years. The discussion covers four main areas: first, the measurement of Unitarity Triangle angles; second, a critical test of the Standard Model involving the isospin sum rule for $B \to K\pi$ decays; third, investigations into $C\!P$ violation in the decays of charged $B$ mesons into charmless three-body final states; and finally, an overview of future prospects for upgrading this experimental sector.

This paper introduces a continual learning framework for Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) that utilizes parameter-efficient transformations of feature maps. The methodology relies on acquiring both global and task-specific parameters; while global parameters remain constant across tasks, the task-specific parameters function as local adapters to efficiently derive task-specific feature maps. Additionally, we introduce an element-wise residual bias addition within the transformed feature space, which further stabilizes GAN training in this context. Our approach also incorporates task similarity metrics derived from the Fisher information matrix, where knowledge from prior tasks significantly enhances performance. Furthermore, this similarity measure aids in minimizing parameter expansion during continual adaptation, facilitating the learning of a compact model. Unlike recent continual learning methods for GANs, our approach offers a memory-efficient solution for effective continual data generation. Extensive experiments on diverse and challenging datasets demonstrate that this feature-map transformation strategy surpasses state-of-the-art continual GAN methods, achieving superior results with substantially fewer parameters. Additionally, the proposed method produces high-quality samples and can enhance generative-replay-based continual learning for discriminative tasks.

This research initiates the investigation of derived functors within extriangulated categories. By employing coends, we modify Yoneda's theory of higher extensions to fit this context. We demonstrate that, in the presence of sufficient projectives or injectives, these newly defined extensions coincide with those previously established via projective or injective resolutions. Furthermore, for categories possessing enough projective or injective morphisms, we establish that these extensions function as the right derived functors of the $\operatorname{Hom}$-bifunctor in either variable. Given that $\operatorname{Hom}$ is only half-exact in each argument, it is anticipated that "negative extensions"—specifically, its left derived functors—should exist and may not necessarily vanish. We define negative extensions relative to both the first and second arguments, proving they generate universal $\delta$-functors when sufficient projective or injective morphisms exist, respectively. Generally, these extensions lack balance; however, in the realm of topological extriangulated categories, a balanced version of negative extensions arises by synthesizing Klemenc's work on exact $\infty$-categories with results from the second and third authors. We examine various criteria ensuring the balance of these bifunctors at both the functorial and numerical levels. Such balance occurs, for instance, in exact or triangulated categories, as well as in the category of $n$-term complexes with projective components over a finite-dimensional algebra. Additionally, for a connected sequence of functors on an extriangulated category $(\mathcal{C},\mathbb{E},\mathfrak{s})$, we identify the maximal relative extriangulated structure rendering the sequence a $\delta$-functor. We also derive several equivalent conditions for the existence of enough projective or injective morphisms within a given extriangulated category.

The integration of optical-frequency combs into photonic platforms promises to expand the application of precision timing signals. In this study, we investigate the creation of an octave-spanning Kerr microresonator frequency comb through the hybrid integration of an InP distributed-feedback laser and a silicon nitride (SiN) photonic integrated circuit. We present electrically pumped, fiber-coupled prototype systems made possible by self-injection locking. This direct coupling of a laser and microresonator circuit, which eliminates the need for intermediate components such as optical modulators and isolators, requires a deeper understanding of self-injection-locking dynamics within the context of octave-spanning Kerr solitons. Specifically, system designs must account for the significant interplay between microresonator back-scattering and the frequency detuning between the laser and microresonator that we have identified. Our findings highlight essential factors for achieving a self-referenced frequency comb using integrated photonics.

Collaborative intrusion detection networks frequently offer superior detection accuracy and cost-effectiveness relative to standalone host-based intrusion detection systems (IDS). By leveraging cooperation, a local IDS can identify novel attacks that are already recognized by other experienced peers. This paper introduces a sequential hypothesis testing approach for aggregating feedback within each IDS in the network. Our simulation outcomes validate our theoretical findings and illustrate the advantages of cost efficiency and accuracy when compared to alternative heuristic methods. Furthermore, the analytical derivation of the lower bound for the average number of acquaintances required for consultation is critical for the design and configuration of IDSs operating in collaborative settings.

This paper investigates nonlinear partial differential equations within a port-Hamiltonian framework grounded in jet-bundle geometry. The study focuses on systems defined over a one-dimensional spatial domain, featuring second-order Hamiltonians alongside specific dissipation models integrated via suitable differential operators. For this class of systems, the paper analyzes and demonstrates energy-based control strategies, including the use of Casimir functionals and energy balancing, through the example of a nonlinear Euler-Bernoulli beam.

The classical model of stochastic reorientations within an asymmetric double well potential (ADWP) is used to analyze the dielectric response of non-interacting dipoles. In the nonlinear regime, this model displays specific anomalies in its static response; notably, the saturation behavior of the symmetric double well potential deviates from the Langevin function, with standard results only emerging in the linear regime. When finite asymmetry is introduced, nonlinear susceptibilities are observed to change signs at several characteristic temperatures dependent on the asymmetry's magnitude, a phenomenon previously noted for third- and fifth-order responses. Assuming the barrier crossing kinetics follow a two-state model yields analytical expressions for these temperatures. Numerical solutions of the Fokker-Planck equation for Brownian motion in an ADWP show behavior very similar to the two-state model when barriers are high. Conversely, for small barriers, a clear separation of time scales between barrier crossing and intra-well relaxation is absent, resulting in multiple time scales. In such cases, the frequency-dependent linear susceptibility at low temperatures is governed by rapid intra-well transitions, shifting to barrier crossing kinetics at higher temperatures. Furthermore, for nonlinear susceptibilities, the barrier crossing process proves more significant, with intra-well transitions playing a role only at the lowest temperatures.

We introduce and assess a new approach for the automated identification of clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa) within bi-parametric magnetic resonance imaging (bpMRI). Given the critical role of prostate zones in MRI-based cancer assessment, we hypothesize that incorporating zonal data can enhance the efficacy of deep learning models for csPCa lesion detection. While segmenting these zones is difficult—rendering deterministic models imprecise—we explored the use of probabilistic zonal segmentation. Our baseline architecture consists of a 2DUNet generating a csPCa heatmap, followed by a 3D detector. We tested the integration of zonal prior information by combining the output of an anisotropic 3DUNet, which produced either deterministic or probabilistic maps for each zone, with our detection model. Furthermore, we examined the impact of early versus late fusion strategies on detection performance. Trained and evaluated on a dataset of 848 bpMRI scans, our results indicate that integrating zonal prior knowledge improves the baseline model, with probabilistic segmentation outperforming deterministic approaches.

Shuttling individual electron spins coherently across quantum dot arrays is essential for building scalable quantum information systems, enabling the efficient resolution of one- and two-qubit gate operations using sparsely populated spin ensembles. However, moving electrons exposes them to site-specific environmental interactions, notably hyperfine coupling with substrate nuclear spins. This study demonstrates that multi-directional displacement of electrons within a $3\times 3$ tunnel-coupled quantum dot array extends spin coherence time through motional narrowing. By investigating up to 10 distinct electron configurations, we observed that fast, repetitive displacement can increase coherence time by a factor of up to 10. A simple model quantitatively describes the physical mechanism behind displacement-induced coherence loss, and its implications for spin dynamics in large-scale quantum circuits are discussed.

This study introduces an adaptive backstepping controller grounded in rigid graph theory, designed to solve distance-based formation control and target tracking for nonlinear multi-agent systems subject to bounded time-delays and disturbances. To handle unknown nonlinearities and disturbances within system dynamics, a radial basis function neural network (RBFNN) is employed. The adverse effects of agent state time-delays are mitigated through a control signal derived from a specific Lyapunov function and Young's inequality, which also facilitates the derivation of the adaptive tuning law for neural network weights. Furthermore, an upper bound for the singular value of the normalized rigidity matrix is established, allowing for a rigorous proof of the uniform ultimate boundedness (UUB) of formation distance errors via Lyapunov stability theory. The efficacy and performance of this approach are confirmed through simulations on nonlinear multi-agent systems, with comparative analysis against an existing displacement-based method to demonstrate the proposed technique's advantages.

Humans possess an innate capacity to acquire new concepts from minimal examples and apply them across various scenarios. Although contemporary machine learning models perform exceptionally well on standard recognition tasks when provided with vast datasets, a significant divide remains between machine-based pattern recognition and human-level concept learning. To bridge this gap, Bongard problems (BPs) were established as a stimulating challenge for visual cognition in intelligent systems. Despite recent progress in representation learning and meta-learning, BPs continue to pose a formidable obstacle for modern artificial intelligence. Drawing inspiration from the original set of one hundred BPs, we introduce a new benchmark called Bongard-LOGO, designed to evaluate human-level concept learning and reasoning. We utilize a program-guided generation method to create a extensive collection of visual cognition problems that are interpretable by humans and expressed in the action-oriented LOGO language. Our benchmark encapsulates three fundamental aspects of human cognition: 1) context-dependent perception, where identical objects can be interpreted differently based on surrounding context; 2) analogy-making perception, involving the exchange of one meaningful concept for another; and 3) the ability to perceive using few samples yet with an infinite vocabulary. Experimental results demonstrate that current state-of-the-art deep learning approaches perform significantly worse than human participants, indicating a failure to capture essential human cognitive properties. Finally, we outline potential research directions aimed at developing a general architecture for visual reasoning to address this benchmark.
It has been demonstrated that if the dual of a separable Banach space satisfies Property($K^*$), then the space itself possesses the weak fixed point property, thereby enhancing earlier findings.

In financial documents like news articles and reports, causality defines the primary relationship between events, consisting of a cause span and an effect span. While prior research has utilized sequence labeling for this task, such models struggle to identify multiple or overlapping causalities within text segments. This paper introduces a generative approach for causality extraction leveraging an encoder-decoder framework with pointer networks. Experiments conducted on the *FinCausal* dataset from the financial domain demonstrate that our proposed framework achieves highly competitive performance.

We introduce a proof-by-simulation framework designed to rigorously regulate the operating characteristics of trial designs across continuous regions of parameter space. This approach achieves two primary objectives: (1) calibrating a design to ensure provable Type I Error control at a specified alpha level, and (2) bounding, with high probability, the operating characteristics—such as Type I Error, FDR, or estimator bias—of a fixed design. The framework accommodates adaptive sampling, nuisance parameters, administrative censoring, multiple arms, and multiple testing procedures. These methods, termed Continuous Simulation Extension (CSE), were initially developed by Sklar (2021) to manage Type I Error and FWER for designs involving exponential family likelihoods with unknown parameters. Our appendix enhances these results through more efficient calibration and bounding techniques, extends the scope to general operating characteristics including FDR and bias, and broadens applicability to canonical generalized linear models (GLMs) and certain non-parametric problems. The main paper illustrates the CSE methodology and accompanying software across three examples: (1) a basic introduction analyzing the z-test; (2) a hierarchical Bayesian analysis of four treatments with fixed sample sizes; and (3) an adaptive Bayesian Phase II-III selection design with four arms, utilizing interim dropping and go/no-go decisions based on a hierarchical model. The latter two examples required trillions of simulations, facilitated by specialized INLA software. Open-source software is maintained at (1).

This study introduces a computational simulation of non-central collisions between two spherical neodymium-iron-boron magnets, designed to illustrate the principle of angular momentum conservation. The simulation solves Newtonian equations of motion by incorporating both an attractive dipole-dipole interaction and a repulsive contact force. We validate angular momentum conservation and analyze energy transformations during the collision. By utilizing the precise formulation of the dipole-dipole force, which accounts for non-central components, our model accurately predicts the final rotational frequencies—a result that simple power-law approximations fail to achieve.

Recent literature has explored various planning-based know-how logics. This paper employs such a logic to achieve know-how-based planning through model checking. Specifically, we address higher-order epistemic planning where goals are defined by know-how formulas; for instance, determining a plan to ensure $p$ such that an adversary cannot know how to falsify $p$ in the future. We provide a polynomial-time (PTIME) algorithm for model checking over finite epistemic transition systems and axiomatize the logic assuming perfect recall.

Accurately forecasting the remaining duration of active business processes is a critical area of study, particularly in retail where timely order delivery serves as a primary driver of customer satisfaction and competitive advantage. While process mining has already yielded numerous techniques for predicting remaining times, this work enhances stochastic Petri nets with generally distributed transitions by integrating the k-nearest neighbors (k-NN) algorithm. This approach applies k-NN to vectors representing the elapsed time of prior activities. By selecting a specific subset of instances, the method generates a more representative and stable stochastic Petri Net, which significantly improves prediction accuracy. We outline the technique and its Python implementation, evaluating its effectiveness using various real-world datasets. The experimental results demonstrate that combining these two methods offers distinct advantages in terms of predictive performance.

Establishing situational awareness relies heavily on the ability to associate and track sensor detections. However, Multi-Target Tracking (MTT) becomes a difficult endeavor when targets are numerous and highly maneuverable. Traditional methods, which address this NP-hard combinatorial optimization problem, often rely on intricate models and extensive parameter tuning, resulting in poor performance within strict computational limits. This paper introduces a model-free, end-to-end solution for airborne target tracking that utilizes sensor data. It integrates the core components of MTT—association, prediction, and filtering—through deep learning with memory capabilities. Specifically, the Bi-Directional Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network handles the challenging association task, while standard LSTM models manage filtering and prediction. These modular components can be trained independently and deployed across various tracking scenarios, accommodating both non-cooperative sensors (such as radar) and cooperative ones (like AIS, IFF, and ADS-B). Furthermore, this modularity improves the interpretability of the deep learning system. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed technique surpasses the performance of conventional state-of-the-art methods, such as the Joint Probabilistic Data Association with Interacting Multiple Model (JPDA-IMM) filter.

This work outlines the rationale, methodology, and validation of the "SKYSURF" project, an archival legacy initiative utilizing the Hubble Space Telescope (HST). Leveraging HST's precision as an absolute photometer, SKYSURF analyzes approximately 250,000 exposures from WFPC2, ACS, and WFC3 instruments across roughly 1,400 independent fields to measure sky surface brightness (SB) in the 0.2–1.7 $\mu$m range. The resulting panchromatic dataset aims to constrain discrete and diffuse components of the sky, including Zodiacal Light (ZL) from the inner Solar System, Kuiper Belt Objects (KBOs) from the outer Solar System, Diffuse Galactic Light (DGL), and both discrete and diffuse Extragalactic Background Light (EBL). The project details three key methodological goals: (1) determining sky-SB levels between detected objects, (2) quantifying the integrated discrete EBL (primarily from galaxies with AB magnitudes of 17–22), and (3) estimating the extent of diffuse light beyond extrapolated discrete galaxy counts. To achieve this, simulations of WFC3/IR images incorporating known sky values, gradients, realistic cosmic ray distributions, and star/galaxy counts were processed using nine distinct algorithms to determine the "Lowest Estimated Sky-SB" (LES). These algorithms successfully recovered inserted LES values within 0.2% accuracy in the absence of gradients and within 0.2–0.4% when 5–10% gradients were present. SKYSURF necessitates non-standard image re-processing to restore the lowest sky level from each visit into drizzled images. A proof of concept using WFC3/IR F125W images demonstrates that residual diffuse light exceeding Kelsall et al. (1998) Zodiacal model predictions is independent of total object flux, thereby supporting the initial SKYSURF results on diffuse light presented in Carleton et al. (2022).

The Two Higgs Doublet model extended with a complex scalar singlet (2HDMS) satisfies all existing experimental limits and represents a compelling framework for physics beyond the Standard Model. This model offers viable solutions for dark matter, baryogenesis, and the generation of gravitational wave signals. Our study specifically investigates the dark matter phenomenology within the 2HDMS framework, treating the complex scalar singlet as the dark matter candidate. We analyze how dark matter observables vary across different model parameters and introduce benchmark points for both light and heavy dark matter mass ranges that comply with current constraints from dark matter detection, flavor physics, and collider experiments. Additionally, we contrast real versus complex scalar dark matter scenarios within this context and evaluate the discovery prospects for these models at the High-Luminosity Large Hadron Collider (HL-LHC) and future electron-positron colliders.

Consider a gravitational field containing multiple macroscopic observers placed within a highly quantum state, constructed as a coherent superposition of distinct classical configurations. What would such a system appear? To investigate this, I employ a spatial distance operator defined among the observers and analyze the characteristics of its expectation values.

The concept of modeling problems using predicates that establish a partial order among global states was originally proposed to enable asynchronous execution in multiprocessor environments. A defining characteristic of these problems is that the predicate creates a lattice within the state space, ensuring correctness even when nodes operate with outdated information from their neighbors. Consequently, compilers aware of this property can disregard data dependencies, allowing applications to proceed with existing data instead of waiting for the latest updates. However, many significant problems lack this lattice linearity. This limitation was addressed through the development of eventually lattice linear algorithms, which impose a partial order on a subset of the state space even when the problem cannot be fully defined by a predicate that forms a partial order across all states.

This paper examines and distinguishes between lattice linear problems and algorithms, introducing a novel category known as (fully) lattice linear algorithms. These algorithms partition the entire reachable state space into one or more lattices, with the initial state confined to a specific lattice. Under certain additional constraints, the initial state uniquely determines the final state. To illustrate this, we present lattice linear self-stabilizing algorithms for the minimal dominating set and graph coloring problems, as well as a parallel processing 2-approximation algorithm for the vertex cover problem. The minimal dominating set algorithm converges in $n$ moves, while the graph coloring algorithm requires $n + 2m$ moves. Notably, the vertex cover algorithm represents the first lattice linear approximation method for an NP-Hard problem, converging in $n$ moves. This study investigates spontaneous asymptotic phase-locking and synchronization in two-qubit systems subject to continuous Markovian evolution governed by Lindbladian dynamics featuring normal Lindblad operators. Employing analytical techniques, the authors identify and categorize all mechanisms that enforce phase-locking within this specific framework. The detailed architecture of the corresponding attractor spaces is examined to elucidate their properties from multiple angles. Among these processes, those that compel identical stationary components for both qubits are distinguished, with the most rigorous form of synchronization serving as a notable instance. A foundational framework is introduced, demonstrating that, physically, two primary categories of phase-locking mechanisms exist. The capacity to retain information regarding the initial state is analyzed, alongside the derivation of an upper limit for the oscillation amplitude in the resulting phase-locked dynamics. The text further discusses the permutation symmetry inherent in both asymptotic states and phase-locking mechanisms. Finally, the hypothesis that entanglement generation acts as a phase-locking witness is refuted through three analytically solvable examples.

Building high-definition (HD) semantic maps is a fundamental aspect of autonomous driving. Nevertheless, conventional workflows demand extensive human effort and resources for annotation and maintenance, thereby restricting their scalability. This paper addresses the challenge of learning HD semantic maps, which involves dynamically generating local semantic information from onboard sensor data. We propose a novel approach named HDMapNet, which encodes visual features from surrounding cameras and/or 3D point clouds from LiDAR to predict vectorized map elements in a bird's-eye view. Evaluated on the nuScenes dataset, HDMapNet surpasses baseline methods across all tested settings. Specifically, our camera-LiDAR fusion variant exceeds existing techniques by over 50% in every metric. Furthermore, we establish both semantic-level and instance-level metrics to assess map learning performance. We also demonstrate that our method can generate locally consistent maps. By presenting this methodology and associated evaluation metrics, we encourage the research community to explore this emerging field of map learning.

Given a prime number $p$ and a non-trivial $p$th root of unity $q$, we outline the primary stages of constructing a local $q$-deformation of the "Simpson correspondence in characteristic $p$" originally established by Ogus and Vologodsky in 2005. This construction relies on the Morita-equivalence linking a ring of $q$-twisted differential operators with its center. Additionally, we discuss the anticipated connections between this approach and recent work by Bhatt and Scholze. To ensure clarity, the discussion is restricted to the one-dimensional case.

Linear off-resonant X-ray Raman spectroscopy can detect ultrafast electronic coherences arising as a photoexcited wave packet traverses a conical intersection. This method utilizes a hybrid scheme where a femtosecond or attosecond probe pulse excites the system and triggers signal photon emission. This study examines the efficacy of attosecond pulse trains generated via high-harmonic generation as probe pulses, replacing traditional single Gaussian pulses within this framework. We analyze various pulse combination strategies and assess how specific pulse train parameters influence the resulting signals. Additionally, we address how Raman selection rules and symmetry considerations impact the spectroscopic output, alongside the role of vibrational contributions. Using two distinct model systems with different molecular symmetries and quantum dynamics simulations, we compare their spectral differences. Our findings indicate that these pulse trains are highly effective at capturing the essential features of electronic coherence.

We introduce a class of angular Gaussian distributions designed to accommodate varying degrees of isotropy for directional random variables in any dimension. Through a series of innovative reparameterizations, this family is defined by parameters possessing clear statistical meanings that span the entire real space of appropriate dimensions. This novel parameterization significantly streamlines the maximum likelihood estimation of all model parameters, resulting in inference procedures that are both theoretically rigorous and numerically stable. Leveraging byproducts from this likelihood-based inference, we develop graphical and numerical diagnostic tools to evaluate the goodness of fit within a data application. Finally, a simulation study alongside an application to hydrogeological data demonstrate the implementation and performance of these inference procedures and diagnostic methods.

This paper examines the Ehrhart polynomial of the dual root polytope of type C, denoted as $C_d^*$, in dimension $d$. We demonstrate that all roots of this polynomial share the same real part of $-1/2$ and establish that the sequence of Ehrhart polynomials for $C_d^*$ across dimensions $d=1,2,\dots$ exhibits the interlacing property.

From 2020 to 2022, the Snowmass Accelerator Frontier (AF) engaged in extensive deliberations through its topical working groups, alongside numerous joint sessions with other Frontiers, Snowmass-wide gatherings, Colloquium-style Agoras, cross-Frontier Forums focusing on muon and electron-positron colliders, and the collider Implementation Task Force (ITF). This Accelerator Frontier report summarizes the results of these efforts.

A defining feature of neural development is the oscillatory movement of nuclei between the apical and basal surfaces of the neuroepithelium, known as interkinetic nuclear migration (IKNM). In this study, we utilize long-term, rapid lightsheet and two-photon imaging of zebrafish retinas *in vivo* during early development to identify the physical mechanisms driving nuclear behavior during IKNM. These imaging techniques enable the reliable tracking of nuclear movements and divisions within densely packed populations during early retinogenesis. By analyzing these tracks, we formulate and validate a theoretical model of retinal IKNM as a diffusive process influenced by a nuclear concentration gradient established by the continuous addition of new nuclei at the apical surface. Our findings elucidate how apical nuclear packing affects migration dynamics, offer a robust quantitative account of nuclear distribution across the retina, and suggest potential implications for stochastic cell fate decisions in this system.

Achieving transaction privacy on account-based blockchains like Ethereum remains a significant challenge. Although Ben-Sasson et al. introduced the Zerocash protocol [BCG+14] as a decentralized anonymous payment (DAP) system built atop Bitcoin, no research has yet explored integrating such a DAP into an account-based ledger. This paper addresses that gap by introducing ZETH, an adaptation of Zerocash designed to operate on Ethereum without requiring modifications to its base layer. Our findings demonstrate that ZETH facilitates not only the transfer of Ether but also other smart contract-based digital assets. Furthermore, we analyze ZETH's privacy guarantees and argue that any inherent information leakages are effectively controlled and well-defined, establishing it as a viable solution for private transactions on both public and permissioned chains.

This study introduces an empirical method for measuring the decline in lexical richness when comparing Machine Translation (MT) outputs to Human Translation (HT). Experimental results confirm that contemporary MT systems struggle to replicate the vocabulary diversity found in human-generated text. The tendency of MT to amplify common patterns while neglecting rare ones, alongside its limited output diversity, may explain underlying causes for contentious issues such as gender bias in translations. Beyond biased training data, can we attribute these problems to algorithms that actively intensify existing biases?

Ionization quenching effects are vital for experiments that measure low-energy recoils, including direct Dark Matter searches. We provide estimated ionization quenching factors for protons, alpha particles, and heavier ions across various energies within H$_{2}$, CH$_{4}$, N$_{2}$, Ar, CO$_{2}$, and C$_{3}$H$_{8}$ gases, derived from corresponding reference W-value measurements. These calculated factors are then compared against predictions made by SRIM.

Controlling the speed and reliability of magnetic domain wall (DW) movement is essential for unlocking the capabilities of DW-based devices in memory and logic systems. A primary obstacle is extrinsic DW pinning caused by shape and material defects, which can persist even with careful sample synthesis. This issue is particularly critical in electrochemically-deposited cylindrical magnetic nanowires (NWs), where significant pinning has hindered the observation of theoretically predicted physical phenomena. This study experimentally examines DW pinning in Co$_x$Ni$_{100-x}$ NWs using quasistatic magnetic fields. We varied wire compositions ($x=20,30,40$) and altered microstructures through annealing or by adjusting the deposition electrolyte pH. Our findings indicate that pinning at grain boundaries is the dominant mechanism, which decreases inversely with both spontaneous magnetization and grain size. Secondary factors include lattice strain inhomogeneities and residual magnetocrystalline anisotropy. In contrast, surface roughness, dislocations, and impurities are not anticipated to significantly contribute to DW pinning in these specific wire samples.

While scientists traditionally regard Euclidean geometry as an objective and a priori framework, adopting an agent-centric perspective requires that route selection account for the agent's capabilities, physical embodiment, and cognitive load. This paper redefines geometry as the navigation between states within a world by integrating information processing costs with spatial distances. As the significance of these informational costs grows, the resulting geometry diverges increasingly from the world's original structure. We visualize this "cognitive geometry" by projecting it onto two- and three-dimensional spaces, revealing specific distortions that highlight the development of epistemic and information-saving strategies, as well as pivotal states. The parallels between conventional cost-based geometries and those shaped by informational expenses suggest extending the concept of geodesics—defined as the cheapest routes—from a simple metric to "infodesics." Inspired by the geodesic property where every point along the optimal path from a start to a goal is also optimally situated relative to the start, infodesics represent routes that minimize cost not just for the destination, but for all intermediate points.

For an undirected graph $G=(V,E)$, a vertex $v \in V$ is considered edge-vertex (ev) dominated by an edge $e \in E$ if $v$ is incident to $e$ or to an edge adjacent to $e$. A subset $S^{ev} \subseteq E$ constitutes an edge-vertex dominating set (or ev-dominating set) when every vertex in $G$ is ev-dominated by at least one edge within $S^{ev}$. The ev-domination number is defined as the smallest cardinality of such a set, and the associated problem seeks to determine this minimum value. This paper establishes that the ev-dominating set problem is {\tt NP-hard} when restricted to unit disk graphs. Furthermore, it demonstrates that a polynomial-time approximation scheme exists for this problem on unit disk graphs and presents a straightforward linear-time approximation algorithm with a performance ratio of 5.

We examine a mathematical framework detailing the dynamics between an insulating rigid object and an incompressible, electrically conductive fluid containing it, incorporating principles from fluid-structure interaction and magnetohydrodynamics. Our primary achievement is demonstrating the existence of a weak solution to the associated system of partial differential equations. This proof employs the Rothe method for time discretization to decouple the system, enabling the handling of test functions in the induction equation's weak formulation that depend on the moving body's position and the system's solution. Additionally, the proof utilizes Brinkman penalization to address the mechanical component of the problem.

The {\it Fermi} satellite has identified approximately 60 radio galaxies (RGs), prompting this study to examine spectral differences between GeV-loud and GeV-quiet RGs. The sample includes 68 objects: 36 detected by {\it Fermi} and 32 that are gamma-ray undetected. We analyzed the X-ray spectra of all 68 sources using data from {\it XMM-Newton}, {\it Chandra}, {\it NuSTAR}, and {\it Swift}. Our findings indicate that while most GeV-loud RGs show no significant absorption, about half of the GeV-quiet RGs do. This implies that the jets of GeV-loud RGs are viewed at small angles, preventing the torus from easily obscuring the emission. Furthermore, we found that RGs with heavy absorption predominantly fall within the X-ray luminosity range of $10^{43}-10^{45}$erg s$^{-1}$, whereas those with lower or higher luminosities rarely exhibit such absorption—a trend consistent with that observed in Seyfert galaxies.

The Black and Scholes (1973) hedging strategy relies on the premise that a continuously rebalanced asset portfolio adheres to the continuous-time self-financing condition. This condition, a specific instance of Merton's (1971) continuous-time budget equation, is widely regarded as the mathematical representation of a portfolio rebalanced continuously without external cash flows. However, we contend through three distinct mathematical proofs that the continuous-time self-financing condition fails for rebalanced portfolios. Furthermore, we identify the error in Merton's (1971) derivation of the budget equation: by mistakenly equating a deterministic variable with a stochastic one, Merton implicitly assumes that rebalancing is independent of asset price fluctuations. If our findings are correct, they invalidate Merton's (1971) continuous-time budget equation, as well as the hedging argument and option pricing formula established by Black and Scholes (1973).

A high-precision technique for establishing predefined PMT gain is detailed, requiring only minimal operator involvement. Following an initial rough adjustment, the automated system fine-tunes the PMT gain to a specified accuracy of up to 2%. This approach was successfully implemented at the Borexino PMT test facility at LNGS to calibrate the 2000 photomultipliers used in the Borexino detector.

We report new findings regarding the light-quark connected component of the leading-order hadronic-vacuum-polarization (HVP) contribution to the muon's anomalous magnetic moment, utilizing $2+1+1$ staggered fermions. By expanding the dataset with two new ensembles and increasing statistics on existing ones, we have substantially reduced statistical uncertainties in the HVP contribution and associated window quantities. Furthermore, we computed the current-current correlator to next-to-next-to-leading order (NNLO) within staggered chiral perturbation theory, enabling corrections for finite-volume effects, pion-mass mistuning, and taste-breaking up to NNLO. We examine the utility of NNLO chiral perturbation theory as a systematic effective field theory (EFT) approach for the HVP contribution, noting its limitations regarding short- and intermediate-distance window quantities, which complicates the assessment of systematic errors for the standard intermediate-distance window currently prevalent in literature. Consequently, we explore a longer-distance window where EFT methods are more robust. Our primary conclusion is that high-statistics calculations at lattice spacings notably finer than 0.06 fm are essential. The ensembles employed were generously supplied by MILC and CalLat.

Deriving ultimate limits for communication across specific quantum repeater networks has established crucial benchmarks for evaluating near-term protocols. However, these bounds typically assume ideal devices, leaving the performance of practical implementations unaddressed. To tackle this, we quantify how losses within repeater stations impact the maximum achievable rates for both linear chains and more intricate quantum networks. By extending the node-splitting framework, we model the loss occurring at repeater stations and subsequently prove the corresponding limits. In linear chain scenarios, we demonstrate that increasing the number of repeaters cannot push the maximum rate beyond a threshold determined solely by the loss of a single station. We also present an adaptation of standard bounding techniques tailored to this realistic context. The key distinction is that while ultimate limits for any strategy can be derived for a fixed channel, repeaters introducing additional decoherence make the effective overall channel dependent on the chosen repeater strategy (e.g., one-way versus two-way classical communication). Consequently, specific classes of repeater strategies can be analyzed through further modeling, allowing the resulting bounds to represent the optimal rate within that specific class.

Amid the ongoing COVID-19 crisis, there is a critical demand for rapid and precise identification of infected individuals. Leveraging deep learning models trained on chest X-rays offers an efficient screening solution, as these approaches are already prevalent in medical practice. However, their accuracy depends heavily on extensive datasets, which, despite collective efforts by the open-source community to collect and annotate, remain insufficient for training robust models. Few-shot learning, a machine learning sub-field designed to achieve objectives with limited data, presents a viable alternative. This study explores established techniques for addressing data scarcity in deep learning—specifically data augmentation, transfer learning, few-shot learning, and unsupervised learning—to detect COVID-19. Additionally, we introduce a custom few-shot learning method utilizing siamese networks for this purpose. Experimental results demonstrate that adopting few-shot learning strategies enables the creation of efficient and accurate deep learning models even with scarce data. Our proposed approach achieved 96.4% accuracy, representing a significant improvement over baseline models which yielded 83%.

Synchrotron radiation, generated when energetic charged particles interact with magnetic fields, is a critical phenomenon in various astronomical contexts, ranging from the interstellar medium to the extreme environments surrounding compact objects. Observations of these sources provide valuable insights into both the sources' intrinsic physical properties and those of their immediate surroundings. Recent multi-wavelength campaigns have uncovered complex features and unique characteristics, particularly near black holes, highlighting the need for numerical tools that complement traditional analytical one-zone models. To address this, we present flaremodel, an open-source Python package designed for such applications. The code's core comprises low-level utility functions, implemented in C for high performance and parallelized using OpenMP to ensure scalability, which describe physical processes relevant to synchrotron sources. While a Python interface facilitates access to these functions and offers built-in source models as a starting point, the package's modular architecture and generic function design allow users to construct diverse models applicable to a wide range of astrophysical synchrotron sources. This paper outlines our methodology, code structure, and provides selected examples to demonstrate its capabilities and potential for future modeling endeavors.

Component-based systems evolve through the addition of new components or the replacement of existing ones with updated versions, making it essential to ensure that safety properties are maintained in the resulting system. Rather than verifying the entire updated system, which can lead to an excessively large state space, it is advantageous to reuse verification results by analyzing the newly added component in isolation. Consequently, this work investigates model checking for component-based, asynchronously communicating systems where a component's behavior is unspecified, focusing on safety properties. The proposed solution employs assume-guarantee reasoning adapted for asynchronous environments to generate the weakest possible assumption. If the new component adheres to this assumption, the entire system retains its safety guarantees. To ensure efficiency and convergence, the approach constructs an overapproximated interface for the missing component; when composed with the rest of the system, this yields an overapproximated system specification. From this specification, traces violating the property are eliminated to derive a refined assumption for the missing component. The method has been implemented and validated through two case studies. When compared with state-of-the-art direct approaches, the generated assumptions were not only smaller in size but also produced more quickly.

This study examines a variable-coefficient Boiti-Leon-Manna-Pempinelli equation. Using the three-waves method, the homoclinic breather approach, and Hirota's bilinear method, we derive numerous multi-wave, breather, and lump solutions. The correctness of all solutions was confirmed via Mathematica software, and their propagation characteristics were analyzed through three-dimensional visualizations. These findings contribute to a better understanding of fluid propagation and incompressible fluids.

The CMS experiment at the LHC analyzed 138 fb$^{-1}$ of 13 TeV proton-proton collision data to search for nonresonant Higgs boson (H) pair production through gluon and vector boson fusion, focusing on the four-bottom-quark final state. By employing a graph neural network to identify Lorentz-boosted H pairs, the study places constraints on the Higgs self-coupling and the quartic VVHH couplings ($\kappa_{2V}$) relative to standard model predictions. Notably, this analysis excludes $\kappa_{2V}$ = 0 for the first time with a significance of 6.3 standard deviations, assuming other Higgs couplings remain consistent with the standard model.

This letter extends Ensemble Kalman inversion methods to broader Bayesian frameworks, moving beyond their prior limitation to additive Gaussian likelihoods, specifically within challenging scenarios where the likelihood can be sampled from but its density may not be directly computed.

Recent observations of angular correlation spectra in the decays $ {\rm ^4He}^*\to {\rm ^4He}+ e^+e^-$ and $ {\rm ^8Be}^*\to {\rm ^8Be}+ e^+e^-$ have been attributed to the formation and decay of a new light particle with a mass of approximately 17 MeV into an electron-positron pair. In this study, we calculate the invariant $m_{e^+e^-}$ mass spectrum for the electromagnetic transition of excited helium states and estimate both the differential and total decay widths. We examine whether the observed signal originates from an $e^+e^-$ pair produced by a new electromagnetic decay of ${\rm ^4He}$, potentially driven by a proposed 12-quark hidden-color Fock state known as the "hexadiquark." Our analysis shows that the signal shape can be fitted using a QCD Fock state at an excitation energy of ${\rm E^*}\simeq 17.9 $ MeV, combined with a Gaussian form factor for the electromagnetic decay. We further discuss the physical implications of these fit parameters in the context of the hexadiquark state. Given these findings, we stress the necessity for independent experimental verification or disproof of the ATOMKI results, as well as additional experiments to detect the proposed new excitation of ${\rm ^4He}$.

Driven by the rapid expansion of the fashion industry, consumer demand for personalized fashion recommendations has significantly increased. This study addresses a practical challenge in this domain: determining the optimal item to pair with existing fashion pieces to create a cohesive outfit. The core of this challenge lies in accurately estimating outfit compatibility. While previous approaches have focused on the compatibility of individual item pairs or treated outfits as linear sequences, they often fail to capture the intricate relationships among multiple items within an ensemble. To address this limitation, we introduce a graph-based representation for outfits. Specifically, we construct a Fashion Graph where nodes denote categories and edges signify interactions between them; consequently, an outfit is modeled as a subgraph by mapping items to their respective category nodes. To derive compatibility scores from this structure, we propose Node-wise Graph Neural Networks (NGNN), designed to more effectively model node interactions and generate superior node embeddings. Within the NGNN framework, the interaction along each edge is unique, governed by parameters specific to the two connected nodes, and an attention mechanism is employed to compute the final compatibility score using these learned representations. NGNN is versatile, capable of modeling compatibility across visual, textual, or multi-modal inputs. We evaluate our method on two tasks: (1) Fill-in-the-blank, which involves recommending an item to complete an outfit, and (2) Compatibility prediction, which entails scoring the compatibility of given outfits. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed method significantly outperforms existing approaches.

Extensive dynamical simulations investigate the potential for sudden, significant energy or rogue fluctuations (RF) to emerge at late stages and within brief time intervals in the strongly nonlinear regime of $\beta$-Fermi-Pasta-Ulam-Tsingou (FPUT) systems. Building upon previous research into RF within non-dissipative granular chains, our findings indicate that rare RF events may be a generic feature of non-integrable, strongly nonlinear systems given sufficient time. We also discuss the impact of initial conditions and the notable effect of harmonic forces on these systems. It is important to note that the RF examined here differ from the well-known Peregrine solitons, which are employed to model rogue waves using the weakly nonlinear Schrödinger equation.

Extensive air shower simulations using LHC-calibrated hadronic interaction models like EPOS-LHC and QGSJetII-04 predict fewer muons than those detected by major cosmic ray observatories. This paper introduces a novel approach to determine muon rescaling factors by analyzing reconstructed simulated showers. The method employs a z-variable, defined as the discrepancy between the initially simulated and reconstructed total detector signals, which correlates with the muon signal, remains largely independent of the zenith angle, yet varies with the primary cosmic ray's mass. Validated against Monte Carlo simulations of the Pierre Auger Observatory's hybrid detector, the technique utilizes individual z-values from simulated hybrid events, the corresponding signal at 1000 meters from the shower axis, and a parametrization of the simulated muon fraction to compute multiplicative rescaling parameters for ground-level muon signals on an event-by-event basis. Furthermore, the study examines how these parameters vary with zenith angle and primary mass. This capability enables not only the testing and calibration of hadronic interaction models but also the derivation of the $\beta$-exponent, which characterizes the rise in muon counts relative to primary energy and mass. Detailed simulations reveal that the $\beta$-exponent depends on hadronic interaction properties, underscoring the importance of determining this parameter to address the muon deficit issue.

Recent observations indicate that our current understanding of mass loss in classical novae remains incomplete, prompting a new theoretical investigation into the physical mechanisms driving nova ejecta. This study utilizes the MESA stellar evolution code to conduct hydrodynamical simulations of classical nova outflows. Our results show that when the binary companion is ignored, white dwarfs with masses of 0.8 solar masses or greater can successfully generate radiation-pressure-driven, optically thick winds that expel the majority of the envelope. However, during most of the mass loss phase, these winds accelerate at distances beyond the white dwarf's Roche radius, assuming a typical cataclysmic variable donor. Consequently, before a standard optically thick wind can form, mass loss is instead initiated and shaped by binary interactions. An isotropic optically thick wind is only successfully launched once the acceleration region retreats within the white dwarf's Roche radius, a point reached after most of the envelope has already been ejected. This interplay between two outflow modes—a primary phase of slow, binary-driven, equatorially focused mass loss accounting for most ejection, followed by a secondary phase of fast, isotropic, optically thick wind—aligns with observational data regarding aspherical ejecta and signatures of multiple outflow components. Furthermore, we find that isolated white dwarfs with masses less than or equal to 0.8 solar masses never develop unbound optically thick winds at any stage, underscoring the critical importance of considering binary companion effects on the resulting outburst.

We report the inaugural lattice QCD computation of distribution amplitudes for longitudinally and transversely polarized vector mesons, specifically the $K^*$ and $\phi$, utilizing large momentum effective theory. This study employs the clover fermion action across three ensembles featuring 2+1+1 flavors of highly improved staggered quarks (HISQ) generated by the MILC collaboration. These simulations are conducted at a physical pion mass with lattice spacings of \{0.06, 0.09, 0.12\} fm and involve three distinct hadron momenta, $P_z=\{1.29, 1.72, 2.15\}$ GeV. The derived lattice matrix elements undergo nonperturbative renormalization using a recently proposed hybrid scheme, followed by an extrapolation to both the continuum limit and infinite momentum. Our findings indicate that longitudinal distribution amplitudes remain close to the asymptotic form, whereas transverse amplitudes exhibit significant deviations. Consequently, our final results offer essential {\it ab initio} theoretical inputs for the analysis of relevant exclusive processes.

By integrating the $b\to s\mu^+\mu^-$ anomaly with dark matter data, we evaluate the LHC's potential to probe dark matter, $Z^{\prime}$ bosons, and vector-like quarks. Our analysis centers on a local $U(1)_{L_\mu-L_\tau}$ framework featuring a vector-like $SU(2)_L$ doublet quark $Q$, a complex singlet scalar, and a dark matter candidate $X_I$ (the lightest component). After applying necessary constraints, we observe that the $b\to s\mu^+\mu^-$ anomaly and dark matter relic density prefer $m_{X_I}< 350$ GeV and $m_{Z^{\prime}}< 450$ GeV, provided $m_Q$ and $m_{X_R}$ (the heavy partner of $X_I$) remain below 2 TeV. Existing LHC searches for jets and missing transverse momentum significantly constrain the vector-like quark mass space, requiring $m_Q$ to exceed 1.7 TeV. Furthermore, we explore probing these particles at the high-luminosity LHC through QCD production processes ($pp \to D\bar{D}$ or $pp \to U\bar{U}$) followed by decays $D\to s (b) Z'X_I$ or $U \to u (c) Z' X_I$, with the subsequent decay $Z'\to\mu^+\mu^-$. Using a benchmark scenario with $m_Q$=1.93 TeV, $m_{Z^\prime}=170$ GeV, and $m_{X_I}=$ 145 GeV, detailed Monte Carlo simulations indicate that this configuration is accessible at the 14 TeV LHC with an integrated luminosity of 3000 fb$^{-1}$.

Massive stars frequently undergo binary interactions that modify the surface and core structures of stripped stars, significantly influencing their ultimate outcomes as core-collapse supernovae. Yet, current simulations have predominantly modeled only single-star evolution. We introduce a systematic study comparing single and binary-stripped stars with identical initial masses (11–21 M$_{\odot}$), identified as supernova candidates. Our results generally show that binary-stripped cores are less compact and feature a deeper, more pronounced silicon/oxygen interface, causing them to explode more readily than their single-star counterparts of the same mass. This behavioral divergence between the two evolutionary paths has profound implications for supernova statistics, including neutron star masses, explosion energies, and nucleosynthetic yields. Furthermore, remnants from binary-stripped stars are uniquely positioned to fill the mass gap between the heaviest neutron stars and the lightest black holes. Our work advances the field by self-consistently modeling both pre-collapse evolution and explosion outcomes; however, our findings underscore the necessity for more detailed stellar evolutionary models to accurately capture the sensitivity of these explosion results.

Cosmological correlation functions offer critical insights into the early universe, potentially revealing signatures of new massive particles at extreme energy scales. Recent advancements, particularly the cosmological bootstrap, provide fresh perspectives and robust tools for analyzing these observables. This paper systematically categorizes inflationary three-point correlators of scalar perturbations via the bootstrap approach. For the first time, we derive a comprehensive set of single-exchange cosmological collider bispectra featuring novel shapes and potentially observable signals. Our analysis focuses specifically on primordial scalar bispectra arising from the exchange of massive particles with all possible boost-breaking interactions during inflation. We introduce three-point "seed" functions to bootstrap inflationary bispectra for both scalar and spinning exchanges using weight-shifting and spin-raising operators. Calculating these seed functions involves solving an ordinary differential equation in comoving momenta, which represents a boundary version of the equation of motion for a propagator that linearly couples a massive particle to external light scalars. The resulting correlators are expressed in analytic form across all kinematic regimes. These shapes are highly relevant for upcoming cosmological surveys, as boost-breaking theories can generate significant primordial non-Gaussianity. We also identify distinct phenomenological features in these shapes that differ from de Sitter invariant cases; for instance, oscillatory patterns in the squeezed limit exhibit varying phases. Additionally, if the massive particle's speed of sound is significantly lower than that of the inflaton, oscillatory features emerge around the equilateral configuration.

The emergence of COVID-19 in late 2019 has captivated media attention as it evolved into a global pandemic. In numerous mathematics and physics classrooms, educators utilize case time series data to illustrate the exponential rise of infections. This manuscript introduces a straightforward diffusion process as the mechanism for infection spread. Although less complex than existing models in the literature, this approach successfully captures exponential growth by relating it to mobility (diffusion constant), population density, and transmission probability. Students can adjust these parameters to calculate growth rates and forecast total cases over time. Furthermore, learners are encouraged to incorporate additional factors beyond those included in the basic diffusion model.

Discrepancies exist between the values of the Cabibbo angle derived from kaon, pion, $D$, and tau decays and those obtained from super-allowed beta decays. This mismatch leads to an approximate $3\,\sigma$ violation of first-row (and first-column) CKM unitarity, a phenomenon recognized as the Cabibbo angle anomaly (CAA). Extracting $V_{ud}$ from beta decay depends on the Fermi constant $G_F$, typically sourced from muon decay; however, since potential new physics could influence muon decay and consequently alter the determination of $G_F$, this introduces a significant interplay with the global electroweak fit where $G_F$ serves as a pivotal input. These proceedings review the CAA and explore its various interpretations regarding physics beyond the Standard Model, beginning with an analysis of the effects within effective field theory followed by an examination of simplified models.

There is increasing focus on creating data-driven reduced-order models for atmospheric and oceanic flows, utilizing training data from either high-resolution simulations or satellite observations. These non-intrusive models provide substantial computational advantages over large-scale numerical counterparts. By employing these low-dimensional representations, researchers can significantly decrease the computational costs associated with forecasting and uncertainty estimation without sacrificing the essential data required for accurate state estimation via data assimilation. This study investigates an equation-free surrogate modeling strategy that bridges machine learning and data assimilation within Earth system modeling. To achieve this, we present an end-to-end non-intrusive reduced-order modeling (NIROM) framework that incorporates advancements in modal decomposition, time series prediction, optimal sensor placement, and sequential data assimilation. Specifically, the approach employs proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) to extract dominant flow structures and a long short-term memory (LSTM) network to capture the dynamics of these modes. The NIROM is coupled with the deterministic ensemble Kalman filter (DEnKF) to assimilate sparse, noisy observations at optimally selected sensor locations determined via QR pivoting. We validate the framework's feasibility and benefits using the NOAA Optimum Interpolation Sea Surface Temperature (SST) V2 dataset. Results demonstrate that the NIROM remains stable for long-term forecasting and accurately models SST dynamics. Moreover, the DEnKF integration enhances prediction accuracy by approximately one order of magnitude. This work offers a pathway for integrating Earth system model outputs with observational data to achieve more precise forecasts.

Tidal interactions between stellar binaries and Sgr A* in the Galactic Centre (GC) can disrupt these systems, ejecting one component at speeds exceeding the Milky Way's escape velocity to become hypervelocity stars (HVSs), which provide valuable insights into the GC's stellar populations. Previous simulations by our group established a robust upper limit of $3\times10^{-2} \, \mathrm{yr^{-1}}$ on the HVS ejection rate from the GC, based on the current absence of main-sequence HVS candidates with precise astrometric data and radial velocities in \textit{Gaia} releases. In this study, we tighten this constraint by also accounting for the lack of post-main-sequence HVSs in the \textit{Gaia} Early Data Release 3 and the confirmed presence of the HVS candidate S5-HVS1. This combined evidence yields degenerate joint constraints on both the HVS ejection rate and the GC's stellar initial mass function (IMF). Assuming a top-heavy IMF as recently proposed, our modeling suggests an ejection rate of $\eta=0.7_{-0.5}^{+1.5} \times10^{-4} \, \mathrm{yr^{-1}}$. However, this rate could reach up to $10^{-2} \, \mathrm{yr^{-1}}$ under a very top-light IMF scenario or drop to $10^{-4.5} \, \mathrm{yr^{-1}}$ if the IMF is extremely top-heavy. Future \textit{Gaia} data releases will further refine these constraints, regardless of the number of HVS candidates identified.

Currently, designing optical multilayer thin-films for specific targets relies on gradient-based optimization combined with methods capable of adding layers. Although Deep Learning and Reinforcement Learning have recently achieved significant success in this domain, trained models typically specialize in a single target and require retraining when optical specifications change. This study employs Conditional Invertible Neural Networks (cINN) to inversely design multilayer thin-films based on an optical target. Because cINN learns the energy landscape of all thin-film configurations within the training set, it can generate a stochastic ensemble of candidate designs that approximate the desired target using only random variables. By further refining these proposals through local optimization, the resulting thin-films achieve the target with substantially higher precision than comparable state-of-the-art methods. Additionally, testing the model on samples outside the training data distribution demonstrated its ability to predict thin-film structures for out-of-distribution targets. These findings indicate that combining established and emerging machine learning techniques is an effective strategy for enhancing the generative design of thin-films to achieve optimal results.

For multiple-input-multiple-output (MIMO) systems employing K-best detection, achieving near-maximum-likelihood (ML) performance requires a sufficiently large K. To lower detection complexity with minimal performance loss, an intelligent MIMO detection network leveraging deep neural networks (DNN) is introduced. This approach treats K as an adjustable variable defined by a fitting function of learnable coefficients. Specifically, the proposed algorithm utilizes meta-learning to derive the coefficients for this fitting function, thereby avoiding the difficulties associated with directly learning K. By applying network fusion to integrate the outputs of the meta-learning sub-networks, simulation results demonstrate that the scheme attains near-ML detection performance with complexity comparable to linear detectors, while also exhibiting rapid training capabilities.

f(Q) gravity extends symmetric teleparallel general relativity (STGR), where gravity arises from nonmetricity as curvature and torsion are zero. This study conducts theoretical analyses of static, spherically symmetric solutions involving anisotropic fluids within general f(Q) gravity. Our findings reveal that the off-diagonal field equation component resulting from a coincident gauge imposes strict constraints on the functional form of f(Q) gravity. Furthermore, while the exact Schwarzschild solution is exclusive to STGR, we derive Schwarzschild-like solutions in nontrivial f(Q) gravity and examine their asymptotic behavior and deviations from the exact solution.

We introduce a cosmic string within a warped five-dimensional spacetime framework governed by Einstein-Yang-Mills theory. Conventional four-dimensional cosmic strings face significant challenges regarding string smoothing mechanisms, particularly due to the constraint that the mass per unit length ($G\mu$) must be approximately $10^{-6}$. In contrast, our warped cosmic string model resolves this issue while also satisfying superstring requirements that $G\mu$ should be of order 1, a value far exceeding current observational limits. Furthermore, this model accounts for the lack of observed axially symmetric lensing effects from cosmic strings by demonstrating that the string's angle deficit is warped down to an unobservable magnitude on the brane relative to its value in the bulk. Finally, consistent numerical solutions for this model are only achievable when the cosmological constant is negative.

Although advancements in large pretrained language models have substantially enhanced their performance on conditional generation tasks like summarization, these improvements are often accompanied by hallucinations. Traditional approaches to mitigate this issue have focused on refining beam search or implementing fact-checking as a post-processing stage. This paper explores the application of Natural Language Inference (NLI) entailment metrics to identify and curb hallucinations during summary creation. We introduce an NLI-assisted beam re-ranking strategy that calculates entailment probabilities between the input context and model-generated beams throughout saliency-enhanced greedy decoding. Additionally, we incorporate a diversity metric to evaluate its efficacy relative to standard beam search. Our proposed algorithm demonstrates significant superiority over conventional beam decoding on the XSum and CNN/DM datasets.

Accurately forecasting the movements of vehicles surrounding an autonomous racecar is essential for effective and efficient planning. While deep neural networks offer high expressiveness, their "black-box" nature makes them difficult to apply in safety-critical domains like autonomous driving. This paper presents a structured method for predicting the trajectories of opposing racecars using deep neural networks, resulting in a constrained set of possible outputs that allow for quality guarantees on predictions. We evaluated the model alongside an LSTM-based encoder-decoder architecture using data from high-fidelity Hardware-in-the-Loop simulations. The proposed approach surpassed the baseline in prediction accuracy while maintaining these quality guarantees, demonstrating its robustness for real-world deployment. The model was successfully implemented on the Technical University of Munich's racecar for the 2021 Indy Autonomous Challenge. The research code is available as open-source software at www.github.com/TUMFTM/MixNet.

This study investigates the asymptotic sum-rate performance of a multi-user multiple-input single-output (MISO) downlink system assisted by a reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS), operating under imperfect channel state information (CSI) with both Rayleigh and Rician fading. Initially, we generalize the standard least squares (LS) ON/OFF channel estimation protocol for multi-user scenarios, deriving minimum mean squared error (MMSE) estimates for all RIS-assisted channels across multiple sub-phases. Additionally, we examine a low-complexity direct estimation (DE) approach, wherein the base station (BS) acquires the MMSE estimate of the aggregate channel within a single sub-phase. Employing maximum ratio transmission (MRT) precoding at the BS and optimizing RIS phases in the large system limit, we derive deterministic equivalents for the signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR) and sum-rate. Our derived asymptotic expressions indicate that under Rayleigh fading, RIS phase-shifts offer negligible improvement to the sum-rate, though the RIS still delivers array gain. Conversely, under Rician fading, the RIS contributes both array and reflect beamforming gains. To optimize phase-shifts under both ON/OFF and DE protocols, we utilize a projected gradient ascent algorithm. Simulation outcomes demonstrate that for large-scale systems, estimating the overall channel via the DE scheme results in superior downlink performance.

We demonstrate that measures generated by the representations of products of generalized Stieltjes transforms are themselves generalized Stieltjes transforms, deriving optimal bounds for their magnitude and examining analogous properties for generalized Cauchy transforms. Specifically, in two distinct scenarios, we establish criteria guaranteeing the positivity of these measures. Consequently, we derive novel, practical conditions for representing functions as generalized Stieltjes transforms, offering a partial resolution to a question raised by Sokal and enhancing understanding of spectral multipliers recently encountered in probabilistic research. Additionally, our methodology refines several established findings concerning Stieltjes and Hilbert transforms.

Numerous constitutive models exist for soft tissue mechanics, yet no standard criterion guides their selection for specific applications. While the model best fitting experimental data is often considered optimal, this approach may fall short due to inter-sample variability. This study introduces a Bayesian framework to determine the relative probabilities of constitutive models using biaxial mechanical testing of tissue samples. Biaxial stretching was performed on 46 porcine aortic valve specimens, each subjected to seven stress ratios along and perpendicular to the fiber direction. Using this selection framework, the probabilities of eight invariant-based models were computed based on the experimental results. The analysis identified the May–Newman model as the most probable for the overall dataset. When samples were categorized by cusp type, the May–Newman model remained dominant for both left- and right-coronary cusps; however, for non-coronary cusps, the Lee–Sacks and May–Newman models were found to be equally probable. This distinction among cusp types correlates with the first principal component (PCA) mode, which showed significant amplitude differences between non-coronary and right-coronary cusps. These findings demonstrate that a PCA-based statistical approach can effectively capture substantial variations in soft tissue mechanical properties. The proposed framework is objective, applicable across tissue types, and offers a structured, rational method for conducting population-based simulations.

Oxide perovskites display a diverse array of structural phases that support various physical phenomena, enabling numerous technological applications.
