Our findings reveal that topological phonons—specifically nodal rings, nodal lines, and Weyl points—are widespread across perovskite oxides, spanning different crystal structures (tetragonal, orthorhombic, and rhombohedral), chemical compositions (BaTiO3, PbTiO3, and SrTiO3), and external stimuli (temperature, strain, and photoexcitation). Notably, while thermal fluctuations stabilize the tetragonal phase with a restricted set of topological phonons, photoexcitation can simultaneously generate all types of these states within the same phase. Furthermore, the concentration of photoexcited carriers offers a mechanism to tune topological phonon states and trigger topological transitions independently of structural phase changes. Consequently, we suggest that oxide perovskites serve as a flexible platform for investigating topological phonons and their manipulation using light.

A smart Ponzi scheme represents an emerging economic crime leveraging Ethereum smart contracts and cryptocurrency to execute Ponzi operations. Although these schemes have caused significant financial harm to numerous investors, research into their detection remains scarce. Current detection approaches suffer from heavy reliance on manual feature engineering and lack model portability. To address these limitations, this paper introduces a data-driven system for identifying smart Ponzi schemes. Utilizing dynamic graph embedding, the system automatically derives account representations from multi-source and multi-modal transaction data. Unlike traditional methods, this approach minimizes human-computer interaction. To our knowledge, this study marks the first implementation of smart Ponzi scheme detection via dynamic graph embedding. Experimental findings demonstrate that the proposed method significantly outperforms existing detection techniques.

We introduce and optimize a vertically-loaded diamond microdisk resonator (VLDMoRt) integrated with a nitrogen-vacancy (NV) center to efficiently capture zero-phonon-line emission into low numerical aperture ($\text{NA}$) free-space modes. This VLDMoRt design yields a Purcell enhancement of 172, collecting 39% of the emitted light within an $\text{NA}$ of 0.6, which results in a total external spin-photon collection efficiency of 0.33. Because the architecture aligns with standard nanofabrication methods and interfaces with low-NA modes suitable for cryogenic free-space optics, it represents a promising platform for developing efficient spin-photon interfaces utilizing diamond quantum emitters.

Test smells represent poor development practices stemming from suboptimal design and implementation decisions within software testing. While the past decade has seen extensive research into their prevalence and impact on test maintainability, this work has primarily focused on unit-level testing, leaving system tests that interact with the System Under Test via a Graphical User Interface (GUI) largely unexplored. To address this gap, we performed an exploratory analysis of test smells in System User Interactive Tests (SUIT). First, utilizing a multi-vocal literature review, we developed a catalog comprising 35 SUIT-specific smells. Subsequently, we conducted an empirical study across 48 industrial test suites and 12 open-source projects to evaluate the frequency and refactoring of these smells. Our findings indicate that while the same categories of smells appear in both industrial and open-source contexts, their remediation strategies differ. Common symptoms such as Obscure Test, Sneaky Checking, and Over Checking are prevalent in over 70% of tests; however, refactoring actions are infrequent, affecting fewer than 50% of the impacted tests. Notably, despite the rarity of active refactoring, certain smells like Narcissistic vanish entirely through the deletion of outdated symptomatic tests and the addition of new tests that do not exhibit such issues.

The ratio of carbon-rich to oxygen-rich asymptotic giant branch (AGB) stars, known as the C/M ratio, is strongly linked to the evolutionary environment of a host galaxy. This study analyzes the C/M ratio across 14 Local Group galaxies using the most comprehensive and purified sample of member stars established in prior research. Boundaries distinguishing carbon-rich AGB stars, oxygen-rich AGB stars, and red supergiants were determined via Gaussian mixture model fitting of number density distributions in the $(J - K)/K$ diagram for LMC and M33 member stars. These boundaries were subsequently applied to other galaxies by adjusting for the positional offset of the tip of the red giant branch (TRGB). Following precise and consistent classification, the C/M ratios were calculated. While galaxies with higher distance moduli exhibit greater uncertainty, the C/M ratio clearly declines as the TRGB color index $(J - K)_0$—a metallicity indicator—increases. This trend aligns with previous findings and supports the hypothesis that carbon stars form more readily in metal-poor environments. Additionally, within M33, the C/M ratio rises with increasing galactocentric distance, consistent with both this scenario and galactic chemical evolution models. Conversely, in M31, the C/M ratio decreases with galactocentric radius, a result that warrants further investigation.

This study examines match data from professional tennis players spanning 1968 to 2010 to construct a directed, weighted contact network. The resulting graph exhibits complex characteristics common to real-world networked systems documented in literature. We devise a diffusion algorithm and apply it to this tennis network to rank players, identifying Jimmy Connors as the greatest player in tennis history according to our methodology. A comprehensive analysis further determines top performers on specific surfaces and for each year within the dataset. When compared against two established methods, our technique demonstrates superior performance, offering higher predictive power without relying on arbitrary external criteria for player assessment. Ultimately, this work provides new evidence of the practical utility of network theory tools and methods.

This study examines Compton scattering by a free electron followed by the reemission of one or two photons, assuming a finite interaction duration. Within the framework of relativistic quantum electrodynamics, the associated cross sections are derived using a modified fermion propagator featuring complex transmitted momentum. The analysis demonstrates that finite-time effects may become observable at sufficiently low scattered photon energies. Furthermore, the proposed approach regularizes the infrared divergence inherent in the double Compton effect cross section, and potential experimental verification of this theoretical model is discussed.

The weak-value-amplification (WVA) method has been a subject of significant discussion in quantum precision measurement, primarily due to the diminished Fisher information resulting from the low probability of successful post-selection. In this study, we demonstrate that employing an optical coherent state as the meter, rather than the conventionally used Gaussian state, allows WVA to definitively surpass standard measurements that do not utilize post-selection. Furthermore, we show that within the WVA framework, a mixture of coherent states can outperform a pure coherent state with the same average photon count, a finding that starkly contrasts with results obtained when post-selection is absent. Additionally, this post-selection strategy enables precision scaling at the Heisenberg limit or even beyond ("super-Heisenberg") without relying on costly quantum resources. These findings may encourage further exploration into the potential of post-selection strategies for enhancing quantum precision measurements.

In the summer of 2017, the NBA implemented rule changes, including a reduction in total timeouts, to improve game flow, making effective timeout management by coaches more critical. Determining the value of a timeout in different game situations, such as when an opponent is on a run, is essential. When facing an opposing run, there are two primary strategies: calling a timeout to rest and regroup, or saving it and hoping the team self-corrects during play. This study examines the validity of these approaches using the Rubin causal model to quantify the causal impact of a timeout during an opponent's run. We carefully address the often-overlooked stable unit-treatment-value assumption (SUTVA) to inform our definition of units. To measure timeout effects, we introduce a novel, interpretable outcome metric based on score differences, which effectively captures broad shifts in scoring dynamics suitable for sports analytics where outcomes fluctuate frequently. Our analysis concludes that although comebacks often follow an opposing run, calling a timeout during such a run is slightly disadvantageous, with the magnitude of this effect varying by franchise.

Various image processing applications, such as video compressed sensing and color image demosaicing, necessitate the separation of constituent images from coded superposition measurements. In these contexts, physically viable code patterns are inherently non-negative, systematically structured, and often lack the incoherence properties found in other patterns like Gaussian codes, which can hinder reconstruction quality. This paper addresses this by designing code patterns for video compressed sensing and demosaicing that minimize the mutual coherence of the matrix $\boldsymbol{\Phi\Psi}$, where $\boldsymbol{\Phi}$ is the sensing matrix derived from the code and $\boldsymbol{\Psi}$ represents the signal basis. Our primary contribution lies in explicitly incorporating the specific structural constraints required by these applications: (1) non-negativity, (2) block-diagonal structure, and (3) circular shifting. Notably, the circular shifting property facilitates accurate and seamless patch-wise reconstruction within certain compressed sensing frameworks.

We have calculated the exclusive electroproduction process, $\gamma^* p \rightarrow V p$, of heavy quarkonia $V$ to Next-to-Leading Order (NLO) within the collinear factorisation framework, a formal proof of which exists for this specific reaction. By incorporating an off-shell virtuality $Q^2$ associated with the photon, this approach extends the phase space of exclusive heavy quarkonia photoproduction to encompass electroproduction kinematics. This process holds significance for diffractive scattering studies at HERA, as well as at the future Electron-Ion Collider (EIC), and the proposed Large Hadron-electron Collider (LHeC) and Future Circular Collider (FCC).

We investigate the development of random hypermagnetic fields (HMFs) within the symmetric phase of the early universe, prior to the electroweak phase transition. This evolution is governed by an analog of the chiral magnetic effect, which incorporates asymmetries in leptons and Higgs bosons; these asymmetries serve as dynamical variables evolving concurrently with the HMFs. Furthermore, we include the effects of hyper-magnetohydrodynamic (hyper-MHD) turbulence on the effective diffusion coefficient and the $\alpha$-dynamo parameter. The realistic seed HMF spectrum comprises two branches: Batchelor and Kolmogorov. We examine the influence of HMFs on the generation of relic gravitational waves (GWs) and the baryon asymmetry of the universe (BAU), as well as the flavor oscillations of supernova neutrinos induced by stochastic GWs. By comparing the spectral density of produced GWs with LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA observations, we derive constraints on the strength of the seed HMF. Additionally, a stricter upper limit on the seed HMF is established based on the requirement that the generated BAU does not surpass observed values.

This study introduces linear mixed models for grouped observations, proposing an L1-penalty on fixed effects coefficients derived from the log-likelihood by treating random effects as missing data. A multicycle ECM algorithm solves the resulting optimization problem, compatible with any variable selection technique for linear models. Notably, the method accommodates scenarios where the number of parameters $p$ exceeds the number of observations $n$ and operates more efficiently than lmmLasso (Schelldorfer, 2011) by avoiding the inversion of an $n \times n$ matrix. Theoretical results from Schelldorfer (2011) hold for our approach when both random effect and residual variances are known. Empirical tests combining the algorithm with a variable selection method (Rohart, 2011) demonstrate superior performance in estimating relevant fixed effects and variances compared to lmmLasso, outperforming it in both standard ($p < n$) and high-dimensional ($p > n$) settings.

Measurements of correlations between flow coefficient moments are presented for Pb-Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}} = 5.02$ TeV, utilizing data from the ALICE detector. These novel results rely on multiparticle mixed harmonic cumulants derived from charged particles within the pseudorapidity interval $|\eta|<0.8$ and transverse momentum range $0.2 < p_{\rm T} < 5.0$ GeV/$c$. The analysis displays the centrality dependence of correlations involving two flow coefficients, as well as those involving three flow coefficients, specifically examining their second moments. Furthermore, for the first time, a set of mixed harmonic cumulants incorporating higher moments of $v_2$ and $v_3$ is reported, revealing the expected pattern of alternating negative, positive, and negative signs for four-, six-, and eight-particle cumulants, respectively. These findings are compared against hydrodynamic simulations using iEBE-VISHNU with AMPT and TRENTo initial conditions. The study demonstrates that the precision of the 2015 LHC Run 2 data enables an investigation into initial-state fluctuation details and the nonlinear hydrodynamic response of $v_2$ and $v_3$ to their respective initial anisotropy coefficients, $\varepsilon_2$ and $\varepsilon_3$. Ultimately, these new investigations into three-coefficient correlations and higher-moment correlations between two coefficients will refine constraints on initial-state models and facilitate the extraction of precise information regarding the dynamic evolution of the hot, dense matter produced in heavy-ion collisions at the LHC.

This research investigates the factors influencing individuals' behavioral intention to adhere to social engineering awareness campaigns. Specifically, it examines the relationships between intention and variables including perceived severity, vulnerability, threat, fear, subjective norms, attitude, perceived behavioral control, self-efficacy, response efficacy, trust in authorities, perceived regulation, authority performance, information sensitivity, and privacy concerns. Utilizing a cross-sectional design, the study administered a survey in Slovenia from January to June 2020. Although 553 individuals participated, 542 responses were deemed valid after excluding incomplete entries, yielding a 27.9% response rate. The original questionnaire was drafted in English, with a Slovenian translation also provided.

Recent research utilizing commonsense knowledge models—pretrained language models (LMs) fine-tuned on knowledge graph (KG) tuples—demonstrates that substantial commonsense knowledge is encoded within the parameters of large language models. Nevertheless, since parallel studies indicate that LMs struggle to independently hypothesize declarative commonsense relationships, it is currently uncertain whether this knowledge is acquired during pretraining or through fine-tuning on KG data. To address this, we trained these models in few-shot scenarios to examine the emergence of their commonsense representation capabilities. Our findings reveal that such models can quickly adapt from limited examples, suggesting that KG fine-tuning establishes an interface to access knowledge already learned during pretraining. Furthermore, our analysis of absolute, angular, and distributional parameter shifts during few-shot fine-tuning offers new insights into the mechanisms by which this interface is developed.

This paper introduces a new deep learning-based approach for SPECT angle interpolation. The model was trained using projection data derived from software phantoms. To assess its effectiveness, Shepp-Logan phantoms with varying noise levels were employed, and the interpolated sinograms were reconstructed via Ordered Subset Expectation Maximization (OSEM) for comparison against reconstructions of the original sinograms. The proposed technique simultaneously quadruples the number of projections and denoises the sinogram. Results indicate that the model substantially enhances reconstruction accuracy. Furthermore, real-world DAT-SPECT sinogram outcomes are provided to validate the method's practical efficacy and capabilities.

This study introduces a model-reduction framework for the material point method applied to nonlinear manifolds. The approach approximates $\textit{kinematics}$ by employing an implicit neural representation to model the deformation map, thereby constraining deformation paths to a low-dimensional manifold. Because the deformation map is explicitly approximated, its spatiotemporal gradients—specifically the deformation gradient and velocity—are derived through analytical differentiation. Unlike conventional model-reduction methods that create manifolds to approximate the finite degrees of freedom of a specific spatial discretization, this method utilizes an implicit neural representation to approximate the $\textit{continuous}$ deformation map directly. This capability renders the kinematic approximation independent of any particular discretization, enabling the technique to handle dynamic discretizations, such as resolution adjustments, during online reduced-order-model simulations.

To define $\textit{dynamics}$ for the generalized coordinates, we introduce a set of projection techniques. At every time step, these methods: (1) compute full-space kinematics at quadrature points, (2) determine full-space dynamics for a selected subset of 'sample' material points, and (3) derive reduced-space dynamics by projecting the updated full-space positions and velocities onto the low-dimensional manifold and its tangent space, respectively. Computational efficiency is significantly enhanced through hyper-reduction, ensuring all three steps operate only on a small fraction of the spatial domain. Large-scale numerical tests involving millions of material points demonstrate that the method achieves an order-of-magnitude reduction in computational cost—enabling $\textit{real-time simulations}$—with negligible error.

We introduce a novel approach leveraging coherently enhanced neutrino pair emission to investigate light-mediator interactions between electrons and neutrinos. Operating at a typical momentum transfer scale of atomic order $\mathcal O(1\,	ext{eV})$, this process exhibits exceptional sensitivity to mediator masses in the range $\mathcal O(10^{-3} \sim 10^4)$ eV. The method can constrain the product of electron ($g^e$ or $y^e$) and neutrino ($g^
u$ or $y^
u$) couplings down to $|y^e y^
u| < 10^{-9} \sim 10^{-19}$ for scalar mediators and $|g^e g^
u| < 10^{-15} \sim 10^{-26}$ for vector mediators, representing significant improvements over current limits.

Multi-label classification involves assigning discrete, non-exclusive labels to instances. While many existing methods adapt or transform binary and multi-class learning techniques, they often struggle to model the joint probability of labels or maintain generalization for unseen label combinations. To overcome these limitations, we introduce LNEMLC (Label Network Embedding for Multi-Label Classification), a novel scheme that embeds the label network to expand the input space for both learning and inference in any base multi-label classifier. This approach captures label joint probabilities with low computational cost, achieving performance comparable to top-tier methods in the literature. We demonstrate that the method yields statistically significant improvements over a simple kNN baseline and offer guidance on selecting robust configurations that perform consistently across various data domains.

This study examines the dynamics of a two-atom system coupled to a quasi-one-dimensional waveguide with a rectangular cross-section. The waveguide accommodates various TE and TM modes, where the latter act as an environment by selectively adjusting the atoms' dipole moments. This environmental interaction induces collective dissipation and coupling between the atoms. When both atoms are centered within the waveguide, a retardation effect is observed; however, shifting one atom off-center disrupts this effect. To maintain complete system dissipation through a dark state mechanism, we propose an arrangement where the atomic connection is perpendicular to the waveguide axis. We anticipate that these findings will contribute to quantum information processing utilizing advanced waveguide architectures.

We systematically identify all circulant good matrices with odd orders divisible by 3, up to an order of 70. This process reveals a previously unknown set of good matrices for order 27 and a new set for order 57. Furthermore, we demonstrate that circulant good matrices cannot exist for orders 51, 63, and 69, providing three new counterexamples to the conjecture that they exist in all odd orders. We also establish a novel relationship between the entries of these matrices and leverage it to enhance our enumeration algorithm. Our approach utilizes the SAT+CAS framework, which integrates computer algebra capabilities with modern SAT solvers to efficiently explore large search spaces defined by both algebraic and logical constraints.

Let $R_+^{n\times n}$ represent the set of $n\times n$ non-negative matrices. For any matrix $A$ in this set, define $\Omega(A)$ as the collection of all matrices generated by permuting the elements within each row of $A$. Formally, $\Omega(A)$ consists of matrices $B$ where each row $i$ of $B$ is a permutation of the corresponding row $i$ of $A$. For any $B \in \Omega(A)$, $\rho(B)$ signifies the spectral radius, or the largest non-negative eigenvalue, of $B$. This study demonstrates that the arithmetic mean of the row sums of $A$ is bounded between the minimum and maximum spectral radii achievable by matrices in $\Omega(A)$. Specifically, we establish the inequality:
$$\min_{B\in\Omega(A)}\rho(B)\leq \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n a_{i,j}\leq \max_{B\in\Omega(A)}\rho(B).$$
When $A$ consists of strictly positive entries, we derive necessary and sufficient conditions under which either inequality (and thus both) becomes an equality. Furthermore, we provide criteria for an irreducible matrix $C$ to achieve the minimum or maximum spectral radius within $\Omega(A)$. These criteria facilitate the development of algorithms to identify such matrices $C$ when all entries of $A$ are positive.

Stars are believed to form by gathering material from surrounding disks, with a general agreement that stellar magnetic fields channel this matter onto the star's surface. This field is thought to be strong enough to cut off the disk near the corotation radius, where the disk's rotation matches the star's. Spectro-interferometric observations of young stellar objects reveal that hydrogen emission originates from a small region, typically a few milliarcseconds wide and located inside the dust sublimation radius. The source of this emission remains debated, with possibilities including the stellar magnetosphere, a rotating wind, or the disk itself. For intermediate-mass Herbig AeBe stars, the spatial resolution of Br gamma emission rules out a magnetospheric origin, as their weak magnetic fields (on the order of tenths of Gauss) create extremely compact magnetospheres. Conversely, T Tauri sources possess larger magnetospheres that should be easier to resolve; however, their small angular size (a few tenths of milliarcseconds) combined with hydrogen-emitting winds complicates interpretation. This study presents direct evidence of magnetospheric accretion by spatially resolving the inner disk of the 60 pc distant T Tauri star TW Hydrae using optical long baseline interferometry. We determine that the hydrogen near-infrared emission arises from a region approximately 3.5 stellar radii ($R_*$) across. This area lies within the continuum dusty disk ($R_{cont} = 7 R_*$) and is smaller than the corotation radius, which is twice as large. These findings indicate that the hydrogen emission stems from accretion columns, consistent with magnetospheric accretion models, rather than from a wind originating at much greater distances (>1 AU).

This paper examines 3D inhomogeneous Navier-Stokes flows containing vacuum, deriving regularity criteria and Liouville-type theorems within the Lorentz space for a smooth solution $(\rho, \mathbf{u})$ that meets appropriate conditions.

This study introduces a consistent microscopic framework for superconductivity in strongly correlated electronic systems using the extended t-J-V model, which incorporates intersite Coulomb repulsion and electron-phonon coupling. An exact Dyson equation is formulated for the normal and anomalous (pair) Green functions of projected (Hubbard) electronic operators and solved via the self-consistent Born approximation for the self-energy. The findings reveal that strong kinematical interactions, comparable to the electronic kinetic energy ($\sim t$), drive high-$T_c$ d-wave pairing through spin fluctuations, a mechanism significantly more potent than the exchange interaction $J$. In contrast, contributions from Coulomb repulsion and electron-phonon interactions to d-wave pairing are minimal. These outcomes validate the spin-fluctuation mechanism for high-temperature superconductivity in cuprates, a concept previously suggested by phenomenological models.

It is established that for a $C^2$ flow on a finite-dimensional compact manifold, sectional-hyperbolic attracting sets contain at most finitely many ergodic physical invariant probability measures. We establish an upper limit on the count of distinct ergodic physical measures within a connected singular-hyperbolic attracting set for a 3-dimensional flow, a bound determined solely by the quantity of Lorenz-like equilibria present in the set. Furthermore, examples of singular-hyperbolic attracting sets are presented to demonstrate that this bound is tight.

Creating intelligent neuromorphic systems remains a difficult task, necessitating a deep grasp of the hardware's core components. Furthermore, accessible and intuitive prototyping tools are essential to accelerate the design process. We have created an open-source Loihi emulator built upon the Brian neural network simulator, which integrates seamlessly into current simulation environments. Our work demonstrates accurate software-based emulation of Loihi for both individual neurons and recurrently connected spiking neural networks. Additionally, we have reviewed and implemented on-chip learning, noting minor discrepancies attributable to stochastic rounding. This study offers a comprehensive overview of Loihi's computational units and introduces a novel, user-friendly prototyping package designed to facilitate the conceptualization and deployment of new algorithms.

This paper introduces a Caristi-Banach type $\mathcal{Z}_{R}^{b}$-contraction within the context of $b$-metric spaces equipped with a transitive relation. By integrating concepts from Caristi and Banach contractions via a simulation function, we define this new notion and provide an illustrative example to support our findings.

Laser experiments are emerging as a vital instrument in astronomical research, offering complementary insights to observational data and theoretical models. Strong magnetic fields have recently been detected at the shock fronts of supernova explosions, and determining the physical mechanisms behind this phenomenon is crucial for understanding the evolution of the interstellar medium. However, simulating the interaction between hydrodynamic instabilities and ambient magnetic fields in a laboratory setting has proven difficult. To address this, we established an experimental platform specifically designed to study the magnetized Richtmyer-Meshkov instability (RMI). Our measurements showed that the growth velocity aligned with linear theory, and magnetic-field amplification was directly linked to RMI development. This experiment marks the first validation of turbulent magnetic field amplification driven by shock-induced interfacial instabilities under astrophysical conditions. Furthermore, clarifying fundamental processes in magnetized plasmas is essential for various applications, including fusion research and planetary science.

In topological stabilizer codes, braiding defects enable the fault-tolerant execution of logical operations. Specifically, twists—defects representing the endpoints of domain walls—are linked to the symmetries of the code's anyon model. This study examines twists across multiple instances of the 2D surface code, establishing that for these twists to function as anyons, they must be self-inverse, and all charges they can localize must remain invariant under their associated symmetry. When these criteria are met, the twist and its localized charges mimic an anyonic model from a hierarchy that extends the Ising anyons. We demonstrate that braiding these twists yields either tensor products of S gates or tensor products of CZ gates. Furthermore, we show that for any number of 2D surface code copies, applying H gates within a copy and CNOT gates between copies is sufficient to generate all possible twists.

Relational inference utilizes connections and relationships between entities within a network to deduce information from limited samples, a technique particularly valuable when comprehensive global data is inaccessible or hard to acquire. However, questions remain regarding the reliability of inferring from small labeled subsets, the optimal sampling approaches, and how these choices influence inference errors. Furthermore, it is unclear how network structure dictates the most effective sampling strategies. This study systematically investigates the interplay between sampling methods, sample size, and the accuracy of relational inference. We constructed a suite of synthetic networks featuring binary node attributes and adjustable homophily levels. As anticipated, high accuracy was achieved in heterophilic networks even with minimal initial labeling, independent of the sampling strategy. Conversely, this did not hold for homophilic networks; strategies effective in heterophilic settings resulted in significant inference errors in homophilic ones. These results indicate that the influence of network structure on relational classification is more intricate than previously believed.

Simulating forest environments serves diverse purposes, ranging from artistic and entertainment projects to commercial and scientific modeling. Although the distinct characteristics and lighting conditions of forests make specialized simulators ideal, existing tools are often proprietary or narrowly focused on specific applications. This work reviews key aspects of procedural generation and rendering tailored for forests to develop a generalized, open-source tool capable of creating interactive and realistic forest scenes. The system employs specialized L-systems to model trees, which are then distributed via an ecosystem simulation algorithm. Rendering is handled through a deferred pipeline utilizing a Blinn-Phong lighting model that includes real-time leaf transparency and post-processing effects. The outcome is a balanced system offering both high natural realism and visual appeal, making it suitable for applications such as training computer vision algorithms for autonomous robots and generating visual media.

Knowledge tracing (KT) seeks to utilize students' past learning records to gauge their proficiency in specific skills, thereby forecasting future performance. In real-world scenarios, a student's history consists of multiple "sessions," which are collections of massed questions, rather than just a simple sequence of isolated answers. Theoretically, learning dynamics can vary significantly both within and between these sessions; thus, effectively modeling these dynamics is essential for solving the KT problem. However, most current KT models treat learning records as a single continuous sequence, failing to account for shifts in a student's knowledge state across sessions. To address this, we introduce HiTSKT, a novel hierarchical transformer model. This model features an interaction-level encoder to capture knowledge gained within a session and a session-level encoder to summarize knowledge acquired across previous sessions. To predict the outcome of a current interaction, a knowledge retriever combines summarized past-session knowledge with prior interaction data to form appropriate representations, which are then used to calculate the student's current knowledge state. Furthermore, to model long-term forgetting across sessions, we incorporate a power-law-decay attention mechanism in the session encoder to prioritize recent sessions. Extensive experiments on three public datasets show that HiTSKT outperforms six existing state-of-the-art KT models, achieving new benchmarks on all of them.

Dialogue systems equipped with social influence capabilities—such as persuasion, negotiation, and therapy—are vital for expanding technological applications into diverse, realistic contexts. Nevertheless, current research predominantly targets either task-oriented or open-domain scenarios, a classification that fails to systematically capture influence skills. Furthermore, there is no formal definition or established category for dialogue systems possessing these abilities, and data-driven initiatives in this area remain scarce. This work formally introduces and defines the category of \emph{social influence dialogue systems}, which utilize natural conversation to alter users' cognitive and emotional states, thereby shifting their thoughts, opinions, and behaviors. We provide a survey of tasks, datasets, and methodologies, synthesizing progress across seven distinct domains. Additionally, we analyze the similarities and disparities among these systems, highlight existing limitations, and propose avenues for future research. Ultimately, this study offers a comprehensive reference intended to stimulate further dedicated inquiry and discourse within this emerging field.

The long-standing challenge in nuclear physics involves understanding how level densities evolve during the transition from spherical to well-deformed nuclei. We have measured level densities for a chain of neodymium isotopes ($^{142,144-151}$Nd) that demonstrate this crossover. To our knowledge, these results constitute the most comprehensive dataset of nuclear level densities for an isotopic series spanning from the neutron shell closure toward the mid-shell. We observed a significant rise in level densities along this chain, with an overall increase of approximately 170 times at an excitation energy of 7.5 MeV, reaching saturation near mass 150. Calculations using the shell model Monte Carlo (SMMC) method align excellently with our experimental findings. Drawing from both our theoretical and experimental data, we provide an explanation for the observed mass dependence of level densities, attributing it to the intrinsic single-particle level density and collective enhancement.

This study examines the Bachelier model incorporating linear price impact, focusing on exponential utility indifference prices for standard European options. We calculate the non-trivial scaling limit of these prices as the price impact vanishes, scaling inversely with risk aversion. Additionally, we explicitly identify a family of portfolios that achieve asymptotic optimality.

This paper examines the effective influence of potentials in wave equations, both with and without damping, on the $L^2$-estimates of their solutions. In the case of the free wave equation, it is established that the $L^2$-norm of the solution typically diverges to infinity as time progresses in one and two dimensions. However, by incorporating a potential under sufficiently broad conditions, one can regulate this growth to achieve $L^2$-bounds. This approach is also applicable to damped wave equations with potentials, enabling fast energy and $L^2$ decay results in low-dimensional settings that have remained open problems for some time. Additionally, applications to heat and plate equations involving potentials are explored. The primary focus of this study is the low-dimensional case.

The complete removal of anomalies across all orders of perturbation theory remains an unresolved challenge. Standard invariance conditions and Wess-Zumino identities fail to eliminate anomalies in the general case of Yang-Mills theories; consequently, introducing a new symmetry could impose stricter constraints on anomalies and potentially solve this issue. This study examines Ojima's anti-BRST transformation within the causal framework to determine if it yields such new restrictions. Unfortunately, the findings are negative: if a theory exhibits BRST invariance up to the second order of perturbation theory, it necessarily possesses anti-BRST invariance to the same order, a result likely valid for all orders. Thus, the anti-BRST transformation offers no novel solutions, necessitating the exploration of alternative concepts to constrain and ultimately eliminate anomalies in general Yang-Mills theories.

**Context.** Quasi-periodic pulsations (QPPs) generally exhibit regular, periodic peaks in light curves during solar flares. While multiple periods can sometimes appear at a single wavelength, simultaneous period variations across different channels are uncommon. **Aims.** This study reports QPPs observed during a solar flare on October 27, 2014, characterized by a period shift contingent on the inclusion of thermal versus nonthermal components. The event was monitored simultaneously by numerous instruments. **Methods.** We employed the fast Fourier transform (FFT) to decompose light curves at various wavelengths into rapidly and slowly varying signals, identifying QPPs as periodic peaks within the rapid components. Periods were calculated using the wavelet method and validated against FFT spectra. **Results.** During the impulsive phase, thermal emissions in soft X-rays revealed a 50-second period, whereas nonthermal emissions in hard X-rays and microwaves showed a period of approximately 100 seconds. The precise 2.0 ratio between these periods may result from magnetic reconnection rate modulations driven by fundamental and harmonic magnetohydrodynamic wave modes. Additionally, the 100-second period was detected across a wide spectral range, including hard X-rays, extreme-UV/UV, and microwaves, suggesting periodic magnetic reconnection. **Conclusions.** To our knowledge, this is the first report of simultaneous period changes between thermal and nonthermal components within a single flare. This novel observation poses a potential challenge to existing theoretical models of flare QPPs.

Since 1987, our work has examined correlation graphs among various organismal features during stress and adaptation. Following 33 years of extensive research, numerous discoveries, and rediscoveries by many authors, we confidently assert that analyzing these correlation graphs is highly beneficial. Furthermore, we emphasize the utility of Hans Selye's concept of adaptability ("adaptation energy"), particularly when enhanced by "adaptation entropy," free energy analysis, and the evaluation of limiting factors. Our 2021 review, titled "Dynamic and Thermodynamic Adaptation Models" (Phys Life Rev, arXiv:2103.01959 [q-bio.OT]), elicited significant engagement from leading experts, sparking discussions on new ideas and challenges ranging from aging dynamics and athletic training to single-cell omics. These discussions also deeply explored methodological foundations such as free energy analysis. In this article, we present an analytical summary of twelve papers that commented on our review, along with several related publications.

The hard $\gamma$-ray spectrum observed in supernova remnant G106.3+2.7 can be accounted for by a hadronic model incorporating the gluon condensation effect. This suggests that PeVatrons and EeVatrons are ubiquitous throughout the universe, including our galaxy, with the capability to accelerate protons to energies exceeding the "ankle" ($10^{19}~eV$). Although these proton beams are extremely faint within the galaxy and undetectable individually on Earth, the gluon condensation effect significantly amplifies the proton-proton cross section. This enhancement offsets the low proton flux, resulting in the observed $\gamma$-ray emission. Furthermore, we demonstrate that gluon condensation in protons serves as an efficient mechanism for converting kinetic energy into $\gamma$-rays across the universe.

This work introduces a learning-based algorithm designed for the distributed formation control of networked multi-agent systems subject to unknown, nonlinear dynamics. Unlike most existing approaches that rely on specific parametric assumptions for unknown dynamics or require excessively large control inputs to ensure theoretical validity, our method circumvents these limitations by combining neural network learning with adaptive control in a two-stage process. In the initial stage, each agent trains a neural network controller using data generated from a variety of formation tasks and agent parameters. These variations are achieved by perturbing nominal agent parameters and altering the specific formation requirements of the assigned task. In the subsequent stage, the trained neural network is embedded within an online adaptive control policy, ensuring that the multi-agent closed-loop system successfully executes the desired formation. Both the learning phase and the adaptive control strategy are fully distributed, meaning each agent determines its actions based solely on local information from its neighbors. Furthermore, the algorithm operates without requiring any prior knowledge of the agents' unknown dynamic terms or specific approximation schemes. We provide rigorous theoretical guarantees confirming the successful accomplishment of the formation task.

Type U radio bursts represent impulsive, coherent radio emissions from the Sun, signaling subrelativistic electron beams traveling along magnetic loops within the solar corona. This study analyzes a Type U burst exceptionally imaged on March 22, 2011, by the Nançay Radioheliograph (NRH) across three frequencies (298.7, 327.0, and 360.8 MHz). Employing a new modeling method, we demonstrate that high-resolution radio heliograph images of Type U bursts can independently and accurately reconstruct the 3D morphology of coronal loops without relying on triangulation, while also fully constraining their physical parameters. Simultaneously, this approach yields unique insights into the dynamics of accelerated electron beams, offering critical clues about the underlying plasma acceleration mechanisms and explaining the relative scarcity of Type U bursts compared to Type III bursts. Finally, we propose plausible explanations for the discrepancy between the modeled radio loops and the extreme-ultraviolet (EUV) structures observed from space in the same coronal region.

This study examines the connection between wavefunction (de)localization and avoided crossings within a quadrupole billiard, utilizing the inverse participation ratio, Rényi entropy, and root-mean-square (rms) image contrast as three distinct metrics. Our findings indicate that these measures behave consistently, reaching a minimum at the center of the avoided crossing where the wavefunction is most delocalized. Consequently, these quantities serve as effective indicators for wavefunction (de)localization, with the rms contrast proving to be the most sensitive of the three.

**Objective:** Historically, the validation of surrogate endpoints has relied on randomized controlled trial (RCT) data, yet such data can be insufficient for this purpose. This study aimed to enhance surrogate endpoint validation by integrating real-world evidence (RWE).

**Study Design and Setting:** We utilized comparative RWE (cRWE) and single-arm RWE (sRWE) to bolster RCT evidence when evaluating progression-free survival (PFS) as a surrogate for overall survival (OS) in metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC). Treatment effect estimates derived from RCTs, cRWE, and matched sRWE—specifically comparing anti-angiogenic therapies against chemotherapy—were employed to identify surrogacy patterns and forecast the impact of PFS treatment effects on OS.

**Results:** A total of seven RCTs, four cRWE studies, and three matched sRWE studies were identified. Incorporating RWE alongside RCTs decreased the uncertainty surrounding the parameters of the surrogate relationship. Furthermore, adding RWE to RCT data enhanced both the accuracy and precision of OS predictions based on observed PFS effects.

**Conclusion:** Integrating RWE with RCT data refined the precision of parameters defining the surrogate link between treatment effects on PFS and OS, as well as improved the prediction of clinical benefit.

We introduced a new method for modifying the time scale of audio signals. Unlike traditional techniques that rely on framing, our spectral approach utilizes the short-time Fourier transform to maintain frequency integrity during temporal stretching. Our neural network model, TSM-Net, converts raw audio into a high-level latent representation called "Neuralgram," where each vector corresponds to 1024 audio samples. Inspired by framing but designed to eliminate clipping artifacts, the Neuralgram is a real-valued two-dimensional matrix that allows us to apply existing image resizing methods. After resizing, our neural decoder reconstructs the time-scaled audio. Both the encoder and decoder were trained using GANs, demonstrating robust generalization across scaled Neuralgrams. Our approach produces minimal artifacts and establishes a new avenue for modern time-scale modification research. The audio samples are available at https://ernestchu.github.io/tsm-net-demo/.

Goal-oriented dialogue systems struggle to balance fluent language generation with specific task control. Although supervised learning using large language models can produce realistic text, determining how to guide these responses toward task completion without compromising linguistic quality remains an unresolved challenge. This study frames goal-oriented dialogue as a partially observed Markov decision process, treating the language model as a unified representation of both system dynamics and policy. This perspective enables the adaptation of learning-based control techniques, such as task relabeling, to create a straightforward and effective method for goal-aware fine-tuning of language models, resulting in substantially enhanced task performance. Furthermore, we propose several training strategies designed to sharpen the model's focus on the immediate objective. We assess our proposed method, Context-Aware Language Models (CALM), on a practical flight-booking scenario using the AirDialogue dataset. Empirical results demonstrate that CALM surpasses state-of-the-art approaches by 7% in task success rate, achieving performance comparable to human levels.

We define an infinite family of universal polynomials, independent of $(g,n)$, within the Miller-Morita-Mumford classes $\kappa_m \in H^{2m}(\overline{\cal M}_{g,n},\bq)$, which are established over the moduli space of stable curves of genus $g$ with $n$ marked points. We propose that these polynomials vanish within a specific range determined by $g$ and $n$.

Bipolar Planetary Nebulae (PN) are characterized by well-defined, low-power outflows, with certain instances displaying shock-induced equatorial spiderweb patterns and hourglass formations around these outflows. These features differ significantly from those found in spherical and elliptical PNe, implying a non-standard mechanism for energizing both structures simultaneously. This study compiles evidence from existing literature concerning bipolar PNe such as Hb\,12 and other sources to support an alternative energization model: accretion from shells deposited during earlier post-AGB and pre-PN phases. Beyond powering the bipolar outflow, a sub-Eddington accretion scenario offers a hydrodynamical explanation for the spiderweb and outer hourglass structures as oblique shockwaves that channel accreting material toward the equatorial region. Furthermore, accretion rate estimates derived from fallback-related spherical accretion appear capable of driving the observed low-power outflows and contributing to the total luminosity of these objects.

Matching text queries to videos or vice versa presents a significant challenge. While current methods predominantly depend on user-generated annotations, this strategy is often impractical. This study investigates the use of the CLIP language-image model to derive video representations independently of such annotations. Since CLIP was specifically designed to learn a shared embedding space for comparing images and text, we adapted its capabilities for video analysis using the techniques outlined herein. Consequently, we achieved state-of-the-art performance on the MSR-VTT and MSVD benchmarks.

Planning presents significant challenges. While employing subgoals can render planning more manageable, identifying these subgoals incurs substantial computational costs. The central question is which algorithms can harness the advantages of subgoal-based planning while minimizing the expense of subgoal selection. We introduce visual scoping, a strategy that interleaves planning and execution by alternately defining a spatial region as the next subgoal and selecting actions to accomplish it. We tested our visual scoping algorithm against two baselines—planning all subgoals beforehand and planning without subgoals—across various physical assembly tasks. Our findings indicate that visual scoping achieves task performance comparable to the subgoal planner while utilizing only a fraction of the total computational resources. Collectively, these results advance our understanding of how humans might efficiently allocate cognitive resources to solve complex planning problems.

Sarnak's conjecture regarding M\"obius disjointness posits that the M\"obius function is disjoint from all zero-entropy dynamical systems. This work establishes the validity of this conjecture for one-frequency analytic quasi-periodic cocycles that are almost reducible, thereby generalizing results from \cite{LS15,W17} to the noncommutative setting. The demonstration depends on a quantitative formulation of almost reducibility.

Schmidt introduced maximum Hermitian rank metric codes in 2018; this paper presents interpolation-based encoding and decoding algorithms for these codes specifically when both the code length and minimum distance are odd.

Accelerating the discovery of new materials offers profound benefits for society and industry, especially within pharmaceuticals and clean energy sectors. While many experimental instruments are increasingly automated to enable continuous operation and higher throughput, sample preparation often remains a manual bottleneck. This reliance on human labor consumes considerable time on repetitive tasks, introducing errors and hindering the generation of statistically significant data. Crystallization experiments, widely used in chemistry for both purification and polymorph screening, typically begin with a solubility screen to determine if a compound dissolves in a specific solvent. This process is often labor-intensive and time-consuming. Furthermore, precise determination of the exact solubility limit is frequently unnecessary; simply identifying a solubility threshold per solvent is sufficient. To overcome these challenges, we introduce a novel cascaded deep learning model inspired by how a human chemist visually evaluates whether a solid has fully dissolved. This paper presents the design, development, and evaluation of the first fully autonomous solubility screening framework, utilizing advanced image segmentation and convolutional neural networks for classification. We established a dataset of various molecules and solvents collected in a real-world laboratory setting. Subsequently, we tested our approach using an eye-in-hand camera mounted on a seven-degree-of-freedom robotic arm, demonstrating that our model achieves 99.13% test accuracy across diverse experimental configurations.

This research examines complex digital platforms in their early two-sided market stages to generate significant network effects. By employing Transfer Entropy, the study identifies "super users" who link hominids across different networks, thereby amplifying these effects within increasingly intricate digital platforms. Additionally, the work seeks to redefine product managers' decision-making criteria, assisting them in pinpointing users who drive stronger network impacts. As technology advances, industry structures have become harder to decipher and business logic more convoluted, presenting the primary obstacle for startups striving to innovate. Ultimately, this study aims to empower product managers to construct novel digital economic networks, facilitate prioritized, data-driven choices, and locate potential network hubs even within small-scale products.

Traditionally, rasterization is utilized for real-time rendering to satisfy interactive frame rate requirements, yet it falls short in generating the visual realism achieved by ray tracing. Consequently, hybrid rendering has been developed to enhance rasterization fidelity by integrating ray tracing within real-time workflows. This study investigates distributed rendering as a method to embed real-time hybrid rendering into metaverse environments for immersive graphics. In standalone extended reality (XR) hardware, achieving ray-traced visuals typically depends on pure cloud-based remote rendering, which requires low-latency networks to deliver real-time ray-traced data in response to user interactions. However, under high-latency network conditions, remote rendering often fails to sustain interactive frame rates, degrading the user experience. By employing a distributed rendering strategy that combines ray tracing on robust remote hardware with raster-based rendering on client devices, our hybrid approach enables standalone XR devices to deliver ray-tracing-enhanced graphics while maintaining interactive frame rates, even when network latency is high.

Deriving the vibrational density of states (DOS) for liquids, specifically its low-frequency linear behavior, has historically proven difficult due to the existence of an infinite number of purely imaginary instantaneous normal modes (INMs). By integrating an analytic continuation of the Plemelj identity into the complex plane with the purely overdamped dynamics of these INMs, we have established a closed-form analytic formula for the low-frequency DOS of liquids. This derivation provides a first-principles explanation for the commonly observed linear frequency term in liquid DOS, noting that its slope correlates with the average INM lifetime. Furthermore, analytical predictions are strongly supported by fitting simulation data for Lennard-Jones liquids and successfully reproduce the expected Arrhenius law for the average INM relaxation time.

Given the limited size of emotion recognition datasets, applying advanced deep learning techniques presents significant challenges. This study introduces a transfer learning strategy for speech emotion recognition, utilizing features derived from pre-trained wav2vec 2.0 models and processed through basic neural networks. Specifically, we integrate outputs from multiple layers of the pre-trained model using trainable weights that are optimized jointly with the downstream network. Additionally, we assess performance using two distinct wav2vec 2.0 variants: one fine-tuned for speech recognition and one that is not. Our approach is evaluated on the IEMOCAP and RAVDESS benchmarks, demonstrating results that outperform existing literature.

To maximize Artificial Intelligence's influence in biology and medicine, it is essential that recommendations are both precise and transparent. While neurosymbolic methods utilizing multi-hop reasoning on knowledge graphs have demonstrated the ability to generate clear explanations in other fields, their application to intricate biomedical datasets and challenges remains underexplored. This study investigates the approach within the context of drug discovery to validate its utility. For the first time, we systematically evaluate this method across various biomedical datasets and recommendation tasks using fair benchmark comparisons. The results indicate that the approach surpasses the best baselines by an average of 21.7% and generates novel, biologically significant explanations.

We utilize mean-field Hartree Fock theory to examine gapped electronic states at charge neutrality in rhombohedral graphite films containing up to thirty layers. For the ground state, while the band gap diminishes as the number of layers increases, the order parameter (representing the band separation at the valley center) stabilizes at a constant non-zero value. We investigate two types of disorder: chiral symmetry breaking via random layer potentials and chiral preserving disorder through random interlayer coupling values. The former decreases the mean band gap magnitude, whereas the latter has a negligible impact due to self-averaging in films with many layers. We also analyze the ground state containing a single stacking fault, which generates two pairs of low-energy bands and yields two distinct order parameters; one governs the zero-temperature band gap, while the other dictates the critical temperature. Consequently, the band gap exhibits a temperature dependence unique to that of pristine rhombohedral graphite. In systems with stacking faults, each $m$-layer rhombohedral segment contributes a pair of low-energy flat bands, creating a Berry curvature peak at a specific wave vector dependent on $m$. Finally, the Chern number per spin-valley flavor for the filled valence bands in the ground state equals half the total number of layers, matching the value found in pristine rhombohedral graphite.

Thermal detectors serve as highly effective tools for identifying rare particle physics phenomena, traditionally utilizing inorganic crystals mounted within copper support frames. This study introduces an innovative operational method for these detectors, involving the cooling of TeO2 crystals to approximately 10 mK using a lightweight structure composed of plastic materials. The benefits of this new approach are analyzed.

We provide a proof of the Riemannian Penrose inequality under the condition $r\leq m+ \sqrt{m^2-q^2}$, where $A=4\pi r^2$ denotes the area of the outermost apparent horizon (which may consist of multiple connected components). This result applies to strongly asymptotically flat initial data sets for the Einstein-Maxwell equations that satisfy the charged dominant energy condition, provided there is no charged matter exterior to the horizon, with $m$ representing the total ADM mass and $q$ the total charge.

Recent research has identified adversarial examples as pervasive threats to deep neural network (DNN) driven speech recognition systems. This study introduces U-Net$_{At}$, a U-Net based attention architecture designed to strengthen adversarial speech signals. We assess the model's efficacy using interpretable speech recognition metrics and analyze its performance through augmented adversarial training. Experimental results indicate that U-Net$_{At}$ significantly boosts speech enhancement capabilities for adversarial inputs, raising the Perceptual Evaluation of Speech Quality (PESQ) from 1.13 to 2.78, the Speech Transmission Index (STI) from 0.65 to 0.75, and the Short-Term Objective Intelligibility (STOI) from 0.83 to 0.96. Furthermore, we evaluated the model on automatic speech recognition (ASR) tasks subjected to adversarial audio attacks. Our findings demonstrate that (i) temporal features extracted by the attention network bolster the robustness of DNN-based ASR models, and (ii) applying adversarial training with additive data augmentation enhances the generalization of these models. Word Error Rate (WER) metrics reveal an absolute reduction of 2.22% under gradient-based perturbations and 2.03% under evolutionary-optimized perturbations, indicating that our adversarially trained enhancement models effectively fortify ASR systems against resilient attacks.

Building upon our previous study in *J. Mol. Liq.* (2020), which demonstrated that methanol suppresses liquid-liquid critical points (LLCP) by inducing spontaneous hexagonal closed packing (HCP) crystallization near the liquid-liquid phase transition (LLPT) via molecular dynamics and core-softened potentials, this work investigates the impact of longer-chain alcohols on supercooled water-alcohol mixtures. We incorporated ethanol and 1-propanol into systems of identical particles interacting through a continuous shouldered well (CSW) potential, alongside the previously used core-softened methanol. Our findings reveal that as the non-polar chain length and alcohol concentration increase, the range of density anomalies in the phase diagrams progressively diminishes until vanishing entirely. This contrasts with the liquid-liquid phase transition and LLCP, which persist across all examined mixtures, consistent with observations reported in *Nature* (2001). In our model, increasing chain length and concentration alter the competition between scales within the CS potential, causing density anomalies to fade as the total maximum density (TMD) point disappears. This occurs when the first coordination shell structure is disrupted, favoring short-range ordering and reducing the competition between short- and long-range ordering. Furthermore, the size of the non-polar chains and their concentration influence solid-state behavior, promoting the formation of HCP and amorphous solids over body-centered cubic (BCC) crystals.

Microrheology determines the local viscoelastic properties of complex fluids by analyzing the movement of embedded colloidal particles, whether driven or free. While theoretical frameworks for forced-probe microrheology typically assume either constant force (CF) or constant velocity (CV), experimental conditions rarely fix either the force or the kinematics. Furthermore, the strict constraints of CF or CV models create challenges in quantifying probe fluctuations due to thermodynamic uncertainty relations. Specifically, for a Brownian particle in a harmonic trap, the product of the standard deviations of trap force and particle position equals $d k_BT$ across $d$ dimensions, where $k_BT$ represents thermal energy. Consequently, preventing fluctuations in force or position leads to infinite fluctuations in the other variable. To address this and enable fluctuation measurement, this study proposes a model where the probe is dragged by a moving harmonic potential, allowing both position and trap force to fluctuate. Beginning with the full Smoluchowski equation for $N$ hard active Brownian particles, we derive a pair Smoluchowski equation describing the probe's interaction with a single bath particle, assuming negligible hydrodynamic interactions in the dilute limit. Using the pair probability distribution, we calculate the mean and variance (fluctuation) of the probe's position. We then analyze the system's behavior under both weak and strong trap conditions, demonstrating that our generalized model reduces to established CF and CV microrheology models through appropriate limiting cases.

This study introduces a new approach for estimating the dates of historical photographs from archives. The core innovation lies in framing date estimation as a retrieval problem: given a query, images are ranked based on the similarity of their estimated dates, with the underlying principle that images with closer embedded representations correspond to closer dates. Unlike traditional models that employ neural networks to learn classifiers or regressors, this work proposes a learning objective grounded in the nDCG ranking metric. Experimental evaluations on the DEW public database, covering both date estimation and date-sensitive image retrieval tasks, demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms baseline approaches.

Query understanding in e-commerce involves deducing customer shopping intent by extracting semantic meaning from search inputs. Recent advancements in pre-trained masked language models (MLMs) within natural language processing offer a promising avenue for building robust query understanding systems. Specifically, MLMs acquire contextual text embeddings by reconstructing masked tokens within sentences, a pre-training phase that heavily depends on ample contextual data. However, this approach is less effective for search queries, which are typically brief. Applying masking to such short texts often results in significant loss of contextual information and potential alterations to the original search intent. To address these limitations in MLM pre-training for short texts, we introduce a novel task specifically tailored for this domain: Extended Token Classification (ETC). Unlike traditional masking, our method expands the input by inserting tokens generated by a network, while training a discriminator to detect these inserted elements within the extended sequence. We validate the efficacy of ETC through experiments conducted on an e-commerce platform.

This study introduces a Natural Language Processing method for identifying spoilers in book reviews, utilizing the University of California San Diego (UCSD) Goodreads Spoiler dataset. We investigated the efficacy of LSTM, BERT, and RoBERTa models for sentence-level spoiler detection, comparing our results against a prior UCSD study that relied on handcrafted features for data preparation. Notably, even without employing handcrafted features, our LSTM model achieved performance that marginally surpassed that of the UCSD team.

An unusual $(2\times2)$ charge density wave (CDW) phase appears in monolayer 1T-TiTe$_2$ but not in its bulk form, with its underlying cause remaining largely unclear. In this work, we examine the evolution of the electronic band structure across the CDW transition using temperature-dependent angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy. We find that the transition is driven by an orbital-selective hybridization between backfolded conduction and valence bands, which generates a substantial electronic energy gain. Conversely, in the bulk material, this energy gain is nearly entirely suppressed due to the three-dimensional nature of the band structure, specifically through a $k_z$-dependent band inversion that alters the orbital character of the valence states. Consequently, our findings offer new insights into how manipulating electronic dimensionality can induce novel collective states in two-dimensional materials.

This paper presents a new likelihood-based inference framework tailored for axion haloscopes operating under the widely used "rescanning" protocol. The proposed approach offers rapid data collection and straightforward detector tuning. By calculating local statistical significance and power analytically, it eliminates the necessity for computationally intensive simulations, while also addressing appropriate corrections for the look-elsewhere effect. The study compares the performance of this strategy against a simpler method relying on the geometric probability of rescanning. Finally, the methodology is demonstrated through an application to a HAYSTAC-style axion haloscope.

Recent developments have revitalized the global discourse on racial justice, with significant attention turning toward the security and privacy risks confronting communities of color. This research examines community-based advocates who lead workshops, clinics, and other programs designed to educate Black populations about digital safety threats and mitigation strategies. Furthermore, the study seeks to identify the online security needs and attitudes of those engaging in these initiatives. By analyzing how advocates operate across various contexts and determining which pedagogical approaches are most effective, we aim to equip other digital safety professionals and activists to serve as advocates within their own communities.

Observations of rocky planets, both within and beyond our solar system, reveal a diverse range of core-mass fractions (CMFs). Imperfect collisions are believed to be the primary driver of this variation, as they can selectively strip away mantle material. However, previous N-body simulations attempting to incorporate such collisions have failed to reliably generate high-CMF super-Earths. To address this, we adjusted our simulation parameters and initial conditions to maximize the frequency of high-energy collisions capable of altering CMFs. Specifically, we aimed to increase the impact velocity relative to escape velocity ($v_{imp}/v_{esc}$) by initiating simulations with high-eccentricity and high-inclination disks to boost orbital velocity differences, thereby increasing $v_{imp}$. Simultaneously, we reduced $v_{esc}$ by starting with smaller planetary embryos. Consequently, the resulting planets experienced numerous debris-producing, high-energy collisions that significantly modified their CMFs during formation. Despite these efforts, we found that various processes conspire to average out planetary CMFs over time, preventing the consistent formation of high-mass, high-CMF planets. We did, however, successfully form high-CMF planets with masses below 0.5 Earth masses ($M_{\oplus}$). Furthermore, in these highly eccentric environments, we observed that collisional grinding leading to debris mass loss significantly impacted final planet masses and CMFs, resulting in smaller planets with higher average CMFs. These findings underscore the necessity of refining measurements of high-density planets to better constrain their core-mass fractions.

Knee osteoarthritis (OA) stands as the most prevalent musculoskeletal condition lacking a definitive cure, with existing therapies restricted to symptom management. Forecasting OA progression remains a critical yet difficult challenge; solving it could hasten the creation of disease-modifying drugs and potentially avert millions of annual joint replacement surgeries. This study introduces a multi-modal machine learning model designed to predict OA progression by integrating raw radiographic data, clinical examination findings, and patients' medical histories. The model was validated using an independent test set comprising 3,918 knee images from 2,129 individuals. The proposed approach achieved an Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC) of 0.79 (0.78–0.81) and an Average Precision (AP) of 0.68 (0.66–0.70). By comparison, a logistic regression-based reference method attained an AUC of 0.75 (0.74–0.77) and an AP of 0.62 (0.60–0.64). Consequently, this method offers substantial potential to refine subject selection for OA drug-development trials and facilitate the formulation of personalized treatment strategies.

Utilizing resonance theory within the context of relativistic quantum field theory, we analyze the time evolution of a two-vector-meson molecular state governed by the total Hamiltonian. Specifically, we model the exotic meson resonance $X(3915)$ as a superposition of two unstable molecular configurations, $D^{*0}\bar{D}^{*0}$ and $D^{*+}D^{*-}$, to compute its corrected mass and width. This detailed calculation demonstrates the derivation of resonance corrections and highlights essential characteristics of the dispersion relation through a novel Feynman diagram. The resulting numerical values align with experimental data.

Nano-size unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) offer significant promise for executing autonomous tasks like inspection, monitoring, and data gathering in intricate settings. Their compact dimensions facilitate safe proximity to humans and agile maneuvering. However, autonomous flight relies heavily on localization, a computationally demanding process that is particularly challenging for nano-UAVs due to strict limitations in processing power, memory, and sensing capabilities. This study introduces a real-time localization method utilizing low-element-count multizone range sensors specifically designed for resource-constrained nano-UAVs. The solution leverages a novel 64-zone time-of-flight sensor from ST Microelectronics and a parallel, ultra-low-power RISC-V processor to achieve accurate, low-latency Monte Carlo Localization directly on-board. Experimental validation on an open nano-UAV platform confirms that the system can localize within a 31.2m² map with 0.15m accuracy and a success rate exceeding 95%, meeting the requirements for typical indoor environments. The research further analyzes trade-offs involving full and half-precision floating-point numbers alongside quantized maps, assessing the impact on accuracy and memory usage across various design configurations. Results indicate that parallelizing execution across 8 RISC-V cores yields a 7x performance boost, enabling real-time on-board operation with latencies between 0.2 and 30ms (variable by particle count) while increasing total power consumption by only 3-7%. Additionally, an open-source implementation of this approach is provided.

Information propagation within Online Social Networks represents a vital and emerging challenge in social network analysis that demands substantial research focus. Efficient dissemination of information is paramount across various scenarios, including pandemic control, advertising, and marketing. Despite the development of numerous mathematical models to date, prior studies have insufficiently analyzed the impact of neighborhood structures on information diffusion. This paper introduces the Common Neighborhood Strategy (CNS) algorithm, which highlights the significance of shared neighbors in propagating information across the network. The CNS algorithm's performance was assessed using multiple real-world datasets, measuring diffusion speed and reach against several established models. Empirical findings indicate that the CNS algorithm achieves superior information diffusion in both speed and extent.

This paper presents a novel concept termed Hawaiian homology, designed for the analysis and classification of pointed topological spaces. This homology group leverages the benefits inherent to Hawaiian groups. Specifically, for path-connected and locally path-connected spaces, the first Hawaiian homology group is isomorphic to the abelianization of the corresponding first Hawaiian group. Due to its concrete elements and abelian nature, computations involving Hawaiian homology are more straightforward. Consequently, we employ Hawaiian homology groups to compare Hawaiian groups, thereby deriving insights into the Hawaiian groups associated with various wild topological spaces.

This research investigates finite-dimensional groups definable within models of the theory of real closed fields equipped with a generic derivation, commonly referred to as CODF. We demonstrate that every such group admits a definable embedding into a semialgebraic group. Furthermore, we generalize these findings to broader settings, including strongly model complete theories of large geometric fields with a generic derivation, model complete o-minimal expansions of RCF featuring a generic derivation, and open theories of topological fields with a generic derivation. Additionally, we present a comprehensive theorem regarding the reconstruction of a definable group from generic data within the framework of geometric structures.

Quantifying the similarities and variations in recorded musical performances has become a prevalent objective within computational musicology. A standard approach entails manually annotating multiple recordings of a single piece along the temporal axis to compare elements such as tempo or to map performance-specific data across versions. This process often involves creating manual annotations for one reference performance followed by the automatic synchronization of other tracks using audio-to-audio alignment techniques. This paper investigates several aspects of these tasks. Initially, we examine multiple human annotations of the same composition to measure timing discrepancies between annotators; a statistical analysis of these timestamps yields (a) an estimate of the expected precision of human timing and (b) a ground truth for future automatic alignment studies. Subsequently, we conduct a systematic assessment of various audio features for audio-to-audio alignment, quantifying the achievable accuracy levels and correlating these findings with the results from the annotation analysis.

Solar type-I noise storms originate from accelerated particle beams produced within active regions experiencing magnetic field reconfiguration. These events exhibit intensity fluctuations across orders of magnitude over sub-second and sub-MHz timescales; however, the morphological evolution of their sources at these resolutions has remained unstudied due to insufficient imaging cadence and fidelity in meter-wave bands. Leveraging data from the Murchison Widefield Array (MWA), this study investigates the simultaneous evolution of a noise storm source's size, sky-orientation, and intensity linked to a weak microflare. The research identifies two correlated evolutionary modes: a sausage-like (\s) mode characterized by an anti-correlation between intensity and size, and a torsional-like (\T) mode marked by a correlation between size and sky-orientation. Furthermore, a flare-mediated mode conversion from \T\ to \s\ is observed for the first time in such sources. These findings support the hypothesis that magnetic stress energy accumulates in braided active region loops until instability triggers flares and particle acceleration, eventually relaxing to a minimally braided state. The identified mode conversion offers potential as a future diagnostic tool for studying these active region phenomena.

The significant growth in computational power and storage capacity has propelled local data and machine learning applications toward cloud environments. However, data owners often lack full trust in these third-party managed systems. Consequently, preserving privacy while sharing data and classifiers among multiple stakeholders remains a critical challenge. This paper introduces a novel framework integrating differential privacy and machine learning techniques, enabling multiple owners to share their data for utilization and allowing the cloud to deliver classification services. The model defines a communication protocol among various untrustworthy parties to process both owner data and the classifier. Furthermore, it offers a robust mechanism to safeguard the privacy of both data and the classifier.
