Experiments were conducted using a Naive Bayes classifier across numerous datasets to evaluate the model's efficiency. The results demonstrate high performance, achieving accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-scores of up to 94%, 95%, 94%, and 94%, respectively. Compared to state-of-the-art approaches, the proposed model shows improvements of up to 16.95%, 20.16%, 16.95%, and 23.33% in these respective metrics.

An in-band full-duplex system enables radios to transmit and receive concurrently within the same frequency band, offering a significant enhancement in spectral efficiency compared to half-duplex systems. However, designing such a system requires mitigating self-interference caused by simultaneous transmission and reception, a challenge that severely restricts the maximum transmit power of full-duplex devices. Furthermore, substantial disparities in power levels within the receiver front-end impose rigorous linearity demands on the transceiver electronics. This paper introduces an advanced architecture for a compact full-duplex multiantenna transceiver that integrates antenna design with both analog and digital cancellation techniques, encompassing linear and nonlinear signal processing.

We have built a one-parameter family of embedded doubly periodic minimal surfaces of genus three, each featuring four parallel ends. The Weierstrass data for every surface in this family is provided, and the two-dimensional period problem has been resolved.

Teams of autonomous systems frequently face missions involving multiple targets within complex, dynamic environments. This study addresses the challenge of a non-communicating team visiting a set of targets in minimal time within a stochastic setting modeled as a Markov decision process (MDP). We begin with the single-agent scenario, demonstrating that it is at least NP-complete through a reduction to the Hamiltonian path problem. While Bellman's optimality equation yields an optimal algorithm with exponential complexity relative to the number of target states, we subsequently propose a suboptimal, polynomial-time algorithm that trades optimality for computational efficiency. We establish that this proposed method generates optimal policies for specific MDP classes. Extending this approach to multi-agent systems, we introduce a heuristic partitioning strategy to assign targets among agents, which approximately minimizes the expected visitation time. Furthermore, we prove that this heuristic yields optimal partitions in environments where targets are naturally clustered. Finally, we evaluate our algorithms on random MDPs and a gridworld scenario inspired by autonomous underwater vehicles in the ocean, demonstrating that our methods are significantly faster than the optimal procedure and more optimal than existing heuristics.

Recent years have seen a surge in congestion control research, characterized by the development of numerous specialized algorithms tailored to specific application requirements. However, these algorithms frequently undergo insufficient testing prior to Internet deployment, where they must interact with diverse algorithms and operate under varying network conditions. Consequently, unforeseen performance problems often arise in real-world scenarios due to algorithmic flaws or implementation errors, which are difficult to detect because packet traces are typically unavailable. To address this, this paper introduces CC-Fuzz, an automated testing framework that employs a genetic search algorithm to stress-test congestion control mechanisms by generating adversarial network traces and traffic patterns. Preliminary results are encouraging: CC-Fuzz has already automatically identified a bug in BBR that causes permanent stalling and successfully discovered the well-known low-rate TCP attack, among other issues.

This study examines the input-constrained binary memoryless symmetric (BMS) channel in the absence of feedback, where the input sequence adheres to the $(d,\infty)$-runlength limited (RLL) constraint, requiring at least $d$ zeros between any two consecutive ones. We focus on constructing explicit codes for this scenario, specifically utilizing the Reed-Muller (RM) code family. Reeves and Pfister (2021) previously demonstrated that RM codes attain the capacity of unconstrained BMS channels when decoded via bit-MAP. We demonstrate that it is feasible to select $(d,\infty)$-RLL subcodes from a sequence of RM codes that achieve capacity on the unconstrained channel, such that these subcodes attain rates of $C\cdot{2^{-\left \lceil \log_2(d+1)\right \rceil}}$ under bit-MAP decoding, where $C$ denotes the channel's capacity. Furthermore, we present methods for establishing upper bounds on the rate of any $(1,\infty)$-RLL subcode derived from a particular capacity-achieving sequence of RM codes.

The emergence of ferroelectricity in hafnia is frequently celebrated as a transformative breakthrough with the potential to reshape the entire field of ferroelectrics. However, despite growing interest, a holistic understanding of the various mechanisms stabilizing this property remains elusive. This study investigates the phase transition using a Landau-theory framework, specifically examining symmetry-allowed distortions that link the high-symmetry paraelectric tetragonal phase to the low-symmetry polar orthorhombic phase. Through first-principles simulations, we observe that the $\Gamma_{3-}$ polar mode exhibits only weak instability, while the other two symmetry-allowed distortions—the non-polar Y$_{2+}$ and anti-polar Y$_{4-}$ modes—behave as hard modes. Neither mode individually, nor any pair of them combined, can drive the transition; instead, the critical factor stabilizing the polar phase is identified as a strong trilinear coupling among all three modes. Additionally, given the recognized role of substrate effects in HfO$_2$ thin film growth and the absence of a definitive order parameter, we extended our analysis to include strain. Our results reveal a complex behavior for the Y$_{2+}$ mode, which becomes unstable under specific strain conditions, and an overall unstable character for the $\Gamma_{3-}$ polar mode across all strain states. A consistent finding emerges: regardless of the type of applied strain (compressive or tensile along orthorhombic axes), the necessity of simultaneously exciting the three coupled modes remains unchanged. Finally, when applied to simulate experimental growth conditions under strain, our analysis demonstrates further stabilization of the ferroelectric phase compared to the unstrained scenario, aligning with experimental observations.

Certain particle physics theories extending beyond the standard cosmological model predict the existence of magnetic monopoles (MMs), a discovery that would represent a monumental breakthrough in high-energy physics. Grand Unified Theory (GUT) has long speculated that MMs existed in the early Universe. If they do exist, the suppression of baryon number violation in GUT gauge theories by inverse powers of the unification mass would be mitigated, making MM-catalyzed nucleon decay a characteristic strong interaction driven by boundary conditions on the monopole core's fermion fields. This paper proposes a mechanism for the formation of the Hot Big Bang Cosmology, utilizing nucleon decay catalyzed by magnetic monopoles (the Rubakov-Callan effect) as its primary component. The model demonstrates that the Hot Big Bang arises naturally because the luminosity generated by the Rubakov-Callan effect significantly exceeds the Eddington luminosity ($L_m > 10^4 L_{\rm{Edd}}$).

Advancements in technology and economics have reshaped the healthcare industry, driving a shift toward IoT-enabled and personalized care. These services rely on control and monitoring applications powered by AI and machine learning algorithms, which significantly enhance the efficiency of conventional healthcare systems. However, existing personalized healthcare solutions are often limited to specific environments, failing to account for the interplay of multiple health conditions. This limitation can result in inaccurate diagnoses and compromise patient sustainability and long-term well-being. In response, Healthcare 5.0 has emerged as a superior evolution of prior technologies, aiming to deliver autonomous services that recognize the interdependent effects of various health conditions. This paper offers a comprehensive survey of personalized healthcare services. It begins by outlining the essential requirements for comprehensive personalized healthcare services within the modern Healthcare Internet of Things (HIoT), defining personalization and illustrating a representative use case. Next, it examines a fundamental three-layer architecture for IoT-based healthcare systems, analyzing both AI and non-AI approaches against key requirements for Comprehensive Personalized Healthcare Services (CPHS), along with their respective strengths and weaknesses. The survey also highlights security threats targeting each layer of the IoT architecture and presents potential AI and non-AI solutions. Finally, the authors propose a methodology for developing reliable, resilient, and personalized healthcare services that overcome the deficiencies of current approaches.

We investigate the Langmuir-Landau-Centrifugal Drive (LLCD) as a potential mechanism converting gravitational energy into particles to explain the extreme thermal luminosity observed in certain active galactic nuclei (AGN). This study analyzes the equations governing the heating of AGN magnetospheres, specifically examining the Fourier components of the linearized momentum, continuity, and Poisson equations. We calculate the growth rates of centrifugally excited electrostatic waves and the rate of Langmuir collapse. Our findings indicate that energy pumping occurs in three phases: initially, rotation efficiently transfers energy to electrostatic modes; subsequently, the Langmuir collapse regime emerges, making energy pumping even more effective; finally, Landau damping terminates the process by releasing vast amounts of energy as heat. We demonstrate that the magnetospheres of supermassive black holes with luminosities around $10^{45-46}$ erg/s can be heated to temperatures between $10^{6-10}$ K.

Although green hydrogen offers a pathway to decarbonize segments of the transportation industry, its interactions with the power sector remain unclear. It could facilitate the integration of variable renewable energy if production capabilities are sufficiently time-flexible. By applying an open-source co-optimization model to the power sector alongside four hydrogen supply scenarios for German fueling stations, we identify a trade-off between energy efficiency and temporal flexibility. In scenarios with lower renewable and hydrogen penetration, the optimal solution is small-scale, on-site electrolysis that prioritizes efficiency over flexibility. Conversely, as shares of renewables and hydrogen increase, large-scale supply chains—which are less efficient but more flexible—become increasingly vital, enabling the decoupling of production from demand through storage. Liquid hydrogen proves to be the most advantageous option, followed by liquid organic hydrogen carriers and gaseous hydrogen. These large-scale systems can yield significant benefits for the power sector, primarily by mitigating excess renewable generation. Consequently, energy modelers and system planners must account for the unique flexibility profiles of various hydrogen supply chains when evaluating the role of green hydrogen in future energy transition scenarios.

Every scheme comes equipped with both small and large Zariski toposes. These toposes provide an internal mathematical language that mirrors standard formal mathematics but is "local relative to the base scheme." Internally, the structure sheaf behaves like a standard local ring rather than a sheaf of rings with local stalks, and vector bundles resemble ordinary free modules instead of sheaves of modules that satisfy local triviality. Translating internal statements and proofs is aided by a straightforward mechanical process.

We explore how the internal language of the small Zariski topos can simplify definitions and offer more conceptual proofs of fundamental algebraic geometry concepts. By constructing a dictionary between internal and external concepts, we demonstrate its value with a concise, fully general proof of Grothendieck's generic freeness lemma. Furthermore, we apply this framework to establish a general transfer principle linking modules to their induced quasicoherent sheaves, investigate how properties propagate from points to open neighborhoods, and compare various definitions of spectra.

Additionally, we use the large Zariski topos to establish a synthetic foundation for scheme theory. This approach resembles the synthetic treatment of differential geometry but possesses a unique algebraic character. A core concept in this theory is synthetic quasicoherence, which has no counterpart in synthetic differential geometry. We also examine how various common subtoposes of the large Zariski topos can be characterized from an internal perspective and derive explicit descriptions of the geometric theories classified by the fppf and surjective topologies.

This research investigates supersymmetric $AdS_5\times \Sigma$ configurations within seven-dimensional $N=2$ gauged supergravity interacting with three vector multiplets, where $\Sigma$ represents a topological disk featuring non-trivial $U(1)$ holonomy at its boundary, often termed a "half-spindle." We examine both compact and non-compact gauge groups, specifically $SO(4-p,p)$ for $p=0,1,2$, identifying numerous $AdS_5\times \Sigma$ solutions that retain $SO(2)\times SO(2)$ and $SO(2)_{\text{diag}}$ symmetries originating from $SO(4)$ and $SO(2,2)$ gauge structures, respectively. Additionally, we discover an $SO(2)_R\subset SO(3)_R\sim SU(2)_R$ symmetric solution interpretable as a pure $N=2$ gauged supergravity solution with an $SO(3)_R$ gauge group, where all vector multiplet fields vanish. These solutions maintain half of the original $N=2$ supersymmetry and serve as supergravity duals to four-dimensional $N=1$ superconformal field theories. Notably, several solutions can be embedded into ten or eleven dimensions, allowing for a description via five-branes wrapped on a topological disk.

The arrival of ultrahigh energy cosmic rays at Earth is influenced by their interactions with background radiation and the magnetic fields encountered along their paths. By integrating the SimProp cosmic ray propagation code with a specific routine to model the average impact of turbulent magnetic fields on particle trajectories, we calculate the spectral modifications caused by the magnetic horizon effect for both primary nuclei and secondary nuclei produced via the photo-disintegration of primaries. Additionally, we present analytic parameterizations describing attenuation effects as a function of magnetic field properties and source density, enabling the derivation of expected spectra in the presence of magnetic fields from those predicted without them. Finally, we address how the discrete distribution of sources with finite density alters the cosmic ray spectrum at the highest energies, where flux suppression occurs due to background radiation interactions, providing corresponding parameterizations for these phenomena.

New experimental findings regarding polarization and spin-correlation parameters in the (p,2p) reaction involving nuclei are introduced. The study focused on investigating modifications to the proton-proton scattering matrix.

This paper introduces ADOP, a new differentiable neural rendering framework based on points. Similar to other neural renderers, ADOP accepts calibrated camera images and a scene proxy geometry—specifically a point cloud—as input. To synthesize novel views, the point cloud is rasterized using learned feature vectors as colors, while a deep neural network interpolates missing areas and shades the resulting pixels. The rasterization process treats points as one-pixel splats, ensuring high speed and enabling efficient gradient computation with respect to all relevant inputs. Additionally, the pipeline incorporates a fully differentiable, physically-based photometric camera model that accounts for exposure, white balance, and camera response functions. Drawing on inverse rendering principles, the system refines its inputs to minimize inconsistencies and enhance output quality. This allows for the optimization of structural parameters, such as camera pose, lens distortions, point positions, features, and neural environment maps, alongside photometric parameters like camera response, vignetting, and per-image exposure or white balance. By integrating these photometric parameters, ADOP effectively manages input images with varying exposures and white balances, producing high-dynamic-range results. We demonstrate that these improvements in input quality yield high rendering fidelity even under challenging conditions, such as imperfect camera calibrations, inaccurate proxy geometry, or inconsistent exposure. Consequently, a simpler and faster deep neural network suffices for reconstruction. Combined with rapid point rasterization, ADOP achieves real-time rendering speeds even for models containing over 100 million points. https://github.com/darglein/ADOP

As digital information becomes increasingly accessible, the prevalence of toxic content has also surged, making its detection critically important. To address this challenge, we employed a hybrid approach combining a state-of-the-art pre-trained language model (CharacterBERT) with a traditional bag-of-words technique. Given that much of the toxic content features misspelled words, analyzing individual characters is essential. Consequently, we utilized CharacterBERT to derive features from word characters via a CharacterCNN module that learns embeddings from context, which were then processed by the established BERT architecture. Complementing this, the bag-of-words method enhanced performance by ensuring that common toxic terms were correctly labeled. In the competition, our system achieved a 4 percent margin difference, securing the 36th rank. The code is publicly available to facilitate further research and result reproduction.

We demonstrate the existence of a $\mathbf{C}_2$ cyclic group action on the $10$-dimensional Floyd manifold that converts it into a conjugation manifold. The fixed point submanifold within this structure is a $5$-dimensional Floyd manifold; its cohomology is isomorphic to that of the larger manifold, with each cohomological degree scaled by a factor of two.

This study presents the initial observations of the Cabibbo-suppressed decays B0bar --> D+ K- pi+ pi- and B- --> D0 K- pi+ pi-, utilizing 35 pb^{-1} of data recorded by the LHCb detector. By comparing these processes to their corresponding Cabibbo-favored counterparts, the branching fractions are determined as B(B0bar --> D+ K- pi+ pi-)/B(B0bar --> D+ pi- pi+ pi-) = (5.9 ± 1.1 ± 0.5) × 10^{-2} and B(B- --> D0 K- pi+ pi-)/B(B- --> D0 pi- pi+ pi-) = (9.4 ± 1.3 ± 0.9) × 10^{-2}, with the errors representing statistical and systematic uncertainties, respectively. Notably, the B- --> D0 K- pi+ pi- decay holds particular significance because it offers a method analogous to B- --> D0 K- for measuring the CKM phase gamma.

The SuperFGD serves as a component of the ND280 near detector for the T2K and Hyper-Kamiokande experiments, aiming to mitigate systematic uncertainties associated with neutrino flux and cross-section modeling. The upgraded ND280 will enable full exclusive reconstruction of final states from neutrino-nucleus interactions, including the measurement of low-momentum protons and pions, as well as event-by-event neutron kinematics for the first time. Since time resolution dictates neutron energy resolution, this study presents results from measurements using a SuperFGD prototype comprising 9,216 plastic scintillator cubes (1 cm³ each) read out by 1,728 wavelength-shifting fibers oriented in three orthogonal directions. Utilizing data from a muon beam exposure at CERN, a time resolution of 0.97 ns was achieved for a single readout channel after applying time calibration and correcting for the time-walk effect. The time resolution improves with the energy deposited in a scintillator cube. By averaging data from two readout channels per cube, the resolution reaches 0.68 ns, indicating that signals across different channels are not perfectly synchronous; consequently, the 2.5 ns contribution from the time recording step is also averaged. Averaging time values from $N$ channels enhances the time resolution by approximately $1/\sqrt{N}$. This suggests that excellent time resolution should be achievable for neutrons, as their recoils typically strike multiple scintillator cubes and generate larger amplitudes than muons. Furthermore, measurements using a laser and a wide-bandwidth oscilloscope indicate that the time resolution obtained with the muon beam is close to its theoretical limit. The intrinsic time resolution for a single channel is 0.67 ns for signals of 56 photo-electrons, which are typical for minimum ionizing particles.

CLIP (Contrastive Vision-Language Pre-training) has established a new framework for learning visual representations through large-scale contrastive image-text pairs, demonstrating remarkable zero-shot transfer capabilities. To improve its few-shot performance, CLIP-Adapter introduced a lightweight residual feature adapter, achieving significant gains in few-shot classification; however, this approach still relies on additional training and computational resources. In this paper, we present **T**raining-Free CL**IP**-**Adapter** (**Tip-Adapter**), which retains CLIP's training-free benefits while matching or exceeding CLIP-Adapter's performance. Unlike traditional methods, Tip-Adapter avoids backpropagation for adapter training, instead generating weights via a key-value cache model derived from the few-shot training set. This non-parametric strategy enables the acquisition of highly effective adapter weights without any training, ensuring both efficiency and effectiveness. Furthermore, the performance of Tip-Adapter can be further enhanced by fine-tuning the properly initialized adapter for just a few epochs, achieving rapid convergence. We validate the superiority of Tip-Adapter through extensive few-shot classification experiments on ImageNet and ten other datasets. The implementation will be made available at \url{https://github.com/gaopengcuhk/Tip-Adapter}.

Distance-based outlier detection is extensively utilized across various domains, such as data mining and machine learning, due to its unsupervised nature, applicability within generic metric spaces, and lack of data distribution assumptions. These fields encounter the challenge of processing large datasets, necessitating efficient algorithms for distance-based outlier detection. With the rise of high-memory computational environments, constructing a main-memory index to facilitate rapid outlier detection has emerged as a promising strategy. Inspired by this, we introduce a novel method leveraging a proximity graph. This approach supports arbitrary proximity graphs and achieves substantial performance gains over state-of-the-art solutions. However, creating an effective proximity graph remains difficult because existing models fail to account for efficient traversal specific to distance-based outlier detection. To address this, we propose the MRPG, a new proximity graph design. Empirical evaluations on real-world datasets confirm that MRPG identifies outliers significantly faster than current leading algorithms.

Current video text spotting benchmarks are largely restricted to single languages and scenarios with limited data. To address this, we present BOVText, a large-scale, bilingual, open-world video text benchmark dataset. BOVText offers four key features: first, it includes over 2,000 videos comprising more than 1.75 million frames, making it 25 times larger than the largest existing incidental text dataset. Second, the dataset spans 30+ open categories across diverse scenarios such as Life Vlogs, driving, and movies. Third, it provides extensive annotations for various text types, including titles, captions, and scene text, to reflect different representational meanings. Fourth, bilingual annotations are included to foster cross-cultural communication. Additionally, we introduce TransVTSpotter, an end-to-end video text spotting framework based on Transformers that efficiently handles multi-oriented text. It utilizes a simple attention-based query-key mechanism, leveraging object features from the previous frame as tracking queries for the current frame while incorporating rotation angle prediction for text instances. On the ICDAR2015(video) benchmark, TransVTSpotter achieves state-of-the-art results with a MOTA of 44.1% at 9 fps. The dataset and code for TransVTSpotter are available at github.com/weijiawu/BOVText and github.com/weijiawu/TransVTSpotter, respectively.

Qualitative data, whether derived from transcribed interviews, blog entries, or tweets, offers readers profound insights into broad trends and the variety of human thought expressed in text. However, processing and analyzing vast quantities of such data is challenging, often demanding numerous time-consuming readings to uncover patterns. This complexity increases further with each additional variable or time point in a dataset. Consequently, a key objective is developing visualizations that facilitate the interpretation of qualitative information by simplifying the identification and exploration of relevant trends. While WordStream previously combined text and visual elements to streamline the retrieval and processing of time-series text, the manual data preparation required to create one remains a substantial hurdle for non-experts. Addressing this gap, this paper introduces WordStream Maker: an end-to-end platform featuring a pipeline that leverages natural language processing (NLP) to assist non-technical users in transforming raw text into customizable visualizations without any coding skills. The discussion includes insights gained from integrating NLP with visualization and scaling these capabilities for large datasets, alongside practical use cases illustrating the platform's utility.

Multi-modal registration is essential for numerous image-guided procedures, particularly ultrasound-guided interventions that depend on anatomical context. Although several registration algorithms exist, they all depend on high-quality initialization to succeed, largely due to the difficult appearance of ultrasound images and their arbitrary acquisition coordinates. This paper introduces a novel method for registering a freehand ultrasound sweep to a pre-operative image. By learning dense keypoint descriptors to estimate the registration, our approach addresses inherent challenges in this domain, including multi-modality and multi-dimensionality, the absence of precise ground truth, and limited training data. The resulting method is fast, generic, and fully automatic, requiring no initialization while naturally producing visualizations that enhance interpretability and explainability. We validate this approach using a clinical dataset comprising paired MR volumes and ultrasound sequences.

Successful full waveform inversion (FWI) relies heavily on an accurate initial model, a requirement that is especially critical in elastic FWI. This is because the short S-wave wavelength intensifies cycle-skipping issues compared to acoustic FWI. This paper expands on our prior research into extrapolated FWI (EFWI) by suggesting the synthesis of low frequencies from multi-component elastic seismic data to seed the elastic FWI frequency sweep. Our approach utilizes deep learning, specifically training separate convolutional neural networks (CNNs) on vertical and horizontal particle velocity components to extrapolate these low frequencies. To ensure a large receptive field, the CNN architecture employs either large convolutional kernels or dilated convolutions. Numerical experiments on the Marmousi2 model demonstrate that extrapolating 2–4 Hz data from band-limited sources above 4 Hz yields effective starting models for both P-wave and S-wave elastic FWI. Furthermore, we evaluated the network's generalization across various physical models and found that training datasets generated through elastic simulations offer superior extrapolation accuracy compared to acoustic simulations, resulting in a reduced generalization gap.

This work investigates various statistical techniques for analyzing variability in the time domain, specifically targeting low count-rate X-ray and gamma-ray sources. Detection of such variability is achievable through both nonparametric methods, including the Anderson-Darling and overdispersion tests, and parametric approaches, such as sequential likelihood-based tests. Upon detection, variability can be characterized using nonparametric tools like the autocorrelation function, structure function, and wavelet analysis, as well as parametric models including Bayesian Blocks, integer autoregressive models, C-statistic, and Poisson regression. The text also introduces new multidimensional strategies for variability detection. While existing software packages for high-energy data analysis are often inadequate, the R statistical environment offers available tools. Notably, most of these methods remain underutilized in the field of high-energy astronomy.

Measure synchronization is a well-established phenomenon in coupled classical Hamiltonian systems that has been studied for the past two decades. This paper investigates synchronization within the coupled Harper system across both classical and quantum frameworks. While measure synchronization, which pertains to phase space, is generally considered restricted to the classical limit, we extend this concept into the quantum domain. In the quantum setting, two many-body systems interact through a potential that varies with time and site, resulting in entanglement between the systems. We apply a technique previously validated in classical contexts to both scenarios, thereby establishing a link between classical and quantum behaviors. Notably, the results from both cases reveal shared characteristics.

The domain of real-time heuristic search has yielded numerous algorithms, yet it is common to observe that an algorithm outperforming another on one set of problems may underperform on a different set. Leveraging the intuition that combining these published methods can create a more powerful algorithmic space capable of solving problem distributions more efficiently, Bulitko (2016) recently framed the task of selecting such combinations as a "survival task." This evolutionary approach defines a search space using published algorithms as building blocks and employs simulated evolution to recombine them, identifying the optimal algorithm within that space. In this paper, we expand the set of building blocks by incorporating the lookahead-based A*-shaped local search space generation method from LSSLRTA-star and an unpublished novel strategy for generating local search spaces using Greedy Best First Search. Experimental results within this expanded algorithmic space reveal that the best algorithms selected by the evolutionary process exhibit a specific property: as the lookahead depth increases, both suboptimality and scrubbing complexity decrease.

The spectrum of doubly heavy tetraquarks ($bb\bar q\bar q$) is investigated using a constituent quark model. By applying a variational method with real scaling techniques to the four-body problem, we identify resonant states situated above fall-apart decay thresholds. Beyond the two bound states previously reported, we have discovered several narrow resonances above the $BB^*$ and $B^*B^*$ thresholds. These states are analyzed through their structural properties and interpreted via quark dynamics. Specifically, a narrow resonance with spin-parity $J^P=1^+$ is identified as a mixed state comprising a compact tetraquark and a $B^*B^*$ scattering state, driven by strong color Coulombic attraction between the $bb$ pair. Furthermore, negative-parity excited resonances with $J^P=0^-$, $1^-$, and $2^-$ form a triplet under heavy-quark spin symmetry. These states exhibit a structure analogous to the $\lambda$-mode of singly heavy baryons, resulting from the strongly attractive correlation of the doubly heavy diquark.

Consider a random variable $\bf{x}$ defined on ${\mathbb R}^d$ with a probability density $\rho(x)$. The goal is to characterize the shape of $\rho(x)$, specifically its orbit $\{ \rho(g\cdot x) | g\in E(d) \}$ under the Euclidean group. By selecting two independent samples $x_1$ and $x_2$ from $\rho(x)$ and defining $\Delta$ as their squared Euclidean distance, we demonstrate that if $\rho(x)$ represents a mixture of Gaussians with identity covariance matrices and means in generic positions, the density $\rho(x)$ can be reconstructed from the distribution of $\bf{\Delta}$ up to a rigid motion in $E(d)$. Consequently, any two such Gaussian mixtures, $\rho(x)$ and $\bar{\rho} (x)$, that share the same distance distribution must be related by a rigid transformation $g\in E(d)$ such that $\rho(x)=\bar{\rho} (g\cdot x)$. Furthermore, an analogous conclusion applies when the distance metric is determined by a symmetric bilinear form.

This paper offers multiple characterizations of uniform amenability for a specific family of finitely generated groups. Specifically, we demonstrate that the Hulanicki-Reiter condition for uniform amenability can be relaxed in various aspects, such as the sizes of supports and specific operator norms.

A primary objective of graph modeling is to identify the fundamental components of network data to analyze diverse physical and natural phenomena. Recent research merging formal language theory and graph theory has investigated graph grammars for this purpose. However, current formalisms, such as Hyperedge Replacement Grammars, are limited to small, tree-like structures. This study addresses that limitation by modifying Vertex Replacement Grammars (VRGs). We demonstrate that a specific VRG variant, the Clustering-based Node Replacement Grammar (CNRG), can be efficiently derived from various hierarchical clusterings of a graph. Although CNRGs provide a concise representation, they maintain the original graph's structural integrity. Furthermore, experiments on large-scale real-world datasets reveal that graphs generated using the CNRG model display a wide variety of properties consistent with those of the source networks.

Computational workflows are essential for data analysis, driving innovation and informed decision-making. In fields such as bioinformatics, image analysis, and radio astronomy, these workflows often involve numerous components developed by third parties in various programming languages. However, the proliferation of competing workflow systems has severely restricted portability, hindering the transfer of workflows across different systems, projects, and environments. This fragmentation leads to vendor lock-in and limits general reusability. To address this, the Common Workflow Language (CWL) project has established free, open standards for describing workflows based on command-line tools. CWL defines a common, streamlined set of abstractions that are both practically applicable and supported by many popular workflow systems. As a declarative language, CWL enables the expression of computational workflows built from diverse software tools, executing each via its command-line interface. By explicitly defining the runtime environment and supporting software containers, CWL ensures portability and reusability. Workflows conforming to CWL standards serve as reusable, executable descriptions of analysis that function across a wide range of computing environments. These descriptions include sufficient detail for advanced optimization without requiring further input from authors. Furthermore, CWL supports polyglot workflows, enhancing portability and reuse, which facilitates scholarly publication, regulatory compliance, and collaboration between academia and industry while reducing implementation costs. The CWL standard has been adopted across numerous domains and industries, with support now integrated into many major workflow systems.

This study examines SIS epidemic models where a large population dynamically decides between adopting protection or remaining vulnerable as the disease spreads. For susceptible individuals, using protection lowers infection risk but incurs a cost that must be balanced against the immediate threat of infection. Similarly, infected individuals who adopt protection transmit the disease at a reduced rate compared to those who do not. We apply replicator evolutionary dynamics to model how protection strategies evolve within both susceptible and infected subpopulations. Our analysis fully characterizes the existence and local stability of equilibria in this coupled system of epidemic and evolutionary dynamics. Furthermore, we demonstrate how stability switches between different equilibrium points as specific parameters vary. Finally, we explore system behavior under conditions where epidemic and evolutionary dynamics operate on different timescales.

This study examines the minimal cost associated with a broad spectrum of combinatorial optimization problems defined on random bipartite geometric graphs within $\mathbb{R}^d$, where edge costs correspond to the $p$-th power of Euclidean distances. Examples include the travelling salesperson problem and the bounded degree minimum spanning tree. Specifically, we demonstrate the almost sure convergence of a renormalized random minimum cost as $n$ increases, provided the points are uniformly distributed and satisfy $d \ge 3$ and $1 \le p < d$. While earlier findings were restricted to the range $p < d/2$, our approach leverages subadditivity methods and relies on novel bounds for random Euclidean bipartite matching instances, derived via optimal transport relaxation and functional analytic techniques.

The paper investigates unique continuation properties for a specific class of evolution equations within Banach spaces from two distinct perspectives. The first approach relies on conserved quantities, which frequently manifest as the preservation of certain solution norms in an appropriate Banach space, while the second focuses on well-posed problems. These findings are subsequently applied to various equations, predominantly modeling physical phenomena such as wave propagation and hydrodynamics, including integrable systems like the $b$-Fornberg-Whitham, potential and $\pi$-Camassa-Holm, generalised Boussinesq equations, and the modified Euler-Poisson system.

This study addresses trajectory planning and task allocation for a Multi-Agent System (MAS) consisting of differential drive robots. We introduce a multirate hierarchical control framework utilizing a planner grounded in robust Model Predictive Control (MPC) with mixed-integer programming (MIP) encoding. This planner calculates trajectories and assigns tasks to each agent in real-time, ensuring the MAS communication network remains robustly connected continuously. Furthermore, we present a data-driven approach to estimate the disturbance sets necessary for the robust MPC formulation. Experimental results in two obstacle-filled environments validate these findings.

In 1990, D. Snow introduced an efficient algorithm for calculating orbits within finite Weyl groups. This original method computes Weyl group elements, weights, and W-orbits. An extension of Snow's approach has been developed to simultaneously identify pairs of mutually inverse elements and calculate W-orbits within a single computational cycle, thereby streamlining the determination of conjugacy classes in the Weyl group. As a demonstration, the complete set of elements for the Weyl group $W(D_4)$, derived using this extended algorithm, is presented. These elements are defined both as reduced expressions and as matrices of the faithful representation. Additionally, the group is partitioned into conjugacy classes with elements specified via reduced expressions. Representatives for the conjugacy classes of $W(D_4)$ are provided in multiple formats: Carter diagrams, reduced expressions, and signed cycle-types. Finally, a Python implementation of the algorithm is included in the appendix.

In recent years, particle filters have demonstrated strong performance in highly nonlinear problems and parameter estimation; however, the issue of particle degeneracy has spurred the development of alternatives such as feedback particle filters. This paper presents a stochastically perturbed feedback particle filter, demonstrating its exactness. The key innovation lies in the stochastic perturbation of the innovation process. Additionally, we introduce the resampled Sinkhorn particle filter. Finally, we evaluate the performance of these methods against other filters in the context of simultaneous state and parameter estimation.

We introduce an exact approach for computing the electronic states of one-electron Hamiltonians subject to diagonal disorder. This method allows for the direct calculation of the disorder-averaged one-particle Green's function by employing a deterministic complex (non-Hermitian) Hamiltonian. Based on the assumption that molecular states follow a Cauchy (Lorentzian) distribution, we apply a supersymmetric technique previously utilized in solid-state physics. Consequently, we derive exact solutions for the states of $N$ molecules confined within a microcavity, valid for any $N$. Our analysis reveals that the width of polaritonic states as a function of $N$ is contingent upon the disorder characteristics, thereby offering a means to investigate the distribution of molecular energy levels. Furthermore, we demonstrate how to obtain exact results for Hückel-type Hamiltonians featuring on-site Cauchy disorder and illustrate their practical application.

Heavy-flavour (HF) quarks, specifically charm and beauty, are generated during the initial phases of ultra-relativistic collisions through hard scattering. Analyzing heavy flavour production relative to charged-particle multiplicity offers insights into how event activity influences production mechanisms and serves as a probe for multiple parton interactions. Additionally, these multiplicity studies are crucial for reference measurements, tuning theoretical models, and characterizing global event properties. At ALICE, measurements of charged-particle multiplicity and HF production in both hadronic and electronic decay channels occur at central rapidity, whereas HF-decay muons and $\rm J/\psi \rightarrow \mu^{+}\mu^{-}$ are measured at forward rapidity. This contribution presents findings on the relative $\rm J/\psi$, average D-mesons, and leptons from HF hadron decays as a function of charged-particle multiplicity in proton-proton (pp) collisions at $\sqrt{s}$ = 5.02, 7, 8, and 13 TeV, comparing these results with theoretical model predictions.

Quantum entanglement between a particle undergoing interference and a detector used to obtain which-path information is fundamental to Bohr's complementary principle; however, the specific quantitative link between this entanglement and fringe visibility has previously remained undefined. In this study, we establish an equality that precisely quantifies this relationship. This equality describes the extent to which an interference pattern can be maintained when a particle, initially possessing a specific level of coherence, becomes entangled with a which-path detector to varying degrees. By uniting coherence theory, this equality offers a novel connection between entanglement and interference, revealing the quantitative complementarity between them for the first time. We experimentally validate this relationship using a superconducting circuit, where a resonator acts as the which-path detector for an interfering qubit. Our results confirm that quantum entanglement is the mechanism preventing any detector from acquiring which-path information without degrading the interference pattern, a finding that was not previously verified.

Data scarcity, often resulting from machine learning over-fitting and the unavailability of manufacturing data for certain computational chemistry tasks, significantly hinders the application of machine learning to molecules. To address this, we propose extracting inherent molecular structural features and rationally distorting them to enhance data availability. This approach enables machine learning projects to utilize physics-informed augmentation, substantially improving predictive accuracy. Validated by predictions of rejection rates and flux for thin film polyamide nanofiltration membranes—which saw relative error decrease from 16.34% to 6.71% and the coefficient of determination increase from 0.16 to 0.75—our proposed deep spatial learning with molecular vibration offers broad utility in molecular science. Experimental comparisons clearly demonstrate its superiority over standard learning algorithms.

This document seeks to resolve ambiguities surrounding electrostatics calculations, particularly within the realm of biomolecular structures and concerning the standard units employed for contouring/visualizing isopotential surfaces and mapping potentials onto molecular solvent-accessible surfaces.

This note demonstrates that the multiplicative Grothendieck-Springer space possesses a natural quasi-Poisson structure. The resolution morphism serves as the corresponding group-valued moment map, with quasi-Hamiltonian leaves defined as the connected components of the preimages of Steinberg fibers. This result represents a multiplicative counterpart to the standard Poisson structure found on the additive Grothendieck-Springer resolution, providing a concrete example of the broader reduction procedure along Dirac realizations recently detailed by the author and Mayrand.

An Intelligent IoT Environment (iIoTe) consists of diverse devices capable of jointly running semi-autonomous applications, such as fully automated manufacturing units or harvesting machines that interact without human intervention. Given that these edge environments typically rely on wireless and battery-powered infrastructure—including e-tractors, drones, Automated Guided Vehicles (AGVs), and robots—energy efficiency is paramount. Total energy usage is influenced by various iIoTe technologies that facilitate edge computing and communication, distributed learning, distributed ledgers, and smart contracts. This paper offers a comprehensive review of these technologies, detailing their functionality and performance while highlighting the trade-offs between resources, latency, privacy, and energy consumption. Furthermore, it outlines a vision for integrating these enabling technologies into energy-efficient iIoTe systems and presents a roadmap to tackle current open research challenges.

Present LHC dark matter searches primarily target mono-X signatures, involving dark matter production alongside a Standard Model particle. A foundational benchmark posits a massive spin-1 $Z^\prime$ mediator connecting dark matter $\chi$ to the Standard Model. Mono-X limits are strongest when the $Z^\prime$ mass exceeds twice the dark matter mass ($M_{Z'}\gtrsim 2M_\chi$), allowing decays into two on-shell dark matter particles. This study extends the experimental reach into a complementary regime where the $Z^\prime$ is significantly lighter than the dark matter. In this scenario, the $Z^\prime$ generates an effective long-range force that enables the formation of darkonium bound states, a feature common in various dark sector models. These bound states become active when $M_{\chi}>M_{Z'}/\alpha_{\rm eff}$, with $\alpha_{\rm eff}$ representing the dark sector's effective fine-structure constant. Additionally, darkonium may decay into Standard Model quarks without generating missing transverse momentum. By analyzing multijet final states, we reinterpret current searches to constrain the simple $Z^\prime$ benchmark in regions inaccessible to traditional mono-X analyses. Furthermore, assuming a baryonic $Z^\prime$ mediator and Dirac dark matter, direct detection constraints can be relaxed by assigning a small Majorana mass to the dark matter. Finally, we examine the interplay between mono-X and darkonium channels at future high-energy colliders, which represents the frontier for exploring this model's parameter space.

Covariant Entropy Principle arguments that do not rely on a specific model suggest that causal diamonds in the primordial universe were completely occupied by a single equilibrated system possessing finite entropy. If this condition were to endure eternally, the universe would contain no localized excitations; however, our universe seems destined to evolve toward such a state. Within a few hundred times its present age, it will likely reach a phase where our local galaxy group resides within empty de Sitter space. Ultimately, this group will collapse into a black hole that subsequently evaporates. In de Sitter space, localized excitations represent low-entropy, constrained states of the vacuum ensemble, and the source of these constraints must trace back to the early universe, where the apparent horizon expanded from an initial constrained state that gave rise to all localized excitations. We contend that within global Friedmann-Robertson-Walker coordinates, this scenario mirrors slow-roll inflation concluding with a dilute gas of microscopic black holes, whose masses are set by the inflationary scale. Furthermore, we examine arguments indicating that these black holes could explain the Hot Big Bang, baryogenesis, a unique pattern of Cosmic Microwave Background fluctuations, and potentially primordial black hole dark matter composed of larger black holes surviving into the matter-dominated era. The more complex issue of whether these small black holes can evolve in a manner consistent with all observational limits remains unresolved, requiring computer simulations that have not yet been conducted.

This short paper finalizes the analysis initiated in [RMF 64 (2018) 662-670, arXiv:1803.02426] concerning the quantifiers of classical correlations and local available quantum correlations for Bell Diagonal states. We refine their prior expressions by incorporating two previously omitted optimization cases.

Accommodating large-scale integration of intermittent renewables necessitates significant demand-side flexibility. Since the built environment consumes roughly 40% of total energy in the EU, unlocking its potential is a critical component of the energy transition. This study concentrates on residential energy flexibility, capitalizing on inherent thermal mass. Drawing on recent advancements in data-driven control, we introduce PhysQ, a physics-informed reinforcement learning framework designed for building control. PhysQ serves as a bridge between traditional model-based control and data-heavy reinforcement learning methods. Experimental results demonstrate that PhysQ learns high-quality control policies that surpass both standard business-as-usual practices and basic model predictive controllers, achieving approximately 9% cost savings. Furthermore, PhysQ effectively incorporates prior physics knowledge to train with fewer samples than conventional reinforcement learning, positioning it as a scalable solution for residential applications. Additionally, by utilizing intuitive building state representations rooted in conventional models, PhysQ offers superior interpretability of its learned policies compared to other data-driven approaches.

We illustrate how employing a reinforcement learning algorithm, specifically the deep cross-entropy method, enables the discovery of explicit constructions and counterexamples to various unresolved conjectures in extremal combinatorics and graph theory. This approach refutes a query by Brualdi and Cao concerning the maximization of permanents in pattern-avoiding matrices, as well as multiple issues regarding the adjacency and distance eigenvalues of graphs.

We analyze the low-energy excitations of a quantum vortex within a quasi-two-dimensional Bose-Einstein condensate (BEC) by employing both the conventional density of states (DOS) definition and an adapted variant that highlights complementary spectral features. The modified approach is especially significant for investigating the polaronic state formed when an impurity is situated inside a vortex. We demonstrate that the impurity responds to the vortex's transverse fluctuations through its residual Kelvin mode and to the phase fluctuations associated with the BEC's Nambu-Goldstone mode. The vortex induces an anomalous excitation spectrum characterized by a finite energy gap and a non-linear DOS at low energies. Furthermore, we identify that the Kelvin mode's high sensitivity to external potentials offers a mechanism for quantum-level control over impurities trapped within a vortex. This additional control pathway could be practically valuable for proposals utilizing vortex-trapped impurities as qubit units in quantum information processing.

It is important to note that a fuzzy conjunction and its corresponding implication constitute a residual pair if and only if the conjunction is left-continuous. To achieve a more comprehensive result regarding residual implications induced by aggregation functions, we relax the definition of general overlap functions by removing the requirement for right-continuity, thereby introducing a novel class of aggregation functions termed semi-overlap functions. We subsequently examine their algebraic properties and analyze their associated residual implications. Furthermore, while various scholars have proposed methods for fuzzy modus ponens (FMP) problems, such as Zadeh's compositional rule of inference (CRI), Wang's triple I method (TIM), and the quintuple implication principle (QIP), the QIP method offers distinct advantages over CRI and TIM in solving FMP. In this paper, we further explore the QIP method for FMP problems, demonstrating that it satisfies the reducibility of multiple-rule fuzzy reasoning. Finally, we propose a new classification algorithm based on semi-overlap functions and the QIP method, designated as the SO5I-FRC algorithm. Comparative tests reveal that the SO5I-FRC algorithm achieves higher average accuracy than the FARC-HD algorithm. These experimental results indicate that semi-overlap functions combined with the QIP method possess significant advantages and broad applicability in classification tasks.

Reconstructing 3D object models is crucial for numerous applications within computer vision. Rather than relying on multiple cameras or sensors as seen in previous research, this study introduces a cost-effective method for 3D reconstruction using a single depth camera supplemented by two or more mirrors. By treating each mirror as a virtual depth camera from a distinct viewpoint, the system captures all scene data from one sensor. This approach enables the reconstruction of moving objects without the need for synchronization protocols typically required by multi-camera setups. Experiments conducted on simple objects validated the accuracy of the proposed system.

The cyclic sieving phenomenon, introduced by Reiner, Stanton, and White, provides a method to count the fixed points of a cyclic group's action on a combinatorial set by evaluating a specific polynomial at roots of unity. A prominent example is Rhoades's theorem, which demonstrates that plane partitions within a rectangular box exhibit cyclic sieving under the promotion operation; in this case, the sieving polynomial corresponds to MacMahon's well-known product formula for the size generating function of these partitions. This work extends Rhoades's findings by incorporating the symmetries of complementation and transposition for plane partitions. The associated polynomial is the size generating function for symmetric plane partitions, utilizing a product formula originally conjectured by MacMahon and later proven by Andrews and Macdonald. Furthermore, we illustrate how these symmetry-based results apply to the rowmotion operator on plane partitions, noting its close relationship to promotion.

The intricacy of biological systems and the growing volume of experimental data compel us to create mathematical models to deepen our comprehension. Since these systems are often poorly understood, most models rely heavily on experimental data, leading to a diverse array of models that appear to describe the same system. To achieve a unified mathematical description, we must determine the relationships between these disparate models. This objective is hindered by the use of various mathematical formalisms for representing identical systems, which complicates direct comparison. In prior research, we established a framework for model comparison by representing models as labelled simplicial complexes and utilizing two approaches: distance-based comparison and equivalence-based comparison. In this paper, we advance our methodology in two key areas. First, we introduce a rigorous and automatable approach for equivalence comparison, specifically identifying conceptually related vertices within the simplicial representation through simplicial operations. This method relies on analyzing vertex symmetry, requiring the development of mathematical theory regarding group actions on simplicial complexes, thereby streamlining and accelerating the determination of model equivalence. Second, we offer an alternative mathematical framework by representing models as groups, enabling the direct application of group-theoretic techniques within our model-comparison methodology.

The evaporation of colloidal droplets often yields intricate patterns, driven by the formation and structural changes of a surface skin. This research examines the drying of colloidal dispersions within a confined space, facilitating direct measurement of skin thickness. The process involves an initial buckling event followed by the expansion of a single depression. These deformations appear to be a universal phenomenon across various colloidal dispersions. The ultimate droplet morphology can be partially rationalized through a basic energy analysis that balances bending and stretching forces. Notably, the final configuration allows for the precise calculation of the critical shell thickness required for buckling. Furthermore, this work validates existing theories for 2D droplets and extends their application to 3D droplets, where direct thickness measurement is impossible.

This work introduces higher order derivations on C*-algebras, serving as the noncommutative counterpart to differential operators in the context of commutative C*-algebras. We demonstrate that the domain of these higher derivations remains closed under smooth functional calculus. Consequently, we establish that Schwartz functions defined on the Connes tangent groupoid are likewise closed under smooth functional calculus.

This study establishes the existence of traveling waves $w: [0,+\infty) \times \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^k$ (where $k \geq 2$) for the parabolic Allen-Cahn system defined by $\partial_t w - \Delta w = -\nabla_u V(w)$ in the specified domain, subject to specific heteroclinic conditions at infinity. The potential $V$ is a smooth, non-negative multi-well potential characterized by a finite null set containing at least two points. These waves propagate horizontally with a positive speed $c^\star$ and a specific profile $\mathfrak{U}$. As $x_1 \to \pm \infty$, the profile $\mathfrak{U}$ connects, in an appropriate sense, two locally minimizing one-dimensional heteroclinics that possess distinct energies. Furthermore, the speed $c^\star$ exhibits certain uniqueness characteristics. The proof relies on a variational approach, which necessitates the assumption of an upper bound on the energy difference between these 1D heteroclinics, where this bound depends on $V$.

While null results from direct detection experiments typically rule out classes of weakly interacting massive particle (WIMP) dark matter coupled to the $Z$ boson, these models remain viable if the particles are superheavy, with masses satisfying $m_{DM} \gtrsim 10^9$ GeV. Future searches may extend sensitivity up to $m_{DM} \simeq 10^{12}$ GeV, reaching the neutrino floor limit. We demonstrate that the observed dark matter abundance of $\Omega_\mathrm{DM}h^2 \simeq 0.1$ for such superheavy WIMPs can be achieved through a reheating temperature of $T_R \simeq m_{DM}/29$ following inflation, provided that direct inflaton decay into dark matter is either negligible or kinematically forbidden.

We introduce a hydrodynamic framework for incompressible polar active fluids subject to quenched disorder. Our theory demonstrates that these fluids can maintain coherent motion, characterized by a non-zero mean velocity in the hydrodynamic limit, despite the disruptive effects of the disorder. Nevertheless, linearized hydrodynamics fails to capture the scaling behavior of these active systems in spatial dimensions ranging from 2 to 5. Despite this limitation, we derive the precise dimension-dependent scaling exponents for these ranges.

A fundamental concept in modern physics, one with a deep historical background, is the fluid—a substance that deforms and flows when subjected to shear stress. In this broad definition, fluids encompass a diverse range of matter phases, including liquids, dense gases, plasmas, and even plastic solids to a certain degree. Fluidity, a primary dynamical trait, is heavily dependent on the specifics of local structure, and conversely, the dominant local structural arrangements of particles over specific time scales are crucial for comprehending fluid dynamics. Orderliness spanning distances similar to inter-particle spacing is termed short-range order, while periodic order extending infinitely is known as long-range order. Neither type of order exists in an ideal gas, yet both liquids and amorphous solids display short-range order. The physics of crystalline solids, characterized by long-range order, is well-established; however, in fluids, atomic structure evolves continuously. The question remains: how do specific structural ordering features influence fluid dynamics? This chapter seeks to address enduring and emerging questions that continue to make fluid dynamics a compelling area for theoretical investigation.

This paper addresses convex finite-sum minimization with explicit convex constraints over strongly connected directed graphs, where constraints represent the intersection of convex sets known individually to specific nodes. We introduce a new decentralized projected gradient algorithm utilizing local averaging and establish its convergence relying solely on the smoothness of local functions.

We fix a Calabi-Yau 3-fold $X$ that satisfies the Bogomolov-Gieseker conjecture by Bayer-Macri-Toda, exemplified by the quintic 3-fold. Utilizing two distinct wall-crossing arguments, we derive two separate explicit formulae connecting rank 0 Donaldson-Thomas invariants (which enumerate torsion sheaves on $X$ supported on ample divisors) with rank 1 Donaldson-Thomas invariants (enumerating ideal sheaves of curves) and Pandharipande-Thomas invariants. Notably, this work establishes a minor adjustment to Toda's formulation of the OSV conjecture for $X$. Furthermore, in cases where $X$ has Picard rank one, we provide an explicit expression for rank two DT invariants in terms of both rank zero and rank one DT invariants.

To investigate fusion hindrance in the synthesis of Super-Heavy Elements (SHE) via very heavy ion collisions, a new framework is introduced. This approach analyzes reaction dynamics through collective degrees of freedom relaxing across various time scales. Utilizing the Nakajima-Zwanzig projection operator method, fast variables are eliminated to generate a dynamical equation for a reduced system containing only slow variables. In this formulation, the time evolution operator is renormalized, introducing an inhomogeneous term that signifies the propagation of the initial distribution and causes a slip in the initial values of the slow variables. It is anticipated that this mechanism provides a dynamical basis for the "injection point $s$" parameter proposed by Swiatecki et al., which is used to match measured absolute cross sections for SHE. The derived formula for this slip, expressed in terms of the system's physical parameters, aligns with recent findings obtained using the Langevin equation.

This study investigates the dynamics of the one-dimensional $\varepsilon$-dependent Cahn-Hilliard / Allen-Cahn equation near an equilibrium featuring $N$ transition layers, a scenario that typically does not conserve mass. We examine two distinct configurations: the first adheres to zero-mass flux boundary conditions at $x=1$, while the second replaces one such condition with a mass-conservation constraint. Drawing inspiration from Carr and Pego's work on layered metastable patterns in the Allen-Cahn equation [10] and Bates and Xun's analysis of the Cahn-Hilliard equation [5], we construct an $N$-dimensional manifold for the first case and a mass-conservative $(N-1)$-dimensional manifold for the second to approximate metastable states with $N$ layers. For both settings, we derive the essential dynamics of the layers as ordinary differential systems governing their motion, formulated using local coordinates relative to the respective manifolds. Specifically, we estimate the spectrum of the linearized Cahn-Hilliard / Allen-Cahn operator and identify broad families of $\varepsilon$-dependent weights, $\delta(\varepsilon)$ and $\mu(\varepsilon)$, applied at various parts of the operator that ensure stable dynamics where the system rests exponentially small in $\varepsilon$. Our findings clarify the role of mass conservation in categorizing the general mixed problem into two primary classes: solutions with profiles resembling Allen-Cahn when mass is not conserved, and solutions approaching the Cahn-Hilliard profile when mass is conserved.

Single-cell magneto-optical Faraday filters are typically implemented using either 'wing' or 'line center' spectral profiles and offer significant utility. We demonstrate that coupling a second cell with an independent axial (Faraday) or transverse (Voigt) magnetic field enhances performance regarding both the figure of merit (FOM) and the spectral profile. In this configuration, the first cell rotates the light's polarization plane to establish a high-transmission window, while the second cell selectively absorbs light to suppress unwanted transmission. Employing naturally abundant Rb vapor cells, we successfully constructed a Faraday-Faraday wing filter and the first-ever Faraday-Voigt line center filter, both of which align closely with theoretical predictions. These filters achieved FOM values of 0.86 and 1.63 GHz$^{-1}$, respectively, with the latter representing the highest FOM ever recorded for an atomic line filter.

Research into correlations lacking a definite causal order has uncovered a complex structure that becomes apparent when involving more than two parties. This finding motivates the investigation of multipartite "noncausal" correlations that remain unattainable even when noncausal resources are accessible to fewer parties. We formally define genuinely N-partite noncausal correlations as those that cannot be generated by partitioning N parties into two or more groups where a causal order exists between the groups. We demonstrate that these correlations can be characterized by their position outside a polytope, where vertices represent deterministic strategies and facets define what we term "2-causal" inequalities. We further show that genuinely multipartite noncausal correlations emerge within the process matrix formalism, a framework where quantum mechanics operates locally but no global causal structure is assumed, though violations were not found for all inequalities. Additionally, we propose two refined definitions that enable different quantifications of the extent to which noncausal correlations function as a genuinely multipartite resource.

Current benchmarks for grounding language in interactive settings either omit real-world linguistic features or struggle to scale due to heavy reliance on human effort for data collection and feedback. To address these limitations, we introduce WebShop, a simulated e-commerce platform featuring 1.18 million real products and 12,087 crowd-sourced text instructions. In this environment, an agent must navigate various webpage types and execute diverse actions to locate, customize, and purchase items based on textual requirements. WebShop presents several challenges for language grounding, including interpreting compositional instructions, reformulating queries, handling noisy webpage text, and conducting strategic exploration. We gathered over 1,600 human demonstrations and trained and evaluated a variety of agents using reinforcement learning, imitation learning, and pre-trained image and language models. Our top-performing model achieved a 29% task success rate, surpassing rule-based heuristics (9.6%) but falling short of human expert performance (59%). Additionally, we analyzed both agent and human trajectories and conducted ablation studies on model components to offer insights for improving future agents' language understanding and decision-making capabilities. Finally, we demonstrated that agents trained on WebShop exhibit meaningful sim-to-real transfer when tested on amazon.com and ebay.com, highlighting the platform's potential for developing practical web-based agents capable of operating in real-world scenarios.

Current machine learning methods are essential for addressing many data-driven real-world challenges. However, when facing complex tasks, practitioners often struggle to decide whether to employ deep learning or forgo it entirely. This paper investigates whether simple statistical machine learning algorithms can match or surpass the performance of deep learning models by strategically understanding the application and processing the data to achieve significant improvements. The study emphasizes that data preprocessing is more critical than algorithm selection. It examines transformations involving trigonometric, logarithmic, and exponential functions, as well as purely trigonometric ones. Finally, the authors validate their arguments through a regression analysis of music signals.

High-dimensional integration is essential across numerous scientific disciplines, prompting the development of numerical methods to compute these intricate integrals. We present i-flow, a Python package that executes high-dimensional numerical integration through normalizing flows—machine-learned, bijective transformations between distributions. Beyond integration, i-flow facilitates the sampling of random points from complex high-dimensional distributions. Our comparison with other high-dimensional integration algorithms demonstrates that i-flow achieves superior performance specifically for correlated integrals in high dimensions. The code is publicly accessible on GitLab at https://gitlab.com/i-flow/i-flow.

By utilizing topos theory, a semantic framework can be established for sequential circuits, treating time-sensitive components like unit delays on equal footing with combinational gates. In this approach, both gate types are represented as functions within a specific topos—the category of presheaves defined over the natural ordering of $\mathbb{N}$. This framework demonstrates that sequential circuits satisfy the equational theory of traced categories.

Functioning as the quantum equivalent of the classical one-time pad, the private quantum channel (PQC) is essential for generating the maximally mixed state from any input, a capability vital for analyzing secure quantum communication and channel capacity. Despite the established link between PQC structure and regular polytopes, no prior report has documented this relationship in higher dimensions. Recent work has already established a one-to-one mapping between single-qubit PQCs and three-dimensional regular polyhedra. This paper elucidates such connections for a qutrit system (three-level states) and four-dimensional regular polytopes by employing two methods: generalized Gell-Mann matrices and a modified quantum Fourier transform. Furthermore, we aim to derive a general formula describing these relationships in even higher dimensions.

Although multi-object tracking (MOT) has advanced significantly in recent years, several challenges remain. The majority of existing MOT algorithms operate under a tracking-by-detection framework, which treats detection and tracking as separate, independent stages. Early versions of this framework required two distinct feature extractions for detection and tracking. While newer approaches have unified feature extraction into a single network, the tracking component still depends on data association and complex post-processing for managing object lifecycles, indicating that these methods fail to fully integrate detection and tracking. This paper introduces the Global Correlation Network (GCNet), a novel architecture designed for end-to-end joint multi-object detection and tracking. Unlike conventional object detection methods, GCNet employs a global correlation layer to directly regress the absolute coordinates and sizes of bounding boxes rather than predicting offsets. The GCNet pipeline is conceptually straightforward, eliminating the need for non-maximum suppression, data association, or other intricate tracking strategies. Evaluated on the UA-DETRAC multi-vehicle tracking dataset, GCNet demonstrates competitive performance against state-of-the-art detectors and trackers.

**Abstract** The magneto-optical trap (MOT) serves as a critical instrument for capturing and cooling atoms, supporting diverse applications. We present a planar-integrated MOT achieved by merging an optical grating chip with a magnetic coil chip. This flat grating chip condenses the traditional six-beam setup into a single laser beam, while the flat coil chip substitutes the standard cylindrical anti-Helmholtz coils. We successfully trapped 10⁴ cold ⁸⁷Rb atoms at a height of 3–9 mm above the chip surface. This innovative design significantly minimizes the device's volume, weight, and complexity, offering advantages for use in gravimeters, atomic clocks, and quantum memory systems.

We present crossingless sheaves within specific equivariant derived categories, which serve as analogues to the Bezrukavnikov-Mirkovic exotic sheaves associated with two-block nilpotents. Furthermore, we determine the classes of these crossingless sheaves in the equivariant K-theory of Cautis-Kamnitzer varieties.

We present a framework for converting problems subject to manifold constraints into unconstrained forms via parametrizations defined in Euclidean space, termed "trivializations." We establish the conditions required for a trivialization to be valid within gradient-based optimization, demonstrating that while two major families of trivializations possess generally advantageous characteristics, they also encounter performance limitations. To address this, we introduce "dynamic trivializations," creating a spectrum of optimization methods that bridge the gap between standard trivializations and Riemannian gradient descent, effectively merging their respective strengths. Furthermore, we detail the practical implementation of these two trivialization families across various matrix manifolds, deriving a formula for the gradient of the matrix exponential that holds independent practical value. Finally, we demonstrate that dynamic trivializations enhance the performance of existing techniques on benchmark tasks designed to evaluate long-term memory in neural networks.

Current theories regarding polymer drag reduction (DR) mechanisms typically apply to long-chain, flexible polymers that create viscoelastic solutions. In contrast, rigid polymer solutions that also induce DR appear to lack prominent viscoelastic properties; however, they exhibit elevated viscosities and distinct shear-thinning behavior, which can be effectively modeled using generalized Newtonian frameworks. This study presents an experimental analysis of turbulent channel flow containing an aqueous xanthan gum solution, covering friction Reynolds numbers ($Re_{\tau}$) from 160 to 680. Drag reduction levels remained relatively stable, ranging between 28% and 33%. Velocity fields were captured via planar particle image velocimetry, while steady shear rheology was assessed using a torsional rheometer. These data characterized flow statistics across varying $Re_{\tau}$ with minimal DR variation—a parametric approach previously limited to numerical simulations. As $Re_{\tau}$ increased, modifications to mean velocity and Reynolds stress profiles mirrored those seen in Newtonian turbulence: inner-normalized mean velocity profiles overlapped across different Reynolds numbers, and Reynolds stresses increased monotonically in magnitude. Mean viscosity profiles versus wall-normal position revealed a thin near-wall layer of low-viscosity fluid, with significantly higher viscosity in the outer region. It is hypothesized that the shear viscosity transition between this inner "lubricating" layer and the outer layer promotes fluid slippage within the buffer layer and elevates the logarithmic layer, a mechanism analogous to drag reduction achieved through wall lubrication or superhydrophobic surfaces.

The analysis of multi-source data, representing multiple perspectives on the same subjects, has grown increasingly prevalent in molecular biomedical research. While recent approaches have focused on uncovering internal and inter-source structures or building predictive models using all available sources, existing methods that integrate both tasks are limited. These limitations arise because such methods either focus solely on shared structures across all datasets while neglecting source-specific patterns, or they extract underlying structures without considering the target outcome. We introduce supervised joint and individual variation explained (sJIVE), a method capable of simultaneously identifying both shared (joint) and source-specific (individual) structures and constructing a linear prediction model for an outcome using these features. These components are weighted to balance the explanation of variation in the multi-source data against variation in the outcome. Simulation results demonstrate that sJIVE outperforms existing methods in scenarios involving substantial noise within multi-source data. Furthermore, an application to COPDGene study data identified gene expression and proteomic patterns predictive of lung function. The sJIVE functions are available in the R.JIVE package at http://github.com/lockEF/r.jive.

Digital painting software utilizes layers to organize artwork, yet these layers are typically not explicitly saved, transmitted, or published with the final image.
