This research investigates non-equilibrium superconductivity in DyBa2Cu3O7-d through photo-induced activation of mm-wave absorption (PIAMA). We tracked the temporal changes in thin film transmissivity at 5 cm⁻¹ following pulsed infrared exposure. Beyond the expected positive bolometric response, we detected a second, more rapid decay with an opposing sign for temperatures above 40 K. We ascribe this phenomenon to the distinctive characteristics of quasi-particles located near the nodes of an unconventional superconductor, which significantly prolongs their recombination time.

This study advances the classification of positive scalar curvature metrics, specifically regarding bordism and concordance. For a closed spin manifold $M$ with dimension $\ge 5$ that supports a metric of positive scalar curvature, we establish lower bounds for the rank of the group of such metrics up to bordism. These bounds are expressed using the corank of the canonical map $KO_*(M)\to KO_*(B\pi_1(M))$, assuming the validity of the rational analytic Novikov conjecture for $\pi_1(M)$.

We investigate the fractional stochastic heat equation defined on the $d$-dimensional torus $\mathbb{T}^d:=[-1,1]^d$ ($d\geq 1$) subject to periodic boundary conditions:
$$ \partial_t u(t,x)=
-(-\Delta)^{\alpha/2}u(t,x)+\sigma(t,x,u)\dot{F}(t,x)\quad x\in
\mathbb{T}^d,t\in\mathbb{R}^+ ,$$
where $\alpha\in(1,2]$ and $\dot{F}(t,x)$ denotes noise that is white in time and colored in space. Under the assumptions that $\sigma$ is uniformly bounded and Lipschitz continuous with respect to $u$, we derive small ball probabilities for the solution $u$, given the initial condition $u(0,x)\equiv 0$.

Multistage stochastic programming offers a framework for addressing sequential decision-making under uncertainty, yet the method of incorporating this uncertainty is frequently underexamined. Traditionally, optimization models rely on simple statistical forecasting techniques, such as first-order autoregressive time-series models, to generate scenarios representing future uncertainty, often without rigorously evaluating their performance. Driven by advancements in probabilistic forecasting, this study integrates a deep learning-based time-series forecasting approach into the multistage stochastic programming framework, contrasting it with traditional methods. We evaluate how improved forecast accuracy affects the quality of two prevalent look-ahead policies—a deterministic and a two-stage policy—within a rolling-horizon setting applied to a practical problem. Our findings demonstrate that higher forecast accuracy significantly enhances model performance, allowing even computationally inexpensive heuristics to produce high-quality solutions. Furthermore, the results highlight that the probabilistic forecasting strengths of deep learning methods are particularly valuable when serving as a sampling tool for scenario-based models and when predicting worst-case scenarios for risk-averse applications.

The goal of singing voice separation is to isolate vocals from instrumental accompaniment. A primary bottleneck for this task is the scarcity of datasets containing separated vocal tracks. While techniques like random source mixing help leverage existing data and yield modest performance gains, we introduce a new method called chromagram-based pitch-aware remixing, which blends music segments exhibiting high pitch alignment. Experimental results in both supervised and semi-supervised contexts demonstrate that incorporating pitch-aware remixing during training significantly enhances the test signal-to-distortion ratio (SDR).

This study examines the impact of the Unruh effect on a quantum Stackelberg duopoly. Our findings demonstrate that the acceleration within a noninertial frame significantly influences firm payoffs. Furthermore, the validation of the subgame perfect Nash equilibrium is restricted to a specific range of noninertial frame accelerations. While initial state entanglement offers benefits in the quantum duopoly model, these advantages are diminished by acceleration. Consequently, the duopoly can only achieve a follower advantage within a narrow acceleration range.

While a classical theorem by Neukirch and Uchida establishes that a number field K is uniquely identified by the structure of its absolute Galois group Gal(K), we demonstrate that this is not the case for the Sylow subgroups of Gal(K), thereby resolving a question posed by Florian Pop.

This paper examines permutation groups that possess the \emph{EKR-Module property}. This property characterizes the largest intersecting sets of permutations within a group by stating that the characteristic vector of any such maximum set is a linear combination of the characteristic vectors of cosets from stabilizer subgroups. While Meagher and Sin previously demonstrated that all $2$-transitive groups satisfy this property, our work identifies several additional infinite classes of permutation groups that do so.

While the path-integral formalism is established as equivalent to standard quantum mechanics, applying it to multi-qubit entangled states remains unclear. Whether viewing entanglement through the lens of high-dimensional Hilbert spaces or as a link between distant spatial configurations, it is not immediately evident that such calculations can rely solely on paths within ordinary space and time. Although prior research demonstrated this approach for specific cases, this paper generalizes the findings to all pure two-qubit states, accommodating arbitrary measurement bases for each qubit. Additionally, certain three-qubit states are analyzed, confirming that path integrals successfully reproduce standard correlations. These advancements facilitate the translation of conventional quantum analysis into a path-integral framework, thereby streamlining specific computations and contributing to broader research in quantum foundations.

Document intelligence, an emerging research field, enables numerous business applications by automatically reading, comprehending, and analyzing documents. However, the wide variety of document formats and layouts poses significant challenges for machine understanding. To address this, we introduce GraphDoc, a multimodal graph attention model designed for diverse document understanding tasks. Pre-trained within a multimodal framework, GraphDoc simultaneously leverages text, layout, and image data. Recognizing that text blocks depend heavily on their surrounding contexts, we integrate a graph structure into the attention mechanism to create a graph attention layer, ensuring each input node focuses only on its neighbors. These input nodes consist of textual, visual, and positional features extracted from semantically meaningful regions in the document image. We achieve multimodal feature fusion for each node using a gate fusion layer, while the graph attention layer models the contextual relationships between nodes. Through Masked Sentence Modeling, GraphDoc learns a generic representation from just 320k unlabeled documents. Extensive experiments on public datasets demonstrate that GraphDoc achieves state-of-the-art performance, validating the efficacy of our approach. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ZZR8066/GraphDoc.

Recently, research has heavily focused on developing link prediction models to automatically complete knowledge graphs (KGs). However, current methods for this task face two inherent challenges: 1) relation distributions in KGs are typically unbalanced, and 2) numerous unseen relations frequently appear in real-world scenarios. These issues restrict both the training efficacy and practical utility of existing models. We propose a unified Generalized Relation Learning (GRL) framework to address these challenges, which can be integrated into current link prediction models. By conducting generalized relation learning, GRL leverages semantic correlations between relations to bridge semantically similar ones. Following training with GRL, the vector space representation improves by bringing semantically similar relations closer together while enhancing the discrimination of dissimilar ones. Comprehensive experiments across six benchmarks demonstrate GRL's superior performance in link prediction tasks. Specifically, GRL enhances existing models, rendering them robust against unbalanced relation distributions and capable of learning unseen relations.

Simulating quantum states on classical hardware is generally challenging due to the substantial memory and computational resources required. However, efficient simulation is feasible for specific quantum state classes, notably Gaussian states within continuous variable systems. This paper presents QuGIT, a Python numerical library utilizing symplectic methods to efficiently simulate multimode Gaussian states and operations. QuGIT offers exact simulations without Hilbert space truncation and supports a broad spectrum of Gaussian operations on arbitrary Gaussian states, such as unitaries, partial traces, tensor products, general-dyne measurements, and both conditional and unconditional dynamics. Several applications relevant to quantum optics and optomechanics are demonstrated to showcase the toolbox.

This study investigates the $\gamma p \to K^+\Lambda(1405)$ photoproduction reaction using a tree-level effective Lagrangian approach to elucidate the underlying mechanism and determine resonance parameters and contents. The reaction amplitudes are constructed by incorporating a minimal set of $N$ resonances in the $s$-channel, alongside $t$-channel $K$ and $K^\ast$ exchanges, $u$-channel $\Sigma$, $\Lambda$, and $\Lambda(1405)$ exchanges, and a generalized contact term. Results indicate that including the $N(2000){5/2}^+$ resonance in the $s$-channel allows for an accurate reproduction of recent differential cross-section data from the CLAS Collaboration. Further analysis reveals that while $t$-channel $K$ exchange dominates the cross sections at high energies, contributions from both $s$-channel $N$ and $N(2000){5/2}^+$ exchanges are particularly significant in the near-threshold energy region. Additionally, predictions for beam and target asymmetries in this reaction are provided.

This paper investigates the dynamics of the higher-order difference equation $x_{n+1}=A+B((x_{n-m})/(x_{n}^2))$, where $A$ and $B$ are positive constants, initial values are positive, and $m$ is a positive integer. We examine the periodicity, boundedness, semi-cycles, and global asymptotic stability of the solutions, as well as the rate of convergence for these difference equations.

This brief note provides a positive resolution to Wu's conjecture regarding practical numbers, originally formulated in [X.-H. Wu, {\it Special forms and the distribution of practical numbers}, Acta Math. Hungar., {\bf 160}(2020), 405-411].

This research examines kinetic models of reversible enzyme reactions, comparing two methods for deriving analytic approximate solutions. Specifically, the Homotopy Perturbation Method (HPM) and the Simple Iteration Method (SIM) are employed to solve non-linear reaction equations for these reversible systems. The findings indicate that the approximations generated by both techniques yield comparable results. Corresponding Matlab programs are provided in the appendices.

Recent research has significantly advanced the study of kagome metals, including compounds like T$_m$X$_n$ (where T is Fe or Co, and X is Sn or Ge) and $A$V$_3$Sb$_5$ (with A being Cs, K, or Rb). A pressing question in this field concerns the characteristics of correlated phases arising when topologically \textit{non-trivial} bands intersect the Fermi level. In this work, we analyze an extended Hubbard model defined on a kagome lattice with spin-orbit coupling, focusing on a Kramer's pair of bands featuring opposite Chern numbers that remain isolated within the band structure. We develop an effective model within a time-reversal (T) symmetric lattice framework. Our analysis identifies density-wave order as a key correlated phase in the system's phase diagram. We demonstrate that this order breaks time-reversal symmetry, a phenomenon stemming from Wannier orbitals that lack a shared Wannier center—a signature of the underlying $Z_2$ topology. Finally, we discuss how these findings influence the understanding of correlation physics in kagome metals.

Nuclear symmetry energy is crucial for characterizing finite nuclei and neutron stars, particularly regarding the crust-core interface at low baryon densities, where its accurate modeling is essential. Although the standard parabolic approximation is commonly used to define symmetry energy, it carries inherent limitations. This study applies a specific class of nuclear models, designed for the inner and outer cores of neutron stars, to investigate how higher-order terms in the energy expansion influence the crust-core transition location. Both thermodynamical and dynamical approaches were utilized to determine the transition density ($n_{\rm t}$) and pressure ($P_{\rm t}$), while a corresponding energy density functional analyzed properties of both nonrotating and slowly rotating neutron stars. Results indicate that a larger slope parameter ($L$) results in slower convergence of the expansion. Furthermore, a universal relationship between $n_{\rm t}$ and $L$ was established using the full expression and dynamical method. The crustal moment of inertia proves highly sensitive to the transition location, whereas the critical angular velocity for $r$-mode instability and minimum mass configurations show moderated effects. Tidal deformability is also impacted, albeit less significantly but still non-negligibly. In all cases, relying on the parabolic approximation leads to an overestimation of $n_{\rm t}$ and $P_{\rm t}$, resulting in inaccurate predictions. Additionally, the matching process at the interface can introduce substantial errors comparable to those arising from the method itself.

This study introduces and analyzes the concept of an intrinsically thinnest transistor: a monolayer ballistic heterojunction bipolar transistor constructed from a lateral transition metal dichalcogenide heterostructure. Unlike Field Effect Transistors, this device lacks the need for top or bottom gates because charge transport is regulated by the electrochemical potential of the base electrode, rendering it inherently thinner. Consistent with bipolar transistor characteristics, the collector current increases tenfold for every 60 mV rise in base voltage across multiple orders of magnitude at room temperature, without requiring complex electrostatic optimization. Our findings rely on detailed self-consistent simulations of electrostatics and quantum transport for both electrons and holes within a pnp configuration, utilizing MoS$_2$ for the 10-nm base and WSe$_2$ for the emitter and collector. These three-terminal simulations validate the operational principle and demonstrate a substantial current modulation ratio of I$_\text{ON}$/I$_\text{OFF}\sim 10^8$ when $\Delta V_{\rm EB}=0.5$ V. Under the assumption of ballistic transport, we achieve a current gain $\beta\sim 10^4$ across various collector current levels and a cutoff frequency extending into the terahertz range. Exploring diverse bipolar nanoscale device concepts in two-dimensional materials holds great promise for future applications in electronics and optoelectronics.

T-Reqs is a text-based requirements management tool built upon the git version control system. It integrates practical conventions, templates, and helper scripts with robust capabilities from the existing git ecosystem to tackle specific requirements engineering challenges in large-scale agile system development. This solution empowers agile cross-functional teams to maintain system-level visibility of requirements and facilitates the efficient proposal of updates. Drawing on our experience with T-Reqs, we i) connect known requirements challenges in large-scale agile development with necessary tool support; ii) outline essential requirements for tools in this context; and iii) suggest concrete solutions to address these challenges.

This paper generalizes the primary findings of arXiv:2001.01312 to the context of twisted groupoids. Specifically, it establishes a decomposition for the C*-algebra associated with a twisted locally compact groupoid possessing a Haar system, provided a normal subgroupoid exists. If both the normal subgroupoid and the twist defined over it are abelian, the result yields another twisted groupoid C*-algebra. These findings are subsequently applied to the study of C*-algebraic deformation quantization and multiplier representations of locally compact abelian groups.

Research indicates that Bundle Adjustment (BA) utilizing parallax angle-based feature parameterization outperforms methods relying on inverse depth or XYZ coordinates. This paper introduces an enhanced Parallax Manifold Bundle Adjustment (PMBA) algorithm, which extends the parallax approach into the manifold domain and incorporates an observation-ray objective function. By aligning the problem formulation more closely with the projective characteristics of image formation, this modification enables BA to achieve superior convergence, accuracy, and robustness, particularly in varied outdoor settings and collinear motion scenarios. Leveraging these advantages, we also propose a pose-graph simplification for PMBA that significantly reduces dimensionality. This convex pose-graph model is straightforward to solve and provides an effective initial guess for the inherently non-convex original BA problem. We offer theoretical proof that our global initialization strategy ensures a near-optimal solution. Extensive experiments across diverse environments and motion types demonstrate PMBA's superior convergence compared to other BA techniques. Furthermore, we show that our global initialization process successfully bootstraps full BA in various sequential or out-of-order scenarios—including datasets from the "Bundle Adjustment in the Large" collection—without relying on incremental initialization or external data.

Recent breakthroughs in multimodal single-cell technologies allow for the simultaneous collection of multiple omics profiles from individual cells, offering deeper understanding of cellular states and dynamics. Nevertheless, deriving joint representations from such multimodal data, modeling inter-modality relationships, and effectively integrating extensive single-modality datasets into downstream analyses remain significant challenges. To overcome these obstacles and enhance multimodal single-cell data analysis, three primary tasks have been established: $\textit{modality prediction}$, $\textit{modality matching}$, and $\textit{joint embedding}$. In this study, we introduce $\textit{scMoGNN}$, a versatile Graph Neural Network framework designed to address these three tasks, demonstrating superior performance across all of them compared to both conventional methods and state-of-the-art approaches. Our method secured the overall first-place ranking in the $\textit{Modality prediction}$ track of the NeurIPS 2021 Competition, and all implementations are now available within the DANCE package~\url{https://github.com/OmicsML/dance}.

Omega Centauri, the Milky Way's most massive globular cluster, is believed to be the surviving core of a disrupted dwarf galaxy, aligning with hierarchical merging models. It hosts multiple stellar populations with varying heavy element abundances resulting from supernova-driven metal enrichment. While M22 resembles Omega Centauri, other globular clusters differ significantly, leading researchers to view the latter two as exceptions; consequently, chemical inhomogeneities in typical clusters are often attributed to "pollution" from intermediate-mass asymptotic giant branch stars. This study reports calcium abundances in seven globular clusters and compares them to Omega Centauri. Since calcium and other heavy elements require numerous supernovae from massive stars to form, yet current cluster gravitational potentials cannot retain most of this ejecta, we conclude that these clusters, like Omega Centauri, are likely remnants of more massive primordial dwarf galaxies that merged and disrupted during the formation of the proto-Galaxy.

This paper investigates multimarginal optimal transport featuring a Coulomb cost, referred to in physics as the Strictly-Correlated Electrons (SCE) functional. We demonstrate that the dual Kantorovich potential corresponds to an electrostatic potential generated by an external charge density, termed the dual charge. Furthermore, we examine its characteristics and apply these findings to discretize the potential across one and three spatial dimensions.

This primarily expository work (though not exclusively so) examines networks modeled as strongly connected, finite directed graphs $X$. Each oriented edge $(x,y)$ carries a positive weight, or conductance, denoted $a(x,y)$. Unlike symmetric cases, we do not assume $a(x,y) = a(y,x)$, nor do we require that an edge in one direction implies the existence of an edge in the opposite direction. These weights define a difference operator; its normalized form serves as our Laplace operator. This operator is linked to a Markov chain with state space $X$. A specific non-empty subset of $X$ is identified as the boundary. The text systematically presents various Laplace equations, beginning with the Poisson equation, followed by the Dirichlet and Neumann problems, where the concept of outer normal derivatives is explained for the latter. The discussion then extends to Laplace equations involving potentials, covering the Robin boundary problem. Subsequently, the bi-Laplacian and its related equations are analyzed, including the iterated Poisson equation, bi-Laplace Dirichlet and Neumann problems, and the "plate equation." Notably, the bi-Laplace Dirichlet-to-Neumann map is highlighted for its significant interest. The work concludes with two comprehensive examples.

This paper introduces a time-evolving graph, composed of sequential snapshots, to represent various real-world networks. We investigate the path classification problem within such graphs, which holds significant practical value, such as forecasting path failures in telecommunication systems and anticipating traffic congestion in road networks. To effectively model temporal dependencies and structural dynamics, we propose a novel deep neural architecture called Long Short-Term Memory R-GCN (LRGCN). LRGCN treats the temporal relationship between consecutive graph snapshots as a memory-based relation and employs a relational Graph Convolutional Network to simultaneously process intra-temporal and inter-temporal connections. Additionally, we introduce a self-attentive path embedding (SAPE) method capable of encoding paths of varying lengths into fixed-length vectors. Experiments conducted on real-world datasets from a telecommunication network and a California traffic network demonstrate that LRGCN outperforms competing approaches in predicting path failures and validate the efficacy of SAPE for path representation.

Precise continuum normalization for merged echelle spectra is a challenging requirement for detailed spectroscopic studies. Existing automatic techniques often struggle due to the diverse features found in stellar spectra, frequently necessitating time-consuming manual intervention. This study aims to create a fully automated tool capable of processing order-merged spectra with optional manual fine-tuning. The method's core relies on a novel fully convolutional deep neural network (SUPP Network) trained to predict a pseudo-continuum, followed by a post-processing step using smoothing splines to provide regressed knots for potential manual adjustments. To mitigate biases from synthetic training data and enhance applicability to features not present in those simulations, active learning techniques were employed. Tested on high-resolution spectra of stars spanning spectral types O to G, the method achieved a root mean squared (RMS) error of 0.0128 across the 3900 Å to 7000 Å range and 0.0081 across the 4200 Å to 7000 Å range. Synthetic spectrum experiments yielded an RMS of approximately 0.0050. These results demonstrate performance comparable to meticulous manual normalization. Furthermore, the approach is versatile and applicable to other astronomical domains requiring background modeling or trend removal. The algorithm is accessible online at https://git.io/JqJhf.

This work introduces a new multimodal learning task called text matching, where the objective is to verify if the text within a single-line image matches a provided transcription candidate. We present the first machine learning model, TextMatcher, specifically built for this purpose. TextMatcher employs a cross-attention mechanism to compare embedding representations of both the image and the text, operating through an end-to-end training process. Our extensive evaluation on the widely used IAM dataset demonstrates that TextMatcher outperforms both baseline methods and existing models related to similar tasks across various configurations, while also offering faster inference speeds. Additionally, we illustrate the practical utility of TextMatcher in an automated bank cheque processing scenario.

This work investigates the long-term dynamics of spin-spin correlation functions within finite geometries, focusing on systems experiencing slow relaxation during phase-ordering kinetics. A phenomenological finite-size scaling framework is proposed and validated by deriving an exact solution for the kinetic spherical model quenched below its critical temperature, applicable across dimensions where $2 < d < 4$.

Recently, matrix factorization has been applied to multi-modal hashing for cross-modality visual search, learning basis functions to map diverse modalities into a shared Hamming space. This paper introduces Supervised Matrix Factorization Hashing (SMFH), a new algorithm that addresses multi-modal hashing through collective non-matrix factorization across modalities. Specifically, SMFH utilizes a carefully designed binary code learning strategy to maintain similarities among original multi-modal features via graph regularization. Furthermore, when available, semantic labels are integrated into the learning process. We hypothesize that these mechanisms help preserve critical information during binary quantization, thereby enhancing retrieval accuracy. Our results on three cross-modality visual search benchmarks—PASCAL-Sentence, Wiki, and NUS-WIDE—demonstrate that SMFH outperforms various state-of-the-art methods.

This analysis investigates supersymmetry (SUSY) within final states featuring one or more jets and missing transverse momentum, utilizing proton-proton collision data at 13 TeV collected by the CMS detector at the CERN LHC in 2016. The dataset corresponds to an integrated luminosity of 35.9 fb$^{-1}$, and the observed signal event counts are consistent with background predictions from standard model processes. These findings are evaluated using simplified SUSY models that posit the pair production of gluinos or squarks, which subsequently decay promptly into quarks and the lightest neutralino. The study probes the masses of bottom, top, and degenerate light-flavour squarks up to 1050, 1000, and 1325 GeV, respectively. When gluinos decay through virtual squark states, their mass reach extends to 1900, 1650, and 1650 GeV. The most stringent limits on neutralino masses derived from these decays are 1150 and 575 GeV. Additionally, the search addresses split-SUSY inspired models with long-lived gluinos, covering proper decay lengths ($c\tau$) ranging from $10^{-3}$ to $10^{5}$ mm, including a metastable scenario. Mass limits of 1750 and 900 GeV are established for gluinos with a $c\tau$ of 1 mm and for the metastable state, respectively, though sensitivity for $c\tau \gtrsim 1$ m relies moderately on specific model assumptions. This investigation offers complementary coverage of the $c\tau$ parameter space for long-lived gluino models compared to other existing LHC methods.

Generating and verifying entanglement between remote qubits is a crucial capability for quantum information technologies. In this study, we introduce a novel method to track and characterize the emergence of entanglement within a half-parity measurement configuration. This approach utilizes the continuous readout of an energetic observable, specifically the half-parity observable itself. Employing a quantum-trajectory framework, we theoretically examine the statistical properties of energy fluctuations for a pair of continuously monitored qubits. We establish a quantitative link between these energetic fluctuations and the rate at which entanglement is generated, subsequently developing an energy-based estimator to detect entanglement within the circuit. Notably, this estimator functions effectively at the single-trajectory level and remains robust despite finite detection efficiency. Our findings advance the fundamental understanding of stochastic energetic processes linked to entanglement creation and offer new avenues for witnessing quantum correlations through quantum thermodynamic metrics.

This study addresses a practical inverse problem aimed at simultaneously recovering the surface heat flux and the thickness of a solid structure using associated ultrasonic data. Within a thermoacoustic coupling framework, both the thermal boundary condition and the structural thickness remain unknown, while ultrasonic sensor propagation times serve as the given measurements. We recast this inverse problem as a PDE-constrained optimization task by defining an appropriate objective functional. Subsequently, we propose an alternating iteration algorithm that integrates the conjugate gradient method with the steepest descent method to solve the optimization challenge. A rigorous convergence analysis is presented for the suggested numerical approach. Furthermore, extensive numerical experiments utilizing real laboratory data are conducted to validate several advantageous characteristics of the newly developed methodology.

Large language models can execute novel tasks without prior training by utilizing natural language prompts that define the required behavior. While these prompts are often manually crafted, they can also be optimized through gradient-based learning using labeled data. Nevertheless, the specific factors contributing to prompt effectiveness, particularly in natural language contexts, remain largely unexplored. This study examines shared characteristics among high-performing prompts. We introduce a human-readable prompt tuning technique called FLUENT PROMPT, which leverages Langevin dynamics and incorporates a fluency constraint to generate a diverse set of effective and fluent prompts. Our analysis indicates that successful prompts are thematically aligned with the task domain and adjust the prior probability of label words. Leveraging these insights, we propose a method for generating prompts from unlabeled data that surpasses strong baselines by an average of 7.0% accuracy across three distinct tasks.

This work demonstrates that the set $\ell^{\infty}\setminus c_0$ is both dense-lineable and dense-algebrable, thereby addressing a question raised by Nestoridis and extending findings by Garc\'ia-Pacheco, Mart\'in, and Seoane-Sep\'ulveda.

A common objective across various domains, including continual and transfer learning, is to accelerate convergence on new tasks by utilizing knowledge gained from prior experiences. This is typically achieved through fine-tuning, which operates under the implicit assumption that neural networks retain plasticity, ensuring that performance on current tasks remains unaffected by previous ones. However, recent findings suggest that fine-tuning a pretrained model on data drawn from the same distribution may yield inferior generalization compared to using a freshly initialized model. We expand upon this observation to propose a hypothesis explaining the underlying mechanisms and examine the consequences of diminished plasticity for continual learning, a field that heavily depends on optimizing pretrained architectures.

Significance often emerges from an entity's function or interactions within a broader system rather than its inherent properties. For instance, the defining characteristic of a hammer is its use for driving nails, not its specific material makeup; similarly, a web page's value often stems from its connections to other pages more than its standalone content. This concept of meaning derived from external relationships is exemplified by methods that identify word meanings through co-occurrence patterns in large text collections. The effectiveness of these approaches implies that human behavioral patterns may underlie conceptual organization. However, written texts do not directly mirror human actions; they serve communication purposes and are typically refined or edited for specific audiences. In this study, we adapt text-analysis techniques to a dataset that directly captures individual behaviors: supermarket transactions. By analyzing product co-occurrence data from approximately 1.3 million shopping baskets, we developed a topic model to identify 25 overarching concepts. These topics were deemed coherent and understandable by both retail professionals and consumers, ranging from specific applications, such as stir-fry ingredients, to broader categories like cooking from scratch. The topics generally reflected goal-oriented and situational needs, aligning with the idea that human conceptual knowledge is adapted to facilitate action. Furthermore, variations in the topics identified by individuals correlated with basic demographic factors. These findings indicate that human activity patterns not only reveal but may also generate conceptual organization.

We announce the identification of 74 new pulsating DA white dwarfs, known as ZZ Cetis, utilizing data from the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) across Sectors 1 through 39, covering the initial three cycles. This dataset encompasses targets from both the Northern Hemisphere (Sectors 14–26) and the Southern Hemisphere (Sectors 1–13 and 27–39), observed with cadences of 120 seconds and 20 seconds. Based on mass estimates derived from fitting Gaia magnitudes and parallax, our sample likely contains 13 low-mass and one extremely low-mass white dwarf candidates. Furthermore, we provide follow-up time-series photometry from ground-based telescopes for 11 of these objects, enabling the detection of additional periods. For every object, we conducted period spectrum analysis and asteroseismological modeling to determine structural parameters, including stellar mass, effective temperature, and hydrogen envelope mass. Excluding the low-mass candidates, the mean asteroseismological mass is approximately 0.635 ± 0.015 solar masses. This figure aligns with the mean mass derived from Gaia data (approximately 0.631 ± 0.040 solar masses) and the average mass of previously identified ZZ Cetis (approximately 0.644 ± 0.034 solar masses). The addition of these 74 new bright ZZ Cetis increases the total population of known ZZ Cetis by roughly 20 percent.

This work establishes multiplicity results for the class of quasilinear problems defined by:
$$ \left\{ \begin{array}{l} -\Delta_{\Phi}u=f(x,u) \quad \mbox{in} \quad \Omega, \\ u=0 \quad \mbox{on} \quad \partial \Omega, \end{array} \right. $$
denoted as $(P)$, where the generalized $p$-Laplacian is given by $\Delta_{\Phi}u=\text{div}(\varphi(x,|\nabla u|)\nabla u)$ with $\Phi(x,t)=\int_{0}^{|t|}\varphi(x,s)s\,ds$. The domain $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^N$ is assumed to be a smooth, bounded region containing two disjoint open subdomains, $\Omega_N$ and $\Omega_p$, such that their closures do not intersect. A key characteristic of problem $(P)$ is that the operator $-\Delta_{\Phi}$ mimics the behavior of $-\Delta_N$ within $\Omega_N$ and $-\Delta_p$ within $\Omega_p$. The nonlinearity $f:\Omega\times\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ is analyzed in two distinct forms; asymptotically, as $|t|$ becomes sufficiently large, it behaves like $e^{\alpha|t|^\frac{N}{N-1}}$ in $\Omega_N$ and like $|t|^{p^*-2}t$ in $\Omega_p$, where $\alpha>0$ and $p^*=\frac{Np}{N-p}$ represents the critical Sobolev exponent for $1<p<N$. Under these conditions, we demonstrate the existence of multiple solutions for one type of nonlinearity $f$ within a general smooth bounded domain, and for the other type, we prove the existence of multiple solutions in an annular domain $\Omega$ that are nonradial and rotationally nonequivalent.

Event cameras represent a new class of sensors that capture per-pixel intensity variations to generate asynchronous event streams, offering significant benefits over conventional cameras, including high dynamic range and the absence of motion blur. While prior research has demonstrated that events can support object tracking through motion compensation or prediction, existing approaches typically assume the target is always in motion and acts as an independent object. Furthermore, these methods struggle to track stationary or non-independent objects within fixed environments. To address these limitations, this paper introduces SiamEvent, a novel event-based tracking framework leveraging Siamese networks and edge-aware similarity learning. Specifically, to identify the target region with the most comparable edge structure, we correlate embedded events across two timestamps to calculate target edge similarity. By maximizing this similarity score, the Siamese network can track arbitrary target edges, thereby extending event-based tracking capabilities beyond independent moving objects to diverse camera and scene configurations. Additionally, we propose methods for target edge initialization and edge detection to mitigate drift. Finally, an open dataset comprising both synthetic and real-world scenes has been created to facilitate the training and evaluation of SiamEvent. Comprehensive experiments indicate that SiamEvent improves tracking performance by up to 15% compared to baselines in real-world scenarios and demonstrates superior robustness under challenging conditions involving high dynamic range and motion blur.

Interferometry is extensively utilized in sensing applications, yet its efficacy is constrained by the finite coherence time of light sources when optical paths are unbalanced. Higher-order interference effects, which rely on intensity correlations across multiple detectors, offer potential advantages over conventional second-order effects observed in single detectors. This discussion examines various fourth-order interference scenarios involving unbalanced delays. We demonstrate that interference can persist even when these delays significantly exceed the source coherence time. Furthermore, we extend this analysis to non-stationary pulsed fields, which necessitate accounting for pulse shapes and require distinct analytical approaches. These findings hold promise for advancing remote sensing technologies.

This study reports the initial detection of spatially resolved oscillation sources using the Siberian Radioheliograph (SRH) within the 3–6 GHz frequency range. Significant flux oscillations with periods of approximately 3, 5, and 13 minutes were identified in Active Region AR12833, where the 3-minute periodicity predominates at higher frequencies. The observed oscillation amplitude varies with the active region's position on the solar disc, diminishing toward the limbs. Detailed analysis of a one-hour interval on June 19, 2021, revealed that the sources of 3-minute oscillations reside above the umbra and exhibit extraordinary polarization. The 5- and 13-minute periods appeared at lower frequencies, extending down to 2.8 GHz; the 5-minute sources were situated near the umbra-penumbra boundary and within pore regions, while the locations of 13-minute sources varied between 3.1 GHz and 4.7 GHz. A consistency was established between the radio and UV (171Å and 304Å) spatial locations of these sources, showing a significant correlation across both ranges. Time delays between microwave oscillations increase as frequency decreases, suggesting an upward propagation of periodic disturbances. The localization of these sources is likely associated with magnetic structures possessing distinct wave cutoff frequencies at different altitudes. These findings demonstrate that the SRH is capable of providing spatially resolved observations of oscillations in both intensity and polarization channels across the 3–6 GHz band.

A critical challenge in many economic experiments involves ensuring adequate statistical power to reject one or more hypotheses. In this work, we adapt methodologies primarily used in clinical trials for testing multiple hypotheses simultaneously within adaptive, two-stage designs. Our primary objective is to demonstrate how this approach can enhance the power of economic experiments. After briefly outlining the underlying theory, we conduct a simulation study supported by the open-source R package `asd` to assess the performance of various designs. The results indicate that the power to reject at least one hypothesis can be increased while maintaining strict control over the overall Type I error rate, all without expanding the total sample size or study costs. Furthermore, we illustrate these derived designs by applying them to two distinct real-world datasets from experimental economics.

This study evaluates the perceptual tolerance for audio-video desynchronization in sports footage. It involved 20 participants who assessed 45 videos created by introducing eight distinct audio-video offsets across five source clips. Findings indicate that humans detect offset errors more readily in speech than in the complex events typical of sports broadcasts, which possess higher thresholds for acceptability. Consequently, this supports the need to tailor audio-video synchronization standards to the specific content being broadcast.

As part of the SRG/eROSITA telescope's performance verification, the eROSITA Final Equatorial-Depth Survey (eFEDS) was executed. This survey covers a 140 deg$^2$ region spanning 126$^\circ <$ R.A. $< 146^\circ$ and -3$^\circ <$ Dec. $< +6^\circ$, with a nominal exposure time of 2.2 ks. Within this area, 542 candidate clusters were identified, detectable down to an X-ray flux limit of approximately $10^{-14}$ erg s$^{-1}$ cm$^{-2}$ in the 0.5-2 keV band. To investigate radio-mode feedback within galaxy clusters, we examined the radio emissions of the Brightest Cluster Galaxies (BCGs) in the eFEDS sample and correlated them with the host clusters' X-ray characteristics. Utilizing LOFAR, we detected 227 radio galaxies residing in the BCGs of the 542 clusters and groups, treating non-detections as upper limits. Our analysis of these radio galaxies included their redshifts, luminosity distributions, offsets from cluster centers, largest linear sizes, and radio powers, alongside an examination of their relationship with the intracluster medium (ICM). We applied statistical methods to account for radio luminosity upper limits. Our findings indicate that BCGs hosting radio-loud active galactic nuclei (AGN) are more centrally located than those with radio-quiet AGN. A significant correlation exists between a cluster's X-ray luminosity and the radio power of its BCG, which statistical tests confirm is not an artifact of radio selection effects. However, no clear connection was found between a radio galaxy's largest linear size and the host cluster's central density. When converting radio luminosity to kinetic luminosity, we determined that the heating supplied by central AGN generally balances the radiative losses of the ICM. Furthermore, after tentatively categorizing the objects as either disturbed or relaxed, we demonstrated that the link between AGN activity and the ICM persists regardless of the cluster's dynamical state.

The rising sophistication and proliferation of threat actors, combined with the rapid velocity of cyberattacks, make the timely detection of such incidents critical for organizational security. As a result, security professionals utilize a wide array of information sources regarding emerging threats, attacker behaviors, and indicators of compromise. Nevertheless, a significant portion of this essential security data exists in unstructured text formats, which hinders the automated and prompt extraction of attackers' Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures (TTPs). To tackle this challenge, we systematically evaluate and compare various Natural Language Processing (NLP) and machine learning approaches for security information extraction in existing research. Based on these findings, we propose a data processing pipeline that automatically categorizes unstructured text according to attacker tactics and techniques, utilizing a knowledge base derived from adversary TTP frameworks.

This paper investigates two Schur complement-based preconditioners designed for twofold and block tridiagonal saddle point problems: one utilizing a nested (or recursive) Schur complement, and the other employing an additive Schur complement following the permutation of the original system. We examine various preconditioners that incorporate exact Schur complements, demonstrating that certain approaches yield positive stable preconditioned systems. These findings offer valuable insights for constructing both exact and inexact preconditioners, as well as iterative solvers, for numerous twofold and block tridiagonal saddle point problems. Furthermore, numerical experiments on a 3-field formulation of the Biot model are presented to validate the theoretical results.

Focusing on the seq2seq framework of TranX for translating natural language into code, we pinpoint four critical elements: grammatical constraints, lexical preprocessing, input representations, and copy mechanisms. To evaluate the influence of these factors, we employ a leading architecture featuring a BERT encoder and a grammar-based decoder, for which a formal specification exists. The study underscores the significance of lexical substitution within existing natural language-to-code systems.

Standard textbooks typically introduce black-body radiation by progressing from the Rayleigh-Jeans law to Max Planck's solution, a sequence that diverges from the actual historical development of the field. The authors argue that presenting the ideas in their true chronological order—rather than a logically structured narrative—offers significant value for both the history of science and pedagogy. Consequently, this work aims to provide a concise historical account of this fascinating area of science.

This work examines the simplicity of map-germs resulting from augmentation and outlines methods for constructing their versal unfoldings. We provide a complete characterization of simplicity when the augmentation originates from an $\mathscr{A}_e$-codimension 1 germ or when the augmenting function is Morse. These characterizations encompass all simple augmentations identified in existing classifications of $\mathscr{A}$-simple monogerms, with the sole exception of the $F_4$ case in Mond's list mapping from $\mathbb{C}^2$ to $\mathbb{C}^3$. Furthermore, leveraging our findings, we generate a list of simple augmentations from $\mathbb{C}^4$ to $\mathbb{C}^4$.

Although Distributionally Robust Optimization (DRO) solutions can occasionally outperform Sample Average Approximation (SAA) in terms of out-of-sample expected rewards, such improvements are not guaranteed. This paper presents the class of Distributionally Optimistic Optimization (DOO) models, demonstrating that it is always feasible to surpass SAA performance out-of-sample by incorporating not only worst-case (DRO) scenarios but also best-case (DOO) scenarios. However, this advantage entails a trade-off: optimistic solutions exhibit greater sensitivity to model errors compared to both worst-case and SAA optimizers, thereby reducing their robustness.

Probabilistic numerical methods for solving ordinary differential equations (ODEs) have become a powerful approach for performing inference and uncertainty quantification within dynamical systems. This study elucidates the underlying mathematical assumptions and implementation strategies required to address high-dimensional ODEs using probabilistic algorithms. Previously, such tasks were infeasible due to the computational cost of matrix-matrix operations at each step; however, this capability is essential for scientifically significant applications, particularly when solving discretized partial differential equations. Essentially, efficient solutions for high-dimensional probabilistic ODEs rely on either independence assumptions or Kronecker structure within the prior model. We assess the performance of these methods across various problems, including the probabilistic simulation of a differential equation involving millions of dimensions.

Strange metals frequently emerge near quantum critical points (QCPs) within diverse strongly correlated systems. Key questions in this field involve the mechanism by which the quantum critical state eliminates quasiparticles, its role in inducing superconductivity, and the degree to which strange-metal phenomena across different correlated material classes are interconnected. This article addresses these challenges through the lens of heavy fermion metals. We outline the concept of Kondo destruction, explaining how it triggers a Fermi surface transition from "large" to "small" across the QCP, results in a universal loss of quasiparticles at the critical point, and produces dynamical Planckian scaling in various properties, including charge responses. Finally, we conclude with a concise examination of the relationships between strange-metal behavior in heavy fermion metals and similar phenomena observed in cuprates and other correlated materials.

We establish a result regarding the generic exactness of supersymmetry in three dimensions and outline a mechanism for F-term spontaneous breaking of 3-D SUSY, utilizing a distinct set of tools compared to O'Raifeartaigh's foundational work on 4-D SUSY. Our approach employs techniques from projective algebraic geometry to effectively address cubic hypersurfaces.

We demonstrate that the spaces of closed finite gap curves in ${\mathbb R}^3$ and ${\mathbb S}^3$ are dense in the spaces of closed curves within those respective manifolds, when measured by the Sobolev $W^{2,2}$-norm.

Transit missions like Kepler and TESS have proven that planets are common, yet their achievements rely heavily on ground-based radial velocity (RV) surveys to determine bulk densities and orbital characteristics alongside transit data. Although many Kepler host stars are too dim for detailed follow-up, TESS has identified planets around nearby bright stars suitable for RV analysis. This paper introduces the TESS-Keck Survey (TKS), an RV initiative utilizing approximately 100 nights on the Keck/HIRES telescope to study TESS-discovered exoplanets. The survey's main goals include exploring the relationship between stellar properties and the composition of small planets, examining how system architectures vary with dynamical configurations or planet multiplicity, pinpointing prime targets for JWST atmospheric studies, and understanding how stellar evolution influences planetary systems. We present a fully automated target selection algorithm that identified 103 planets in 86 systems for the final TKS sample. The majority of TKS hosts are inactive, solar-like main-sequence stars with effective temperatures between 4500 K and 6000 K, spanning a broad range of metallicities. The selected sample features 71 small planets (Rp < 4 Re), 11 systems with multiple transiting candidates, 6 sub-day period planets, and 3 planets located in or near their host stars' habitable zones. This selection strategy will enable comparisons between measured planetary masses, densities, and eccentricities and predictions from population models. Our target selection software is publicly available at https://github.com/ashleychontos/sort-a-survey and can be customized for any survey requiring a balanced approach to multiple scientific objectives within a specific telescope allocation.

The Open Images Dataset comprises roughly 9 million images and serves as a standard benchmark for computer vision research. Consistent with large-scale datasets, its annotations are partial, providing bounding boxes and attribute labels for only a subset of classes within each image. This paper introduces a new annotation set for a specific portion of the Open Images dataset, termed the MIAP (More Inclusive Annotations for People) subset, which includes bounding boxes and attributes for every person visible in the selected images. The MIAP annotation methodology was specifically crafted to facilitate research on model fairness. Furthermore, we examine the original annotation approach for the person class and its subclasses, analyzing emerging patterns to guide future annotation strategies. By utilizing both the original and our exhaustive annotation sets, researchers can now investigate how systematic biases in training labels influence model performance.

Temporary forks represent a core characteristic of proof-of-work blockchains, and their analysis has recently garnered significant interest. Unlike prior research that concentrates on system-level variables like block size, network latency, or block generation rates, this paper investigates a novel dimension: the competition for computing power among miners. We first introduce a comprehensive mathematical model to quantify how mining pool competition influences temporary forks. Furthermore, we derive closed-form equations for the probability of temporary forks and the anticipated mining rewards for individual pools. To uncover long-term trends in computing power distribution across competing pools, we establish an evolutionary game framework grounded in our fork model to identify stable equilibrium sets. Finally, extensive numerical simulations and evaluations using real blockchain data validate our theoretical models and findings.

Voiculescu's concept of freeness arises when analyzing the asymptotic spectral behavior of polynomials on $N\times N$ random matrices whose eigenspaces are in generic positions; specifically, these matrices are randomly rotated using a uniform unitary random matrix $U_N$. This article expands on that idea by introducing a new random matrix model called the Vortex model, in which $U_N$ follows the distribution of a uniform unitary random matrix conditioned to preserve a single deterministic vector $v_N$. As $N$ approaches infinity, we demonstrate that matrices randomly rotated by $U_N$ become asymptotically conditionally free with respect to the normalized trace and the state vector $v_N$. To characterize second-order asymptotics, we introduce "cyclic-conditional freeness," a novel notion of independence that unifies infinitesimal freeness, cyclic-monotone independence, and cyclic-Boolean independence. Leveraging this new framework, we compute the infinitesimal distribution within the Vortex model. Furthermore, we extend the Vortex model to construct random matrix models representing ordered freeness and indented independence.

Reasoning about sequential events naturally invites probabilistic inquiries like predicting the next occurrence of an event or calculating the likelihood of one event preceding another, with relevance to fields including finance, medicine, and user modeling. Despite the rise of neural autoregressive architectures such as transformers and RNNs, the ability to perform such queries has remained limited primarily to simple next-token prediction. This constraint stems from the difficulty of efficiently marginalizing over vast path spaces required for future querying within these models. This paper proposes a comprehensive typology for predictive queries in neural autoregressive sequence models, demonstrating that they can be systematically decomposed into elementary components. Utilizing this framework, we develop novel query estimation techniques leveraging beam search, importance sampling, and hybrid approaches. Evaluated across four extensive datasets from diverse domains and the GPT-2 language model, we show that answering arbitrary queries within exponentially large predictive path spaces becomes tractable, while also identifying distinct cost-accuracy trade-offs between search-based and sampling-based methods.

We report lattice QCD calculations of the scalar, vector, and tensor form factors for $B\to K\ell^+\ell^-$ decays, covering the complete physical spectrum of momentum transfer. Our analysis employs the highly improved staggered quark (HISQ) formalism for all valence quarks across eight gluon field configurations provided by the MILC collaboration. These ensembles feature four flavors of HISQ quarks in the sea, with three sets utilizing physical masses for the light $u/d$ quarks. In this first fully relativistic determination of these form factors, we apply the heavy-HISQ method, enabling us to derive the form factors as a function of heavy quark mass from charm to bottom. Consequently, we also present new results for the $D\to K$ tensor form factor. The primary benefit of this relativistic approach is the enhanced accuracy in matching lattice weak currents to their continuum equivalents compared to prior studies: our scalar and vector currents are renormalized fully nonperturbatively, while a well-matched intermediate momentum-subtraction scheme is utilized for the tensor current. The uncertainties for our scalar and vector $B\to K$ form factors remain below 4% throughout the entire physical $q^2$ range, with the tensor form factor uncertainty under 7%. Furthermore, the heavy-HISQ method facilitates an examination of the heavy-quark mass dependence of the form factors, and by comparing with earlier HPQCD results for the same weak transition but involving heavier mesons, we can assess the impact of varying spectator quark masses.

Effective teamwork relies fundamentally on clear communication. As groups interact, they cultivate distinct communication patterns, frequently demonstrating entrainment, where individuals synchronize their linguistic choices. This study investigates predicting team performance using embeddings derived from multiparty dialogues, aiming to position teams with comparable conflict levels closely together within a vector space. The analysis incorporates embeddings based on three feature types: dialogue acts, sentiment polarity, and syntactic entrainment. While all three features can successfully forecast performance, their effectiveness shifts depending on the stage of the collaboration. We segmented dialogues from a cooperative game into three phases: early (knowledge building), middle (problem-solving), and late (culmination). Contrary to syntactic entrainment, embeddings based on dialogue acts and sentiment polarity prove effective for classifying performance even in the initial stage. These insights hold significant implications for creating conversational agents designed to enhance team collaboration.

A theoretical framework is introduced that unifies the complete Standard Model (SM) field content into a solitary superfield. This model features an $E_8$ gauge group and simple supersymmetry within a 10-dimensional spacetime. By orbifolding the extra dimensions, the model simultaneously breaks supersymmetry and reduces the gauge symmetry to that of the Standard Model. At low energies, the theory retains only the SM fields with viable unified Yukawa couplings. Unification occurs at low energy scales ($10^{6-9}\ \rm{GeV}$) while maintaining controlled proton decay.

This work evaluates the performance of Orthogonal Time Frequency Space (OTFS) modulation within cell-free massive MIMO systems. By exploiting the sparsity inherent in the delay-Doppler (DD) domain representation of time-varying channels, we utilize an embedded pilot-aided channel estimation technique that employs reduced guard intervals. This approach enables the derivation of the minimum mean-square error (MMSE) estimate for channel gains using uplink pilots received at access points (APs), where each AP subsequently applies conjugate beamforming for data transmission. We present a closed-form expression for individual user downlink throughput, dependent on the counts of APs, users, and DD channel estimation parameters. A comparison between OTFS and Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiplexing (OFDM) under high-mobility conditions reveals that, in scenarios with uncorrelated shadowing, cell-free massive MIMO using OTFS achieves up to a 35% improvement in 95%-likely per-user throughput relative to OFDM. Furthermore, the enhancement in per-user throughput is significantly more evident at median rates when correlated shadowing is present.

This paper introduces a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) model designed to interpolate irregularly distributed measurements across the spatial domain, creating a smooth radio frequency map (RFMap) for subsequent localization via a deep neural network. Monitoring wireless spectrum across spatial, temporal, and frequency dimensions is becoming essential for enabling dynamic spectrum access (DSA) in beyond-5G and 6G systems. Distributed spectrum sensing is pivotal for applications such as localization, wireless signal detection, and spectrum policy formulation, yet detecting and positioning emitters remains a significant challenge over large spectral and spatial areas. Building a high-quality RFMap database typically demands extensive measurements that are costly and time-intensive. A practical solution involves collecting finite localized measurements and interpolating them to build the database. While existing literature relies on channel modeling for RFMap construction—which often lacks the granularity required for precise localization—our proposed method generates a generalized RFMap. We present localization results and compare them against conventional channel models.

Galactic flat rotation curves represent a key astrophysical puzzle requiring gravitational acceleration beyond what Newtonian physics predicts for observed baryonic matter. The primary explanations are either the presence of unseen dark matter or a modification to Newtonian gravity at low accelerations, termed Milgromian dynamics (MOND). Wide binary stars near the Sun offer a direct test for MOND, as these systems are expected to contain negligible dark matter relative to the Galaxy's total content. Under MOND, such binaries should orbit approximately 20% faster than predicted by Newtonian dynamics. This paper outlines a detailed strategy for executing this test, with particular attention to computationally intensive phases. We estimate the memory and processing requirements for these stages. Our conclusion is that the critical cost function can be evaluated deterministically in just a few seconds, enabling the calculation of a model's absolute binomial likelihood. This efficiency allows the cost function to be integrated into a Markov Chain Monte Carlo sampler or a more economical gradient descent method to identify optimal model parameters. Consequently, the wide binary test is deemed feasible with existing technology.

Slot filling is a core component of dialog state tracking within task-oriented dialog systems. In multi-domain settings, both user inputs and system replies often contain multiple named entities and attribute values, requiring the system to identify user-confirmed information and populate the corresponding slots. A primary challenge arises because deep models like BERT struggle with limited input token capacity and GPU memory when processing all tokens across multiple turns of a dialogue session. This paper proposes an ontology-enhanced method that matches named entities from all dialogue turns using an ontology. These matched entities from prior turns are accumulated and encoded as supplementary inputs for a BERT-based dialog state tracker. Furthermore, our approach incorporates ontology constraint validation and refines slot name tokenization. Experimental results on the MultiWOZ 2.1 dataset demonstrate that our ontology-enhanced tracker increases joint goal accuracy (slot F1) from 52.63% (91.64%) to 53.91% (92%).

We present our system for the DSL 2016 shared task, which focuses on distinguishing between similar languages. Our approach, called ResIdent, relies exclusively on byte representations within a deep residual network (ResNet) and was trained solely on the task-provided data using a closed training setup. The system achieved 84.88% accuracy on subtask A, 68.80% on subtask B1, and 69.80% on subtask B2. We observed a significant gap between development and test accuracy despite only minor adjustments to the network's architecture and hyperparameters; consequently, we anticipate that fine-tuning these parameters will result in improved performance.

We present measurements of heating in silica nanospheres levitated within a vacuum by thermal light generated from a superluminescent diode. We quantified the heating of the spheres' motion along all three trap axes across varying gas pressures and for two distinct particle sizes. Furthermore, we compared these heating rates to the significantly lower reheating observed when the same spheres were levitated by a laser. Our findings indicate that the measured trap heating rates are primarily driven by the substantially higher heating rates predicted from the recoil of thermal photons.

The legal domain has significantly advanced through the adoption of Transformer-based Pre-trained Language Models (PLMs) trained specifically on legal corpora. While existing models like LegalBERT are based on European and US texts, the surge in NLP applications for Indian legal documents, combined with the unique features of such texts, necessitates the development of models pre-trained on Indian data. This study presents Transformer-based PLMs trained on a substantial corpus of Indian legal documents. We evaluate these models across various benchmark legal NLP tasks, utilizing both Indian legal texts and datasets from other jurisdictions. The experimental tasks include identifying legal statutes from facts, performing semantic segmentation on court judgments, and predicting court judgment outcomes. Our results highlight the effectiveness of these India-specific PLMs.

This correspondence addresses power control within an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) system designed for ultra-reliable and low-latency communications (URLLC), featuring deep neural network (DNN)-based channel estimation. Specifically, the power control issue is framed as an optimization problem that satisfies URLLC demands for uplink control and non-payload signaling while guaranteeing high-speed downlink payload transmission. This task is difficult to solve due to the necessity of analytically tractable channel models and the inherent non-convexity of the problem. To overcome these obstacles, we introduce a new power control algorithm that builds analytically tractable channel models using DNN estimation outcomes and employs a semidefinite relaxation (SDR) approach to handle non-convexity. Simulation outcomes confirm the precision of the DNN estimation and validate the efficacy of the proposed algorithm.

The Lunar Lander Neutron and Dosimetry (LND) experiment, installed on the far side of the Moon aboard the Chang'e-4 lander, detects energetic neutral and charged particles while monitoring associated radiation levels. During periods of solar quiet, galactic cosmic rays (GCRs) constitute the primary component of charged particles at the lunar surface. Additionally, LND measures upward-directed albedo protons generated by the interaction of GCRs with the lunar regolith. This study utilizes calibrated LND data to analyze both primary GCRs and albedo protons. Specifically, we computed the average GCR proton spectrum ranging from 9 to 368 MeV and the average albedo proton flux between 64.7 and 76.7 MeV for the period spanning from June 2019 (the 7th lunar day post-landing) to July 2020 (the 20th lunar day). A comparison between LND's primary proton measurements and those from the Electron Proton Helium INstrument (EPHIN) on SOHO reveals reasonable consistency in GCR proton spectra across different instruments, thereby demonstrating LND's effectiveness. Similarly, LND's albedo proton data align well with measurements from the Cosmic Ray Telescope for the Effects of Radiation (CRaTER) taken during solar minimum. Our findings corroborate predictions made by the Radiation Environment and Dose at the Moon (REDMoon) model. Furthermore, we present the ratio of albedo protons to primary protons for the 64.7–76.7 MeV energy range, which supports simulations conducted over a wider spectrum.

Model-based reinforcement learning (RL) typically demonstrates superior sample efficiency compared to model-free RL by training a dynamics model to synthesize samples for policy optimization. While prior research has focused on learning a "global" dynamics model to approximate the state-action visitation distribution across all historical policies, this study reveals that such an approach does not inherently benefit model predictions for the current policy, as policies continuously evolve during training. This evolution induces shifts in the state-action visitation distribution. We provide a theoretical analysis of how the distribution of historical policies influences model learning and rollouts. Consequently, we introduce a novel model-based RL framework called \textit{Policy-adaptation Model-based Actor-Critic (PMAC)}, which employs a policy-adaptation mechanism to learn a dynamics model tailored to the evolving policy. This mechanism dynamically adjusts the mixture distribution of historical policies, ensuring the learned model remains aligned with the state-action visitation distribution of the current policy. Experimental results across various continuous control environments in MuJoCo indicate that PMAC achieves state-of-the-art asymptotic performance and exhibits nearly double the sample efficiency of previous model-based methods.

This study introduces two rational expectation models featuring heterogeneous arbitrageurs and positive feedback mechanisms that generate self-reinforcing, transient stochastic price dynamics accelerating faster than exponentially. These nonlinear feedbacks result in bubble termination marked by a finite-time singularity within the price formation process, concluding at a specific critical time $\tilde{t}_c$ and transitioning into mean-reversing stationary dynamics. Due to the diversity in rational agents' expectations, a synchronization issue arises regarding the optimal exit times of arbitrageurs, enabling the bubble to persist nearly until its theoretical conclusion. The models yield explicit, exact analytical solutions that define nonlinear transformations, facilitating new tests to detect bubbles in financial time series. By circumventing the complexities of parameter estimation for the stochastic differential equations governing price dynamics, these operational procedures allow for the diagnosis of emerging bubbles and the forecasting of their collapse. Empirical tests conducted on the US S&P500 (1980–2008), the US NASDAQ composite (1980–2008), and the Hong Kong Hang Seng index (1986–2008) indicate the viability of early warning systems for bubbles.

We introduce a graph generative adversarial network designed to create sparse datasets comparable to those from the CERN Large Hadron Collider (LHC). This method is validated by training on and producing sparse representations of MNIST handwritten digits and particle jets resulting from proton-proton collisions, similar to LHC events. The model effectively generates both sparse MNIST digits and particle jet data. To assess the similarity between real and synthetic data, we employ a graph-based Fréchet Inception distance for the MNIST dataset and a particle and jet feature-level 1-Wasserstein distance for the jet dataset.

This paper introduces TradeChain, a privacy-preserving framework that separates participant trade events through decentralized identities. Grounded in Self-Sovereign Identity (SSI) principles, TradeChain offers three key innovations: first, it utilizes two distinct permissioned blockchains—one for identity management and another for tracking trade flows; second, it employs Zero Knowledge Proofs (ZKPs) on private credentials to authenticate multiple identities on the trade ledger; and third, it enables data owners to establish dynamic access rules for verifying traceability data via access tokens and Ciphertext Policy Attribute-Based Encryption (CP-ABE). A proof-of-concept deployment on Hyperledger Indy and Fabric demonstrates that the system incurs minimal overheads, as confirmed by comprehensive evaluations of execution time, latency, and throughput.

Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) have recently proven highly effective for processing non-Euclidean data. While existing research utilizes deeper layers in Euclidean structures to extract advanced features, applying excessively deep GCNs to non-Euclidean data leads to issues such as "neighbor explosion" and "over-smoothing," and hinders scalability on large datasets. To overcome these challenges, we introduce PathSAGE, a model designed to capture high-order topological information and enhance performance by expanding the receptive field. PathSAGE randomly samples paths originating from a central node and aggregates them using a Transformer encoder. By employing a single-layer architecture for node aggregation, the model avoids the aforementioned pitfalls. Evaluation results demonstrate that PathSAGE achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art models in inductive learning tasks.

We report next-to-leading order QCD calculations for Higgs boson production through gluon-gluon fusion accompanied by one or two extra jets. The H+jet computation incorporates the top-quark mass exactly, while the H+2jets calculation approximates two-loop virtual amplitudes using a reweighting of leading-order mass effects, retaining full top-quark mass dependence in real radiation terms. This work on H+jet production corrects an error found in prior studies and provides updated total and differential cross sections. Furthermore, we compare QCD corrections against the infinite top-mass limit, observing excellent agreement when all amplitudes are scaled by their leading-order mass dependence.

Although temperature influences the timing and results of animal development, the specific effects on early developmental stages remain poorly understood. To investigate how temperature impacts the sequence and duration of events during *Drosophila melanogaster* embryogenesis, researchers utilized time-lapse imaging to monitor embryos from shortly after egg-laying until hatching across seven precisely controlled temperatures ranging from 17.5°C to 32.5°C. By combining automated and manual annotation, they identified the timing of 36 distinct milestones. *D. melanogaster* embryogenesis lasts approximately 33 hours at 17.5°C, accelerating to 16 hours at 27.5°C, after which the rate slows slightly. Remarkably, despite a two-fold variation in total duration, the relative timing of events from cellularization through hatching remains constant regardless of temperature. Expanding the study to ten additional *Drosophila* species with diverse climatic origins revealed further patterns: six tropical species exhibited similar temperature-dependent development times. *D. mojavensis*, a sub-tropical species, developed more slowly than tropical flies at lower temperatures, whereas the temperate *D. virilis* showed slower development across all temperatures. The alpine species *D. persimilis* and *D. pseudoobscura* developed as quickly as tropical flies in cooler conditions but showed reduced acceleration above 22.5°C and drastically slowed development by 30°C. Despite total embryogenesis times varying from 13 hours (*D. erecta* at 30°C) to 46 hours (*D. virilis* at 17.5°C), the relative timing of events from cellularization through hatching remained constant across all species and temperatures, indicating the presence of a universal timer governing embryogenesis.

Within quantum information science, highly nonlinear regimes capable of supporting solitons remain only marginally explored. Despite their potential to function as entanglement sources or self-organized quantum processors, general methodologies for quantum solitons are currently lacking. To address this, we introduce a computational framework employing a neural network as a variational ansatz for quantum solitons within waveguide arrays. Through training a resulting phase-space quantum machine learning model, we identify diverse soliton solutions by adjusting particle counts and interaction strengths. We utilize Gaussian states to quantify entanglement levels and sample probability distributions for many-particle events. Furthermore, we calculate the probability of particle pair generation and reveal that soliton bound states emit correlated pairs. These findings hold significance for boson sampling in nonlinear systems and the development of quantum processors utilizing entangled nonlinear waves.

At finite temperatures, the Geodesic rule posits that a field along a linear segment of correlation length should trace the shortest path in field space between two endpoints. This study calculates the probability that field variations over correlation-length distances adhere to this rule within theories possessing $O(2)$ global symmetry, specifically examining a ferromagnetic $O(2)$ spin model and a complex $\phi^4$ theory. Utilizing Monte Carlo simulations to generate equilibrium configurations at finite temperatures, the numerical findings indicate a substantial deviation from the Geodesic rule at temperatures pertinent to investigating topological defect formation during second-order phase transitions. Furthermore, the research analyzes the equilibrium density and distribution of vortices in two-dimensional $O(2)$ spins, comparing these results against the Kibble-Zurek Mechanism for defect formation.

Utilizing nucleons and antinucleons derived from the quark combination model at kinetic freeze-out, we investigate the formation of light nuclei and antinuclei via the (anti-)nucleon coalescence mechanism in relativistic heavy ion collisions. We establish analytic expressions for the momentum distributions of various light nuclei, employing them to calculate transverse momentum ($p_T$) spectra for (anti-)deuterons ($d$, $\bar d$) and (anti-)tritons ($t$, $\bar t$) in Au-Au collisions across center-of-mass energies ranging from 7.7 to 54.4 GeV. Our analysis demonstrates that existing experimental data for these $p_T$ spectra are accurately reproduced. Furthermore, we examine the yields and yield ratios of different light (anti-)nuclei, offering a natural explanation for their observed energy-dependent behaviors. Notably, we emphasize that the multi-particle yield ratio $tp/d^2$ requires careful correction for hyperon weak decay effects on protons to effectively probe light nucleus production characteristics.
