Overall, our findings indicate that the coalescence mechanism is the dominant process for generating light nuclei and antinuclei at the beam energies scanned at RHIC.

We introduce a Poisson geometric framework designed to investigate the representation theory of contragredient quantum super groups at roots of unity. This study is conducted uniformly by examining the quantum doubles of the bozonizations of all distinguished pre-Nichols algebras (referenced in arXiv:1405.6681) within a specific one-parameter family; we designate these as \emph{large} quantum groups. We demonstrate that each of these quantum algebras possesses a central Hopf subalgebra that generates a Poisson order, as defined in arXiv:math/0201042. Furthermore, we explicitly characterize the underlying Poisson algebraic groups and Poisson homogeneous spaces using Borel subgroups of complex semisimple algebraic groups of adjoint type. The geometry of these structures and their implications for the irreducible representations of the algebras $U_{\mathfrak{q}} \supset U_{\mathfrak{q}}^{\geqslant} \supset U_{\mathfrak{q}}^+$ are also detailed.

Beyond encompassing the multiparameter big quantum groups of De Concini--Kac--Procesi and big quantum super groups at roots of unity, our framework also includes characteristic 0 quantizations of the 34-dimensional Kac-Weisfeler Lie algebras (in characteristic 2) and the 10-dimensional Brown Lie algebras (in characteristic 3). Previous methods for these problems depended on reducing to rank two cases and computing Poisson brackets directly, an approach that fails in the super case due to 13 distinct types of additional Serre relations involving up to 4 generators. Instead, we employ a novel method based on perfect pairings between restricted and non-restricted integral forms.

We examine a one-dimensional diffusion process with continuous coefficients that is positive recurrent, proving stable central limit theorems for a specific class of its additive functionals. Specifically, we identify explicit criteria for these functionals such that their long-term fluctuations mimic an $\alpha$-stable process for $\alpha\in(0,2]$.

A wide range of robotics challenges, including motion planning and object manipulation, can be formulated as mixed-integer convex programs (MICPs). Nevertheless, current state-of-the-art algorithms fail to solve MICPs for control tasks quickly enough for real-time application, and existing heuristics often yield suboptimal results that may compromise robotic performance. To address this, we adopt data-driven techniques and introduce the Combinatorial Offline, Convex Online (CoCo) algorithm, designed to rapidly identify high-quality solutions for MICPs. CoCo employs a two-stage framework: in the offline phase, a neural network classifier is trained to map problem parameters to a "logical strategy," defined as the discrete variables and relaxed big-M constraints corresponding to the optimal solution. During the online phase, this classifier selects a candidate logical strategy based on new parameters, enabling the original MICP to be solved as a convex optimization problem. Numerical experiments demonstrate that CoCo achieves near-optimal solutions for MICPs in robot planning and control, delivering a 1 to 2 orders of magnitude improvement in solution speed compared to other data-driven methods and solvers.

The ALICE detector at the LHC has investigated $\phi$ meson production in proton-proton collisions within the rapidity range $2.5 < y < 4$ using the dimuon decay channel. This study presents differential cross section measurements (${\rm d}^2\sigma/{\rm d}y {\rm d}p_{\rm T}$) as a function of transverse momentum ($p_{\rm T}$) for center-of-mass energies of 5.02, 8, and 13 TeV, alongside comparisons with previous midrapidity findings. Additionally, cross sections at 5.02 and 13 TeV were analyzed across various rapidity intervals relative to $p_{\rm T}$, and as a function of rapidity across three distinct $p_{\rm T}$ ranges. Results indicate that the $p_{\rm T}$-differential cross section hardens as collision energy increases; however, at a fixed energy, $p_{\rm T}$ spectra soften with higher rapidity, while rapidity distributions become slightly narrower at elevated $p_{\rm T}$. These new data, which extend prior measurements from $\sqrt{s}=2.76$ and 7 TeV, enable the determination of energy dependence for $\phi$ meson production and facilitate comparisons with phenomenological models. Notably, none of the examined models successfully describe the evolution of the cross section with both $p_{\rm T}$ and rapidity across all energy levels.

This research investigates how group dynamics influence the toxicity of Twitter exchanges. First, it analyzes how the presence of others can dilute individual accountability when responding to a toxic direct reply. Second, it assesses whether the toxicity of an initial reply to a harmful tweet sets the tone for subsequent interactions in a conversation. Consequently, the study identifies bystander presence and the tone of early responses as key determinants influencing whether users feel free to post further abusive content. This hypothesis is tested using a random sample of over 156,000 tweets from approximately 9,000 conversations. The analysis draws on social psychological concepts regarding the "bystander effect," which suggests that the presence of observers can significantly alter social interactions. Specifically, if the first response reinforces a divisive atmosphere, it often encourages others to do the same. The findings confirm a bystander effect, demonstrating that a higher number of participants prior to receiving a toxic tweet correlates with fewer non-toxic responses. Furthermore, the study highlights the critical impact of initial reactions; posting a toxic reply immediately after another toxic comment is negatively linked to subsequent non-toxic contributions, thereby driving the conversation toward greater toxicity.

Let $\lambda_k$ represent the $k$-th successive minimum of a lattice $L$. This work investigates the lengths of specific bases within $L$. For a basis $v_1, \dots, v_n$ that is Minkowski-reduced, we demonstrate that $\lvert v_k \rvert^2 \leq \frac{k}{4} \lambda_{k}^2$ holds for $k = 6, 7$, thereby validating a conjecture by Schürmann and achieving the first enhancement of Van der Waerden's classical bound. Furthermore, we present a sequence of lattices where $\lvert v_n \rvert$ is notably longer than the longest vector in a Korkin-Zolotarev reduced basis, thus addressing a query posed by Schürmann. Finally, in an appendix co-authored with Lior Hadassi, we introduce a lattice $L$ exhibiting the unexpected characteristic that any basis including $L$'s shortest vector fails to be the shortest possible basis.

This paper examines geometrical scaling (GS) as it applies to prompt (direct) photons generated in heavy ion collisions. We begin by defining GS and demonstrating its development using charged particles as a case study. Subsequently, we evaluate direct photon measurements from both RHIC and the LHC, revealing that the data corroborate the GS hypothesis when analyzed in terms of participant numbers across various centrality classes. Furthermore, we investigate GS across different energy levels; however, a more comprehensive analysis will require data from at least three distinct energies within a single experiment, alongside results from both large systems (Cu+Cu, Au+Au, Pb+Pb) and small systems (p+p, d+Au, p+Au).

Investigating how high-energy partons lose energy as they traverse the dense medium created in heavy-ion collisions offers a crucial window into understanding the properties of that medium. The Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) detector, equipped with high-resolution calorimeters and a precise silicon tracker, is ideally suited for measuring such hard scattering events. By analyzing data from proton-proton and lead-lead collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 2.76 TeV, researchers observed parton energy loss manifested as a significant imbalance in dijet transverse momentum. To better comprehend the mechanisms behind this energy loss, the study examined how quenched jet energy redistributes by analyzing the transverse momentum balance of charged tracks relative to the leading jet's direction. Unlike in proton-proton collisions, the momentum balance for asymmetric jets in these heavy-ion events is largely carried by low-momentum particles located far from the jet axis. Additionally, reconstructed fragmentation functions for both leading and subleading jets showed no modification compared to proton-proton benchmarks. These findings collectively provide a detailed view of parton propagation within the hot QCD medium.

We investigate the isometry group of the open unit ball within a specific complex Banach space of bounded linear operators, utilizing the Carath\'eodory metric. In doing so, we establish a characterization of normal isometries based on their distinct class of fixed points.

This study presents a two-color formaldehyde planar laser-induced fluorescence (PLIF) thermometry approach utilizing a 355 nm wavelength-switching, injection-seeded Nd:YAG laser. By targeting the formaldehyde peaks at 28183.5 cm⁻¹ and 28184.5 cm⁻¹, the method measures temperatures within low-temperature combustion regions. Employing a burst-mode amplifier and a high-speed camera, the system achieves high-repetition rate (20 kHz) temperature field measurements. This technique was validated on a laminar coflow diffusion flame and further demonstrated in a turbulent confined jet within a hot crossflow flame.

Mental health continues to be a major global public health issue. As online platforms gain popularity, many individuals use them to disclose their conditions, express emotions, and seek assistance from both communities and counselors. While some platforms, like Reachout, are specialized forums requiring user registration, others, such as Reddit, offer anonymous subreddits for public posts regarding mental distress. Regardless of post length, creating concise yet informative summaries is advantageous for enabling counselors to process content efficiently. To support research in summarizing these online mental health posts, we present the Mental Health Summarization dataset, MentSum. This collection comprises over 24,000 carefully selected user posts from 43 Reddit subreddits, paired with their original English "TLDR" summaries. This domain-specific resource is valuable not only for summarizing Reddit threads but also for dedicated mental health forums like Reachout. Furthermore, we assess state-of-the-art extractive and abstractive summarization baselines using Rouge scores and perform a detailed human evaluation comparing user-written and system-generated summaries, thereby identifying key challenges in this field.

Heatmaps are a widely used geovisualization technique that interpolates point observations across a map surface. While most online web mapping libraries employ a one-pass algorithm utilizing HTML5 canvas or WebGL for efficient generation, these implementations rely on additive operations that accumulate point weights on the map grid. Consequently, they are unsuitable for visualizations requiring the simultaneous highlighting of both low and high weights. We introduce \textit{hilomap}, an online heatmap algorithm designed to emphasize surface areas containing points with both low and high trends. Additionally, an HTML5 Canvas-based reference implementation using OpenLayers is presented and evaluated.

Biological process models are typically realistic yet complex, featuring multi-scale interacting components driven by environmental shifts and intrinsic stochasticity, often rendering them analytically or numerically unsolvable. We re-examine a dynamic maximum entropy approach that merges static maximum entropy with a quasi-stationary approximation. This technique simplifies stochastic non-equilibrium dynamics described by the Fokker-Planck equation into a lower-dimensional deterministic framework, eliminating the necessity to track microscopic details. While this method has previously been applied to a limited number of intricate population genetics cases, our primary objective is to elucidate and deepen the understanding of its operational mechanics. We showcase the method's efficacy in two prominent stochastic problems, emphasizing its precision in capturing key macroscopic quantities even during rapid, non-stationary environmental changes. Specifically, the method retrieves exact dynamics for the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process and maintains high macroscopic accuracy across diverse scenarios for a stochastic island model involving migration under dynamic environmental conditions.

The challenge of detecting magnetic fields via NV centers—specifically determining the presence of weak fields—can be addressed through quantum state discrimination theory. In this context, we identify POVMs that maximize measurement confidence, factoring in both interaction duration and decoherence effects. Our formalism is applied across diverse scenarios, including constant and oscillating magnetic fields, while incorporating techniques like dynamical decoupling to enhance confidence and extending the analysis to NV center ensembles.

This study examines the one-dimensional discrete Schrödinger operator featuring a complex-valued, sparse periodic potential. The spectrum associated with such a potential forms a complex compact set in the complex plane, characterized by the real intersections of algebraic curves defined by a discriminant. By expressing this discriminant through Chebyshev polynomials and analyzing perturbations of the discriminant, we investigate the spectral properties.

This study introduces an automatic music tagging algorithm based on content analysis, utilizing fully convolutional neural networks (FCNs) composed exclusively of 2D convolutional and subsampling layers. Using the MagnaTagATune dataset, we assessed architectures of varying complexities and input types via AUC-ROC scores, identifying a 4-layer model with mel-spectrogram input as achieving state-of-the-art results. Additionally, evaluations on the larger Million Song Dataset revealed that increasing the number of layers in the architectures led to superior performance compared to the 4-layer baseline. These findings indicate that mel-spectrograms serve as an effective time-frequency representation for automatic tagging and that more intricate models leverage additional training data to enhance their capabilities.

This study investigates the pair production of heavy fermionic top partners carrying a charge of 5/3 (X$_{5/3}$) using proton-proton collision data recorded at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV by the CMS detector at the CERN LHC, with an integrated luminosity of 35.9 fb$^{-1}$. Assuming the X$_{5/3}$ quark decays into a top quark and a W boson, the analysis examines both right-handed and left-handed coupling scenarios. The search targets final states containing either same-sign dilepton pairs or single leptons. No statistically significant excess over the predicted standard model background was found. Consequently, 95% confidence level lower limits on the X$_{5/3}$ quark mass are established at 1.33 TeV for right-handed couplings and 1.30 TeV for left-handed couplings, combining results from both the same-sign dilepton and single-lepton channels.

This study presents findings from a search for the rare two-body charmless baryonic decays $B^0 \to p \bar{p}$ and $B_s^0 \to p \bar{p}$. The analysis is based on a data set with an integrated luminosity of 0.9 fb$^{-1}$ from $pp$ collisions recorded by the LHCb experiment at a center-of-mass energy of 7 TeV. An excess of $B^0 \to p \bar{p}$ candidates relative to background expectations is observed with a statistical significance of 3.3 standard deviations, marking the first evidence for a two-body charmless baryonic $B^0$ decay. No significant signal is detected for $B_s^0 \to p \bar{p}$, which improves previous upper limits by three orders of magnitude. Assuming the observed excess represents the signal, the branching fraction intervals at 68.3% confidence level are:
$$ \cal{B}(B^0 \to p \bar{p}) = (1.47 \,^{+0.62}_{-0.51} \,^{+0.35}_{-0.14}) \times 10^{-8} $$
$$ \cal{B}(B_s^0 \to p \bar{p}) = (2.84 \,^{+2.03}_{-1.68} \,^{+0.85}_{-0.18}) \times 10^{-8} $$
where the first uncertainty corresponds to statistical variation and the second to systematic effects.

The chiral anomaly represents a fundamental quantum mechanical effect that is crucial for both particle and condensed matter physics. Within Quantum Electrodynamics (QED), it appears as the violation of chiral symmetry under electromagnetic fields; however, anomalous chiral symmetry breaking can also arise solely from interactions, as seen in one-dimensional interacting systems. This study examines how these two mechanisms interact within interacting Weyl semimetals. By employing Fujikawa's path integral technique, we demonstrate that interactions modify the chiral charge continuity equation, an effect interpretable as incorporating the electric and magnetic fields produced by the interacting quantum matter itself. This phenomenon can be further elucidated through dimensional reduction and a Luttinger liquid framework describing the lowest Landau level. These interactions result in non-linear system responses, specifically an interaction-dependent density response driven by changes in the magnetic field, as well as contributions to the non-equilibrium and inhomogeneous anomalous Hall response, while maintaining the equilibrium value.

To mitigate security risks associated with data storage, software vendors have introduced file-based encryption (FBE) schemes. Although encrypting data-at-rest appears conceptually simple, major mobile device proponents have developed seemingly disparate FBE solutions. Because design choices are often outlined in high-level whitepapers or revealed through low-level source code analysis (for Android) or reverse engineering (for iOS), comparative studies and discussions on their respective strengths remain limited. This paper introduces a formal framework for analyzing file-based encryption systems, with a focus on two leading implementations: those found in Android and Linux, and those in iOS. Our formal model and detailed algorithmic descriptions rely on documentation from various sources, including whitepapers, technical reports, presentations, and blog posts. Leveraging this framework, we evaluate the security of existing key derivation chains and overall system designs under standard symmetric cipher assumptions, such as IND-CPA or INT-CTXT security, within the random-oracle model.

RISC-V represents a relatively recent, open instruction set architecture backed by a robust ecosystem and an official, machine-readable formal specification, making it an ideal candidate for formal-methods research. Nevertheless, we note that various formal-methods initiatives focus on distinct facets of RISC-V, necessitating the simplification, abstraction, approximation, or exclusion of other features. Additionally, differing encoding requirements often compel each project to develop its own formalization from the ground up. Our objective is to uncover shared elements among these projects and model the RISC-V specification as a program containing placeholders, allowing diverse projects to instantiate these gaps according to their specific needs. Implemented in Haskell, our formalization utilizes existing tools rather than introducing new domain-specific ones, distinguishing it from alternative methods. To our knowledge, this is the first RISC-V specification capable of bridging processor-correctness proofs and compiler-correctness proofs, while simultaneously accommodating multiple projects with varying requirements.

Past observations have identified several multi-messenger anomalies, such as spectral hardening or excesses for nuclei and leptons, variations in $\bar p/p$ and B/C ratios, and anisotropic reversal. Additionally, the AMS-02 experiment detected distinct spectral breaks for electrons at 284 GeV and positrons beyond the TeV range. This study explores whether these diverse anomalies stem from a single unified physical framework by employing spatially-dependent propagation (SDP) coupled with a nearby supernova remnant (SNR) source. Given the likelihood of dense molecular clouds (DMCs) surrounding SNRs, secondary particles may be generated through $pp$-collisions or fragmentation between accelerated primary cosmic rays and these clouds. This mechanism successfully reproduces spectral hardening for both primary and secondary particles, as well as the observed B/C and $\bar p/p$ ratios. Due to energy losses associated with an SNR age of 330 kyr, the primary electron spectrum exhibits a characteristic cutoff near 1 TeV, consistent with current measurements. Furthermore, since secondary electrons and positrons derived from charged pions account for only 5% of their parent particles' energy, the positron spectrum shows a cutoff at approximately 250 GeV. Consequently, this unified scenario explains the differing spectral breaks for electrons and positrons alongside other anomalies. Notably, the model also predicts a distinctive spectral break-off for secondary Li, Be, and B nuclei at 5 TV, offering a testable signature. Future observations by the next-generation space experiment HERD are expected to detect these features, thereby validating the proposed model.

This study investigates the $D\bar{D}$, $DD$, $D\bar{D}_s$, $DD_s$, $D_s\bar{D}_s$, and $D_sD_s$ tetraquark molecular states possessing $J^{PC}=0^{++}$ using QCD sum rules. The calculated mass for the $D_s\bar{D}_s$ state, $M_{D_s\bar {D}_s} = 3.98\pm0.10\, \rm{GeV}$, aligns closely with the LHCb experimental measurement of $M_{X(3960)} = 3956 \pm 5\pm 10 \,\rm{MeV}$, thereby supporting the identification of $X(3960)$ as a $D_s^+D_s^-$ molecular state with $J^{PC}=0^{++}$. Building on our prior research into four-quark systems formed by two color-neutral clusters, we have derived the mass spectrum for ground-state hidden-charm and doubly-charm tetraquark molecular states.

This work explores the potential for achieving current rectification in graphene nanoribbons (GNRs). Since physical asymmetry is a prerequisite for rectification, we introduce this asymmetry by incorporating nanopores into the GNR structure, analyzing how varying nanopore configurations influence rectification properties. Our findings indicate that both the shape and orientation of these nanopores are critical and highly sensitive factors determining the extent of current rectification. Furthermore, we examine the explicit dependence of rectification on Fermi energy for a specific nanopore shape, given its pivotal role in achieving significant rectification. Finally, we address the impact of nanopore dimensions and the spatial distribution of electrostatic potential profiles across the GNR. Due to the simplicity of this approach and its promising outcomes, it may offer a novel pathway for inducing current rectification in various materials where selective nanopore formation is feasible.

This study investigates mechanical instability arising from growth in an isotropic circular hyperelastic plate. Using a variational method, consistent two-dimensional governing equations for a plate under general finite strain are established. The compound matrix method is employed to solve these equations for two axisymmetric growth scenarios: purely radial and combined radial-circumferential growth. The impact of growth on the plate's buckling behavior—specifically the critical growth factor and corresponding mode shapes—is examined across various thicknesses. These findings provide a framework for modeling growth-induced deformations in planar soft tissues, such as skin.

This study examines a particular transfer learning method for deep reinforcement learning, specifically designed for scenarios where two tasks share identical internal dynamics but possess different visual representations. We derive a low-dimensional encoding of the environment to capture summarizing abstractions, from which internal dynamics and value functions are subsequently learned. Transfer is achieved by freezing these learned components, thereby reusing the shared low-dimensional embedding space. During the retraining of the encoder for transfer, we observed two key phenomena: (i) local minima can exist with minimal loss but mismatched embedding spaces, leading to suboptimal task performance, and (ii) in the absence of such minima, the encoder converges to the same embedding space in our experiments, enabling fast and efficient transfer compared to training from scratch. These local minima arise from the reduced degrees of freedom in the optimization process due to the frozen models. Furthermore, we found that transfer performance is highly dependent on the base model, as some yield successful transfers while others frequently fail.

This work outlines a rigorous derivation of the density functional through the effective action within the Hohenberg-Kohn framework. By employing the auxiliary field method—which does not require the electric coupling constant $e^2$ to be small—we demonstrate that the loop expansion of the exchange-correlation functional can be reorganized to depend exclusively on Kohn-Sham single-particle orbitals and their corresponding energies.

In the quadratic theory of gravity incorporating a scalar field, exact solutions have been derived for wave-like space-time models exhibiting spatial homogeneity. These solutions facilitate the integration of test particle equations of motion within the Hamilton-Jacobi framework using the separation of variables method, specifically applying Shapovalov spaces of type II. The study determines the specific form of the scalar field and the associated functions embedded in the theory's Lagrangian. Consequently, these exact solutions provide a description for primary gravitational wave disturbances in the Universe.

The International Linear Collider (ILC) is currently being designed in stages, beginning with an initial run of 2 ${\rm ab^{-1}}$ at 250 GeV, followed by subsequent phases to reach the project's full specifications of 4 ${\rm ab^{-1}}$ at 500 GeV. This presentation outlines the potential for precise Higgs boson measurements during the 250 GeV phase. It demonstrates that this initial stage will yield significant insights into Higgs physics, offering unique data unattainable at the Large Hadron Collider, model-independent constraints on critical parameters, and the ability to distinguish between various new physics scenarios.

Reduced quasilinear and gradient-driven nonlinear models, which rely on scale separations to analyze experiments and predict turbulent transport in magnetised plasmas, are evaluated against nonlinear flux-driven models that lack such separations. The study examines two turbulence regimes—those far above threshold and those near marginal stability—using Boltzmann electrons. The accuracy of reduced models depends heavily on their ability to replicate nonlinear fluxes. While reduced models align well with other models above the threshold, they significantly underestimate fluxes near marginality by neglecting mesoscale flow organization and turbulence self-advection. The paper concludes by discussing constructive methods to enhance these reduced models.

This study examines how lossy compression impacts the processing of sensor signals required for detecting anomalies within a system. We formalize the intuitive link between quality degradation at elevated compression levels and the ability to distinguish anomalous behavior from normal operation using information-theoretic metrics. Analytical derivations are performed under a Gaussian framework, potentially extending to asymptotic regimes for the specific signal ranges considered. These theoretical findings are validated against the performance of practical detectors in a simplified scenario, enabling an evaluation of various compression and detector configurations.

We develop a biophysical framework to describe the behavior of lipid vesicles interacting with surfactants. The insertion of surfactant molecules causes membrane solubilization, which reduces the vesicle's surface area while maintaining a nearly constant volume. This process generates a rate-dependent rise in membrane tension, ultimately triggering the formation of a micron-scale pore. Our analysis demonstrates that surfactant-driven solubilization kinetics dictate pore behavior, resulting in either short-lived pores that reseal within a second or long-lived pores that remain open for several minutes. Initially, we validate the model against existing experimental data on pore dynamics. Subsequently, we explore how solubilization rates and membrane characteristics influence pore evolution, constructing a phase diagram to distinguish between short- and long-lived regimes. Furthermore, we analyze sequential pore formation, revealing that cyclic short-lived pores occur at intervals inversely proportional to the solubilization rate. By deriving a theoretical formula for this cycle period, we offer an analytical method to quantify the solubilization rate of lipid vesicles by surfactants. These insights illuminate fundamental biophysical mechanisms enabling simple cell-like structures to maintain integrity under environmental stress and may assist in designing vesicle-based drug delivery systems.

We introduce a novel secure transmission framework designed for uplink multiple-input single-output (MISO) orthogonal-frequency division multiplexing (OFDM) environments facing multiple eavesdroppers. This approach exploits OFDM sub-channel orthogonality to concurrently deliver data and secret key symbols. Specifically, the base station (Bob) and the legitimate user (Alice) exchange secret key symbols via wiretap coding across a subset of sub-channels. Simultaneously, Alice encrypts data symbols using a one-time pad (OTP) cipher with keys drawn from her accumulated secret-key queue, transmitting the encrypted data over the remaining sub-channels to Bob. In scenarios where Alice's key queue is insufficient, she resorts to wiretap coding for data protection. We present both fixed and dynamic sub-channel allocation strategies to partition resources between data and keys. Furthermore, we derive the secrecy outage probability (SOP) and secure throughput for this scheme, while quantifying system security under practical non-Gaussian transmission conditions involving discrete signal constellations. Finally, numerical simulations confirm our theoretical results and assess the influence of various system design parameters.

Systems dependent on the collective actions of decision-makers are susceptible to various adversarial threats. This paper investigates the extent to which a system operator can safeguard performance against such risks, specifically within the framework of graphical coordination games. In this model, network agents select between two conventions to gain benefits from aligning with neighbors, with overall performance evaluated by agent welfare. We evaluate an operator's capacity to counter two distinct attack types: broad attacks, which incentivize all agents, and focused attacks, which compel a specific subset of agents to adhere to a designated convention. As a defense mechanism, the operator employs distributed algorithms to regulate agent decision-making. Our primary contribution delineates the fundamental trade-off an operator faces between security against worst-case broad attacks and exposure to focused attacks. We demonstrate that this trade-off improves substantially when the operator adopts a randomized decision-making process. Ultimately, our findings underscore the design challenges inherent in ensuring the resilience of networked distributed systems.

Quality Estimation (QE) models hold the promise of transforming how machine translation systems are evaluated and potentially trained; however, their widespread adoption is hindered by insufficient robustness. Our findings reveal that even state-of-the-art QE models struggle significantly in Parallel Corpus Mining (PCM) scenarios due to poor generalization on out-of-domain data. To address this, we introduce a framework combining multitask training, data augmentation, and contrastive learning to enhance both performance and robustness. Our approach yields substantial improvements in QE accuracy within the MLQE challenge and demonstrates markedly better resilience in PCM settings. Specifically, we boost PCM accuracy by over 0.80, bringing it to the level of existing state-of-the-art methods that rely on millions of sentence pairs. Notably, our novel low-resource PCM strategy achieves these results using only 7,000 parallel sentences—approximately one-thousandth of the data required by current leaders.

This work investigates the discrete symmetries of the Dirac field within the de Sitter manifold, distinguishing between its expanding and collapsing sectors as potential physical spacetimes. While improper discrete isometries that switch between these sectors hold only mathematical significance, proper isometries that preserve a specific sector possess physical relevance. Focusing on the expanding portion within physical frames, the study examines discrete symmetries arising from proper isometries combined with charge conjugation. It demonstrates that all transformations reversing cosmic time are local and contingent upon a local boost matrix. Consequently, the discrete group for Dirac theory in the de Sitter expanding universe is determined to be of order 16, featuring a multiplication table analogous to that of special relativity. Furthermore, all de Sitter discrete isometries, including the improper ones, are analyzed in conformal frames to provide a comprehensive global perspective on these symmetries, despite their inability to form a larger discrete group with physical implications.

Nucleation typically acts as the rate-limiting stage in the kinetics of numerous self-assembly mechanisms, yet its specific role in DNA-origami self-assembly—which entails both staple strand binding and scaffold strand folding—remains ambiguous. Through Monte Carlo simulations employing a lattice model of DNA origami, we discovered that while certain designs exhibit a nucleation barrier, others do not; furthermore, this barrier vanishes at reduced temperatures, thereby explaining the efficacy of isothermal assembly methods. Our findings indicate that the magnitude of the nucleation barrier is chiefly dictated by the coaxial stacking of adjacent staples on the same helix, a feature that can be tuned through staple design. Engineering a nucleation barrier could enhance assembly yields and optimize timing, whereas removing such a barrier would be crucial for developing rapid molecular sensors capable of folding or unfolding without hysteresis in response to environmental fluctuations.

The evolution of Information Technology has transformed information exchange, creating a demand for digitizing printed documents. Amidst rising fraud in the current era, verification processes utilizing Optical Character Recognition (OCR) and Natural Language Processing (NLP) for ID card extraction have been implemented to prevent account fraud. OCR technology converts images into text, enabling the extraction of data from Indonesian identity cards (KTP) to facilitate easier data entry for service operators. To enhance accuracy, NLP methods are employed to correct the extracted text. Testing on 50 Indonesian ID card images yielded an F-score of 0.78, with an extraction time of 4510 milliseconds per card.

We examine a scenario where experience tickets are distributed via lottery. Agents are organized into groups, and a group achieves success only if its members secure sufficient tickets for all. A lottery is deemed efficient if it maximizes the count of successful groups and fair if it grants every group an equal probability of success. We analyze the efficiency and fairness of current methods and suggest practical alternatives. When agents must identify their group members, a logical approach is the Group Lottery, which randomly orders groups and processes them sequentially. We establish tight bounds on the inefficiency and unfairness of this mechanism and outline modifications to achieve greater fairness. Conversely, if agents can request multiple tickets without revealing group identities, the standard Individual Lottery randomly orders agents and fulfills requests until tickets run out. Since any group member can apply and win, this method can produce outcomes that are both arbitrarily unfair and inefficient. As an alternative, we propose the Weighted Individual Lottery, which biases the processing order against agents making large requests. While multiple winners within a group remain possible, this simple adjustment significantly reduces that likelihood. Consequently, the Weighted Individual Lottery is both approximately fair and efficient, resembling the Group Lottery when the number of agents greatly exceeds the number of tickets.

Divacancy spins in silicon carbide offer qubits with exceptional properties within an industrial semiconductor platform. However, significant gaps remain in understanding the physics of these divacancy point defects, particularly regarding spin relaxation, which has not been fully investigated. This study presents a theoretical analysis of environmental spin-induced relaxation mechanisms for divacancy qubits in 4H-SiC. We identify all critical magnetic field strengths where the longitudinal spin relaxation time ($T_1$) decreases resonantly due to coupling with either nuclear or electron spins. Furthermore, we quantitatively examine the relationship between $T_1$ and both the concentration of point defect spins and the applied magnetic field across key scenarios, deriving an analytical expression. Our results demonstrate that dipolar spin relaxation is a dominant factor in both as-grown and ion-implanted samples, frequently limiting coherence times in 4H-SiC.

This study explores the potential to detect Flavour Changing Neutral Current (FCNC) $tqZ$ couplings through two production mechanisms that result in trilepton signatures: top-antitop pair production ($pp\to t\bar{t}$) where one top decays into a $Z$ boson and a light jet, and anomalous single top production accompanied by a $Z$ boson ($pp\to tZ$). We analyze these channels across several future Large Hadron Collider successors, including the approved High-Luminosity LHC (HL-LHC), the proposed High-Energy LHC (HE-LHC), and the Future Circular Collider in hadron-hadron mode (FCC-hh). By conducting a comprehensive simulation of both signal and relevant Standard Model backgrounds, we derive constraints on the Branching Ratios (BRs) for $t\to qZ$ (where $q=u,c$), specifically targeting the trilepton final state arising from $t\to b W^{+}\to b\ell^{+}\nu_{\ell}$ and $Z\to \ell^{+}\ell^{-}$ decays. Upper limits on these FCNC branching ratios at 95% Confidence Level (CL) are established for the HL-LHC at $\sqrt{s}=14$ TeV with 3 ab$^{-1}$, the HE-LHC at $\sqrt{s}=27$ TeV with 15 ab$^{-1}$, and the FCC-hh at $\sqrt{s}=100$ TeV with 30 ab$^{-1}$.

The Liquid State Machine (LSM) has emerged as a promising framework for neuromorphic and edge computing due to its biological plausibility and low training complexity. Originally conceived as a model of brain computation, the LSM adjusts internal weights without relying on gradient backpropagation, a limitation that typically yields lower performance than multi-layer neural networks. However, recent neuroscience insights reveal that astrocytes—previously overlooked non-neuronal cells—play a crucial role in modulating synaptic plasticity and brain dynamics, guiding networks toward a critical phase transition between order and chaos. Drawing inspiration from this self-tuning mechanism in the brain, we introduce the Neuron-Astrocyte Liquid State Machine (NALSM), which mitigates performance deficits through self-organized near-critical dynamics. Mirroring its biological counterpart, the astrocyte component in NALSM incorporates neuronal activity to deliver global feedback to spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP), thereby self-organizing the system around a critical branching factor linked to the edge of chaos. Our results demonstrate that NALSM attains state-of-the-art accuracy comparable to other LSM approaches, all without requiring data-specific manual tuning. Specifically, NALSM achieved 97.61% accuracy on MNIST, 97.51% on N-MNIST, and 85.84% on Fashion-MNIST, matching the performance of fully-connected multi-layer spiking neural networks trained via backpropagation. These findings indicate that advancing brain-inspired machine learning methods could enable deep learning-level performance while simultaneously supporting robust, energy-efficient neuromorphic computing for edge applications.

This study examines the phase space dynamics of a nonminimally coupled scalar field model across various potentials, including KKLT, Higgs, inverse, and inverse square. Our analysis identifies novel asymptotic regimes and derives a stable de-Sitter solution. Specifically, the KKLT potential fails to yield a stable de-Sitter solution, while the Higgs model meets the de-Sitter criteria but lacks stability in the conventional sense due to a zero eigenvalue. We successfully derive a Hubble constant time derivative of $\dot{H}=0$, an equation of state $w_{\phi}\simeq -1$, a constant scalar field $\phi$, and a positive effective gravitational constant ($G_{eff}>0$)—features absent from our previous research. Consequently, for $F(\phi)R$ coupling where $F(\phi)= 1-\xi\phi^2$, combined with inverse and inverse square potentials, a true stable de-Sitter solution is trivially achieved.

Cross-chain interaction involves communication between distinct blockchains. As the number of blockchains grows, establishing either a single star or a fully connected topology becomes challenging. Unlike legacy networks, blockchain propagation must ensure data validity, making topology design and propagation methods two critical issues that require strict adherence during data transmission. This paper introduces a confirmation-based propagation method to maintain the validity of cross-chain data by sealing transactions synchronized from other chains. Furthermore, we establish that a valid topology necessitates strong connectivity among blockchains and propose several topologies tailored to various connection scenarios. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed methods securely propagate cross-chain data while offering flexible connection options.

This study presents numerical simulations examining the jamming transition of non-spherical particles in a two-dimensional setting. Specifically, we analyze how physical quantities at the jamming point evolve as particle shapes deviate slightly from ideal disks. To ensure computational efficiency, we first derive an analytical expression for the gap function using perturbation theory centered on reference disks. Beginning with perfect disks, we examine the impact of shape deformations introduced by the $n$-th order term of a Fourier series, $\sin(n\theta)$. Our findings demonstrate that various physical metrics—including contact counts, gap distributions, and characteristic frequencies of the vibrational density of states—exhibit power-law scaling with respect to the linear deviation from the reference disks. Crucially, these power-law behaviors remain independent of $n$ and align perfectly with mean-field theories for non-spherical particle jamming. This outcome indicates that mean-field theory applies broadly to nearly spherical particles whose geometries can be described by Fourier series.

Clustering plays a vital role in numerous data mining systems focused on analyzing and exploring diverse datasets. The heterogeneity of data necessitates clustering algorithms that are both precise and stable—meaning they yield deterministic and robust outcomes regardless of input network variations. Furthermore, the prevalence of large-scale datasets in modern systems imposes implicit limits on algorithmic complexity. While current clustering methods offer partial stability by guaranteeing either determinism or robustness, they fail to provide both. To resolve this, we present DAOC, a Deterministic and Agglomerative Overlapping Clustering algorithm. DAOC utilizes a novel Overlap Decomposition technique to deterministically identify fine-grained clusters that capture multiple optimal solutions. Additionally, it employs a new consensus strategy called Mutual Maximal Gain to ensure robustness, enhance result stability, and enable the detection of micro-scale clusters. Empirical evaluations on both synthetic and real-world networks demonstrate that DAOC produces stable clusters that are, on average, 25% more accurate than state-of-the-art deterministic algorithms without requiring parameter tuning. This approach aims to significantly streamline and accelerate data analysis tasks involving iterative processing (requiring determinism) and data fluctuations (requiring robustness), thereby delivering accurate and reproducible results.

Using Hyper Suprime-Cam weak lensing data, we derive mass estimates for 458 galaxy clusters from the redMaPPer SDSS DR8 catalogue by implementing a rapid estimation method based on shear. We apply this technique to determine the weak lensing mass for every cluster in the sample, then constrain the mass-richness relation and the intrinsic scatter between richness and mass. For the full sample with richness $\lambda>20$, we identify a tension in the slope of the mass-richness relation compared to the Dark Energy Survey Year 1 stacked weak lensing analysis. However, when analyzing a restricted subset of clusters with $\lambda>40$, our findings align with the Dark Energy Survey Year 1 results.

This paper practically resolves the problem of describing overgroups of the subsystem subgroup $E(\Delta,R)$ within the Chevalley group $G(\Phi,R)$ over the ring $R$, where $\Phi$ is a simply laced root system and $\Delta$ is a sufficiently large subsystem. Specifically, we introduce objects termed "levels" and demonstrate that for any such overgroup $H$, there exists a unique level $\sigma$ satisfying $E(\sigma)\le H\le \mathrm{Stab}_{G(\Phi,R)}(L_{\max}(\sigma))$. In this context, $E(\sigma)$ denotes an elementary subgroup defined by the level $\sigma$, while $L_{\max}(\sigma)$ represents the associated Lie subalgebra in the Chevalley algebra. Distinct from all prior works, the levels introduced here can be more complex structures than mere nets of ideals.

A frequent challenge in deriving causal conclusions from observational data is that measured covariates often fail to capture all confounding sources, frequently serving only as proxies for latent confounders. While recent studies demonstrate that proxy variables can identify causal effects even when the standard 'no unmeasured confounding' assumption is violated, most of this work focuses solely on total effects, neglecting the analysis of direct and indirect pathways mediated by intermediate variables. This study presents three distinct proximal identification results for natural direct and indirect effects under unmeasured confounding. Furthermore, we establish a semiparametric framework for inferring natural (in)direct effects, yielding locally efficient and multiply robust estimators.

Risk arbitrage, or merger arbitrage, is a recognized investment approach that bets on the outcome of M&A transactions. Accurately forecasting deal outcomes beforehand is crucial for arbitrageurs; misclassifying a deal as completed can lead to significant financial losses from investing in target shares, while incorrect predictions may result in missed profit opportunities. This paper introduces a machine learning and deep learning framework designed to predict takeover success. The process begins with data preprocessing using various ML techniques, including kNN for imputing missing values, PCA for reducing the dimensionality of numerical data, MCA for handling categorical variables, and LSTM autoencoders for generating sentiment scores. To address class imbalance, the study tests different cost functions, evaluation metrics, and oversampling methods. Subsequently, feedforward neural networks are employed to forecast deal outcomes. Preliminary findings suggest that this methodology surpasses benchmark models like logit and weighted logit. Although sentiment scores were integrated using diverse architectures, the results showed minimal performance improvement over the basic feedforward neural network framework. Future research will focus on exploring alternative architectures and conducting comprehensive hyperparameter tuning to optimize the use of sentiment scores.

Superconducting on-chip filter-banks offer a scalable and compact approach for building imaging spectrometers in the millimetre and sub-millimetre wavelength ranges. We introduce a lithographically fabricated superconducting filter design that exhibits high resilience to manufacturing imperfections. By employing a capacitively coupled $\lambda/2$ microstrip resonator to establish a narrow spectral passband ($\lambda/\Delta\lambda = 300$), the output from each spectrometer channel interfaces directly with a Lumped Element Kinetic Inductance Detector (LEKID). Our tolerance analysis confirms that a single realistic fabrication error alters the filter quality factor by less than 11%, and we project a full filter-bank efficiency of 60% once fabrication errors and dielectric loss tangent are factored in.

N132D stands as the most luminous gamma-ray supernova remnant (SNR) within the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC). Utilizing the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) and the Atacama Submillimeter Telescope Experiment, we conducted $^{12}$CO($J$ = 1-0, 3-2) observations targeting this remnant. Our results reveal diffuse CO emission not only at the previously identified southern edge but also within the X-ray shell. With an angular resolution of $5''$ (equivalent to approximately 1 pc at the LMC's distance), ALMA resolved nine distinct molecular clouds. These clouds exhibit typical dimensions and masses of roughly 2.0 pc and 100 $M_\odot$, respectively. Observed CO $J$ = 3-2 / 1-0 intensity ratios exceeding 1.5 toward these clouds indicate shock-heating events. Spatially resolved X-ray spectroscopy demonstrates that thermal X-rays in N132D's center originate both behind and in front of molecular clouds. The lack of a thermal component linked to a forward shock toward one specific cloud along the line of sight to the remnant's center suggests this cloud is shock-engulfed and located on the near side. If hadronic processes dominate the gamma-ray emission, these shock-engulfed clouds likely serve as targets for cosmic rays. We estimate the total energy of cosmic-ray protons accelerated in N132D to be a conservative lower limit of $\sim$0.5-$3.8 \times 10^{49}$ erg, a value comparable to those observed in Galactic gamma-ray SNRs.

Reliable channel estimation is vital for vehicular communication systems because of the doubly-dispersive characteristics of these channels. However, the IEEE 802.11p standard provides an inadequate number of pilots for precise channel tracking, causing conventional estimators to degrade significantly, particularly under high-mobility conditions. Although recent deep learning (DL) approaches have been applied to 802.11p channel estimation, they often struggle with performance drops in extremely high mobility or incur excessive computational costs. This paper addresses these drawbacks by introducing an LSTM-based estimator that utilizes an LSTM unit for channel prediction followed by temporal averaging (TA) to mitigate noise. The study analytically determines the noise reduction ratio, confirming TA's effectiveness in enhancing overall performance. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms recent DL-based estimators while achieving a substantial decrease in computational complexity.

Training segmentation networks typically demands extensive annotated datasets, a significant challenge in medical imaging. Although this limitation exists, data augmentation for brain tumor segmentation remains underutilized. This project evaluates various augmentation strategies—including flipping, rotation, scaling, brightness adjustment, and elastic deformation—applied to a standard 3D U-Net, demonstrating that these methods substantially enhance performance in numerous scenarios. We conclude that brightness adjustment and elastic deformation yield the best results, and that combining multiple techniques offers no additional benefit over using a single method. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/mdciri/3D-augmentation-techniques.

We investigate the quasi-periodic oscillation (QPO) present in the historical light curve of the FSRQ PKS 0405-385, utilizing data from the Fermi LAT spanning August 2008 to November 2021. To detect and characterize the QPO signal within the $\gamma$-ray light curve, we employed four time series analysis methods operating in both frequency and time domains: the Lomb-Scargle periodogram (LSP), the weighted wavelet z-transform (WWZ), REDFIT, and epoch folding. Our findings indicate that PKS 0405-385 exhibits a quasi-periodic behavior of approximately 2.8 years with a significance level of $\sim$4.3$\sigma$ during Fermi's long-term monitoring. Notably, we also conducted QPO analysis on the G-band light curve recorded from October 2014 to October 2021 using LSP and WWZ techniques. The resulting $\sim$4$\sigma$ significance aligns with the periodicity detected in $\gamma$-rays, suggesting that the optical emission may originate from the same electron population responsible for the \gr\ emission. Regarding the potential mechanisms driving this quasi-periodic behavior, either helical motion within a jet or a supermassive black hole binary system offers a viable explanation for the 2.8-year QPO, with relevant parameters having been estimated.

There is increasing attention on analyzing bulk samples containing mixed cell types through cell-type-specific approaches. A fundamental prerequisite for these analyses is the precise estimation of cell-type proportions within the bulk sample. Despite numerous recent methodological proposals, the quantification of uncertainties inherent in these proportion estimates remains underexplored. Neglecting such uncertainties can result in erroneous or overlooked findings in subsequent analyses. This paper presents a flexible statistical deconvolution framework capable of accommodating general, subject-specific covariance structures for bulk gene expressions. Within this framework, we introduce DECALS, a decorrelated constrained least squares method designed to estimate cell-type proportions and their corresponding sampling distributions. Simulation results indicate that while other methods fall short, DECALS accurately quantifies the uncertainty in estimated proportions. Furthermore, applying DECALS to bulk gene expression data from post-mortem brain samples in the ROSMAP and GTEx projects demonstrates that accounting for these uncertainties enhances the accuracy of identifying cell-type-specific differentially expressed genes and transcripts across various subject groups, including comparisons between Alzheimer's disease patients and controls, as well as between males and females.

Rank aggregation seeks to synthesize preference rankings from multiple voters into one consensus order. While this model is valuable for many real-world applications, solving it remains computationally difficult. This paper introduces an efficient hybrid evolutionary ranking algorithm capable of handling both complete and partial rankings. The method incorporates a semantic crossover mechanism utilizing concordant pairs and a late acceptance local search enhanced by an efficient incremental evaluation strategy. Experimental results demonstrate that the algorithm achieves highly competitive performance on benchmark instances when compared to state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, its practical utility is illustrated through its application to label ranking, a significant machine learning task.

We simulated the ground states of quantum harmonic oscillators subjected to either constant forces of varying magnitudes or time-dependent driving forces. Expectation values of position were computed for different combinations of mass, natural angular frequency, and the coupling constant $\lambda$ under both driving conditions. Under constant forcing, the simulations yielded coherent states. The outcomes for both scenarios align almost perfectly with theoretical predictions. To perform these simulations, we implemented the Metropolis algorithm on a discrete time lattice to evaluate the systems' imaginary time path integrals.

This research investigates small perturbations applied to Dirichlet problems involving second-order elliptic equations that degenerate at the boundary. We determine the limiting behavior of the solution as the perturbation vanishes, a result grounded in a specific form of asymptotic self-similarity near the boundary that occurs in generic cases. The final section briefly addresses the stabilization of solutions for corresponding parabolic equations containing a small parameter, where metastability effects emerge, causing the solution's asymptotics to depend on the time scale. Additionally, the last section examines an initial-boundary value problem subject to Neumann boundary conditions.

This study proposes substituting Proportional-Integral and Proportional-Integral-Derivative controllers, which are fundamental to control engineering, with intelligent Proportional-Derivative feedback loops (iPDs) based on model-free control. This perspective is supported by laboratory experiments.

In Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM), high-level landmarks offer the advantage of creating more compact and informative maps compared to conventional point-based landmarks. This study concentrates on parameterizing common geometric primitives, such as points, lines, planes, ellipsoids, cylinders, and cones. We initially introduce a unified representation grounded in quadrics, which yields a consistent and concise formulation. Subsequently, we examine a decomposed quadric model that reveals the symmetric and degenerate characteristics of these primitives. Leveraging this decomposition, we construct geometrically interpretable quadric factors within a graph-SLAM framework. Simulation results indicate that the decomposed approach outperforms baseline parameterizations in terms of efficiency and robustness to observation noise. Furthermore, real-world experiments demonstrate that the proposed back-end framework effectively generates compact and regularized maps.

This study examines the $D_s^+ \to a_0(980)(f_0(980)) e^+ \nu_e$ reactions to investigate the various mechanisms of isospin violation that enable $a_0(980)$ production. We determine that kaon loops constitute one source of isospin violation, as the mass differences between charged and neutral kaons prevent these loops from canceling out. However, we identify the primary source as the isospin breaking within the meson-meson transition $T$ matrices, which encode information regarding low-lying scalar mesons. Consequently, this reaction offers high sensitivity to the intrinsic nature of the $a_0(980)$ and $f_0(980)$ resonances. Our findings align with the current upper limits for $a_0(980)$ production, falling only by a factor of three, suggesting that future experiments with increased statistics will be able to measure the actual reaction rates. These measurements will provide deeper insights into the origin and nature of scalar resonances.

Historically, quantum metrology has centered on the resolution improvements derived from entangling $N$ probes, typically yielding a quadratic enhancement that shifts resolution from the $1/\sqrt{N}$ limit of the central limit theorem to the $1/N$ Heisenberg bound. This work shifts focus to quantum squeezing, establishing a unified framework for squeezing-based metrology. We demonstrate that, analogous to entanglement, a quadratic gain in resolution is generally attainable when comparing squeezed probes against the optimal $N$-probe classical strategy utilizing equivalent energy. Specifically, we quantify the Heisenberg squeezing bound applicable to arbitrary estimation strategies involving squeezing. While our theory encompasses established results in quantum optics and spin squeezing, it relies on the general theory of squeezing and remains valid for any quantum system.

The Clifford group is defined as the quotient of the normalizer of the Weyl-Heisenberg group in dimension $d$ by its center. We demonstrate that when $d$ is composite, the Clifford group fails to constitute a group unitary 2-design. Additionally, we establish that the multipartite Clifford group is not a group unitary 2-design, with the sole exceptions being cases where the local Hilbert space dimensions are a constant prime number. We also elucidate the structure of projective group unitary 2-designs. Specifically, we show that the adjoint action generated by a group unitary 2-design splits into precisely two irreducible components; furthermore, a group qualifies as a unitary 2-design if and only if the character of its associated $U\overline{U}$ representation equals $\sqrt{2}$.

It is established that Abstract State Machines (ASMs) can simulate the step-by-step execution of various machine types, such as Turing machines and RAMs. However, we seek to address two limitations: first, that simulation does not equate to identification, and second, that ASMs designed to simulate specific machine types do not form a natural class within the broader set of ASMs. To resolve this, we adapt Gurevich's concept of ASMs into "Evolving MultiAlgebras" (EMAs) by substituting the syntactic program with a semantic object—a functional that must be simply definable over the static component of the ASM. We demonstrate that natural classes of EMAs map through "literal identifications" to slightly extended versions of standard machine models and grammar models. While these models undergo minor modifications, their fundamental computational approach remains intact, with only certain contingencies adjusted. Consequently, EMAs emerge as the mathematical framework that unifies all sequential computation paradigms.

Grasping the carrier dynamics within nanostructures is essential for developing and optimizing new semiconductor nano-devices. In this study, we investigate the optical characteristics and carrier dynamics of (InGa)(AsSb)/GaAs/GaP quantum dots (QDs) using non-resonant energy and temperature modulated time-resolved photoluminescence. Given the growing application of such QDs in nano memory technologies, analyzing this material system is particularly significant. Our structural set includes a solitary QD layer, QDs capped with a GaSb layer, and exclusively a GaAs quantum well. Analytical theoretical models help distinguish common spectral features near the 1.8 eV emission energy, which are associated with both the GaAs quantum well and the GaP substrate. We detect type-I emission from the QDs with recombination times ranging from 2 ns to 10 ns, increasing as energy decreases. This distribution indicates the simultaneous presence of momentum direct and indirect QD transitions. Furthermore, leveraging the significant tunability of the dots via Sb incorporation, we propose their use as quantum photonic sources integrated into complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) platforms, noting that GaP is nearly lattice-matched to silicon. Finally, our analysis validates that the pumping power-induced blue-shift in emission stems from alterations in wavefunction topology caused by charged backgrounds.

This study investigates the structural and magnetic characteristics of a novel spin-$\frac12$ antiferromagnet, NaZnVOPO$_4$(HPO$_4$), utilizing x-ray diffraction, magnetic susceptibility, high-field magnetization, specific heat, and $^{31}$P NMR, alongside density-functional band-structure calculations. Although the thermodynamic behavior aligns well with the $J_1-J_2$ square-lattice model, *ab initio* calculations indicate a substantial distortion of the spin lattice. Analysis of magnetic susceptibility yields averaged nearest-neighbor and second-neighbor exchange couplings of $\bar J_1\simeq -1.3$ K and $\bar J_2\simeq 5.6$ K. The experimentally observed saturation field of 15.3\,T agrees with these values when 20\% spatial anisotropy in $J_1$ is considered. Specific heat measurements indicate the onset of magnetic long-range order at $T_{\rm N} \simeq 2.1$ K, corroborated by a distinct peak in the NMR spin-lattice relaxation rate. Furthermore, the NMR spectra reveal two non-equivalent phosphorus sites: a broad line with strong hyperfine coupling and short $T_1$ corresponds to the P(1) site within the magnetic planes, whereas a narrow line with weak hyperfine coupling and long $T_1$ identifies the P(2) site situated between the planes.

The broad utility of rheological matter stems from the interaction between fluid dynamics and material characteristics, sparking significant interest in the rheology of active fluids. These fluids generate spontaneous flows and exhibit complex, non-equilibrium behaviors due to their internal architecture and constant energy input. We introduce and validate a flexible, highly tunable technique for managing flow patterns, topology, and composition in active films. This method creates rheological coupling by embedding fully submerged micropatterned structures within a thin oil layer beneath the active film. Simulations indicate that these structures act as effective virtual boundaries for the overlying active nematic layer, driven by variations in viscous dissipation across different depths. By enabling position-dependent, effective dissipation in a non-intrusive manner, this accessible approach offers a viable route for engineering active microfluidic systems.

This research introduces a modified approach to functional constraints to derive exact solutions for nonlinear reaction-diffusion equations involving delays and variable coefficients. The study addresses a highly generalized class of such nonlinear equations, employing a novel technique to generate new traveling-wave solutions. These solutions incorporate arbitrary functions and free parameters, enhancing their utility for addressing specific modeling challenges and validating both numerical and approximate analytical methods. Furthermore, the findings offer applications for solving more complex forms of partial differential equations. The paper presents specific examples of delayed reaction-diffusion equations alongside their exact solutions, and includes graphical representations of solutions for certain reaction-diffusion equations.

For a short time, the machine learning community has focused on automatically coloring images without human input. This task is inherently ill-posed due to its vast degrees of freedom, meaning that for any given image, there is rarely one definitive correct color combination. Beyond colorization, image reconstruction also involves Single Image Super Resolution, which converts low-resolution images into higher-resolution ones. This research proposes an automated solution tailored specifically for astronomical images by employing Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). The study investigates various models across two color spaces, RGB and L*a*b. Due to the limited dataset size, transfer learning is utilized, employing a pre-trained ResNet-18 as the backbone encoder for a U-net architecture, which is then further fine-tuned. The resulting model generates visually compelling images that hallucinate high-resolution, colorized details absent from the original inputs. Performance is evaluated quantitatively using distance metrics, specifically L1 and L2 distances across all channels in each color space, to facilitate comparative analysis. Additionally, the Frechet Inception Distance (FID) is applied to compare the distribution of generated images against real images, thereby assessing the model's overall effectiveness.

It is established that generalizing the structure of coherent states can enhance the Helstrom bound, making the design of quantum measurements capable of reaching this improved limit crucial for advancing quantum communication. This article analytically demonstrates that such an enhanced bound is attainable through a projective measurement utilizing orthogonal, non-standard Schrödinger cat states. Furthermore, numerical results indicate that an indirect measurement scheme grounded in the Jaynes-Cummings model can nearly achieve this improved bound. Given that the Jaynes-Cummings model characterizes the interaction between light and a two-level atom, we highlight that this indirect measurement approach holds significant promise for experimental realization.

Features within the primordial power spectrum provide a critical insight into the inflationary epoch, with the cosmic microwave background (CMB) historically serving as the most sensitive method for detecting them. This study demonstrates that large-scale structure observations can surpass the CMB in probing these primordial signatures. We establish that signatures present in galaxy surveys can be distinguished from the broadband power spectrum and remain as resilient to the nonlinear evolution of matter as standard baryon acoustic oscillations. Consequently, analyses can leverage a substantial range of scales extending beyond the linear regime. By developing a feature search for large-scale structure and applying it to the final Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey data release, we derive new constraints on oscillatory features that exceed Planck's sensitivity across a significant frequency range. Furthermore, we project that upcoming galaxy surveys like DESI and Euclid will enhance current limits by up to an order of magnitude over a broader frequency spectrum.

The recent surge in RDF adoption has driven the standardization of the SPARQL query language and spurred the creation of both local and distributed engines for executing these queries. This survey offers a thorough examination of methods and systems designed for querying RDF knowledge graphs. Unlike other reviews that primarily concentrate on distributed environments, this work centers on a comprehensive overview of cutting-edge storage, indexing, and query processing techniques for efficiently evaluating SPARQL queries in a local context (on a single machine). To ensure the survey remains self-contained, it also includes a brief discussion on graph partitioning methods used in distributed settings. The paper concludes by addressing current research challenges aimed at further enhancing SPARQL query engines. This extended version additionally surveys over one hundred SPARQL engines and their respective techniques, alongside twelve benchmarks and their characteristics.

This paper investigates an analogue of Serre's modularity conjecture concerning projective representations $\overline{\rho}: \operatorname{Gal}(\overline{K} / K) \rightarrow \operatorname{PGL}_2(k)$ over totally real number fields $K$. By leveraging automorphy lifting theorems over CM fields developed by the authors in prior research, we establish new instances of this conjecture specifically for the case $k = \mathbb{F}_5$.

On-demand and resource reservation pricing models are prevalent in cloud computing to address diverse user needs. However, in Multi-Access Edge Computing (MEC), where edge resources are more constrained than cloud resources, on-demand users risk delayed or failed job execution if reservation plan users monopolize capacity. Conversely, reservation users may hold underutilized quotas. To resolve this resource mismatch, we introduce a Sharing Quota Model (SQM) that enables reservation users to resell unused quotas to on-demand users, with the mobile network operator (MNO) collecting a commission. To analyze equilibrium user behavior and the MNO's incentives, we model this as a three-stage non-cooperative Stackelberg Game. Solving this game reveals the optimal strategies for buyers and resellers. We demonstrate that aggregate user strategies create four distinct regions based on MNO pricing and supply levels, allowing us to derive the MNO's optimal prices for on-demand services. Numerical results indicate that the MNO achieves maximum revenue when both sharing and on-demand pools are available, particularly when on-demand supply is low and the MNO's commission is minimal.

This study highlights that in the mean-field majority-rule opinion dynamics model, the relationship between consensus time and population size operates across two distinct regimes. This behavior is governed by the distribution of group sizes that form at each evolutionary step to achieve agreement. Specifically, when the mean group size is finite, the consensus time follows the previously established logarithmic dependence on population size. Conversely, if the mean group size diverges, the consensus time scales with the population size according to a power law. Numerical simulations confirm these semi-quantitative analytical findings.

We employ luminous red galaxies identified in imaging surveys for Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) targeting, paired with Planck CMB lensing maps, to investigate the amplitude of large-scale structure between redshifts $0.4\le z\le 1$. Our sample, covering 18,000 square degrees with an angular number density of roughly $500\,\mathrm{deg}^{-2}$, is split into four tomographic bins based on photometric redshifts, with distributions calibrated via DESI spectroscopy. Using models grounded in cosmological perturbation theory and focusing on large scales where these models are reliable, we analyze galaxy autospectra and galaxy-convergence cross-spectra. Within the $\Lambda$CDM framework and applying background cosmology priors from supernova and baryon acoustic oscillation data, we derive $S_8=\sigma_8(\Omega_m/0.3)^{0.5}=0.73\pm 0.03$. This value falls below the $\Lambda$CDM prediction conditioned on Planck data, indicating that our data suggest a slower growth of structure at low redshift than the model anticipates, albeit at modest significance.

Small-angle neutron scattering studies reveal that the vortex lattice (VL) in UPt3 gradually disorders over time due to 235U fission. This process temporarily heats sample regions above the critical temperature; upon subsequent cooling, the vortices become trapped in a quenched vortex glass state. The rate of this disordering scales with the magnetic field, indicating that collective VL properties, such as elastic moduli, govern the mechanism. Furthermore, the ability to restore an ordered VL through small field oscillations demonstrates that fission does not inflict significant radiation damage on the UPt3 crystals, even following prolonged exposure.

This study establishes a cut-and-join operator framework for the generating functions encompassing all intersection numbers of $\psi$, $\kappa$, and $\Theta$ classes on the moduli spaces $\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,n}$. These operators provide an algebraic formulation of topological recursion, enabling the recursive calculation of the aforementioned intersection numbers. Under specific parameter values, the resulting generating functions correspond to the volumes of moduli spaces of (super) hyperbolic Riemann surfaces featuring geodesic boundaries, a concept also linked to JT (super)gravity.

The greatest potential for labor unions to exert political influence stems from their direct access to millions of individuals within the workplace, where they can shape the political perspectives of both unionized employees and their non-unionized management, a group often considered the most pertinent out-group. This study examines how unionization affects campaign contributions from both workers and managers at specific workplaces across the United States from 1980 to 2016. To do so, we merge establishment-level data on union elections with transaction-level records of contributions to federal and local candidates. Using stacked Difference-in-Differences models, we demonstrate that unionization causes a leftward shift in campaign contributions, boosting support for Democrats over Republicans among both workers and managers. To validate these findings, we conduct Regression Discontinuity analyses, which reveal no differential trends across placebo vote share thresholds and confirm that results remain robust when examining increasingly tight elections. Additionally, we present evidence indicating that our findings are not attributable to changes in the composition of the workforce.

Effective adoption of mobile health (m-health) applications increasingly relies on the successful visualization of personal data. Consequently, grasping the specific needs and obstacles users face when interacting with mobile personal data visualizations is vital for promoting these tools. This study reports on a user survey designed to explore demographics, tasks, requirements, and difficulties associated with mobile data visualization, gathering 56 complete responses. Key findings reveal that 51% of users employ multiple health tracking applications to meet their objectives; bar and pie charts are identified as the preferred formats for viewing health information; and users favor a combination of text and charts, emphasizing the necessity of explanatory content. The three most frequently cited challenges are excessive data volume, text overlap, and a lack of utility in information exploration. Conversely, the primary drivers for user satisfaction include readable data presentation, intuitive navigation, and high-quality chart content. Additionally, fun and curiosity are recognized as the main motivations for using m-health tracking apps. Based on these insights, the paper proposes design and development guidelines aimed at mitigating reported challenges and enhancing user satisfaction. Future research will contextualize these findings and investigate the benefits and drawbacks of data visualization across specific m-health domains, including sports, heart monitoring, blood pressure, sleep patterns, and dietary habits.

Recent advances have introduced various Bayesian deep learning techniques for semi-supervised medical image segmentation. Despite achieving encouraging results on standard benchmarks, these methods face two key limitations. First, their discriminative architectures rely solely on labeled data during early training phases, creating a risk of overfitting. Second, they are only partially grounded in Bayesian principles because their overall structures are not inherently designed within a Bayesian framework. Unifying the entire architecture under a Bayesian perspective would provide a rigorous theoretical foundation, ensuring that every component has a clear probabilistic interpretation. To address these issues, we propose a novel Generative Bayesian Deep Learning (GBDL) architecture. As a generative model, GBDL aims to estimate the joint distribution of input medical volumes and their corresponding labels.
